}

Note also that rounding a span takes time zone transitions like daylight saving
time into account. For example, let’s take
2024-11-02 17:30
and

2024-11-03 04:45
in New York. Because New York stopped daylight saving time
at 2AM on 2024-11-03, the amount of physical time between them is 12 hours and
15 minutes:

let

zdt1

=

date
(
2024
,

11
,

2
).
at
(
17
,

30
,

0
,

0
).
in_tz
(
"America/New_York"
)
?
;

let

zdt2

=

date
(
2024
,

11
,

3
).
at
(
4
,

45
,

0
,

0
).
in_tz
(
"America/New_York"
)
?
;

assert_eq!
(
zdt2

-

zdt1
,

12.
hours
().
minutes
(
15
).
fieldwise
());

Normally, if we rounded to the nearest day, this would round up to 1 day. But
since the midpoint of this particular day is actually 12 hours and 30 minutes,
this duration will round down to 0 days when we request it:

use

jiff
::
{
civil
::
date
,

RoundMode
,

ToSpan
,

Unit
,

ZonedDateTimeDifference
};

fn

main
()

->
anyhow
::
Result
<
()
>

{

let

zdt1

=

date
(
2024
,

11
,

2
).
at
(
17
,

30
,

0
,

0
).
in_tz
(
"America/New_York"
)
?
;

let

zdt2

=

date
(
2024
,

11
,

3
).
at
(
4
,

45
,

0
,

0
).
in_tz
(
"America/New_York"
)
?
;

let

difference

=

ZonedDateTimeDifference
::
new
(
&
zdt2
)

.
largest
(
Unit
::
Day
)

.
smallest
(
Unit
::
Day
)

.
mode
(
RoundMode
::
HalfExpand
);

assert_eq!
(
zdt1
.
until
(
difference
)
?
,

0.
days
().
fieldwise
());

Ok
(())

}

Next we’ll continue our discussion of rounding, but when applied to datetimes
themselves.

Date Rounding

Date rounding in Jiff is limited to units of days or lower. Therefore, it’s
only available on
ZonedDateTime
,
Timestamp
,
civil::DateTime
,

civil::Time
but not
civil::Date
.

A common example for rounding a datetime is to reduce precision. For example,
a system clock might provide nanosecond precision, but maybe we only care about
the nearest half-hour:

use

jiff
::
{
civil
::
date
,

Unit
};

fn

main
()

->
anyhow
::
Result
<
()
>

{

let

zdt

=

date
(
2024
,

11
,

2
)

.
at
(
17
,

46
,

20
,

123_456_789
)

.
in_tz
(
"America/New_York"
)
?
;

assert_eq!
(

zdt
.
to_string
(),

"2024-11-02T17:46:20.123456789-04:00[America/New_York]"

);

// Round to the nearest half hour.

let

rounded

=

zdt
.
round
((
Unit
::
Minute
,

30
))
?
;

assert_eq!
(

rounded
.
to_string
(),

"2024-11-02T18:00:00-04:00[America/New_York]"

);

Ok
(())

}

As with rounding spans, rounding a
ZonedDateTime
is aware of time zone
transitions:

let

zdt

=

date
(
2024
,

11
,

3
)

.
at
(
11
,

45
,

20
,

123_456_789
)

.
in_tz
(
"America/New_York"
)
?
;

// Round to the nearest day.

let

rounded

=

zdt
.
round
(
Unit
::
Day
)
?
;

assert_eq!
(

rounded
.
to_string
(),

"2024-11-04T00:00:00-05:00[America/New_York]"

);

Notice that in the above example, our time of 11:45AM is
before
noon, yet the
result still rounds
up
to the next day. This is because the midpoint for this
day is 11:30AM since, by 11:30AM, 12.5 hours have already elapsed because of
the repeated 1AM hour in the move away from daylight saving time in New York.

Other Calendars

Jiff itself doesn’t support any calendars other than the proleptic Gregorian
calendar. One can instead use the
ICU4X
crate to work in non-Gregorian
calendars, and convert between datetime types using the
jiff-icu
crate:
(Use
cargo add icu jiff-icu
to make this example work.)

use

icu
::
{

calendar
::
{
types
::
Month
,

Date

as

IcuDate
},

time
::
{
DateTime

as

IcuDateTime
,

Time

as

IcuTime
},

};

use

jiff
::
civil
::
DateTime
;

use

jiff_icu
::
ConvertTryFrom

as

_
;

fn

main
()

->
anyhow
::
Result
<
()
>

{

// Firstly, create an ICU datetime using the Hebrew calendar.

let

datetime

=

IcuDateTime

{

date
:
IcuDate
::
try_new_hebrew_v2
(
5785
,

Month
::
new
(
5
),

4
)
?
,

time
:
IcuTime
::
try_new
(
17
,

30
,

0
,

0
)
?
,

};

// Secondly, convert it to a civil datetime.

// This will automatically use ICU to convert

// the date from the Hebrew calendar to the

// Gregorian (or ISO) calendar.

let

zdt

=

DateTime
::
convert_try_from
(
datetime
)
?
;

assert_eq!
(
zdt
.
to_string
(),

"2025-02-02T17:30:00"
);

Ok
(())

}

The ICU4X API supports
many more calendars
.

Which DateTime Type Do I Use?

There are 3 potentially confusable datetime types in Jiff:

civil::DateTime

Timestamp

ZonedDateTime

When should you use each one versus the other?

To a first approximation, if you
can
use a
ZonedDateTime
, then that is
probably the type you want to reach for. It represents a specific instant in
time in a particular geographic location. That is, it has both a
Timestamp

and a
TimeZone
.

If you only ever need to work in UTC or just deal with system time, then a

Timestamp
is probably the right choice. This is useful for representing a
specific instant in time that is not connected to any time zone.

A
civil::DateTime
is useful in contexts where you don’t care about a specific
instant in time and when calcuations should be done independent of time zone.
For example, when parsing datetime information from a user interface datetime
picker.

Remember that both a
civil::DateTime
and a
Timestamp
can be converted to a

ZonedDateTime
by supplying a time zone.

Span Manipulation

We’ve already seen how to add spans to datetime values and how to get spans
as a difference between datetime values. But we haven’t yet explored the APIs
available on a
Span
itself.

First and foremost, we can build a
Span
through its constructor, which
returns a
Span
with all of its units set to
0
:

use

jiff
::
Span
;

let

span

=

Span
::
new
();

A
Span
is both
Copy
and immutable. We can create new spans through method
chaining:

let

span

=

Span
::
new
().
hours
(
1
).
minutes
(
30
);

assert_eq!
(
span
.
to_string
(),

"PT1H30M"
);

Or we can use the
ToSpan
convenience trait, which adds methods on integer
types for constructing spans:

use

jiff
::
ToSpan
;

let

span

=

1.
hour
().
minutes
(
30
);

assert_eq!
(
span
.
to_string
(),

"PT1H30M"
);

Note though that methods like
Span::hours
and
ToSpan::hours
will panic
when the integer is outside the limits of what
Span
supports. This is fine
when your spans are literals in your program, since a panic would indicate a
bug. But if your inputs come from an end user, it’s better to use fallible
methods:

let

span

=

Span
::
new
().
try_hours
(
1
)
?
.
try_minutes
(
30
)
?
;

assert_eq!
(
span
.
to_string
(),

"PT1H30M"
);

Spans preserve each individual unit value. This means that 90 minutes and 1
hour 30 minutes, while they represent the same duration, are actually different
values in memory:

let

span1

=

1.
hour
().
minutes
(
30
);

let

span2

=

90.
minutes
();

assert_eq!
(
span1
.
to_string
(),

"PT1H30M"
);

assert_eq!
(
span2
.
to_string
(),

"PT90M"
);

This permits callers maximum flexibility when it comes to representing
durations. This makes it possible to represent durations in a specific unit
even when they add up to larger units. For example, the runtime duration of
films is typically conveyed in minutes, even when the runtime exceeds one hour.
This can be adjusted programmatically using
Span::round
:

use

jiff
::
{
SpanRound
,

ToSpan
,

Unit
};

fn

main
()

->
anyhow
::
Result
<
()
>

{

let

span1

=

1.
hour
().
minutes
(
30
);

let

span2

=

span1
.
round
(
SpanRound
::
new
().
largest
(
Unit
::
Minute
))
?
;

assert_eq!
(
span2
.
to_string
(),

"PT90M"
);

Ok
(())

}

You can go the other way as well:

use

jiff
::
{
SpanRound
,

ToSpan
,

Unit
};

fn

main
()

->
anyhow
::
Result
<
()
>

{

let

span1

=

90.
minutes
();

let

span2

=

span1
.
round
(
SpanRound
::
new
().
largest
(
Unit
::
Hour
))
?
;

assert_eq!
(
span2
.
to_string
(),

"PT1H30M"
);

Ok
(())

}

Neither of these examples do actual rounding, despite the name of the API.
Instead, since we’re only setting the largest unit, this API is doing unit
balancing. Unit balancing is when all unit values rollover into larger units
up until the largest configured unit. This works even for calendar units too,
but you need to provide a relative date:

use

jiff
::
{
civil
,

SpanRound
,

ToSpan
,

Unit
};

fn

main
()

->
anyhow
::
Result
<
()
>

{

let

span

=

2756.
hours
();

let

dt

=

civil
::
date
(
2020
,

1
,

1
).
at
(
0
,

0
,

0
,

0
);

let

round

=

SpanRound
::
new
().
largest
(
Unit
::
Year
).
relative
(
dt
);

assert_eq!
(
span
.
round
(
round
)
?
.
to_friendly
(),

"3mo 23d 20h"
);

Ok
(())

}

Without a relative date, it’s not possible to know how many hours are in a
single month. That is, once calendar units are involved, a span cannot be
interpreted as a physical duration of time until some context is applied.

The same even applies to days themselves, since days can sometimes be more or
less than 24 hours. Take the above example. What happens if we use a zoned
datetime as our relative date instead?

use

jiff
::
{
civil
,

SpanRound
,

ToSpan
,

Unit
};

fn

main
()

->
anyhow
::
Result
<
()
>

{

let

span

=

2756.
hours
();

let

zdt

=

civil
::
date
(
2020
,

1
,

1
).
at
(
0
,

0
,

0
,

0
).
in_tz
(
"Europe/Rome"
)
?
;

let

round

=

SpanRound
::
new
().
largest
(
Unit
::
Year
).
relative
(
&
zdt
);

assert_eq!
(
span
.
round
(
round
)
?
.
to_friendly
(),

"3mo 23d 21h"
);

Ok
(())

}

Notice that the duration’s hour component changed from
20
to
21
. Why?
Because we started with 2756 hour in both cases and because
2020-03-29
in
Rome was only 23 hours long (in a move from standard time to daylight saving
time). That means that one of those days in
3mo 23d
was only 23 hours long.
So an extra hour needed to be added to make up for it.

The
round
API can also do actual rounding:

use

jiff
::
{
SpanRound
,

ToSpan
,

Unit
};

fn

main
()

->
anyhow
::
Result
<
()
>

{

let

span

=

2.
hours
().
minutes
(
30
);

let

round

=

SpanRound
::
new
().
smallest
(
Unit
::
Hour
);

assert_eq!
(
span
.
round
(
round
)
?
.
to_friendly
(),

"3h"
);

Ok
(())

}

You can also change its rounding mode from the default (“half-expand”, or like
you were taught rounding in school) to truncation (or one of several other
modes):

use

jiff
::
{
RoundMode
,

SpanRound
,

ToSpan
,

Unit
};

fn

main
()

->
anyhow
::
Result
<
()
>

{

let

span

=

2.
hours
().
minutes
(
30
);

let

round

=

SpanRound
::
new
().
smallest
(
Unit
::
Hour
).
mode
(
RoundMode
::
Trunc
);

assert_eq!
(
span
.
round
(
round
)
?
.
to_friendly
(),

"2h"
);

Ok
(())

}

One can also specify a rounding increment to round to the nearest unit value.
For example, to the nearest half-hour:

use

jiff
::
{
SpanRound
,

ToSpan
,

Unit
};

fn

main
()

->
anyhow
::
Result
<
()
>

{

let

span

=

2.
hours
().
minutes
(
31
);

let

round

=

SpanRound
::
new
().
smallest
(
Unit
::
Minute
).
increment
(
30
);

assert_eq!
(
span
.
round
(
round
)
?
.
to_friendly
(),

"2h 30m"
);

Ok
(())

}

Because a
Span
value cannot easily be compared correctly based purely on its
value in memory, a dedicated comparison
Span::compare
routine is provided:

let

span1

=

2.
hours
();

let

span2

=

120.
minutes
();

assert!
(
span1
.
compare
(
span2
)
?
.
is_eq
());

Also, one can convert a
Span
to a floating point value in terms of any unit.
For example:

use

jiff
::
{
ToSpan
,

Unit
};

fn

main
()

->
anyhow
::
Result
<
()
>

{

let

span

=

90.
minutes
();

assert_eq!
(
span
.
total
(
Unit
::
Hour
)
?
,

1.5
);

Ok
(())

}

Converting to calendar units requires a relative date for the same reasons
discussed above:

use

jiff
::
{
civil
,

ToSpan
,

Unit
};

fn

main
()

->
anyhow
::
Result
<
()
>

{

let

span

=

24.
hours
();

assert_eq!
(

span
.
total
((
Unit
::
Month
,

civil
::
date
(
2026
,

6
,

1
)))
?
,

0.03333333333333333

);

assert_eq!
(

span
.
total
((
Unit
::
Month
,

civil
::
date
(
2026
,

7
,

1
)))
?
,

0.03225806451612903

);

Ok
(())

}

Conclusion

So far, we’ve explored a good chunk of Jiff’s API. We didn’t talk about every
nook and cranny, but I think we’ve covered the most important pieces.

We’ll wrap up by briefly discussing motivation and inspiration.

Motivation

Whenever I needed datetime handling in Rust, I always got confused. Should I
use
chrono
or
time
? How do I get my local time from a timestamp? How do I
use my system’s time zone database? How do I do calendar arithmetic?

Before I started working on Jiff, this confusion got annoying enough for me to
consider writing my own crate. I felt like the APIs of both
chrono
and
time

could be improved upon. I personally found the domain quite interesting and so
set out to build something better.

Why not improve on an existing solution, like
chrono
or
time
, instead of
adding yet another choice into the ecosystem? I do think there are material
downsides of having too many choices, but I had concluded that both
chrono

and
time
(in 2024) had reached a local maximum. Moreover, in 2024, I was not
an expert in datetime handling. It took building a datetime library to become
one. So convincing crate maintainers to go in a radically different direction
would have been a tall order.

Jiff’s
design
and
comparison
documentation contain much more detail
regarding the motivation and specific examples between Jiff,
chrono
and

time
.

Inspiration

Jiff is heavily inspired by
Temporal
, which is JavaScript’s standard library
solution for date and time management. Jiff inherits API design, functionality
and even parsing/formatting of datetime values. Note though that Jiff is not
and does not aim to be a 100% compatible implementation of the Temporal
specification. Jiff is meant to be a Rust ecosystem library first and foremost.

With that said, if you’re familiar with Temporal and Rust, then it’s likely
you’ll find Jiff to be a relatively straightforward translation of Temporal’s
API to Rust. This example shows how to use Temporal to round a calendar span
to the nearest number of days relative to a date:

const

duration

=

Temporal
.
Duration
.
from
({

months
:

1
,

days
:

1
,

hours
:

1

});

const

roundedDuration

=

duration
.
round
({

largestUnit
:

"days"
,

smallestUnit
:

"days"
,

relativeTo
:

Temporal
.
PlainDateTime
.
from
(
"2022-01-01"
),

});

console
.
log
(
roundedDuration
);

// "P32D"

And here’s the equivalent operation in Jiff:

use

jiff
::
{
SpanRound
,

ToSpan
,

Unit
};

fn

main
()

->
anyhow
::
Result
<
()
>

{

let

span

=

1.
month
().
days
(
1
).
hours
(
1
);

let

rounded_span

=

span
.
round
(

SpanRound
::
new
()

.
largest
(
Unit
::
Day
)

.
smallest
(
Unit
::
Day
)

.
relative
(
"2022-01-01"
.
parse
::
<
jiff
::
civil
::
Date
>
()
?
),

)
?
;

assert_eq!
(
rounded_span
.
to_string
(),

"P32D"
);

Ok
(())

}

The main difference between these examples is that Jiff’s duration type is
named
Span
instead of
Duration
. This was done to avoid confusion with
Rust’s standard library
std::time::Duration
type.

Here are some other differences:

Temporal’s
Instant
type in Jiff is named
Timestamp
in order to avoid
confusion with Rust’s standard library
std::time::Instant
type.

Temporal’s “plain” date and time types are called “civil” in Jiff.

Jiff only supports the Gregorian calendar.

Jiff’s datetime range only extends to +/- 9999, whereas Temporal’s range is
larger.

It’s easy to say that without Temporal, Jiff wouldn’t exist in its current
form today.

title: Test/verification technique effectiveness with Astra
content:
When we looked at
how well agents used test/verification techniques in August
1
, we saw that GPT-5.6 Sol generally did what you might call a caricature of various techniques when asked to use a technique or library such as TDD, QuickCheck, Lean 4, etc.; not specifying any particular test method (which we'll call Default) resulted in many worthless unit tests, which was one of the best performing conditions because asking agents to test in specific ways mostly made them worse. In that eval, we gave agents the Zstd RFC and asked them to implement Zstd (with an addendum for how they should test for all conditions other than Default).

On re-running the same eval with GPT-6 Astra, we see two big differences:

Astra's capability has increased by enough that we need a more difficult eval (on the Zstd implementation eval, almost every condition gets 100% correctness almost every time on medium regardless of technique)

Agents seemed to use test and verification techniques more effectively

On (1), we previously saw that, when implementing Zstd from the RFC with 5.6 Sol, on average, agents spent $3.50 on medium effort and $5.50 on xhigh effort to get full (holdout) test correctness about 63% and 77% of the time, respectively. With Astra, agents cost $1 to get full test correctness over 99% of the time at medium effort.

On (2), an example would be that when we asked 5.6 Sol to do fuzzing, it would generate many worthless random inputs, which would mostly hit the same code paths and not test anything interesting. With 6 Astra, we see agents that are asked to do fuzzing in a structured way that actually exercises code paths and finds non-trivial bugs, but we can't tell if this improved correctness or not because the Zstd implementation benchmark is saturated.

We also tried giving 5.6 Sol the IMAP RFC, but it was too hard for 5.6 Sol. When trying again with 6 Astra, we get the following distribution of results (the y-axis is the percent of runs where all tests pass; agents are not given the tests and the points are the results across 80 runs of each condition).

Default once again looks pretty good. Some conditions result in somewhat better correctness, but also with higher cost. Although the IMAP RFC isn't saturated, it would be nice to also see results on a harder task since most of my time goes to tasks that agents can't one-shot most of the time. To test this, we'll try the
pandoc eval we looked at when comparing programming languages
. A reason I want to see results on larger evals is that, as we observed
when looking at caveman mode
and as we saw with languages, models often perform fairly differently on larger tasks. With caveman mode, the large wins that people reported became smaller or disappeared and with languages, we saw this in multiple ways, such as C and C++ implementations of Zstd being at least somewhat ok on memory safety, whereas C and C++ implementations of Pandoc were plagued by memory safety issues.

Pandoc is significantly harder, and even after running multiple turns (roughly 14 on average), no condition reached 100% correctness, so we'll look at the fraction of tests passed instead of fraction of runs that got to 100%.

For this, we only ran each condition 25 times due to the cost involved. At MSRP, this cost about $90k.

Recall that, in past evals we ran on languages and test/verification techniques, the failures were often idiosyncratic results of how agents operate, such as agents using Clojure writing incorrect byte conversion code by default or agents using Verus writing vacuous proofs. This kind of thing is quite different from the reasons I've seen people say that agents should use some particular language or test/verification technique, which are generally nice-sounding explanations for why something ought to be better that sound appealing in a very human way but appear to be unrelated to reality when we look at what agents actually did
2
.

Because we "only" ran $90k worth of evals here, we don't really have enough information to say why almost anything happened. We can observe that some conditions performed better than others, but it's difficult to say what it means. As a result, we shouldn't read too much into this, but we do see some things that seem consistent with what one might expect, in that we might expect most of the test techniques and libraries suggested to give better generalization, which would then give better holdout vs. test scores (result is up and to the left of the Default line when viewing visible vs. holdout test scores), with TDD giving worse generalization (down and to the right of the Default line).

But, if it's true that testing properties gives us better generalization and conditions like TDD that result in a lot of small tests give less general results, we'd expect the built-in condition to also have a low holdout:visible relative to Default and that's not what we saw. Why this is is unclear and I don't think we can really determine this without a lot more runs.

For the actual results, the line shown for cost vs. holdout and cost vs. visible show curves fitted to the shape of all graph trajectories across multiple turns, fit to Default. Things that are below / right of the line can be thought of as worse and above / left can be considered better. With 5.6 Sol, it was clear that the test conditions generally weren't doing useful work for a combination of reasons:

Almost no condition outperformed Default

On other evals (not discussed in detail), similar prompts also did not outperform Default

The tests produced by non-Default conditions were mostly ridiculous and didn't capture the value of the technique

Here, we have a situation where many different techniques have a better result than Default. The conceptual error bars on each condition are quite wide (more so than indicated by the bootstrap intervals shown on the plots), but the number of conditions that outperform Default makes it
plausible that one or more conditions truly outperforms Default
even if we don't know which ones exactly. Furthermore, some conditions likely truly outperform other conditions, but we don't really have sufficient data to tell which conditions are generally better. It's much simpler when almost everything looks bad across a wide variety of techniques.

Here are some questions I have about the results:

To what extent can these results be extrapolated to running more turns to get to
near-complete correctness for Pandoc
? In general, conditions do maintain something like their rank order with additional turns, so it's plausible the ranking will continue as-is, but this is untested

How much of the results are due to a small sample size (with respect to each condition)? For the Pandoc eval, we "only" ran each condition 25 times. Many different turns were run, but we know from previous experiments as well as just using agents that there's a high degree of path dependence when looping over generated code

How much of the results are due to a small sample size (with respect to minute / trivial variations)? From having run a few silly evals, I know that it's possible to get very different results when asking for the same thing due to trivial changes (such as changing sentence structure, changing capitalization, etc.); how much of the current results are due to something arbitrary like this?

How much of the results are due to a small sample size (with respect to the problem being solved)? We looked at one "Pandoc-sized" problem. If we looked at 100, how representative would Pandoc be?

If I really wanted to answer these questions, I'd want to run at least 100x what was run here to run the full matrix. Steve Yegge has mentioned using ~20 Claude subscriptions to spend ~$120k/mo of MSRP token spend. Getting to 100x isn't plausible with a setup like that, but 2x to 3x could be done with testing expanded in a limited fashion and some guesswork and extrapolation. I don't know that it really makes sense for me to do that given how much time it would take and how little spare time I have, but considering
what kinds of things academics have looked at when studying programming productivity
, maybe it makes sense for a grad student to do this, since it would be more informative than a number of widely cited studies. But, in industry, I'm not sure who would do this outside of an AI lab.

That being said, if you keep in mind that we don't know how well any of these results generalize, I'll note a few things that I thought were interesting.

Differential testing caused agents to examine tests and invariants in a way that engendered better "understanding" than other conditions

TDD once again underperformed, but not all conditions that caused agents to write a lot of small tests underperformed

ACL2 (a theorem prover) performed well (
it also performed well in the 5.6 Sol Zstd eval
)

Property-based testing (not the named condition, but a number of libraries that force the use of the technique) finally resulted in tests that do what one might hope from PBT

(1): I tried to get agents to do this with the hastily written skill I wrote for the 5.6 Sol Zstd eval; although the skill performed decently, agents basically didn't do this. However, for the Pandoc eval, differential testing did cause agents to closely examine boundary conditions and figure out how to write tests (and therefore how to write code) that correctly implements both sides of the boundary. I'm not confident that this generalize, but it would be interesting to see if it does generalize and what else can get agents to do this kind of thing systematically.

(2): Although TDD underperforming is exactly what I'd expect (recall that I added TDD to the 5.6 Sol eval because I thought it would underperform), the lack of underperformance of other conditions that cause many small tests to get generated should reduce confidence in the plausible sounding reason that writing many small tests underperforms.

(3): I've felt for a long time that ACL2 is underrated relative to other verification tools (it was heavily used to good effect in industry in some areas relative to the amount of academic work on it). I had low confidence in this opinion and continue to have low confidence, but it has performed well in evals I've done so far. Given how much effort is being poured into getting agents to use Lean effectively, I'd expect that Lean will eventually outperform ACL2 even if ACL2 outperforms today, but ACL2 doesn't seem like a bad choice today. For people doing verification or proofs with Lean 4, I'd be curious how the results compare to using ACL2.

(4): Yay (perhaps). For all the reasons I noted above, I have low confidence that this generalizes, but Proptest once again performed well. And, this time, the testing was a lot better than we saw in the 5.6 Sol Zstd eval. I have no inside information on this, but I would guess that there wasn't a major effort on improving PBT / fuzzing / etc. between 5.6 Sol and 6 Astra and that this comes out of better generalization and higher capability. If that's true (and this isn't just some artifact of my only spending $90k MSRP and not $9M MSRP), this bodes well for better testing in the future in that we should expect models to get better at testing without any particular effort to improve testing capabilities.

Between my running these tests and publishing this post, a claim that you should tell agents not to write tests (based on running DeepSWE) went viral. The specific claim was

ok it's official...[ellipses from original quote] AI-written unit tests and integration tests are empirically proven to be unhelpful. you should tell your agents to stop writing tests by themselves

As we previously noted
, I find DeepSWE unrepresentative of work that I do and therefore meaningless to me personally. Additionally, that was done with Sonnet 5.5 High, so it generally only passed on problems that are much easier than the problems discussed here, and as observed here and in other recent evals, which techniques are effective often doesn't generalize across problem size or problem difficulty. I find it plausible that for problems coding agents find very easy, telling them not to test reduces cost (which is what was actually shown conditional on someone caring about DeepSWE). Generalizing this to "AI-written unit tests and integration tests are empirically proven to be unhelpful" based on the test that was run seems wrong regardless of whether or not this holds for other problems, and it seems unlikely that the claim holds. The claim was based on asking for no tests, which resulted in similar correctness and a small cost savings (9%, on average). In our tests here as well as before, we find differences in correctness as well as a larger than 9% difference in cost, so it seems unlikely that a claim like "AI-written unit tests and integration tests are empirically proven to be unhelpful" based on a 9% difference in cost on a benchmark of small problems is correct. Another thing to note is that DeepSWE's grader is broken with respect to testing because (among other issues),
an agent can add a test name that conflicts with a grader's secret test name, which will then cause a failure
. Given issues like that, adding tests is inherently penalized in a way that isn't representative of real-world usage.

You can argue the claim was highly effective, in that making overstated claims that something is empirically proven is a good way to go viral
3
or
get a lot of citations
, but it's not a good way to figure out how to use coding agents effectively.

In Nolan Lawson's recent post on how JavaScript framework choice impacts agents
, he noted:

My goal here is not to write the end-all-be-all benchmark for “I’m a vibe-coder, which framework should I choose?” The point of this post is to demonstrate that it’s possible in the era of AI coding to still make decisions based on evidence rather than vibes.

I feel the same way here, in that I think it's valuable to run some toy evals and see what the results are. Even if someone had the resources of an AI lab available to them, I don't think they could say that X or Y are "empirically proven to be unhelpful [or helpful]", but we can still get some kind of information.

From what we've seen in our testing evals, I'd be inclined to try proptest if I wanted a property-based testing library in Rust, and for any problem that I'd use Lean on, I'd be inclined to try ACL2 as well to see how results vary and if I get better results, and there's also a fair amount of information that fits into some kind of vibes-based feel for things.

As I've noted in my N most recent posts, I've been trying to write up each of these in 30 minutes because there are too many results to write up and not enough time, so I'm not going to provide
an accounting of what happened for each condition like I did for the 5.6 Sol Zstd eval
. I'm already over 30 minutes on this post, so I'll stop here and perhaps we'll look more into testing and verification in a future post.

Thanks to Laurence Tratt, Edward Z. Yang, Sophia Wisdom, and Marco Primi for comments/corrections/discussion.

Appendix: why don't AI labs publish more comparisons on what techniques are effective?

Unlike us randos, they actually have the resources to run relatively comprehensive evals and there's a general lack of information about what's effective. If people understood how to use AI better, it seems like that would result in more AI usage. Also, my experience has been that different techniques are effective with OpenAI's models vs. Anthropic's models. If one of these companies published good information about what works with their models, that could move people towards interacting with agents in a way that's advantageous for them.

I guess the case against this is something like, revenue growth is so rapid that more money can be made by doing other work and/or differences in how people prompt don't really matter anyway. As someone on the outside of these labs, the former seems plausible to me, whereas the latter doesn't seem like it can be true (because I've repeatedly observed reasonable people who aren't doing obviously silly things get very different results, to the point where one person might fail to get a working solution to a problem where another person easily makes things work). To the extent the results are "real" and not an artifact of testing a broad enough set of things, the impact is larger than it might seem from just skimming the graph because, as we put more effort/turns/dollars into implementing Pandoc, we get dimishing returns with respect to correctness. This can be observed by looking at the Default fit line, which has a slope far below what we'd get if we fit a straight line from (0,0) to the Default point, as well as by looking at the curve of the fit line. Despite that, the differences I've observed w.r.t. the impact of how people prompt in practice are much larger than what we see from variying test techinque by adding a few words about how to test. I think this is fairly unsurprising (we dont really expect there to be some magic testing/verification words that give us a 10x improvement), but this kind of thing makes it difficult/expensive to run an eval that gets at differences in how people prompt.

David R. MacIver noted:

Btw one thing I'm noticing in my evaluations on the skill is that ChatGPT is way less into PBT than Claude is. Claude will pretty eagerly write property-based tests and seems to benefit from them during development in my current benchmarks, but ChatGPT sol doesn't do that unless you're really insistent. So there might be some prompt sensitivity going on here, or it might be model specific. I've not yet optimised the skill for ChatGPT at all so it's possible I've inadvertently fucked something up for it. BTW I don't actually know that Claude is
better
at PBT than ChatGPT (I should really check this). It's just more proactive about doing it, but it's plausible that when they actually write properties they're about the same level of quality.

I haven't done the same breadth of testing with Claude. Given what MacIver said, it's plausible that Claude is better at property-based testing or that it's not. Also, given that he develops Hegel and is generally using Claude, it's also plausible that Hegel works better with Claude than with Codex and we'd see better results from Hegel if we tried with Claude. So there might be some prompt sensitivity going on here, or it might be model specific.

Although it's not shown on the graph, the original Hegel skilled used for the 5.6 Sol Zstd eval and the updated one that was created as a result of MacIver doing more testing on the skill after that eval both fared worse than Hegel with no skill. Correctness was pretty similar, and both cost a lot more, with the updated skill being the more expensive of the two. I think it's pretty interesting that this skill, which was improved for some cases got worse for other cases. As we discussed in the last post, it seems very difficult to write certain kinds of skills (such as test technique skills) that are effective across models and effort levels. A related thing we can observe here is that the Skill condition, which was a skill I quickly whipped up based on my experience driving agentic testing with GPT-5.5 and GPT-5.6 Sol outperformed in our 5.6 Sol eval, but underperformed here with 6 Astra on Pandoc. Someone who has more experience driving testing with 6 Astra on larger problems could probably write a skill that outperforms in those circumstances, at least on problems that are similar in nature to what that person has worked on, but I haven't seriously looked at Astra test effectiveness enough to write that skill myself.

On a related note, for various arbitrary reasons, I've gotten used to using Codex. I seem to do ok with it. This gives me little idea how effective I would be with Claude.

Roman Leventov commented:

Hi Dan, I was encouraged by your post about ai-coding to try fuzz/generated testing.

A part of a system I develop has a statechart-like architecture. Think of it as a support chat where automation could suggest actions or messages for support agent (human) to send to the user. LLM is not used to author messages, but just to classify some of the support intents, but state transitions are deterministic. There could also external events about the subject of the ticket that materially affect possible next actions or decisions. All of this gives rise to a rich statechart system. It is written in TypeScript.

So I had to rewrite a significant chunk of that system so to derisk rewrite but also to try fuzzing I decided to go with it during the rewrite. I used sol xhigh for the first 5 days of the rewrite, then mostly astra medium or high for 4-5 days more (it was around astra release). I instructed agent to develop generate traces of all the possible kinds of events and effects that affect the logic.

For the first 4 days it couldn't make the generated testing system find a single de novo defect that agent reviewers themselves didn't find first. I always use my approach where I define many angles/scopes/areas of review (for this rewrite there were about 15), make agents generate quite detailed prompt for these areas based on my templates, then start subagents in these areas with verbatim prompts in the areas as long as they find any defects or things to fix.

In total throughout the whole rewrite, agent reviewers found about 210 bugs/defects, generated tests took off the ground a bit towards the end and produced about 20 de novo defects that agents themselves didn't notice. In total about 230.

Production code change was about 30k lines, the generated testing harness and everything that was written specifically to support this generated testing approach was about 300k lines at the end. Probably it was very ineffective, but I didn't look into it.

After the deploy, there were a few (4-5) very "stupid" bugs that you would think a process that run well over 100 agent reviewers and found 230 bugs couldn't have missed. Still, I consider this a good result for a rewrite of such a complex statechart system.

Overall I consider this a negative result because generated tests helped find just 10% of the defects, and required gargantuan amount of code (300k lines) and agent tokens to develop and support.

I think this is interesting and I would love to see more people writing up case studies of what they observe.

That post was published in September, but the tests were run in August. The bulk of the work for this post was done in September, but I didn't get around to publishing until November. Despite trying to spend near-zero effort on writing in order to write up experiments I've done, I'm getting further behind while simply not writing up some results that I would've published before agents.

[return]

One I heard recently is that Rust is particularly good for agents because it has nice errors that guide agents toward the correct solution. I've seen this mentioned a few times and, while I'm not going to say this absolutely can't be true as, perhaps, a large scale set of evals that I can't really afford to run might be able to find some kind of effect, I've looked a lot harder at this than anyone who I've seen make this statement and it doesn't seem to be true for any problem that I've looked at, at least at a sample size that I can afford to run. If the statement is true, its effect seems dominated by other factors in most circumstances, so it shouldn't be a reason to choose a language; it seems like the wrong thing to mention if you're going to give a single reason Rust is a good agentic language (which is what happened when I last saw this come up).

Another thing to note here is that the plausible "human sounding" reasons for effectiveness are probably just as untrue when evaluating humans; it's just that we can't afford to run the human eval, so people pass around these irrefutable but also unsupported reasons. Recall that
we looked at the literature on the effectiveness of static vs. dynamic types
because people frequently said that studies show that static types are more effective than dynamic types, but the evidence for this claim was nearly non-existent when we looked at the major studies that had been published at the time.

[return]

Some variant of the saying "a lie can run round the world before the truth has got its boots on" seems to hold for this kind of thing. The viral tweet making the overstated claim has 2.8k likes, 2.8k saves, and 395 retweets as of this writing, a bit less than a month after it was tweeted out. What's your best guess for how much traction
the tweet about this post
will get? I don't think I can make a real money bet that the more accurate tweet will get less traction because someone could take the bet and use some service to give the tweet fake engagement, but for any topic I see being discussed on social media, the most viral claims are almost always overstated and wrong, and more nuanced claims that are less wrong can't really keep up. People seem to really like confidence even (or perhaps especially) in cases where the level of confidence indicates that the claim is almost certainly incorrect.

[return]

title: The Fossils That Haunted Lovecraft
content:
A nest of fossilized eggs at the Flaming Cliffs (Gobi, 1923). Photo: Walter Granger / James B. Shackelford (Central Asiatic Expeditions, 1923). Courtesy of the American Museum of Natural History Library, Special Collections (Image #108751)

In November 1923, newspapers such as
The New York Times
reported on a desert whose name was unfamiliar to most Westerners: the Gobi. The Central Asiatic Expeditions of the American Museum of Natural History (AMNH), led by Roy Chapman Andrews, had returned with tons of fossils and what the press hailed as the first dinosaur eggs ever discovered, preserved in the sandstone of the Flaming Cliffs. The museum took them for the eggs of Protoceratops. Some papers gave their age as ten million years, about seven times too young. The eggs were shipped to New York, where they caused a sensation. The nests had remained intact for seventy million years. Next to them lay the skeleton of a small, toothless, beaked dinosaur, with its skull just four inches (about 10 cm) above the eggs. Henry Fairfield Osborn named
Oviraptor
, the
‘egg-seizer’
, combining the Latin
‘ovum’
(egg) with
‘raptor’
(robber, plunderer). The species name,
philoceratops
, “lover of ceratopsians,” completed the verdict: that beak seemed made for cracking the eggs of
Protoceratops.
Osborn later recognised that this might mislead us as to its feeding habits. He was right. In 1993, a team from the AMNH and the Mongolian Academy of Sciences found an embryo inside an egg of the same type, showing that these eggs were oviraptorid, not
Protoceratops
(Norell et al., 1994). In the following years, oviraptorids such as
Citipati
were found fossilized sitting on their nests with their arms spread over the clutch (Norell et al., 1995; Clark et al., 1999). The supposed thief had been a devoted parent, and one of the researchers, James Clark, even titled a 1995 article “An egg thief exonerated.”

Citipati osmolskae
(IGM 100/979), Ukhaa Tolgod, Mongolia. Joint AMNH–MAS Expedition (1993). Photo: Mick Ellison / Courtesy of AMNH.

Howard Phillips Lovecraft’s love of science is well known, and it gave him an overwhelming sense of the vastness of time, in which humanity is a mere accident. In
The Shadow Out of Time
, his narrator warns that, if his experience was real, humanity must accept notions of the cosmos and of “his own place in the seething vortex of time”. Around 1922, during his early trips to New York, Lovecraft and his friend Frank Belknap Long apparently visited the American Museum of Natural History together, and the idea of a story about a dinosaur egg took shape there. Lovecraft, however, treated it as Long’s. On January 26, 1924, he wrote to Long that H. G. Wells’s
“Æpyornis Island”
did not anticipate
“your dinosaur egg story,”
and urged him to write it anyway. A dinosaur, he argued, belongs to aeons utterly remote from human experience, so a hatching in a museum cellar could be handled with a creepiness wholly unlike anything in Wells. He even threatened, jokingly, to punish Long if he did not. Long never wrote it. In August 1924, Lovecraft saw the Gobi eggs that had reached the museum the previous November. He was not especially impressed: they were, after all, the eggs of a very small dinosaur. The “thief” had not yet been formally named: Osborn’s description of
Oviraptor
appeared in November 1924.

Cover of
Weird Tales
(November 1930):
“A Million Years After.
” Source: Deep Cuts in a Lovecraftian Vein

Lovecraft noticed the November 1930 issue of
Weird Tales,
which featured
“A Million Years After”
by Katharine Metcalf Roof, a story about a dinosaur hatching from a million-year-old egg. By modern paleontological standards, the creature is a mess: a snake-like neck, a small head, spotted skin and a bipedal run, while the cover shows something closer to a sauropod. In a letter to Frank Belknap Long written on October 17 of that year, Lovecraft complained that someone else had gotten there first; he voiced the same frustration to Clark Ashton Smith the same day. A few months later, Lovecraft began to write
“At the Mountains of Madness.
” In the novella, Professor Lake finds a cave in Antarctic limestone full of fossils from many ages:

“This was my first word of the discovery, and it told of the identification of early shells, bones of ganoids and placoderms, remnants of labyrinthodonta and thecoiidea, great mosasaur skull fragments, dinosaur vertebræ and armor plates, pterodactyl teeth and wing bones, Archaeopteryx débris, Miocene sharks’ teeth, primitive bird skulls, and other bones of archaic mammals…”

In 1931, no dinosaur had been found in Antarctica, yet Lovecraft filled a cave there with dinosaur bones. The first dinosaur remains on the continent were discovered during the 1986 Antarctic campaign on James Ross Island by two Argentine geologists, Eduardo Olivero and Roberto Scasso: an armored dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous, later named
Antarctopelta oliveroi
. Lovecraft’s guess turned out to be right.

References:

H. P. Lovecraft to Frank Belknap Long, Jan. 26, 1924,
Selected Letters
, vol. 1, p. 287

H. P. Lovecraft to F. B. Long, Oct. 17, 1930,
Selected Letters
vol. 3, pp. 186-187

H.  P. Lovecraft to C. A. Smith, Oct. 17, 1930,
Dawnward Spire, Lonely Hill
, pp. 245-246

Lovecraft, H. P. (1936).
The Shadow Out of Time
.
Astounding Stories
, June 1936. New York: Street & Smith.

H. P. Lovecraft (1936).
At the Mountains of Madness
.
Astounding Stories
, February–April 1936. Electronic transcription: Project Gutenberg, EBook #70652, April 27, 2023.

Deep Cuts in a Lovecraftian Vein, “A Million Years After” (deepcuts.blog).

Weird Tales
, November 1930 (Internet Archive).

“Bring Dinosaur’s Eggs,”
The New York Times
, Nov. 2, 1923.

“Scientists Motor to a Mystery Land,”
The New York Times
, Nov. 11, 1923.

The Illustrated London News
, Dec. 15, 1923

American Museum Novitates
144 (1924)

M. A. Norell et al., “A theropod dinosaur embryo and the affinities of the Flaming Cliffs dinosaur eggs,”
Science
266: 779-782 (1994). doi:10.1126/science.266.5186.779

J. M. Clark, “An egg thief exonerated,”
Natural History
104(6): 56-57 (1995).

American Museum Novitates
3265 (1999)

Geological Evolution of Antarctica
(pp. 617–622). Cambridge University Press

title: Comcast's "fiber-powered Wi-Fi" is cable, AT&T says in false advertising case
content:
AT&T on Friday accused Comcast of false advertising in a lawsuit challenging the marketing claim that Comcast’s cable broadband service and Wi-Fi is “fiber-powered.”

“This case challenges Comcast’s false advertising campaign for its residential Internet service, marketed under the Xfinity brand to consumers nationwide,”
AT&T’s lawsuit
said. “At the center of that campaign is Comcast’s claim that Xfinity Internet and its associated Wi-Fi service are ‘Fiber-Powered.’”

While Comcast has deployed plenty of fiber throughout the US, its cable Internet service makes the final connection to homes with coaxial cable. This results in upload speeds being far slower than download speeds.

In contrast, fiber-to-the-home service can provide symmetrical upload and download speeds. Comcast has deployed fiber-to-the-home in only
small portions
of its cable territory while advertising its service as fiber-powered in the majority of areas where cable makes the final connection.

AT&T’s lawsuit said that in describing its cable broadband as fiber-powered, Comcast “conveys to reasonable consumers the misleading impression that Xfinity Internet is a fiber-to-the-home service comparable to AT&T Fiber. In fact, the vast majority of Xfinity Internet runs over a hybrid fiber-coaxial (‘HFC’) network, where the critical ‘last mile’ connection to the customer’s home uses copper coaxial cable, not fiber.”

AT&T has its own history of ads that mislead customers about the nature of its network. It used to advertise 4G LTE service as “5GE” or “5G Evolution,” and
displayed a 5GE network icon
on 4G phones. AT&T claimed that its 5G Evolution ads “served to educate customers about the billions of dollars AT&T has invested to give customers an outstanding experience,” but the BBB National Programs’ National Advertising Division found the term was likely to mislead consumers into thinking they had 5G connections.

AT&T: Fiber-powered is “literally false”

AT&T’s lawsuit said that Comcast’s fiber-powered claim “is literally false” because the cable firm’s HFC “architecture is fundamentally different from true fiber-to-the-home services like AT&T Fiber, which deliver fiber optic cables directly to the customer’s premises.”

“Describing that service as ‘Fiber-Powered,’ ‘Powered by fiber,’ and ‘the most reliable, fiber-powered Wi-Fi’—particularly alongside Comcast’s own representations that fiber connections outperform ‘copper-based’ alternatives—is literally false or false by necessary implication,” AT&T wrote. “In that context, Comcast unambiguously conveys that Xfinity Internet is delivered to the home over fiber or is equivalent to fiber-to-the-home service, like AT&T Fiber.”

AT&T sued Comcast in US District Court for the Northern District of California, telling the court that Comcast violated US and California competition laws. AT&T alleged that Comcast’s fiber-powered advertising is a fraudulent business act or practice and an unfair method of competition.

“Comcast should be required to restore to AT&T any and all profits earned as a result of its false and misleading advertising or provide AT&T with any other restitutionary relief the Court deems appropriate,” the lawsuit said. The lawsuit asked for a permanent injunction “requiring Comcast to cease describing its hybrid fiber-coaxial service as ‘Fiber-Powered.’”

AT&T said that even if the court doesn’t find Comcast’s advertising to be literally false, it should determine that it is “misleading because it deceives or has the capacity to deceive a substantial segment of reasonable consumers into believing that Xfinity Internet is delivered to the home over fiber alone.”

Comcast is cutting jobs in its cable division, which for the past few years has been losing Internet customers to fiber and fixed wireless competitors. Comcast lost 144,000 residential broadband customers in Q3 2026, up from a 91,000-customer loss in the same quarter a year ago.

Comcast is struggling against cheaper Internet service providers, including fiber ISPs. Comcast co-CEO Mike Cavanagh
complained in an earnings call
last month that some competitors are offering what he called “irrational pricing.” Comcast CFO Jason Armstrong said fiber ISPs are offering $30 to $40 monthly broadband deals in certain markets, and he said this is irrational because deploying fiber costs $1,500 or more per home.

What’s fiber-powered Wi-Fi?

In December 2025, a
Reddit user reported
receiving a Comcast advertisement for “fiber-powered Wi-Fi” with speeds of up to 300Mbps for $40 a month before taxes and fees. The Reddit user asked what fiber-powered Wi-Fi technology is and whether Comcast provides an adapter to connect fiber to its Wi-Fi equipment.

“Trying to understand what equipment is this Wi-Fi, because I have a hard time merging radio waves with light waves. Doesn’t match any of my tech knowledge, and I’m very curious about it,” the Reddit post said.

A person commenting in response explained that it’s still the same cable service and that “fiber-powered” is Comcast’s new marketing term to describing the existing cable-and-fiber network. “It’s marketing,” the Reddit user wrote. “Now that so many places are offering fiber to the premises, Xfinity needs to work the word ‘fiber’ into their advertising to hide the fact that they still use decades-old, unreliable, DOCSIS technology to get Internet to your home. Their backbone network is fiber, so they call it ‘fiber-powered.’”

AT&T previously challenged Comcast’s fiber-powered claims through the advertising industry’s self-regulatory system operated by BBB National Programs’ National Advertising Division (NAD). The NAD
determined in June
that Comcast accurately described its mix of cable and fiber technology in a disclosure, but that Comcast didn’t make the disclosure prominently enough.

The NAD said:

In the challenged advertising, “fiber-powered” appears alongside several other claims, including pricing offers accompanied by separate disclosures. As a result, the coaxial cable disclosure does not stand out within the larger block of disclosures, reducing its prominence. NAD also noted that in certain advertisements, including the “Overview Ad,” the disclosure appears several panels away from the “fiber-powered” claim and may require consumers to scroll to view it. In addition, the advertising does not include an asterisk or other signal directing consumers to the disclosure. While the disclosure appears in readable black font against a contrasting background, NAD concluded that the disclosure should be more prominent or placed closer to the triggering claim to increase the likelihood that consumers will notice and read it.

The NAD recommended that Comcast make the disclosure “more prominent and more proximate to the ‘fiber-powered’ Wi-Fi claim as necessary to ensure that the disclosure is clear and conspicuous.” Comcast said it would comply with the decision, but AT&T’s lawsuit makes it clear that it isn’t satisfied with the current state of Comcast’s advertising. We contacted Comcast and will update this article if it provides a response.

AT&T filed similar lawsuit against Charter

AT&T has a similar ongoing battle against Charter, which also describes its cable Internet service as fiber-powered. Charter
modified its disclosures
in response to an AT&T complaint to the NAD in March, and
AT&T sued Charter
in August.

“Charter deceives consumers by manipulating the word ‘fiber’ in its advertising so it can tout its ‘Spectrum Fiber Broadband Network’ and hide the fact that its network mainly connects to customers’ homes using copper wire,” said the lawsuit filed in US District Court for the Northern District of Texas.

Charter filed a
motion to dismiss
the lawsuit in October. “Charter’s description of Internet services delivered over an HFC network as ‘fiber-powered’ fits the definition of the word ‘powered,’ for much as computers are ‘powered by Intel chips,’ Charter’s HFC network—and the Internet service it delivers to customers—are powered by fiber,” Charter said, arguing that it uses the term “to describe the critical role fiber technology plays in its HFC network.”

AT&T’s lawsuit against Charter said a Spectrum commercial didn’t make it clear enough that the broadband service uses cable. AT&T wrote, “When ‘Spectrum Fiber-Powered Internet’ first appears onscreen, it is accompanied by a miniature, momentary disclosure at the bottom of the screen amid loud music and rapidly moving visual stimuli. The disclosure says, ‘Spectrum Internet is powered by fiber and connected to the premises by coaxial lines,’ but the voiceover does not read it aloud. That disclosure is inadequate to cure the deception caused by Charter’s ‘Fiber-Powered Internet’ claim.”

Charter said its disclosures are prominent enough and that it is not deceiving customers. “A company bent on hiding its coaxial connection does not illustrate it, explain it in an FAQ, and disclose it on-screen in its advertising,” Charter told the court.

Disclosure: The Advance/Newhouse Partnership, which owns 14 percent of Charter, is part of Advance Publications, which owns Ars Technica parent Condé Nast.

Jon Brodkin

Senior IT Reporter

Jon Brodkin

Senior IT Reporter

Jon is a Senior IT Reporter for Ars Technica. He covers the telecom industry, Federal Communications Commission rulemakings, broadband consumer affairs, court cases, and government regulation of the tech industry.

title: Formal Verification Is Not Verifiable
content:
Formal Verification is Not Verifiable
.

Posted on
2026-11-13

::

8 min read

:: Tags:

🏷
software engineering
,

🏷
ai
,

🏷
formal methods
,

🏷
software testing

AI
is
making formal verification go mainstream...

...I
wrote in December 2025
, well, after the last 12 months I believe it is hard to argue otherwise. AI
has
made formal verification go mainstream.

Not only did the number of formal verification startups skyrocket, Claude also wrote
a billion lines of Rocq
for a single verification project, everyone from
the creator of Claude Code
to
the Vercel CEO
, lead
Codex
/
Cursor
developers is talking about formal verification. The early startups have started to show economic value in software on top of simply producing math proofs:
Theorem's binary verification work with Anthropic
,
Harmonic verifying C programs and hardware designs
... With the cybersecurity risk going through the roof, formal verification is not just easier, it is also getting more economically valuable.

The questions people ask now are not "how can we prove X", but rather "what can we prove about X"; or "what is left that we can't prove"? These are good questions to ask, I am writing this post in part to answer them; and in part as a follow-up to last year's post
"Test, don't (just) verify"
. To tease the ending, I am very optimistic about formal verification, but I think people mean lots of different things when they say something is "formally verified", which I will try to break down into the parts I'm optimistic and pessimistic about.

Let's start from the title, I'm what an SF person would call a "verifiability-pilled" person, I've argued for long (well, 2 years) that
verifiability was the limit
of how much leverage AI can give us; my rough long-term view is that we will build our technology stack around these spikes of verifiable components in our systems. Nowadays, when verifiability is mentioned formal verification very quickly jumps into the discussion. However, somehow, formally verified systems can still have bugs, and when I hear someone has formally verified their systems I am genuinely not filled with a flow of confidence in the correctness of their system. On the other hand, when someone says they found a bug in a system, I am fairly confident that they did so. I argue that this is because testing is verifiable, it produces a well-defined, reviewable, understandable object, a good old bug report.
Testing is verifiable (by a HUMAN)
as in UI components are verifiable, that's why they're both very easy to use AI with.

Formal verification on the other hand has "verified" components that require no external review, the proofs; and hard to verify components, the definitions themselves, the underlying models of the object we are proving facts about, the provers that are doing the verification. The claim of formal verification is also very strong--formal verification makes
forall
claims, testing makes
exists
claims--any mistake in any of the hard-to-verify components might lead to the downfall of the proofs.

There are a few paths to make formal verification more "verifiable", the simplest is to reduce the amount or the size of these trusted components. A great example of this is the recent "binary verification" approach, where instead of proving facts about the programs themselves, we prove facts about the compiled binaries of those programs. This allows us to (1) elide modelling the semantics of the high level programming language, we can instead model the semantics of the machine--presumably simpler semantics--and also drop our reliance on compiler correctness (which really isn't a good idea, compilers have
many
bugs
); (2) avoid modelling semantics of not one, but many high level languages, because source level verification requires you to model every language separately, but at the binary level they all converge to the same model.

This however, in my opinion, solves a small part of the problem. The trusted surface is still huge, you have both the machine semantics and the Linux process semantics in your trusted computing base, both of which need extra validation. More importantly though, talking about "formally verifying X" is still a mistake, the specifically correct term is "formally verifying X properties of Y". This distinction in terminology used to be a colloquially accepted notion, when we heard "
CompCert
is a formally verified compiler" or "
seL4
is a formally verified microkernel" we assumed the authors did not verify vacuous or trivial properties, because the work of verification itself was held to a high standard that highly affected the reputation of the researcher. It is actually a huge disservice to the scientific method and formal verification community to say we assumed these things, because in reality these works have undergone extensive peer review, people have built other formally verified systems on them,
and they had bugs
. However, just as AI has shaken up code review in software engineering, it has a similar, even more aggressive effect on proof engineering. If AI has 10x'd the volume of software in the world, it has perhaps 1000x'd the volume of "formally verified software" in the world. This democratization affects our traditional validation strategies in almost every domain, but the more niche a field originally was, the more crucially affected it is due to this change in volume.

It is my opinion that we must
as soon as possible
abolish the notion of "formally verified software", nuance has to arise. Every discussion of formal verification must come with a list of caveats, a precise understanding of what is trusted, what is proven and what is not. Some of this is already here, new Lean proofs are discussed under the possibility of a kernel soundness bug an LLM could've exploited,
comparator
is becoming the standard device for validating a new Lean proof, major announcements like
Anthropic<>Theorem crash freeness verification
as well as
Google DeepMind's Signal verification
state the limitations of the proof as well as the trusted computing base.

It is also important to develop a conversation around bugs in software with formally verified attributes.
It is normal for software to have bugs!
This is not an indictment of software engineers but the result of the inherent complexity of software; a complex software system deals with not millions or billions, but trillions of different types of events. Engineers constrain this complexity by building layers of abstractions, capturing complex behavior behind manageable, general patterns of well-tested primitives. However, as these layers come closer to the users, the mathematically well-defined abstractions are harder to create. The easiest way to think about this is to imagine a piece of software like a car, the engine is similar to the database, both well-engineered, both providing a simple interface; the car seat is similar to the user interface, there is no mathematical formula for it, there are general guidelines, there are user demands, there are aesthetic choices, in the end it feels "
bouba
", compared to the engine or the database which feels more "kiki".

The more "bouba" a piece of software or a given layer is, the harder it is to talk about what makes it correct. We can always talk about some correct attributes, but to talk about a uniform notion of correctness is not possible in my opinion. That means to talk about formally verifying bouba software is a hopeless endeavour, and any statements of "formally verifying everything" or "bug-free software" need a huge asterisk next to it.

We can't prove bouba software
correct
, but we can prove plenty of things
about
it. For general properties of software we can specify, regardless of whether these facts show up in the inner kiki layers or outer bouba layers, I am very optimistic about proving them. Specifically in the context of single-threaded programs, I think our existing proof frameworks give us the latitude to prove large, real production systems with the help of machine-generated proofs. I had previously made a personal bet that we might solve single-threaded code translation by 2030; I'm now at the stage where I believe we can not only solve translation, but single-threaded program verification as well. For any first-order universally quantified property of a program we can write as a
property-based test
, I think we will be able to generate proofs at the binary level, against architecture models that have themselves been validated by millions of hours of testing. The challenge of extending this to multi-threaded programs, distributed systems, higher-order properties, non-functional properties, real deployment settings will be years more of work we must conduct across thousands of verification engineers and researchers.

In solving these challenges, I think random testing and random exploration in general will prove to be invaluable tools. A test execution is a measurement, so it produces information about the real underlying system that we can leverage to falsify, harden and validate the models we use for verification. The verifiability of testing will continue to be a huge driving force of its adoption as well as a gateway into the rest of formal methods, and maybe it will even help us trust when we hear software is "formally verified" instead of wondering what was left out or when someone will find a bug in there.
