title: Effects of a Nuclear Detonation in Low Earth Orbit
content:
Physics > Physics and Society

[Submitted on 6 Nov 2026]

Title:
Effects of a Nuclear Detonation in Low Earth Orbit

Authors:
Zachary Petersen
,
Hong Qin
,
Sarah Thiele
,
Sébastien Philippe

View a PDF of the paper titled Effects of a Nuclear Detonation in Low Earth Orbit, by Zachary Petersen and 3 other authors

View PDF

HTML (experimental)

Abstract:
More than 13,000 satellites operate in low Earth orbit (LEO), and concern has grown that nuclear weapons could be used in space to target them. Beyond the initial X-ray burst, electrons released by radioactive fission products can become trapped in Earth's magnetic field, repeatedly exposing satellites as an artificial radiation belt. Here we couple prompt radiation, electron trapping and belt evolution to satellite failures, collisions and atmospheric drag. For a 1-Mt detonation at 500km over the South Atlantic, repeated belt exposure disables approximately 98% of modeled satellites within one week in our central case. Tripling the assumed radiation tolerance delays widespread failure by only days: approximately 97% are still disabled within two weeks. The loss of maneuverability sharply increases collision risk, with approximately 20 collisions expected within two years. Drag removes many disabled spacecraft from lower altitudes, but replacement satellites could remain exposed to radiation and debris for years. These findings show how a single detonation could devastate orbital infrastructure and support efforts to prevent the deployment and use of nuclear weapons in space.

title: Who Builds the Machines That Build the Machines?
content:
Who Builds the Machines That Build the Machines? Section 232 and America's Machine Tool Gap
The Russian doll of physical AI’s bottlenecks
Michelle Sun
Nov 17, 2026
∙
Paid
On October 28, 2026, the White House issued a proclamation under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962. This followed a Commerce Department investigation that concluded
imports of robotics and industrial machinery “threaten to impair the national security.”
No new tariffs have been set yet. Section 232 opens a 180-day window till April 26, 2027 to negotiate with trading partners.
This ties back to one theme that keeps coming back to me as I write on Core Matter.
The bottleneck for scaling physical AI sits below the finished machine, in the components inside it, the materials inside those components (eg, rare earth magnets), and the machines that build them (this piece’s topic)
, as we covered in
Part 4 of the actuator series
. It’s like a Russian doll, layer after layer.
With the fresh Section 232 news, I went down the rabbit hole of the US machine tool landscape. Here’s what I found.
The US imports about half of the machine tools it uses
, $5.8bn of $11.4bn in 2025. Assuming demand (which is not the trend, see point 3) stays flat, US output would need to grow 63% to 83% ($4.4bn to $5.8bn a year) to replace imports with domestic machines.
The US builds everyday machines and imports the precise ones.
About 55% of import value is the high-end versions of machines US plants already make, such as 5-axis machining centers. Precision machines, small-module gear grinders, precision grinders and the heaviest forging presses have no confirmed US volume builder. Imports rose 29.5% for grinders and 76.7% for gear machines in Jan to Sep 2026. These machines make the ball screws, bearings, gears and forgings that aircraft, turbines and robots depend on.
Orders are at a record by value since 1998, while a domestic ramp is limited by people and components.
US machine tool orders grew 45.0% to $5.76bn in Jan to Sep 2026, after 3 straight years of decline. Aerospace, power generation, munitions and shipbuilding are pulling it up. A domestic ramp is limited by people, castings and imported components (the components that make the machines, the next doll in). We dive into the key cost drivers and where industrial AI could change the cost structure.
This piece also launches our first Core Matter model
, a US machine tool demand model built up by end market. It puts US machine tool consumption at $12.7bn to $15.4bn a year on average over the 2026 to 2030 build-out, up from $11.4bn in 2025. Paid subscribers can download the full model, with every input and source, at the end of this piece.
Exhibit 1. The. Core Matter Industrial. Machinery Model, year by year from 2025 to 2031 (access at bottom of this article)
In this piece
US Machine Tool Imports Are Half of an $11.4bn Market
Which Machine Tools the US Makes vs. Imports
Aerospace, Gas Turbines, Munitions and Ships Drove Machine Demand in 2026
Who Builds Machine Tools in the US, and How Fast Can Supply Ramp?
Fixed Costs and People Keep New Machine Tool Builders Scarce
Machine Tool Startups Building the Machines That Build the Machines
Section 232, the 1986 Machine Tool Precedent and What the 180 Days Decide
1. US Machine Tool Imports Are Half of an $11.4bn Market
Assuming domestic demand stays flat, which is not the trendline as we’ll discuss in section 3, closing the import gap means $4.4bn to $5.8bn of new US machine output a year, or output up 63% to 83%.
The low end replaces net imports, and the high end replaces every imported machine.
In 2025 the US produced $7.0bn of machine tools, consumed $11.4bn, imported $5.8bn and exported $1.4bn, per Gardner’s World Machine Tool Survey.
Exhibit 2. The US imports 51% of the machine tools it used in 2025.
Forming and stamping ($1.48bn) and machining centers ($1.43bn) are the top 2025 imports.
Imports of precision grinders or gear grinders rose rapidly at 29.5% and 76.7% in January to September 2026, against about 9.6% for all machine tool imports. We could not confirm US volume production.
Exhibit 3. US machine tool imports by type, 2025. Machining centers and forming machines are top imports, while grinders and gear machines are harder to ramp domestically.
2. Which Machine Tools the US Makes vs. Imports
The US imports
5-axis machines, horizontals with pallet systems, large gantries and boring mills, precision and gear grinders, and presses.
It builds in volume
entry and mid-range 3-axis mills and lathes.
“Japanese and DACH (Germany, Austria and Switzerland) machines generally fulfill buyer needs in the higher segment while US and Taiwanese (ROC) generally fulfill them in the lower.”
One distributor analyst put it succinctly in a filing to the Section 232 docket.
What do higher vs. lower segments mean? Higher means more axes, tighter precision, bigger work envelopes and more automation, at a higher price.
The average imported machining center cost about $196k in 2024, roughly 2x our estimate of about $96k per machine at Haas, the largest machine tool builder in North America.
See the table below of what these machines do, and who the main buyers are.
Exhibit 4. The US builds the everyday machine tiers in volume, while imports precision and heavy machines.
While Okuma (Charlotte), Makino (Ohio), United Grinding (Ohio), Kapp Niles (Colorado) and DN Solutions (New Jersey) have large US sites, the sources we found describe them as sales, service or headquarters sites.
The largest two import classes feed autos, aerospace and defense.
Forming and stamping machines make stampings, shell bodies and aerospace forgings. Machining centers make everything from brackets and housings to aerospace structures and turbine parts. My guess is that a cutoff at the high end would hit aerospace, defense and power first.
The US built its own heavy forging presses in the 1950s. The newest ones came from a German builder.
Heavy forging presses squeeze titanium, aluminum and nickel into one-piece parts such as landing gear, airframe bulkheads and turbine discs.
Because so few exist, these presses can cap how many aircraft and engine parts get made here.
Robot reducers need ultra-precision gear machines, which are imported and in low volumes.
Robot joints use reducers, small gearboxes whose teeth are cut and ground on gear machines. Leaderdrive, a Chinese reducer maker, told the Shanghai stock exchange that a plant for 1 million harmonic reducers a year needs 30 ultra-precision gear machines, at about $833k each.
Assuming 23 reducers per humanoid (on the low end, based on Unitree G1 teardown), 1 million humanoids a year (Tesla’s stated line capacity) would need about 690 of those machines, or about $115mn a year bought over the 5 years to 2030. That is 2.3x and 1.2x all US gear-machine imports, $50.7mn in 2025 and about $100mn a year at the 2026 pace.
Exhibit 5. At 1m humanoids a year, the demand for gear machines will exceed all US gear-machine imports by 1.15X
I ranked the hardest machines to ramp domestically based on, a) which are whether we found a US builder making them in volume, b) how long new capacity takes, and c) how much it costs.
Details are in the Core Matter Industrial Machinery Model.
Machines to build in the US, ranked from hardest to ramp:
Small-module gear grinders.
They finish the gears in robot reducers and aerospace gearboxes. We could not confirm volume production of these at any US builder.
Precision cylindrical and thread grinders.
These grinders make the ball screws and bearings that other machines need. United Grinding, the Swiss grinding group, serves the US from an import and service site in Ohio. We found 2 US builders, Weldon (Pennsylvania) and Drake (Ohio), and could not confirm volume production at either.
Heavy forging presses.
The 2 largest US presses we found built or rebuilt since 2000 came from a German builder. Each project took years and $100mn or more.
Large gantries and boring mills.
Ingersoll and Fives build them here, so these are the likeliest candidates to ramp. The constraint is size and lead time.
High-end 5-axis machines and automated horizontals.
Mazak and DMG MORI already build some in the US, so expansion of existing plants is the shorter path here.
3. Aerospace, Gas Turbines, Munitions and Ships Drove Machine Demand in 2026
US machine tool orders have picked up significantly in 2025 and 2026. Order value rose 22.5% to $5.74bn in 2025, and another
45.0%
to $5.76bn in January to September 2026. That was after 3 straight years of decline, including a 3.8% fall in 2024. AMT calls
the first half of 2026 its strongest half since the series began in 1998.
Exhibit 6. US machine tool orders have significantly rebounded in 2025 and 2026
Who buys these machines in the US?
Aerospace
orders rose 45.1% in 2025, and in the first half of 2026 aerospace ordered more machinery than in any half on record. AMT ties 2026 demand to the space economy, commercial aircraft backlogs and munitions, so commercial demand is part of it alongside defense.
Power generation
orders in the first half of 2026 ran 14% above automotive.
Contract job shops
, AMT’s largest customer group, grew orders 19.1% in 2025.
Data centers
drive gas turbines machinery demands. Klingelnberg says that in the US “the rising energy needs of these data centers are providing additional momentum, for example through investments in gas turbines.”
The US buys $11.4bn of machine tools a year today. Four build-outs (munitions, ships, gas turbines, commercial aerospace) add $1.0bn to $2.9bn a year of extra buying for 5 years, on top of 1% to 3% normal growth. That puts US buying at $12.7bn to $15.4bn a year in 2026 to 2030.
Munitions is the largest piece. The one new US plant we found, Haas Henderson, adds about $0.5bn of machines sold at home.
So imports rise from $5.8bn to about $6.9bn to $9.5bn a year, and the import share goes from 51% to 54% to 62%.
Exhibit 7. US machine tool consumption in 2025 and on average in 2026 to 2030, and build-out demand by end market.
4. Who Builds Machine Tools in the US, and How Fast Can Supply Ramp?
Exhibit 8. Where machine tools are built in the US.
A domestic ramp-up faces four limiting factors.
Workforce.
This is the manufacturing story repeating all over again. Gleason’s executive put it first, saying “First you need a large enough, trained workforce. This needs to be the top priority to expand the industrial base.” Haas is hiring more than 1,000 people for Henderson at starting pay of about $23 an hour.
Castings.
Castings are the heavy iron bed and columns of a machine. Haas bought “more than 100 million pounds of castings each year” back in 2006 and worried that shrinking US foundry numbers “could limit their company’s growth.” At 10,000 to 13,000 machines a year, that is roughly 7,700 to 10,000 pounds (3.5 to 4.5 tonnes, about the weight of 2 to 3 cars) of castings per machine.
Imported components.
The parts inside the machines are imported too, including controls (FANUC, Siemens, Heidenhain, Mitsubishi), spindles, ball screws and linear guides. Tariffs raise their cost, and control deliveries have seen delays.
In April 2025 Haas asked for “tariff exemptions for raw materials and components vital to the U.S. machine tool industry.” DMG MORI’s 2025 results blame late deliveries partly on “delays in switching to new European-made CNCs.”
Time.
“A shift in global production takes a lot of time,” per GMTA, a US importer of German gear machines. One example is Haas’s plant in Henderson, Nevada. The city closed the land sale in November 2019, with completion planned for 2022. Haas asked the city to extend its deadline, citing the pandemic, supply chains and construction costs. They eventually held the groundbreaking in October 2024. The plant is scheduled to open in Q1 2027, 5 years behind schedule.
Imports are slow to fill a jump in demand too, since foreign builders hold about 7 months of sales in backlog, with DMG MORI at 7.0 months on September 30, 2026 and Klingelnberg at about 7 at the end of March 2026. Klingelnberg’s backlog has halved since 2023.
5. Fixed Costs and People Keep New Machine Tool Builders Scarce
Would this spur a new generation of startups to build the machines that build the machines? As I read the filings of listed builders, the economics are brutal.
Exhibit 9. People cost as much as materials for European and Japanese builders, at 30-41% and 38%-41% revenue respectively.
What I took away from these financials is that for European and Japanese builders,
people cost about as much as materials.
Personnel is 30% to 41% of revenue or operating output and materials 38% to 41%. At Chinese builders, total employee pay is 15% to 19% of revenue (Haitian and Kede, 2025) and materials 50% to 62%. Personnel, depreciation and overhead are fixed costs, so margins swing with the cycle. 2025 was a weak year. In 2023 Hermle earned an operating margin of about 21.8% and DMG MORI 10.0%. Labor productivity in US metalworking machinery “has grown only 0.9% per year over the last 30 years.”
What are the key materials? Neway, a Chinese CNC machine builder (688697.SS)’s IPO prospectus published their bill of materials. Of Rmb840.0mn ($122mn) of purchases in 2020, the split is below.
Functional components
(hydraulics, tool magazines, rotary tables) are 25.6%
Castings
are 22.3%
Electrical parts
(mainly the control) are 20.9%. The control alone is about 17.7% of purchases.
Transmission parts
(spindles, guides, screws, bearings, gears) are 15.4%
Accessories, machined parts, sheet metal and other
are 15.8%
Control and distribution are two levers that can help expand margins.
The control.
A CNC control is the machine’s computer, software, servo drives and motors. Most builders we checked buy it from FANUC, Siemens, Heidenhain or Mitsubishi, and FANUC earns a 21.4% operating margin (company-wide) against 3% to 10% at most builders we checked.
Cutting the middlemen.
US distribution typically has 2 levels, “a wholesaler and a dealer,” and “each level marks their cost up as much as 20%.”
6. Machine Tool Startups Building the Machines That Build the Machines
Could venture capital close the machinery gap with the next wave of startups? I went searching and
found no venture-backed US company building production machining centers, grinders or gear machines.
(If you are building them, I’d love to hear from you!)
What we can learn from history.
Haas, the largest machine builder in North America, was founded in 1983, during the import surge behind the 1983 machine tool Section 232 petition. It started with indexers and built its first vertical machining center in 1987. Today it builds about 10,000 to 15,000 machines a year on about $1.2bn of revenue, and is private.
The small US builders popped up in the 2000s. They include Tormach (Wisconsin, 2001), Pocket NC, now Penta Machine (Montana, 2011), and Langmuir Systems, a plasma-table maker bought by ShopSabre in 2023. They design and sell desktop and small-shop machines.
US venture money has gone to companies that use machine tools or build equipment for their own factories.
Examples include Hadrian, Machina Labs, Divergent, VulcanForms, Freeform and Seurat. Hadrian’s new Alabama factory is the first of three supported by a $900mn Navy contract, with a goal to “automate 80% of the work.”
This year’s capital went to factory software and sensing.
Arda, led by OpenAI’s former research chief Bob McGrew, came out of stealth in October 2026 with $232mn of funding, its Series A at a $1.5bn valuation, building AI that turns product designs into assembly lines. Matter, whose cofounder and CEO Adi Prasad came from Tesla, offers final assembly, test and packaging for robots in the US. In machining software, CloudNC raised $20mn (UK, September 2026, with Lockheed’s venture arm), Limitless Labs $20mn (Israel) and IPercept $16.5mn (Sweden, entering the US).
Funded machine builders abroad tell a different story.
Ethereal Machines (India) raised a $28.5mn Series B in 2026. It builds its own multi-axis CNC machines, sells machining as a service from them, and is building its own controller and a 300,000 sq ft plant. Shanghai Xinghe (China) builds gear grinders and raised several hundred million yuan in July 2026.
Government money has gone to training and adjacent supply.
America’s Cutting Edge, a national CNC machining training initiative backed by Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL), received $42mn from the Defense Department from 2020 to 2022 for machine tool training and R&D. The Pentagon’s industrial base program has awarded over $3.3bn since FY2024. The releases we read do not name any machine tool builder.
With Section 232, I believe two opportunities arise domestically in the US.
Foreign builders establish US bases to build machines. They are more experienced in navigating thin margins, but that would likely still require government incentives to boost investments.
Startups in the same spirit as Ethereal Machines launch in the US. They would need to think carefully about how to cut labor cost, solve the materials supply chain bottleneck, and build the control in-house from day one.
7. Section 232, the 1986 Machine Tool Precedent and What the 180 Days Decide
This Section 232 has until April 26, 2027 for its first negotiation update. Section 232 last came for machine tools in 1983, 43 years ago. Will history repeat or rhyme?
The US lost its lead in the 1970s and 1980s.
Japanese machine tool exports to the US rose over 1,200% between 1964 and 1967, and by 1986 imports were 75% of the numerically controlled (NC) machines sold in the US, the category that includes today’s CNC machines. Across all machine tools, imports went from about 10% of US consumption in the mid-1970s to 25% by 1981 and about 50% by 1986.
March 1983.
The builders’ association petitions for import quotas under Section 232.
May 20, 1986.
Reagan chooses negotiation. “Voluntary restraint agreements will be sought with Taiwan, West Germany, Japan, and Switzerland.”
Dec 16, 1986.
Japan and Taiwan agree to 5 years of restraint from January 1987. The White House projects up to 16,500 more domestic machine sales over the 5 years and cites industry estimates of about $115mn of new plant investment. The full outcome is hard to score. One NBER study found US output rose from 41,992 machines in 1987 to 48,668 in 1988.
By Oct 1991.
Reports said “at least 10 Japanese machine-toolmakers have established plants in the U.S.”
Dec 1991.
Bush keeps the restraints on computer-controlled machines for a 2-year phase-out from January 1992. Japan’s extension ran to Dec 31, 1993, so 5 years became 7.
Effects.
The US International Trade Commission estimated that in 1987, the first year, the restraints raised prices 4.4% to 4.9% and protected 658 to 671 jobs. AMT says the domestic share held near 50% for the next decade, so the restraints stopped the fall without reversing it. Imports are about 51% of consumption today.
Here is our view.
A tariff alone raises prices, but buyers keep importing the precise machines.
Back in 1987, during the last Section 232, the domestic share held near 50% for the following decade. Fast forward to today, imports are 51% of consumption. One can argue that without the 1987 restraints, the domestic share would be even lower today. This time, imports fell where US plants offer an alternative and kept rising where buyers have few US options. So either the buyers are not price sensitive, or the cost are passed down to the customers. In January to September 2026, with duties in place, machining-center imports fell 3.7% while orders rose 45.0%, and grinder imports rose 29.5% and gear machine imports +76.7%.
For reindustrialization startups, the openings are in the control and in automation that cuts labor cost.
The control is where the profit sits. Builders buy it from suppliers such as FANUC, Siemens, Heidenhain and Mitsubishi, and FANUC earns a 21.4% operating margin (company-wide) against 3% to 10% at most builders we checked. Automation goes after the other big cost. On our numbers, personnel is 30% to 41% of revenue or operating output at European and Japanese builders, about as much as materials. Service margins come from machines already in the field, so they follow once the core machine business is running. This in my opinion is an opportunity for agentic robotics, manufacturing AI founders to shine.

title: Munich Laser Emits a Beam of Matter Waves (1999)
content:
Science News

from research organizations

Munich Laser Emits A Beam Of Matter Waves

Date:

March 17, 1999

Source:

Max Planck Society

Summary:

German scientists at the Max Planck Institute for Quantum Optics in Garching and the University of Munich have developed a laser that emits a continuous heam of matter waves instead of light. Such unprecedented control over atomic motion becomes possible by the laws of quantum mechanics at very low temperatures, close to absolute zero, where the atoms reveal their wave nature.

Share:

FULL STORY

German scientists at the Max Planck Institute for Quantum Optics in Garching and the University of Munich have developed a laser that emits a continuous heam of matter waves instead of light (to be reported in Physical Review Letters).

Such unprecedented control over atomic motion becomes possible by the laws of quantum mechanics at very low temperatures, close to absolute zero, where the atoms reveal their wave nature.

Atom lasers open new prospects in many areas of science and technology. For instance, it should become possible to accurately deposit atoms on surfaces and thus to produce tiny nanostructures, as needed in future computer circuits. Atom lasers may also lead to extremely precise atomic clocks for future navigation and communication systems.

In their experiments, Tilman Esslinger, Immanuel Bloch and Theodor W. Hänsch have taken pictures of the shadow cast by their atom laser beam. The pencil-like beam contains about half a million rubidium atoms and is accelerated downwards by gravity.

Just as a beam of light, an atom laser beam can be focused and reflected by using lenses or mirrors consisting of laser light (or of magnets). It appears feasible to focus an atom laser beam to a spot size of one nanometer, which is a thousand times smaller than the smallest focus of a laser beam.

The atom laser is based on Bose- Einstein condensation. If a gas is cooled to a few millionth of a degree above absolute zero, the atoms lose their identity and behave as a single entity, some kind of "super atom". Such a Bose-Einstein condensate was first produced by American scientists in 1995.

In the Munich experiment, a dilute gas of rubidium atoms is captured in a sophisticated low-power magnetic trap and cooled down to reach Bose-Einstein condensation. With the help of a radiofrequency field the scientists flip the atomic spin so that atoms are allowed escape from the magnetic trap. In vacuum, the atoms are accelerated by gravity and form a parallel beam of coherent matter waves.

It the radiofrequency field is turned on before condensation sets in, the atom laser can only reach threshold, if there is laser "gain". Unlike a Bose-Einstein condensate, such a laser relies on matter wave amplification by stimulated elastic scattering of rubidium atoms just as an optical laser relies on light amplification by stimulated emission of radiation.

Two years ago, a group at MIT demonstrated the first pulsed atom laser. The Munich group is the first to produce a continuous matter wave beam which can be maintained for a tenth of a second. The wave packet of each atom extends over the entire length of this beam, so that a quantum object of truly macroscopic dimensions is created. The high brightness and coherence of such a matter wave beam opens exciting perspectives for the young fields of atom optics and atom interferometry.

title: Not Everything Needs an LLM
content:
Not everything needs an LLM
How we use decision models
Jina Yoon
Nov 09, 2026
LLMs love to yap. Ask a simple question and you get a few hundred words of "it depends." It's annoying as hell.
This is why we love
decision models like Jev
for simpler tasks. You ask a structured question and get a typed answer with a probability, which looks something like this:
Noul.
Are hedgehogs mammals? → Yes, 0.99
Choice.
Which animal family do hedgehogs belong to? → Mammal, 0.99
Score.
What is the current conservation status of hedgehogs? → Least Concern, 0.77
Whereas LLMs return free-form and overly confident prose, decision models make model uncertainty explicit. In a calibrated model, answers that score 0.8 are right about 80% of the time. That means a score of 0.5 is a coin flip.
We've been experimenting with them at PostHog and several use cases have made it to production. This is everything we've learned about using decision models so far: when to use them, how to use them, and mistakes to avoid.
1. Use them to gate expensive LLM calls
Decision models are up to 444.6x cheaper and 193.6x faster than frontier models,
1
so you can use them to check whether you even need to make an expensive LLM call at all.
We do this in a pipeline that scrubs personal info in
Replay Vision
, our product that watches and summarizes user session recordings for you. Here's how it works:
Each session summary goes through 2 yes/no questions from a decision model. Using narrow questions like this cuts false flags to about a tenth of what a single question produced.
1. “Does this name a real person?”
2. “Does this show contact details or an ID?”
If either scores 0.4 or above, Gemini rewrites the summary without the personal info and it gets checked again.
Otherwise, it's clean and passes through the gate.
In production
, 98.7% skip the LLM call entirely.
Without the decision model, we'd have to keep fussing with prompts and regexes that miss things, or sending every summary to Gemini to catch the 1% that need it.
But remember they make mistakes
A probability score of 0.85 still means ~150 wrong answers per 1,000 checks, so plan ahead for false positives and false negatives.
In the PII example, a false positive only costs us an extra LLM call, whereas a false negative stores personal data as clean. That's why we set the threshold low at 0.4.
When false positives are the costlier mistake, use
higher
thresholds. For example, we recently updated the PostHog in Slack bot, so it can answer questions
without being tagged
. To avoid being annoying, it checks every message in a channel to see (1) whether it's asking for information, and (2) whether PostHog could answer it. Only messages that pass both at 0.85+ go through.
Takeaway:
Use decision models to filter jobs before they hit an expensive LLM call, and set the threshold based on which mistake costs you more.
2. Use them as model routers
Our
PostHog in Slack
bot also uses a decision model as a
model router
.
When the bot gets tagged, it first checks whether the message asked for a specific model. If not, one
choice
question picks from the list:
“Pick the cheapest option that will most likely finish the task correctly on the first try. A failed run costs more than a smarter option.”
Each option in the list carries a short note on what that model is good for. GPT Luna is described as “a light and very cheap model. Good for short answers, lookups, summaries and very small edits.” The decision model then scores the request against each option’s text.
But don't assume they're interchangeable
Different tasks, models, and providers all have different thresholds.
We were experimenting with using them to auto-merge similar logs in
Error Tracking
and found that thresholds changed between v1 and v2 of the same model. We had to make its thresholds configurable per PostHog project and keep the judge in shadow mode while recalibrating based on
hand-labeled data
.
This is one of the reasons why
Fernando
on our growth team pushed for a model-agnostic interface early. We now have an internal AI gateway for swapping and testing models, including self-hosted ones.
Takeaway:
Use a
choice
question to route free-form LLM requests to the cheapest model that can handle it. Keep in mind that thresholds don't carry over, so set them per task and per model.
3. Use them for face-value checks
If a question requires more context or chains of reasoning, it's better to use an LLM. However, you can still use a decision model if you have a way to flatten, or pre-process the input, so it's checkable at face-value.
In Replay Vision, when a user searches for a theme like "onboarding friction," there's a chance for the query to return a few unexpected results because of the way embedding distance works.
A decision model can’t "Rank the top 10 sessions that contain summaries that match the user's search query." It’s too complicated.
Instead, we use the embeddings first to derive an initial list of session recordings to pass to the decision model. Then, the only task left for the decision model is to look at how closely each result in the list matches the user's original search term:
"Does this summary describe a session that matches what the search looks for?"
Results are then
reranked
by that probability. On 20 test queries, this improved ranking quality by about 25%.
But avoid multi-step reasoning
We've tried
using a decision model
for multi-step reasoning before. Before embeddings were ready in Replay Vision, we tried ranking a "Highlights" feed of sessions worth a human's time. The questions were:
Is this session worth watching?
If so, why is it worth watching? (With choices like “error on screen,” “slow or stuck,” “user confused”, “user gave up", etc.)
Processing these two questions in order required an hourly job that sent large requests – up to 32 sessions and 12-38k tokens each – which flooded the model server and blocked other products' calls for hours.
So yes, technically, you can chain decision models into multi-step judgments, but it's not operationally worth it. Leave that to LLMs, or do the heavy lifting before the decision model sees the data like in the embedding search example above.
Takeaway:
Decision models judge what's in front of them in a single pass. Leave multi-step reasoning to LLMs.
4. Use them in place of overqualified LLMs
Decision models can take any job where an LLM is overkill, either because it's too slow or too expensive.
One example is our
smarter chart picker
for SQL queries. PostHog used to pick a visualization using deterministic rules like:
A date column, a number column and multiple rows → Line chart
Two or more text columns plus a number → Heatmap
Any number column → Bar chart
Now, a decision model looks at both the SQL itself if your org opts in, and the first three rows of the results to suggest a better chart.
The example below is based on a simple query about pageviews by browser. The original rules picked a basic aggregate line chart; with Jev, it chose a bar chart split by browser:
But keep LLMs for open-ended jobs
Anything more open-ended should still go to an LLM.
Still, out of curiosity, we tried Jev on ranking our internal PR review agent's findings with five noul questions that roughly asked if the change is worth a developer's attention. The results were inconclusive with an AUC of 0.52.
If Jev were an LLM, we’d solve this by sending more context, but Jev can’t handle large requests. Its long-context mode is also slower and less accurate.
2
Typical decision models just aren’t built for this kind of reasoning.
Hybrid decision models like
Jeeves
can help bridge this gap, though. Developed by our
in-house AI research team
, Jeeves is a decision model that reasons before deciding when it’s unsure.
It's now our default for any decision call at PostHog that doesn't name a model, and there are similar variations by other developers, like
Kev
.
Takeaway:
Use decision models as evaluators for inputs that are too simple for a language model, yet too fuzzy for a regex. Anything more complex is still too much to hand over to a decision model. For now, at least.
Words by Jina Yoon, who expects this article to be obsolete in two months.

– Karri Saarinen

The sleep framework: A new way for LLMs to retain knowledge in continual learning
– Ali Behrouz, Vahab Mirrokni

– Juraj Majerik

title: Mouse Party
content:
Let’s

Have

a

Mouse

Party!

The Aboard Newsletter

A free, secure way to watch videos with friends on the web—no server needed.

By
Paul Ford
·
11 Nov 2026

Get your squeak on.

It’s a
holiday in the U.S.
and many folks are home today, so rather than talking about enterprise software, I thought I’d give you one more app.
Meet Mouse Party!
It lets you watch videos with friends via the web, but it doesn’t need a web server.

Mouse Party is very simple. It’s an open-sourced MacOS App.
You download and install it
and double-click the icon, which is a mouse in a party hat. When you open it, it looks like this:

It used to have about fifty buttons but my business partner Rich yelled, “Two buttons! Two!” And you know what? He was right.

Open the app.

Drag a video onto it. Then it’ll make you a link you can copy and share.

Hit play. Everyone with the link can watch the video and chat.
When you quit the app, the server is gone, and the chat is gone.

A normal conversation between friends.

You can add all kinds of videos as well as MP3s, FLACs, Word docs, PDFs, ePubs, and more kinds of files. It also has fun little mini apps that let you share documents and work together. You can do graffiti, or play word games.

Why Mouse Party?

Why did I build this? The male loneliness epidemic. A little over a year ago, a friend of mine in San Francisco told me about an open-source app called
Owncast
. Owncast lets you set up a web server for video streaming. People can visit and watch the video on the website and talk via the chat interface. According to my pal, it was really helping everyone stay connected.

I set it up, too, and played some movies, but my friends all complained about the interface. I thought it was great, but they whined about how the chat works, the mobile app, and the video player. They wanted me to move it to Discord, then figure out a way to show video inside of WhatsApp.

Ultimately I realized the problem: My friends are not chill San Francisco people with open-source vibes. My friends are annoying East Coast product manager tech scrooges. So I looked around for replacements. There are other tools like
Watch Party
, but everything was hard to tweak to the exacting requirements of my very special peers.

Go ahead and scribble.

So I built my own. At first, it was janky and required me to be online and monitor a bunch of command-line scripts; it broke all the time and everyone kept complaining. But over time, I fixed a lot of bugs, until they started complaining about other things that were not my software. I know it sounds terrible, but I do love them.

The app had one problem, though: In order to watch a movie, you had to stream the video to a web server. Setting up web servers is hard and costs money. I felt dumb. I’d built another piece of software that was only for nerds—one that requires you to be a systems administrator if you want to set it up. So we watched movies with it, but I figured that was that.

Then I learned about the Cloudflare
“quick tunnel” tool
and…that solved it. You can open a secure, random link right into your desktop, with no login, for free, and when you break the connection (quit the app, restart your computer, whatever) that link vanishes forever. It’s something Cloudflare created to make it easier for nerds to do a particular class of programming-and-testing nerd activities, but there’s no real reason it couldn’t work for everyone. The links are weird-looking to normies, but they’re also free and disposable.

I remade Mouse Party from a command-line app into a desktop application for Mac that sets up a web server from your desktop or laptop and lets people “tunnel” to it through Cloudflare. Now you can serve web video without setting up a web server. It uses the same technology as video calls, just for a different purpose. You can probably stream to four or five people using your home internet, or ten or more if you have a faster connection (After a certain number, set in preferences, it tells people they can’t get in.)

Throw a Great Mouse Party

Want to host your own Mouse Party? A few tips:

Download a few short things to show while people gather. Old commercials, music videos, and so forth.
Archive.org
has all of it.

Drop the link in the chat with no explanation. Surprise people and let them complain about new things for a while. They will ask why you can’t show Netflix videos. They will want you to make it like YouTube. They will post profanity. Let them do it. Before long, you’ll be hosting every week, because if you give humans a bright glowing thing to gather around, they can’t help themselves. We’ve been doing it for hundreds of thousands of years.

Optimize for complaining. Terrible movies work better than good ones. Retro horror films are good, too. Depressing documentaries. Familiar stuff. Things that get people rambling are better for this kind of set-up than wonderful art. Even really boring stuff is good conversation fodder. Remember, people will literally stare at a fire for an hour. We need less stimulation, not more.

Watching old TV shows, like
MTV’s
120 Minutes
, is another good way to get everyone rambling.

You don’t have to download things. Just find video on
Archive.org
and paste the URL in using the “Add URL” menu items. I made it smart about
Archive.org
URLs.

Ultimately, Mouse Party has been good for the group chats. It gives us something to do. It’s a way to introduce people from one chat to another. In my case, it’s a lot of dads who appreciate being able to talk world-historical amounts of trash after they’ve begged their teens to go to sleep. People ask me to kick off Mouse Parties pretty often, and I’m trying to convince them they can host, too.

I did want to prove to myself that you can make, share, and create things on the web without setting up a web server. I don’t think this will replace Hulu or WhatsApp or Google Docs. It’s not a perfect approach for the software of the future, because you don’t want people running random web servers off their desktops for anyone. But there’s a lot of prior art around how to lock down web serving and keep hosted things running in sandboxes, away from any of your other files, and that’s applied here, too.

That said, this really is designed for use with friends. You are inviting people to your digital house to hang. For example, there are no moderation tools at all for the chat. If someone sucks, you can’t kick them out; you have to quit the app and end the party. You need to upgrade your friends, not your apps.

Concluding Thoughts

I find the future of software absolutely fascinating because no one has any idea what’s coming next—and anyone who tells you they do is absolutely high on their own token supply. At work, we build a lot of large, durable platforms with hundreds or many thousands of users. At home, I like to keep things a little more ephemeral. In both cases, everything is evolving at ridiculous speeds. But as ever, users will decide what they like, in their own time.

That’s it. It’s all
open source
, and I hope you enjoy it and do with it what you will. Unfortunately, it’s a couple hundred megabytes—that’s because it uses a lot of open-source code for handling all the different video file types. I learned a lot making it. I’d enjoy hearing your thoughts on how your own Mouse Party goes. Feel free to invite me to one, or send me a screenshot in strictest confidence!

title: How the Claude Code team thinks about verification
content:
Engineering
How the Claude Code team thinks about verification
How end-to-end, property and differential tests let coding agents verify their work with evidence, and what the Claude Code team does to keep its verifiers honest.
AUTHOR
Addy Osmani
CATEGORY
Engineering
PUBLISHED
Nov 16, 2026
READING TIME
10
min
On the Claude Code team, the vast majority of our code (~90%) is written and
reviewed by Claude
. At this scale, how we equip our agents to verify their work with evidence becomes extremely important.

Verification loops are the building block that lets you delegate more work to Claude. Without them, you can really only run one or two Claudes at a time, because you have to check everything yourself. With them, you can run dozens or hundreds in parallel.

That’s because giving agents a
way to verify their output
is an effective way to improve quality. In internal testing around structured file generation, having a separate grader check Claude’s work against a rubric
improved task success by up to 10 points
over a standard prompting loop, with the largest gains on the hardest problems.

What was once expensive to verify (tests, benchmarks, specs, real end-to-end runs) is now cheap to request from an agent. Like code, agents can quickly generate tests, benchmarks, and specs. And once generated, these tests and benchmarks run as software so they can be run frequently without using many additional tokens.

You can also close the verification loop by using the results to improve the agent’s performance on that task. For example, if an agent repeatedly fails a test that checks logs for user data, you can create a hook or a more explicit rule in your CLAUDE.md to avoid future issues. This (mostly) stops issues from happening again.

So if verification is critical to producing quality code at a high velocity, what types of tests should you use and how should you apply them across your pipeline? This article answers those questions and also shares the process used by the Claude Code team.

NOT ALL TESTS ARE CREATED EQUAL: 3 TESTS WORTH INVESTING IN

No matter which test type you choose, there are a few failure modes to avoid.

If your tests are flaky you’ll train the agent to run them again rather than fixing the failing code. If your tests are slow, the agent will do fewer tests across batches which can make pinpointing issues difficult. Heavier tests are best deployed before you’ve committed the changes.

Now, here are the three types of tests I think are most worth investing in.

E2E tests

If you have to focus on one test type, pick end-to-end. These tests describe real user flows like adding an item to a cart, checking out, and moving to a confirmation page.

The reason E2E tests are so effective is that they are difficult to fool–either the whole feature works or it doesn't. They also have definitive done criteria and can concretely tell you what’s broken.

FIG A
A unit test may show “Error: Timeout after 30 seconds,” but an end-to-end test can show a screenshot with a description of what’s broken.

While unit tests are faster and less flaky, it’s possible to pass them and still break the feature. This is because both the agent and the test don’t understand the full task.

With E2E tests, it is effective to give your agent hands and eyes on the real running system. You can use a skill to boot, drive, and inspect the app with tools like
CDP
, simulators, or API harnesses.

The feature map can serve as a guide and grading rubric for agents as they typically list features from the user’s point of view with descriptions of paths, keyboard shortcuts, selectors, and expected results.

Property tests: constraints that can’t break

A lot of tests are based on what you thought might go wrong. Property tests look at the edge cases that people tend to miss, which is where agents often fail.

You start by writing a statement you think can’t fail and then use a test library (
fast-check
for JS/TS,
Hypothesis
for Python,
proptest
for Rust, etc.) to generate thousands of inputs that try to prove otherwise.

There are many properties in virtually every software project like:

Round-trip encoding
: “if you encode X then decode it back, you get X.” This works for parsing and serialization as well.

Invariants
: Things that must always be true, like “account balance can never become negative.”

Idempotency
: Doing an action (migration, normalization, retry) twice has the same effect as doing it once.

Equivalence
: Optimized code produces the same result as naive but correct code.

Property libraries are a great way to keep agents honest by using edge cases that aren’t created with the same bias as the agent that created the original code. They are also particularly helpful for rewrites when the spec has drifted from production behavior and is no longer a reliable source for verification.

Differential tests: the old system is the oracle

Differential tests are particularly effective for
large-scale migration
use cases where functionality is expected to remain the same. For these tests, you run both the old system and the new system with the same inputs and see if you get different results. If you do, there is a bug or breaking change that needs to be fixed.

The key for differential tests is to use randomly generated inputs or a sample of production traffic. You’ll also want to normalize irrelevant factors like whitespace and keep a list of approved changes for situations where the new environment should differ from the old.

HOW THE CLAUDE CODE TEAM THINKS ABOUT VERIFICATION

We have previously written about
how code review works at Anthropic
, but this article aims to go deeper on how we verify our work.

Verification means running the change

Running the app end to end matters more than tests. You wouldn't ship an iOS change without trying it in a simulator, and the same goes for Claude.

Claude can test the whole app the way a human or QA engineer would. Ask it to use the Claude Chrome extension for web changes, an iOS or Android MCP for mobile, computer use for desktop, or to run the service locally for backend work.

To codify how to start the simulator or run your app, create a skill called verify. Put it in a .claude/skills/ folder in your repo, as close to the relevant code as you can, and add as many as you need. Claude knows to use the verify skill before committing changes.

Then invest in making your verify skill fast and reliable. Ask Claude to iterate on it and stress test it. It's your smoke test harness, so you want it rock solid.

When you give Claude a way to smoke test its changes end to end, you get much better results. You'll see it iterate and catch real mistakes faster, the way a human would. This is how we test nearly all changes at Anthropic.

Failing tests require human attention

Nobody can read every change, so we use failures as one way to decide what needs a person. Claude runs the checks and tries to fix anything that fails. If a check is still failing after three rounds, Claude stops and brings in a human.

Code owners write their own checks

The people who own the code write the checks for it, and refine them until they flag what the owner would flag. When a check pulls in a reviewer, it should say why, so they don't have to work it out from the diff.

Reliability checks trigger on the diff

We maintain a reliability checklist with 39 items, each with a trigger that can be read from a diff, a check, and the incidents or PRs behind it. One is “--resume loads old transcripts.” When session storage or message types change, we ask whether a new field loads safely, since older transcripts won’t have it.

Claude reads the diff and checks only the items whose trigger matches–usually 3 to 10–so nobody has to memorize past outages.

One reviewer, multiple rounds

We don't try to improve reviews by stacking on more reviewers. Adding a second, more expensive, reviewer on top of the primary one is often a worse approach than tuning the primary. Instead, we have a
REVIEW.md
that says what the reviewer should pay attention to for this code.

We also think review and verification rounds should build on each other. We point each pass at context from earlier rounds and past failures rather than re-checking everything from scratch. It’s cheaper and finds more.

Changes can't modify their own checks

If a change can modify the check that judges it, the check is broken. Code Review reads the REVIEW.md file from the base or default branch,
never from the pull request's changes
. The Claude Code team ensures the rules that gate changes are on a branch that the change can't modify.

The Claude Code team also reserves reviews for commits. If someone's pushing while the review is happening, then the review result is no longer useful. A passing review on an out-of-date commit means nothing.

The team also runs cheap checks first. If an agent pushes before testing locally, it has spent shared review and CI time when it could have caught the bug itself. On our team, Claude runs the tests, build, and linter before opening a pull request. You can enforce this with a
hook
that runs the tests when Claude finishes, or a
/goal
of a passing test suite.

Start a new gate in observe mode

In our own repos, we stamp each commit with how it was verified. The stamp even includes "none" so we can query for commits that weren't verified.

We've also created a commit gate that can block a commit if the session did not contain /code-review or /verify. We've set it up with off, observe, and enforce modes.

Observe mode will log what would have been blocked, so that we can review any false positives and ensure no one is impacted.

Enforce mode will block the commit. Any commit can carry an explanation in its message as to why it didn't get verified. If commits have been blocked twice in the session, the next one will be allowed through so Claude doesn't get stuck – Claude Code isn't perfect.

Test your checks on what actually matters

The Claude Code team also regularly reviews the reviewers. We track how many merged changes were reverted, how many changes a maintainer rejected before merging, and a size-matched subset of changes that have stayed clean.

This can also be done with a formal evaluation. In our
code review post
, we described how the Code Review team has set up an evaluation based on previous incidents and reverts. They recreate the repo to the state at the time of review for each example, and provide a one-sentence answer key to what the bug was. Only findings that correctly describe the bug in question get points. They use merged and stable changes as a control to prevent over-flagging. Their tuning set is split out from the fixed test set they use to evaluate their system.

They also evaluated the recall rate for raw findings, post-verification, and final review separately. This lets them see if the system is losing bugs it had already found. Any evaluation that treats all these as one end-to-end score won't capture this nuance.

In addition to validity, the other dimension we care about is how important it is to make the change. A good reviewer will catch most things that are technically correct, but people care about whether a given bug is a must-fix, a should-fix, or a nit.

Code Review has this exact idea, and it will tag things as
Important, Nit or Pre-existing
. The "pre-existing" tag means that the reviewer shouldn't hold the author responsible for something that was already a bug.

Finally, the Claude Code team tunes recall up to the point where the next improvement would be overfitting to the eval rather than actually catching bugs.

Turn misses into rules

In the Claude Code repo, we have two methods of turning missed cases into rules. The first is extracting patterns in human code review comments and PR reverts to identify common issues. These must occur in at least two PRs and be identifiable from a diff to be considered a potential rule. Three agents will try to disprove them, and they will be reviewed and approved by a human in a PR.

The second method is replaying three bug finders against a PR that is associated with a known incident. If at least two find the bug, it's a detectable bug. If the bug is missed on a small diff, this is a gap that is worth turning into a rule in REVIEW.md.

Flaky tests get the same treatment. Claude can't skip them, add sleeps or retry until they pass. If it can't find the root cause, it deletes the test and writes down why.

Rules need cleaning up too. Test suites, verification steps and .md files only grow if you let them, so we tidy them up on a routine.

GOOD TESTS, GOOD RESULTS

We’ve found that giving your agent a way to verify its work with a strong feedback loop makes all the difference. Treat your verification layer like you would any other system. Keep it out of reach of the changes they judge, grade them against the bugs that mattered to you, and write down lessons when they miss something so that it doesn’t happen more than once, and prune those lessons so they stay worth running.

Do that and your job shifts from reading every diff to defining what “done” looks like and reviewing the evidence, which is what lets you run many Claudes at once.

title: Unauthenticated remote code execution in Nginx
content:
Executive Summary
Wiz Research, Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint independently uncovered two critical remote code execution vulnerabilities in NGINX, software used to receive and route traffic to production applications and APIs.
NGINX is a common default for the front door of modern web architectures, where it handles HTTPS and routes incoming traffic to the right application or API. As the
world's most widely used open-source web server
, it powers
more than 225 million websites
.
Successful exploitation could let attackers take control of affected NGINX servers, steal sensitive data, tamper with websites, or disrupt services.
The vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, are both rated Critical, with a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2. The flaws are in NGINX itself. Websites and APIs can be exposed even when their own application code is secure.
Both vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 to be enabled on the affected NGINX server.
Additional conditions are described below. CVE-2026-123007 affects versions dating back to NGINX 1.9.5 in 2015.
We reported our findings to F5, the company behind NGINX, and collaborated with its security team on remediation and coordinated disclosure. Organizations should identify affected deployments and apply the security updates when released.
We recommend updating affected NGINX deployments to the latest release which includes multiple security fixes.
Responsible disclosure timeline
October 21, 2026:
Wiz reports the HTTP/2 use-after-free vulnerability, later assigned CVE-2026-123633, to F5, including confirmed remote code execution with an ASLR bypass and a proposed fix. F5 confirms that another research team had previously reported the same vulnerability.
November 10, 2026:
F5 supplies a patch for CVE-2026-123633 for review.
November 16, 2026
: Wiz reports the second HTTP/2 vulnerability, later assigned CVE-2026-123007, to F5.
November 17, 2026
: F5 confirms that the second report matches CVE-2026-123007 and is included in the planned November 18 security release.
November 18, 2026:
F5 security release and coordinated public disclosure.
Overview
Wiz Research, Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint independently uncovered  CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, two critical unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerabilities in NGINX, and reported them to F5, the company behind NGINX. Successful exploitation can compromise the server running NGINX, allowing attackers to execute code, steal sensitive data, tamper with websites, or disrupt services.
NGINX often handles traffic for several applications, so a single affected deployment can put multiple services at risk. The flaws are in NGINX itself and can affect websites even when their own application code is secure.
Both vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 to be enabled on the affected NGINX server.
Our testing of CVE-2026-123007 demonstrated code execution on NGINX serving ordinary static files, without a backend application or third-party modules.
Wiz Research used
Wiz Atlas
, the harness powering Wiz’s
AI Code scanning solution
, to discover both vulnerabilities. Our researchers used Gemini 4 Carbon and ChatGPT 5.6 Sol to validate the impact of both vulnerabilities, confirming that each could allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code on the server. We reported our findings to F5 and worked with its security team on remediation and coordinated disclosure.
The integer underflow vulnerability dates back to NGINX 1.9.5 in 2015, meaning it had been hiding in the code for more than a decade. The use-after-free vulnerability had been there for nearly six years. Like the
PHP2Shell
vulnerabilities we reported last month and
Java4Shell
, disclosed yesterday by Calif, these are memory-safety flaws that have historically been extremely difficult to discover and exploit. Finding them often requires tracing subtle interactions between memory operations and multiple code paths. For years, that complexity itself created a practical barrier. AI is fundamentally dissolving that barrier. As AI models get better at following those interactions, both researchers and attackers can uncover longstanding flaws in software that powers the internet and modern applications. The fact that multiple independent research teams uncovered the same vulnerabilities in both PHP and NGINX, after they had remained in the code for years, makes this shift particularly striking. And as AI capabilities advance, each new generation of models may uncover even more complex vulnerabilities that were previously beyond practical reach. Complexity can no longer be relied upon as a barrier to discovery or exploitation. This changes not only which vulnerabilities can be found, but how quickly longstanding risks can become real threats.
Over time, finding and fixing these flaws can harden the software we all depend on. In the near term, faster discovery and a shorter window between disclosure and exploitation add to an already demanding workload for security teams. Turning a published fix into protection in production still takes substantial manual work, from validating patches to coordinating rollouts with service owners. We recommend focusing on how quickly you can reduce exposure in production. Identify deployments running the affected version and configuration, prioritize those an attacker can reach, and apply mitigations while patches are tested and rolled out.
In this post, we explain the vulnerabilities and their impact, and provide mitigation and detection guidance. Organizations should identify affected deployments and apply the security updates as soon as they are available. If upgrading is not immediately possible, temporarily disable HTTP/2.
What is NGINX?
NGINX is the
world's most widely used open-source web server
, powering
more than 225 million websites
. It is commonly used as a
reverse proxy
in front of websites and APIs. In this role, NGINX accepts incoming requests, forwards them to the appropriate application server based on its configuration, and returns the response to the user.
NGINX can also serve web content directly and act as a
load balancer
, distributing traffic across multiple servers. A single NGINX deployment can serve several applications, making it a shared entry point for the websites and APIs behind it.
The Vulnerabilities
Both vulnerabilities are memory-safety issues in how NGINX handles HTTP/2 traffic. In CVE-2026-123633, a connection's memory is freed while a request still needs it, creating a use-after-free. In CVE-2026-123007, incorrect flow-control accounting leads to an invalid memory copy. Each can lead to unauthenticated remote code execution on the NGINX server.
Tracking ID
The bug
What an attacker can achieve
CVE-2026-123633
HTTP/2 connection use-after-free
Execute arbitrary code on the NGINX server without authentication.
CVE-2026-123007
HTTP/2 send_window integer underflow
Execute arbitrary code on the NGINX server without authentication.
Both vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 to be enabled, but their additional requirements differ. CVE-2026-123633 affects reverse-proxy processing when available connection slots run low. CVE-2026-123007 can also affect NGINX serving content directly, as demonstrated in our testing over HTTPS on 64-bit systems. Typical memory safety mitigations such as ASLR do not protect against these issues, as attackers can use either vulnerabilities for memory read access prior to code execution.
Impact
On affected NGINX versions with HTTP/2 enabled, these vulnerabilities can allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code on the server.
The flaws are in NGINX itself. Exploitation does not depend on a bug in the website or API behind it, so applications with secure code can still be exposed. For CVE-2026-123007, we demonstrated remote code execution on a server serving ordinary static files, without a backend application or third-party module.
An attacker could use this access to run commands, steal sensitive data, tamper with websites, or disrupt services. Because one NGINX deployment can serve several applications, the impact could extend across multiple websites and APIs.
Illustrative deployment: an attacker exploits NGINX to run code on the server, putting the applications and data it serves at risk.
Coordinated disclosure
We reported both vulnerabilities to F5 and collaborated with its security team on remediation and coordinated disclosure. We also shared proposed fixes. Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint also independently discovered and reported these issues to F5. We thank the F5 and NGINX teams for their work on the fixes.
Vulnerabilities Addressed in the Release
F5's security release addresses several other vulnerabilities in NGINX. Below is a summary of these additional CVEs, as well as the two critical HTTP/2 remote code execution flaws detailed in this post (captured in the first two rows of the table):

Mitigation and detection
Identify affected NGINX deployments with HTTP/2 enabled and upgrade to a release that fixes both vulnerabilities as soon as it is available.
Product
CVE and first affected version or branch
Fixed releases
NGINX OSS
CVE-2026-123633: 1.19.7
1.30.7 stable; 1.31.9 mainline
NGINX Plus
CVE-2026-123633: R33; 37.0.0
37.0.7.1; 37.2.0.1

CVE-2026-123007: 1.9.5
1.30.7 stable; 1.31.9 mainline
NGINX Plus
CVE-2026-123007: R33; 37.0.0
37.0.8.1; 37.3.0.1
If you cannot upgrade immediately, temporarily disable HTTP/2 on affected NGINX instances:
Set
http2 off;
in affected server blocks on NGINX 1.25.1 or later, and remove the
http2 parameter from any listen directives
.
Test application compatibility,
reload NGINX
, and confirm the old workers have exited.
Re-enable HTTP/2 after upgrading.
Investigate unexpected NGINX worker crashes or commands launched by NGINX; these are general warning signs, not confirmed indicators of these vulnerabilities.
Technical deep dive
CVE-2026-123633: An active connection marked as reusable
NGINX keeps a list of connections that it can close when it needs room for new ones. An HTTP/2 connection can join this list when it has no active requests, but must leave it when a request starts.
We start by sending only part of a
HEADERS
frame, which carries an HTTP/2 request's headers. With no active request streams,

ngx_http_v2_handle_connection()
marks the connection as reusable while waiting for the rest:
ngx_reusable_connection(c, 1);
if (h2c->state.incomplete) {
return;
}
When we send the rest of the frame,

ngx_http_v2_create_stream()
creates a request stream and increments
h2c->processing
. However, it does not remove the connection from the reusable list. We now have a request being processed on a connection that NGINX still considers safe to close.
Triggering the use-after-free
Next, we need NGINX to close this connection while the request is still running. Forwarding the request to an application server can trigger this.
Opening an upstream connection calls
ngx_get_connection()
.
When free connection slots run low,
ngx_drain_connections()

selects reusable connections to close. Our HTTP/2 connection is still on that list, so NGINX can select it while processing its own request.
Before closing it, NGINX tries to send a
GOAWAY
frame to notify the client. Even creating this frame can fail, for example, if NGINX has reached its
internal frame limit
for the connection and has no frame available for reuse. In that case, the
error path
closes the connection and frees the memory associated with it. Processing then resumes in the original request, which still uses that memory. We have reached the use-after-free.
From use-after-free to remote code execution
The freed memory can now be reused for other data. The request-processing code still follows its old pointers, treating the new contents as the original request or connection.
This use-after-free can lead to unauthenticated remote code execution on the NGINX server.
CVE-2026-123007: HTTP/2 send_window integer underflow
Returning credit for unsent data
HTTP/2 allows several requests, called streams, to share one connection. Flow control limits how much response data NGINX can send before the client is ready to receive more. NGINX tracks the connection's remaining allowance in a counter called
h2c->send_window
.
When NGINX queues response data, it subtracts that data's size from the counter before sending it. If a stream is canceled while its data is still queued,
ngx_http_v2_filter_cleanup()
removes the unsent data and returns the unused allowance:
h2c->send_window += window;
This refund does not check HTTP/2's maximum allowed window. If the client has already increased the allowance while data was waiting to be sent, the refund can push the counter above that maximum. NGINX is now tracking a value the rest of its HTTP/2 code assumes cannot occur.
A bounds check that no longer works
The next problem is in
ngx_http_v2_state_window_update()
, which checks whether an increase would exceed the limit:
if (window > NGX_HTTP_V2_MAX_WINDOW - h2c->send_window)
The check subtracts the current allowance from the maximum to calculate how much room remains. But the refund has already pushed the allowance past that maximum. Because the calculation uses an unsigned integer, which cannot represent a negative number, the subtraction wraps around and underflows to a very large positive value. The check now treats an invalid counter as though it has plenty of room left and allows further increases.
From an invalid length to remote code execution
The invalid counter eventually reaches
ngx_http_v2_send_chain()
, where it is converted to the signed integer type
off_t
to calculate how much data to send. A sufficiently large value becomes negative. That negative length then reaches the code that describes a portion of a response buffer, leaving its end pointer before its start pointer.
When the TLS send path in
ngx_ssl_send_chain()
processes this malformed buffer, further signed and unsigned conversions turn the invalid length into an out-of-bounds memory copy. An attacker can use this to disclose memory, corrupt the heap, and lead to unauthenticated remote code execution on the NGINX server.
We confirmed remote code execution with an ASLR bypass on official NGINX 1.31.7 and 1.31.8 builds. The tested path used HTTP/2 over TLS on 64-bit systems serving response data from memory. Ordinary static files can reach this path through standard TLS processing, without a backend application or third-party module.
Exploitation
To confirm these vulnerabilities, Wiz Research built proof-of-concept exploits and managed to run them in multiple lab settings against servers running common NGINX configurations we’ve seen in customer environments. In the interest of customer protection, we will not be releasing these exploits at this time.
Like other memory-safety issues, such vulnerabilities are difficult to exploit remotely and require the attacker to disclose memory addresses, groom and shape the heap correctly, and handle different NGINX versions, builds, and configurations. In reality, attackers may not need to target every single configuration, and we have seen in
PHP2Shell
that widespread attacks initially start against packaged products where many customers use the exact same build and configuration. Motivated attackers may tailor exploits for specific targets.
Any exploit assumes the attacker is able to communicate directly with the affected NGINX server. CDNs and WAFs that terminate HTTP/2 may mitigate parts of the exploit by not reflecting the exact payload back to the underlying NGINX server. This depends on implementation.
Specifically, CVE-2026-123007 requires the attacker to send a large number of WINDOW_UPDATE records to increase it to an arbitrary value. Detection rules covering long standing HTTP/2 connections sending large amounts of data may hint at an attack associated with this vulnerability. CVE-2026-123633 has different exploitation constraints and is more likely to be exploited when NGINX is configured in proxy configuration.
How Can Wiz Help?
Wiz customers can use the pre-built query and advisory in the
Wiz Threat Center
to search for vulnerable instances in their environment.
Conclusion
With NGINX handling traffic for critical websites and applications, the impact of flaws in its core extends far beyond a single service. This research is another example of AI uncovering critical vulnerabilities in widely deployed infrastructure. The flaws were already there; AI helped us find them.
As we saw with
PHP2Shell
, AI is changing the economics of vulnerability research. The same capabilities that help defenders uncover flaws can also help attackers investigate them. Software that has been used and reviewed for years still needs to be examined as these tools improve.
The opportunity is to make this work routine: finding vulnerabilities in the software organizations depend on and working with maintainers to fix them. Our collaboration with F5 brings that approach to NGINX, helping protect the applications and services behind it.
Stay in touch
Hi there! We are
Nir Ohfeld
and
Tomer Schwartz
from the Wiz Research Team (
@wiz_io
). We are a group of veteran white-hat hackers with a single goal: to make the cloud a safer place for everyone. We focus on finding new attack vectors in cloud software and uncovering isolation issues in the systems organizations depend on. We would love to hear from you on X or at
research@wiz.io
.
