Transcript

Below is a
polished and edited transcript
.

Ben Lorica.
All right. Today we have an old friend, Pete Warden of Useful Sensors, and their main website is actually at moonshine.ai. If you go to the website, you’ll see that they’re very much about voice on-device, and we will definitely talk to Pete about all things speech and all things edge computing. But I do want to take advantage of Pete being one of the OG deep learning engineers to get his sense of what’s going on these days. And with that, Pete, welcome back to the podcast.

Pete Warden.
Thanks for having me, Ben.

Ben Lorica.
All right. So I would say, Pete, I don’t know if this is a fair characterization, but one of the main thrusts of your work is the whole idea that local AI does not have to be compromised. In fact, it’s something that people should take more seriously. As I mentioned, we’ll definitely talk about your work on speech models on-device. But broadly speaking, Pete, for our audience that doesn’t really follow local models, where are we for someone who wants to run a model on a laptop, not a phone, just a laptop? What’s the state of ease of use? I guess one of the obstacles is that it’s always easier to use a cloud API, right? So where are we in terms of the tooling around local AI?

Pete Warden.
Yeah. So at the moment, it’s like many open-source projects. Every year is going to be the year of the Linux desktop. I think there’s always going to be a bit of a lag in usability for the average user with this stuff, but I think there’s an even bigger lag in marketing because it’s very hard to make money off local models.

That means the big companies like Anthropic and OpenAI, and even the big tech companies generally, aren’t going to push that. If you give them a choice between a SaaS service that you can actually make money on and this other thing where you’re not even going to know that people are using it because they’re not contacting your service, every company is going to go for the one that has an easy subscription revenue model.

That means you have a massive amount of marketing around all of these tools that are basically a little text box on a website. And so it means that most people have never heard of these local models.

Now, if you use something like Ollama, which is probably the most well-known, I think people will be pleasantly surprised by how straightforward it is to use and by the quality of the models. I saw some news recently that Anthropic is actually a bit concerned because people are turning to more specialized models versus always going for the most sprawling, expensive model that’s available.

Local models are actually doing very well in the benchmarks. They continue to be only a few months behind the capabilities of the big commercial Anthropic and OpenAI models. But I also believe that local models have gotten to the point where they can do the things that people want to use them for.

What I’m really hoping is that it’s one of those situations, for those of us old enough to remember the dot-com boom, when people were paying thousands of dollars for SPARC servers or using Microsoft IIS and paying massive amounts of money because web servers were seen as such an arcane thing. Then, of course, Apache, Nginx, and all of these alternatives, once people actually had time to look around and the alternatives had a little bit of time to improve, just wiped the floor with the commercial alternatives.

I don’t know if we’re going to quite get there, but that’s the pattern I’m seeing.

Ben Lorica.
Yeah, my sense is that open models, whatever your definition of open is, mainly open weights, I guess, will ultimately prevail. It just seems like that makes a lot more sense to me.

As you mentioned, in the early days of Linux versus Solaris, or even Postgres and MySQL versus Oracle, it was far from clear that these open-source projects would ever get to the point of us having to take them seriously. But ultimately, I think they’re such important parts of the stack that the open alternatives are what people will opt for.

Speaking of which, Pete, you mentioned Ollama, right? And obviously, there are other alternatives. Let’s say, for the sake of argument, that they are in fact easy to install and use. As far as the models are concerned, you have things like Gemma, I suppose, and other small models, right? What kind of hardware does someone need to have in order to run these models so that they don’t have to wait 20 minutes for each prompt?

Pete Warden.
So a lot of it comes down to your model choice.

Ben Lorica.
Yeah.

Pete Warden.
You can get very capable models that are like 9 billion parameters these days. Especially if you look around at the Qwen family of models, they tend to be doing very well, though there are a bunch of other alternatives.

Ben Lorica.
But translate that, Pete. To someone with a normal laptop, is 9 billion big or small?

Pete Warden.
So the key thing is whether you can fit that into your graphics card’s memory. With weight quantization, 9 billion, if it was eight bits, is like nine gigabytes. A lot of decent midrange laptops that are shipping now have more than that.

But using Q4, and there are all sorts of schemes, you can actually get that down into a four-gigabyte graphics card, and that’s widely available. There are a lot of even older laptops that have that amount of GPU memory, VRAM, in them.

So really, the hardware barriers are a lot lower than people think. And the other piece of good news is that all of the hardware manufacturers are looking at this. They’re slightly hobbled by the DRAM craziness, the price increases. But if you look at the new M5 Studio from Apple, they have a configuration that’s 256 gigabytes of system memory.

Apple does a great job of actually making that available to the accelerators that they build into all of their Macs now, too. And with that, you’re looking at something like a model with hundreds of billions of parameters that you can actually run at a decent speed.

Once you get up into those numbers, you’re really looking at something where it can be hard to tell if you’re using Claude or if you’re using an open-weights model at that point. They have different characteristics, but one isn’t clearly worse than the other.

Ben Lorica.
So as I mentioned, we’ll definitely dive deep into voice and speech in a second here. But sticking with this notion of local models, obviously privacy and IP security are arguments for it.

Do you think, if we look ahead, let’s say 12 to 24 months, these local models are going to be capable enough that people doing knowledge work in an enterprise might even consider them here and there?

For example, someone who travels a lot is on an airplane, not connected to the internet, and needs to keep writing a document or generating images or even coding, vibe coding, on a laptop. Do you think we’ll get to the point where, with these local models, you essentially feel like you’re not compromising when you’re doing your knowledge work?

Pete Warden.
I think you can actually get to that point right now, and I know that’s a fairly bold statement.

Ben Lorica.
But when you say you, does that mean Pete Warden, who’s going to compile all of these? We want normal people. We want civilians, Pete.

Pete Warden.
I think the biggest barriers are usability. If you look at the benchmarks, it really is no longer a question of model quality.

Ben Lorica.
Model quality.

Pete Warden.
Yeah, a question of model quality. There are still things around the edges where you might prefer some of the commercial online models, but it’s not clear-cut.

And people are finding that some of the models actually work better, especially if you’re dealing with things like, I don’t want to call it censorship because I feel like that’s a loaded term, but a lot of commercial models have restrictions. They may be intended to prevent a bad use case, but pretty often they can also trip you up even if you’re trying to do something benign.

I know a lot of people who work in cybersecurity, for example, who are white hats, but they’re having to work with a lot of stuff where they’re asking questions about malicious actions. With the commercial models, you’re going to keep tripping over the restrictions and the guardrails that are built in with good intentions, but they can really impact your work.

Ben Lorica.
Right, right, right. By the way, Pete, the model is one component, but then there are the things surrounding the model, the so-called harness, or even context, memory, knowledge.

You can imagine someone, and this is actually something I’ve thought about. You know how people are starting to use these LLMs as therapists or friends, right?

Pete Warden.
Yes.

Ben Lorica.
Then if you’re going to do that, why not do that on a local model? Why do it on something connected to the cloud?

I guess one argument against it is that if you do it locally, you’re responsible for model upgrades and things like that, right? Whereas if you use one of these digital or AI therapist services, they take care of all your history and all of this.

Do you think it will become easier for consumers to use local models that are essentially something they trust 100% because they own it?

Pete Warden.
Yeah, I mean, these should be part of the OS. At this point, it’s really an operating system capability that should be available to apps, and I feel like Apple is moving in this direction.

Ben Lorica.
I see. Yeah, that makes a lot of sense.

Pete Warden.
Yeah, they’re getting the hardware capabilities.

The other thing I would say is that local doesn’t have to mean on your laptop. Especially as an enterprise user, you can host on-prem or even spin up a cloud instance that your enterprise has control over, run these models there, and have the same experience.

One thing I do want to emphasize is that people are finally having to pay something approaching the real cost of running these models through Anthropic and OpenAI, and hosting locally or hosting on-prem can cost a lot less, too.

Ben Lorica.
Although if you look at their consumer offerings, it’s still insanely cheap, right? So $20 a month. I mean, you probably blow through that in a day.

Pete Warden.
Yeah. Especially on the enterprise side, there are a bunch of options that don’t require high-end NVIDIA GPUs. You still need those for training, but for inference, for just running models, as an enterprise, you might already have the capacity lying around.

Ben Lorica.
So another important aspect of what you’ve been doing is getting people excited about voice and speech, right? This notion that speech could become a basic computing primitive. It doesn’t necessarily have to feel like some remote service.

I still remember you demonstrating to me this voice transcription service in a loud coffee shop near Precita Park.

Pete Warden.
Yes. Right. Yeah.

Ben Lorica.
This was several years ago. The accuracy of this thing was insane, and it was running not even on a laptop. I think it was just running on a Raspberry Pi.

Pete Warden.
That’s right. Yeah.

Ben Lorica.
And so talk to us about the state of voice as an actual interface, similar to a mouse or a keyboard. Where are we?

Pete Warden.
I think a lot of people are skeptical of voice because they’ve used Siri and Alexa, and it’s a very stilted way of communicating.

But the question I often ask people when I’m having a conversation about this stuff and I encounter that resistance is, when you’re sitting on the couch and you’re trying to decide what TV show to watch with your significant other next to you, do you text them or do you talk to them?

Ben Lorica.
Right.

Pete Warden.
Apart from a few Gen Z people, almost everybody says talk to them.

And so following on from that, it’s like, okay, well, it’s not that people don’t like voice interfaces. It’s that people don’t like bad voice interfaces.

So the problem becomes an engineering and user experience problem of how do we make voice interfaces that are pleasant and efficient to use?

I think once we do that, voice can really take its place as maybe even a more frequent input medium than the keyboard or touchscreen.

Ben Lorica.
Yeah, because I think the general impression people have is that voice and speech are much less deterministic than a keyboard or a touchscreen, right?

Although people now interact with their LLMs and misspell things right and left, and it doesn’t seem to matter.

But the impression people have is that there’ll be problems with accents, background noise, phrasing, and so on and so forth. So where are we in terms of all of these things?

Pete Warden.
We have solutions available to most of those problems, or at least big improvements. But because there’s no commercial incentive to pull them all together, it really hasn’t hit the mainstream yet.

I feel like we’re still dealing with interfaces that are from the previous generation. They haven’t taken on board the LLM era fully, and they’re still suffering from a lot of those problems you listed.

And that’s why I think open source can be a really strong lever.

Ben Lorica.
So as you’ve been trying to solve a lot of these interface problems, what are some of the lessons that you’ve learned? In fact, maybe some of them might even apply to people who are not working with voice but are just building AI applications.

I think one of the things you mentioned to me years ago is that with voice, you don’t have to wait until someone has finished talking to start doing work, right? So what are some of these interface lessons?

Pete Warden.
I think latency is a massive deal. That is something you just don’t get with cloud-based voice interfaces.

You’re usually waiting at least a couple of seconds, and that’s long enough for people to wonder if they were actually heard.

Ben Lorica.
Yeah, it’s like being on a Zoom call or phone call with someone, and then there’s a pause.

Pete Warden.
Yeah, and they’re just sitting there. It feels like the other person is just sitting there, ignoring you.

We know from general user experience research that you really want to be in that 200-millisecond or lower range to feel responsive.

I often ask people to imagine that you press a key on the keyboard and it takes two seconds for the key to show up in the window. That would be very awkward.

Ben Lorica.
By the way, this is something that people who work with LLMs also have to deal with, but on the output side, right? They want to make sure that the response is not too long. Otherwise, people get impatient, right?

Pete Warden.
Yeah, absolutely.

And I do want to mention another thing, which I think might be helpful to people thinking about local AI in general as well.

When you’re no longer paying per token, when you’re no longer having to pay to use a voice interface, the way you can use these things, the world of possibilities, becomes so much wider.

If you imagine that every app developer had to pay a few cents every time somebody touched an icon on the touchscreen in their app, you would design apps very differently, and a lot of apps wouldn’t exist because of that tax.

So once LLMs are built into the OS and just generally available with no cost, and the same with voice, that is not just an incremental change going from a cent to zero. That massively increases the number of viable things that you can use those for.

Ben Lorica.
So I imagine, Pete, this is one thing where you’ve done a lot of work, which is basically designing for failure, right? Because in voice, a lot of things can go wrong.

What are some of the lessons there in terms of designing your applications with failure in mind?

Pete Warden.
One of my favorite examples of designing for failure is the use of snippets in Google Search.

Google Search, from the beginning, knew they couldn’t always get the number one result right. There’s a reason you didn’t just hit “I’m Feeling Lucky.”

Ben Lorica.
Yeah, exactly. “I’m Feeling Lucky.”

Pete Warden.
What was genius about their approach was that they actually let you browse, just scan with your eyes.

They hoped to get the right result in the top three most of the time, and then you actually narrow it down by looking at the snippets, which tell you enough to click on the right one.

And the same thing for voice. The more you can actually read the body language of somebody, as we’re talking, you’re nodding a little bit to indicate what’s happening.

Ben Lorica.
Wait a minute, I’m only voice, so you can’t see me.

Pete Warden.
No, I can see.

Ben Lorica.
No, no, but in general, right? In general.

Pete Warden.
Well, that’s actually a whole other part of this that I haven’t mentioned.

I think having a little camera that’s completely local-only will be a massive part of this. But even without a camera, if you hear supportive noises, or if you start giving a response and somebody reacts, all of those things that we recognize as people, we respond to them and ask more questions versus assuming that we picked the right thing.

So really trying to understand all of those cues that we use as people. Some of them are verbal, some of them are body language and visual, but really having them all understood locally.

And ensuring that all of those recordings never get recorded, because you can verify that locally. You don’t know what happens to audio and video once you send it up to the cloud. It’s impossible to audit, basically.

With local stuff, you can audit. So I’m hoping that opens up the chance to use cameras without increasing the risk to users around privacy.

Ben Lorica.
So there are the people who work on speech models, and there’s been a lot of work in that area.

In fact, one thing that I think is vastly underappreciated is that people talk about deep learning having an ImageNet moment, but actually the first impressive deep learning models were in speech, before ImageNet, right?

So there are people working on speech models. They’ve even talked about end-to-end models, but obviously we have LLMs.

For the people who don’t follow this closely, Pete, what’s the relationship between the LLMs and the speech models, or do people not use LLMs? Do they just use speech models?

Pete Warden.
There’s been a massive debate, a split between what I think of as LLM maximalists, who expect everything to be an end-to-end model.

Ben Lorica.
“Machines of Loving Grace.”

Pete Warden.
Yes, exactly. And I see usually Anthropic, OpenAI, the big AI companies.

Ben Lorica.
Or, you know, the hype machine has to be fed, right?

Pete Warden.
Well, the hype machine has to be fed, and specifically, if the future is end-to-end models, then only the people with the most money can actually build and train them.

Now, I’m very strongly in what Berkeley calls the compound AI camp, where you actually build your applications out of multiple models, each of which has a specialized task.

So there, instead of having a model that takes speech in and outputs speech audio, you actually have a model that takes speech audio in, converts it to text, feeds that into an LLM, and the LLM then outputs text, which is converted into speech.

Now, every time you convert the audio into text, you actually lose a bunch of expressiveness. It’s like a bottleneck of information.

You can’t tell how somebody’s asking it, whether they’re asking it with a particular intonation and all of this other stuff.

Ben Lorica.
Can’t you, as you’re doing that translation, add metadata?

Pete Warden.
You kind of can, but the whole point of compound AI is that you can take models from different sources and plug them together. So you need some kind of common language, and at the moment, the only thing that all LLMs speak is text input and text output.

But the advantages are that you can actually train all of the models independently. With a speech end-to-end model, if you have a new accent, then if it’s a true end-to-end model, you have to do a whole bunch of training.

If you have a new input accent, if you have new output voices or new capabilities, if it’s a true end-to-end model, then you’re having to train the whole thing.

If it’s not actually, if end-to-end is just a marketing term, then you can train individual components, individual modules separately.

But then you’re always agreeing on some settled interface data, like some schema, some language. Even if it’s not text, even if it’s an embedding, you still have to have those fixed points.

So yeah, I see end-to-end as much more of a marketing term and something to justify the insane amounts of money that are flowing into these companies.

Ben Lorica.
Pete, what about, for our listeners who’ve heard of the term multimodal, right? Gemini is supposed to be multimodal.

And coincidentally, I just spoke to someone who works in the visual reasoning and understanding space, and they said actually Gemini is quite poor in terms of understanding video.

So what is the state of these multimodal models for your domain, speech?

Pete Warden.
They’re actually often pretty good. Qwen, 1.7 billion, I think it is, actually does a better job than Whisper, a significantly better job on some languages like Mandarin. And the same goes for Gemma.

The trouble is that, as general-purpose models, one of the failure cases with Gemma is that you upload audio of some speech, it transcribes it, but it then gets confused by the content of that speech and thinks you’re asking it a question, say, if there was a question in the transcribed speech.

So it’s one of these things where you’re trying to use a Swiss Army knife, and it’s a lot easier to use an actual wood saw versus the thing that can do everything and has a little saw attachment with it.

So that’s another drawback of the end-to-end models.

Ben Lorica.
By the way, obviously you’re the king on this topic. General-purpose models are dead on arrival on the edge, right?

Pete Warden.
I mean, right now, only…

Ben Lorica.
For the types of, I mean, some of the really small pieces of hardware that you work on.

Pete Warden.
One of the things I recently did was get a full voice interface where you could connect to Wi-Fi, set the password, and all of this sort of stuff, running on a Raspberry Pi Pico microcontroller that only has 500 kilobytes of RAM.

Now, there, you’re never going to have a general-purpose model that’s going to work well for you. But as always…

Ben Lorica.
And by the way, one of the things that you’ve also worked on, which is interesting, and which I don’t see a lot of people working on, is taking the browser more seriously, right?

So tell us, what’s the motivation behind that, and what has been the reception?

Pete Warden.
Yeah, so it’s tricky because I sometimes think of “We’ve done X, but in the browser” as Hacker News bait, because that always gets a lot of attention as a novelty. But it’s often hard to find practical uses for a lot of these things.

With the voice capabilities, with voice input and voice output, what I’ve seen is that it makes it part of the browser operating system, or feel like part of the browser operating system.

And once you’re able to transcribe fast and accurately in the browser, it’s a way for people to easily start experimenting with this stuff, and there aren’t any costs for this at the moment.

I’ve tried to put a few examples. If you go to Moonshine AI…

Ben Lorica.
But the whole notion of using the browser as a point of inference, right? You can imagine other models doing that too, not just yours, which focuses on speech.

You can imagine text, I mean, browser inference for text kinds of applications, right?

Pete Warden.
Well, if you’re running Chrome, you’ve already got a very capable model installed. You’ve got a 4-billion-parameter model.

I actually did a blog post last year showing how you could just go through Chrome settings and start using it as a chatbot, just typing in the window and getting responses.

I think that’s an example of the models becoming part of the operating system, because Chrome is essentially an operating system that sits on top of other operating systems.

You can already access that built-in LLM, I think now from any website. It used to be just extensions, but now I think any website can access that from JavaScript.

And again, we’re still figuring out what the best use cases are for that. But once it becomes free and you can rely on it being everywhere, I really feel like it’s an iPhone moment for a lot of these new LLM technologies.

Ben Lorica.
Or even what you mentioned earlier, which is for people on a laptop, it’ll be part of the OS somehow, right?

So looking ahead, Pete, and again, for our listeners, you can follow Pete’s work at Moonshot AI. Moonshine. Ah, Moonshine. Moonshine.ai. And a lot of the work is open source, and you can take advantage of that.

So looking ahead, Pete, 12 to 24 months. I hate to put you on the spot. Where are we in terms of, I guess, local or edge models, number one, and number two, just the state of open models in general?

Pete Warden.
Yeah, and I’m always terrible at predictions.

Ben Lorica.
But one thing Pete is super good at, for our listeners, is knowing what to work on. So that’s an indication. Just tell us what you’re working on.

Pete Warden.
Yes. So what I see from being deep in the technical side, most of what I end up working on is because I’ve been working on something, and it becomes blindingly obvious that the only reasonable technical solution is X, and so of course I want to work on X.

And what I see, and what I’ve seen for the last few years, is the gravitational pull of running this stuff locally or on-prem, or however you want to call it.

I often say, “AI wants to be local.”

If you think about something like Google Search, you need massive databases, you need armies of servers, you need all of this stuff. If you look at what Claude and ChatGPT are doing, you can run that entirely on one laptop with no internet connectivity.

So the shape of these models is perfect for running locally, unlike almost everything else we’ve seen over the last couple of decades, where the cloud has made more sense.

So what I expect is all of these pressures: cost for enterprises especially, worries about privacy, worries about capabilities going away, worries about changes.

If you built an application on top of a particular version of Claude, even if you’re using the same version in the dropdown, what’s actually happening behind the scenes can change from day to day.

So if you want stability, you actually need to host your own, at least in your own cloud infrastructure, if not locally on users’ laptops.

And I can keep going on and on.

Ben Lorica.
Yeah. And then the other thing, too, is I think a lot of enterprises are recognizing that the moat, or their moat, is really not the model. It’s that compounding loop around the model, right?

As you use the model more, you learn more and things like that. So why in the world would you send that to a commercial proprietary model?

Pete Warden.
And why not do fine-tuning on your own model?

Ben Lorica.
Yeah, I mean, with that data.

Pete Warden.
Yeah, exactly.

Ben Lorica.
And then, as you point out, you actually control your timing and roadmap as well, because you have the model and you know when it’s safe to replace that model with something else.

No one is going to replace that model underneath you, right?

Pete Warden.
Nobody’s going to start charging 10 times as much overnight.

Ben Lorica.
Right, right, right. And then also, even if they keep the cost the same, they may weaken the model for some reason, right?

Pete Warden.
Yep. Yeah, and it could even be pressure from outside.

Ben Lorica.
So by the way, one last question for you, Pete, because obviously you work in a space where you really care about hardware, right?

Right now, we’re in a world where Jensen Huang seems to own everything. So what’s your prediction about the state of AI hardware?

Are we going to get more diversification? Is AMD going to up its game, or what’s going on in hardware in general?

Pete Warden.
So watch Apple.

And disclaimer, I worked at Apple for five years in the 2000s. My wife worked there for 13 years.

But if you look at what they’re doing, they’re getting lots of RAM, increasing the RAM speed so that you can actually run models much faster, and they have their own inference-only accelerators.

I think with those three, you don’t need a GPU.

Ben Lorica.
So you just run everything on a CPU?

Pete Warden.
Well, run everything on a different kind of accelerator.

Ben Lorica.
Oh, okay. That’s not a…

Pete Warden.
GPU.

Ben Lorica.
I see. I see. So CPU…

Pete Warden.
Could actually be pretty fast. Obviously, the…

Ben Lorica.
The NVIDIA answer is why we have all the HBM, high-bandwidth memory, on the GPU, right?

Pete Warden.
And I like to think of GPUs as being designed for large batches and training.

I like to think of a GPU as trying to use an oil tanker to go and do your shopping.

They’re fantastic for these large training jobs, but they’re complete overkill for inference. Inference has a very different shape to the workload that it places on hardware.

Ben Lorica.
One thing that I’ve started to pay attention to lately, and it’s very, very early, is high-bandwidth flash.

Pete Warden.
Absolutely.

Ben Lorica.
Right. So what’s your take?

Pete Warden.
So that’s another example.

I see the massive amount of money that NVIDIA is pulling in, and that also has its own gravitational pull on all of these hardware companies, where they’re looking from a technical side.

I don’t have any special insights. I’ve just worked with these things. I know what the workloads look like. Other people are looking at those too, and they’re like, “Oh, I see. We have to stream all of the weights. All of the weights have to be processed for every token.”

So if you have something, even if you’re running on the CPU, if you have something that’s got high enough bandwidth to pull the 27 billion weights in a fraction of a second, then the rest of it is fairly easy in terms of actually doing the processing. It’s very much memory-bound, usually.

So it’s been awesome seeing high-bandwidth flash, what Apple is doing, increasing the bandwidth on regular RAM.

I think we’re going to see a lot of really imaginative solutions now that people understand what the workload looks like.

Ben Lorica.
Yeah, and with that, thank you, Pete. And again, the website is moonshine.ai.

title: Rebuilding my local voice assistant pipeline
content:
Rebuilding my voice assistant pipeline

https://blog.platypush.tech/article/Rewriting-my-voice-assistant-pipeline

📝

Swapping openwakeword for microwakeword and making voice detection smarter

Fabio Manganiello

Nov 19, 2026

#platypush

#voice

#voiceassistant

#microwakeword

#openai

Wake word detection: a new assistant.microwakeword plugin

Speech-to-text: assistant.openai, with a much better ear

Responses and context: the openai plugin

Text-to-speech: tts.openai

The full configuration

What changed on the code side

Caveats

I
wrote an article
a couple of months ago describing how I rebuilt my old voice assistant pipeline in
Platypush
.

And I wrote earlier articles describing my journey through self-hosted voice assistants -
in 2024
(with
Picovoice
),
in 2020
(diving into the legacy
assistant.google
integration, the now defunct
assistant.alexa
integration, the now defunct Snowboy integration, the now defunct DeepSpeech integration and Picovoice) and the
original article in 2019
describing the Google Assistant integration.

For a couple of months I used the voice pipeline described in my latest article as my main driver, but after getting used to the robustness of commercial voice assistants I was unhappy with the high rates of false positives/negatives of my self-hosted pipeline, as well as its lack of robustness in detecting start/end of speech, especially in noisy environments and using cheap microphones.

After a bit of experimentation, I decided to swap and fine tune a few parts, and after a couple of days of trying the results are satisfying enough for me to write a short article about it.

The resulting pipeline is:

Wake word detection: a new
assistant.microwakeword
plugin

Until recently I used
assistant.openwakeword
, which wraps
openWakeWord
.

It works, but the project has been quiet for a while and all of its pre-trained models are
v0.1
files from 2023, mostly trained on synthetic speech.

In practice I was getting both false positives (the hotword triggering on background noise) and false negatives (the hotword not detected unless I was close to the microphone).

I added a new plugin,
assistant.microwakeword
, on top of
microWakeWord
through the
pymicro-wakeword
Python bindings.

microWakeWord
is the engine used by ESPHome and Home Assistant Voice, its models are actively maintained, and the built-in models (
okay_nabu
,
hey_jarvis
,
hey_mycroft
,
alexa
) ship with the package — no download required.

The current official models are provided under the
ESPHome micro-wake-word-models repository
.

Custom models are supported too: drop a
microWakeWord
JSON manifest (with its
.tflite
model) in the plugin's models directory and reference it by name.

The plugin exposes the same API as
assistant.openwakeword
(same
models
,
detection_threshold
,
frame_duration
,
patience_frames
,
input_device
,
input_volume
parameters, same
list_models
action, same
HotwordDetectedEvent
), so switching is a matter of just changing the configuration to point to the new plugin:

assistant.microwakeword
:

models
:

-

alexa

A few design notes:

Without an explicit
detection_threshold
, each model uses the
probability_cutoff
from its own manifest (0.9 for
alexa
), which is the value the model was validated against.

Models already smooth their output over a sliding window, so unlike openwakeword,
patience_frames
defaults to 0 here.

The audio thread never touches the TFLite models directly: it queues frames (and a reset marker) to the main thread, because
MicroWakeWord.reset()
reloads the interpreter and isn't safe to call concurrently.

Like
assistant.openwakeword
, the plugin releases the audio device when another assistant plugin starts a conversation, and re-acquires it when the conversation ends.

Speech-to-text:
assistant.openai
, with a much better ear

assistant.openai
records audio when a conversation starts and transcribes it through Whisper.

The tricky part has always been
end-of-speech detection
: knowing when the user has finished talking. The previous implementation used a per-frame boolean from WebRTC VAD, and any single frame classified as speech would reset the silence timer. With even a bit of background noise, phrases would only end when the maximum conversation duration was hit.

The audio preprocessing layer (
AudioPreprocessor
, shared by the STT integrations) has been reworked:

Silero VAD
as the primary backend
(through
onnxruntime
, no
PyTorch
required), with WebRTC VAD and a plain RMS-based detector as fallbacks. To get an idea of Silero VAD's performance compared against other solutions for speech activity detection, take a look at the insightful article
One voice detector to rule them all
. The Silero model is downloaded on first use into the Platypush workdir and checksum-verified:

assistant.openai
:

# auto = silero -> webrtc -> energy, depending on what's installed

vad_backend
:

auto

Hysteresis + sliding window
: a frame becomes speech above the VAD threshold and stays speech until its score drops by a margin, and the per-frame decisions are smoothed by majority vote over a 0.5s window. A single noise burst can no longer keep a conversation alive.

Adaptive noise floor
: the background noise level is tracked over time, and frames that aren't louder than
noise_floor_factor
(default 2.0, ~6 dB) times the floor are never considered as speech.

On a synthetic benchmark (Piper-generated phrases mixed with babble and burst noise), the old settings kept conversations open for 6–10 seconds after the speech had ended; the new pipeline ends them 1.0–1.6 seconds after the last word, which is the configured
conversation_end_timeout
plus the smoothing lag.

Since the changes on Platypush have been performed directly in the
AudioPreprocessor
also used by other native speech-to-text engines, other speech-to-text plugins also benefit from them - e.g. if you use
assistant.vosk
for full on-device detection.

Responses and context: the
openai
plugin

The transcribed phrase is processed by the
openai
plugin, which handles both the API key and the conversation context. By default the assistant renders the response through the configured
tts_plugin
; if the response ends with a question mark, the conversation continues with a follow-up.

Custom hooks can intercept phrases before the default response kicks in — for example, to handle home automation commands locally without an LLM round-trip:

from

platypush

import

run
,

when

from

platypush.message.event.assistant

import

SpeechRecognizedEvent

@when
(
SpeechRecognizedEvent
,

phrase
=
'play (the)? music'
)

def

play_music
():

run
(
'music.mpd.play'
)

And the hotword event is wired to the conversation start with a similar hook:

from

platypush

import

run
,

when

from

platypush.message.event.assistant

import

HotwordDetectedEvent

@when
(
HotwordDetectedEvent
)

def

on_hotword
(
**
_
):

run
(
'assistant.openai.start_conversation'
)

Text-to-speech:
tts.openai

Responses are rendered by
tts.openai
, with volume and voice configurable. In my tests however
tts.piper
also yielded good results, and it runs entirely locally. In my tests on a RaspberryPi 5 however it added ~3-4s of latency to process the response to audio compared to
tts.openai
.

Since the TTS output goes to the speakers and the wake word detector listens on the microphone, the assistant plugins pause hotword detection while a conversation is active — otherwise the assistant would hear itself.

The full configuration

openai
:

api_key
:

YOUR_API_KEY

# Or, for a custom setup using a model provider compatible with the OpenAI API,

# e.g. a local Ollama instance:

# base_url: http://localhost:8000/v1

# model: gpt-5

# Optional context that can be passed to initialize the assistant

# context:

#   role: system

#   content: You are a useful assistant.

assistant.microwakeword
:

models
:

-

alexa

assistant.openai
:

tts_plugin
:

tts.openai

conversation_start_sound
:

~/sounds/wake_word_detected.wav

input_volume
:

100

# assistant.vosk:

#   model: /path/to/vosk/model

#   conversation_start_sound: ~/sounds/wake_word_detected.wav

#   input_volume: 100

tts.openai
:

output_volume
:

80.0

# Or, for a fully local setup that uses tts.piper:

# tts.piper:

#   output_volume: 80.0

What changed on the code side

New
assistant.microwakeword
plugin
: microWakeWord hotword detection through
pymicro-wakeword
, same API as
assistant.openwakeword
, built-in models bundled with the package, custom models via JSON manifests.

assistant.openwakeword
fixes
: frames are now 80ms (1280 samples, the size openWakeWord recommends) instead of 500ms — longer chunks only return the highest score over their sub-frames and can miss hotwords — plus a
patience_frames
parameter (consecutive frames above threshold) and an explicit
detection_threshold
parameter (default 0.5).

Shared
AudioPreprocessor
rework
: Silero/WebRTC/energy VAD backends with
vad_backend: auto
selection, threshold hysteresis, sliding-window majority vote, and an adaptive noise floor. Used by both
assistant.openai
and
assistant.vosk
.

New
Silero VAD wrapper
: ONNX inference through
onnxruntime
, recurrent state carried across frames, checksum-verified model download into the workdir.

Caveats

The microphone on my RPi doesn't support 16 kHz natively, so audio is captured at 44.1 kHz and software-resampled — it works, but if detection feels sluggish software resampling is usually the first suspect.

The VAD and threshold defaults were tuned on synthetic audio plus a couple of my audio recordings.

Different rooms, microphones and acoustics may yield different results. You may want to adjust
detection_threshold
on the wake word plugin and
noise_floor_factor
on the STT plugins if you don't feel satisfied with your mileage.

Technical details

Root cause

Most of Ruby's single-byte encodings have no capital

The output buffer is allocated as the input length plus 20

The same loop is in several ISO-8859 and Windows-125x encodings

Copying the result out of the buffer then reads one byte out of

title: Adding Fortran Support to LLDB (GSoC 2026)
content:
GSoC 2026 - Adding Fortran Support to LLDB
GSoC 2026 - Adding Fortran Support to LLDB (LLVM)
While Flang has matured, the developer tooling around it has lagged behind. In particular it lacks a dedicated debugger. LLDB lacks native Fortran support, it is only able to resolve basic breakpoints via raw line tables. This project adds support for Fortran in LLDB and lays the foundations on which a fully-featured Flang-backed debugger can be built.
Specifically, this work introduces native support for:
Primitive types (
INTEGER
,
REAL
,
LOGICAL
,
COMPLEX
)
Arrays
Pointers
Functions
Current Status & Running the Code
Because the upstreaming process for a project of this scale is ongoing, not all features have been merged into the LLVM main branch yet. However a working implementation is available for anyone to test. You can view the full set of changes, clone the code, and compile it yourself from my
personal branch
.
To keep up to date with the ongoing integration of this project, you can follow the
tracking issue
.
High-Level Architecture
Adding a new language to LLDB requires teaching it how to extract, represent, and display the values from compiled binaries. This relies on three core components:
DWARFASTParser
:
Parses compiler-generated DWARF debug information and extracts raw type metadata (e.g., symbol names, byte sizes, and layouts).
TypeSystem
:
Represents the internal type model of the language within LLDB. It takes the metadata parsed from DWARF and constructs native LLDB type representations.
Language Plugin
:
Registers Fortran with LLDB and supplies language-specific pretty-printers, value formatters, and synthetic children providers.
For more details on how to add a new language to LLDB, see the official
documentation
.
RFC process
When proposing any significant change to LLVM, it first needs to go through the
RFC process
. In short, a proposal is written providing an overview of the change, the motivation behind it, the overall architecture of what will be changed, and open questions. It then receives feedback, and if consensus is reached, the change is accepted and can be upstreamed.
Reaching consensus on
my RFC
took approximately two months since it was a major new feature, but it taught me a lot about how to communicate an idea and interact with other developers.
The most important decisions we reached in the RFC were:
Figuring out where and how testing would be performed, including setting up buildbots (x86_64 / AArch64) to prevent bit-rot.
Expression evaluation will eventually be supported using Flang, but later in the project’s lifetime and outside the scope of GSoC.
LLDB will not link directly to Flang at this stage due to Flang’s demanding build requirements. For now, only a Fortran compiler is needed to run tests.
Array support will be added using synthetic children, rather than making intrusive changes to LLDB’s core infrastructure.
Language-specific details like Fortran’s case insensitivity will be handled inside the plugin via DWARF attributes (
DW_AT_identifier_case
) without polluting core LLDB.
Testing and Upstreaming
For a large part of GSoC, development took place on my
personal LLVM fork
while waiting for community consensus on the RFC. Once consensus was reached, the focus shifted to breaking the work into small, incrementally testable pull requests that were easy for maintainers to review.
To ensure long-term stability without regressions, the implementation leverages LLDB’s
lit-based testing infrastructure
across two distinct levels:
Unit Tests (C++):
Added three test suites to test core components in isolation:
TypeSystemFortranTests
: Verifies that
TypeSystemFortran
correctly instantiates, constructs, and queries Fortran types.
DWARFASTParserFortranTests
: Tests that raw DWARF debug info is parsed accurately into internal types.
FortranLanguageTests
: Validates language plugin registration and synthetic child provider hooks.
API Tests (Python / SB API):
End-to-end integration tests using LLDB’s
Scripting Bridge API
. These compile sample Fortran programs, launch debug sessions, and verify that the plugin, DWARF parser, and type system communicate properly to inspect variables and print output.
For more details on LLDB testing standards, see the official
testing documentation
.
Features added
1. Laying the Foundation
For API tests, LLDB needs to compile sample Fortran programs. This patch updated LLDB’s test runner to automatically detect an installed Fortran compiler and conditionally enable the Fortran test suite.

PR #208298
Before adding actual language features, LLDB requires substantial boilerplate to satisfy its internal interfaces, specifically the
TypeSystem
, which demands numerous stub methods just to compile. To keep patches incremental and easy to review, this initial scaffolding was split into three minimal PRs that contain no active feature logic (except for registering the language plugin itself):
Language Plugin Registration:
Registers Fortran as a supported language within LLDB.
PR #218014
TypeSystem Stubs (
TypeSystemFortran
):
Adds the class skeleton and required interface overrides.
PR #218016
DWARF Parser Stubs (
DWARFASTParserFortran
):
Adds the parser skeleton to prepare for DWARF type parsing.
PR #218024
2. Primitive Types
Primitive types in Fortran consist of the INTEGER, REAL, LOGICAL and COMPLEX types and they are all described by the
DW_TAG_base_type
DWARF tag.
Type System Implementation
TypeSystemFortran
manages the lifetime and representation of all Fortran types in LLDB:
Memory Management & Deduplication:
For memory management without leaks, types are stored as unique pointers in a vector. To avoid redundant allocations, an LLVM
FoldingSet
uniques types so existing instances are reused whenever a matching type is requested.
Primitive Type Representation:
To represent basic primitive types (
INTEGER
,
REAL
,
LOGICAL
,
COMPLEX
), the type system tracks three essential properties:
Type name
Byte size
Type kind
Add support for basic types in TypeSystemFortran PR #218269
DWARFASTParser Implementation
DWARFASTParserFortran
bridges the raw debug symbols generated by the compiler and LLDB’s internal type system:
Tag Recognition:
Parses the
DW_TAG_base_type
and its children, collecting information about the type.
Scope Extraction:
Calculates the scope/context of the type.
Type Construction:
Forwards the extracted information to
TypeSystemFortran
to instantiate and cache the corresponding type.
3. Functions & Subroutines
Type System Implementation (Functions & Subroutines)
To represent Fortran functions and subroutines,
TypeSystemFortran
tracks three key elements:
Parameters:
Stores the name and type of each parameter, which are used to construct the function signature and resolve argument inspection at runtime.
Name:
Receives the base identifier from the DWARF parser and formats the complete Fortran signature (e.g.,
INTEGER sample(INTEGER arg1)
).
Return Type:
Tracks the return type for functions (or absence thereof for subroutines) to build the signature and provide accurate type info.
DWARFASTParser Implementation (Functions & Subroutines)
When encountering a Fortran function or subroutine,
DWARFASTParserFortran
handles two main tasks:
Parsing Subprogram Information:
Identifies
DW_TAG_subprogram
(and Fortran subroutines) and extracts the symbol name, parameter metadata, and return type, passing them to
TypeSystemFortran
to instantiate the function type.
Calculating Frame Bounds:
Determines the start and end memory addresses (low/high PC) of the subprogram. This address range is essential for stack frame unwinding and allows
frame variable
to correctly locate and display local variables in the current scope.
4. Variable Printing
For variable values to be printed correctly, the TypeSystem provides information about how they should be displayed, such as their encoding and formatting, along with implementing
DumpTypeValue
to format and dump the value to a stream.
With this addition,
frame variable
can print variables in a predictable way:
(lldb) frame variable num_real

(REAL) num_real = 2.71828175

(lldb) frame variable num_int

(INTEGER) num_int = 152

(lldb) frame variable num_logical

(LOGICAL) num_logical = true

(lldb) frame variable z1

# TypeSystemFortran formats complex as (real, imaginary) to match how Fortran prints them

(COMPLEX(KIND=8)) z1 = (3, 4)

With this addition API tests were also added, since the output could not be tested before.
5. Pointers
Pointers assosciated with non-array types are similar to C-like languages. So to handle them all that is needed is the pointee type.
Type System Implementation
The TypeSystem creates a pointer type from the pointee type. It can also provide the pointee type from the pointer type and vice-versa.
DWARFASTParser Implementation
The
DW_TAG_pointer_type
has a reference to the pointee type as a child, so the pointee type is recursively parsed using this reference and is forwarded to the TypeSystem.
Output
(lldb) frame variable target_val

(INTEGER) _QFEtarget_val = 42

(lldb) frame variable int_ptr

(INTEGER *) _QFEint_ptr = 0x000055555563d1e8

(lldb) frame variable &target_val

(INTEGER *) &_QFEtarget_val = 0x000055555563d1e8

(lldb) frame variable func_ptr

(INTEGER <unnamed function>(INTEGER * ) *) _QFEfunc_ptr = 0x0000555555556740

(lldb) image lookup -a 0x0000555555556740

Address: pointers[0x0000000000002740] (pointers.PT_LOAD[1]..text + 896)

Summary: pointers`square at pointers.f90:24

Note on output: Variables appear with a mangled name because LLDB does not have access to the Flang demangler.
6. Explicit Arrays
Arrays in Fortran can have custom bounds (e.g., indexing from
-1
instead of
1
) and custom byte strides (such as creating a slice consisting of every second element). In addition, Fortran arrays are column-major, unlike C/C++ which is row-major. For example, in a 2D array, elements of each column are stored in contiguous memory locations, whereas in C/C++ the elements of each row are contiguous. Furthermore, in Fortran, partial subscripting (such as indexing only one dimension of a multi-dimensional array) is invalid, unlike in C where it yields a pointer to a sub-array.
The array type structure
Below is a representation of how arrays are stored in the TypeSystem:
+-----------------------------------------------------------+

| ArrayType                                                 |

|   - Element Type : CompilerType (e.g., INTEGER)           |

|   - Metadata     : Flags, Rank                            |

|   - Dimensions   : vector<ArrayShape>                     |

+-----------------------------------------------------------+

|

v (Per Dimension)

+-----------------------------------------------------------+

| ArrayShape                                                |

|   - Byte Stride   : Memory step between elements          |

|   - Element Count : Extent of this dimension              |

|   - Lower Bound   : ArrayBound                            |

|   - Upper Bound   : ArrayBound                            |

+-----------------------------------------------------------+

|

v

+-----------------------------------------------------------+

| ArrayBound                                                |

|   - Kind  : Explicit | Star (*) | Colon(:)                |

|   - Value : Bound index                                   |

+-----------------------------------------------------------+

Note:
Star describes
assumed-size
arrays and colon describes
allocatable
arrays.
TypeSystem Implementation
When executing
frame variable
for an array, LLDB resolves subscripts iteratively: it first resolves the base array, processes the first subscript, then resolves subsequent subscripts based on the previous result. Consequently, when a user queries
arr[1]
on a multi-dimensional array, LLDB should return a valid sub-array rather than an error. Because Fortran arrays are column-major, the elements of this sub-array are not contiguous in memory, but are instead separated by a byte stride.
To handle this, a new sub-array type is created which strips the outermost dimension and scales the byte stride based on the extent and stride of the peeled dimension. This intermediate type is then returned, enabling LLDB to display the slice or continue stripping dimensions for chained subscripts.
The diagram below illustrates this resolution process:
Logical 2D Fortran Array: A(1:3, 1:2)

Col 1      Col 2

+--------+ +--------+

Row 1| A(1,1) | | A(1,2) |

Row 2| A(2,1) | | A(2,2) |  <-- User queries intermediate slice: A[2]

Row 3| A(3,1) | | A(3,2) |

+--------+ +--------+

Physical Memory Layout (Column-Major):

Offset:   0x00     0x04     0x08        0x0C     0x10     0x14

Bytes:   [ A(1,1) | A(2,1) | A(3,1) ]  [ A(1,2) | A(2,2) | A(3,2) ]

^                             ^

|                             |

+------ stride = 3 * 4B ------+

(12 bytes)

Intermediate Sub-Array Type created by LLDB for A[2]:

- Base Offset : 0x04  (idx * sizeof(elem))

- Stride      : 12 B  (count(dim 1) * sizeof(elem))

- Elements    : [ A(2,1), A(2,2) ]

Assumed-Size Arrays (*)
Assumed-size arrays use an asterisk (*) for their final dimension’s upper bound, leaving the total element count unknown in debug metadata. While handling follows the standard path, it differs in two ways:
Unbounded Indexing:
Upper-bound checks are bypassed, allowing direct element access (e.g., arr[10]) without failing on an unknown extent.
No Trailing Sub-Array Display:
Because the final dimension lacks a known element count, LLDB cannot calculate child boundaries, meaning intermediate slices cannot list or display the sub-arrays that follow.
Note:
While Fortran source syntax uses parentheses for multi-dimensional indexing (e.g.,
A(row, col)
), LLDB’s frame variable expression path parser currently only supports chained C-style bracket notation (
A[row][col]
).
DWARFASTParser Implementation
A
DW_TAG_array_type
tag is emitted in DWARF, with its children consisting of the element type as well as
DW_TAG_subrange_type
tags, one for each subrange, which can contain the following information:
Lower and upper bound
Element count
Byte stride
This information is collected and forwarded to TypeSystemFortran to create the array type.
Output
(lldb) frame variable a

(INTEGER(2, 2)) a = {

[1] = ([1] = 1, [2] = 3)

[2] = ([1] = 2, [2] = 4)

}

(lldb) frame variable a[1]

(INTEGER(2)) a[1] = ([1] = 1, [2] = 3)

(lldb) frame variable a[1][2]

(INTEGER) a[1][2] = 3

(lldb) frame variable arr

(INTEGER(3, *)) arr =

(lldb) frame variable arr[1]

(INTEGER(*)) arr[1] =

(lldb) frame variable arr[1][2]

(INTEGER) arr[1][2] = 12

7. Dynamic Arrays
Dynamic arrays in Fortran are described by an array descriptor, which holds information about the byte stride, lower/upper bounds, and each subrange’s element count. Because this information can change at runtime, it must be evaluated dynamically at the point of inspection.
Fortran compilers expose this metadata by emitting
DWARF expressions
, which evaluate the target memory state to calculate the runtime address and value of each attribute.
The primary architectural challenge was that LLDB as a whole assumes array geometry is static. Root structures like ValueObject and TypeSystem assume that while the values of array elements change at runtime, the structure of the array (such as its bounds and element count) does not, and if it does there is no way to know what that structure is. This model works for C, but breaks for Fortran, where the array’s true shape and element count can change during execution and the debugger can know what the array’s structure is.
Rather than making intrusive changes to core LLDB interfaces, a provider for synthetic children was used. Its job is to read the runtime descriptor in target memory and instantiate a new, concrete type containing the active bounds and strides. This cleanly accommodates Fortran’s dynamic layouts while keeping the TypeSystem isolated from runtime state.
Automatic-arrays
For arrays whose properties depend on runtime variables (such as bounds determined by function arguments), compilers emit a hidden variable in the DWARF metadata containing the required values. Because this information resides in runtime memory, it is resolved by the synthetic children provider using the same mechanism as array descriptors.
Assumed-rank arrays
These arrays appear in functions, allowing callers to pass arrays of varying dimensions to the same routine. For these arrays, the compiler emits a single
DW_TAG_generic_subrange
instead of one subrange tag per dimension, along with a rank attribute (
DW_AT_rank
) that provides the actual rank. Using the DWARF expressions found in the generic subrange’s children, the runtime properties of each dimension are determined. This resolution is handled by the synthetic children provider.
TypeSystem Implementation
The required DWARF expressions are stored directly within the array type, ensuring the
TypeSystem
does not process arrays containing runtime information. During
frame variable
evaluation, LLDB first attempts to retrieve a child from the
TypeSystem
. If the static type cannot provide one, the request falls back to the synthetic children provider. The provider resolves the runtime metadata into a concrete type and passes that resolved type back to the
TypeSystem
for standard processing.
DWARFASTParser implementation
The DWARF information for arrays can either be a DWARF expression, a reference to a variable or a number. The DWARFASTParser has to figure out what type of array it is and activate the appropriate flags. Its job is to inform the TypeSystem what to expect and forward all information.
8. Case-insensitivity
Fortran is a case insensitive language and LLDB did not have support for performing case-insensitive lookups. Compilers emit a
DW_AT_identifier_case
attribute which gives information regarding the casing. Using this attribute LLDB sets the correct appropriate casing.
For mixed-language executables, where one language is case-insensitive and the other isn’t, LLDB defaults to being case-sensitive.
Next steps
Unfortunately, arrays proved to be a lot more complex and time-consuming than we originally anticipated, so the scope of the project changed. The following features will be implemented in the future:
Strings
Derived types
As discussed in the RFC, the ideal end-point of this project is to have an expression evaluator using Flang, rather than relying only on the
frame variable
command (which uses a language-agnostic parser called
DIL
).
Biggest struggle
This was my first professional project and also my first time collaborating with many people. The hardest thing for me was learning how to communicate effectively and finding my voice in a large community. Thankfully, my mentors helped me a lot with this, enabling me to become much more confident in group discussions.
Learnings
I learned a lot about navigating a large codebase. By the end of the project, I was completing tasks much faster and finding information more easily. Just as importantly, I realized how vital clear communication is in a big project, and how much difference a supportive, helpful community can make.
Acknowledgements
I want to say a big thank you to my mentors, Shivam Gupta and Tarun Prabhu. They were immensely helpful throughout this project and taught me a lot. I also want to thank the LLVM community—especially the LLDB team—for taking the time to give me feedback on the RFC for this project and helping me along the way.

title: Do not buy RAM, compress
content:
Do not buy RAM, compress!
19 Nov, 2026
AI has changed a lot. We do more work in parallel. This increases the memory demand on our workstations.
Also, memory is expensive and often not extendable. So buying more RAM is not an easy option.
Recently I was running out of memory, I found my solution in
zram
, a solution to compress memory.
Memory compression is not new. If you have a Windows or Mac device you are already using it.
Also, many Android smartphones utilize the technique of using compression to put more data into the RAM.
Unfortunately not all Linux environments have RAM compression enabled by default.
Fedora, Pop!_OS do, but Ubuntu doesn’t. Amazon Linux only enables zram on smaller virtual machines.
Most other distributions do not have it enabled.
Compressing memory does come with small, but not really noticeable, downsides. It takes a little bit more from your CPU and adds latency to some processes.
What you gain is gigantic amounts of extra capacity. It is not uncommon to see compression ratios up to 1:4.
I remember that in the early days of writing SaaS software we would often need double the size of the machines when we added more features to our monolithic app.
Often the CPUs were under little stress, so we could have avoided upgrading if we had enabled RAM compression.
This could have cut our Cloud spend in half!
How it looks in practice
I opened a lot of websites in Firefox. So many, it would almost fully take all system memory. (I have 32GB with some reserved for the graphics)

title: Distributed, high-performance blob storage on SQLite
content:
TLDR;
We built Blobasaur, a sharded, distributed, lightweight blob storage server on top of SQLite to solve our high-throughput blob read/write usecase. JSON blobs varying from a few KBs to MBs are now written and read thousands of times per second on commodity hardware while maintaining single-digit millisecond latency.
On
Kite
, our trading platform with ~20 million customers, users are able to customize their investment and trading screens heavily. They save multi-chart layouts, financial indicator templates, vector drawings, and various kinds of arbitrary UI preferences. In addition, we offer a Terminal mode that allows users to design their own workspaces by dragging, dropping, and customizing widgets. Under the hood, our backend services store these user preferences and metadata as opaque blobs (mostly JSON) ranging from a few kilobytes to several megabytes.
Many years ago, we stored such blobs in CouchDB, which turned out to be ill-suited for the kind of throughput we were starting to see. We then moved to SSDB (
ssdb
), a C++ disk-backed store that speaks the Redis protocol. This made it very easy to integrate as well. SSDB solved our immediate performance problems and ran reliably in production for several years.
Over time, two problems forced us to look for a replacement:
As we added features like the Terminal mode and onboarded more internal services, we needed a robust solution. Our criteria were:
So we investigated FOSS databases optimized for high-throughput blob storage and looked at the following:
Around this time, we were toying with SQLite for another project and were marveling at its
35% Faster Than The Filesystem
claim. We also happen to have a query cache system that creates
millions of tables
every day in a Postgres instance, which pushes the database to its limits quite successfully. Putting two and two together, we thought, why not build a system on top of SQLite to store millions of blobs and see what happens?
So we ended up building
Blobasaur
, an open source sharded blob server written in Rust that speaks the Redis protocol and uses SQLite as its storage engine. It is a single binary application that is high performance, and super simple to deploy and maintain. It is in production at Zerodha and it has successfully replaced SSDB.

We had several Go and Python services already talking to SSDB via the Redis protocol, with more waiting to onboard. We wanted the new solution to meet these requirements:
We had a few options for the storage. The obvious one is the raw filesystem, with one file per blob. But with that, we’d need to invent everything ourselves:
SQLite pretty much gave us everything that the raw filesystem lacked. For small blobs, SQLite is up to 35% faster than raw filesystem I/O. While raw files start to beat SQLite above ~100 KiB, we compress blobs before writing them. And thankfully, 99% of our compressed values sit well below 100 KiB.
Using SQLite also meant inheriting a battle-tested storage engine with ACID transactions, crash recovery, and standard tooling. Any shard on disk can be inspected with the standard
sqlite3
CLI or queried with plain SQL for analytics, etc.
While most of our backend stack is written in Go, we wrote Blobasaur in Rust. Go’s standard SQLite driver requires CGo, which complicates static builds, pins OS threads during C calls under high concurrency, and adds garbage-collection pressure when allocating and compressing multi-megabyte buffers. With Rust (
sqlx
,
rusqlite
, and
tokio
), we call SQLite’s C API directly with predictable memory usage and ship a single static binary.
In WAL (Write-Ahead Logging) mode, a single SQLite database allows concurrent readers, but still permits only one writer at a time. Since writes make up roughly 50% of our production traffic, a single SQLite file per node would bottleneck quickly.
To get write concurrency on a single machine, Blobasaur splits data across multiple SQLite database files on disk, called shards:

We benchmarked 1 shard against 16 shards using a load generator opening 64 concurrent connections. Each request used a 64 KiB JSON blob payload (close to our production average), which zstd compresses roughly 9x.
All runs used 100,000 keys, synchronous writes, and
batch_size = 50
, with the data directory on
tmpfs
to isolate SQLite locking and CPU overhead from disk variance. Both setups received the same total resources: 1,600 MB of SQLite page cache and 64 total read connections.
With 16 shards, write throughput increases 3.3x and median write latency drops from 8.2 ms to 2.1 ms. Read throughput stays nearly identical because SQLite WAL mode already serves concurrent readers without contention.
At 25,324
HSET
operations per second, each carrying a 64 KiB payload, Blobasaur processes roughly
1.66 GB/s of uncompressed JSON
through zstd. Both the server and load generator ran on the same 16-core laptop, sharing its CPU resources.
Our services use both plain keys (
SET
/
GET
) and Redis hashes (
HSET
/
HGET
) to group blobs by service or feature (for example,
HSET prefs userID <json>
).
Inside each shard, plain keys live in a
blobs
table:
SET
writes to
blobs
.
HSET
writes to a table for its namespace,
blobs_<namespace>
, with the same columns. For example,
HSET prefs user42 ...
stores
user42
in
blobs_prefs
.
Expiry is stored in
expires_at
on the same row. Read queries filter out expired rows at read time (
expires_at IS NULL OR expires_at > ?
), while a background worker reaps expired rows asynchronously. Because the index on
expires_at
is a partial index (
WHERE expires_at IS NOT NULL
), rows without a TTL take up no space in the expiry index.
Blobasaur supports zstd, lz4, gzip, and brotli compression before writing to SQLite. We run zstd in production.
Here is the compression ratio across one hour of production
HSET
traffic:
With SQLite’s default 4 KiB pages, shrinking a 63.6 KiB payload to 5.5 KiB reduces its storage footprint from roughly 16 pages to roughly 2, before accounting for row and index overhead. Fewer pages holding blob data means less pressure on the page cache and less data to write through the WAL and into the database.

Because we don’t require strict durability for our specific use case of UI preferences, shards run in WAL mode with
PRAGMA synchronous = NORMAL
. SQLite does not fsync on every transaction commit. An OS crash or power loss can lose recent committed transactions that have not yet been synced to durable storage, while preserving database consistency.
For workloads that want even lower write latency, Blobasaur also supports an optional
async_write
mode that acknowledges writes as soon as they enter the shard’s memory queue, before the SQLite batch commits.
To scale beyond a single server, Blobasaur implements the Redis Cluster protocol, making it compatible with standard cluster-aware Redis clients. Like Redis Cluster, the keyspace is divided into 16384 hash slots using
CRC16
. Each Blobasaur node owns a configured range of slots, and nodes discover each other via gossip. If a client sends a key to the wrong node, the node responds with a
MOVED
redirect pointing to the owner node.

This gives Blobasaur two-level routing:
There are some limitations right now. At present, slot assignment is static in config. Live slot rebalancing between running nodes and automatic failover are not implemented yet.
We chose multi-probe consistent hashing so resharding a node only has to move minimal data, without needing virtual nodes. With naive
hash % num_shards
, increasing from 4 to 5 shards moves ~80% of keys. With consistent hashing, only ~20% of keys move (the share belonging to the new shard).
Resharding is currently an offline operation via the built-in CLI:
The migration tool moves keys whose target shard changed. With
--verify
, it checks that keys are in the expected shards and reports post-migration row counts.
We rolled out Blobasaur in a phased deployment strategy:
After running dual-writes for a month with zero discrepancies, we turned off SSDB.
Early on, we noticed disk usage only grew, even after millions of keys expired or were deleted. By default, SQLite keeps freed pages on an internal freelist for future writes rather than returning space to the OS.
To fix this, we enabled
PRAGMA auto_vacuum = INCREMENTAL
across every shard and added a
blobasaur shard vacuum
subcommand to reclaim unused freelist pages within a set allocation (128 MB default). Since shrinking the actual database file in WAL mode requires a checkpoint, Blobasaur runs
PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE)
right after executing an incremental vacuum.
When
async_write
is enabled, a write returns
OK
while still sitting in the shard’s memory queue waiting for the next batch commit. To preserve read-your-writes consistency, queued writes are also placed in an in-memory pending map that reads check before querying SQLite.
During testing, we hit edge cases where certain read and existence-check paths bypassed this pending map or didn’t account for deletes. For example, a
DEL
followed immediately by a
GET
could return the old value from SQLite because the queued
DEL
hadn’t committed yet. We fixed this by storing explicit tombstones in the pending map and routing every read (
GET
,
HGET
,
EXISTS
,
TTL
) through it first.
In production, our p99 write latency normally sat below 5 ms, but we occasionally saw spikes to 30 to 50 ms.
We traced the spikes to the background TTL cleanup task. Initially, the cleanup worker opened its own write connection and ran a single large
DELETE
statement for all expired rows. That large
DELETE
contended with the shard’s main writer for SQLite’s single write lock, stalling normal client batches.
We fixed this in two ways: routing cleanup batches through the shard’s existing writer connection so they take turns cleanly with client writes, and bounding each pass with
cleanup_chunk_size
(1,000 rows by default). Since expired rows are already filtered out at read time, spreading physical deletion across smaller chunks eliminated the latency spikes without affecting correctness.
Our current Blobasaur deployment runs as a three-node (4 vCPU, 8 GB RAM) cluster. Over a full trading session (09:00 to 15:30), p99 latency across all commands stays around 2 ms on every node, and p50 sits between 250 and 550 µs.

Broken down by command,
HSET
p99 sits around 2 ms,
HGET
p99 around 1.4 ms, and
HDEL
p99 mostly under 1 ms.

Blobasaur is open source under the AGPLv3 license and available on GitHub
@iamd3vil/blobasaur
. Find other projects from the Zerodha.tech hacker collective at
4th Cross Labs
.

title: Fuck Your AI Safeguards
content:
Fuck your AI safeguards
2026-11-19

engineering
,
ramblings
While refrigerators were getting hacked in Estonia,

I half-seriously took a project I’m working on and asked Claude Code if there are any low-hanging fruit regarding
security that we could improve. It found one issue that was easy to fix, simple oversight with a one line fix, so I just
went along with it.
Then it got stopped because of bullshit “AI safeguards”. Oh no, how dare
I
, the senior product engineer with

my
product that I provably have control over, try to
fix
and prevent security issues and ensure compliance
with local laws and regulations?
“Oh but you can just apply to get an exemption from them here
bla bla fucking blah
”
Have you
READ

the requirements?
First of all, you will have to wait for multiple business days to get a response.
You forfeit any data retention exemptions, so hope you don’t have any IP to protect!
Oh, and oh so
please
give us your fucking ID or passport! We won’t leak it later, promise!
WHAT.
And you may just get fucked anyway and not get approval.
Approval to appropriately protect your own service!
This wasn’t the first time I ran into this issue. As maddening as it sounds, I
try
to keep up with the security
landscape and to apply appropriate mitigations because leaking sensitive information is
a big fucking no-no
and I
can’t let that happen.
If there’s a popular exploit out there that applies for our technical stack, I need to know if the public
proof-of-concept snippets can be adapted and used maliciously against my services. But no, Claude will tell you to fuck
off and use an older model that
still
will try to stop you from applying adequate protection.
You know who don’t need to ask for approval? Criminals. They just go and use the models that don’t have safeguards in
place. Abliterated open weights models don’t care. Bad actors reach their goals with or without your “safe” models.
You can use a knife to cut up some food, or seriously hurt someone. Yet I don’t get asked to put in an application with
my government-provided ID to buy one. Why is this tool so special?
Predictably, the only way to
actually
make our own service more secure ended up involving the use of EU-hosted
open weights models, such as GLM 5.3, that actually complied with our intentions, proved that the issue is there, and
then helped fix and verify that the issue is now resolved, for good.
Congratulations, Anthropic, you’ve made the world an unsafer place.
Or maybe that was your plan all along to get regulators to react and build that moat for you right before your IPO to
fend off competitors?
Either way, I’m just incredibly frustrated. Big AI labs use the same tools without restrictions to make the security
landscape a fucking mess, and then they go and prohibit others from using the same tools to protect themselves from the
threats they just created. Fucking asshats.
1
and that’s my swear word quota hit for the year.
