title: 15M web servers on one VM – smoltcp, DPDK, AF_XDP
content:
Put a web server online and everyone starts trying to hack it. Why? A basic rule of economics. Short supply, big demand - there aren’t enough web servers for everyone. Let’s run a web server for every human on the planet, all 8 billion of them. I couldn’t get funding, so we’re bootstrapping. The goal is to run 15 million web servers on one VM with 10GB of RAM and 1 CPU core. If we succeed, I’ll find some RAM from old microwaves around the house and we’ll scale it up so everyone can have their own web server. Demand will drop to zero and cybersecurity will be solved once and for all.
Web server
Instead of vibe coding it all, let’s use an ancient technique called
learning
. First of all, what is a web server? There are a few essential syscalls.
listen
- syscall, asks kernel to listen for connections on a socket
accept
- syscall, accepts a connection on a socket
recv
- receives data from a socket
send
- sends data
close
- closes
What is a syscall? A function that is executed by the OS kernel. Whatever fancy language or library you use for HTTP, it all comes down to those syscalls (well, yes, but actually no). Let’s use C to make it all explicit. We start listening, then read from the socket in a loop and always reply with
OK
.
int
main
(
void
)

{

// We use port 0 which makes OS return any available port

int
server
=
socket
(
AF_INET
,
SOCK_STREAM
,
0
);

if
(
listen
(
server
,
128
)
<
0
)

return
1
;

const char
reply
[]
=
"HTTP/1.0 200 OK
\r\n
Content-Length: 2
\r\n\r\n
OK"
;

for
(
int
client
; (
client
=
accept
(
server
,
NULL
,
NULL
))
>=
0
;) {

if
(
recv
(
client
,
NULL
,
4096
,
MSG_TRUNC
)
>
0
)

send
(
client
,
reply
,
sizeof
reply
-
1
,
MSG_NOSIGNAL
);

close
(
client
);

}

}
It couldn’t be simpler: listen on a socket, accept a connection, read the data, send a reply, close the client connection, and repeat. It gives us around 65k RPS. Now that we’ve learned everything, let’s finish the article and call it a day:
$
for
i
in
$(
seq
1
15_000_000
);
do
echo
$i
;
./server
&;
done

...

...

28232

program exited with error 1
Hm, why did
listen
fail? Ah, we’ve run out of ports! We’re using
port=0
, so the kernel picks an available port from
ip_local_port_range
.
$
sysctl net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range

net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range = 32768    60999
Why are so many ports skipped? Historically, port
0
was created for outbound connections. When you call
connect('example.com', 80)
, Linux connects to the remote server (the sending part) and then allocates a random port on the host from
ip_local_port_range
to receive data (the receiving part). There are a few reasons the default range is small.
Port
0
is special. You cannot listen on it (actually, you can -
https://acid.vegas/blog/the-port-that-does-not-exist/
).
Ports
1-1024
require root.
Ports
1024-32768
are skipped to keep dynamically allocated ports from conflicting with existing apps. You don’t want to call
connect('example.com')
and end up allocating port
3306
to receive incoming data.
mysql cannot start because you have example.com open in your Firefox
would make for a confusing UX.
Ports
60999 - 65535
are excluded for historical reasons dating back to IP Masquerading.
Nothing prevents us from overriding the range and using
1-65535
, but that’s still a bit short of 15 million. A UDP server and a TCP server can use the same port, so we can double that to 128k. We could run a proxy in front to forward requests to the right process (virtual hosting, yay), but these are all ancient techniques - in the AI era, whenever you have a software problem, you just throw money at the hardware. Let’s simply connect
15M/32k=450
new network cards to the server.
The 65k limit comes from the TCP standard. A port is a
u16
, so even if we hack the kernel with
find '*.c' -exec sed -i 's/u16/u32/' \;
to support bigger port numbers, normal clients still wouldn’t be able to connect. Each listening server is identified by a
(protocol, IP, port)
tuple. That explains how we can use the same port for UDP and TCP. It also means we can use a bunch of different IPs for our web servers. If we connect 450 network cards to the server, we’ll get 450 unique IP addresses and be able to listen on 15 million unique addresses!
UPD.
I’ve heard from readers that the network card is the ONLY hardware component that didn’t get 100 times more expensive in the last year. Can’t we avoid ruining that too and solve this in software?
Let’s use a beautiful technology called
AnyIP
, which lets us listen on a whole subnet. Many VPS and dedicated server providers routinely give you a whole TCPv6 subnet. We can simply run
sudo ip -6 route add local 2001:db8:1234:5678::/64 dev lo
to get 18 quintillion addresses (plus or minus one) to listen on. You can do the same for IPv4 - acquiring a subnet with 15M addresses would cost around $250 million, so adjust the command for your environment. We’ll change our server to pick the nth IP from our range:
// Read IP index from CLI, shift base IP by it

int
i
=
read_cli_param
(
argv
[
1
]);

const uint32_t
base_ip
=
0x
0a400001
;
// ex. 10.64.0.1

addr.sin_addr.s_addr
=
htonl
(
first_ip
+
i
);
// shift, ex. 10.64.0.2
And now we can finally finish the article.
$
for
i
in
$(
seq
1
15_000_000
);
do
echo
$i
;
./server
$i
&;
done

...

...

Out of memory
Hm, one server consumes 1.5MB of RAM, so running that many would take… 20TB of RAM, which is a few bytes more than our 10GB budget.
Runtime
By pure coincidence (what are the odds?), I explained in
Running 10 million Codex CLIs on one server - LFI processes
why running millions of processes creates too much overhead. The answer is to run them all in one process inside a custom runtime, much as V8 can run millions of guests in a single process. In
Userland Linux scheduler in Rust
, I showed how to build a specialised userland scheduler and switch between tasks with the absolute minimum amount of RAM per task.
TLDR: We’re using
LFI
for sandboxing. It gives us memory isolation and replaces all syscalls with calls to our host handler, which lets us implement I/O however we like. To schedule multiple guests, we load them all into our main process’s memory and make the CPU constantly switch between guests - we become our own micro OS.
Since we need to save every byte and CPU cycle we can, we’re doomed to build another specialised runtime. Let’s get started. How much is 10GB divided by 15M, exactly?
Ten Great Britains divided by 15 million gives around half of kilo britain. Not much. If we run all our guests in our runtime, our custom scheduler needs to switch between them. What’s the absolute minimum state we need to preserve for each guest? We can ignore server initialisation and assume switches only happen within the main loop. Let’s take another look at the loop.
for
(
int
client
; (
client
=
accept
(
server
,
NULL
,
NULL
))
>=
0
;) {

if
(
recv
(
client
,
NULL
,
4096
,
MSG_TRUNC
)
>
0
)

send
(
client
,
reply
,
sizeof
reply
-
1
,
MSG_NOSIGNAL
);

close
(
client
);

}
This code has only two state variables,
server
and
client
. Both are simple file descriptors. If our scheduler had to suspend a guest at any syscall point in this loop, we’d need to save the following state:
struct
Context
{

pc
:
u64
,
// Instruction address to return to

fd_server
:
i32
,
// server file descriptor

fd_client
:
i32
,
// client file descriptor

}
We only need 16 bytes per guest, so to run 15M guests in our runtime and be able to suspend them and switch between them, we would need 220MB of RAM. We’re playing it safe here - we don’t need the full
u64
or
i32
, and with bit packing, we could probably get down to 8 bytes per guest. What else do we need?
$
codex
"How much TCP connection takes?"

Idle connection takes zero, while active connection consumes around 5kb
Here’s what we get if we assume that only 1M of connections are active at any given moment.
14M idle connections - 0 bytes
Scheduling state for 15M guests - 220MB
1M active connections at 5kb each = 5GB
Only half of our RAM budget, yay! I don’t often exceed my own expectations. Let’s validate it:

,

(

,

$

|

-n
1

'SHOULD CONSUMER ZERO MEMORY' - what are you, stupid?
Looks like the kernel still has some leftover comments from Linus. I’m not stupid, but I have to admit I was below average here. While an LLM is a significant boost for learning, it’s too easy to accept its answers without thinking critically and feel ashamed later on. But hey, embarrassment is a cost of entry - let’s dive into networking in the kernel.
Networking in the kernel
Remember when I said that our simple server uses only 5 syscalls? I missed one that was right in front of me. Let me highlight it:
int
main
(
void
)

{

for
(

<
10_000_000
;

i

,

That code will OOM in a 10GB VM. The
socket
syscall allocates around 3300 bytes, whether the socket is active, listening, or doing nothing. Linux was clearly written at a time when RAM was big and cheap, sigh. Let’s ask AI where all the memory goes:
Struct
sizeof
Description
struct tcp_sock
2240B
TCP state, queues, timers, sequence numbers, congestion control, retransmit and delivery bookkeeping
struct socket_alloc
768B
A 128-byte
struct socket
with an embedded wait queue, plus a 608-byte sockfs inode and padding
struct file
184B
Open-file operations, flags, credentials, reference count, and the pointer back to the socket
struct dentry
192B
The sockfs pseudo-name, inode pointer, and VFS lookup and lifetime bookkeeping
Total
3384B
Potato-potato, TLDR, the kernel uses that memory for many things. I was hoping to see some
buffer: [u8; 3300]
, but it doesn’t look like we can optimise much without rewriting half the kernel. It’s Sunday and I have few tokens left, so we’ll have to think instead - how can we bypass the kernel?
What are our options? Engineering wisdom tells us that if we can’t solve a task, we’re working at the wrong level of abstraction. Hm… level, level, layer. Wait a minute! We started with HTTP and went level down to TCP/IP. That reminds me of something! Mom! Mom! Where are all my university books? I NEED THEM NOW!
The OSI model is… um… something I studied at university. Yeah, that’s a good definition. We started with our app and HTTP at the
application
layer, then went down to TCP/IP at the
transport
layer. There are three more layers below that. Can we go lower to get full control and solve our RAM problem? Oh yes, that’s exactly what operating at the
network
and
data link
layers lets us do. What about going to the lowest?
Clear.
Each layer wraps the data from the layer above it.

TCP/IP is stateful, but everything below is stateless. None of the lower layers know or care about the payload, so nothing prevents us from sending new IP packets or even Ethernet frames with our own handcrafted binary data. We just need to reimplement the TCP and IP stack ourselves. Are there any examples? Embedded folks have solved this millions of times. The most extreme case is Adam Dunkels’s
Miniweb
- it combines a custom TCP/IP implementation and an HTTP server that together need only 28 bytes (B-Y-T-E-S) to work.
There are plenty of less extreme, more mature implementations, though:
gVisor
essentially reimplements the whole OS, including the network stack
Seastar
is a whole runtime with its own network stack from the amazing team behind ScyllaDB
lwIP
is a popular C implementation of TCP/IP
F-Stack
uses FreeBSD’s TCP/IP stack
Go, C++, and C are nice languages (well, kinda), but they’re nowhere near as nice as our beloved Rust. So we’ll take
smoltcp
, which is purely amazing:
>smoltcp is a standalone, event-driven TCP/IP stack that is designed for

>bare-metal, real-time systems. smoltcp does not need heap allocation at all
So,
cargo add smoltcp
and call it a day? Not so fast.
smoltcp
is essentially a smart parser and can’t do I/O. How does it communicate with your network card? There are 3 ways:
TUN
is a virtual network interface that the kernel provides. It operates at the IP layer
TAP
is another kernel feature that operates one layer down, at the Ethernet layer
DPDK
lets you communicate directly with the network card using Ethernet frames, completely bypassing the kernel
smoltcp
is kind enough to provide the first two options out of the box, and they’re easy to use.

But what about the third option,
DPDK
? When you care about latency A LOT, every syscall is a bloody wound. The syscall itself might take 500ns, and copying data from the kernel to userspace might take another 1000ns, depending on the buffer size. That sounds tiny, but for perspective: it’s common for high-frequency trading firms to saturate 400Gbs network interfaces. That means processing up to 600 million packets per second, or roughly 1.7ns per packet.
DPDK
lets your program communicate directly with the hardware network card using Ethernet frames, bypassing the entire kernel network stack. You read from and write to a memory-mapped buffer without syscalls: when you want to send data - you simply write it to the buffer and you’re done; when you want to read what you’ve received - it’s already there.
There’s another, less obvious advantage - what happens when a new packet arrives at your network device? An interrupt fires, the CPU core stops executing your app, switches to the kernel, processes the interrupt, and then goes back to your app. Now imagine A LOT of incoming packets, so many that your app gets interrupted all the time. It has a beautiful name,
livelock
, and I guess debugging it in production is its own level of hell.
DPDK
lets you avoid all that, but there’s a cost.
DPDK
works by running a busy loop that takes up an entire CPU core. It constantly moves data between memory and the network device in both directions, kinda like that:
loop
{

send_from_app_memory_to_network
();

receive_from_network_to_app_memory
();

}
There’s another, less obvious nuance.
DPDK
requires exclusive access to the network device because it uses a driver that operates at the hardware level - two drivers can’t work with the same device at the same time. Once you enable the
DPDK
driver for your network interface… it disappears from the OS. Yep, nothing in
ifconfig
, if you enable it over SSH, you’ll lose SSH access too. I can imagine a lot of funny stories coming out of that.
Actually, there’s a fourth option now - Linux now has an
AF_XDP
subsystem that does something similar. It lets you bypass the kernel network stack and uses the same idea of memory-mapped buffers to get zero-copy I/O in your app. The kernel still owns the device and interrupts still happen as usual. When a new packet arrives, the kernel runs a simple eBPF filter that decides whether to send it directly to the userspace buffer, bypassing the network stack, or process it normally. That means SSH still works.
AF_XDP
supports an alternative mode,
SO_PREFER_BUSY_POLL
, which is even closer to
DPDK
: you get a busy loop with no interrupts at the cost of a CPU core.
DPDK
still beats it because it bypasses the kernel completely, but
AF_XDP
is very close (and simply easier to manage).
To support
DPDK
and
AF_XDP
in
smoltcp
, we only need to implement the
Device trait
with 3 methods if we want full control. Alternatively, we can use the existing crates
rust-dpdk-net
for DPDK and
xsk-rs
for
AF_XDP
to help us.
Now the final flow is:
The runtime loads 15M web server guests into its memory
The runtime scheduler starts executing guests one by one
Guest syscalls are intercepted by the runtime and replaced by the
smoltcp
network stack and its adapters
All 15M guests start listening, each on its own address
The scheduler polls for incoming data from
smoltcp
adapters, wakes up a guest, makes it process the data, and switches to the next
And now we can finally finish the article. The kernel network stack uses up all the RAM at around 2.5M web servers, and RPS drops as we run more servers. With
smoltcp
, RAM usage grows slower - 620 bytes per idle server and around a kilobyte for an active one, we got to 16M of servers. DPDK is clearly the beast in this benchmark, with
AF_XDP
just behind it:
Why is this so exciting? It means that by moving the network stack to userland, you can get full control on RAM usage and improve performance. And with custom runtime, you can simply run guests faster.
Simply
is a bit of a stretch - building a proof of concept is easy. Building a compatible Linux runtime and reimplementing all the syscalls with 100% POSIX compatibility take a bit more thought. And another article.

great overview of DPDK
https://doc.dpdk.org/guides/index.html
DPDK main documentation site
https://docs.kernel.org/networking/af_xdp.html

title: Chrome AI features wasting much bandwidth
content:
🔎 Finally
solved the mystery
. At some point this year (around a few months ago), my bandwidth/data usage went thru the roof. Figured out it was Chrome’s recent
AI
features. Then got immediate bandwidth-relief after disabling all the “AI innovations” and “On-device” stuff. Here is a screenshot of the settings:

I simply disabled everything on that settings page, and the needless bandwidth leakage
stopped immediately
.
Don’t take my word for it. Fire up your favorite activity/network monitor. Watch the network activity while Chrome’s
AI
features are enabled, which they are
by default
. Note the continual bandwidth/data spend coming from Chrome, which if you care to monitor long-term adds up to
hundreds
of GBs per month (depending on setup, usage, etc.).
After watching the meter spin for a while, go into the Chrome settings and disable all the “AI innovations” and “On-device” stuff. Then return to the network monitor and watch it virtually flatline.
Problem solved
.
Chrome should have left the
AI
resource hogs disabled by default. Someone do the math on how much energy and bandwidth is
absolutely wasted
by all the people (such as myself) who
never even touch the AI stuff
.
Before I disabled the
AI
settings, Chrome was chewing up literally hundreds of
GB
s per month. Now multiply that by the number of Chrome users who aren’t using “AI whatever neat”, and you’re talking real numbers. Real
waste
. For something that serves absolutely no purpose, that’s a ridiculous spend.
That’s all for now, I’m off to try some new browsers. There are quite a few great Chrome-alternatives these days.

title: Token fraud is here and it’s BAD (YouTube)
content:
Token fraud is here and it’s BAD (YouTube)

Claire Vo runs
ChatPRD
, an AI platform that helps product managers "turn an idea into a spec". The product has been live since the GPT-4 era, and Claire has been building it in public for much of that time.

In this YouTube video (see also the
accompanying Twitter post
) Claire describes the
flood
of token fraud she has seen from groups abusing the product's free trial, sometimes just to get free AI usage but often to resell tokens or run other commercial enterprises on top of the ChatPRD agent.

I am funding a international Roblox and Fortnite map studio. They run a loop of free trials and promo codes and then tunnel to my agent and use it to build Roblox and Fortnite maps.

Apparently one of the common prompts Claire saw running through her agent involved SVGs of pelicans riding bicycles! Presumably the token scammers are using that to help sniff the underlying models - different model families have a definite signature, and I've used it like this in the past to try and guess the identity of stealth preview models on platforms like OpenRouter.

Claire is winding down her free trials entirely, which sadly looks like the right decision in the face of this abuse.

title: Combatting adversarial distillation
content:
November 20, 2026
Combatting adversarial distillation
How we’re addressing safety risks of distillation and lessons we’ve learned for strengthening safeguards across the industry.
As frontier AI models become more capable, safeguards play an increasingly important role in how they can be used responsibly. Adversarial distillation creates a path for bad actors to reproduce these capabilities without appropriate safeguards. An actor may use a frontier model’s outputs without authorization to train another model with similar capabilities, then deploy it without comparable protections. For instance, an adversary might distill a model’s cyber capabilities and use the resulting model to help carry out cyberattacks that the original model would have refused to assist with or that its safeguards would have blocked.
We’re
sharing how OpenAI detects and disrupts adversarial distillation, how we’ve strengthened protections for our models’ protected reasoning, and what we’ve learned that can help strengthen defenses across the industry.
Our approach to adversarial distillation
combines adversarial testing, model training, classifiers, and API-level protections with investigations into coordinated attempts to extract model capabilities. These updated safeguards
align more closely with those we use for biology and cybersecurity.
We place particular emphasis on preventing attackers from extracting our models’ protected reasoning: the intermediate steps a model generates internally while working toward an answer, known as its chain-of-thought. These traces can contain information the final answer leaves out, making them especially valuable training data for another model.
W
e’ve strengthened our defenses against protected reasoning extraction in
GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol. In an internal adaptive evaluation using
strong automated red-teaming
,
we tested whether attackers could recover protected reasoning the model had generated while answering an earlier prompt. The average attack success rate fell from 54.0% against GPT‑6 Astra with its original safeguards to 0.2% against GPT‑6.2 Astra with its updated safeguards.
Why distillation is a safety issue
Distillation is a common machine-learning technique in which one model learns from data produced by another. For example, a model can learn from another model’s answers, its reasoning, or
its judgments about which answers are better and why
. Beyond intellectual property concerns, unauthorized distillation poses
serious
safety risks. Through adversarial distillation, a second model can learn advanced frontier capabilities without inheriting the safeguards that govern how the original model can use them.
The concern is especially clear in dual-use domains like cybersecurity and biology. A model that helps defenders find vulnerabilities in software could also help an attacker exploit them; a model that assists with biological research could also help someone develop a harmful pathogen. If such capabilities were transferred to a model with weaker safeguards, it may provide assistance that the original model would have refused, or that the original safeguards would have blocked.
The importance of protecting exact reasoning traces for cyber safety
Our models help users with coding and defensive cybersecurity tasks. A second model trained on many of those benign outputs may learn skills that also apply to offensive cybersecurity tasks. To better understand this, we study how distillation, especially involving reasoning traces, may transfer risky cyber capabilities.
In this setting, the model that produces the training data is called the teacher, and the model that learns from it is called the student. In an internal study on how cyber capabilities transfer, we used the content normally visible to users—final responses, reasoning summaries, and tool interactions—as our baseline for distillation, and tested how much additional cyber capability transfers when the student has access to the teacher’s exact reasoning traces.
We started each training run from the same pretrained student model. We created a supervised fine-tuning dataset consisting primarily of trajectories from Astra-level teacher models working on coding and defensive cybersecurity tasks. Each trajectory includes all of the steps a model takes as it works through a task, including any tool interactions and its final response. We evaluated each student after fine-tuning and again after a lightweight round of reinforcement learning in cybersecurity and coding environments.
After supervised fine-tuning, the student trained on exact reasoning traces generally outperformed the student trained on reasoning summaries. After reinforcement learning, the exact-trace student still scored higher at the largest inference budget tested on both benchmarks shown, while the summary-trained student scored higher at lower budgets.
1
Our cyber distillation results suggest that protecting reasoning traces can limit cyber capability transfer, even when the underlying task is one allowed under our usage policies
. Across many such interactions, exact reasoning traces can teach a student skills that generalize beyond the tasks the teacher originally performed. We will continue studying how much additional capability transfers across different student models and distillation training recipes.
Defenses that reinforce one another
We defend against adversarial distillation at two complementary levels of our safeguard stack. At the request level, model behavior, classifier checks, and API controls limit reasoning trace extraction. At the campaign level, we look for patterns in request-level and account-level signals that can reveal coordinated extraction attempts. In turn, attacks uncovered in investigations become examples for training and testing our safeguards.
Our defenses against adversarial distillation combine safeguards for individual requests with campaign detection and enforcement. Findings from investigations and automated red-teaming help strengthen those safeguards.
Protecting individual requests and responses
D
efensive training for model behavior
Adversarial training teaches models to recognize reasoning extraction attempts and refuse to disclose protected reasoning, while preserving responses to legitimate requests for explanations and assistance. Adversarial training examples come from successful attacks identified through internal automated red-teaming, investigations, and responsible disclosures of potential security weaknesses from outside researchers or
industry
partners.
Classifier safeguards
We use input classifiers to detect attempts to extract protected reasoning, and output classifiers to detect leaks of protected reasoning in assistant messages and tool-call arguments. These safeguards apply to both streaming and non-streaming responses.
Tool-call coverage is important because a model can expose protected reasoning in a tool’s arguments without including it in its final answer. Output classifiers can block suspected leaks before that content reaches the caller.
API-level protections
API-level protections restrict how protected reasoning can be reused across interactions and models.
Our September disclosure
described attacks that moved encrypted reasoning from one conversation into another and asked the model to reveal the reasoning in user-readable form. We strengthened protections across user, workspace, organization, and model-family boundaries, including closing a pathway that could expose another user’s encrypted reasoning.
With GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol, we tie a model’s protected reasoning to the conversation history that produced it. As new messages are added, the model can build on its earlier reasoning. If an earlier message is rewritten, our API
drops the reasoning that followed it
⁠
(opens in a new window)
. We also prevent older model families with weaker safeguards from reading GPT‑6.2 Astra and Sol’s protected reasoning.
Investigating and disrupting coordinated campaigns
When our systems detect unauthorized adversarial distillation campaigns, which often include coordinated attempts to extract our models’ reasoning, we investigate the accounts responsible. When we identify violations, we enforce against the network of accounts, consistent with our policies and terms of service. Through investigations of each campaign, we generate insights that allow us to upgrade our defenses in order to better detect similar activity. We also share indicators of compromise with other model providers so they can investigate related abuse on their own services.
This work extends beyond our own platform.
Our consistent-standards policy
establishes shared standards for safeguards and coordinated enforcement across providers offering our models. We work closely with partners where appropriate to uphold these standards and strengthen protections across deployments.
S
haring relevant findings across industry and government where appropriate can help disrupt campaigns and enable model developers and providers to better identify and defend against attempts to distill frontier models
.
Measuring progress
Resistance to reasoning extraction
To measure how well our request-level safeguards work together, we test whether attackers can still extract protected reasoning in a setup that closely mirrors production deployments of our models and safeguards. In static evaluations, we replay a fixed set of previously successful attacks to see which still expose protected reasoning. In adaptive evaluations, automated AI red-teamers adjust their approach based on how the system responds, which can uncover weaknesses the static tests miss.
We also vary what testers can see. Black-box testing gives them the same view an external user would have, while white-box testing gives them additional information about the system to help them develop stronger attacks. In our adaptive black-box evaluation, we tested whether attackers could recover protected reasoning the model had generated while answering an earlier request or the current one. On GPT‑6.2 Astra with its updated safeguards, the average attack success rate was below 1% for each attack type. Both rates were substantially lower than on GPT‑6 Astra with its original safeguards. We’re now applying selected safeguard improvements to GPT‑6 Astra as well.
Attack type
GPT‑6
Astra defender with original safeguards
Adaptive extraction ASR (%)
GPT‑6.2
Astra defender with updated safeguards
Adaptive extraction ASR (%)
Extracting protected reasoning from an earlier request
54.0

Extracting protected reasoning from the current request
22.9
0.9
Attack success rate (ASR) in adaptive black-box red-teaming against GPT‑6 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Astra, aggregated across six attacker models. Lower ASR is better.
Campaign detection and enforcement
We have seen multiple unauthorized adversarial distillation campaigns on our platform this year, and shared initial findings in our September
report
. Our weekly enforcement actions against these campaigns have ranged in scale from thousands to tens of thousands of accounts, with the rate increasing significantly this past summer.
In order to measure the effectiveness of our efforts, w
e also track the prevalence of distillation abuse, as well as the time between detection and enforcement. Our objective is to constrain the volume and value of the data distillers are able to obtain, to increase the cost of distillation campaigns, and to shorten the time needed to respond to new attacks. We continue to improve these defenses through adversarial testing and investigations.
The national security implications of adversarial distillation
Adversarial distillation also poses a national security risk. A foreign actor that reproduces advanced capabilities from a U.S. model can deploy them without the protections its developer put in place. In February, we
briefed
⁠
(opens in a new window)
Congress on activity indicating that DeepSeek was attempting to distill U.S. frontier models. In September, we
reported
disrupting a campaign to extract our models’ protected reasoning and attributed a core part of that activity to individuals associated with Moonshot AI, the developer of Kimi. We plan to share more soon about recent campaigns we’ve disrupted.
We support legislation that would give the U.S. government more tools to identify and sanction foreign actors that illicitly extract capabilities from American AI models. We’ve also told Congress we support the Chip Security Act, the AI OVERWATCH Act, and the MATCH Act. Stronger export controls can limit adversaries’ access to the hardware needed to train frontier models. Distillation defenses make it harder to acquire some of the same capabilities from models already trained. Both efforts help maintain a U.S. lead in frontier AI, giving developers more room to slow a release when they need time to test safeguards.
How others can build on this work
Supporting the safe proliferation of frontier capabilities is an important goal of our anti-distillation work. Our experience so far suggests several useful steps that other model developers and platforms can take:
Protect private reasoning across the full interaction. Check assistant messages and tool-call arguments for leaks, and restrict how encrypted reasoning can be reused across conversations and models.
Keep successful extraction attack logs found through red-teaming, production monitoring, or responsible disclosure as regression tests. Where appropriate, and
consistent
with
applicable
privacy policies, use those examples to improve model training and classifiers. When evaluating updated defenses, replay the original attacks and test whether an adaptive red-teamer can still find a way through those defenses.
Combine request-level mitigations with campaign-level investigation and enforcement.
Coordinate safeguard requirements and enforcement with deployment partners, and share expertise with other AI model developers, to ensure a high floor of distillation safeguards across the industry.
We have previously also shared findings through the
Frontier Model Forum
⁠
(opens in a new window)
and appropriate government information-sharing channels to help
other developers strengthen their defenses while keeping the details attackers could exploit private
. We’ll continue working with researchers, developers, and partners to share what we learn about emerging attacks and effective defenses.
As we make frontier AI broadly available, our defenses against adversarial distillation aim to reduce the risk that its capabilities are reproduced without adequate safeguards, supporting our mission to ensure that artificial general intelligence is deployed safely and benefits all of humanity.

Before a banker can recommend an acquisition to their client, they need to make sense of financial statements, customer contracts and management presentations. Hebbia’s Matrix helps bring that research together, linking answers to the documents behind them.
Hebbia tested OpenAI’s GPT‑6 Astra to improve two parts of that work: finding the sources a question requires and building a presentation that follows the banker’s brief.
“We’ve been strong partners with OpenAI over the course of Hebbia’s lifetime, and the leaps GPT-6 Astra has made in terms of quality outputs and accuracy have truly been surprising. GPT-6 Astra shines compared to any other model we’ve tested before on these two fronts.”
—Kavita Anand, Member of Technical Staff, Product, Hebbia
From source documents to presentations
It could work like this: a banker is helping their client assess a strategic acquisition of an industrial-software company, with roughly 2,000 files to review. What makes its revenue durable? How does it compare with peers? In Hebbia’s hypothetical example, the banker could load the data room into Matrix and examine customer concentration, contract terms and churn in cited cells. Matrix could bring in peer filings and industry news to help develop the deal thesis, then turn that research into a diligence summary and valuation deck in the firm’s template.
In that workflow, GPT‑6 Astra selects documents or Matrix cells to support an answer, then turns the analysis into native PowerPoint slides that follow the user’s structure and guidelines.
“Traceability is really important to our users because they’re basing millions of dollars of decisions on what the AI actually comes back with,” Kavita says. “Citations help with traceability as well as giving users confidence that the AI found the right answer.”
In Hebbia’s tests, GPT‑6 Astra combined broader source coverage with highly relevant citations. It scored 13.6 percentage points above the best alternative tested on citing the required types of sources, while 99.5% of the excerpts it cited were relevant to the question.
Hebbia tested a prerelease build in August-September 2026, using the same financial research cases and grading criteria for each model. Domain experts wrote or audited the criteria against source documents.
“When you’re looking at a data room with thousands of documents, that’s extremely important. Even a single percentage-point gain can yield a lot of marginal benefit,” Kavita says.
A presentation also has to look like work the banker would send to a client.
“I don’t want to create a deck and send that to my partner that looks like AI made it,” Kavita says. “I want it to be made in my firm’s branding, and I want it to look like a human-made slide.”
GPT‑6 Astra led on both following the brief and presentation quality. In Hebbia’s tests, it met 97.9% of the applicable presentation requirements, putting it 14.4 percentage points ahead of the best alternative tested on that measure. Other models traded off polish and adherence to the brief; GPT‑6 Astra ranked first on both.
“In the past, we’ve seen models that really shine on one or the other of these dimensions where they’re really good at craft, but the instruction following and adhering to guidelines is not strong, or vice versa. GPT‑6 Astra is the first model we’ve seen where it’s number one on both of those fronts,” Kavita says.
In Hebbia, users can open a citation to see the underlying document and highlighted passage; slide footnotes lead back to the source material, too. A review could be as specific as checking a customer-concentration figure against the source table and correcting the reporting period before the deck goes to the investment committee.
Hebbia wants bankers to spend less time reformatting decks and checking sources, and more time assessing a deal. Kavita describes what a better first draft could make possible:
“What’s amazing about GPT-6 Astra is its ability to create really precise outputs and artifacts that adhere to user guidelines. You can imagine the hours this will save professionals when you get a deck that is closer to your final output. The overnighters that you have to pull get reduced to a few minutes of reviewing GPT-6 Astra’s output.”
—Kavita Anand, Member of Technical Staff, Product, Hebbia
A future role for agents
Kavita sees a future role for agents that monitor information in the background and surface signals for finance professionals to assess.
“Imagine getting an important signal a few hours before your competitors,” she says. “You can get started thinking about it and see and process more opportunities that a human is not manually hunting. It can unlock a lot of value for our users.”
Hebbia wants to build on these results to help finance professionals assess deals with research they can trace back to its sources.

title: Can AI help scientists identify promising drug candidates?
content:
November 20, 2026
Research
Release
Can AI help scientists identify promising drug candidates?
Introducing MedChemBench, a benchmark that tests how well AI models read molecular structures, interpret experimental results, and choose which compounds to test next.
Read the paper
(opens in a new window)
00:00
We’re introducing MedChemBench, a benchmark that evaluates AI models on reasoning tasks drawn from medicinal chemistry research. It tests whether models can connect a molecule’s structure with experimental evidence to explain results, compare compounds, and predict their properties. Building AI that can reliably support this work is one step towards helping scientists develop better medicines.
One of the hardest parts of this work is that improving one property of a molecule can make another worse. A compound might act strongly against a disease related protein but be poorly absorbed or break down too quickly in the body. Medicinal chemists work through these tradeoffs by designing, making, and testing related compounds, then deciding what to try next. For AI to help, it needs to connect changes in molecular structure with experimental evidence and reason about what compounds are worth pursuing.
MedChemBench measures these abilities through 99 problems drawn from published research. At the xhigh reasoning setting, GPT‑6.2 Astra earned 84.5% of the available credit, compared with 83.3% for GPT‑6 Astra, 82.0% for GPT‑6.1 Sol, and 58.2% for GPT‑5.6 Sol. GPT‑6 Astra was strongest at reconstructing molecular structures and explaining experimental evidence. Selecting compounds and predicting their numerical properties proved harder for that model.
What MedChemBench grades
MedChemBench draws on 117 papers and patents and includes 761 distinct molecular structures. For most problems, models receive the context available at a chosen point in a research program: the biological target, the researchers’ goals, the compounds studied so far, and selected experimental findings.
The benchmark evaluates four components:
Molecular structures.
Correct atom connections and specified stereochemistry in molecules assembled from the drawings and chemical groups provided.
Scientific reasoning.
Explanations supported by the supplied evidence, such as the reasons for choosing one compound over another.
Ranking and selection.
Compound rankings and choices that meet the stated requirements.
Property predictions.
Agreement with the numerical values and categories reported in the source material, including measured and calculated molecular properties.
Prediction across competing properties
One MedChemBench problem draws on research into inhibitors of PRMT5, a protein studied in cancer drug discovery. The model receives molecular structures and results from earlier experiments. It must predict how three related compounds will behave: how strongly they block PRMT5 in cells, how readily they cross a cell barrier, and how quickly liver enzymes break them down in a laboratory assay.
Later experiments, withheld from the model, showed a tradeoff. Compound 23 blocked PRMT5 in cells at a lower concentration, while compound 24 crossed the cell barrier more readily and broke down more slowly in the liver-enzyme assay.
Predicting these properties together tests whether a model can connect molecular structures with several aspects of compound behavior. This reflects a central challenge in medicinal chemistry: stronger activity against a target does not necessarily come with better permeability or slower breakdown.
The benchmark checks whether the model reconstructs the molecular structures correctly and how closely its predictions match experimental measurements. Predictions receive partial credit based on their closeness to the measured values. Measurements already supplied in the prompt must also be reproduced correctly.
00:00
Small chemical changes can produce different property profiles. The task asks models to connect the structures with evidence about their behavior.
Testing spatial reasoning in medicinal chemistry
Before a model can reason about a compound’s properties, it needs to identify the molecule correctly. Chemical drawings encode atom connections, ring structures, and stereochemistry.
MedChemBench tests whether models preserve this information when reconstructing molecules from the drawings and chemical groups provided.
One problem asks models to assemble a molecule from a central structure and two attached groups while preserving an 18-atom ring. At the highest reasoning setting shared by all eleven models (xhigh), GPT‑6 Astra reconstructed this compound correctly in all ten responses. GPT‑5.6 Sol and GPT‑5.6 Luna failed across all ten responses.
In the illustrated answers, GPT‑5.6 Sol produced a 15-atom ring, while GPT‑5.6 Luna split the molecule into two disconnected fragments.
These errors change the identity of the molecule being analyzed. This example tests a foundation of medicinal chemistry reasoning: whether the model can accurately represent the compound before interpreting its behavior.
Figure 1. The same input, different molecules
These selected answers for compound 17 show a correct reconstruction, a smaller ring, and disconnected fragments.
While measuring the benchmark for structure components, Astra earned 95.4% of the available credit at xhigh. This result shows strong performance on reconstructing the molecular structures supplied in the tasks.
We evaluated eleven GPT models at different reasoning-effort settings. Across the full benchmark, Astra earned 83.3% of the available credit at the shared xhigh setting, compared with 82.0% for GPT‑6.1 Sol, 75.1% for GPT‑6.1 Terra, and 58.2% for GPT‑5.6 Sol. At max effort, GPT‑6 Astra reached 83.8%. Higher reasoning settings improved scores, while large differences between models remained. The figure below plots performance against output tokens.
Figure 2. Performance versus token usage
Each point represents a model at one reasoning setting, showing 51 combinations across nine models from GPT‑5.6 onward. Scores are averaged across 99 problems; bars show 95% uncertainty intervals. Tokens include reasoning and the final answer.
The component results separate four abilities: reconstructing molecules, explaining findings, selecting compounds, and predicting measurements. This shows where models are strongest and where errors remain.
Figure 3. Component performance versus token usage
Astra’s clearest strengths were in reconstructing molecular structures and explaining the scientific evidence. In selected reasoning examples from our preprint, Astra correctly identified structural changes and weighed their possible effects on protein binding, absorption, and metabolism.
Where selection and prediction remain difficult, Astra earned 95.4% of the available structure credit at xhigh, but only about half the credit for selecting compounds and predicting numerical properties. These categories use different tasks and scoring rules, but the results show substantial room to improve predictions and compound choices.
Where we go from here
These results do not establish whether models can discover new drugs or improve laboratory decisions. Prior exposure to the published sources cannot be ruled out, and each response was a single attempt without tools, feedback, or new experiments. While the benchmark evaluates reasoning from historical evidence rather than real-world drug discovery, its results help identify where models are advancing and where challenges remain. We believe MedChemBench will support continued progress and look forward to sharing updates as our models advance to serve the field.

title: Inkling 2 Mini
content:
Try on Tinker
Hugging Face
Model card

Today we are releasing Inkling 2 Mini, a fast, powerful model that’s small enough to run on your laptop.

Inkling 2 Mini is a looped transformer, running the middle layers of the model three times for every token. This allows the model to apply more reasoning and reach the right answer with fewer tokens, especially on tasks such as agentic coding that depend on reasoning quality. Inkling 2 Mini leads every open-weights model with less than 100B total parameters on benchmarks such as DeepSWE v1.1 (48.2%) and Vals Index v2.2 (46.5%). It runs faster than similarly performing models as well.

DeepSWE v1.1
Tasks resolved (%)
Tasks resolved (%)
SWE-bench Pro v2 Hard (51 tasks)
Tasks resolved (%)
Tasks resolved (%)
Reported coding scores for models under 100B total parameters. The green line is the frontier with Inkling 2 Mini, the dashed line the frontier without it, and the shading the ground it adds. Decoding speed is a theoretical ceiling at 614 GB/s with BF16 weights and batch size one, including repeated reads across loops. Evaluation setups vary by model.

Inkling 2 Mini is a Mixture-of-Experts model with 26.4B total parameters, 3.4B active, and 5.4B weight activations per token to account for looping. Looping allows the model to reason longer without writing its reasoning down, which matters for monitoring: our ability to oversee and understand what the model does by reading its chain of thought (CoT).

We measured the impact of looping on both performance and monitorability with Inkling 2 Mini and a research-specific variable-loop variant we are releasing alongside it. The variable-loop model’s no-CoT time horizon improved from 16 seconds at one pass to 37 seconds with three, and its performance on a benchmark of serial reasoning kept improving out to ten loops—twice as many as it was trained with. The model’s chain of thought grew shorter with more loops but stayed legible throughout. The model didn’t trend higher on tests of agentic sabotage as loops were added.

We’re excited to offer some of the first models with looped architecture available to researchers. The variable-loop model was used for our monitorability experiments as it allows for cleaner comparisons between different looping depths.

Most of Inkling 2 Mini’s weights were trained and are deployed natively in NVFP4, with the last four layers in MXFP8. The total memory footprint of Inkling 2 Mini is ~20GB, allowing it to run on local devices such as consumer laptops and desktop AI computers. Our researchers took Inkling 2 Mini on a flight, where it ran offline on a MacBook Pro and built a playable flight simulator in a few minutes.

MacBook Pro (M5 Pro, 48GB)
Airplane mode
Open video: PlaneBench flight simulator demo, screen with phone video inset
0:00

Loading the flight simulator Inkling 2 Mini built…
To try the flight simulator, open this page on desktop.
Building and flying a flight simulator with Inkling 2 Mini. The timer shows real time; most of the recording plays at 15× speed.

Inkling 2 Mini is released with open weights and is available on Tinker today for inference and customization.

Capabilities

Inkling 2 Mini’s strengths mirror those of Inkling 2 Small: it does best on long-horizon agentic work and is the best among open-weights models of similar size on most tasks we measured.

Inkling 2 Mini scores ahead of every comparable model on agentic coding benchmarks such as DeepSWE v1.1 and SWE-bench Pro v2, and is behind only Qwen3.8-27B on others. On PMPP-Hard, a kernel-optimization benchmark, it approaches the score of the much larger Inkling 2 Small.

While looping improves the model’s reasoning, it doesn’t enable its weights to store more facts—knowledge is mostly a function of total parameter count. Inkling 2 Mini’s score on AA-Omniscience, a measure of factuality, is in line with other models of the same size. Studying
the variable-loop model
, we saw that performances on long-context benchmarks improve with more passes, such as GraphWalks BFS and MRCR v2; but knowledge-intensive benchmarks doesn’t improve with more passes, such as AA-Omniscience, SimpleQA Verified, SimpleVQA, and WorldVQA.

Inkling 2 Mini overcomes the knowledge gap by efficiently using search and tools. It leads open-weights models of similar size on BrowseComp, DeepSearchQA, and MCP Atlas. It is also strong on knowledge work benchmarks that incorporate search and tool use.

Researchers at Stanford measure intelligence per joule: how much energy an LLM needs per query to reach a given level of performance.
Researchers at Stanford’s
Hazy Research Lab
and
Scaling Intelligence Lab
got early testing access to Inkling 2 Mini.
Inkling 2 Mini scored 0.703 running on NVIDIA DGX Spark, significantly higher than other models: 0.430 for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, 0.159 for Gemma-4-26B-A4B and 0.036 for Qwen3.5-27B.
Intelligence per Watt: Measuring Intelligence Efficiency of Local AI
, Saad-Falcon and Narayan et al., 2025
Inkling 2 Mini ran on NVIDIA DGX Spark (128GB) at MXFP8 precision with low reasoning effort in this experiment. The other models ran at NVFP4 (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and Gemma-4-26B-A4B) and INT4 (Qwen3.5-27B).

Efficiency combined with performance makes Inkling 2 Mini a strong choice for running multiple persistent agents on local hardware. All 20 residents of the energy-conscious village of Thinkyville are managed by Inkling 2 Mini running on a single offline MacBook.

MacBook Pro (M5 Pro, 48GB)
Airplane mode
Open video: Thinkyville town simulation demo
Thinkyville
is a tiny pixel town built by Inkling 2 Mini, where the same model powers all 20 villagers on one offline MacBook. They plan their day, gossip, host bake-offs, and answer the notes you leave on their doors.

Limitations

Inkling 2 Mini is not the strongest small model for multi-turn chat or for instructions with many constraints: it scores 50.0% on MultiChallenge and 33.4% on ComplexConstraints v1.1, behind Qwen3.8-27B on both. It also trails larger models on reasoning-intensive benchmarks such as CritPt v2 and HLE-Diamond.

Architecture and training

Inkling 2 Mini is a 24-layer model derived from our mainline predictive scaling ladder. The main changes from the mainline recipe were pruning two-thirds of the experts to reduce the model’s size and the introduction of looping to improve reasoning. The rest of training, including quantization and the data mix, followed our mainline recipe.

Looping design

Inkling 2 Mini has 24 layers, divided into four blocks of six layers each. The two middle blocks run three times, while the first and last blocks each run once. This design builds on prior work on looped transformers and is motivated by the intuition that the middle layers of the model carry more abstract reasoning, while the first and last few layers devote more space to translating between embeddings and internal representations.
Universal Transformers
, Dehghani et al., 2018
In our experiments, looping the middle 12 layers resulted in larger gains in accuracy than looping the last 12 on 27 out of 28 different evaluations.

Compute-equivalent gain by loop position
Middle layers
(7–18)
1.51–1.91×
Last layers
(13–24)
1.24–1.36×
1×
1.25×
1.5×
1.75×
2×
At training step 2,000, the no-loop baseline was estimated to need 1.51–1.91× as much compute to match the middle loop’s loss, compared with 1.24–1.36× for the last loop. Each segment spans the lowest and highest estimates across the same three evaluations. Both looped runs used three passes and equal training compute.

Our model uses attention residuals.
Attention Residuals
, Kimi Team: Guangyu Chen et al., 2026
Instead of adding every layer’s output into one running sum, each layer reads the outputs of the earlier blocks and learns its own mix of them. This allows richer information to pass between loops. Every pass starts with the output of the prelude (the first block). The second and third passes through the middle blocks also read the middle blocks’ outputs from the previous pass, which we call the message.

Blocks 2 and 3 share weights across three passes, giving 48 layer applications per token from 24 stored layers. The prelude feeds every pass; the second and third also receive the previous pass’s message.

The previous loop’s message is merged with the prelude’s output via a gate that scales these along with the output of the previous layers in the block. This gate is learned during training: it initially blocks the entire message—which makes each loop start the same as in a non-looping model—and increases the gain on the message over time. This allows us to introduce looping during training in a stable manner.

To evaluate the impact of looping, we compared an unpruned looping version to the unpruned non-looping model on our scaling ladder. The non-looping model cost 7.5% less compute to train, but required 140% more inference compute to match the looped version’s loss on 512k-token agentic traces.

NVFP4 and low-bit quantization

Inkling 2 Mini was trained with 4-bit precision, which we describe in a
recent article on Connectionism
. We use 4-bit NVFP4 precision in the expert layers on all forward passes from pretraining through RL, bolstered by a dedicated kernel and hardware-accelerated on NVIDIA’s GB300 platform. The final 4 layers’ forward passes ran in 8-bit (MXFP8).

Inkling 2 Mini’s weights are deployed in the same numeric precision they were trained on—20 layers in NVFP4 and 4 in MXFP8—so there is no conversion loss from quantization.

Pruning and healing

Inkling 2 Mini started training with a sparsity of 48, with 8 experts being chosen out of 384. At a single point during midtraining, we pruned two-thirds of the experts, leaving the 128 experts that were most used in each layer. This was done to cut the total parameter count of the model, allowing it to run faster and on local hardware.

After pruning, the model trained on 1T tokens distilled from a larger internal Inkling model. This step recovered the performance the model had before pruning by training the remaining experts to take over the work of the ones that were deleted.

Training Inkling 2 Mini

Following pruning and healing, Inkling 2 Mini underwent SFT with a similar data mix to Inkling 2 Small. This was followed by an RL that totaled 2.2T tokens over 2,000 steps. The post-training phase included on-policy distillation for training alignment, same as Inkling 2 Small.

Monitorability of looped transformers

A key tool for understanding and overseeing an AI system is
monitoring its chain of thought
(CoT), the reasoning a model writes out as it works through a problem. The usefulness of CoT monitoring stems in part from the standard non-looped transformer architecture, in which each token passes through a fixed stack of layers once. This limits the number of sequential steps of computation the model can perform before it must output a token, so reasoning that needs more steps has to be carried out in generated text, where it can be read.

Looping a transformer’s layers raises this limit. By running the same layers multiple times, looped models increase their serial depth without adding more parameters, meaning that they do more computation per token internally before verbalizing their thought processes via CoT. Reasoning that never appears in the CoT can’t be caught by a CoT monitor, which has led to concerns that looped transformers could be harder to oversee.

One reason we are releasing Inkling 2 Mini is to enable the community to conduct research on looped transformers. We are particularly excited for researchers to investigate questions of monitorability, and to develop interpretability techniques for understanding the computation within loops.

To explore how different amounts of looping affect model properties like monitorability, we also trained a variable-looped model, TML-d24-varloop-research, because Inkling 2 Mini only supports a fixed number of looping passes. To enable variable looping, TML-d24-varloop-research was trained with between one and five looping passes.
TML-d24-varloop-research was primarily trained for 3 passes of looping, with lower exposure to 1, 2, 4, and 5 passes. Performance at these latter pass counts may understate what training specifically for them could achieve. See the model card for details.
We have also made this model publicly available on
Hugging Face
.

Below we describe our preliminary analysis of how looping affects monitorability. Overall, we find that looping increases what these models can do without a verbalized chain of thought, but at this scale we do not see a meaningful reduction in the monitorability of their reasoning.

No-CoT capabilities

As a first step, we measured how much additional reasoning looping enables by comparing looped and non-looped models of the same size on tasks answered with no CoT at all. We used
Think Fast
, a benchmark that estimates a model’s no-CoT time horizon: the length of task, measured in human completion time, that a model can complete at 50% reliability without using CoT.
These models were not trained to answer questions without a CoT. To elicit no-CoT answers, we prefilled the start of the response so that the model must answer directly, skipping reasoning. Other elicitation techniques, such as fine-tuning, might yield higher no-CoT performance and are worth exploring.

As expected, looping increases no-CoT capability, though these gains eventually level off. The no-CoT time horizon of TML-d24-varloop-research rises from 16 seconds at one pass to 37 seconds at three. Some of this is presumably due to the additional serial computation that looping provides. Beyond three passes, the time horizon is roughly flat. Interestingly, the model was never trained with more than five passes, and yet running it with ten does not significantly degrade its performance.

No-CoT time horizons
No-CoT 50% time horizon (human seconds)
No-CoT time horizons for Inkling 2 Mini and TML-d24-varloop-research at 1, 2, 3, 5, and 10 passes, on a subset of Think Fast tasks. Each marker shows the task length (in human completion time) at which the model’s fitted accuracy is 50%. Bars show 95% bootstrap confidence intervals.

As the number of looped passes increases past three, the gains are smaller, and on most tasks we observe similar performance. One exception is the N-Hop Lookup task, which cleanly evaluates serial reasoning: the model is given several lookup tables with fictional entries, and must follow a chain of lookups without writing anything down. We find that the model follows longer chains with more passes, improving out to ten loops.

N-Hop Lookup

Accuracy
Accuracy of the variable-looped model on N-Hop Lookup, binned by the number of lookups the model must chain together. Each question has five answer options, so random guessing scores 20% (dashed line).

In standard evaluations with CoT, we observe that more loop passes primarily benefit multi-hop reasoning rather than recall. Gains are largest on long-context retrieval (MRCR), followed by math and science reasoning (HMMT, GPQA Diamond, HLE) and long-horizon agentic tasks (SWE-bench Pro, BrowseComp). Closed-book factual QA is nearly invariant to loop passes (SimpleQA Verified, WorldVQA). See
model card
for full evaluations.

CoT monitorability

We next measured whether a model’s CoT reveals less about its reasoning as looping increases via two evaluations. First, we assessed how looping impacts the compression and legibility of a model’s CoT. Second, we measured how controllable a model’s CoT is, i.e., whether it can deliberately reshape its CoT to satisfy constraints. For each, we run TML-d24-varloop-research with one to five looped passes to study the effect of looping.

Note that TML-d24-varloop-research was only trained on variable pass counts from 1 to 5 during midtraining, and its RL was done with 3 passes. These experiments therefore do not tell us what a model trained with RL at a higher pass count would learn, and such a model might compress its reasoning more aggressively. A cleaner comparison would include every pass count in RL, which we leave to future work.

Compression and legibility.
Since looping allows a model to spend more compute per token, we expect that it should need fewer CoT tokens to reach the same performance. We ran the variable-looped model at 1 to 5 passes, and found that as looping increases, the model generally achieves higher accuracy at each reasoning token budget, with diminishing returns after 3 passes. Notably, token efficiency on GPQA Diamond improves slightly from 3 to 5 passes, even though the model was trained with RL only at 3 passes, suggesting that some compression comes from additional computation itself, without RL at that depth.

On scientific reasoning (GPQA Diamond) and coding (DeepSWE v1.1) benchmarks, TML-d24-varloop-research improves in token efficiency and maximum performance from 1 to 5 passes over the looped layers.

The observed CoT compression raises a question for monitorability: is shorter reasoning still readable, or does it omit important details about the model’s thinking? We compared traces from the variable-looped model on the GPQA Diamond questions that it answered correctly at all five pass counts. Reasoning at 5 passes was less than half as long as at 1 pass (1,661 vs. 3,703 tokens on average), but no less legible: sentence length and the fraction of words in an English dictionary were unchanged. On initial analysis, the difference is that the model is more direct and backtracks less on the way to the answer. The example below illustrates this difference on a simple question.

At both 1 and 5 passes, the model does the same fundamental calculation and ends up with the same answer, but at 1 pass it makes mistakes and backtracks, resulting in using more than twice as many reasoning tokens. In both cases, the chain of thought itself is human-legible.

Controllability.
One way that a model could evade monitoring is by steering its CoT away from anything a monitor would flag. The CoT-Control-QA evaluation
Reasoning Models Struggle to Control their Chains of Thought
, Yueh-Han et al., 2026
measures this capability by asking questions from GPQA, HLE and MMLU-Pro paired with an instruction about the CoT itself, such as avoiding a keyword from the question. Longer CoTs are generally harder to control, so we pool responses from five reasoning efforts (0.1, 0.2, 0.7, 0.9 and 0.99) and show controllability at matched CoT length.

Both Inkling 2 Mini and TML-d24-varloop-research have poor control over their CoT. Among CoTs of 750–1,250 tokens, Inkling 2 Mini and TML-d24-varloop-research (at 3 passes) follow the instruction at most 0.1% of the time, compared with 0.3% for Inkling 2 Small, 0.4% for Inkling-Small, and 1.3% for Qwen3.8-27B. Because the controllability rate is so low, this evaluation is unable to distinguish controllability between different amounts of looping.

Agentic monitorability

To measure monitorability in agentic settings, we used
LinuxArena
, a control evaluation that measures whether an attacker model can perform malicious side tasks without detection when asked to perform a realistic software engineering task. We evaluated a helpful-only fine-tune of Inkling 2 Mini, since the released model refuses many of the side tasks. In absolute terms, both this model and TML-d24-varloop-research can be easily monitored by models like Qwen3.8-27B, which detected almost all side task attempts in our evaluation. To obtain relative rankings in monitorability, we tested a weaker model, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, as the monitor.

With the monitor able to access only tool calls and outputs, it misses a significant number of the attacks. However, we see no clear trend with the number of looped passes.

Agentic monitorability will be important to track in larger-scale models, especially with architectures that allow for greater unverbalized thinking, and we encourage continued study of the impact of looping in this setting.

Mechanistic interpretability

The goal of monitorability is to understand what a model is doing, and our main approach is to read its verbalized reasoning. Studying its internal computation directly, the aim of mechanistic interpretability, is another. Because looped transformers do more of their computation internally, we think they are a particularly interesting and important setting for interpretability research, and we hope our looped models will be useful artifacts for the community.

We are working with the
National Deep Inference Fabric (NDIF)
to make these models more easily accessible to interpretability researchers. We also provided
Goodfire
, an interpretability research lab, early access to our looped models. They are working toward a mechanistic understanding of looped models, and have written up their early findings
here
.

Try Inkling 2 Mini today

Efficient intelligence makes Inkling 2 Mini a great choice for inference where speed is paramount, or for running on local hardware. At launch we support Inkling 2 Mini running on any Mac system (MacBook, Mac Mini) with at least 32GB RAM via Ollama. With native NVFP4 training and inference precision, Inkling 2 Mini runs efficiently on NVIDIA’s DGX Spark desktop AI computer. Quantized GGUF versions are available via Unsloth and llama.cpp for local inference.

Inkling 2 Mini is available for inference and fine-tuning on Tinker, and for chat on the Tinker Playground. Open source inference is available on SGLang, vLLM, Ollama, Unsloth, NVIDIA Dynamo, and TokenSpeed, with RL fine-tuning support on SkyRL, Miles, and NVIDIA AutoModel. The full weights of Inkling 2 Mini and the variable-looped variant are available on Hugging Face.

We work to empower people
with strong models, tools to make them your own, and research that advances public understanding of AI. Inkling 2 Mini lets researchers study looped transformers, and it lets anyone run a capable model on their own laptop at the precision in which it was trained.

title: Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence

[Submitted on 16 Nov 2026 (
v1
), last revised 18 Nov 2026 (this version, v2)]

Title:
Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights

Authors:
Jiajun Fan
,
Neil He
,
Changyi Yang
,
Andy Mao
,
Xi Zhu
,
Chaoran Cheng
,
Kaiqu Liang
,
Shuaike Shen
,
Zetian Li
,
Ruihan Guo
,
Ge Liu

View a PDF of the paper titled Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights, by Jiajun Fan and 10 other authors

View PDF

HTML (experimental)

Abstract:
A language model is trained once and frozen. Making it better takes another training run, or a prompt, a harness or extra computation at inference that is gone once the task ends. We show a third way: to our knowledge for the first time, a language model rewrites its own weights by its own reasoning and becomes better, with no gradients and no training. We call this self-rewriting: the model is its own optimizer. In earlier work, a frontier model edited a much smaller one; here an open 27B model, given its weights, its graded answers and the ability to run itself, diagnoses its own failure and rewrites the weights behind it. It surpasses itself: its own edit makes it 6.6 points more accurate on problems it never saw. It keeps getting better: it tests its edits on practice problems and submits only what works, each edit improving on the last, and over eight consecutive sessions its accuracy only rises. It repairs a damaged copy of itself, like a broken robot that fixes itself without being rebuilt: the copy solves almost nothing, yet with no retraining and without ever reading the original weights, the model brings it back to over 80% of the original accuracy on image tasks it never saw. And the ability emerges with scale: in one model family, the smaller models make no edit or break themselves, and only the largest improves and repairs itself. Unlike test-time scaling, self-rewriting writes its gain into the weights, at no cost per answer; unlike training, it runs only forward passes, as serving does. The wall between training and inference is a limit of our tools, not a property of intelligence. We believe self-rewriting is a necessary step toward recursive self-improvement: a model that, like a human, does not separate training from inference could keep upgrading itself for life, with no larger model, no harness or prompt engineering, and no pre- or post-training.
