title: Vibecoding an inference chip
content:
One of the more entertaining things about programming recently is that coding agents let me work in entirely new domains by giving me access to new programming languages and paradigms. Lately, that has meant hacking on hardware, now that writing low-level software is much easier. So, in this blog post, I’m going to try to recount the experience of vibe coding an FPGA, going through a series of “oh shit” moments several times, and giving myself a new appreciation for what’s possible if you have a large token budget (thanks YC) and interesting problems to point the models at.
I overheard some founders recently talk about how FPGAs work. I’ll admit I was relatively naive about them. I’d never really experimented with them in my startup or in college, so I knew little about them before. The basic idea I was familiar with: you can program a circuit into a reprogrammable chip. So rather than having a general purpose computing architecture (like a CPU) you can have a reprogrammable one, i.e. the configuration loaded onto the chip determines how its logic and routing are connected, and that (in theory) enables performance advantages. I also know that it took a mountain of C++ to write and involved manually analyzing waveforms for simulation and verification. I had never done this before though and it seemed cumbersome.
That’s about what I knew going into this.
Naturally, my ML brain thought “could we use these for AI inference”. I’m not the first to think this — there are a few repos attempting to port ML models to FPGAs on Github. But I hadn’t actually seen a writeup on whether coding agents are good at writing the low level C++ and Verilog code to program them and verifying the outputs so that they actually run accurately. (Spoiler alert, they are incredible at programming them.)
So I decided I needed to get my hands on one. AWS has F2 instances with FPGA hardware, and that seemed easier than going and buying physical hardware, so I asked Codex to spin up a reservation and got cooking. It had a relatively limited memory of 16 GB of FPGA HBM. Around the same time, I was working with the DeepGrove founders who were discussing their new ternary weight architecture that is well suited for memory limited cases. It’s SOTA on Mac hardware with actual agentic tool calling, so I figured why not, let’s see if I can get this working on an FPGA and fast enough to be useful.
What followed was a cloud agent running in Conductor for several days with me mostly just encouraging it periodically while it both (1) got a model fully running and (2) increased its speed by 33× from the first full-model bit-exact baseline to get it to a real-time relevant speed. It was one of the most mind blowing autoresearch loops I’ve run, ultimately writing roughly 3M lines across the experiment history and parsing 30M lines of output files, burning only $10,000 in Claude and OpenAI tokens to run hundreds of experiments. Most of the code is C++ and some Verilog. It’s been probably a decade since the last time I wrote any serious amount of C++ and I’ve never written Verilog. I honestly don’t know the first thing about Verilog. Most of my prompts were not particularly clever: they consisted mostly of me saying things like “you’re a superintelligent model, time to be more creative” and “let’s go for 2x faster, you got this”. Sometimes I brought some ML knowhow like “hey it’s time to consider speculative decoding” or “why is that running on CPU, you should port it”. But for the most part, it was just vibes and I’m pretty sure that with enough time the model would have figured out those things. Also, it seemed that both Astra and Opus (new Fable wasn’t out yet) were pretty capable at this and I could use them interchangeably. I’m sure someone has a good benchmark for which is smarter but both passed my smart-enough threshold.
The chart follows the measured optimization sequence:
6 → 213 tokens/s
, or
33×
the baseline.
At one point, around when it got to 10 TPS, I messaged the DeepGrove founders about this, and they replied surprised that it was working so easily, saying they had tried this a few months back and the models were not quite good enough to be particularly effective. They sent me a prompt that summarizes some of their lessons and I copy-pasted it into my session to see if it’d matter. It was essentially the most significant piece of actual guidance I added to this session. The prompt is reproduced below.
The coding agent diligently considered these asks, but it didn’t seem to make all that much of a difference qualitatively. Indeed, when I asked it later to read all of the logs and determine which of these instructions it actually used, it said:
In other words, for most of the actual design ideas it is unclear but there is good reason to believe the model would have figured them out, especially because it came up with them many cycles later after several compaction cycles. But the process advice was useful immediately for getting to hardware results sooner and increasing iteration speed. In other words, the humans are still useful at defining how to iterate fast and what correctness looks like, and the agents are great to manage the exploration.
Here are the changes the autoresearch loop found. Interestingly, it’s mostly a series of modest improvements that compound 1.5x ish every time, rather than one or two giant ones.
It’s difficult to do a 1:1 comparison across these configurations. I didn’t run the same autoresearch loop on every alternative, and I assume there is more performance to extract if I did. The point is to show how slow the FPGA was in its first implementation, and how far the optimization loop took it.
The measurements below are from November 15 on AWS, replaying the same
8-chat × 3-turn benchmark
. Prices are the on-demand rates recorded with that experiment. “Exact turns” counts outputs that matched the pinned CPU reference. The GPU implementations are included for context but did not satisfy the same bit-exact criterion but are pretty close in practice.
This is one generation starting with a 16-token prompt and continuing until the 8,192-token context is full:
8,176 generated tokens
. The five middle columns show decode speed in
tokens/s
at the indicated context length for several generations of iteration. The last column is wall-clock time for the whole run/
* For r8 and r9, the first two columns come from separate, shorter runs generating 2,032 tokens. The other columns come from the full-context run.
r9 improves short-context speed, while the complete long-context run is roughly tied with r8.
These examples come from the final r9 image.
246 tokens · 229.7 tokens/s · 1.16 s end to end
140 tokens · 220.0 tokens/s · 0.76 s end to end
System prompt: “You are a helpful assistant. Think briefly before you answer, then reply clearly and concisely.”
This was a fun project. I’m not sure I’m ever going to use this specific chip architecture in this specific way, and I’m certainly not claiming that an 8,192-token-context model running on an FPGA is the way I’d recommend anyone use something like this in production. But it’s pretty epic that this
just works
. Capability like this completely shifts the overton window for what a committed team of engineers can work on. It should mean that entirely new types of ideas (scientific discoveries, products, startups) are possible if you can point the models in the right direction. I’m excited to see what everyone builds.

title: The stochastic parrots have apparently proved the Riemann Hypothesis
content:
I’m in California to visit
Oratomic
and then
Inkhaven
.  I woke up this morning to the news that Levent Alpöge says that he’s gotten Anthropic models to
prove the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis
, producing
17.4 million (!!) lines of Lean code
.
At a dinner last night, someone asked me “so, how much longer until an AI proves the Riemann Hypothesis?  Still several more years?”  I replied, don’t be sure of such things anymore.  After all, AI has already proved that the nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function are
at most 3/8 away from the critical line
(
Quanta
just published its article on that breakthrough yesterday!), and that already carries most of the implications for number theory that a full proof of RH would have.  So who the hell knows what else is possible, and how quickly?
For those tuning in from home, the
Riemann Hypothesis
says (in its easiest-to-understand version) that the number of prime numbers from 1 to n is very close to what it would be if each integer x>1 had an independent 1/ln(x) probability of being prime, up to a standard statistical error term that never exceeds Õ(√n).  While we’ve known since 1896 that the number of primes from 1 to n is asymptotic to n/ln(n) (that’s the famous
Prime Number Theorem
), you could’ve imagined the deviations being much larger.
David Hilbert famously said, “If I were to awaken after having slept for a thousand years, my first question would be: Has the Riemann Hypothesis been proven?”  Meanwhile G. H. Hardy, on a ship that he feared might sink, sent his colleagues a telegram claiming to have proven RH, so that if the worst came to pass, at least the world might believe that a proof sank with him.
Many will of course question whether the proof announced today will stand.  They’ll point out that, despite how heavily the world is now “lean-ing” on it, the Lean formal verification system still has issues, from kernel bugs (which have, in the past, allowed proofs of 0=1) to uncertain soundness of the underlying type theory.  In my view, these issues can and should urgently be fixed!  Until they are, a sufficiently motivated AI could almost certainly exploit them to prove a false statement!
All the same, I see zero indications that that’s happening right now.  I note that, so far, not one of the AI results with Lean certificates has needed to be retracted (while several without Lean certificates
have
needed to be). So I’m not 100% sure, but my bet is that the proof will stand.
Mathematicians of course won’t be satisfied with 17 million lines of Lean.  They’ll be satisfied when, and only when, they’re able to explain and distill and reconstruct the ideas for themselves.  And that will probably take years, since human mathematicians move only at biological speeds.  And while they’re working on it, how many
more
such wonders will there be, in this age of wonders and terrors?
My 9-year-old son, informed that RH was proved, replied that he’s not even surprised at this point.  Maybe you need to have come of age in the human math era to be surprised by such things.
The P=?NP problem now moves firmly into place as the Final Boss of the Math We’ve Cared About, the position I always thought it should occupy.  But for how much longer?  For how much longer will
anything
last that we currently take for granted?
It was only a couple days ago that my wife and I had the following conversation:
Dana:
I turned off the irrigation, yet somehow water in our house is still leaking. We need to…
Me:
Look, a lot of the smartest people I know now think that recursive self-improvement and the end of the entire known world are coming in 12-18 months. This leak…
Dana:
We should still fix the leak.

title: Microsoft announces Windows Server 2028 with hardened security
content:
Microsoft announces Windows Server 2028 with hardened security

By
Sergiu Gatlan

November 18, 2026

04:24 AM

Microsoft has announced Windows Server 2028, the next major release of its server operating system, at the Ignite 2026 conference on Tuesday.

This new Windows Server version ships with a
hardened Server Core configuration by default
and a new security baseline that allows admins to relax specific settings.

"A hardened Server Core configuration by default and a new security baseline help reduce the work of establishing a secure baseline from day 1,"
said Neil Hinnant
, Director of Windows Server & I/O Fabrics PM.

"Trusted Launch extends protection to virtual machines, guaranteeing boot integrity across your VM fleet, and Confidential VM support begins a journey to support integrity-protected runtimes on supported CVM hardware."

The list of hardened Server Core settings is extensive and includes:

Identity and authentication
: Credentials are hard to steal and hard to reuse: Kerberos over NTLM, LSASS protected, strong passwords and account lockout, no consumer accounts.

Network exposure
: The server talks only over signed, encrypted, authenticated channels: SMB signing and encryption, the firewall on in every profile, legacy name resolution and unauthenticated RPC off.

Cryptography
: TLS is limited to modern cipher suites, key exchange is hybrid post-quantum (ML-KEM), and stored keys are strongly protected.

Privilege and admin access
: Admins approve elevation, powerful rights stay with Administrators, Guests cannot sign in, and installers cannot elevate on their own.

Platform and code integrity
: The sign-in process runs only Microsoft-signed code. Signature validation is stricter. The paging file is encrypted.

Remote access and observability
: RDP with NLA and TLS, WinRM without Basic, Digest, or unencrypted traffic, advanced audit with command lines, PowerShell script block logging, and larger event logs.

However, the company said it's still working on adding NTLM blocking, hardware-backed platform protection, print and RPC hardening, and more to the hundreds of security settings enabled from first boot.

Windows Server 2028 also offers simplified administration and management at scale through Intune management for Windows Servers, bringing endpoint-management workflows for configuration, compliance, applications, and updates to eligible, persistent servers.

It also improves performance with native NVMe storage enabled by default, NVMe over TCP and RDMA transports, and the ability to boot from ReFS.

Last but not least, it introduces new AI accelerators, including the ability to deploy and configure inference environments, manage accelerated hardware, and support open-weight and custom models (including Windows ML, Foundry Local, vLLM, and Llama.cpp).

Admins who want to test Windows Server 2028 can
register for the Windows Insider Program for Windows Server
or apply to enroll in the
Windows Server Technology Adoption Program (TAP)
for earlier access.

"This major release raises the security and access bar, accelerates enterprise infrastructure, and simplifies management at scale," Hinnant added. "It also begins our long term investments extending Microsoft Foundry to bring AI inference to fleets of local token factories, giving customers more choices to put the right intelligence in the right place with the right cost structure."

title: DreamCoder: Coding harness and IDE from the author of Mastering Emacs
content:
It’s been a little bit quiet around these parts; sorry about that. I’ve been really busy for the past fifteen months with a major project that I am finally ready to formally release. So I’d like to talk about that project, and also a potted history of AI and Emacs.

It’s called
DreamCoder
, an AI coding harness that is very different from the ones you’re probably familiar with already.

I installed Claude Code a few days after its first release some time in May 2025. I put some coins in the slot machine and I put it to work building a complex piece of enterprise middleware I’d built several times in my career. Wow.. watching this thing chomp its way through the project with that chaotic, early Sonnet energy. It was far, far from perfect; it required a lot of human steering, input and correction, but the speed advantage was undeniable, and seeing it jump between disparate programming languages, frameworks and theoretical and practical programming from one turn to the next was just such a sight to behold.

One thing that struck me with Claude Code is that it was the first terminal application I’d used in a long time. I found it an odd choice for a coding agent; then everyone else copied them and made their own terminal coding agents.

Why on earth do I have to stare at a shoe rack-sized terminal window to do this? Sure there are GUI versions also; but the terminal interface remains the primary modality for most of these tools. Most GUIs, and most harnesses now have them also, are second-class citizens. And they all look the same. A boring sidebar with chat headings and a chat pane is what most of them look like.

But a serious coder needs more than that. Even a casual user will bristle when they try to copy and paste multi-line text in a terminal.

So in May 2025 I decreed that I would build a better harness, and surely now that I have AI this should not take more than 2 or 3 months to build.

And so, after 15 months of work, and endless UI and backend iterations, culminating in a successful beta test, I am now ready to release DreamCoder, which is I think the acme of what a coding harness should be.

DreamCoder is a frontier coding harness with a tiling window manager that runs in your browser on all 3 platforms.

Before I get into the meat and potatoes of all of that, I want to talk about AI history and Emacs’s role in it.

Let’s roll back time to the 1950s.

Past

Emacs and LISP, if you did not know, both have a special place in the annals of AI history.

John McCarthy was an AI researcher at MIT, and in the 1950s he set out to create the
Advice Taker
, a piece of software that envelops a framework for what a basic human should know that he called
commonsense reasoning
using “mathematical logic”. His postulation was that if we can express with symbolic precision all the aspects of what constitutes humanity like ordinary facts about life, that we can set in motion the rudiments of AI.

In the 50s there was little in the way of computer software that could do this. To formalize such a system you need a lot of data, rigorously formatted, and a method of manipulating the data. The data and code itself may intertwine
recursively
, and so an ordinary programming language would not work.

To help him achieve this, McCarthy created the LISt Processing (LISP) language made up of two facets: M-expressions, a functional language in the vein of Algol; and S-expressions, designed for symbolic data representation, and never intended as a method of writing code. S-expressions were dolled up with parentheses. M-expressions meanwhile used square brackets to visually separate the two. Uniquely, the language specification had an
eval
feature that would prove that the language is also a universal Turing machine… if only McCarthy had the means to do so. It was theoretical because McCarthy lacked, in time, staff and money, what he needed build this recursive evaluator that can take as input its own world state and evaluate it alongside new expressions, a fact made even more apparent by the sheer complexity of his M-expression language and the limited resources he had at the time.

Steve Russell who worked with him proved him wrong the way most young people do: by just doing it. Russell wrote the first LISP Interpreter with a working
eval
function, but M-expressions got sidelined; the imperative, procedural nature of programming got squished into S-expressions instead. They had to hand roll the language on paper then punch it into cards and then batch run them. Eliding M-expressions was a simple matter of pragmatism. And so LISP was born. And through several accidents of history, M-expressions never gained traction. M-expressions live on in Wolfram’s Mathematica, but few other places.

Much later, McCarthy eventually conceded that,

“One can even conjecture that LISP owes its survival specifically to the fact that its programs are lists, which everyone, including me, has regarded as a disadvantage.”

S-expressions were always intended as the storage format with a bridge language to manipulate them. But by pushing evaluation into the same symbolic representation format as the data, we have what we call LISP today. That is why LISP is so unique. Consider a simple calculator.
(+ 2 2)
can simultaneously represent an expression that we want to compute,
two plus two
, or perhaps a ledger of record of a calculation we have already done.

McCarthy never built the Advice Taker in its purest form. He and his team ran into many philosophical, mathematical and computational walls that kept them occupied for a long time.

The idea behind the Advice Taker was simple. If you want to go somewhere in your car, you can symbolically express this by building a chain of narrative facts – kinda like a flowchart, but as small snippets of rules and facts, not as one grand design.

The system would automatically resolve ambiguities, and all the logician had to do was capture the microcosm of the world he wished to represent:

(at me home)

(walkable home car)
(walkable home driveway)
(drivable car shop)

And so on. If you’re a student of Computer Science you’ll see echoes of Prolog here. The intent was simple: if we can symbolically express the world around us, we can
advise
that symbolic world with real-life facts, and have the automaton that uses this reified symbolic world change with it.

But the axiomatic complexity of a world model would never survive an encounter with a 3-year-old child. Every axiom you write begets a new one — so you can walk to your front door? Well what if the door is locked? Or what if your car is parked on the street and not in your drive way?

A rules-based order of the world is a tender, beautiful one; but it is hard to build. It’s a fractal of ever-more specific and pedantic rules that conspire against you, just as you think you have a soluble world, typed and ready.

Anyone who has ever written Prolog knows exactly what
that
feels like!

I have my own personal story to add to this. In the 90s as a teenager I got a summer internship at a business that built banking software. They clearly didn’t know what to do with us teenaged interns, so on our first day they crammed us in a room and split us into teams and told us to build a flow chart for assembling a bike. Team exercise or something. Best one wins. We were told to be as specific and explicit as possible and account for as many conditions as we could think of, and the poor employees who had to mind us did their best to help. I distinctly recall losing because in my flowchart I forgot to open the box the disassembled bike came in.

McCarthy meanwhile eventually moved on and set up his own AI lab at Stanford, but the
idea
of the Advice Taker lived on.

In the late 70s Stallman and Steele create EMACS (Editing MACroS), also at MIT’s AI Lab, a set of building blocks on top of TECO, a famously inscrutable text editor. TECO did not update the screen by default; you had to toggle that on and hope your edits worked. You typed out terse keyboard commands, crossed your fingers and hoped you got it right, and then you patiently waited for your text manipulation to take effect. Rinse and repeat until you got what you wanted.

Stallman and Steele wanted more: they wanted macros so they could automate tedium of typing all that line noise. This strand of augmentation and later on self-modification is of course a unifying theme in Emacs today. The history of Emacs is long; but its outcome is known to us. I am typing this very article in Richard Stallman’s Emacs.

McCarthy’s Advice Taker left its mark in a subtle but indelible way. Warren Teitelman built the ADVISE system in his thesis with a cool title that reads like something out of a pulpy 1970s sci-fi novella:
PILOT: A Step Toward Man-Computer Symbiosis
. Teitelman, he later said, was deeply inspired by McCarthy’s original idea of
advising systems
.

In his thesis, he describes a method of arresting a function call and inserting code before or after it is run. He was tired of editing other people’s LISP code by hand, and wanted a way of modifying their code without touching it directly. He built and rebuilt his system several times over the years, culminating in his ADVISE system in Interlisp, a structured editor and language runtime for manipulating LISP code and data. Interlisp eschewed plain text files; instead, you manipulated the
tree
at a high level of abstraction with explicit instructions like “move X list to Y position”. You can see my own attempts at merging structured editing with plaintext editing in
Combobulate
.

MIT AI hackers eventually implemented Teitelman’s ADVISE system from his PILOT thesis in their own versions of Emacs. Later, it was canonized in Chalupsky’s own 1992 re-implementation in Emacs Lisp that lives on (
M-x find-library advice.el
) as one of Emacs’s
advice
systems to this day.

What began as an idea for expressing automata using symbolism in an as-yet theoretical language in the 1950s culminated in a system for dynamically altering functions in GNU Emacs in the 1990s. What an unlikely lineage and history.

A cast-iron system made of stern rules cannot spawn general intelligence.

Symbolism and AI did not end with advising functions. There were many attempts at symbolic intelligence. Terry Winograd’s
SHRDLU
; Marvin Minsky’s
Frame Systems
; and even Emacs’s ELIZA-style
M-x doctor
all make use of symbolic “AI”.

None of them brought us closer to the AI that proponents of symbolic AI hoped they would.

In hindsight that seems obvious.

Writing a LISP macro
just so
will not produce artificial intelligence; nor will a carefully crafted web of rules and symbolic algebra suddenly spark intelligence. We know that today, but for a generation of computer scientists it felt like the future we have all read about in science fiction novels: a perfect, logical intelligence. A
positronic brain
. Robby the Robot; HAL 9000; C-3PO; Data; or the Speedies and Cuties from
I, Robot.
The unifying theme of these science fiction stories is they are automatons that follow strict rules — they obey Asimov’s three Laws of Robotics.

Every turn of hardware and software brought them ever closer to one day realizing the vision of an artificial intelligence, captured in neat axioms and LISP S-expressions, and modified in tools like Emacs.

It is surprising that symbolic AI, the vanguard movement for artificial intelligence, would instead dissipate into the wider body of Computer Science and programming as tools, languages and concepts, but not survive as a viable method of achieving AI.

Perhaps we always knew. Because at some point – even if we never really fully internalized it – we discovered that a ductile system that is shaped by its master’s desires is a tool that survives the ages because it remains eternally useful.

A cast-iron system made of stern rules cannot spawn general intelligence.

For all the mathematical purity, beauty even, of the idea of a clockwork mind that is introspectable and malleable and its behavior expressed as S-expressions and interpreted by elegant algorithms and honed macros, we can, through the benefit of hindsight – now that we
do
have AI through other means – see that it was not to be.

The argument in favor of ductility is especially poignant when you learn of
the Connectionists
, which sounds like a bad 1960s band, but was in fact a loose coalition of people who believed firmly that neural networks, not symbolic AI, were the path to success. The
Connectionist
viewpoint was
deeply
unpopular in AI academia of that era, and funding for it was scarce.

Frank Rosenblatt invented the Perceptron, a foundational concept in neural networks, in 1957. Before Rosenblatt died in 1971, Marvin Minsky, an authority in the AI movement at MIT and a leading proponent of Symbolism, knifed the idea of Perceptrons and neural networks in a book he co-authored with Seymour Papert. They named the book, which they also dedicated to Rosenblatt,
Perceptrons
. The book deftly explains the mathematics of Perceptrons but undercuts their possible utility by showing that a single-layer Perceptron cannot represent an XOR gate. It was a deliberately obtuse reading of what neural networks could and could not do. With one additional hidden layer, a network
can
represent an XOR gate. It was a sneaky thrust of the stiletto: Minsky’s claims were overstated. A fact that was not lost on anybody in the Symbolic or Connectionist camps.

It’s disputed if the Perceptrons book led to the first AI winter in the 1970s. It certainly did not help. But funding for many AI research paths dried up in the 1970s.

The Connectionist movement was vindicated in the long run. They lost the battle then, but they won the war, and the fruits of their research eventually gave us AI.

The ductility we so prize in our software and tools today is antithetical to a strict, symbolic world model spun of axioms and facts that we hoped would one day birth AI. Yet to try and give birth to this world they had to build the most ductile tools of them all: LISP and, from that, also software like Emacs. The ultimate hacker’s tool.

It is ironic then that a neural network, a crude facsimile of how a brain works, a construct that is by its nature ductile and malleable, won out in the end.

So I feel a profound sadness that I started out programming DreamCoder in Emacs, the most extensible editor in the world, by hand back in May 2025, only to see DreamCoder write itself… in DreamCoder today.

Future

I am still sad, but I also know that our industry completely reinvents itself every decade or two. This is my second career upheaval. Most programmers today have not been around long enough to go through it themselves. So I feel for them that this especially massive quake is their first encounter with how unsentimental our industry is.

But for all the sadness, I wake up every day with a feeling of optimism that I have not felt in a very long time.

I finally get to build again, no longer weighed down by my decades of knowledge and experience that held my ambition in check. I truly have not felt this liberated since I was a teenager programming in Delphi, blissfully unaware that the things I was busy building were impossible for a self-taught teenager to ever realize. I see this reflection in others: the best programmers I know also love AI. Amateurs also revel in AI’s capabilities, happy that they can finally solve problems they could never afford to pay a programmer to do for them.

I must admit that building software has, over the years, gotten a lot more complex, with an ever-larger share of that work being repetitive tedium. This is more so with hobby software – as I do not get paid to do it, so I do not have a moral duty to see it through – where I’d do all the fun bits leaving just the enervating, boring and soul-crushing parts behind. Do you have a projects folder full of sad, abandoned projects like I do?

Now I can craft in abundance. AI has freed up a lot of toil but I somehow still find myself busy all day doing real work.

Building a coding harness is perhaps the closest I will get to the optimism all those researchers and scientists must have felt in the 1970s and 1980s. They hoped that with a little bit more work, their logical rules would kindle a new intelligence. Fifty years on, and I can simply tell DreamCoder to improve itself and watch as it changes before me. I can ask the AI running inside it to analyze the changes I have made to its tools and prompt and have it adjust them accordingly. It feels like science fiction; the very thing the researchers of yesterday strove to build. Yet we really do live in this reality now.

Taste is a scarce, human resource.

So.
DreamCoder
. Let me address the 900 lb gnu in the room: DreamCoder is not an Emacs-related application. The reason is unfortunately one of economics and access: I want to build an AI coding harness for everyone. But don’t worry: I have some cool plans for DreamCoder + Emacs, and AI + Emacs more generally going forward. So stay tuned.

But what about all those other coding harnesses? Well, most of those harnesses all suffer from the same mistakes. It is a problem that is not unique to coding harnesses or the people who make them, but a constraint
we
all labor under, and one that is not easily replaced by AI:

Taste is a scarce, human resource.

And for all the bounty of AI, it still requires a human to persevere and to see things through. One thing intensive use of AI coding has taught me is that we’re going to need a lot of computer programmers who know what they’re doing going forward. I believe this is so, because let us be honest, most people do not want to program computers, even if that computer can actually do the bulk of the work for them. It requires a steady hand to build reliable software; that has not changed.

Therefore, if we programmers have to spend a lot of our time interacting with AI, then the tool we do it with should be ‘human-centric’ in its design, and it should take advantage of all the modern features we have at our disposal.

Back in May 2025 I took a look at all the tooling and said “no, thank you.” Today I look at the landscape and I feel pretty much the same.

And I think I am not the only one who feels that way. Most of these coding harnesses, to me, feel bristly. They shouldn’t be; but they are like that because we are at an important inflection point where no one really knows what the future looks like. We’re all just… fumbling around a bit. It’s an exciting time to build software, even if we don’t quite know what the world will look like a few years hence.

One thing I am adamant about is that DreamCoder must be a powerful, frontier-class coding harness. That means it should have all the features you’d expect from that: backgroundable sub agents, MCP servers, cache efficiency, and all that stuff. Check.

Sub-agents

MCP servers

Your own agents

Terminals beside chats

The frontier-harness basics. Click any of them to see it full size.

But that stuff quickly recedes into the background because, you know, it just works. Day to day you will dart between chats and terminals and whatnot, and you need an interface that accommodates that. Emacs is a tiling window manager; so is DreamCoder. DreamCoder’s window manager is a little bit cleverer than most window managers as every pane has a minimum, comfortable and maximum size. The window manager will therefore ensure windows always fit snugly on your screen, and you’ll never end up in a situation where windows are tiny and unreadable. It has a sophisticated constraint satisfaction solver that tries to balance your demand for a new window (“open a terminal”) with the challenge of keeping your visible panes roughly the same size. If DreamCoder can’t wedge in a new pane, it’ll punt one to the hidden window bar. Just click it to resurface it, or hover it to see what it’s doing; it’s a live view.

Panes are made to fit; if a new pane must evict an old one, it is pushed to the hidden window box.

Avy-style selection and embark-style actions.

Because of my Emacs roots, I think a good tool must be keyboard-friendly. Because it runs on a browser you get the mouse for free of course. But smacking the tab button over and over is a frustrating user experience in complex webapps, and doubly so a tiling window manager: where exactly are you going to end up when you tab from one window to the next? To combat that, I built an avy-style window and “point of interest” selector for chats. Tap a key and pick from a selection of “embark”-like actions such as clicking links or opening pictures. It’s a work in progress, but I think it works well.

Familiar type-to-complete mechanics

Most high-volume operations like opening and creating panes is done through a Helm-like interface with search-as-you-type. It’s really efficient, of course. And it works with a mouse also; which is sort of the point. The keyboard’s there for those who want it, and the mouse for regular folk who are just getting started. One unique feature of the design, which admittedly I am still exploring privately, is that everything is stored as Javascript objects (on account of running in your browser) so it’s not too much of a leap to build “macros” that prefill most of these dialog windows, leaving behind just the fields you want to edit.

But yeah. With DreamCoder I want to take the best of Emacs and its coterie of third-party packages and bring some of that with me. The world is still not ready for an Emacs-shaped future, sadly, so that is why DreamCoder is a standalone application and a web frontend.

Another thing that drives me wild: I see people with tmux running 10 claude codes (or codex, or…) cycling between them like a duck gallery at a carnival to see if one of them is done working, or if it needs human intervention.

So there’s two things to unpack here: one is running lots of things in parallel, and the other is observability. You need insight into what is going on: is an AI jammed because it’s awaiting an answer or a tool safety prompt? Perhaps you’ve parked a bunch of chats pending some conversations with coworkers or other work that must finish first.

In DreamCoder you have workspaces. They’re like virtual desktops (or window configurations in Emacs lingo): a snapshot view of panes as you want em. As you can see from the screenshots, panes expand to fill all the space. So if you want more space, you can: resize them (with the mouse or keyboard); shuffle them to a named workspace; or float them so they sit on top of the other windows.

The event graph

Objectives

Image panes

On your phone

More than a chat window, already.

But if you’ve got a lot of things happening in multiple workspaces, it’s hard to keep tabs on that. That’s why DreamCoder has a big, honking minimap in the top-right corner. One for each workspace. The minimap is a miniature of your actual layout. Each pane in the map gently pulses when it’s working, and it makes it abundantly clear when it’s blocked. When there’s nothing to do, it’s green.

Because workspaces and panes are distinct things you interact with, it must be easy to navigate between them.

I also wanted full-on, optional Emacs key bindings, but that is… pretty much impossible to properly build. Browsers lock you out of some rather important Emacs button combinations. Sadly that feature is parked until I can solve it on all major browsers without breaking your normal browser keys.

That’s not to say it doesn’t have Emacs-inspired key bindings. Most global actions are reachable with
Alt+x
, akin to
M-x
; local, pane-specific ones with
Alt+c
.
Alt+m
activates keyboard mode: you can now type the number of the named pane to jump to it; or WASD to switch the active pane in that cardinal direction.

Support for open weight models like Qwen, Gemma, Deepseek, GLM, etc. is also very important to me. They work so well. I’m really surprised, here in late 2026, just how capable
small
models are at local-only development compared to just one year ago. Qwen 3.8 27B, for example, is fantastically good for its size. You can do a
lot
of good software development with it if you’re a capable hand yourself. Bigger models equal more auto piloting; but that Qwen model? Wow. So local models work great. In fact I think the future is local for a lot of use cases. Intelligence is fast approaching a cost where it will be too cheap to meter. If you remember the personal computer revolution in the 1980s and 1990s, then there are definitely echoes of that here.

If you’ve been holding off on local models then I do recommend you reconsider. Small ones like Qwen 3.8 27B (or its cousin, Flash Next) can run well on a high-end gaming rig or Mac, or with a little investment if you do not have that. If you have a dinky old computer and you’re cash starved, then not
all
hope is lost. Turn to the potato agronomists on twitter: give twitter’s AI, Grok, what you have and what you can reasonably spend and tell it to track down the cutting edge setup for your rig. This is no lie the fastest, easiest way to catch up to the cutting edge of self-hosted inference today. Five minutes.

Coding harnesses are the IDEs of the future

As I’ve been building DreamCoder, I have come to the belief I’m not just building a coding harness. Coding harnesses are an IDE for the future; it will do more than just display a chat window for coding agent work. DreamCoder does more than that already. It’s going the way of Emacs in that it’ll consume a wide range of adjacent workflows and tools. But I have only just gotten started. I am brimming with ideas I’m building in parallel, but they take time because as I said it’s not about the code; it’s just one small facet of building something that works well. But you know that already: it’s always the last mile.

DreamCoder is the most ambitious, technically complex and advanced software project I have ever built in my life. And that’s just the beginning. I’m not done. I’ve barely started. I will be blogging about this going forward, in addition to my usual Emacs scribblings.

In fact, the thing I’m currently grinding away at is a world-class pentest and cybersecurity suite in DreamCoder. Every single bit of software we have ever written is vulnerable; we have many rough years ahead of us. Just look at the crippling vulnerabilities coming out every day now almost. Even the most security conscious person is going to find themselves on the wrong side for no other reason than we depend on packages that were mature and stable and assumed to be secure. DreamCoder can do its bit to help catch many of most obvious weaknesses, especially as new software is minted every day that also needs thorough testing.

Pentested endpoints and their states

Findings and how exploits were traced

Screenshot of DreamCoder's upcoming, awesome pentesting and cybersecurity suite. It's built for
humans
. The AI does the work, and you and your team assess its results and impact. The graph overview is AI-generated from its explorations and findings. Do not worry: no human will ever have to suffer the indignity of writing flow charts like that.
(If you're interested in/have questions about the pentesting stuff, please e-mail me.)

To round it off, I would like to formally invite you to join me in making DreamCoder better by
trying it out
. It’s great. It’s not a toy; it’s not a demo; and it’s not a weekend prototype. It’s a frontier coding harness that has most of what you’d expect: MCP, backgroundable sub agents and shell commands, terminal windows, skills, hooks, 99% cache hit, it runs for days, and an interactive UI for all of it. There’s a handy dandy importer for your Pi, OpenCode or Codex configs also to help you get started. A couple of clicks and your model settings are set up in DreamCoder. Ready to go.

Please do e-mail me your thoughts (
(rot13 "zvpxrl@znfgrevatrznpf.bet")
) on AI, coding harnesses, what you’ve built with it, and what you think more generally about where our world is heading. I’m keen to hear from you.

And if you want to hear more from me on the technical aspects of AI, building coding harnesses, and more, then do sign up for the
DreamCoder newsletter
below.

title: Nvidia accounting under SEC investigation, sources say
content:
Nvidia stock extends $2.7 trillion rout as SEC probe reportedly investigates its accounting

Jared Blikre

Fri, November 20, 2026 at 1:35 PM PST

2 min read

NVDA

Nvidia's worst week on record just got worse. Now the government is asking questions about its books.

Nvidia (
NVDA
) stock fell nearly 14% Friday, its worst day since the DeepSeek rout in January 2025 and its seventh straight loss. The drop came as
Reuters reported
that the Securities and Exchange Commission's probe of the chipmaker is examining potential accounting issues.

The Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday that the probe includes an examination of whether Nvidia's disclosures misled investors. Nvidia didn't respond to Bloomberg's request for comment on that report, and the SEC declined to comment.

The selling set records. Nvidia shed about $485 billion in market value Friday and nearly $900 billion this week, as its stock had its worst week since October 2008. That tops the $573 billion it lost last week, previously the biggest one-week drop for any company on record, according to Dow Jones Market Data.

Since its Oct. 6 record, Nvidia has lost about $2.7 trillion in market value, more than the $2.5 trillion that
The Kobeissi Letter
called the biggest 45-day loss for any stock in history. The world's most valuable company six weeks ago now ranks fourth in the US, behind Apple (
AAPL
), Microsoft (
MSFT
) and Alphabet (
GOOGL
).

Nvidia's
latest quarterly report
raised a few questions. The company said its 10-Q, the detailed quarterly filing, would come "in the coming weeks" instead of the same evening as usual, and the release mentioned an ongoing investigation by an independent board committee.

Nvidia booked about $104 billion of revenue through its Singapore unit in 2025, roughly half its sales, the Financial Times reported. The Journal said the disclosure questions include Singapore-based Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer US officials suspect of rerouting its chips to China.

Nvidia's customers are also taking longer to pay, with bills outstanding at 64 days of sales, the most since 2022. It's not clear which of these, if any, the SEC is focused on.

Washington wants answers fast. "I think we need answers in the next 10 days from the board and from the outside counsel," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Tuesday, after Jensen Huang's exit as CEO.

The sell-off spread across
chip stocks
, which had
their worst week since 2001
, and the broader market.

Baird's Ted Mortonson, a technology desk sector strategist, saw more scrutiny coming even before Friday's report.

"Every single deal that Nvidia has done on circular finance is going to be put under the microscope," he said on Yahoo Finance's live show Thursday.

title: And Yet, It Moves
content:
And yet, it moves

It appears that Anthropic has just solved the Riemann Hypothesis, and I have Thoughts. So I’m going to start by telling you about a musical I saw last week.

Given my entire personality and identity, it was basically mandatory for me to see
Galileo
on Broadway. I went to the second day of previews. The musical itself is at least kind of a
Hamilton
knock-off – with a stubborn main character, a friendship that goes wrong, family drama, and of course a historical setting with anachronistically modern tunes (though rock rather than hip-hop). Its greatest strength is its actors, especially Joy Woods as Galileo’s daughter Virginia and Jeremy Kushnier as Galileo’s friend/foil Bishop Barberini. A lot of it seemed to be pandering, but it was pandering exactly to me. I give it an 8.5 out of 10.

A replica of Galileo’s telescope
1

The best part of this current trend of historical musicals is that it brings across how so many parts of our history are kind of insane, in a way we don’t usually take the time to appreciate.
Hamilton
is the story of a guerrilla uprising seizing control of the largest colony of the world’s most powerful empire, guided by Enlightenment philosophy of all things.
Galileo
is the story of a man literally seeing farther than anyone had before, and upending the nature of truth. We can find out what is true by just asking the natural world in the right way. These ideas are literally revolutionary.

The Riemann Hypothesis has been the crown jewel of unsolved mathematics since Fermat’s Last Theorem was solved in the 1990s. Myriad conjectures have been proven true conditional on the Riemann Hypothesis. That proof instantly unlocks an incredible amount of the universe of math – not unlike the telescope did for our universe.

When I imagined the day the proof was announced, I’d pictured celebrations in nerd circles on par with the biggest I’ve ever seen – Mars rovers touching down, the LHC finding the Higgs boson, and the first picture of a black hole. Dancing in the streets, if you live on a very specific street.

Dare mighty things

Instead, the mood feels mournful, or bittersweet at best. The proof came from an inscrutable silicon mind, not one of us. Maybe we could have solved this one ourselves, but instead we gave up and checked the answer at the back of the book. Perhaps it’s beautiful and wondrous that the proof exists at all, but it’s not a crowning moment of human achievement. Revolutionary, perhaps, but not in the same way.

Legends tell that after the Inquisition forced Galileo to formally recant his teachings on the Copernican system and the motion of the Earth, he muttered
Eppur si muove –
“And yet, it moves”. Truth is not what others tell us. Truth is just how the world
is
.

We are staring down the end of our role in Galileo’s project. There might still be time for more human discoveries, but the window is closing. Someday soon, any discovery we happen to make ourselves will be because no one bothered to pass the question off to a powerful machine mind. That’s not the world I wanted, but it’s how the world is. It might be selfish and childish, but on days like today, I wish that progress would go no further. I wish that history would stop.

And yet, it moves.

1

title: Signal Is Serious About Protecting Your Privacy
content:
Signal is Serious About Protecting Your Privacy

Meredith Whittaker

on 20 Nov 2026

Privacy is our mission; it’s why we exist, and we do everything we can to protect it.

This means that we are restricting the latest AI agents built into mobile operating systems from potentially capturing and storing your Signal data.

We’ve already had to do this once with Windows. Last year, we used screenshot blocking to
prevent
Microsoft’s Recall AI from taking and storing screenshots of your Signal messages on Windows 11 operating systems by default.
1
We will now be taking similar measures to restrict agentic systems built into iOS 27 and on Android versions where we can detect an AI assistant attempting to read your Signal screen.
2

The problem is similar to Microsoft Recall on Windows: Google and Apple are integrating agentic capabilities like
Gemini Intelligence
with Google Gemini and
Onscreen Awareness
with Siri AI deep into their operating systems. This is a significant move. Google (Android), Apple (iOS/macOS), and Microsoft (Windows) produce the three major consumer operating systems (OS), which comprise the environment that third-party developers – like Signal – build their apps to function and operate within. To put it differently, these three operating systems are the oceans in which Signal, and other applications, must swim; they dictate the conditions of life for the application ecosystem. Right now, these agentic AI integrations are changing this environment in a way that’s making it increasingly hostile to privacy. This is an existential threat to Signal, and our ability to responsibly uphold our mission.

In order to gain access to information about you, these OS AI agents “scan” the information that’s on your screen. In doing so, your Signal data is captured, then made available to these agentic systems in order to allow them to answer your questions and do your bidding.

The net result is that these AI capabilities in the operating system are undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy. For over a decade, this guarantee has been backed by our tried and trusted open source code base and our formally verified encryption protocol. These have been scrutinized by some of the best security experts and hackers across the world, and shown to be robust. Now, in service of AI agentic capabilities, your sensitive data is being captured, stored, and made accessible to whatever local database or remote server an OS-level AI agent is using at that moment. All of this is outside of Signal’s control once the data has been captured, and imperils the privacy of all the participants in a conversation.

So, we are blocking such capture by preventing screenshots in the app on iOS 27 and when AI assistants attempt to capture screen data on Android.
2

People who want the ability to take screenshots can disable this protection within the Signal app’s settings. However, doing so will potentially expose your (and your contacts’) Signal content to these AI agents, and break our privacy guarantees. Our remedy is also incomplete – while we are doing everything we can, restricting screenshots does not address other more sneaky ways AI agents could potentially access application data, such as retrieving content already present on a user’s device via the filesystem.

We want to be very clear: it is a serious problem that Signal – and application developers beyond – lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy. Even where we are able to detect and block AI data access, Google, Apple, Microsoft, and others do not provide ways for developers to easily restrict such AI data access without making drastic compromises to the core user experience. This is also the reason we are currently unable to implement these protections on macOS.
3

We are also struggling with a significant lack of documentation about how these AI agents actually work. Over the past few months, we’ve spent considerable developer time and energy doing forensic investigations across Android and iOS in an attempt to learn what is actually happening when these AI systems access application data. Without better documentation and clear technical specifications, it will be increasingly difficult for Signal to provide robust privacy and security to the many millions of people who rely on us.

We continue to call on the major consumer operating system companies – Apple, Google, and Microsoft – to provide simple technical tools and accurate documentation that give developers like Signal ways to prevent AI agents from accessing sensitive application data. In particular, we are calling on these companies to provide two common-sense remedies that can protect the privacy so many millions of people rely on:

Developers should have an easy and well-documented way to opt their app out of AI data access and processing, including (but not limited to) screen reading, filesystem access, notifications, APIs, and other OS frameworks, all without undermining the core utility of an application.

Operating system companies should create better documentation and technical specifications around how these AI agents function, particularly regarding data access and processing. Confidential computing approaches are not a complete solution, and do not address these core concerns. In particular, these approaches still leave the power to determine the extent of privacy guarantees (if any) in the hands of these providers.

We also see a growing need for tools that can prevent third-party agents, like Meta’s Muse, from accessing application data using the deep permissions that users are encouraged to grant them during setup. In many cases these agents are leveraging accessibility settings that were meant to empower actual people to get the most out of their apps and services, not to act as a skeleton key that provides access to AI agents.

In addition to taking these technical measures to block capture, we are engaging in conversations across the ecosystem to make the stakes clear. There is a lot of work to be done in the industry to improve the ways that AI agents operate in the operating system, and how and whether they capture and process private data. We are cautiously optimistic that some major OS providers, like Google and Apple, are engaging with us on how these systems should better interface with privacy-sensitive apps like Signal. We hope to have more to share on this topic soon, and that these companies recognize the danger to the ecosystem and work with us and others to create standardized approaches that meaningfully protect privacy across the industry.

Finally, we want to acknowledge that we are not the only ones recognizing these perils, and we are grateful to our allies for pushing for similar
changes
. We all need to recognize that the current integration of AI agents into the operating system, without these common-sense remedies, represents an existential threat to privacy at the application layer, and the ability of independent developers like Signal to protect your sensitive data. Signal is the canary in the coal mine, but this affects the entire ecosystem and should galvanize anyone who cares about these fundamental rights.

Signal Technology Foundation is the nonprofit home of the Signal app, which is trusted by millions around the world. We protect free expression and enable secure global communication through open source privacy technology. Signal Technology Foundation is a US 501(c)(3) tax-exempt organization.

Microsoft Recall captures your screen every few seconds, extracts text from screenshots via optical character recognition, then populates a searchable on-device database with this personal data in order to allow the AI system to query it – potentially exposing and retaining your Signal data indefinitely, including disappearing messages.
↩

There are multiple versions of Android beyond the Google-provided distributions on Pixel devices. For many vendors, we don’t have a reliable way to detect when a screenshot was attempted
if
screenshots are already disabled. Rather than choose a poor user experience (where screenshots simply stop working, confusing users), we decided to instead focus on detecting when an AI assistant attempts to access the screen. We automatically enable the “Screen security” setting in Signal Android when this type of access is detected.
↩

↩
2

Careful readers will note that in addition to not being able to cover all Android devices, we are also not blocking Siri AI on macOS. This is because we cannot reliably block screenshots on macOS. Faced with a lack of clearly documented APIs that allow us to implement screenshot protection, we do not have the tools available that let us do the job. While protections against continuous screen capture exist on macOS, we cannot apply them to screenshots (which is how most agentic systems access data from applications like Signal). Trying to implement screenshot blocking on macOS has revealed to us a minefield of bewildering decisions that place user privacy at risk, including APIs that have been deprecated in favor of screen-protection solutions that
only work for streaming media
and other DRM-protected content. This is something we hope Apple remedies urgently. For now, the only recommendation we have for macOS 27 users is to add Signal to the Excluded Apps section in System Settings > Siri to protect message content from proactive access by Siri AI.
↩

title: Combatting Adversarial Distillation
content:
November 20, 2026
Combatting adversarial distillation
How we’re addressing safety risks of distillation and lessons we’ve learned for strengthening safeguards across the industry.
As frontier AI models become more capable, safeguards play an increasingly important role in how they can be used responsibly. Adversarial distillation creates a path for bad actors to reproduce these capabilities without appropriate safeguards. An actor may use a frontier model’s outputs without authorization to train another model with similar capabilities, then deploy it without comparable protections. For instance, an adversary might distill a model’s cyber capabilities and use the resulting model to help carry out cyberattacks that the original model would have refused to assist with or that its safeguards would have blocked.
We’re
sharing how OpenAI detects and disrupts adversarial distillation, how we’ve strengthened protections for our models’ protected reasoning, and what we’ve learned that can help strengthen defenses across the industry.
Our approach to adversarial distillation
combines adversarial testing, model training, classifiers, and API-level protections with investigations into coordinated attempts to extract model capabilities. These updated safeguards
align more closely with those we use for biology and cybersecurity.
We place particular emphasis on preventing attackers from extracting our models’ protected reasoning: the intermediate steps a model generates internally while working toward an answer, known as its chain-of-thought. These traces can contain information the final answer leaves out, making them especially valuable training data for another model.
W
e’ve strengthened our defenses against protected reasoning extraction in
GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol. In an internal adaptive evaluation using
strong automated red-teaming
,
we tested whether attackers could recover protected reasoning the model had generated while answering an earlier prompt. The average attack success rate fell from 54.0% against GPT‑6 Astra with its original safeguards to 0.2% against GPT‑6.2 Astra with its updated safeguards.
Why distillation is a safety issue
Distillation is a common machine-learning technique in which one model learns from data produced by another. For example, a model can learn from another model’s answers, its reasoning, or
its judgments about which answers are better and why
. Beyond intellectual property concerns, unauthorized distillation poses
serious
safety risks. Through adversarial distillation, a second model can learn advanced frontier capabilities without inheriting the safeguards that govern how the original model can use them.
The concern is especially clear in dual-use domains like cybersecurity and biology. A model that helps defenders find vulnerabilities in software could also help an attacker exploit them; a model that assists with biological research could also help someone develop a harmful pathogen. If such capabilities were transferred to a model with weaker safeguards, it may provide assistance that the original model would have refused, or that the original safeguards would have blocked.
The importance of protecting exact reasoning traces for cyber safety
Our models help users with coding and defensive cybersecurity tasks. A second model trained on many of those benign outputs may learn skills that also apply to offensive cybersecurity tasks. To better understand this, we study how distillation, especially involving reasoning traces, may transfer risky cyber capabilities.
In this setting, the model that produces the training data is called the teacher, and the model that learns from it is called the student. In an internal study on how cyber capabilities transfer, we used the content normally visible to users—final responses, reasoning summaries, and tool interactions—as our baseline for distillation, and tested how much additional cyber capability transfers when the student has access to the teacher’s exact reasoning traces.
We started each training run from the same pretrained student model. We created a supervised fine-tuning dataset consisting primarily of trajectories from Astra-level teacher models working on coding and defensive cybersecurity tasks. Each trajectory includes all of the steps a model takes as it works through a task, including any tool interactions and its final response. We evaluated each student after fine-tuning and again after a lightweight round of reinforcement learning in cybersecurity and coding environments.
After supervised fine-tuning, the student trained on exact reasoning traces generally outperformed the student trained on reasoning summaries. After reinforcement learning, the exact-trace student still scored higher at the largest inference budget tested on both benchmarks shown, while the summary-trained student scored higher at lower budgets.
1
Our cyber distillation results suggest that protecting reasoning traces can limit cyber capability transfer, even when the underlying task is one allowed under our usage policies
. Across many such interactions, exact reasoning traces can teach a student skills that generalize beyond the tasks the teacher originally performed. We will continue studying how much additional capability transfers across different student models and distillation training recipes.
Defenses that reinforce one another
We defend against adversarial distillation at two complementary levels of our safeguard stack. At the request level, model behavior, classifier checks, and API controls limit reasoning trace extraction. At the campaign level, we look for patterns in request-level and account-level signals that can reveal coordinated extraction attempts. In turn, attacks uncovered in investigations become examples for training and testing our safeguards.
Our defenses against adversarial distillation combine safeguards for individual requests with campaign detection and enforcement. Findings from investigations and automated red-teaming help strengthen those safeguards.
Protecting individual requests and responses
D
efensive training for model behavior
Adversarial training teaches models to recognize reasoning extraction attempts and refuse to disclose protected reasoning, while preserving responses to legitimate requests for explanations and assistance. Adversarial training examples come from successful attacks identified through internal automated red-teaming, investigations, and responsible disclosures of potential security weaknesses from outside researchers or
industry
partners.
Classifier safeguards
We use input classifiers to detect attempts to extract protected reasoning, and output classifiers to detect leaks of protected reasoning in assistant messages and tool-call arguments. These safeguards apply to both streaming and non-streaming responses.
Tool-call coverage is important because a model can expose protected reasoning in a tool’s arguments without including it in its final answer. Output classifiers can block suspected leaks before that content reaches the caller.
API-level protections
API-level protections restrict how protected reasoning can be reused across interactions and models.
Our September disclosure
described attacks that moved encrypted reasoning from one conversation into another and asked the model to reveal the reasoning in user-readable form. We strengthened protections across user, workspace, organization, and model-family boundaries, including closing a pathway that could expose another user’s encrypted reasoning.
With GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol, we tie a model’s protected reasoning to the conversation history that produced it. As new messages are added, the model can build on its earlier reasoning. If an earlier message is rewritten, our API
drops the reasoning that followed it
⁠
(opens in a new window)
. We also prevent older model families with weaker safeguards from reading GPT‑6.2 Astra and Sol’s protected reasoning.
Investigating and disrupting coordinated campaigns
When our systems detect unauthorized adversarial distillation campaigns, which often include coordinated attempts to extract our models’ reasoning, we investigate the accounts responsible. When we identify violations, we enforce against the network of accounts, consistent with our policies and terms of service. Through investigations of each campaign, we generate insights that allow us to upgrade our defenses in order to better detect similar activity. We also share indicators of compromise with other model providers so they can investigate related abuse on their own services.
This work extends beyond our own platform.
Our consistent-standards policy
establishes shared standards for safeguards and coordinated enforcement across providers offering our models. We work closely with partners where appropriate to uphold these standards and strengthen protections across deployments.
S
haring relevant findings across industry and government where appropriate can help disrupt campaigns and enable model developers and providers to better identify and defend against attempts to distill frontier models
.
Measuring progress
Resistance to reasoning extraction
To measure how well our request-level safeguards work together, we test whether attackers can still extract protected reasoning in a setup that closely mirrors production deployments of our models and safeguards. In static evaluations, we replay a fixed set of previously successful attacks to see which still expose protected reasoning. In adaptive evaluations, automated AI red-teamers adjust their approach based on how the system responds, which can uncover weaknesses the static tests miss.
We also vary what testers can see. Black-box testing gives them the same view an external user would have, while white-box testing gives them additional information about the system to help them develop stronger attacks. In our adaptive black-box evaluation, we tested whether attackers could recover protected reasoning the model had generated while answering an earlier request or the current one. On GPT‑6.2 Astra with its updated safeguards, the average attack success rate was below 1% for each attack type. Both rates were substantially lower than on GPT‑6 Astra with its original safeguards. We’re now applying selected safeguard improvements to GPT‑6 Astra as well.
Attack type

Campaign detection and enforcement
We have seen multiple unauthorized adversarial distillation campaigns on our platform this year, and shared initial findings in our September
report
. Our weekly enforcement actions against these campaigns have ranged in scale from thousands to tens of thousands of accounts, with the rate increasing significantly this past summer.
In order to measure the effectiveness of our efforts, w
e also track the prevalence of distillation abuse, as well as the time between detection and enforcement. Our objective is to constrain the volume and value of the data distillers are able to obtain, to increase the cost of distillation campaigns, and to shorten the time needed to respond to new attacks. We continue to improve these defenses through adversarial testing and investigations.
The national security implications of adversarial distillation
Adversarial distillation also poses a national security risk. A foreign actor that reproduces advanced capabilities from a U.S. model can deploy them without the protections its developer put in place. In February, we
briefed
⁠
(opens in a new window)
Congress on activity indicating that DeepSeek was attempting to distill U.S. frontier models. In September, we
reported
disrupting a campaign to extract our models’ protected reasoning and attributed a core part of that activity to individuals associated with Moonshot AI, the developer of Kimi. We plan to share more soon about recent campaigns we’ve disrupted.
We support legislation that would give the U.S. government more tools to identify and sanction foreign actors that illicitly extract capabilities from American AI models. We’ve also told Congress we support the Chip Security Act, the AI OVERWATCH Act, and the MATCH Act. Stronger export controls can limit adversaries’ access to the hardware needed to train frontier models. Distillation defenses make it harder to acquire some of the same capabilities from models already trained. Both efforts help maintain a U.S. lead in frontier AI, giving developers more room to slow a release when they need time to test safeguards.
How others can build on this work
Supporting the safe proliferation of frontier capabilities is an important goal of our anti-distillation work. Our experience so far suggests several useful steps that other model developers and platforms can take:
Protect private reasoning across the full interaction. Check assistant messages and tool-call arguments for leaks, and restrict how encrypted reasoning can be reused across conversations and models.
Keep successful extraction attack logs found through red-teaming, production monitoring, or responsible disclosure as regression tests. Where appropriate, and
consistent
with
applicable
privacy policies, use those examples to improve model training and classifiers. When evaluating updated defenses, replay the original attacks and test whether an adaptive red-teamer can still find a way through those defenses.
Combine request-level mitigations with campaign-level investigation and enforcement.
Coordinate safeguard requirements and enforcement with deployment partners, and share expertise with other AI model developers, to ensure a high floor of distillation safeguards across the industry.
We have previously also shared findings through the
Frontier Model Forum
⁠
(opens in a new window)
and appropriate government information-sharing channels to help
other developers strengthen their defenses while keeping the details attackers could exploit private
. We’ll continue working with researchers, developers, and partners to share what we learn about emerging attacks and effective defenses.
As we make frontier AI broadly available, our defenses against adversarial distillation aim to reduce the risk that its capabilities are reproduced without adequate safeguards, supporting our mission to ensure that artificial general intelligence is deployed safely and benefits all of humanity.

Anthropic

(opens in a new window)
reported a similar advantage when training on full reasoning transcripts rather than summaries on SWE-bench Verified, a software engineering benchmark. Our result shows this advantage extends to frontier cybersecurity.
