title: Google Workers Tell Their Employer Not to Punish Schools That Don't Want AI
content:
Chromebooks are distributed to students through a fence at a Los Angeles Unified School District high school for during the Covid quarantine.
Sarah Reingewirtz/MediaNews Group/Pasadena Star-News/Getty

Get your news from a source that’s not owned and controlled by oligarchs.
Sign up for the free
Mother Jones Daily
.

Hundreds of workers
at Google are pushing senior leadership to retract a policy that would block schools who turn off its Gemini AI tools from access to the company’s search engine starting next year.

Google made
the surprise announcement
two weeks ago, on Election Day, with executives saying they wanted to address teachers and parents’ concerns around AI in the classroom. Since then, communities across the country have protested Google’s tight hold on tech in many schools.

As I
wrote last week
after attending a rally in New York City:

Attendees of all ages held signs reading, “NO AI IN MY SCHOOL!”, “A.I. Gets an F,” “Stop stealing our imaginations,” and “SCHOOL Librarians = THE BEST Search Engines.” Some students handed out fliers to passersby while younger children ran around and drew pictures off to the side.

Many cars driving by honked their horns in support, and a few construction workers on the other side of the one-way street cheered the protesters on.

That day, protests took place in
six other cities
—Los Angeles; Chicago; Boston; Portland, Oregon; Boulder, Colorado; and Durham, North Carolina—all organized by a nationwide alliance of parent and community advocacy organizations.

School districts across the country use the company’s software and
Chromebooks
, which were more affordable than Windows and Apple computers when many were quickly assembling remote learning programs during the early years of the Covid pandemic. The Chromebooks have built-in AI classroom tools, and Google Search
embeds
AI Overview and AI Mode powered by Gemini.

Responding to the backlash, three of the largest school districts in the US—New York City, Los Angeles, and Chicago—are now
discussing
alternative search engines.

“Any opportunity to drive positive change with AI in education will rely on educators having the freedom to choose how to implement it in their curriculum,” employees wrote in
a petition
brought by
the Alphabet Workers Union
, which represents
more than 1,000 workers
at Google’s parent company. “Cutting off access to Search for schools that don’t wish to use AI will not help persuade our users, and will more likely result in them shutting out Google products altogether.”

“It is our job as Googlers to respect the user, and listen to them when they have concerns about our products,” they continued, addressing Alphabet and Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Google vice president and general manager of education Chris Phillips, and Elizabeth Reid, its vice president and head of search.

A software engineer in Google’s education department told me on Thursday that most workers did not know about the Google Search decision before it was publicly announced. Corporate leadership has now acknowledged the letter but has not responded to any of its

specific demands.

AI classroom tools should be “built responsibly and prioritize the best interests of the students, not the company’s bottom line,” the Google engineer said.

Another engineer and union member in New York, who also signed the petition, said to
Mother Jones
that the executive team “seems convinced that resistance to AI adoption is because people don’t see the vision.”

That goes beyond teachers, parents, and students: the Google staffer said their colleagues are also concerned about how the company is implementing their work on AI tools.

“If the tech is really as useful and desirable as they think it is, why don’t they trust us to choose to use it on our own terms?” the engineer asked.

Google has been contacted for comment.

title: PostgreSQL 19: A hands-on tour with runnable browser examples
content:
A release you can try at the prompt

PostgreSQL 19 brings useful new SQL alongside maintenance and replication improvements. Try
IGNORE NULLS
,
get-or-create inserts
,
JSON export
,
JSONPath transformations
, and
range subtraction
, then explore planner advice and real replication.

PostgreSQL 19.0 · released 19 November 2026.
The
stable release announcement
introduces the version installed in this sandbox. Each feature links to its official documentation. The
release notes
remain the complete change log.

About this terminal.
Experiments run on a real PostgreSQL 19 server as
student
, in a disposable guest. Maintenance tables live in
blog_lab
. Replication experiments start additional real servers on demand: a logical subscriber on
5433
, and a physical standby on
5434
, both fed by the primary on
5432
. To fit the guest’s memory budget, only one of these extra instances runs at a time: each replication card stops the other and starts its own. Re-run that card before checking its current state again. Their first runs take longer because they initialize a cluster or take a base backup. Reset discards all three clusters and their data.

How to compare with 18.
Sidenotes offer older SQL/workflows that you can run on 19, or a setting that disables a particular new optimization. These show the difference in expression or behavior. They do not turn PostgreSQL 19 into PostgreSQL 18. For timing claims, run the same workload on actual 18 and 19 servers with equal data, settings, cache conditions, and hardware.

Run the experiments in any order. Commands beginning with
\!
run a shell command from psql. The logical replication walkthrough shows its server setup and SQL directly;
as-postgres
runs server utilities as the Linux
postgres
account. Query and comparison examples state when to use another port or the administrative SQL role.
01
Start with the server you actually have
Before reading a release article, ask the server which release you are actually running.
SELECT 1
is also a pleasantly boring connectivity test: a result beats a spinning status indicator.

The version returned below belongs to the
sandbox
, not to the release covered by the article. The SQL role is
student
; ownership of the prepared demo database gives you room to experiment without administrative credentials.

Look for:
one row, a real server version, and the expected role. Keep that baseline when you compare an upgrade later.
↳ TRY IT / CURRENT IMAGE
Live SQL
From the shell, open the demo database (
PGDATABASE=
blog_lab
):
psql
Then run this at the SQL prompt:
SELECT 1 AS terminal_is_alive,
current_setting('server_version') AS actual_version,
current_user AS sql_role;
Expected:

One row with terminal_is_alive = 1, the installed server version, and student.

02
REPACK — rewrite and reclaim space
Deleting rows leaves reusable space behind. Regular vacuum cleans that space; PostgreSQL 19’s native
REPACK
rewrites the table and returns unused bytes to the OS. The card deletes middle rows, preserving occupied tail pages so ordinary vacuum cannot simply truncate them. Compare the file size after vacuum with its size after a real rewrite. The tiny table demonstrates the operation, not a storage benchmark.
REPACK documentation
.

The concurrent variant uses logical decoding to capture intervening writes and takes an access-exclusive lock for the final swap. After the card, run this example at the same
psql
prompt.
REPACK
requires the table's
MAINTAIN
privilege;
student
owns
events
, so no role change is needed.

REPACK (CONCURRENTLY, ANALYZE) events;

Compare with 18:

VACUUM (FULL, ANALYZE) events;
performs the older blocking rewrite. For physical index ordering, compare
CLUSTER events USING events_pkey;
with
REPACK events USING INDEX events_pkey;
. Restore the same bloated table before each run. Use a second connection to try
SELECT
/
INSERT
while a larger rewrite runs, and inspect
pg_locks
: the concurrent form still locks briefly at the swap. PostgreSQL 18 has no native concurrent equivalent; the separately installed
pg_repack
extension is another workflow.

↳ TRY IT / CURRENT IMAGE
Live SQL
DELETE FROM events WHERE id BETWEEN 301 AND 700;
VACUUM (ANALYZE) events;
SELECT pg_relation_size('events') AS bytes_before_repack;
REPACK (ANALYZE) events;
SELECT count(*) AS surviving_events,
pg_relation_size('events') AS bytes_after_repack
FROM events
WHERE id <= 1000;
Expected:

DELETE 400 on the first run, VACUUM, REPACK, then 600 original surviving events. Compare bytes before/after; sizes vary.

03
Autovacuum — inspect the real priority scores
Autovacuum now prioritizes tables using real scores and can parallelize index work. The card reads
pg_stat_autovacuum_scores
and the configured score weights. Use
\x on
to show the wide scores view as readable records, then
\x off
to return to a table for the two-column settings query. Scores change with workload and statistics, so zero after maintenance is a useful result too.
Autovacuum scheduling
,
statistics views
.

autovacuum_max_parallel_workers
controls the server-wide allowance;
autovacuum_parallel_workers
is a per-table setting. The sandbox’s current parallel allowance is zero, so the card inspects priorities rather than launching parallel vacuum work. PostgreSQL 19 can also mark eligible pages all-visible during ordinary scans, improving future index-only scans.

Compare with 18:
On an administrative connection, set
autovacuum_max_parallel_workers = 0
with
ALTER SYSTEM
, then reload using
SELECT pg_reload_conf();
to disable this new parallel index work. Restore the previous value afterward. Manual
VACUUM (PARALLEL 0)
versus
VACUUM (PARALLEL 2)
is also runnable on 18, but measures manual vacuum. There is no faithful switch back to PostgreSQL 18’s autovacuum scheduler; compare the scheduling on separate installations.

↳ TRY IT / CURRENT IMAGE
Live SQL
\x on
SELECT *
FROM pg_stat_autovacuum_scores
WHERE relid IN ('events'::regclass, 'orders'::regclass);
\x off
SELECT name, setting
FROM pg_settings
WHERE name LIKE 'autovacuum%score_weight'
OR name = 'autovacuum_max_parallel_workers'
ORDER BY name;
Expected:

Expanded records for per-table scores, then a two-column table of configured weights; recently vacuumed tables may score zero.

04
Plan advice — constrain one query, then release it
pg_plan_advice
generates a description of planner choices and lets you constrain selected choices.
pg_stash_advice
stores advice by query identifier for automatic reuse. In this database setup has enabled the advice module for the student’s sessions; on another installation an administrator can use
LOAD 'pg_plan_advice'
or configure preloading.
Plan advice
,
stored advice
.

The first plan emits generated advice; the second requests
SEQ_SCAN(orders)
. Look for
matched
feedback. Advice restricts the normal planner and can become stale when data changes.

Compare with 18:
Run the settings, query, and resets in the same connection:

SET enable_indexscan = off;
SET enable_bitmapscan = off;
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT sum(amount)
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 1;
RESET enable_indexscan;
RESET enable_bitmapscan;

These broad settings discourage whole classes of paths. PostgreSQL 19’s advice can instead target a named table in a query. Our small table is likely to choose a sequential scan already; the interesting evidence is the advice and its feedback.
↳ TRY IT / CURRENT IMAGE
Live SQL
Inspect the generated plan advice.
EXPLAIN (PLAN_ADVICE, COSTS OFF)
SELECT sum(amount)
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 1;
Apply session advice, inspect the plan, then reset the setting.
SET pg_plan_advice.advice = 'SEQ_SCAN(orders)';
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, COSTS OFF)
SELECT sum(amount)
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 1;
RESET pg_plan_advice.advice;
Expected:

Generated Plan Advice, then Supplied Plan Advice with matched feedback and an Aggregate plan.

05
Logical replication — see what moves between two servers
Follow one row and one counter from source to destination.
The publisher on
5432
owns the source data. The subscriber on
5433
is a separate PostgreSQL process with its own data directory. Both databases are named
pg19_repl
; the port identifies which one you are changing.

Object
Publisher · 5432
Subscriber · 5433
messages
Write a row
The publication copies the row
scratch
Write a row
Excluded from the publication; remains empty
ticket_numbers
Consume 50 values
Explicit refresh copies the sequence state

The commands below show the entire setup.
Run them in order
, or use
Run all steps
to enter the same visible commands.
\!
runs a shell command from psql.
as-postgres
runs the following command as the Linux
postgres
account;
initdb
initializes the cluster and
pg_ctl
starts it.
\connect database role host port
chooses the SQL connection. Administrative SQL here explicitly uses the SQL role
postgres
. Local trust authentication is for this disposable guest.

The standby from experiment 06 is stopped first to fit the guest's memory budget. The subscriber uses small buffers and synchronous I/O for this runtime. Its log is
/tmp/pg19-subscriber.log
. Conditional setup preserves existing objects on repeat runs; each repeat advances the publisher counter again.

What is new in 19?

FOR ALL TABLES EXCEPT (TABLE scratch)
excludes a table, and
ALL SEQUENCES
includes sequence state. Initial subscription creation copies sequence values; later publisher calls to
nextval
can leave the subscriber behind.
REFRESH SEQUENCES
requests another copy. We wait for the initial copy before advancing the publisher so it cannot mask the before/after comparison. The visible polling loops have a deadline because synchronization is asynchronous. Definitions must match on both servers.
Sequence synchronization
,
publication syntax
.

The subscription receives data over loopback TCP; psql uses local Unix sockets for administration. Compare
wal_level = replica
with
effective_wal_level = logical
on the publisher after creating the publication: PostgreSQL 19 enables logical WAL when required without restarting this primary.
WAL configuration
.

Compare with 18:
Publish the included table explicitly with
FOR TABLE messages
. The publisher needs
wal_level = logical
and a restart. Sequence state is not replicated: at cutover, stop publisher writes, read
last_value
and
is_called
, and apply
setval('ticket_numbers', captured_value, captured_is_called)
on the subscriber. In 19, repeat the steps below and compare the counter before and after
REFRESH SEQUENCES
.

↳ TRY IT / CURRENT IMAGE
Live SQL
1 · Make room for the subscriber. Stop the physical standby only if experiment 06 has started it.
\! if as-postgres pg_ctl status -D /tmp/pg19-standby >/dev/null 2>&1; then as-postgres pg_ctl stop -D /tmp/pg19-standby -m fast -w; fi
2 · Initialize a separate cluster. initdb creates its data directory; the condition preserves it on repeat runs.
\! if ! as-postgres test -f /tmp/pg19-subscriber/PG_VERSION; then as-postgres initdb -D /tmp/pg19-subscriber -U postgres --auth=trust --locale=C -E UTF8; fi
3 · Start that cluster on port 5433. pg_ctl waits for startup; the -o options choose the port, sockets, and small memory settings for this guest.
\! as-postgres pg_ctl status -D /tmp/pg19-subscriber || as-postgres pg_ctl start -D /tmp/pg19-subscriber -l /tmp/pg19-subscriber.log -w -o "-p 5433 -h 127.0.0.1 -k /tmp -c dynamic_shared_memory_type=mmap -c shared_buffers=16MB -c max_connections=10 -c io_method=sync"
4 · Publisher, port 5432. Create the source database if absent. psql’s \gexec executes the CREATE DATABASE text only when the SELECT returns it.
\connect postgres postgres /tmp 5432
SELECT 'CREATE DATABASE pg19_repl OWNER student'
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT FROM pg_database WHERE datname = 'pg19_repl') \gexec
5 · Publisher schema and publication. messages is included, scratch is excluded, and ticket_numbers is explicitly published through ALL SEQUENCES. The existence checks make setup repeatable.
\connect pg19_repl postgres /tmp 5432
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS messages (id integer PRIMARY KEY, body text);
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS scratch (id integer);
CREATE SEQUENCE IF NOT EXISTS ticket_numbers START 1;
SELECT 'CREATE PUBLICATION pg19_pub FOR ALL TABLES EXCEPT (TABLE scratch), ALL SEQUENCES'
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT FROM pg_publication WHERE pubname = 'pg19_pub') \gexec
SELECT pubname, puballtables, puballsequences FROM pg_publication;
SHOW wal_level;
SHOW effective_wal_level;
6 · Subscriber, port 5433. Create the destination database and matching objects. Logical replication does not create their definitions.
\connect postgres postgres /tmp 5433
SELECT 'CREATE DATABASE pg19_repl'
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT FROM pg_database WHERE datname = 'pg19_repl') \gexec
\connect pg19_repl postgres /tmp 5433
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS messages (id integer PRIMARY KEY, body text);
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS scratch (id integer);
CREATE SEQUENCE IF NOT EXISTS ticket_numbers START 1;
7 · Subscriber. Subscribe to the publisher on 5432. The connection string is the source; the current psql connection is the destination.
SELECT $sql$CREATE SUBSCRIPTION pg19_sub
CONNECTION 'host=127.0.0.1 port=5432 user=postgres dbname=pg19_repl'
PUBLICATION pg19_pub$sql$

FROM (SELECT nextval('ticket_numbers') AS n FROM generate_series(1, 50)) q;

FROM pg_subscription_rel ORDER BY 1;
\connect blog_lab student /tmp 5432

title: LZ-RDO lands in ARM's astc-encoder
content:
Jon Olick

LZ-RDO lands in ARM's astc-encoder

11/17/2026

My rate-distortion optimization work for ASTC is now in
ARM's astc-encoder (PR #781)
. Fabian "ryg" Giesen took my original implementation, added a round of optimizations and improvements, and landed it. If you ship ASTC textures inside Oodle, zlib, zstd, LZ4 or LZMA-compressed packages, your downloads can now get smaller with one command-line flag.

​The problem: ASTC looks like noise to LZ

​ASTC is a fixed-rate format. Every block is exactly 128 bits, whether it's 4x4 or 12x12. On the GPU that's what you want, but nobody ships raw textures. They go into packages that get compressed with a general-purpose LZ codec. To an LZ compressor, a normal ASTC bitstream looks almost random: each block's endpoints and weights are fitted to that block's pixels, so neighboring blocks rarely share bytes. That leaves the compressor nothing to match.
RDO fixes this by choosing, among encodings that look nearly as good, the ones that repeat bits the encoder has already emitted. The GPU sees a valid ASTC texture of exactly the same size, and LZ sees matches. It's a quality-for-package-size trade, and a single knob controls it.

​How it works

1. Encode normally, plus a "restricted" encoding
First the image goes through the regular astcenc encode. With LZ-RDO enabled, each block also gets one extra trial encode using the most common configuration: 1 partition, 1 weight plane, endpoints quantized to at most 32 levels, and only the always-available block modes for 2D. Blocks that share a configuration are much more likely to share bits, so this gives the optimizer more chances to find repeats.​
2. Measure where errors will be visible
Raw squared error (PSNR) is the wrong measure when you're adding error on purpose. Errors in smooth areas and slow gradients are easy to spot. Errors in noisy texture or near edges are mostly hidden.
So before encoding, the image is split into tiles (about 256×256, or 32³ for 3D) and each texel gets an activity weight:
Low-pass filter the image (Gaussian, σ = 2.2).
Take the squared difference from the original. That's the local high-frequency energy.
Blur that energy a little (σ = 1.25) so it spreads.
Map it to a weight that falls off with the square root of the energy.
Smooth texels keep tight error tolerances. Busy texels get looser ones.
3. ​Move-to-front histories for endpoints and weights
ASTC packs weights from the top of the block downward and the mode and endpoints from the bottom up. That makes splitting a block into "endpoint bits" and "weight bits" a simple bitmask. The optimizer keeps two move-to-front lists of recently used values:
Endpoint history: mode, header and endpoint bits.
Weight history: weight bits.
The -rdo-endpoints and -rdo-weights options set their sizes. Defaults range from 16/4 at -fastest up to 512/160 at -exhaustive.
4. Build candidates for each block
For every block, the encoder scores:
the original encoding;
the restricted encoding;
endpoint substitution: take endpoints from the history, compute the ideal weights for this block's pixels with those endpoints, and quantize. A quick check on endpoint-axis alignment skips pairs that can't work. The best few candidates are kept.
weight splicing: combine every weight entry in the history with each surviving endpoint candidate that has the same weight bit count. If both halves came from the same earlier block, it's one long LZ match.
5. ​Score with a simple LZ cost model
Each candidate's cost is
cost = weighted_SSD + λ · estimated_bits
The bit estimate is deliberately simple:
Unmatched bits are billed as literals.
A match costs about 10 + log2(mtf_position + 32) bits.
If the endpoints and weights match the same earlier block, they're billed as one match.
The first two bytes (where the mode lives) are costed from an adaptive histogram, so frequently used modes get cheaper.
A partial byte at the endpoint/weight boundary is billed as literal bits.
The code comments say "don't over-tune this," and I mean it. The goal is to point the search in the right direction, not to simulate zstd.
λ is scaled by texel count, so the same value behaves about the same at 4x4 and at 12x12.
6. Multiple passes, in parallel
The image is processed in independent chunks of blocks, so it spreads across threads. Each pass seeds the histories with random blocks from the chunk, and passes alternate between forward and reverse order. Because splicing produces the same bit pattern many different ways, a small hash-table cache of decoded blocks avoids decoding them again during error checks.

Using It

Command line:
astcenc -cl albedo.png albedo.astc 6x6 -thorough -rdo-lambda 20
API:
astcenc_config_init(ASTCENC_PRF_LDR, 6, 6, 1, ASTCENC_PRE_THOROUGH,
ASTCENC_FLG_USE_LZ_RDO, &config);
config.lz_rdo_lambda = 20.0f;
Tuning guidance:
λ is tuned so that a step of about 10 is a visible difference.
Diffuse/albedo: 20–40 is usually fine.
Normal maps: stay low, around 10 or even below, depending on your quality bar.
-rdo-passes 2 (the -exhaustive default) squeezes out a bit more, at a real cost in encode time.
Progress callbacks and cancellation work across both stages: the base encode reports the first 33%, and the RDO passes report the rest.

​Limitations

LDR only. Nothing prevents HDR in principle.
In-memory size doesn't change. The gain only shows up after LZ compression on disk or over the wire.
It costs encode time. It's meant to be paired with the higher-quality presets.

Results

Thanks

​Huge thanks to Fabian for the optimizations, fixes and for getting this merged, to ARM for taking it upstream, and to Charles, Fabian and Sean for the Oodle Texture work this comes from.

title: Reverse Engineering my cat's litter box
content:
Maisie likes to touch the litter box while it is running. I would prefer that she find something else to do during that time.

My idea was to bring the litter box into Home Assistant, add some buttons, and eventually use presence sensors to start a cleaning cycle when she is in another room and distracted. There are probably many more automations I will come up with once I have that working. First, I needed a way to talk to the box.

The phone app already knew how to do everything I needed. I started by watching its traffic with Wireshark and inspecting HTTP requests with HTTP Toolkit, then decompiled the Android app to understand the parts I could not reproduce from the traffic alone.

This turned into two related projects. I needed to reproduce the signed HTTP requests used to access account and device data, then rebuild the binary messages used to operate the box over MQTT.

Recreating the HTTP Requests

The HTTP traffic exposed devices on the account, configuration, waste drawer levels, and records of litter box visits. I could also see how authentication worked. The app logs in to obtain a token, then includes that token in the
Authorization
header on later requests.

My first attempts to reproduce the requests returned
401 Unauthorized
. Copying the endpoints and headers from a capture had not been enough. A 401 did not identify exactly which part of my reproduction was wrong, so I went back to comparing the app’s requests.

The
X-UBT-Sign
header kept changing. I could not work out its algorithm just by looking at the captured values. To generate my own requests, I needed to see how the app created it.

I used JADX to decompile the Android APK, then searched the recovered source for the header name and familiar backend strings:

grep
-R
-n
-E
'X-UBT-Sign|catbox-server|airrobo-home'
\

furrytail_decompiled/sources

The header name gave me a useful place to start in the decompiled code. It appears in
sources/com/ubtrobot/infrastructure/a0.java
, an obfuscated class whose retained metadata identifies it as
UrcsSignInterceptor
from
HttpInterceptors.kt
. The interceptor builds the signature and attaches it to outgoing HTTP requests. Its hashing helper,
a.b.t
, calls
MessageDigest.getInstance("MD5")
.

The decompiled code shows the final header being assembled and added to the request.

Finding the algorithm still left the application settings to sort out. During implementation, a mismatched client configuration produced an “illegal client” response. I followed the app’s regional bootstrap flow. In

There were a few similarly named fields to keep straight:

X-UBT-AppId
identifies the application configuration and needs to match the app key.

X-UBT-DeviceId
is a stable client/app-install identifier. It is also included in the signature calculation; it is not the litter box’s serial number.

The login request separately hashes the account password with MD5. Its response includes
token.token
, the value to send in

, and

, the expiration time in milliseconds. I wrapped this in a small asynchronous HTTP client that reuses the token, logs in again shortly before expiration, and retries once after a 401.

With that in place, I could turn the vendor’s responses into useful API endpoints like

and

. That gave me the data for a dashboard. Making a cleaning button required another layer of work.

Finding the Command Path

The next clue came from something I did not see in Wireshark. When I pressed Clean in the app, there was no new HTTP request corresponding to the action.

For a moment, I wondered whether the app was talking to the box over Bluetooth. But I could also operate the box remotely, so Bluetooth would not explain the whole command path.

Looking more closely at the app’s startup requests, I found
/v1/ubtechinc-im-manager/im/login
. Its response included
mqttUserName
,
mqttPassword
,
clientId
,
pubTopic
, and

. That gave me another protocol to investigate, plus the credentials and topics needed to connect.

From

From

:

public
class
MqttInfoBean
{

public
String clientId;

public
String mqttPassword;

String pubTopic;

public
String subTopic;

public

}

After connecting to the broker as a subscriber, I pressed Clean again. This time I could see a message arrive. It was binary, which gave me the next problem to solve.

The command path uses MQTT. The app publishes a message to a broker, which routes it to the box. MQTT carries messages over its own connection. An already-open connection can carry a publish, so each button press needs neither a new HTTP request nor a new connection. This is the
publish/subscribe model used by MQTT
.

The HTTP API supplies the MQTT session credentials, and a contacts endpoint helps identify the device’s messaging user ID.

I needed to keep track of both the client sending the message and the litter box receiving it. The serial number used by the HTTP endpoints is not the destination field used by the messaging protocol.

My wrapper fetches the MQTT credentials at runtime and uses the device’s messaging ID to address commands. Now I had somewhere to send a message. I still needed to work out what that message should contain.

Four Bytes, Several Wrappers

At the center of a cleaning command is a small Protocol Buffers message:

message
d2c1019_intelligent_dev_airpet_op_rq
{

uint32
op_mode
=
1
;

uint32
op_state
=
2
;

}

For a request to start cleaning, both values are
1
. Serialized, the payload is just four bytes:

08 01 10 01

Unfortunately, publishing those four bytes is not enough. The device expects a series of wrappers around them:

MQTT payload

└── IM Message

└── MessageContent ("custom")

└── google.protobuf.Any

└── google.protobuf.BytesValue

└── Command

└── RISP frame

├── Header

└── Operation payload

There is quite a lot of packaging involved in asking a litter box to rotate.

The RISP frame starts with a magic byte,
0xDB
, followed by the length of a serialized header. That header includes the device category, command number, payload length, request attribute, and sequence number. An operation request uses command
1019
.

The frame also includes separate CRC-8 checksums for the header and payload. The implementation uses polynomial
0x07
with a final XOR of
0x55
. These details are small, but they are part of the format the receiver expects.

The frame goes inside a protobuf
Command
. The serialized command is then wrapped in
BytesValue
, packed into
Any
, and placed in a custom instant-messaging message. That outer message carries the sender, recipient, message identifiers, timestamp, and protocol version.

The
Any
wrapper took some care. The outgoing message contains a
BytesValue
holding serialized command bytes. Packing the command directly into
Any
would produce a different message. Knowing the innermost schema only solves part of the problem.

Looking Inside the Running App

Decompiled code helped explain the structure, but I also wanted visibility into the bytes the app was building.

I added a Frida script to inspect several points in the serialization path. It hooks the operation request, the RISP converter, the command’s
toByteArray
, and the outer messaging object’s
toByteArray
. Each hook logs the bytes at that layer and returns the original result.

This makes the nesting much easier to inspect. Instead of trying to understand one large binary payload all at once, I can look at the operation bytes separately from the command wrapper and the final MQTT message.

I also added an Android log capture script and an MQTT subscriber that prints raw payloads alongside decoded messages. On the Python side, I recreated the protobuf definitions and generated serialization classes from them. That lets the code build messages from named fields instead of maintaining long strings of hex.

The decoder works back through the same layers, exposing the RISP header and known payload types. State responses include the work mode, work state, and sensor fields, which are much more useful for debugging than an unexplained byte array.

Bringing It Into Home Assistant

Once the message construction was in place, I could expose the operation through a normal HTTP endpoint:

curl
-X
POST
http://localhost:8000/device/clean

The wrapper handles the MQTT login, builds the nested message, and publishes it. The recreated command successfully operated the physical box, which was a satisfying result after working through all those layers.

The API also supports clear and smooth operations, plus start, pause, resume, and stop states. Home Assistant buttons can call these endpoints without needing to know anything about protobufs or checksums.

For the data side, I added a script that pushes values into Home Assistant entities. It combines HTTP data, such as waste drawer percentage and visit history, with decoded MQTT state fields. This gives me a starting point for displaying the box’s status alongside the rest of the house.

My Home Assistant dashboard combines Maisie’s weight history, litter box statistics, and a cleaning button.

There is still a dependency on the vendor’s cloud. The service runs locally, but it uses the vendor’s HTTP API and MQTT broker to communicate with the box. What I have now is a bridge that lets my own tools use those interfaces.

Next, I want to add presence sensors and figure out when Maisie is occupied elsewhere. That was the idea that started this project. Getting a button to operate the box was the first milestone. Deciding when to press it should give me plenty more things to work on.

The code is on
GitHub
.

title: The G1 Garbage Collector
content:
The G1 Garbage Collector

Introduction

The Garbage-First Garbage Collector (G1) is the default garbage collector on the JVM as of JDK 27, with
JEP 523: Make G1 the Default Garbage Collector in All Environments
, which made it the default in all environments. It had been the default garbage collector in "server" environments since JDK 9, with
JEP 248: Make G1 the Default Garbage Collector
. G1 seeks to balance throughput and latency and is a good option for many workloads. In this article, we will cover a brief history of G1, its key design concepts, and how to use it.

A Brief History of G1

G1 was originally introduced in JDK 6u14 as an experimental feature, promoted to a standard feature in JDK 7u4, and designated the default garbage collector in JDK 9, taking over that role from ParallelGC. While G1 has taken over the role of default garbage collector from Parallel, it was originally introduced to replace the CMS (Concurrent-Mark-Sweep) Garbage Collector, which was deprecated in JDK 9 and removed in JDK 14.

At the time of its introduction, G1 was designed for server environments. Systems using G1 were expected to have multiple processors and large amounts of system memory (tens of GB) available. Continued development of G1 has reduced its system requirements, and now G1 can provide good performance even in resource constrained environments with only a single CPU and less than 2 GB of available system memory. This is why, as of JDK 27, it is the default garbage collector across all system configurations.

In garbage collector design, the three primary design constraints are throughput, latency (pause time), and memory footprint. G1 seeks to maintain a balance between latency and throughput, rather than heavily optimizing for either. By comparison, ParallelGC primarily focuses on maximizing throughput, and ZGC focuses on minimizing latency. G1 also aims for more consistent pause times than the CMS collector it replaced.

As of the writing of this article, 12 JEPs relating to G1 have been delivered since JDK 8, with more changes planned for the future. Continued development has steadily improved G1's throughput, latency, and memory footprint.

G1 Design and Collection Cycle

G1 is a generational, incremental, parallel, mostly concurrent, stop-the-world, and evacuating garbage collector. For an explanation of each of these terms, check the
Garbage Collection Concepts and JVM Collectors
article on dev.java. This section covers some of the key design characteristics of G1.

As mentioned in the previous section, G1 was originally designed with large "server-like" environments in mind. G1 is capable of efficiently marshalling the resources of systems with dozens of cores and addressing heaps measured in tens of GB.

G1 Heap Layout

Figure 03-01: Simplified representation of the G1 heap layout

G1 divides the heap into a set of regions (increments) of uniform size. Figure 03-01 is a simplified example of what the G1 heap space would look like. The size and number of regions, unless otherwise configured, are based on internal heuristics, with the overall heap size being the primary influence on both. These regions are then divided up into eden, survivor, old, and humongous regions.

Eden and survivor regions are both part of the "young" generation. On creation, an object is placed in an eden region. If that object survives a collection, it is evacuated (copied) into a survivor region. Unreachable objects are not deleted individually; rather, the region they are a part of is considered empty and is eligible for reuse by G1. Surviving objects, if they remain reachable, will be evacuated to a new survivor region on subsequent collections. If an object survives enough collections, based on internal heuristics unless otherwise configured, it will be evacuated to an old region, which is checked less frequently.

A humongous region is a contiguous space of one or more regions, reserved for a single "humongous" object. An object qualifies as "humongous" if it's larger than half the size of a single region. Humongous objects bypass the eden and survivor regions and are treated as equivalent to an old region by G1.

G1 Garbage Collection Cycle

Figure 03-02: Simplified representation of the G1 garbage collection cycle

The G1 garbage collection cycle (GC cycle) consists of both stop-the-world and concurrent behavior, both of which can run in parallel. Again, check
Garbage Collection Concepts and JVM Collectors
for definitions of these terms. Figure 03-02 is a simplified visualization of the G1 GC cycle and will help to contextualize this section.

At a high level, the G1 GC cycle consists of two phases: Young-Only and Space-Reclamation. G1 will start in the Young-Only phase, which, as the name suggests, means only young regions are collected. In G1, when a collection happens, the application is
paused
while G1 evacuates objects to new regions or performs other GC work.

The concurrent behavior of G1 is primarily concerned with determining which objects in old regions are still active. The concurrent phase can be broken into three distinct parts and starts when old-generation occupancy reaches a threshold.

Concurrent Start
is the first step in the concurrent phase and is a special pause. During this pause, normal evacuation of young regions still occurs, and G1 also initiates concurrent marking of old-generation regions to determine which objects are still reachable. It is also possible that G1 determines there is no need to follow through with marking, in which case a Concurrent Mark Undo pause occurs, and the Young-Only phase continues.

Remark
is the second step in the concurrent phase. This is a special pause where no evacuation of young regions happens. Instead, during this pause, G1 finalizes concurrent marking and performs other work, such as reference processing, class unloading, and reclaiming empty regions. Between this phase and Cleanup, G1 will concurrently calculate information to be used during the Space-Reclamation phase.

Cleanup
is the third and final step in the concurrent phase. This is also a special pause where no evacuation of young regions happens. During this pause, G1 determines if it should proceed to the Space-Reclamation phase. If a Space-Reclamation phase is determined to be necessary, the Young-Only phase will complete with a single Prepare Mixed young collection.

The Space-Reclamation phase consists of multiple mixed collections: collections where young and old regions are evacuated. G1 uses an efficiency algorithm to determine which old regions to collect first. A major factor in this algorithm is the amount of garbage in each old region, as regions with more garbage are more likely to yield large amounts of space. This is what "Garbage-First" in the G1 name refers to: it will reclaim the regions with the most garbage first.

The Space-Reclamation phase ends when G1 determines that evacuating more old regions is no longer worth the effort. At this point, G1 shifts back to the Young-Only phase.

For more technical details on G1, check the
Garbage-First Garbage Collector guide
and the G1 Stack Walker video at the bottom of this page.

Using G1

G1 is explicitly enabled with the JVM argument
-XX:+UseG1GC
. If you are on JDK 27 or later, this argument is never necessary, as G1 was designated the default GC in all environments. From JDK 9 to JDK 26, G1 was chosen by the JVM if it detected two or more CPU cores and more than 1792 MB of available system memory; otherwise, SerialGC was used. If you are on JDK 8, you will need to explicitly set
-XX:+UseG1GC
to use G1, as ParallelGC is the default GC.

Configuring G1

Generally speaking, users should avoid applying too much configuration to garbage collectors. Often, "less is more," and the engineers who develop and maintain garbage collectors, G1 included, have worked toward having internal heuristics provide the best performance in most use cases "out of the box." As of the writing of this article, an upcoming change to G1,
Automatic Heap Sizing
, would handle one of the most important remaining aspects of G1 configuration: configuring the heap size.

When thinking about configuring a garbage collector, consider the three major constraints garbage collectors are designed around: throughput, latency, and memory footprint. G1 aims for a balance between latency and throughput. When a user provides custom configuration to G1, some tradeoff
will be
happening. A user increasing the heap size is trying to trade a larger memory footprint for reduced latency. A user setting a higher pause time goal for G1 will be trying to trade reduced latency for improved throughput. As a user considers configuring G1, there are no settings for simply "better" performance, but, at best, a tradeoff. Some configuration combinations simply lead to worse observed performance. Below are some key configuration parameters for G1.

-Xmx
: Sets the maximum heap size. Increasing this value can improve throughput and/or reduce latency, but at the cost of increased memory footprint. When setting the maximum heap size, provide some headroom above the expected live set size. The general guidance is to set the maximum heap size 25% above the expected live set size, but the ideal amount depends on your application's behavior and your performance goals.

-Xms
: Sets the minimum and initial heap size. Setting this to the same value as the maximum heap avoids heap resizing and allows G1 to prepare the heap when combined with
-XX:+AlwaysPreTouch
, which can reduce latency during the early life cycle of an application.

-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis
: Sets the
target
for the maximum GC pause time. This is a soft goal that the JVM will try to achieve but cannot guarantee. A higher setting can improve throughput at the cost of increased latency; a lower setting would likely have the opposite effect.

For a deeper dive into configuring G1, check
the guide
maintained by the G1 engineering team.

title: Pill to treat pancreatic cancer hailed as 'biggest breakthrough in decades'
content:
A year after starting treatment, 76.6% of patients were alive; usually 40-45 % of patients given chemotherapy alone survive a year.
Photograph: Jeff Moore/PA
A year after starting treatment, 76.6% of patients were alive; usually 40-45 % of patients given chemotherapy alone survive a year.
Photograph: Jeff Moore/PA
Pill to treat pancreatic cancer hailed as ‘biggest breakthrough in decades’
Cancer undetectable for one in 12 patients in daraxonrasib trial, while nearly all participants’ tumours stopped growing
A pill that can shrink and potentially eliminate pancreas tumours is being hailed as the biggest breakthrough treatment for the cancer in decades.
In one in 12 of the patients given
the drug, daraxonrasib
, during a trial, the cancer became undetectable, and the tumours stopped growing in almost all of the 61 patients. The trial participants had recently been diagnosed with advanced pancreatic cancer that had spread to other parts of the body.
Though doctors have said the pill cannot yet be considered a cure, and they do not know how long it can keep the disease at bay, they have said it is encouraging news because it appears it will offer patients more time, even if it does not cause full remission.
‘The undruggable became druggable’: a gamechanging treatment for the world’s deadliest cancer – podcast
Read more
Half of all people diagnosed with pancreatic cancer die within three months, and only about 3% of patients survive for five years when the disease spreads to other organs. It has the lowest survival rate of all common cancers in the UK and has a similarly poor prognosis globally.
Patients were followed for a year and a half during the trial on average and some did not see the cancer return during this period. Longer studies will be conducted to see if any of the cancers can be put into remission. During the trial, tumours stopped growing in 90% of patients, just over 60% of patients had their tumours shrink or disappear, and for about 8% of patients tumours became undetectable on CT scans.
A year after starting treatment, 76.6% of patients were alive; usually 40-45% of patients given chemotherapy alone survive a year.
Dr Wungki Park, a gastrointestinal medical oncologist at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York, who presented the findings, said “this is the closest to cure”, adding that he had never seen so many tumours disappear in patients whose cancer had spread.
He presented the findings at the EORTC-NCI-AACR Symposium on Molecular Targets and Cancer Therapeutics in Barcelona. “We are beginning to see not only a higher percentage of tumour response rates, but also deeper responses and a near doubling in the duration of disease control, which may eventually translate into longer survival,” he said.
FDA gives expedited approval to new groundbreaking pancreatic cancer drug
Read more
“The median follow-up is 18 months. Just imagine, in an average of 18 months your disease just disappears on the CT scan … that’s closest to complete remission … it’s incredible.”
Daraxonrasib is a KRAS inhibitor treatment, which works by locking on to and shutting off certain mutations found in most pancreatic cancers. These mutations drive tumour growth.
There are hopes the treatment could work for dozens of other cancers because they can have similar mutations.
Michelle Mitchell, Cancer Research UK’s chief executive, said more research was needed, but added: “This is the biggest leap forward we’ve seen in decades for pancreatic cancer patients and could offer real hope to people facing one of the deadliest and most difficult-to-treat cancers.
“These results raise the exciting possibility that this breakthrough could eventually pave the way for treating other cancers that carry Kras gene mutations. More trials are now needed before this treatment can be assessed for use on the NHS and despite this advance, pancreatic cancer survival is still very low.”

title: Lean verification of the Riemann Hypothesis
content:
Lean verification of the Riemann Hypothesis

Joint statement by the Lean and Mathlib communities, endorsed by the Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative.

On November 20, 2026, Levent Alpöge
released
a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis as a Lean library comprising 17 million lines of code.

We have full confidence that Alpöge's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement.

Our rationale is outlined below.

The codebase depends directly only on Mathlib. Over the past day, the Lean and Mathlib communities have rallied to verify the proof's correctness. We hereby certify that both the statement and the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis are correct. The four criteria in
https://xenaproject.wordpress.com/2026/11/12/and-the-proof-is-checked-in-lean/
are all satisfied.

The statement of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct.
This statement is part of Mathlib:
RiemannHypothesis
and has been carefully vetted by experts in Lean and number theory.

Alpöge’s library compiles correctly.
By now, dozens of people have reported correct compilation of the codebase, reproducing the same raw proof export file. The library compiles without errors or build failures.

The code proves the correct statement.
Crucially, the community has added a file that isolates the statement of the Riemann Hypothesis and imports only Mathlib. That statement was compared against the theorem proved by Alpöge using two independent tools (
comparator
and
con-leche –compare
), both confirming that the theorem proved in Alpöge’s library is exactly Mathlib’s statement of the Riemann Hypothesis.

The Lean proof is valid.
The exported raw proof has been checked by several proof checkers, including Lean’s official kernel, the
con-leche
and
con-ron
checkers, and several independent checkers contributed by third parties and implemented in different programming languages. The checkers
con-leche
and
con-ron
come with a formal proof, relative to set theory, that they cannot accept a false proof, thus addressing concerns that Lean’s logic itself might have flaws that the proof could exploit. An extensive overview is available at
https://math.mit.edu/~drew/grh/
. These checks ran on an inert export of the proof, out of reach of hypothetical malicious code in the Lean proof sources.

Thanks are owed to
everyone in the community
who provided resources for the verification.

We look forward to all the activity in the mathematical community that will help explain the new ideas in this proof.

title: Brazil's tax authority open-sources its tax calculator on GitHub under MIT
content:
Notícias

Serviços

Receita Federal publica primeiro código-fonte aberto no GitHub e amplia transparência da Reforma Tributária

Iniciativa fortalece a transparência, a segurança jurídica e a previsibilidade na implementação dos novos tributos sobre o consumo.

Publicado em

16/11/2026 12h40

A Receita Federal deu mais um passo na implementação da Reforma Tributária do Consumo ao autorizar a publicação do código-fonte da Calculadora de Tributos em repositórios públicos no GitHub. A medida foi formalizada pela Portaria Cotec nº 342, de 12 de novembro de 2026, publicada no Diário Oficial da União.

Pela primeira vez, a Receita Federal disponibiliza oficialmente um projeto de software em ambiente público de desenvolvimento colaborativo, adotando a licença MIT, uma das mais utilizadas no mundo para código aberto. A iniciativa fortalece a transparência, a segurança jurídica e a previsibilidade na implementação dos novos tributos sobre o consumo.

O que muda na prática?

A Calculadora de Tributos é uma ferramenta que materializa as regras de cálculo da CBS e dos demais tributos da Reforma Tributária. Ao disponibilizar seu código-fonte de forma aberta, a Receita permite que empresas, desenvolvedores e fornecedores de software incorporem exatamente a mesma lógica utilizada pela administração tributária em seus sistemas de faturamento, gestão e compliance.

Na prática, isso significa que empresas poderão calcular os tributos da Reforma Tributária utilizando um mecanismo alinhado às regras oficiais, com memória de cálculo e fundamentação legal integradas. O resultado esperado é a redução de dúvidas, retrabalho e custos de conformidade.

Benefícios para empresas e gestores

A transição para o novo modelo tributário exigirá adaptações em milhares de sistemas corporativos. Com a Calculadora de Tributos disponível em código aberto, empresas ganham um componente oficial, auditável e interoperável para apoiar essa adequação.

Entre os principais benefícios estão:

- Maior segurança na implementação das regras tributárias;

- Redução de custos de desenvolvimento e manutenção;

- Transparência sobre a forma como os tributos são calculados;

- Uniformidade na interpretação das regras;

- Facilidade de integração com sistemas já utilizados pelo mercado.

A iniciativa também está alinhada ao conceito de Administração Tributária 3.0, defendido pela Organização para Cooperação e Desenvolvimento Econômico (OCDE), em que a conformidade tributária ocorre diretamente nos sistemas utilizados pelos contribuintes.

Vantagens para desenvolvedores

Para as software houses e equipes de tecnologia, a publicação no GitHub facilita o acompanhamento das evoluções da Calculadora, o controle das versões e a incorporação das atualizações aos processos de desenvolvimento e integração contínua.

Outro aspecto relevante é que a Portaria registra os hashes das versões iniciais dos repositórios, permitindo verificar a autenticidade e a integridade do código disponibilizado.

A proposta não é substituir os sistemas atualmente utilizados pelas empresas, mas fornecer um componente oficial que possa ser integrado às soluções já existentes, ampliando a confiabilidade e a padronização dos cálculos tributários.

Transparência e inovação no setor público

Embora o código da Calculadora já estivesse disponível para download na Plataforma CBS desde 2025, sua publicação no GitHub representa um avanço importante ao levá-lo para o principal ambiente utilizado pela comunidade global de desenvolvimento de software.

A medida reforça princípios que orientam a implementação da Reforma Tributária, como transparência, colaboração, interoperabilidade, inovação e participação do ecossistema tecnológico na construção das soluções necessárias para a transição ao novo sistema tributário.

Além disso, o projeto é resultado do trabalho conjunto entre Receita Federal e Serpro, demonstrando como a transformação digital pode contribuir para simplificar obrigações, aumentar a previsibilidade e fortalecer a relação entre Fisco e contribuintes.

: Reforma Tributária, CBS, Calculadora de Tributos, GitHub, código aberto, Receita Federal, Serpro, Administração Tributária 3.0, inovação, transformação digital.

title: Getting the mind to steer the body to steer you
content:
getting the mind to steer the body to steer you
Nov 20, 2026
Often in life, your body is the one steering you. And sometimes, to get to do the thing you want, you can’t just convince yourself with reason or arguments, or will yourself, or do the exercises to get there - you need to learn the magic formula, the secret words, to trick the body into acting in a way that gets you the outcome you want.
As a kid, spending time on the internet forums for bands I loved, I kept hearing about some magical book called
The Easy Way to Stop Smoking by Allen Carr,
that cured people of their smoking addiction. Middle-aged man after middle-aged man would praise the miracles of this book - not by the patch, not by gum, not by sheer will, only by reading this book could they quit smoking - and not only that, everyone they had given the book to had the same result.
As a 12 year old, unable to find out what this book actually said, I spent hours thinking about this - trying to figure out what secret trick the book could be sharing that was so powerful. [to clarify, I have never smoked a cigarette in my life]
So after countless nights thinking through this, this is what I came up with: you want to smoke because the craving feels bad, not because you actually want the cigarette. So you need to find a way to tame the cravings, and each time you don’t smoke, your cravings become smaller and smaller. Maybe you could do this by saying to yourself - this is just a craving and nothing to do with the goodness of smoking, and while the craving really sucks, the thing I’m trying to satisfy is just a craving. Each time I don’t smoke, I win this battle, and the craving will be smaller. And so long as I can go to war and bring all my focus to defeating this craving in this one battle, eventually each craving will become smaller until they all go away.
I forgot all about this book, and cigarettes, and whether or not I was right - until one day I realized I had become addicted to sugar and was experiencing lots of cravings to eat something sweet after every meal. I realized I could finally try this technique for the first time, and shortly after doing so, I overcame all the cravings. (I later learned that the book basically had the same idea as me, that there is a little “craving” monster inside you that dies when you stop feeding it - so I give 12 year old Daniel a lot of credit for this one.)
Something similar happened when Scott Alexander reviewed
The Body Keeps the Score
, a book about PTSD and the theory that trauma gets stuck in the body. Even though Scott was unimpressed by the contents of the book, he retells recommending it to a severely traumatized patient who hadn’t gotten better after years of conventional treatment, and the next week the patient came back saying they were cured. Shockingly, the patient hadn’t tried any of the techniques in the book. Reading it just helped them find some “indescribable mental motion” that made the problem go away. Scott had no idea what to make of this.
The same thing happens with John Sarno’s book, Healing Back Pain: The Mind-Body Connection. Patrick Collison
Patrick Collison

patrickc

amazon.com/Healing-Back-P…
. While it sounds like preposterous woo, it has worked in 4/4 cases of people I personally know trying it. (One account:
aaroniba.net/how-i-cured-my…

just by reading the reviews on Amazon

The theory seems to be that the pain starts with some discomfort, which causes you to think something is wrong, which causes you to focus on the area and tense up, which convinces the body to focus on and tense this area further, until it materializes into actual awful and generally incurable pain. But once you convince yourself that there is nothing structurally wrong with your body, you can break this cycle and the pain goes away. It’s the same as the smoking book. No matter how badly one wants something, no matter how much they try, or how much “rehab” they do, they cannot get the body and mind aligned until they learn the magic formula to steer the body.
If I lie in bed at night and tell myself I want to fall asleep in twenty minutes, I can’t. But if I tell myself I need to lie in bed scanning how my body feels, and noticing any time my mind starts to wander, for twenty minutes as timed by my watch, I will be asleep before the twenty minutes are up - and I can do this basically on command, but funny enough, only if my watch is actually timing me.
When I feel even mildly stressed, or angry about something, I feel my body as being heavy. But if I tell myself to smile and imagine my body being filled with air like a balloon - I not only immediately feel physically lighter, but I also feel much more relaxed and the tension evaporates. It’s as if my body’s weight is what determines my mood, and I can manipulate my body’s “weight” just by thinking about the balloons. I can’t just tell myself to be happier or less stressed, I need to think about the balloons. I need to trick my body in a way that it understands, so the body can lead the mind to the right place.
Often in life, we think about things through facts and logic and abstract arguments. But knowing what we should do, and all the reasons for it, is not enough to get the body to do it. For many things, we can’t just tell ourselves to be stronger, or to be tougher, and get the body to do the thing we want, and sometimes even therapy or rehab can’t get us there. Sometimes we need to find a way to steer the body, and the body only listens when you say the magic words. I like these examples, not only because they are all actually powerful and useful, but also because it feels like I am whispering the secrets of the universe - that through saying the magic words, I am being granted special root access to my own programming.
And then I think about how many other things like this there are in life - whether through ritual, or art, or doing something in some particular way, like my watch actually timing me, we get ourselves to reach an outcome that otherwise, no matter how much we want to get to, or how much we try, is closed off to us. Because our bodies not our minds govern so many of our outcomes - and our body is not persuaded by facts and logic. I am sure there are many more examples like those I shared here, if you have one, please share it.

title: PostgreSQL Extensions in Go
content:
PostgreSQL extensions in
Go
gopgext builds PostgreSQL extensions from plain Go code, using TinyGo. Mark a function with
//gopgext:function
and it becomes a SQL function: gopgext writes the C glue, the install script and the control file.
Get started

Documentation

GitHub
Experimental
gopgext is experimental. Don’t use it in production: a bug in the generated code or the Go runtime runs inside the server, where it can crash it or corrupt data, and the API and generated SQL may change without notice.
Just Go
A project is plain Go files. The standard library works:
fmt
,
regexp
,
encoding/json
,
crypto/*
, maps, generics, iterators,
defer
/
recover
.
Types map to SQL
Strings, numbers, arrays,
NULL
s, sets, rows, timestamps, UUIDs and JSON map to SQL types. Define your own data types and composite types in Go.
Queries and errors
Run SQL through SPI, return errors with SQLSTATE codes, log, read settings and stay responsive to query cancellation.
Beyond functions
Write triggers, aggregates, GiST, GIN, SP-GiST and BRIN operator classes, index access methods, foreign data wrappers and query hooks.
Proven on contrib
Ports of PostgreSQL’s contrib modules (
pgcrypto
,
hstore
,
pg_stat_statements
,
cube
, …) pass upstream’s regression tests.
Safe coexistence
Several Go extensions load in one backend. PostgreSQL errors never unwind through Go frames, and results are copied into PostgreSQL memory.
Hello, world
#
package

main

import

(

"strings"

"gopgext/pg"

)

// Hello returns a greeting for name.

//

//gopgext:function immutable parallel=safe

func

Hello
(
name

string
)

string

{

return

"Hello, "

+

name

+

"!"

}

// Shout upper-cases s. An empty string raises an error.

//

//gopgext:function immutable parallel=safe

func

Shout
(
s

string
)

(
string
,

error
)

{

if

s

==

""

{

return

""
,

pg
.
Errorf
(
pg
.
CodeInvalidParameterValue
,

"nothing to shout"
)

}

return

strings
.
ToUpper
(
s
)

+

"!"
,

nil

}

func

main
()

{}

// runs once per backend, when PostgreSQL loads the library

gopgext init hello
# creates hello/go.mod and hello/main.go

gopgext install hello
# builds hello.so, hello.control, hello--1.0.sql and installs them

psql -c
'CREATE EXTENSION hello'
-c
"SELECT hello('world')"

#     hello

# ---------------

#  Hello, world!

The
tutorial
walks through it step by step.
A sibling project
#
gopgext uses the same approach as
gokm
,
which builds Linux kernel modules from Go: a custom TinyGo target and runtime
layer for the host, a C runtime compiled by the host’s own build system
(PGXS here, kbuild there), and generated glue.

title: My monitor was cutting my download speed by 75%
content:
My Monitor Was Cutting My Download Speed by 75%
2026-11-15
Oscar Molnar
8 min read (1684 words)
#
networking

#
debugging

#
apple

#
macOS

#
usb

#
unifi

Somehow I am one of those few very lucky people to have the opportunity of owning a 2.5 gig symmetrical line for my internet. But one day, when I wanted to brag to my equally nerdy friends, shock and horror: 600 Mbps down? Luckily my upload speed was still 2.4 Gbps, so I didn’t lose all my bragging rights, but that’s weird, right? If anything, you’d expect the opposite!
My ISP is pretty cool. It’s run by this one guy (Hey Keith!), and I know I can always message them and they respond promptly, as they did this time. We tried to run through a few debugging steps, they checked on their end, and everything was normal. I tried my work laptop too, same speed.
I didn’t have time for debugging, because I needed to travel 2000 km to the other side of the continent for a family emergency.
But as soon as I got back, I got curious again. What could it be? In retrospect, I now know when it started: when I moved all my connections onto my
Studio Display XDR
. I wanted to have a one-cable setup, and the monitor offered me that. I’ve had it for half a year now, and I don’t think I’ve ever run a speed test through it. 600 Mbps was more than fast enough for me to never realise I wasn’t getting three quarters of the speed I was paying for 🤦
The setup
#
MacBook Pro M3 Pro
2026 Studio Display XDR, with everything plugged into it so switching laptops is one cable
UGREEN USB-C to 2.5G Ethernet adapter, plugged into the display
UniFi Dream Router 7, the same one from my
WiFi 7 debugging post
What I thought was interesting
#
Pings to other wired computers during a download would fail 10% of the time over Ethernet through the adapter plugged into my screen, and 0% of the time over Wi-Fi. What made it stranger was that there were no dropped frame errors in macOS’s logs at all. This was the big hint for me: the adapter was dropping them before the computer could know.
I then plugged the adapter straight into my Mac instead of the monitor, and ran an iperf3 server on my UDR 7: 2.3 Gbps. So the cable, the router and the adapter are all fine? What about fast.com? Perfect speeds there too! 2.2 down and 2.3 up when connected straight in. As soon as I connected it to the display, it was back to 600 down again.
So it’s the display, right? Well, I would find out: sort of yes, sort of no, which is why I wanted to write this blog post. I couldn’t find anything online explaining the exact cause, and it’s quite a cool reason.
The driver and flow control
#
The adapter uses a Realtek RTL8156B, which on macOS binds to Apple’s generic USB networking driver. But Realtek ship
their own driver on their website
, so I thought I’d give that a go! I installed it and, to my surprise, it almost doubled the download speed to 1.1 Gbps, but that was still nowhere close to 2.5. First hint that it couldn’t just be the monitor’s fault.
Then I tried
flow control
. I had never truly looked into this before, and I think it’s quite neat to know about if you were also ignorant of it like me. Basically, when a device receives Ethernet frames it can’t keep up with, it just drops them. With flow control (it’s something your router or switch has to support), it can send the sender a “pause” frame, and the sender then buffers the data on its side, instead of the receiver (the adapter in this case) on its side. I turned it on in my UniFi console and guess what, download jumped to around 2 Gbps, with upload still at full speed! Yay! Well, not so fast…
I don’t like it always being on, because it can add latency to other systems like my gaming PC. Can you work around it? For sure, you can disable it on those computers, but it’s janky, and it’s another thing I need to remember when my
Sauerbraten
game starts lagging. I need fewer things to remember, considering I am 30 in a couple of months. My memory is not what it used to be.
But the upload was always fine
#
Yeah, isn’t that weird? First of all, it looks like the port can indeed do 2.5 in both directions. I already knew that, because I get much more than that from my external SSD through the monitor’s Thunderbolt port. So the issue is not the monitor again? But it has to be!
Well, I had another idea. How about I connect to my Linux box, which is also on 2.5, and send perfectly smooth UDP traffic at a fixed rate with flow control off? Then I can check the chip’s own counter of dropped frames:
Sent
Lost behind the display
Frames/s reaching the Mac behind the display
Lost direct on the Mac
1.46 Gbps
0%
123,800
0%
1.75 Gbps
0.05%
148,600
0%
1.94 Gbps
0.1%
165,000
0%
2.03 Gbps
2.7%
168,000
0%
2.12 Gbps
7.2%
168,000
0%
2.20 Gbps
10.5%
168,000
0.001%
2.28 Gbps
13.5%
168,000
0.02%
So basically no drops whatsoever when connected straight to my Mac, but loads of drops after about 168k frames per second (roughly 2 Gbps). Remember that number. That number comes from the adapter’s own counters: however much I sent, the number of frames it managed to hand over to the Mac each second flattened out at about 168,000, and everything above that was dropped.
Why did this not happen on my SSD? What was the only difference I could find? Bursts!
When the Mac reads data from a USB 3 device, the device sends some packets, then has to wait for the Mac to say “lgtm, send more!”. The SSD enclosure sends 16 packets before needing a go-ahead message back. The RTL8156B in my Ethernet adapter sends 4.
Here is a diagram of my best understanding of why this is an issue. I made this diagram 100 times, and I think I can probably improve it more, but if it helps you understand the issue, I have done my job.
As you can see, the speed of packets coming into the adapter is 2.5 Gbps. That’s what the router pushes in. The speed going out is around 2 Gbps. The reason is that if you add up the average time it takes to get the go-ahead through my monitor’s hub, which is around 7.6 µs, to the average time it takes to send 4 KB, around 8.2 µs, you can find what the maximum speed is.
Well, if the speed of the drain from my adapter to my Mac is half a gig slower than the speed of the input, then you can imagine the buffer getting filled more and more until it overflows. Those are dropped packets, which result in a hard backoff when the router resends them, so you drop loads in speed. And that’s the reason for all of this.
OK, well, what now?
#
I have a cupboard full of USB-C Ethernet adapters. Don’t ask.
The problem is they’re all 1 gig adapters, so any of the tests I made would not tell me anything, because the issues don’t start at 1 gig. They start at around 2… If I run my 2.5 gig adapter at 1 gig speeds, I get 1 gig downloads with the official driver. If I run it at 1.5, I get 1.5. If I run it at 2, well, I get 1…
So I thought I would do what any human would do, and I spent more money on a new adapter. Another UGREEN, but this time it’s one that promises 5 Gbps and uses the RTL8157 chip instead:
UGREEN 5G USB-C Ethernet adapter
. My reasoning was that if this one could get me better speeds, it would help me understand how. And that it did!
With this adapter, I dropped 0 frames:
Sent
Frames/s reaching the Mac
Dropped by the adapter
1.5 Gbps
124k
0
1.9 Gbps
157k
0
2.1 Gbps
173k
0
2.3 Gbps
187k
0
2.4 Gbps
194k
0
Why? Well, looking through what each adapter tells me about itself:
$ python3 -c "import usb.core; e = usb.core.find(idVendor=0x0bda)[0][(0,0)][0]; print('packet size', e.wMaxPacketSize, 'bMaxBurst', e.extra_descriptors[2])"

# old adapter (RTL8156B)
packet size 1024 bMaxBurst 3

# new adapter (RTL8157)
packet size 1024 bMaxBurst 7

# bMaxBurst counts the packets after the first one, so 3 means 4 packets and 7 means 8

I can see that instead of sending 4 1 KB packets per burst, it would send 8! And the speed of the link was also 2x faster, so those 8 KB would go 2x faster to the Mac. That means the time spent was 8 times lower to send the same data, and while the wait for the go-ahead was identical, the theoretical speed from the adapter to the Mac, including the wait for the go-ahead, was a maximum of 4.5 Gbps. That’s much bigger than the 2.5 coming into the adapter, so the buffer would never fill up, packets would never drop and everything was great, even if the “go-ahead” response was still much slower than when connected directly to the Mac.
Final thoughts
#
I think the big takeaway from this is that all the things you think are quite easy to understand, such as transfer speeds, have so many cool intricacies that it’s worth diving deep every so often. Who would’ve thought that the speed of the link between the adapter and the Mac was defined not only by the link speed itself in Gbps, but also by the time it took your Mac to reply, by the amount of packets, by the speed of those packets, by the number of packets in a burst, and by the size of those packets?
See you next time, when I will spend just as much time on another trivial thing that we can all learn from!

title: Tropical Rainforests Species may be surprisingly young
content:
November 17, 2026

Species in tropical rainforests may be surprisingly young with emergence linked to geological upheavals

by
University of Turku

edited by

Swati Mestri
, 																								reviewed by
Robert Egan

Editors' notes

This article has been reviewed according to Science X's

editorial process

and
policies
.

Editors
have highlighted
the following attributes while ensuring the content's credibility:

fact-checked

trusted source

proofread

The GIST

Add to Preferred Sources

Spread of the Danaea genus ferns from one region to another and speciation in different areas in the past 53 million years. The Amazon has been the most important area for speciation. Credit: Venni Keskiniva

How did the rich biodiversity in the tropics originally emerge? One traditional explanation is that tropical regions have provided species with favorable habitats for millions of years. While, for example, Europe's flora and fauna have been subjected to repeated ice ages, many ancient evolutionary lineages have persisted for a long time in the tropics.

However, tropical regions have not remained unchanged. The uplift of mountain ranges, the drying of coastal bays and the formation of different types of soil have forced species to adapt to new conditions and have opened up opportunities for the emergence and spread of new species.

Researchers from the University of Turku in Finland and Aarhus University in Denmark investigated the link between environmental changes and the evolutionary history of the fern genus Danaea, which grows in tropical America.

"We have conducted extensive research at the University of Turku in order to understand the biodiversity of the Amazon rainforest," says professor of ecology Hanna Tuomisto.

"In the last 25 years, we have discovered and described 47 new Danaea species previously unknown to science and have clarified the distribution and phylogenetic relationships of the species in the Danaea genus. We have now been able to link this information to the geological and climatic history of tropical America."

Danaea kessleri, one of the new species described by the University of Turku researchers in 2024. It diverged from its sister species approximately 3 million years ago in western Amazonia, on the edge of the Andes. Credit: Hanna Tuomisto

Ancient family, young species

According to the
study
published in the journal
Frontiers of Biogeography
, the Danaea genus diverged from its closest living relatives as early as the Early Cretaceous period, some 128 million years ago, and the common ancestor of the present-day Danaea species lived around 53 million years ago.

While the genus has a very long evolutionary history, around half of its extant species emerged only within the last 6 million years.

This relatively recent speciation coincided with significant geological and climatic changes. During the Miocene epoch, the uplift of the Andes reshaped the climate and soil of tropical America, and the vast megawetlands of the western Amazon were drained. At the same time, new landmasses emerged in Central America, enabling species to spread and diversify.

Tropical America divided into different regions where Danaea fern species can be found. Credit: Venni Keskiniva

Danaea ferns most diverse in the Amazon

In general, fern species are most diverse in tropical mountain forests. However, in the case of the Danaea genus, the greatest number of species has developed in the Amazon throughout the history of the genus.

The difference could be explained by the growth habits of various fern genera.

"Mountain rainforests are home in particular to an abundance of epiphytes—plants that grow on top of other plants. Danaea ferns, on the other hand, grow on the forest floor. These research results are, in fact, similar to those obtained for trees, which are also the most species-rich in lowland rainforests," says postdoctoral researcher Venni Keskiniva from the University of Turku.

Research into different plant groups may therefore reveal quite different responses to the same environment, which may explain tropical biodiversity to some extent.

Adapting to mountainous environments opened up new avenues for dispersal

The study found that Danaea lineages adapted to mountainous conditions began to appear as the uplift of the Andes accelerated around 20 million years ago.

Interestingly, the lineages that had spread into the mountain forests often dispersed to new areas farther away from the equator. On the other hand, lineages specialized in the lowland conditions of the Amazon tended to stay put in the Amazon.

"As the plants had already adapted to the cooler climate of the mountains, it may have been easier for them to spread to areas where the temperature differences between the seasons are greater," says Keskiniva.

The study shows that the dynamic geological history of the American tropics has contributed to the development of the region's staggering biodiversity. Although the plant lineages in rainforests may be very old, their current species may be surprisingly young.

"The biodiversity in rainforests is the result of a long history, but its formation has also been greatly influenced by events that are relatively recent on a geological time scale," Keskiniva concludes.

More information

Venni Keskiniva et al., Out of Amazonia: Biogeography of a Neotropical fern radiation,
Frontiers of Biogeography
(2026).
DOI: 10.21425/fob.19.211246

Key concepts

biogeography
paleogeography
species diversity
ferns and fern allies
Biological Evolution

Provided by

University of Turku

Swati Mestri

Swati Mestri holds a bachelor's degree in Electronics Engineering and has worked as a content editor since 2019. She has experience editing research documents across technology, health care, and materials science, and has a particular interest in technology and space.

Bachelor's in mathematical biology, Master's in creative writing. Well-traveled with unique perspectives on science and language.

log

lean4lean (
67f63b0c
, built with Lean v4.33.1) on the compiled files, module by module

, above, does. (

unknown constant 'Decidable.intro'
)

What was verified

Five theorems, proved in the submission's
Main.lean
. Their statements are below exactly as they appear in the challenge file, which imports only Mathlib. All the mathematical notions in them (
riemannZeta
,
DirichletCharacter
,
DirichletCharacter.LFunction
,
IsPrimitive
) are Mathlib's.

1. The Riemann Hypothesis
, using Mathlib's own definition (
Mathlib/NumberTheory/LSeries/RiemannZeta.lean
): every zero of ζ other than the trivial zeros −2, −4, −6, … has real part 1/2. The condition
s ≠ 1
is there because Mathlib assigns ζ a conventional value at its pole.

def RiemannHypothesis : Prop :=
∀ (s : ℂ) (_ : riemannZeta s = 0) (_ : ¬∃ n : ℕ, s = -2 * (n + 1)) (_ : s ≠ 1), s.re = 1 / 2

theorem riemannHypothesis : RiemannHypothesis

2. The same statement written out
in the submission's own words. Lean accepts the two as equal by definition.

theorem riemannZeta_eq_zero_re :
∀ s : ℂ, riemannZeta s = 0 → (¬∃ n : ℕ, s = -2 * ((n : ℂ) + 1)) → s ≠ 1 → s.re = 1 / 2

3. No zeros to the right of the critical line, for every Dirichlet L-function.
For every modulus
N ≥ 1
and every Dirichlet character χ modulo N, primitive or not, L(χ, s) ≠ 0 whenever Re s > 1/2. The one excluded case is the trivial character at
s = 1
, where the L-function has its pole.

theorem LFunction_ne_zero_of_half_lt_re :
∀ (N : ℕ) [NeZero N] (χ : DirichletCharacter ℂ N) (s : ℂ),
1 / 2 < s.re → (χ ≠ 1 ∨ s ≠ 1) → DirichletCharacter.LFunction χ s ≠ 0

4. Zeros in the critical strip lie on the critical line, for every Dirichlet L-function.

theorem LFunction_eq_zero_re :
∀ (N : ℕ) [NeZero N] (χ : DirichletCharacter ℂ N) (s : ℂ),
0 < s.re → s.re < 1 → DirichletCharacter.LFunction χ s = 0 → s.re = 1 / 2

5. The same for primitive characters
, the form in which the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis for Dirichlet L-functions is usually stated.

theorem LFunction_eq_zero_re_of_isPrimitive :
∀ (N : ℕ) [NeZero N] (χ : DirichletCharacter ℂ N), χ.IsPrimitive →
