title: Show HN: Zero C# – C# without a runtime or GC
content:
C# with nothing underneath

A fork of bflat compiles C# straight to a small native program: no .NET runtime, no garbage collector, nothing to install where it runs.

You keep C#'s syntax, type checking and generics. Memory comes from arenas you free all at once, and a small library gives you strings, collections, input and output on those terms. The same source runs on Linux, macOS and Windows, on WebAssembly, and on DOS on a 386.

Get started

Build the quiz tutorial

Run it in your browser

// Read into a stack buffer: nothing allocated per answer.

Span
<
char
> buffer =
stackalloc char
[
32
];

Out
.Write(
$"Q
{i}
:
{a}
+
{b}
= "
);

int
length =
In
.ReadLine(buffer);

// Kept until the end, so it goes into an arena.

mistakes.Add(
Str
.Format(keep,

$"
{a}
+
{b}
=
{a + b}
, not
{value}
"
));

From the quiz the
tutorial
builds, step by step.

The language stays, the runtime goes

The compiler still checks everything it checks in .NET. What's missing is what a runtime would do while your program runs.

You keep

C# 15
Unions, extension members and the new memory safety rules.

Real generics
A specialized copy for each type, and static abstract members.

Interfaces and virtual methods
Default interface methods, casts,
is
and
as
.

Records, tuples, anonymous types
Value equality,
with
, and the generated
ToString
.

Lambdas and queries
Where
,
Select
and
GroupBy
, from a small library instead of LINQ.

Threads
Parallel.For
runs a loop on every core.

You do without

Garbage collector
Arenas free their memory all at once, when you say.

.NET runtime
Hello world is 11 KB on Windows and 40 KB on Linux, with nothing to install.

Catching exceptions
throw
ends the program. Return errors as unions.

Reflection and async
A type can be compared, but it has no name.

One program, five machines

The hello-world sample, unchanged, built for each target. Each build is checked by the same test suite, which requires the same output everywhere.

$
./build.sh Minimal

$
./run.sh Minimal
Hello from zero-mode!

$
wc -c bin/Minimal
39848 bin/Minimal

Linux, x64 or arm64

A native program that needs only the C library. On macOS it builds and runs in a container.

$
./build.sh --mac Minimal

$
bin/mac/Minimal
Hello from zero-mode!

$
wc -c bin/mac/Minimal
64728 bin/mac/Minimal

macOS on Apple Silicon

A native Mac program: bflat compiles it, the Mac's own clang links it. No container to run it.

$
./build.sh --win Minimal

$
./run.sh --win Minimal
Hello from zero-mode!

$
wc -c bin/win/Minimal.exe
10752 bin/win/Minimal.exe

Windows x64

A console program on Windows' own C library, built from Linux or macOS. Tested under Wine.

$
./build.sh --wasm Minimal

$
./run.sh --wasm Minimal
Hello from zero-mode!

$
wc -c bin/wasm/Minimal.wasm
15833 bin/wasm/Minimal.wasm

WebAssembly

A WASI module, through NativeAOT-LLVM. Runs under wasmtime.

C:\>D:
D:\>PROGRAM

Hello from zero-mode!

D:\>DIR PROGRAM.EXE
PROGRAM  EXE     16,384

D:\>

DOS on a 386

The same bitcode compiled for a 386, run by the HX DOS extender. Tested on Bochs's i386 model.

What's different, and what you get

Without a runtime, a few things work differently. Each has a page that explains why and what to do instead.

Memory is yours to free

There is no garbage collector, so
new
is never freed. Arenas hand out memory and free it all at once, one per lifetime.

Memory without a garbage collector

Text without throwaway strings

Out.Line($"...")
formats straight into the output buffer, and
In.ReadLine
reads into a span. Strings that must last go into an arena.

Strings without a garbage collector

Collections that live in arenas

List
,
Dict
, and their versions for references and string keys, all handles into an arena.

Choose a collection

C# 15, with the safety rules on

Every program compiles under the updated memory safety rules: creating a pointer is safe, reading through one is marked and explained.

The memory safety rules

Where to start

If you're new to it, these four pages take you from nothing to an interactive program.

Install
The bflat fork and the prerequisites.

Your first program
Build it, run it, see how small it is.

Run it on DOS
The same program under FreeDOS, in an emulator.

The tutorial
A quiz: output, input, bad input, arenas.

Looking for something specific? The
task guides
answer one question each, and the
reference
lists every type in the library.

title: I'm quite pleased by the tech architecture of my art website
content:
I’m quite pleased by the tech architecture of my art website
This piece has embedded interactive widgets from my art website!

It is a truth universally acknowledged, that every developer blog begins by explaining the new static site generator they wrote to make it. This post isn’t
exactly
that, but maybe only on a technicality, in that it’s not about
this
website…

The problem

Earlier this year I decided to put a some of my paintings and sketchbook pages online. I don’t much use social media besides Hacker News, but I wanted to share my work with friends and family. So I’d been sending scans of my work in group chats. That was fine for a bit but so messy and disorganized. Sometimes someone asked, “Where did you paint this?” Sometimes a friend wanted to see what it looked like in real life. My little brother suggested a map with a marker for each piece. That was a good idea! For that I’d need a website and some code. Here, take a look at the map, its done now! You can zoom and click on markers to see the painting!

When it comes to tech side projects there are two wolves inside me. One is the Wolf of Pragmatism, which wants to smash every problem with whatever hammer is nearest at hand: “Isn’t this just some trivial React? Dump the images in S3 and call it a day. This website is for friends and family; you have no traffic to speak of. Put a CDN in front so your parents in India get reasonable performance.”

The other is the Aesthetic Wolf: “This should be a static website. The content almost never changes.”

Yes. This is a static website. I do at most four, and on average less than 0.3, paintings a day. The content almost never changes. Why should javascript render the page on the user’s browser? Why should any code even run on the server? I should have the bytes for every page just sitting there, ready to be shipped. The correct server implementation for this problem is
open
followed by
sendfile
inside the event loop (I’m joking but only kind of?). The Aesthetic Wolf won.

But the problem with a static website is that for every new post, I need to add a file, and run a build, and deploy it to production. I made a hundred paintings this year! Even if I automate a lot of it, I wanted a better UI for stuff like adding tags and setting location. And the best UI for what’s essentially a CRUD app is … probably a web UI. But if I have a web UI that changes the content of the website, that’s not a static website any more.

Now look at this colorful house!

So what I really want is a website that’s static for everyone else, but dynamic for me. I want a build system but I want it triggered by actions in a nice CRUD UI that I make, not GitHub actions or a terminal.

Here’s my silly little solution to this silly conundrum. I’m sure the design I’m about to describe isn’t novel, but I did come up with it. I’m just pleased by it because it’s an efficient solution to the exact problem I happened to have. It’s dollar-efficient for me, i.e., it’s free*. It’s resource-efficient for Cloudflare, because the static assets are rarely rebuilt and mostly sit there cached. And it’s fast, because the bytes are mostly sitting there in a CDN waiting to be sent.

(Asterisk: the compute and bandwidth are free. The storage is currently free, but if I paint enough then I’ll go past the 10 GB free tier and pay a couple cents per month.)

The solution

The main idea is that every html page
is
rendered on the server, but with a cache header telling Cloudflare’s infrastructure to cache the response forever (well, for 30 days). Then, whenever I upload a new art piece or change the set of tags or anything like that, the request handler for this write operation invalidates all cached pages. That’s it.

There’s one detail that makes this work well for an image-heavy website: we generate several smaller sizes of each image
at upload time
, and I actually do it on the client’s browser. Since I’m the only uploader, that would be my browser. We need the smaller sizes for thumbnails and cards, where sending the full archival images would be way too slow. Those downsampled images are uploaded along with originals to Cloudflare’s R2, their S3-equivalent.

Why downsample at upload time? Cloudflare does offer an image service that’ll do the resizing the first time you make a request for that image at that size, and it’ll cache that resized copy. But in my case I already know the three sizes I want, so it’s faster to just precompute and store them. The additional storage doesn’t add up to much, because the archival images are enormous compared to downsampled copies.

All the metadata for all pieces goes in a single json file that also lives in R2. When someone requests a dynamic html page, like the one for
pieces tagged #summer
, a piece of code runs in a Cloudflare worker. It reads the json and generates the html, which is then cached until the next invalidation. Cloudflare’s CDN handles the rest: if someone in India later requests the same page, the cached artifact is sent to an edge machine in India and cached there for a while. I suppose Cloudflare can choose to rerun the worker instead of copying the artifact, which is fine by me. Based on my testing that’s not what happens: the generator writes a timestamp on each page so I can see when it was generated.

Now look at these cool rocks!

Interactive elements

The website has some interactive stuff like maps and timelines. Those are just embedded javascript that run on the client’s browser and read that single metadata json file to initialize. They don’t write anything back to the server, so there’s no database or anything. They’re just displaying the information in different ways. For example, here’s an interactive timeline of my pieces over the years. I haven’t uploaded everything I’ve ever made, so this is biased toward recent stuff.

(To be very technically correct, this timeline component doesn’t read the json directly. Its bars are drawn on the server, and it gets a per-month list derived from the metadata to handle clicking and paging.)

Here’s what the page for a piece looks like. The metadata json has the information to figure out what pieces were done nearby and around the same time, so I show all that. This is an embedded iframe so you can scroll and click:

Why invalidate everything?

This is where Pragmatic Wolf won. Here’s the possible optimization: whenever I make an edit, we should invalidate only those pages that are potentially affected by that edit. A good build system certainly works this way: when you change one file, it recompiles only those artifacts that (transitively) depend on it.

In my case, however, dependencies aren’t explicitly written down anywhere. The code to generate a page just runs, and potentially any change in the metadata json could cause its output to be different. I could try to encode the dependencies for each page and component, but it’s so easy to get this wrong and introduce bugs in the future. The result is a half-updated website, i.e., a correctness bug.

So while it’s true that adding a new piece only changes the
#evening
page if the new piece actually has that tag, I considered it too tricky to get this cache invalidation right, and decided to just invalidate everything. If I were using a normal static site generator then the CDN could potentially do this optimization by noticing that the hash of an artifact hasn’t changed, so it doesn’t need to be updated on every edge machine.

Anyway here is a waterfall in Washington, the one in Twin Peaks apparently:

And here’s the view from right outside my house in Brooklyn:

By the way, the specific javascript framework I ended up using is called Astro. Cloudflare bought them so they’re pretty nicely integrated. But you don’t really need it for this, you could write your own code to run in the Worker to generate the page. The whole trick is in some careful management of cache.

title: Bolt's Scooters Are Becoming Accessibility Sensors
content:
#GeoAI

#News

Bolt’s Scooters Are Becoming Accessibility Sensors

Aleks Buczkowski

09.28.2026

Founder and Editor-in-Chief at Geoawesome. Raised around maps, spatial thinking is part of my DNA. By day, I’m a Director at PwC, leading a global drone and geospatial team.

Bolt has demonstrated that a shared scooter can be more than a vehicle. It can also be a mobile geospatial sensor.

During its Wheels4Wheels pilot in Tallinn, Estonia, the company used sensors already installed in its scooters to assess pavement conditions, curb transitions and other features affecting wheelchair users and people with reduced mobility.

Bolt says the project covered approximately 550 kilometres across all eight Tallinn districts, producing 40.5 million accelerometer readings and more than 66,000 surface-quality assessments. The resulting information was contributed to OpenStreetMap, according to
Bolt’s accessibility programme page
.

Publishing the results as open data makes the project more significant than a conventional corporate mapping exercise. Municipalities, routing applications and accessibility services could all potentially use the observations.

The larger opportunity is the conversion of commercial vehicle fleets into continuously operating urban-observation networks. Thousands of scooters already traverse city streets during everyday operations, potentially detecting damaged surfaces and deteriorating infrastructure without requiring a dedicated municipal survey.

According to
Geo Week News
, Bolt combined GPS with accelerometers, gyroscopes and cameras. The company reports that the pilot increased available surface-quality data in Tallinn by 26%. These figures have not been independently audited.

The difficult step is converting motion signals into reliable accessibility information. A vibration could represent broken pavement, cobblestones, a drainage channel or an abrupt rider manoeuvre. Results may also vary with speed, tyre pressure, weather and scooter model.

Coverage presents another limitation. Scooters primarily travel where their use is permitted and commercially viable. They may miss residential streets, pedestrian paths and disconnected sections that create the greatest problems for wheelchair users.

Each observation therefore needs provenance, a confidence level and an effective validation method. The most important validators should include wheelchair and mobility-aid users, who can determine whether a detected anomaly represents a genuine barrier.

Wheels4Wheels complements rather than replaces existing accessibility platforms.
Wheelmap
maps the accessibility of public places, while
Project Sidewalk
combines crowdsourcing, machine learning and street imagery to identify curb ramps and obstacles. Bolt adds passive, recurring fleet sensing.

A future workflow could use scooter telemetry to flag anomalies, imagery to classify them and local contributors to confirm their significance before the information enters OpenStreetMap.

Public discussion of the project has also highlighted a contradiction: poorly parked scooters can themselves block sidewalks and curb ramps. Bolt’s accessibility strategy must therefore address parking and obstruction management alongside data collection.

If the company can demonstrate reliable classification, transparent data handling and meaningful participation by accessibility users, Wheels4Wheels could evolve into more than a mapping experiment. The sensing capacity already exists. The next challenge is turning it into trustworthy, routable and genuinely inclusive geospatial infrastructure.

The Superspectral Shift: Why the Remote Sensing World Is Moving Away from Old Multispectral Limits

Harshaditya Gaur

09.23.2026

Harshaditya Gaur is a Senior Remote Sensing Engineer at BharatRohan Airborne Innovations Limited, specializing in satellite and UAV-based Earth observation, hyperspectral imaging, and geospatial data analysis. He holds a Master’s degree in Remote Sensing and GIS from the Indian Institute of Remote Sensing (IIRS–ISRO), with a specialization in Satellite Image Analysis and Photogrammetry. His work focuses on applying remote sensing, machine learning, and open-source geospatial technologies to precision agriculture, environmental monitoring, and automated image-processing workflows. He is also actively involved in technical research, knowledge sharing, and mentoring through workshops, webinars, and geospatial community initiatives.

For decades, “more bands” in Earth observation meant one of two things: you either work with multispectral sensors; four to ten broad bands, cheap, fast and familiar or else transition to the hyperspectral domain, which has hundreds of narrow, contiguous bands, costly and enormous data volumes. However, this gap is closing not by making hyperspectral high-resolution accessible, but by rethinking what “enough bands” actually means. A category is quietly establishing itself between the two:
Superspectral
, a curated set of roughly a dozen to a few dozen
discrete
bands, placed purposely at specific wavelengths that correspond to something physically meaningful, rather than being sampled continuously across the electromagnetic spectrum.

The Multispectral Ceiling

Multispectral sensors were built around a simple idea: a handful of broad bands such as blue, green, red, red-edge, near-infrared are enough to compute NDVI & NDRE, delineate landcover, and monitor vegetation vigour at scale. Many of these systems also carry a panchromatic band: a single high-resolution spectral channel spanning across the visible spectrum (400-800 nm), used purely to sharpen spatial detail rather than to add spectral information. That’s the multispectral-era trade-off at minimal where spatial resolution and spectral resolution were treated as two separate problems, solved by two different types of bands. It works and it still works, for a huge share of remote sensing applications.

However, broad bands average out the very features that distinguish stressed vegetation from healthy vegetation, one water body from another, or one mineral from the next. A 100-120 nm wide band cannot resolve a narrow absorption or reflectance feature within it. Indices tied to specific physiological or physical processes such as pigment ratios, early-stage stress signatures and water turbidity, often require reflectance captured at precise, narrow wavelengths which a standard four or five-band setup was never designed to capture.

Why Hyperspectral isn’t the Universal Answer

Hyperspectral imaging solves the problem by capturing contiguous and narrow bands. A 20-band sensor covering 500-700 nm at 10 nm interval is hyperspectral by this definition, while a sensor with 20 discrete, non-adjacent bands spanning the visible through infrared is still, technically a multispectral. That distinction matters because hyperspectral sensors carry real expense; complex optics, strict calibration requirements, and data volumes that stretch onboard storage, downlink bandwidth, and downstream ML pipelines. For most applied problems, that’s more data than the underlying problem statement actually needs.

The Middle Category: Superspectral

Superspectral fits between the two. Rather than sampling the electromagnetic spectrum continuously, it samples it
selectively
– a dozen-plus discrete, narrow bands chosen because they align with known absorption or reflectance features, not because they happen to be adjacent on a continuum. It’s a knowledge-first approach to sensor design: instead of asking “how much of the spectrum can we cover continuously,” it asks “which specific wavelengths actually carry the signal we care about.”

This only works if the band selection is grounded in the underlying physics or biology of the target. Which is exactly where the reasoning gets interesting — because the “right” dozen bands look completely different depending on what you’re trying to measure.

Building the Case: Three Domains, Three Different Superspectral Stacks

Coastal & Aquatic — A dedicated coastal-blue region

Water quickly absorbs longer wavelengths, which is exactly why coastal and bathymetric applications require the shorter wavelength of the visible spectrum. In clear, deep water 400-450 nm wavelength penetrates furthest, making it the band of choice for shallow-water bathymetry and seafloor mapping. In turbid or CDOM-rich coastal water the picture inverts: suspended sediment and dissolved organic matter absorb and scatter strongly in the blue, and the transmission peak migrates toward green. On sediment loaded reef sites it has been observed shifting by around 100 nm into the green-yellow, peaking near 575 nm. A standard multispectral blue band, which is broadly tuned for atmospheric correction and land applications, is not optimized for this; a narrow, purpose-placed coastal-blue bands are. This is a case where one extra, carefully positioned band is more beneficial for the application than several additional generic ones.

Agriculture & Forestry — How discrete spectral selection works?

Green/yellow region (515–570 nm):
Chlorophyll absorption is weak in the region, so carotenoids and anthocyanins dominate the signal, and small changes in the pigment show up as measurable changes in reflectance. Photochemical Reflectance Index (PRI), which pairs a band at 531 nm tracking the xanthophyll cycle, the fast photoprotective response of the canopy against a reference band near 570 nm where that cycle has no effect. The 531/570 pairing is the clearest illustration in the whole vegetation stack of why
discrete
placement matters, a single broad green band averages both of them into one number that carries neither.

Red region (650–690 nm):
Tracks pigment concentration, with the chlorophyll absorption maximum near 670-680 nm. When, paired with the red-edge bands, it helps constrain the shape of the absorption feature rather than just its depth. At 687 nm band, it allows retrieval of solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence, a direct proxy for photosynthetic activity rather than just the presence of pigment.

Red-edge region (700–750 nm):
The single most diagnostic region for vegetation stress. Healthy vegetation shows a redshift (the edge moves toward NIR); stressed or drought-affected vegetation shows a blueshift. This one narrow region does more stress-detection work than broad NIR alone ever could.

NIR region (780–1000 nm):
Reflectance is dominated by scattering, not absorption; biomass, leaf area index, and water absorption through near 970 nm that supports biochemical property retrieval independent of pigment signals.

Urban — Where the same spectral logic becomes more conditional.

Extending the vegetation logic straight into urban environments using Red-edge and NIR bands, but the physics doesn’t transfer as cleanly. Red-edge and NIR bands are diagnostic of chlorophyll and canopy structure, which makes them excellent for mapping urban vegetation fraction: street trees, park canopy, green-roof coverage, and green-space stress, all of which are legitimate and useful urban indicators, especially as proxies for urban surface extent and heat island risk. But Red-edge and NIR bands are not, a strong basis for classifying
built materials themselves
— asphalt, concrete, and rooftops don’t have a red-edge-style feature the way vegetation does. The spectral region that most cleanly separates impervious surfaces from vegetation and bare soil sits further out, in the shortwave infrared, where built materials and natural surfaces diverge most sharply. A Red-edge/NIR-only superspectral stack can tell you a great deal about a city’s green infrastructure; it can’t, tell you what the non-green parts of the city are made of. Getting that requires extending the band selection into SWIR — which is a fair, extension of the same superspectral principle: add exactly the band the physics calls for, nothing more.

Superspectral Sensors Exists: Drones to Satellites

Micasense Drone payload: RedEdge-P Triple.
A stacked triple narrowband camera bodies on one drone platform, each contributing a handful of 15 discrete, narrow, non-contiguous bands, pan-sharpened to 4 centimetres per pixel, enough to compute pigment and stress-sensitive indices that a standard five-band multispectral sensor can’t generate. This is the smallest-scale, most accessible end of the superspectral sensor; no continuous spectral coverage, just a deliberately chosen set of narrow bands.

Commercial VHR satellite: WorldView-3.
Launched in 2014, WorldView-3 is explicitly described in the remote sensing literature and by its operators as a “Superspectral” sensor, a term used specifically to distinguish it from hyperspectral. Its imager collects 8 discrete VNIR bands (coastal, blue, green, yellow, red, red-edge, and two NIR bands), 8 discrete SWIR bands, and a separate 12-band CAVIS instrument for atmospheric correction (clouds, aerosols, water vapor, ice, and snow) 29 bands in total, but none of them contiguous in the way a hyperspectral band are. That distinction matters: WorldView-3 has been used for tasks like hydrocarbon and mineral detection that’s the domain of hyperspectral, precisely because its SWIR bands were placed at known diagnostic absorption features rather than spread evenly across the spectrum.

Research microsatellite: VENμS.
A joint French–Israeli mission (CNES and the Israel Space Agency, launched 2017), was purpose-built VENμS Super-Spectral Camera (VSSC) with exactly 12 narrow bands between 415–910 nm, at 5.3 m resolution with a 2-day revisit. The band placement was designed specifically around vegetation status and the chlorophyll red-edge, plus atmospheric correction. It’s one of the cleanest real-world matches to the “12-18 narrow, targeted bands” definition of superspectral, since it was purpose-built as a science mission rather than adapted from a broader commercial sensor.

Next-generation Landsat constellation: Landsat Next.
Planned for launch in late 2030/early 2031, the USGS and NASA’s Landsat Next mission is explicitly presented as “26-band Superspectral”, more than double the 11 bands on Landsat 8 and 9. It combines refined versions of Landsat’s legacy bands, ten new bands targeting applications like harmful algal blooms and snow hydrology, and five thermal infrared bands. When, a government agency formally classifies its flagship imaging mission as “superspectral” rather than multispectral or hyperspectral, that’s a strong indication the category has moved from marketing language to an accepted technical classification.

Why This Matters for GeoAI Pipelines

The pattern across all three domains is the same, and it’s the real reason for superspectral as a category:

Information density over band count.
A dozen bands selected against known absorption features carry more discriminative signal per band than a broader, generic stack, without the storage and preprocessing burden of a full hyperspectral cube.

Physics-informed feature engineering.
Bands chosen for red-edge stress detection, coastal water penetration, or pigment-specific absorption effectively encode domain knowledge directly into the input, reducing how much a downstream model has to learn from raw reflectance alone.

Where This Is Headed: Future

The multispectral or hyperspectral is a simple binary choice. Superspectral won’t replace either, broadband multispectral remains the workhorse for large-scale, low-cost monitoring, and hyperspectral remains necessary where continuous spectral coverage matters, like detailed mineral mapping or ore detection. But for the growing set of problems that need
specific
physical or biological signals – water quality, vegetation stress, urban green infrastructure and many more; without the overhead of a full hyperspectral sensor system, superspectral is becoming the realistic answer. It’s less “how much of the spectrum can we see” and more “how much do we actually need to see, and where.”

Superspectral systems, by design, only see what they were told to look for. That’s a real trade-off, not a compromise to gloss over, it’s the whole point of this technology.

title: RCE in Gnupg
content:
[Announce] GnuPG Security Advisory for GPGME (T8557,CVE-2026-129975)

Werner Koch

wk at gnupg.org

Fri Nov 20 19:01:51 CET 2026

Messages sorted by:

[ date ]

[ thread ]

[ subject ]

[ author ]

Hello!

We are pleased to announce the availability of a new GPGME release:
version 2.3.1.  This version fixes a *critical security bug* found in
all prior versions.  We also release a new Gpg4win versions and and
GnuPG Desktop and GnuPG VS-Desktop versions which all make use of GPGME.

Description
===========

By using an OpenPGP key containing a crafted very long user id it is
possible to trigger a double free.  This double free can be used
exfiltrate data from applications by sending for example signed data.
Exploiting this bug to mount an Remote Code Execution attack (RCE) can't
be ruled out.  Thus an immediate update is highly suggested.

Our internal ID is T8557 (
https://static.dev.gnupg.org/T8557
)
The CVE-id is CVE-2026-129975.

This vulnerability was discovered by Johan Carlsson and we were informed
by GitLab on 2026-11-12.  Initially we set 2026-11-25 for a coordinated
disclosure; due to the new Ruby2Shell bug GitLab had to update earlier
and thus we also disclosed the GPGME bug on 2026-11-20.

The root cause for this bug are two GPGME internal functions to read the
status lines and key listings from gpg.  Initially a buffer of 1024
bytes is allocated which is reallocated if more space is required.  When
reallocating the pointer to the new buffer is used by the function but
it is only assigned back to the context object at the end of the
function.  Thus if the function returns early due to an read error or
other events the context is not updated and keeps the stale pointer to
the freed memory.  Eventually the context is released and the memory
freed a second time.  Due to other allocations in between the common
double free checks of memory allocators may not be triggered.

Impact
======

All software using a GPGME version prior to 2.3.0 either as shared
libary, DLL, or statically linked is affected.  Examples of software
using GPGME are

- Gpg4win
- GnuPG Desktop
- GnuPG VS-Desktop
- Most mail clients
- Many XMPP clients
- Samba
- Flatpack

Solution
========

Please update your GPGME shared library to version 2.3.1.  If you need a
DLL you may take it from from the updated Gpg4win version.

For statically linked binaries remmeber to build them against GPGME
2.3.1.

If for some reasons GPGME can't be updated, you may patch your GPGME
version using the attached patch which likley applies cleanly even to
very old versions.

There is no need to udpate GPGMEPP or GPGMEQT.

Noteworthy changes in version 2.3.1 (2026-11-19)
================================================
[compared to version 2.2.0]

* New constants GPGME_PK_MLKEM, GPGME_PK_MLDSA, and GPGME_PK_DLTHM.
Add mappings for algos used bei backends.   [rMa85fa49236]

* Fix a double free in the status line read code.
[T8557,CVE-2026-129975]

* Interface changes relative to the 2.2.0 release:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
GPGME_PK_DLTHM                NEW.
GPGME_PK_MLKEM                NEW.
GPGME_PK_MLDSA                NEW.

Release-info:
https://dev.gnupg.org/T8427

Getting the Software
====================

Please follow the instructions found at <
https://gnupg.org/download/
> or
read on:

The GPGME source code compressed using BZIP2 and its OpenPGP signature
are available here:

https://gnupg.org/ftp/gcrypt/gpgme/gpgme-2.3.1.tar.bz2
(1393k)

https://gnupg.org/ftp/gcrypt/gpgme/gpgme-2.3.1.tar.bz2.sig

A sufficient patch to solve the security bug for older versions is
attached.   Note that version 2.3.0 was never publicly available.

Debian Packages
===============

We also provide Debian style packages for a couple of Debian variants.
See
https://repos.gnupg.org/deb/gnupg/trixie/
or use the menu to switch
to other distros/releases.

Windows Installer
=================

A new version of Gpg4win (5.1.2), our full featured Windows installer,
including the fixed version of GPGME, the Kleopatra GUI, and a PDF
reader has also been released.  Head over to
https://gpg4win.org/

Checking the Integrity
======================

See
https://gnupg.org/download/integrity_check.html

The checksum for gpgme is:

1134a407b50204ee6fb9efaa6e1451c2460e543e  gpgme-2.3.1.tar.bz2

*Thank you all*

Your GnuPG hackers

p.s.
This is an announcement only mailing list.  Please send replies only to
the gnupg-users at gnupg.org mailing list.

* List of Release Signing Keys:
To guarantee that a downloaded version has not been tampered by
malicious entities we provide signature files for all tarballs and
binary versions.  The keys are also signed by the long term keys of
their respective owners.  Current releases are signed by one or more
of these five keys:

ed25519 2020-08-24 [SC] [expires: 2030-06-30]
6DAA 6E64 A76D 2840 571B  4902 5288 97B8 2640 3ADA
Werner Koch (dist signing 2020)

title: How I made a custom game engine for Satelital
content:
Seven years ago I decided to start learning how to make a game from scratch. And last week I released Satelital, a rule-discovery game about learning alien logic.

As a solo developer, I decided to start this project from scratch. My motivation was to learn the actual fundamentals behind the technology of videogames. This meant I had to build most of the tools I would need myself, including the game engine, renderer, puzzles, editors, UX, design, art and music.

Now that I've finally managed to release the game, I think it's a good moment to share how I built it.

The main reason I got into programming was the idea of eventually working on games. I spent many years working on web and building mobile apps. It was fun, but I felt like I wasn't going in the direction I really wanted to.

So one day, after listening to every Jonathan Blow talk I could find and playing too much The Witness, I decided to finally give it a try.

I spent many days and countless hours looking for the best tool I could use to make a game, but nothing left me satisfied. The closest I got to having fun with gamedev was with the
LÖVE framework
making a few jam games. But even with that, it felt quite limiting to not really know what was happening behind the graphics I somehow managed to animate on my screen.

Early prototype of a tile-based level editor built with LÖVE and Lua

I remember hearing about shaders and parallel programming. The concept always felt very arcane and mysterious to me, but now writing them is the thing I enjoy the most while coding.

I finally decided to jump into the swimming pool and actually learn C⁠+⁠+. I had to learn how to manage memory and how not to shoot myself in the foot with the wrong tools. I started using SDL2 while trying to use the C⁠+⁠+ standard library as little as possible.

Before getting too deep into the engine, I actually finished a prototype of the puzzles not long after learning how to draw some simple graphics with C⁠+⁠+. It had very early versions of four kinds of puzzles that mostly survived until the final game. It was made entirely with SDL2, but I soon realised that if I wanted more interesting graphics, I would need to use shaders and decided to switch to OpenGL.

Early prototype gameplay with SDL2

This puzzle was the first one I made, also the only one that survived until the end

With the help of
LearnOpenGL
I quickly had a triangle on the screen. From there, learning things like lighting, tonemapping, normal maps, shader effects and everything else opened up a whole new way of looking at computers for me. Before, my idea of how a computer actually draws to the screen was quite naive. When I started learning graphics I just wanted to be able to manually change the color of each pixel individually, but in the end the idea of running a program in parallel for every pixel clicked for me.

One thing that made a huge difference while working on shaders was having code reloading. Before that, I had a complex system that stored constant values in config files, which would later get passed through uniforms into shaders. Then a custom development menu would provide some UI to tweak those values at runtime. With that I stopped having to reload and compile everything for every little change I wanted to make.

It worked, but having to maintain all this extra scaffolding was slowing me down. Another unexpected downside of this setup was that, in some cases, the shader compiler couldn't optimize the code as well as it otherwise could, since knowing constant values ahead of time helps it make better decisions.

Having shader reloading made a huge difference. Being able to change some code, save the file and immediately see the result on screen was very useful. Iterating on shaders became much faster and more fun. This was probably my biggest regret about not having it from day one.

Color modification preview using shader hot reloading

For a big part of the development I was using SDL2, mainly to create a window, read input and get a surface to draw on. But it felt wrong to depend on a library that was several times bigger than my entire game just to handle a few seemingly simple tasks. I decided to drop that dependency and make my own platform layer that I could understand and maintain. I wouldn't have to wait for someone else to fix a bug anymore because now I could just change it myself. It wasn't that hard to end up with a single file with a few thousand lines of code that supported both macOS and Windows. I'm now looking forward to working on mobile and console ports, it feels like it might be a fun thing to work on.

At some point during development, compile times were getting longer, so I decided to look into what was going on. I checked where all that time was going, and to my surprise a lot of it was spent compiling standard library things. Stuff like
std::function
was particularly slow for example.

Eventually I realised that I wasn't actually forced to use the standard library just because it was there, and the subset I needed wasn't that hard to implement myself. It took me a month to replace it with my own base library, but it was so worth it. Not only did compile times get faster, but I also learned how a lot of things I had always taken for granted in other languages actually worked.

At some point I started looking into Vulkan because I wanted HDR. I couldn't get it working on macOS through OpenGL and I was worried about OpenGL being deprecated in the future. Also I didn't really want to build the whole engine around an API that might become deprecated.

Testing alpha blending with my first Vulkan triangles

Moving to Vulkan was rough at the beginning. There was so much boilerplate to type and understand. Also, when I started working on the engine, there wasn't much documentation around how to implement a good backend with it. In hindsight, I feel that even though I got a lot of valuable things from tutorials and books, most of them were overcomplicating something that could be much more straightforward. I still have nightmares about trying to resize a window...

Getting Vulkan working on macOS was actually surprisingly easy thanks to MoltenVK. It was nice not having to learn Metal and being able to keep the same codebase on Windows. The engine started out only working on macOS, so I was afraid I'd run into a lot of issues when porting it to Windows. But I was quite nice to see Vulkan just working the same day I tried it.

Funny looking bug I got doing the Vulkan port

My philosophy from day one was to only grow the engine towards exactly what I needed. This was a long solo project, so trying to build a general purpose engine first, without knowing what I needed, would probably have meant never finishing the game. I did waste time on things I thought I would need, but I cut them when I knew I wouldn't be using them. Because I was also learning C/C⁠+⁠+ along the way, I made many coding mistakes but I wasn't afraid of big refactors. Cleaning the codebase helped me bring up my morale.

From the beginning I wanted to avoid making a 3D engine since I knew that might complicate things too much. But after I finished the prototype, I kept learning about shader techniques and effects. So in the end, my goal was to get as close as possible to a 3D look without actually having to load any 3D polygons.

To do this, I chose an orthographic top-down view so I could just prerender the assets in Blender and then load their albedo, normal and height maps as textures. Having a fixed camera meant I could render all the assets from exactly the same perspective, so they would always fit together properly in the game. Other things that needed to be animated were drawn in the pixel shader using SDFs. The terrain of the planets was too big to be stored entirely in textures, so in most cases I had to procedurally generate them in shaders too.

Final frame

Albedo

Normals

Light & Shadows

Since I wanted a 3D look with dynamic lighting, I also needed dynamic shadows. The final approach I settled on was ray marching. With the height map of each prop, I could make them look as if they were actually sitting in a 3D space, even though everything was still rendered in 2D. In the shader I basically march along the direction of the light and sample the height map to figure out where a shadow should be drawn.

Having the height map was also useful for other things. For example, I could use that information to make objects interact with the water in a convincing way. Objects can actually submerge in the ocean instead of looking like flat images drawn on top of it. This is also how the waves can interact with the shore around an island.

Moving a tree into the ocean

The engine was only one part of making a complete game. I also had to build a custom level editor. I wanted to make it as easy as possible to design and iterate on puzzles, so I integrated an edit mode that allowed me to change puzzles and the enviroment at runtime and see the changes in real time.

It was quite fun to quickly draw and tweak puzzles directly in the game. It helped me discover so many ideas. After making thousands of puzzles, you start to develop a sense of beauty about how a puzzle should be. Having this editor allowed me to get into the zone. I could spend hours making puzzles without actually thinking about the tool I was using.

Puzzle level editor

Alongside the in-game editor I made a custom Blender plugin that could load my level config files into Blender. The game had a file watcher that could detect changes in the baked textures of the 3D models rendered by Blender. But it could also load level data and provide another way to edit. The upside was being able to just use Blender tools like multi-select, but aside from that, it wasn't actually that useful. It was cool to make though, and it's an interesting demo. But just being able to edit things in-game was much better, since you can see how it will actually look in the end. Though having said that, looking at the levels in an actual 3D environment feels quite nice.

Environmental level editor with a custom Blender plugin

Building the game with all these custom tools brought some issues. They worked on my machine, but when I started playtesting I began to find lots of bugs that were tricky to reproduce. The hardest ones were related to graphics, due to differences in hardware and drivers on machines I didn't have access to. Tools like Vulkan validation layers were quite useful, though they didn't catch everything.

Another thing that was tricky to deal with was shader compatibility. When using GLSL, if you rely heavily on making visual effects with noise related functions, you will find issues with things like
sin
or
pow
because the specification doesn't guarantee their precision. So I had to be constantly checking that everything looked the same on as many different hardware configurations as I could find. For a while, I didn't notice that the distribution pattern of my stars looked different across vendors. It looked correct, but I wanted to have the same placement of stars wherever you played to make it feel more like an actual place.

Early concept of parallax for stars

Having good logs to see how the internals of the game were working ended up being very useful. It was essential for me to have them after I released the demo and started getting feedback from users who were seeing errors I couldn't reproduce. Many of them reported a black screen when trying to open the game for the first time, and these were caused by many different kinds of problems. Sometimes it would be a missing extension, sometimes a third party Vulkan layer injecting code that prevented the frame from being drawn, or some other particular driver issue. Without the logs showing the exact point when the error happened, it would have been almost impossible to fix these bugs without having the actual hardware.

The logs ended up being quite useful for performance. For example, when trying to do optimizations for Intel GPUs, I noticed that some of the biggest shaders were being compiled in a non-optimal way. I basically ran the whole game in just 2 big shaders, one to blend the scene with all the quads, and another pass where I do lighting, shadows and effects like water, where the final normal and height map of the scene are presented. Because these shaders were so big, they couldn't be compiled for SIMD16.

These integrated Intel GPUs are quite common on laptops, and they can shade 16 pixels at once, but only if everything in the shader fits in a small amount of very fast memory. Because my shaders grew so much and I wasn't even aware that this would be an actual issue, the driver was quietly falling back to shading 8 pixels at a time, making the game run noticeably slower. Once I had this information in the logs, I could see what I needed to trim down. I reduced the number of values I needed to keep around as much as possible, while also avoiding duplicated code caused by things like macros until everything fit again.

Menu graphics options

During development I was always careful about how demanding the game was, but after switching to a faster computer I started paying less attention to it. It's quite easy to just settle for something that looks good enough and move on to the next thing when you're busy. That's why I started targeting the Steam Deck and aiming for stable 90 FPS. It helped me keep performance in sight and avoid things that would make the game too slow on low-powered platforms.

I feel like I threw away a lot of work during development because the art and design of the game changed several times. In hindsight, I think it was good to keep the mentality of avoiding things that would make the game slow and keeping an eye on the performance stats. But it was only towards the end of the game that I could simply focus on performance without worrying about optimizing things in a way that would make them hard to generalize or reuse in the future, since the game was finished.

In the end I actually added a performance mode that tones down a few special effects, but I think it was a good decision to do that when the game was finished. Otherwise, you suddenly need to be testing and tweaking more than one version of the game while making changes and adding new things.

A frame limiter was something else I added to help slower laptops maintain a stable framerate. This also brought the necessity of adding an option to draw the cursor in hardware. For the whole development I was drawing the cursor within the game in software, and that meant some lag was unavoidable. Many users complained about this when the demo was released.

This happens when you use Vsync because the last frame you're seeing is actually buffered, so the frame is already behind the input. The OS has a special mode for drawing the cursor that prevents these issues, but then you lose the ability to apply effects to it, like fluid animations or doing some lighting around it. Being aware of this also helped me focus on reducing the input lag of the game as much as possible. When running the game with the frame limiter, you notice immediately that the cursor becomes super laggy. For that case, having a hardware cursor was necessary.

Proof of concept for the level selection view

Looking back on all these details, being able to change basic engine things like that is super hard, or almost impossible, with closed engines. I worked with Unity before, doing some ports, and the mentality there was that you had to follow a set of "good practices" and deal with whatever was decided for you, even though the hardware in most cases could do better. It was very rough and slow at the beginning when making a custom engine, but the freedom you get at the end of development is very satisfying.

I feel lucky about how I got the chance to take this long journey and actually make it to the end. I feel like I stumbled into something really interesting that made me lose count of all the nice moments of realization I had while working on this project.

After all these years, I'm quite happy now to have found the perfect excuse to actually study the things I love the most to work on.

If you enjoyed this article, consider giving Satelital a try. The game is available on Steam, with a free demo available.

title: Context-Generic Programming v0.8.0 – Pluggable trait implementations for Rust
content:
Context-Generic Programming
(CGP) v0.8.0 is out!
This release is about making CGP easier to learn and maintain. It introduces cargo-cgp, a new tool for one of CGP's longest-standing problems: compile errors that describe the code the macros generated rather than the code you wrote. cargo-cgp explains those errors in your terms. When a provider needs a field your type lacks, for example, it can tell you which field to add, and the expanded documentation explains why the provider needs it. Later, as your application grows, the new namespaces let you choose the providers for a whole group of components in one wiring entry.

CGP is a language extension for Rust, with pluggable trait implementations at compile-time. It is an ordinary library on stable Rust: applications select providers through wiring that resolves to static calls, and you can adopt it one component at a time. The
Overview
explains the model.

I'll start with cargo-cgp and the new documentation, then work through namespaces using a social-media application. The namespace walkthrough is the longest part, so you can read the tooling and documentation news on their own if you prefer. Allow about 35 minutes for the full post, including the code, or jump to the section you need:

Diagnosing wiring with cargo-cgp

Expanded documentation and AI agent support

Grouping component wiring with namespaces

Sharing default implementations

Other improvements

Breaking changes and migration

Diagnosing wiring with cargo-cgp
​

Since CGP began, verbose and confusing compiler errors have been one of the largest obstacles to adopting it. Leave out a field or a component binding, and the error message can name a generated trait or show a field name encoded as a Rust type. The compiler checks the Rust produced by macro expansion, so its explanation can be far removed from the code where we made the mistake.

For a newcomer, that can mean learning advanced Rust traits and generics, along with CGP's internals, just to diagnose a small mistake. You might understand the program you are trying to write and still have little idea why it does not compile. Because the difficulty lies in how the compiler reports the expanded code, better syntax alone cannot address it.

So I built
cargo-cgp v0.1.0
, CGP's new error toolchain, to report those errors in terms of the code you wrote.
cargo cgp check
checks CGP code and explains a missing dependency through the fields, components, and providers involved, leading with the root cause. It does not yet reshape every class of error, though, so some still reach you in the compiler's own words. When you want to look deeper,
cargo cgp expand
shows the Rust that the macros generated.

Find a missing field
​

Let's try it on a small mistake from the
area-calculation tutorial
. We have an area provider that multiplies
width
by
height
, and a
Rectangle
that supplies only
width
. Here, the rectangle itself is the context: it is the value the operation acts on, and its fields supply the provider's inputs.

Save this library example as
src/lib.rs
in a Cargo package using
cgp = "0.8.0"
:

use

cgp
::
prelude
::
*
;
#[cgp_component(AreaCalculator)]
pub

trait

CanCalculateArea

{

fn

area
(
&
self
)

->

f64
;
}
#[cgp_impl(new RectangleArea)]
impl

AreaCalculator

{

fn

area
(
&
self
,

#[implicit]
width
:

f64
,

#[implicit]
height
:

f64
)

->

f64

{
width
*
height

}
}
#[derive(HasField)]
pub

struct

Rectangle

{

pub
width
:

f64
,

}
delegate_and_check_components!

{

Rectangle

{

AreaCalculatorComponent
:

RectangleArea
,

}
}

The table selects
RectangleArea
, whose
#[implicit]
arguments read the rectangle's fields. Because we used
delegate_and_check_components!
, the compiler checks those dependencies at the wiring entry. Run
cargo cgp check
, and it points to the field we forgot:

error[E0277]: [CGP-E001] missing field `height` on `Rectangle`
--> src/lib.rs:23:9
|
23 |         AreaCalculatorComponent: RectangleArea,
|         ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
|
= note: root cause: [CGP-E110] missing field `height` on `Rectangle`
this is required through the dependency chain:
[CGP-E101] consumer trait impl `CanCalculateArea` for context `Rectangle`
└─ [CGP-E102] provider trait impl `AreaCalculator` with context `Rectangle` for provider `RectangleArea`
└─ [CGP-E110] missing field `height` on `Rectangle`
= help: add the field `height: f64` to `Rectangle`

The help line gives us the edit,
height: f64
. To see why the provider needs it, the dependency tree takes us back through
RectangleArea
to the area operation. For comparison, plain
cargo check
describes the same mistake through generated traits and a nested
Symbol
type:

Compare the output from cargo check

error[E0277]: the trait bound `Rectangle: CanUseComponent<AreaCalculatorComponent>` is not satisfied
--> src/lib.rs:23:9
|
23 |         AreaCalculatorComponent: RectangleArea,
|         ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ unsatisfied trait bound
|
help: the trait `HasField<Symbol<6, Chars<'h', Chars<'e', Chars<'i', Chars<'g', Chars<_, cgp::macro_prelude::Chars<'t', Nil>>>>>>>>` is not implemented for `Rectangle`
but trait `HasField<Symbol<5, Chars<'w', Chars<'i', Chars<'d', Chars<'t', Chars<_, Nil>>>>>>>` is implemented for it
--> src/lib.rs:17:9
|
17 |     pub width: f64,
|         ^^^^^
note: required for `RectangleArea` to implement `IsProviderFor<AreaCalculatorComponent, Rectangle>`
--> src/lib.rs:8:1
|
8 | #[cgp_impl(new RectangleArea)]
| ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
= note: required for `Rectangle` to implement `CanUseComponent<AreaCalculatorComponent>`
note: required by a bound in `__CanUseRectangle`
--> src/lib.rs:21:1
|
21 | / delegate_and_check_components! {
22 | |     Rectangle {
23 | |         AreaCalculatorComponent: RectangleArea,
24 | |     }
25 | | }
| |_^ required by this bound in `__CanUseRectangle`
= note: this error originates in the attribute macro `cgp_impl` which comes from the expansion of the macro `delegate_and_check_components` (in Nightly builds, run with -Z macro-backtrace for more info)

Following that suggestion, we add the missing field:

#[derive(HasField)]
pub

struct

Rectangle

{

pub
width
:

f64
,

pub
height
:

f64
,
}

The wiring check now passes, and the provider can read both fields to calculate the area. Fixing the mistake did not require decoding the type-level spelling of
height
.

To produce this explanation, cargo-cgp wraps a nightly compiler and uses the Rust compiler's API to inspect the failed dependencies. It can follow their chain using information that would be difficult to recover from the printed diagnostic alone. That access is why the tool has its own compiler-linked driver.

Try the checker
​

With cargo and rustup available, you can install the tool and set up its compiler-linked driver, then check your own project. The install needs Rust 1.96 or newer, and the tool is tested on Linux only so far:

cargo

install

--locked
cargo-cgp
cargo
cgp setup
cargo
cgp check

cargo cgp setup
installs the tool's pinned nightly and builds the matching driver. That nightly runs only cargo-cgp's checks, so your application keeps its normal toolchain for ordinary cargo builds. CGP itself still compiles on stable Rust, and you can use it without installing cargo-cgp at all.

Use plain cargo to build, run, and test applications. cargo-cgp supplies
check
for diagnostics and
expand
for reading the Rust generated by macros, with CGP's type-level constructs restored to readable notation. The
installation guide
covers setup, updates, and the Nix alternative, and the
cargo-cgp v0.1.0 release notes
list what this first release supports.

Expanded documentation and AI agent support
​

A release post can show you an interesting feature and still leave you unsure how to use it in your own program. For too long, CGP left readers in that position. Most explanations lived in blog posts like this one, with each post introducing features as they arrived. There was little room to explain every construct or give readers a complete account of how the pieces fit together.

CGP is a side project, and finding the time to fill those gaps has been difficult. Writing a comparable body of documentation entirely by hand would likely take me months of full-time work. I do not expect to have that time in the near future, and waiting would leave readers facing the same gaps.

Advances in AI and agentic coding made it practical to take on that work. Agents, primarily Claude Code, wrote much of the new documentation under my direction, over many iterations of planning and revision. If a blog post leaves you wanting more detail, you can now turn to:

Reference
: look up a construct's accepted syntax, examples, and generated code.

Concepts
: work through ideas such as provider composition, abstract types, and namespaces.

Comparisons
: connect CGP to approaches you already know from other programming languages, with the limits of each comparison explained.

Projects
: follow the code and patterns of CGP projects highlighted in earlier blog posts.

The
/cgp
skill
: give an AI assistant the foundations to help you read and write CGP, as described below.

The knowledge base
: explore the fuller record written for agents working on CGP itself, including its implementation and documentation.

Across more than 360 pages, the website now contains roughly 365,000 words of documentation prose, excluding code blocks and the mirrored skill files. At 300 words per printed page, that would be about 1,200 pages before code listings.

I understand why readers may be skeptical of AI-written explanations. A word count says little about their usefulness, and I would not expect a one-shot prompt to produce useful material at this scale. The planning, source checks, and repeated revisions are essential to the quality I am aiming for. I encourage you to read the pages and tell me where an explanation is vague, incorrect, or reads like generic AI output.

How the documentation is written
​

I direct the work, set the rules, and choose what gets documented. The process starts with the knowledge base, where agents record how CGP works and check claims about syntax and macro expansions against the implementation, tests, and expansion snapshots. That account becomes the basis for the website pages, which agents write and revise against the project's writing guides.

When a page needs an update, the agent can pick up from the same record. That saves me time because each revision starts from what the record already holds about CGP. The
knowledge-base overview
explains how the record supports the project.

I review the pages myself, though not all in the same depth. I read in full every page that explains CGP's ideas or the decisions behind its design, which includes the Concepts pages and the blog posts. The reference pages for individual constructs follow their writing guides, and I spot-check them. But neither kind of review catches everything. Like the source checks, it can miss mistakes, so the knowledge base
can still contain errors
. I remain responsible for what the project publishes.

I would like to explore the methodology further in a dedicated follow-up post. For now,
How CGP's Documentation Is Written
explains the process and where its checks stop. The
AI disclosure
describes who writes and reviews the documentation, tooling, and core library.

Optional help from the
/cgp
skill
​

If you already work with an AI assistant, try exploring a small CGP example together. With the
/cgp
skill
loaded, you can ask it to explain an unfamiliar wiring entry, trace which provider a method uses, or help investigate a compiler error. This gives you a way to explore the internal details as they become relevant, with explanations suited to your Rust experience.

The skill gives the assistant a condensed guide to current CGP: the consumer/provider model, wiring, dependency declarations, and debugging with cargo-cgp. It can help the assistant investigate macro expansions and guide you through installing and using the checker. For deeper questions, it can consult the fuller knowledge-base record.

Before it works on your code, the skill checks which
cgp
release your project uses and tells you when that differs from the release it describes. You still need to review and verify the assistant's suggested code. The
installation page
explains how to install the skill in your agent, and
Using the Knowledge Base with Your Agent
covers deeper investigation. Neither is required to use CGP.

Grouping component wiring with namespaces
​

The release also introduces
namespaces
, for grouping components as an application grows.

When an application has only a few components, writing out its
delegate_components!
table is straightforward. Each time we split behavior into another component, though, we add a routing entry. Eventually, someone opening the application has to sort through a long list of bindings before they can see which ones belong together. The implementations have become more reusable, but the configuration has become harder to follow.

I have tried a few ways to address this difficulty. Provider bundles collect implementations, but applications still have to list the components they forward to each bundle. The earlier preset system reduced some repetition too, with limitations I will return to below.

With namespaces, we can now give those groups names and select their implementations together. I'll work through a social-media application whose production and test configurations share a PostgreSQL-backed core but use different content filters. By the end, that difference will be visible in one wiring entry.

If you have already maintained a large wiring table, you may prefer to jump to
the namespace syntax
or
the migration guide
. Otherwise, let's start with the small application and see how its wiring grows.

Suppose we are building a social-media service that manages users and posts. We need a database handle and a place to choose the implementations the service uses, so our context will represent the application. This is a different role from the earlier
Rectangle
, where the context was the data being operated on.

The snippets illustrate wiring rather than a complete web service. They assume
use cgp::prelude::*;
and omit domain type declarations and database query bodies. The
web-app walkthrough
follows the same example, and its
compiling source
uses placeholder database operations.

#[cgp_component]
lets us write their implementations separately from the application that uses them: it generates a provider trait such as
UserManager
and a wiring key such as
UserManagerComponent
. The application will choose a provider through that key.

Choosing a manager provider chooses all its methods together. A component can hold several methods, associated types, and constants, just like an ordinary trait, and grouping the user operations keeps this first version simple. As the service grows, we will see where choosing those methods together becomes inconvenient.

For the PostgreSQL implementations, each method declares the database handle it needs as an implicit argument. The providers can then work with any application supplying that dependency:

Add dependencies as the service grows

Now suppose the service needs to reject censored usernames and spam posts. Before inserting a user or a post, its manager must consult a filter. We can add a component for each check and declare the manager's dependency on its consumer trait with

#[uses]
attribute declares the new trait dependency, while
#[implicit] database
still supplies the database handle. The remaining manager methods are omitted here.

In production, filtering might involve an AI model or a cloud service. We would rather not make those calls every time we test the rest of the application. A deterministic string-matching filter lets tests run more quickly while keeping the same PostgreSQL managers:

#[derive(HasField)]
pub

struct

ProductionApp

{

pub
database
:

PostgresDb
,

}

PostgresUserManager

The wiring has grown along with the dependency tree. Each context now has four entries, so the two contexts together already have eight to keep in step, even in this small service.

Split independently reusable operations
​

Adding
CanCensorUsername
to the user manager looked straightforward. But that bound belongs to the whole
PostgresUserManager
implementation, so even
get_user
now requires a context with a censor. Retrieving a user never runs the filter. The dependency arrives because retrieval and creation share a provider. The post manager has the same problem with spam detection, and every unrelated dependency we add makes the managers harder to maintain and test.

As we add operations, the domain boundaries become less obvious too.
get_user_profile_picture
might fit in the user manager, but it could need an entirely different set of dependencies.
get_user_posts
concerns both users and posts. Naming a manager after an entity does not settle which operations are useful to group together.

There is also a reason to keep the caller's interface narrow. Deleting a user is destructive, and we may not want every piece of code that works with users to be able to do it. Yet if we added
delete_user
to the manager, even generic code that only retrieves users would gain access to deletion. Giving retrieval its own trait lets that code ask for exactly the operation it needs, and nothing more.

That points to a simple but powerful pattern that CGP makes practical: splitting each manager into
fine-grained traits
, each holding one operation or a few closely related ones. Each provider can then declare only the dependencies it uses. For the user operations, that gives us:

GetUserWithPostgres
can be used with a database alone, while
CreateUserWithPostgres
keeps its censor dependency. A caller bounded by
CanGetUser
can retrieve users without depending on creation or deletion. The same split gives us separate post-creation, retrieval, update, and deletion components.

Separate filtering from database access
​

Splitting the components solved the getter's problem, but
CreateUserWithPostgres
still does two jobs: it checks the username, then inserts the user into PostgreSQL. Only the insert has anything to do with the database. If we added a provider for SQLite, it would have to repeat the same check. Because creation now has a component of its own, we can move the check into a wrapper instead, and apply it to whichever user-creation provider we choose:

#[cgp_impl(new FilterCensoredUsername<InnerCreator>)]
#[uses(CanCensorUsername)]

Why the earlier grouping approaches were insufficient
​

Ideally, the configuration would say something like this, with a key for each group:

delegate_components! {
ProductionApp {
???: // all user components
PostgresUserComponents,
???: // all post components
PostgresPostComponents,
???: // all content filter components
AiContentFilterComponents,
}
}

The
???
keys are the hard part. Each entry in the table becomes a trait implementation for one key, so
UserCreatorComponent: …
gives the application one implementation that answers lookups for user creation. A key that stood for all user components would need to produce one implementation per component in the group, and Rust's trait system has no way to expand a single entry like that. So CGP needs another way to recognize a group: either its own lookup rules, or a macro that expands the group into its keys. Namespaces take the first route, but the macro route is worth a look first.

One possibility would be a helper macro that supplied the list of keys for each group. That would let us write a hypothetical table like this:

delegate_components! {
ProductionApp {
all_user_components!():
PostgresUserComponents,
all_post_components!():
PostgresPostComponents,
all_content_filter_components!():
AiContentFilterComponents,
}
}

Here,
all_user_components!()
would expand to
[UserCreatorComponent, UserGetterComponent, UserUpdaterComponent]
, with corresponding lists for posts and filters. Like the
???
keys above, these helpers are pseudocode rather than supported syntax.

Unfortunately, this runs into the order in which Rust expands macros. Rust expands them lazily, from the outside in, so
delegate_components!
runs first and receives
all_user_components!()
as literal tokens. At that point the helper has not expanded, and the component list does not exist yet. The table would need eager expansion, where a macro expands the macros inside its input before reading it, and stable Rust offers no way for a macro to do that. Even if it did, CGP would still have to generate helpers like
all_user_components!
and export them so that their names and imports keep working in other crates, and Rust's macro system has limited support for that.

My earlier
preset system
tried to solve the same problem, but it supported only a hierarchy like single inheritance. A context could inherit one preset, such as a user preset, and Rust's coherence restrictions then stopped it from also inheriting an independent post preset. I also experimented with combining several presets through macros, but the lack of eager macro expansion, together with the way imports and aliases resolve inside macro output, made that approach tedious to use.

Those attempts helped clarify what I wanted from the feature: an application should be able to name a group and choose its implementation bundle without enumerating every key. In v0.8.0, namespaces express that choice through trait resolution and paths. Existing preset users can find the conversion in the
migration section
.

The check lists the individual operations, even though the wiring now routes them in groups. A group entry only says where a lookup goes, so the check confirms that every operation we rely on actually resolves. Run it on the real application context, which supplies the database field and the other dependencies. An aggregate provider is only a bundle of implementations, so checking a bundle as if it were the application would ask it for dependencies that only the context can supply.

Sharing default implementations
​

So far, we have organized the wiring around choices we might want to change: PostgreSQL or SQLite, production or test filters. Bundles work well for that arrangement. We could add a
PostgresWithLoggingCoreComponents
variant, for example, and select the logging-backed core in the same place.

But an application starting out with PostgreSQL may have little reason to define interchangeable database bundles yet. Early in a project, developers often prefer one implementation per feature, tied to its interface on purpose, because that keeps the application easy to reason about. If several contexts should always use the same user and post implementations, having each one select those bundles repeats a choice that never varies. We can instead record those choices once in a namespace and leave only the varying parts to each context. These are
default implementations
.

I see defaults as a way to adopt CGP gradually. Ordinary traits may already be enough for a single-crate application with one implementation of each operation. If that application later needs more modularity, it can move code into CGP components and record its initial provider choices as defaults. Bundles can follow when there are useful groups to swap.

Let's keep the routes we already registered in
DefaultNamespace
and define a configuration namespace that inherits them using the new
cgp_namespace!
macro:

{
new
DefaultAppComponents
:

DefaultNamespace
}

These are alternative ways to register the same binding, so writing both would create a conflict. The namespace body looks like a
delegate_components!
table, but its choices apply to every context that joins the namespace. We bind the provider at the full path because the bare key is already taken. The route inherited from

uses

to send lookups on to
@app.core.user.UserGetterComponent
, so a second entry for the bare key would conflict with it.

These defaults are fixed choices. Once the namespace binds a provider, a joining context or inheriting namespace cannot override it, even with a more specific entry. A context also cannot disable just one default while retaining the rest of that namespace. So a choice that should vary between contexts belongs on a path the namespace leaves open, as we will do with the filters below.

There is also a constraint on where we write the registration. With a prefixed path, the binding must live in the crate that owns the namespace, here
DefaultAppComponents
. The path expands to CGP's
PathCons
type, and owning a component marker nested inside that type does not satisfy Rust's
orphan rules
. An unprefixed local component marker has different ownership rules, covered by the
#[default_impl]
reference
.

We kept the prefixes in
DefaultNamespace
and the provider choices in
DefaultAppComponents
for a reason. Another configuration, such as a SQLite one, can then inherit the same routes without also inheriting PostgreSQL choices it could not override. So the routes belong in a base namespace, and the fixed choices in a configuration namespace that inherits it.

If we later need to replace one of these fixed defaults, we choose a namespace that leaves its destination open. We could return to the base
DefaultNamespace
and supply the required bindings explicitly, as in the earlier bundle examples.

While the application lives in one crate,
#[default_impl]
conveniently keeps each binding beside its implementation. Once providers move into crates of their own, that attribute would sit in a crate that does not own the namespace, which the ownership rule above forbids. So we move the bindings into the configuration namespace's body instead, and the namespace's crate assembles the providers from there.

There is room to start with direct wiring, share fixed choices through defaults, and introduce interchangeable bundles as the application needs them. I would choose whichever arrangement makes the current decisions easiest to see, rather than build the full hierarchy in anticipation of future growth.

Other improvements
​

Namespaces are the largest change, but several smaller additions also make CGP easier to write, read, and use in more kinds of crates. You can use these without following the full application refactoring above:

Choose a provider per type with
open
.
If a generic component needs one provider for a rectangle and another for a circle, you can put those selections directly in the context's table. You do not need to declare a namespace or a nested
UseDelegate
table. The
delegate_components!
reference
shows the syntax.

Assemble separate tables with
for
.
A backend and an API surface may each have their own table of defaults. You can bring entries from another namespace table onto a path in your context, keeping those concerns independently defined. See
namespace statements
.

Keep implementation details out of trait parameters.
Sometimes a
#[cgp_fn]
body needs a generic type only because it reads a field of that type. With
#[impl_generics]
, the implementation can infer the type from the implicit field without adding a parameter to the generated trait.

Write data shapes as declarations.
A field list is easier to recognize when it looks like the struct or enum it describes.
Struct!
and
Enum!
provide that notation, and cargo-cgp uses it when displaying shapes too.

Use fieldless variants directly.
If an enum contains a state such as
Closed
, you can now use the extensible-variant derives without giving it a placeholder payload. The derives accept
Closed
,
Closed()
, and
Closed {}
, representing the payload as
Nil
. A
no_std
crate using the mutable extractor must have
Box
in scope.

Build without the standard library.
With its default features,
cgp
needs neither
std
nor an allocator, so it fits a
no_std
crate on a target without either. The two error providers that format an error into a
String
,
DebugError
and
DisplayError
, need the new
alloc
feature.

Borrow any string field.
An
#[implicit]

name: &str
argument now reads any field whose type implements
AsRef<str>
, such as
String
,
Box<str>
, or
Cow<'static, str>
, where v0.7.0 required a
String
. An
Option<&str>
argument reads an
Option
of any of them.

Document what the macros generate.
Every macro that declares a public item gives it a short doc line when you write none, so a crate can turn on
#![warn(missing_docs)]
without the lint flagging a component marker or a provider struct. A provider trait's doc also names its component key, so hovering the trait in an editor shows the key to import.

Get help with a missing component key.
A provider written as
impl Greeter
needs the key
GreeterComponent
in scope, so a provider in another module imports the key along with the trait. If you forget,
cargo cgp check
reports
CGP-E041
and offers a fix that adds the
use
line. You can also skip the import by naming the trait by its path, as the
#[cgp_impl]
reference
explains.

For the smaller changes, such as clearer errors from the handler macros and the restrictions this release lifts, see the
v0.8.0 release notes
.

Breaking changes and migration
​

Upgrading from v0.7.0 needs source changes. The largest is the removal of presets, which namespaces replace in this release, and most applications will also need explicit imports for items that used to come from the prelude. The
v0.8.0 release notes
list every change, with the upgrade steps in order.

Two projects built with CGP move to v0.8.0 at the same time.
cgp-serde
0.3.0 can now serialize and deserialize enums, and
Hypershell
0.2.0 assembles its language from a namespace instead of presets. If your code builds on either, the
cgp-serde v0.3.0
and
Hypershell v0.2.0
release notes give the upgrade steps.
