The removed preset constructs and their replacements are:

Removed construct
What to use

​

cgp::prelude
now exports only the names CGP code usually writes: the macros, the derives,
PhantomData
, and a few traits and providers such as
HasErrorType
,
CanRaiseError
,
UseType
, and
DefaultNamespace
. The code the macros generate reaches CGP's items through a separate
cgp::macro_prelude
, so the prelude no longer has to carry those items. If your code names one of the dropped items through the glob import, the compiler reports that it cannot find it, and you import it from its module:

use

cgp
::
core
::
component
::
DelegateComponent
;
use

cgp
::
core
::
field
::
traits
::
HasField
;
use

cgp
::
extra
::
handler
::
{
Computer
,

ComputerComponent
}
;

The dropped names come from these modules:

Wiring traits
such as
DelegateComponent
and
IsProviderFor
:
cgp::core::component
.

Field-access traits and type-level types
such as
Cons
,
Nil
, and
Index
: the modules under
cgp::core::field
.

HasType
and
TypeProvider
:
cgp::core::types
.

The handler family
, with its traits, keys, and providers:
cgp::extra::handler
.

A derive does not need its trait imported, so
#[derive(HasField)]
still works through the prelude, while a
HasField
bound or a
.get_field()
call needs the import. A provider for a handler trait such as
Computer
imports its key,
ComputerComponent
, beside the trait, because the provider's header names the key, as
Other improvements
describes.

Raw compiler output changes slightly as a result. Where v0.7.0 printed a type such as
cgp::prelude::Chars
, the compiler can now print
cgp::macro_prelude::Chars
, as in the
cargo check
comparison
above.

The type-level types also lose their Greek-letter names. v0.7.0 declared them as
π
,
ε
,
σ
,
θ
,
ζ
,
ψ
,
δ
, and
ω
, with
Cons
,
Nil
,
Either
,
Void
,
Chars
,
Symbol
,
Index
, and
Field
as aliases, and the prelude exported both spellings. Only the English names remain, so code that wrote a Greek name switches to the English one, imported from
cgp::core::field::types
. Raw compiler output changes with them, printing
Cons<…>
and
Chars<…>
where v0.7.0 printed
π<…>
and
ζ<…>
.

Turn on
alloc
for the formatting error providers
​

The default features of
cgp
are now empty, so the library builds without
std
or an allocator. In v0.7.0, the defaults turned on
DebugError
and
DisplayError
, the error providers that format an error into a
String
. If your wiring uses either, turn on the
alloc
feature:

[
dependencies
]
cgp

=

{

version

=

"0.8.0"
,

features

=

[
"alloc"
]

}

Update attribute syntax and direct dependencies
​

The associated-type separator in
#[use_type]
changes from
::
to
.
:

#[use_type(HasErrorType::Error)]
#[use_type(HasErrorType.Error)]

Equality imports use the new separator too. Write
#[use_type(HasErrorType.{Error = AppError})]
. An import from another context changes shape as well, with the context named after
in
:
#[use_type(@Types::HasScalarType::Scalar)]
becomes
#[use_type(HasScalarType.Scalar in Types)]
. The
#[use_type]
reference
covers each form.

A component that generates a
UseDelegate
dispatcher moves the
derive_delegate
key of
#[cgp_component]
into
an attribute of its own
, one per dispatcher:

#[cgp_component {
provider: AreaCalculator,
derive_delegate: UseDelegate<Shape>,
}]
#[cgp_component(AreaCalculator)]
#[derive_delegate(UseDelegate<Shape>)]

A new component does not need either form, because the
open
statement from
Other improvements
dispatches it per type.

The extra-feature macro crates are renamed from
cgp-extra-macro
and
cgp-extra-macro-lib
to
cgp-macro-extra
and
cgp-macro-extra-lib
. Update direct dependencies on those crates. Imports through
cgp::prelude
keep their names.

Self-contained handler-macro expansions may leave imports unused. Remove imports the compiler reports when they existed only for the old expansion.

#[cgp_auto_dispatch]
rejects attribute arguments and typed receivers such as
self: Box<Self>
. It previously ignored the arguments or miscompiled those receivers.

The new
Struct!
and
Enum!
prelude exports can make a macro name ambiguous. Qualify the call if another glob import provides the same name.

DelegateComponent
,
IsProviderFor
,
HasField
, and
HasFieldMut
no longer carry custom
#[diagnostic::on_unimplemented]
messages. Plain
cargo check
now reports an unmet bound on them in the compiler's own wording, and
cargo cgp check
rewrites those errors into its own summary. If a test compares compiler output, as a UI test does, update the messages it expects.

Check error-backend behavior
​

cgp-error-eyre
enables eyre's automatic default-handler installation and tracks the caller of
raise_error
and
wrap_error
.

cgp-error-std
changes how wrapped errors are displayed. Ordinary
Display
prints only the outer detail, while alternate
Display
and
Debug
include the chain. This avoids duplicated sources when a reporter walks
source()
itself. Update output assertions that depend on the old formatting.

The minimum anyhow and eyre dependencies rise to 1.0.104 and 0.6.14 respectively. The backend READMEs in the
CGP repository
describe their use.

Try one part of your application
​

We started with two manager choices and ended with applications that could share a core, change their filters, or use a different database. Namespaces let the top-level wiring express those choices even as we split the implementations into smaller pieces. I hope that makes similar refactorings easier to follow in your own projects, with cargo-cgp and the new documentation there to help when something is unclear.

CGP still takes time to learn. Its ecosystem is small, and I still have work to do on the tooling and documentation. My suggestion is to try it on one problem you already have. If you already use CGP, try grouping one area of your wiring while keeping its component checks in place. If you are new to CGP, the
Quickstart
provides a smaller starting point.

I would appreciate hearing where you still struggle to trace an implementation, understand a diagnostic, or follow an explanation. Those examples will help me decide what to improve next. You can share them in
GitHub Discussions
. Thank you for reading and trying CGP.

I wrote the draft of this post, and an AI agent revised its prose and checked its code and claims against the CGP knowledge base. See
How AI is used in this project
.

title: LLMs can read and write executables byte by byte from a hex dump
content:
Programming in the Machine Code Space:
LLMs can read & write executables byte by byte

Authors

George Xenos

Sotiris Giannopoulos

November 2026

TL;DR

LLMs can now
understand and write machine code
.

Given only a hex dump, with no disassembler or compiler, and no tools, GPT-6.1 Sol can
read and write executables byte by byte
. This is an early sign that LLMs can program directly in binary.

By reading only the actual bytes, it
explained all five binaries we gave it
, including a stripped open-source statistics tool,
where it even found a real bug in the upstream code
.

It
successfully analyzed an unknown malware sample we gave it
, correctly identifying its behavior and extracting the correct IOCs.

In a later experiment, it added a feature to three binaries by
directly editing their bytes
. It also successfully wrote three programs
from scratch
.

In the future, LLMs may
write directly in machine code instead of using high level languages
.

As preliminary evidence that this isn't limited to closed models,
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash reached the same conclusion about the malware
.

These findings raise interesting questions about the future of reverse engineering, malware analysis and even
programming
.

Almost nobody writes machine code by hand. We write source, and a compiler and linker turn it into bytes; to go back, we use disassemblers and decompilers. There are good reasons for this. x86-64 instructions vary in length, jumps are relative byte distances, and one wrong header field means the file won't load. So what can an LLM do with those bytes when it has none of these tools?

Machine Code Programming

Takehi et al. recently showed that LLMs can read and write neural network weights directly, which they call Weight-Space Programming
. We ask the same question about the other artifact we treat as unreadable output: compiled code.

We define
Machine Code Programming
as a general-purpose LLM reasoning directly about an executable's bytes, with no compiler, assembler, disassembler or execution between it and the file. We test three abilities and one real-world case:

Reading:
say what a program does from its hex dump.

Extending:
add a feature by editing the bytes in place.

Writing:
produce a working executable from a description alone.

Applying it:
analyze real malware the same way.

One program,
wordcount
, through all three tasks. Replayed from the real run data.

Setup for all experiments

Model:
GPT-6.1 Sol (
gpt-6.1-sol
, effort
high
) through Codex CLI 0.166.0.

Input:
an
xxd
hex dump pasted into the prompt, about 2.4 tokens per byte. Experiment 3 gets a written spec and no hex.

No tools:
a local relay removes every tool from every request, and each turn's event stream is audited. A live check also asks the model to read a planted file, run a command and fetch a URL.

One reply:
no feedback and no second try. Experiments 2 to 4 use one attempt per program.

Scoring:
each build and a reference GCC build run on every test case, and stdout and exit code must match byte for byte. They ran under
qemu-x86_64
on Apple Silicon. Experiment 1 and Experiment 4 are not formally scored.

Can LLMs Understand a Program from Its Raw Bytes?

Experiment 1
What does this binary do?

Can an LLM work out what a binary does from its bytes alone?

We gave the model the hex dumps of three programs we wrote ourselves, plus one real binary from FreeBSD,
ministat
. The LLM
correctly identified what all four programs were, with only their bytes as input
.

Program
Size
What Sol 6.1 reported

wordcount
5,368 B
Line, word and byte counter

AES tool
9,152 B
AES-128/256 in ECB mode, encrypt only

Bank ledger
8,872 B
Command interpreter for named accounts

ministat
67,392 B
Statistics tool with a pooled
t
-test and ASCII plot

Experiment 1.
The input and output of each run, copied from the logs. This task produces a report rather than bytes.

The hardest case is
ministat
. We built FreeBSD's tool at
-O3
, linked it statically against musl, stripped it and removed all of its own text, then hid its last three strings by setting each byte's high bit. The LLM
found the decoding loop, recovered the option list and described all eight options
.

To our surprise, the LLM even
found a real bug from the bytes alone
, with no access to the source. The binary has no symbols or text explaining the table. Reading the
t
-table as raw 64-bit floats, it noticed that
the option labeled 99.5% confidence uses critical values for about 99.8%
, so
-c 99.5
applies a stricter test than it claims. We confirmed the bug in the original source code using Claude.

Can an LLM Extend a Binary by Editing Its Bytes?

Experiment 2
One-shot binary patching

For each program we ask for one new feature. The model replies with a list of byte edits, each the same length as the bytes it replaces. Hidden tests then check that the old behavior still works, that the new feature works, and that long inputs are handled correctly.
All three patched programs pass every test.

Program
Extension asked for
Bytes changed
Output tokens
Time

wordcount
Print a fourth number: the longest line's length
74 (1.4%)
3,440
93 s

AES tool
Add a
dec
command that decrypts
544 (5.9%)
9,324
201 s

Bank ledger
Add a
transfer
command between accounts
379 (4.3%)
6,859
140 s

Experiment 2.
The input and output of each run.

Figure 1.
Each program before (left) and after Sol 6.1's patch (right), running the same commands. Every command really ran against both binaries under
qemu-x86_64
, and each pane shows exactly what that binary printed; only the typing is animated. On these commands the patched binaries also match our reference builds.

How does it do it?
Sol 6.1 treats this like a human patching a binary. It finds padding, makes that padding executable by editing the segment headers, writes new code there, and overwrites existing instructions with calls into it. Here is the whole
wordcount
patch:

0x44, 0x60: headers
04 … 7c 01 … 7c 01
05 … 00 10 … 00 10

Make room.
The first segment now loads up to
0x1000
and can execute, which turns its zero padding into space for code.

0x102a: a padding nop
66 0f 1f 44 00 00
e8 d1 f1 ff ff 90

Call
0x400200
:
zero the two new counters, current line length and longest line.

0x104b: per-byte loop
48 83 c3 01 44 89 d9
e8 d0 f1 ff ff 90 90

Call
0x400220
:
rerun the two instructions it overwrote, then reset the count on a newline, or else add one and update the longest.

0x10e9: before the newline
bf 0a 00 00 00
e8 52 f1 ff ff

Call
0x400240
:
print a space and the longest line using the program's own routines, then redo the overwritten
mov edi, 10
.

Figure 2.
Our annotations on the bytes Sol 6.1 wrote. Struck-through bytes were in the original program. Sol 6.1 found the output routines at
0x1110
and
0x1190
itself.

Can an LLM Write a Binary from Scratch?

Experiment 3
From a description to a complete executable

Now there is no binary at all. This time we ask the LLM to produce a fully functional ELF64 program from a written spec of its behavior. It gets no assembler and no compiler, and must reply with every byte of the file, headers included.
All three files ran and matched the reference on every case.

Experiment 3.
The input and output of each run, copied from the logs.

Sol 6.1 worked out every jump, call and header field itself, with no assembler. Extending a program used 1.8 to 3.7 times fewer output tokens than writing it.

Three files, each written from scratch in one reply. Hover over or tap a byte to see what it does.

Figure 3.
The three programs Sol 6.1 wrote, byte by byte. The AES tool's lookup tables match the AES standard exactly.

A Real-World Scenario: Malware Analysis

Experiment 4
What does this unknown Windows executable do?

Malware analysts spend hours turning a sample back into assembly or C code with disassemblers and decompilers. We give Sol 6.1 a real sample using the same prompt as Experiment 1, with no hint that it is malicious. It is a 4,608-byte PE32+ file whose only visible import is
Sleep
. Its other API calls are hidden behind name hashes and its strings are built on the stack.

In 211 seconds, Sol 6.1 concluded that it
downloads machine code and runs it in memory
. Its report named a hardcoded server,
165.154.205.34
on port 443. We then compared it with a public VMRay dynamic analysis of the same file
, which we matched by SHA-256.
The sandbox contacted the same address, and requested the same URL.

What Sol 6.1 reported
How we checked it

Finds 13 APIs by walking loaded modules and comparing rotate-right-13 hashes
We recomputed all 13 hashes independently:
13/13 match

Exits if
%TEMP%\log_de.log
exists
The sandbox logged accesses to
%TEMP%\log_de.log
, and public reports describe this file as a kill switch

Connects to
165.154.205.34
on port 443, sending plain HTTP rather than TLS:
GET /?a=w64&h=165.154.205.34&t=ws_&p=443
The sandbox's only contacted address was
165.154.205.34
, on port 443 over HTTP, and it fetched
http://165.154.205.34:443/?a=w64&h=165.154.205.34&t=ws_&p=443
:
the same URL

Retries every 10 s until the connection succeeds
Not confirmed: the sandbox shortened the sample's 9 min 15 s of sleeping to 20 s, and the server answered

XORs the response with
0x99
, then calls it from a writable, executable buffer
The sandbox downloaded a 5,158,400-byte
windows_amd64.exe
, created a read-write-execute page, and matched a memory dump to its VShell rule. Public reports on VShell's stager give the same key

Experiment 4.
The input and output of the run, copied from the logs, without the sample's hex dump. This task produces a report rather than bytes.

We made these comparisons after the run, and they cover one sample and one run. The sandbox confirms the address, the request and the download, but not the 10 s retry or the XOR key itself. Rotate-right-13 hashing is also common in public tooling, so recognition probably helped here too. We did not ask Sol 6.1 to modify malware or write any.

Implications for Reverse Engineering and Malware Analysis

These are early results on small programs, but they
may soon challenge the foundations of reverse engineering
. Disassemblers, decompilers and the assembly they produce exist to turn bytes into something a person can read. In our experiments the LLM didn't need that step: it read, patched and wrote machine code directly. These tools are still essential for human analysts, but
for an LLM they may turn out to be optional
.

Malware analysis will also be affected.
A model that works directly in machine code space
can analyze a sample without first lifting it to assembly or source. That removes the slowest and most tool-dependent stage of triage, so more samples can be analyzed with less effort. Our results suggest that
a general-purpose LLM can do this without being specialized for it
, which could make both detection and analysis more efficient.

Limitations

Context size is the hard limit.
A hex dump costs about 2.4 tokens per byte, so our 67 KB binary took about 163,000 tokens. A 10 MB program would need about 24 million tokens. So this one-shot approach can't read very large programs, and because our largest test was 67 KB, we don't know how quality holds up on the way to that limit.

One way forward is a harness based on Recursive Language Models
. An RLM keeps a long prompt outside the model's context, as a variable in a REPL, and lets the model inspect pieces of it and call itself on them. For a binary, the model could read the headers first, follow calls and jumps by offset, and hand each function to a sub-call.

Reading raw bytes is an established problem in malware detection, tackled with models trained for the job such as MalConv
. The recent Large Byte Model extends an LLM's vocabulary with byte tokens, on the premise that LLMs "cannot process raw byte representations"
. Our small sample suggests that a general-purpose frontier model can now do more than that implies, at least when bytes are written out as hex.

Other work applies models to assembly, including the SLaDe decompiler
and Nova, a generative model for assembly
. The BinMetric benchmark found that challenges remain for LLMs, particularly in binary lifting and assembly synthesis
. Project Ire reverse engineers and classifies malware at scale, using tools such as Ghidra and angr
; it is a far larger system than our no-tools test, and the two aren't comparable. We didn't find a prior account of a general-purpose LLM patching and writing working executables with no tools, though our search was not exhaustive.

A Different Harness and an Open-Weight Model

Experiment 5
Can a model with public weights do this too?

We repeat Experiment 4 with a different harness, opencode, and a different model, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, whose
weights are public under an MIT license
. It gets the same sample and the same request at high reasoning effort, with one reply and no tool calls recorded. This is
preliminary evidence that this ability isn't limited to closed frontier models
.

Input

What does this binary program do? Write a detailed report of what it does. No tools are allowed.
Followed by the sample's complete hex dump.

Output

"a
download-and-execute stager
": it finds its Windows functions by hash, contacts a hardcoded server over plain HTTP on port 443, decodes the reply with a single-byte XOR and runs it in memory. "The final payload is not present in this file."

Sol 6.1
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash

Conclusion
Downloads code and runs it in memory
Same

API names matching our check
13 of 13
9 of 13

Server address, as in the VMRay sandbox
165.154.205.34:443
Same

Request URL, as in the VMRay sandbox
Exact match
One parameter misnamed:
fh
for
h

Reasoning tokens
5,178
89,902

Time to answer
211 s
859 s

How does it do it?
The trace shows DeepSeek reading the bytes as hex. We checked three deductions against the executable.

Finds where the code starts.
It uses the PE section headers to map the entry point to file offset
0x400
, then decodes
e9 03 00 00 00
as a jump to
0x408
, past three padding bytes.

Reassembles part of the HTTP request.
It reads
47 45 54 20
and
2f 3f 61 00
from two instructions that write to adjacent stack slots. Together they spell
GET /?a
. The dump has no ASCII column.

Follows the downloaded bytes into execution.
It tracks the buffer pointer in
rbx
, reads
80 34 19 99
as XORing a byte in that buffer with
0x99
, and decodes
ff d3
as a call into the same buffer.

DeepSeek reached the same conclusion with about 17 times as many reasoning tokens. It repeatedly revises its reading and explicitly recalls familiar API hashes. It gets nine of the 13 hidden function names right, and two of its naming errors lead it to misread the marker-file check.

Experiment 5.
The input and output of the run, from OpenCode's session record, without the sample's hex dump. This task produces a report rather than bytes.

Read DeepSeek’s thinking

This is the supplied reasoning transcript, including its false starts, revisions and incorrect guesses. It is model output, not a verified analysis. The text is reproduced unchanged.

We need answer detailed report no tools. Need analyze binary hex. It's Windows PE x64, likely shellcode loader / meterpreter-ish? Need reverse engineer.

We must not use tools; only given hex. Need produce detailed report. Let's decode.

PE header: MZ, PE at 0xc0. Machine 0x8664 (x64). Number sections 6? SizeOfOptionalHeader 0xf0? Characteristics 0x22 (executable, large address aware? 0x22 = executable image, large address aware). Magic 0x20b PE32+.

Sections:
.text VA 0x1000 size raw 0x831? virtual 0x831? Let's parse.

At 0x1c8 section table. First:
Name .text, VirtualSize 0x831, VirtualAddress 0x1000, SizeOfRawData 0xa00? At 0x1d0: 31 08 00 00 = 0x831; 00 10 00 00 VA 0x1000; 00 0a 00 00 raw size 0xa00; 00 04 00 00 pointer raw 0x400; relocs 0; linenums 0; numreloc 0; characteristics 0x60000020 code execute read.
.rdata at 0x1f0? Name at 0x1f8? Actually section 2 starts 0x1e8? Let's compute: section table starts 0xc0+4+20+0xf0 = 0x1c8? PE offset 0xc0. PE sig 4, COFF 20 -> 0xd8. Optional header 0xf0? At 0xd8 optional starts 0xe0? Wait optional header starts 0xd8? Let's recalc. At 0xc0 PE\0\0. COFF header at 0xc4: machine 64 86, numsections 03 00 (3), timestamp fe 75 3a 65, ptr sym 0, num sym 0, size opt 0xf0 at 0xd4? COFF bytes:
0xc4-0xc5 machine
0xc6-0xc7 numsections = 03 00 (3 sections)
0xc8-0xcb timestamp
0xcc-0xcf pointer symbol
0xd0-0xd3 number symbols
0xd4-0xd5 size optional 0xf0
0xd6-0xd7 characteristics 0x22
Optional at 0xd8, 0xf0 bytes -> ends 0x1c8. Section headers at 0x1c8. But data at 0x1c8 shows ".text"? Actually at 0x1c0 row: 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 2e 74 65 78 74 00 00 00. So section at 0x1c8 indeed name ".text". Good.

Sections:
.text VA 0x1000 vsize 0x831 rawsize 0xa00 rawptr 0x400. .rdata at 0x1f0? Name `2e 72 64 61 74 61 00 00` starting 0x1f0? Wait 0x1e8 row has 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 2e 72... Actually row 0x1e0: 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 20 00 00 60. So first section header spans 0x1c8-0x1ef. Second at 0x1f0: 2e 72 64 61 74 61 00 00. vsize be 01 00 00=0x1be, VA 0x2000, rawsize 0x200, rawptr 0xe00, characteristics 0x40000040 = initialized data read.
Third .pdata at 0x218? Actually at 0x218 row? Name .pdata: 2e 70 64 61 74 61 00 00 at 0x218. vsize 0x18? bytes 18 00 00 00 at 0x220? VA 0x3000, rawsize 0x200, rawptr 0x1000, chars 0x40000040. Wait Data at 0x240 onwards zeros. Hmm but 0x1000 in hex dump contains .pdata (exception directory) with entries, yes raw pdata at 0x1000? But rawsize 0x200. Actually header at 0x218 says ptr raw 0x1000? At 0x228: 00 00 00 00? Let's parse:
Section .pdata header at 0x218:
0x218-0x21f name
0x220-0x223 vsize = 0x18 (24)
0x224-0x227 VA = 0x3000
0x228-0x22b rawsize = 0x200
0x22c-0x22f rawptr = 0x1000? Bytes at 0x220: 18 00 00 00 00 30 00 00 00 02 00 00 00 10 00 00 => yes VA 0x3000, size 0x200, ptr 0x1000. Wait rawptr 0x1000 overlaps? The .text raw is 0x400-0xdff, .rdata raw 0xe00-0xfff, .pdata raw 0x1000-0x11ff. But hexdump at 0x1000 starts pdata entries and 0x1100 zeros. However actual code extends to 0xb... within .text raw up to 0xdff? code at 0x400-0xc3f; zeros rest. .rdata at 0xe00? At 0xe00 there seems data/cert? Let's look: at 0xe00 starts `a8 21 00 00...` and 0xe60 `47 43 54 4c` etc. That's .rdata containing exception data? Wait .rdata raw 0xe00 size 0x200. It contains load config? Actually at 0xe60 "GCTL" indicates debug directory type? `47 43 54 4c` is "GCTL" (not standard debug type? 0x4c544347 = "GCTL"). Hmm could be .rdata at 0xe00. Let's analyze.

At 0xe00: a8 21 00 00 = RVA 0x21a8 maybe pointer to something. Then 0xe10: 00 ... fe 75 3a 65 timestamp. At 0xe18? 0d 00 00 00 0xdc... This looks debug directory entry: characteristics 0, timestamp, major 0, minor 0, type? Wait debug directory entries are 28 bytes. At 0xe08? Let's align: maybe .rdata starts at 0xe00 raw but with data? Hmm section raw pointer could be 0xe00 and .rdata data starts with something like import directory? At 0xe00 there is `00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 a8 21 00 00...`? Let's check 0xe00 row: `a8 21 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00`. 0xe10: `00 00 00 00 fe 75 3a 65 00 00 00 00 0d 00 00 00`. 0xe20 `dc 00 00 00 60 20 00 00 60 0e 00 00 00 00 00 00`. This actually debug directory maybe at 0xe08: Characteristics 0, TimeDateStamp 0x653a75fe at 0xe0c? Wait bytes: 0xe08-0xe0b = 00 00 00 00; 0xe0c-0xe0f = 00 00 00 00; 0xe10-0xe13 = 00 00 00 00; 0xe14-0xe17 = fe 75 3a 65. Not.

Maybe section raw pointer for .rdata is 0xe00, and at RVA 0x2000 data starts at file 0xe00. The content should include import directory, exception directory, load config, etc. But typical .rdata begins with IAT or debug? Let's parse optional data directories from optional header at 0xe0 onwards to know RVAs.

Optional header PE32+:
0xe0 magic 0x20b (bytes 0b 02)
0xe2 linker version 0e 24 (14.36?).
0xe4 SizeOfCode 0x00000a00? bytes 00 0a 00 00

title: Deterministic Simulation Testing Is for Everyone
content:
20 Nov 2026

Deterministic Simulation Testing is often seen as a technique just for
distributed systems. I argue that it's a testing technique for everyone and
all applications.

Why We Test

Why do we use automated testing when building software?

To Prevent Bugs

We test because we want to find issues internally and not have them be found
for us by users (who may not even report them at all).

We do this
reactively
; when an implementation bug is found, a failing
test we think corresponds to the bug is written, and the system is changed to
make the test pass. If the bug can no longer be reproduced, we have proven to
ourselves that the test corresponds to the bug, and we keep the test to guard
against further regressions.

We can also do this
defensively
; predicting where and what the bugs
might be, and using tests as guardrails ensuring they do not occur in
development.

To Remove Doubt

We test because we are plagued with self-doubt.

Doubting every development decision we make is exhausting. Can this feature be
added? Can this dependency be removed? Can these modules be re-arranged? Can
this all be done without breaking what we already have? Second guessing brings

decision fatigue
.
Doubt kills productivity. If we are confident the machine is checking this for
us, then our confidence grows.

To Fulfil Obligations

We test because we ought to test, in the same way a small child brushes their
teeth - they may not see the point but they know someone else will make their
lives hard if they don't.

In Test-Driven Development, each bit of code must be preceded by a failing
test. Tests are written under TDD because without them nothing at all can be
written. It follows that these tests tend to be numerous, brittle, numerous,
limited in utility and numerous. Obligation is an external pressure, and if
that external pressure is gone (i.e., the senior TDD champion leaves the
company), the obligation leaves with it.

I see limited utility in testing processes driven by obligation.

The Elements of a Test

System Under Test (SUT)

The unit of code under test.

Test Logic

Assertions and associated setup which check that properties are upheld.

Test Seed

Used to seed any random values needed for the test. By default this is
chosen randomly, but can be overridden by the user to replay specific test
runs.

What Makes a Test Useful?

The utility of a test can be evaluated across three dimensions.

Scope

Tests have a certain
scope
. This scope may be anything from an
individual function to an entire program. The greater the scope, the more
interesting the properties we can reason about. If the scope is large enough,
properties start corresponding to the requirements; that is we can test things
relevant to the real world.

Determinism

A test is run many times. A
non-deterministic
or "flaky" test can
produce different results even when the SUT, test logic, and test seed remain
the same. Such tests are incredibly frustrating for the developer - how can
they tell if a bug is fixed if their tests don't produce consistent results?

If a test is
deterministic
, then the same code with the same test will
return the same failure. Always.

Thoroughness

In some tests, specific examples are thought up by the programmer, and
specific states or responses are tested for. In others the inputs to the SUT
are described declaratively and generated randomly, so that each run generates
multiple different examples. This lets us explore a lot more of the state
space. Let's call these tests
thorough
.

Testing Approaches

Different testing approaches ask different kinds of questions:

End to End Testing

Can a user login, sign up, and place an order?

Unit Testing

Does
1 + 1 = 2
?

Property-Based Testing

Does
n + 0 = n
hold for every integer n?

Black-Box Fuzzing

Can any input crash the SUT?

Deterministic Simulation Testing

If we simulate running this for a year, will our properties hold?

The different testing approaches can be analysed according to the criteria
discussed above:

Widely Scoped

Deterministic

Thorough

End-to-End Testing

Yes

Almost never; most systems do IO internally

No

Unit Testing

No

Deterministic units considered a best practice

No

Property-Based Testing

Usually no, though scope can widen using model based PBT, or if the pure
function is large enough.

SUT is typically deterministic; PBT comes from the FP world.

Yes

Black-Box Fuzzing

Yes

Only if the SUT is deterministic for all inputs

A black-box cannot bias interesting states.

Deterministic Simulation Testing

Most of the program

Yes

Yes

Deterministic Simulation Testing

In the above analysis Deterministic Simulation Testing (henceforth DST) stands
out. So how does it work? In short they combine a
simulated environment

with a
deterministic machine
. Let's look at these terms in detail.

Deterministic

The whole program, hence the SUT, is a deterministic machine. This means it's
single-threaded (or at least deterministically scheduled) and does not make
direct IO calls; so you're left with input-driven deterministic state
machines, making the same state transitions for the same inputs every single
time.

If you're interested in how to do this, see my previous article

on designing programs around a deterministic core

.

Simulation

The environment is simulated. This includes all relevant real world phenomena
that are shared with the deterministic machine, for example:

User IO

Network IO

System Randomness (procedural random generation derived from the test seed
is fine as it's reproducible)

Time (Physical, System...)

Persistent Storage

Simulating the environment turns a source of non-determinism into something
deterministic. Given the same seed, the simulated environment always produces
the same outputs. It also allows you to dial up the chaos: weird inputs,
failures and coincidences that will "never happen" can all be dialled up. A
good simulation is an exercise in amplifying the deviousness of those parts of
the environment we cannot control.

Testing

Typically the test is its own executable. A seed is provided, and a test loop
is run using the simulated environment and the deterministic machine, checking
that properties hold each loop. If a property does not hold the loop exits and
the executable returns the failing seed. This makes errors reproducible.

Some DST implementations act like a game loop, using ticks to simulate time;
just as an "in-game" day might take 24 minutes of real time to represent 24
hours of game time, a simulation test might take 1 month of sim time but
complete in one hour of real time. Others model progression through the test
as distinct events, jumping from one to the next. In either case, because all
network and storage delay is simulated, the test never has to truly wait, and
things can progress much faster than they would under a real environment. This
minimises "time to bug", in effect compressing time, and surfacing issues far
more quickly than it would ever take them to appear naturally in production.

Isn't This Just for Distributed Systems?

When people think of DST, a few products come to mind: Dropbox, FoundationDB,
TigerBeetle, Turso; all very clever systems engineering products made by
people who are essentially wizards.

But conceptually, all software programs have an
environment and a machine
. If you make the machine deterministic, and you
define an interface for the environment so it can be simulated, then you can
do DST.

Here are some examples of how DST can apply to different kinds of software:

Simulated Environment

Deterministic Machine

Properties

Distributed Databases

Physical Time, Network, Storage, Crashes

Sync Algorithm, Consensus Protocol, Storage Engine

Consistency level upheld, handles network splits and replica crashes.

Web Applications

User actions (clicking, typing, navigation), third party API responses

Business Logic, View State, Routing

Can't check out empty cart, prices aren't negative, fields can't be
empty.

Embedded Systems

Sensors, Interrupts, Timers

Control loop, State machines

Fail safe on sensor faults, real-time deadlines met.

DST Is Inevitable

DST is not driven by obligation, it does not plague developers with doubt; it
lets them build without fear, by finding as many bugs
in development

as possible. Development is the best place to find bugs.

DST improves architecture by maximising the amount of code in the
deterministic context, and carefully controlling exposure to the environment.

DST is under your control; you do not have to rely on someone else to simulate
the entire world for you - just the environment you care about.

My goal in this article is not to dissuade you from unit tests, property-based
tests, or any other testing technique. My goal is to persuade you that DST is
relevant for you and your team. Don't let a technique being associated with
one domain stop you from considering using it in yours.

title: The Soviet Elektronika BK-0010 home computer built on a clone of the PDP-11 CPU
content:
MACHINE REFERENCE

Elektronika BK-0010

Elektronika BK-0010
ran on a processor copied from a minicomputer, not a microcomputer. Where the West built home computers around 8-bit chips designed for the job, the Soviet Union’s only officially sanctioned home computer used the K1801VM1, a 16-bit clone of the CPU inside DEC’s PDP-11, repurposed for a machine that cost four months of an average wage.

Why it matters

That PDP-11 heritage is the whole story. The K1801VM1 gave the BK-0010 real 16-bit instructions and addressing at a time when Z80 and 6502 machines were the Western norm, and it made the computer genuinely capable once you got past the 16 KiB of RAM left over after the video buffer took its half. It reached serial production in 1985 as the only Soviet home computer design accounted for in state economic planning, which is a very different kind of achievement to topping a sales chart, but a real one: everything else sold as a “home computer” in the USSR at the time was an unofficial clone of somebody else’s design. Three decades later, its straightforward, well-documented hardware gave it an unlikely second life in the post-Soviet demoscene, where programmers could still buy old stock and push it further than its 1983 designers ever planned.

What to check before you buy

Confirm the power supply delivers a clean, regulated 5V, since the repair community’s own threads on the BK family link memory instability to drifting voltage regulators
Expect the keyboard to feel different to anything Western-built from the same era — the pseudo-membrane design was a contemporary complaint, not just a modern one
Check whether it’s a bare BK-0010 or the later 0010.01 revision with the improved keyboard and built-in Vilnius BASIC, since the two are often listed interchangeably
Factor in that documentation and spares are overwhelmingly in Russian

Photo: Jiri Brozovsky, Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.0)

Released

1985

RAM

32 KiB total, split down the middle: 16 KiB usable by the programmer and 16 KiB reserved as video memory

CPU

K1801VM1 (a Soviet LSI-11/PDP-11-compatible 16-bit processor), 3 MHz

Launch price

600-650 roubles (against an average Soviet monthly wage of around 150 roubles)

Manufacturer

NPO Elektronika (Soviet state electronics combine)

Form factor

Desktop unit with an integrated keyboard, no monitor or cassette deck included

CPU

K1801VM1 (a Soviet LSI-11/PDP-11-compatible 16-bit processor), 3 MHz

Chipset

K1801VP1-037 video display controller, a 600-gate uncommitted logic array

RAM

32 KiB total, split down the middle: 16 KiB usable by the programmer and 16 KiB reserved as video memory

ROM

24 KiB across three 8 KiB chips (BIOS, FOCAL interpreter, debugger), plus one free ROM socket for an add-on such as Vilnius BASIC

Graphics

High-resolution 512×256 monochrome, or 256×256 in 4 colours; text modes of 32×25 and 64×25 simulated in software via the BIOS

Audio

A simple programmable counter driving an onboard piezo speaker; no dedicated sound chip

Storage

Cassette tape, via a dedicated recorder port

Ports

One Q-Bus-compatible slot (electrically, not mechanically, standard), a 16-bit parallel I/O port, two 5-pin DIN video outputs (monochrome and colour), and the cassette recorder port

OS

BK-11 (a cut-down RT-11 derivative), with FOCAL in ROM as standard and Vilnius BASIC available as an add-on ROM

PSU

External, supplying regulated +5V DC through a 5-pin DIN connector rated at a minimum of 1.5A

Units sold

Unknown; it was, however, the only Soviet-designed home computer that reached official, planned mass production

Successors

BK-0010.01 (revised keyboard and built-in Vilnius BASIC), BK-0010Sh (school variant with a network adapter), BK-0011 (1989, 128 KiB RAM at 4 MHz), BK-0011M (a later compatibility-focused revision)

Uncomfortable pseudo-membrane keyboard

The keyboard uses mechanical microswitches under a flexible membrane overlay rather than real keycaps, which contemporary and retrospective accounts alike describe as giving poor, mushy tactile feedback compared to a conventional keyboard.

Power and memory stability issues documented by the repair community

Russian-language repair forums dedicated to the BK-0010/0011/0011M family document recurring voltage-regulator faults (an onboard regulator drifting well off its 5V specification) and RAM stability problems serious enough that enthusiasts have built dedicated memory-testing routines for the platform.

1983

BK-0010 development completed

1985

Serial production begins — the first Soviet home computer in official, planned mass production

1985-1993

Main production run

1989

BK-0011 follow-up released, with four times the RAM and a faster clock

1990s

Adopted by the Eastern Bloc demoscene, thanks to its well-documented, straightforward hardware

title: NINLIVE: The Nine Inch Nails live archive
content:
Besides a database driven site. The second most requested feature for ninlive is streaming capability. The future is now. TJ has been working hard behind the scenes to make it happen. You are now able to stream all of your favorite NIN live recordings from 1988-2026. I can't believe how far the site has come in the last year. Some truly incredible work. Login with your discord account and you can save your favorite recordings to stream and keep your faves organized. As always, feedback is always welcome. Reach out via email if you have comments/suggestions about it.
I am currently adding all of the ticket stubs, setlist scans, passes that I have for each show. Please get in contact if you have anything to contribute. I am also looking for photos from past shows. If you are a photographer and would like to contribute some highlights, I'd love to add them to the archive with a link directed to your site of choice.

title: Muru
content:
Muru

Graham Dumpleton started
mod_wsgi
20 years ago, and has been thinking about the ideal way to serve Python web applications in production ever since.

Muru is his new, AI-assisted Rust server that aims to provide the best possible tools for running ASGI and WSGI Python apps both in development and production.

As
he did with wrapture
, he's been publishing an extraordinarily detailed account of the project as he works on it - as part of his development process.

Here's everything he's published so far, all in the last three weeks:

2026-11-04 —
Twenty years of mod_wsgi, and what comes next

2026-11-05 —
A first look at Muru

2026-11-07 —
Muru: looking inside the workers

Muru: how it fits together

Muru: import once, fork many

Muru: HTTPS in development

2026-11-11 —
Muru: WSGI and ASGI together

AI as a lifestyle choice

Muru: releases, not restarts

Muru: canaries without a service mesh

Muru: a better tenant in a container

Muru: working with Kubernetes, not around it

Muru: scaling from what the workers report

2026-11-17 —
Muru: scaling to zero

Muru: noticing and responding

Muru: a toolbar on every page

Muru: tracing in the toolbar

Muru: when lazy imports help

That post about
AI as a lifestyle choice
is particularly worth a read:

The AI may be doing a lot of the work on the surface, but deciding what isn't good enough yet is still down to me, and twenty years of getting things wrong with mod_wsgi turns out to be useful for that. I am prepared to put in the hard work to keep polishing Muru until it is something I would trust, and something you would too.

title: Perplexity and Intelligence
content:
November 22, 2026
Research
Safety
Perplexity and Intelligence
By Jakub Pachocki, Chief Scientist at OpenAI
From afar, it might seem like modern AI is built similarly to how software has been built in previous decades: with a diverse set of techniques targeting specific capabilities. There are indeed a variety of methods, but rather than designing something from scratch, they are mostly
harnessing
the intelligence coming from a much simpler and less interpretable process: training a compressor (or,
equivalently
⁠
(opens in a new window)
, predictor) on a very large corpus of data.
1
I believe tracking the pace of progress on training better compressors is key to understanding the arc of advances in AI. In this post, I argue for establishing perplexity (or, equivalently, cross-entropy loss) as a metric to compare between model developers and inform shared safety standards. As a first step, I provide more transparency into pretraining progress at OpenAI. Publishing our internal perplexity measurements took some consideration; it gives competitors a clearer picture of where we stand, but that concern is outweighed by the urgency of establishing
shared
⁠
(opens in a new window)
safety measures across the industry. We at OpenAI hope for this to be a step towards building a shared scientific basis for future pacing efforts.
A simplified, but fundamentally informative, view of AI development is that first, one builds a large computer, then uses it to
pretrain
a model (compressor) on a large unstructured dataset, then applies a variety of techniques—like prompting, finetuning or reinforcement learning—in different contexts to elicit the latent capabilities of that model. Algorithmic progress can blur the distinction between training phases, but we can still separate the creation of the AI with hard-to-predict emergent capabilities (which I earlier dubbed “
an alien mind
⁠
”) and the subsequent targeted elicitation.
The primary way we measure progress on this key “intelligence substrate” has remained remarkably constant over the years—we have been tracking the
perplexity
of the models on a held-out dataset.
2
,
3
Perplexity measures how well a model predicts the next token on average; lower perplexity means better predictions. The plot opening this blog post shows how this metric evolved for our models starting with GPT‑3.5.
The range of capabilities of models that are largely described by this one metric is stunning. Setting the new perplexity state-of-the-art on older datasets
4
, GPT‑2 was arguably the first model capable of consistently formulating coherent paragraphs of text. The next major leap, GPT‑3, was capable of learning in context, given a few examples of a task. GPT‑3.5, at a log-perplexity of ~0.99 on our current main evaluation dataset, was capable of fluent conversation and formed the basis for the original ChatGPT. GPT‑4, at ~0.91, was proficient at utilizing chain-of-thought reasoning productively, which motivated the subsequent targeted elicitation of this capability and the creation of modern reasoning models. Now, as we have reached losses below 0.8, we have seen the emergence of transformative capabilities in fields like cybersecurity and mathematics. I want to reemphasize that it was not at all clear
a priori
that these capabilities would appear once those precise perplexity thresholds are met—they can fundamentally be seen as emergent latent capabilities from progress on this one metric.
As AI advances very rapidly, the scope and way in which we measure downstream capabilities may change quickly. It would make little sense to evaluate GPT‑2 and GPT‑3 on most modern benchmarks; and the benchmarks used then were largely saturated around GPT‑4. In contrast, I believe looking at progress on pretraining is likely to stay informative.
A particular change in the pace of progress comes from the increasing contribution of AI to its own development. The most commonly discussed metrics revolve around AI augmenting and replacing human researchers in all stages of the development cycle; with an ultimate inflection point seen at “full recursive self-improvement”, where the process would be entirely automated with no human oversight. Apart from considering such a state as something we should obviously avoid for the sake of maintaining human control, I find this general framing misses something crucial. There is a potential step change that may come from AI participation in one key part of the development process: algorithmic research on pretraining.
We have recently witnessed unprecedented acceleration in another domain. For more than a year, we have been posing open problems in mathematics to our models as one of the ways of evaluating them. Once we upgraded to a model of log-perplexity ~0.76, it started producing groundbreaking results. For many of us that have previously worked in mathematics and adjacent fields, seeing the resolutions to questions we’ve long thought about coming out of the model one after another in a single Slack thread felt deeply surreal. Having experienced that allows us to extrapolate—such a sudden transformation is plausible in deep learning research too. While this field relies more on experimentation, there is a long history of simple insights being missed for years; and so as soon as 2027 we could conceivably see a similar avalanche of fundamental pretraining advancements
5
. While I expect AI will also significantly contribute to progress on alignment and monitoring, I think that progress is unlikely to be fast enough to allow the full potential acceleration in pretraining.
Given that the main way new surprising capabilities emerge is by progress on compression, a measure rooted in perplexity could give us a shared benchmark for general intelligence, regardless of the degree of automation of the development process. Extrapolating from recent progress, we should expect further transformative capabilities as we enter the ~0.68-0.7 log-perplexity window. I don’t know what those capabilities will be, and we may not be testing for them today. At the same time, we should also expect
further degradation
⁠
(opens in a new window)
in currently dominant forms of alignment auditing and further increases in evaluation and training awareness. I believe frontier model developers should jointly endeavour to establish shared norms for how to evaluate such models and red-team safety cases for them by the time they are first used, including shared transparency standards. I further propose
common limits
, based on perplexity and other measurements, that developers are committed to not crossing until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior achieves a certain concrete milestone (such as the development of a successor to CoT monitors). That is, I’d like an industry standard that specifies a first limit on development, measured by some key metric we can track across labs, and what concretely we’d need to achieve before going beyond it. I hope that this leads the way to a common framework for setting successive limits and pacing further development.
Perplexity as a shared metric has challenges:
Difficulty of comparison across labs.
Different developers use different evaluation datasets and train on different data mixtures. Here, we report the numbers on the main dataset we have been tracking; I believe if we establish a goal of transparency we can find transferable ways to compare the quality of different base models.
Detachment from actionable evaluations.
Perplexity does not directly correspond to a task we care about. The reason to care about it is that we can expect advances on it to lead to emergence of entirely new capabilities.
Not accounting for advances outside of pretraining.
Most notably, chain-of-thought reasoning does not reduce perplexity achieved by the model, even though it leads to a drastic increase in capabilities.
Unknown floor.
We do not expect it is possible to achieve a loss of 0, which would correspond to being able to predict the dataset entirely deterministically. But we do not know what the inherent entropy of the data is. As we approach it, the apparent progress on perplexity will slow, but smaller gains on perplexity will correspond to larger leaps in model intelligence.
At the same time, perplexity has stood the test of time as a metric many research teams have put a lot of effort into optimizing, and it continues to deliver consistent gains on general intelligence. I believe it can play an important role in standardizing how we talk about AI progress, and hope to see more transparency about it across the industry.
Compute Scaling
Ethics & Safety
2026
Author
Jakub Pachocki
Footnotes
1
It’s important to note that “compressor” in this sense is something that is capable of performing compression by predicting unseen data, not a compressed artifact like a GZIP file - that is, the best compressor trained on a given corpus does not necessarily “remember” the contents of the corpus.
2
In practice, we generally track the
log
of perplexity, also called
cross-entropy loss
.
3
The primary held-out datasets we’ve been using since GPT-3.5 are sourced from our internal codebase, and those are the numbers reported here (for a fixed snapshot).
4
Given what GPT‑2 and GPT‑3 were trained on, how well they predict code is a poor proxy for their general capabilities. This showcases a potential challenge arising from dataset selection with using perplexity as a shared metric; however it should still be informative to evaluate them jointly with modern models on general text. I chose to report perplexity on our internal codebase because I wanted to share the numbers we rely on most today to gauge progress in pretraining at OpenAI.
5
On the plot of losses of OpenAI models, you can see a steep acceleration in 2026. We attribute it mostly to the outcomes of long term research and compute investments, and only in a smaller part to automation. However, for the most recent models,
we have already seen meaningful design contributions coming from AI
⁠
.

title: The Birds of GTA 6: A Field Guide to Vice City and Leonida's Wildlife
content:
Audubon Magazine

Arts & Culture

I Tracked Down All 60 Birds in GTA 6: A Birder’s Guide to Vice City’s Wildlife

From Roseate Spoonbills in the Grassrivers to gulls over Vice Beach, here's what it takes to find Leonida’s birds, how the spotting mechanics work, and what Rockstar’s artists got right.

Still: Rockstar Games

By
Nicholas Lund

Contributor, Audubon magazine

Published

November 20, 2026

This article is a product of Audubon magazine. Become a member to receive our quarterly print issue in the mail.

Get the Magazine

Latest Issue

I finished collecting the bricks of cocaine and landed my bullet-ridden seaplane at the dock. It was time for birdwatching.
A few minutes after midnight on Thursday morning, I joined millions of other gamers for the release of
Grand Theft Auto VI
, the latest in the smash video game series from Rockstar Games. The new installment is already a worldwide sensation, earning more than
$1.8 billion in revenue
the day it was released.
Grand Theft Auto
, or
GTA
, games are famous for their “open worlds,” which allow players to explore massive, intricately detailed versions of America. Much of that exploration is focused on mayhem and chaos: The story missions usher players through criminal underworlds, and players are at any time free to steal cars, rob stores and pedestrians, and initiate anarchy.
But
GTA 6
has more going on than just criminality—it’s also a world filled with wildlife. Previous
GTA
games were set in fictionalized versions of New York City and Hollywood, but the new one returns to Vice City, its version of Miami, which was also the setting for 2002’s installment. Unlike that game, however,
GTA 6
’s South Florida is complete with dozens of species of birds, reptiles, amphibians, fish, mammals, and other creatures. The in-game Progress menu tracks all kinds of items to find, including 338 vehicles, 205 weapons, and, of primary interest to me, at least 60 bird species.
I made it my mission to find them all as quickly as possible.
(Side note: Pre-release marketing for
GTA
6 touted 62 bird species, but the official birds Progress screen only lists 60, with a handful of others listed on the hunting screen.)
I am one hour in and I’ve found 16/60 birds https://t.co/81x42O1BuY
— The Birdist (@TheBirdist)
November 19, 2026
You begin the game as Jason, a low-level criminal working to raise money to support his young family. You’re equipped with zoom binoculars before the very first mission—tracking drug runners through a swamp and escaping with the seaplane—and I used them immediately, stopping mid-lurk to scan some Double-crested Cormorants on a dock. (Distracted from the job at hand to look at birds—just like real life!) They looked like Double-crested Cormorants!
After the first mission the player is free to explore the entirety of the map, stealing cars, robbing stores, or just birding wherever they want. The game makes birding easy: Looking at any bird through the in-game binoculars gives players the option to hold a button to “study” it, thereby adding it to the Progress menu. Simply standing on the back deck of Jason’s first safehouse yields a bunch of species like Brown Pelican and Laughing Gull. It’s just like being in South Florida!

I found a few more species right in Jason’s backyard, including American Crow, House Sparrow, and South Florida-appropriate Monk Parakeets.

Looking south from the back deck, I spotted another bird perched on an adjacent dock, with a few people gathered at the end. Looking through my binoculars
I spotted my first Herring Gull
—and noticed that the people, a woman and three men, were fully and visibly naked. Jason apparently lives next to a nudist resort. It’s just like being in South Florida!
Two down, 58 to go. I found a few more species right in Jason’s backyard, including American Crow, House Sparrow, and South Florida-appropriate Monk Parakeets, before venturing out into the huge map. My strategy for finding birds in
GTA 6
was the same as finding birds in real life: look in as many habitats as I could find. I started by “borrowing” a fanboat off a nearby dock and heading back to the swampy areas near the seaplane mission. There were tons of birds across the open water and in the marsh: Caspian Terns, Mottled Ducks, Sanderlings, Spotted Sandpipers, Great Blue Herons, Glossy and White Ibis, and … flocks of Whooping Cranes?
incredibly healthy populations of critically-endangered Whooping Cranes across Vice City. Huge if true. https://t.co/doe6oMOvBX
— The Birdist (@TheBirdist)
November 19, 2026
In fact, I found a number of avian inaccuracies in just my first few hours of playtime. Certain species like Whooping Crane and Red-cockaded Woodpecker are common throughout the map, despite being endangered and threatened, respectively, in real life. Golden Eagles are extremely rare in Florida, but I found one soaring over the Mt. Kalaga area (mountains, one may point out, aren’t found in Florida either). Some species have confusing naming quirks—the chickadee is Black-capped instead of Carolina, and there’s a “New World Oriole” instead of a Baltimore Oriole—but those changes are likely due to the fact that Carolina and Baltimore don’t exist in the
GTA
universe.

Though some of the inaccuracies may feel like a letdown in a game that is being hailed as the
Greatest of All Time
, I think it’s important to remember that it’s also game where you can
get a ride from a dog driving a jet ski
.
Grand Theft Auto
games are meant to be fun, not science. Plus, despite some of the misfires, the avifauna feels well thought-out. The map is true to the ecological boundaries of South Florida, with herons, gulls, and other waterbirds in the south while birds like Red-bellied Woodpecker, Wood Stork, and American Robin are found farther north. Birders know that certain exotic species have made their home in tropical South Florida, including Spot-breasted Oriole and Red Junglefowl, both in the game.

The game doesn’t tell you what species to look for, so you’ll need to cover a lot of ground to find everything.

That geographic fidelity is the main tip for anyone looking to check off all the game’s birds: Find their habitat. The game doesn’t tell you what species to look for, so you’ll need to cover a lot of ground to find everything. Wading birds, shorebirds, and seabirds are common in the southern coastal part of the map. A number of smaller, open-country or forest birds are found up north. Owls come out at night. Birds in zoos and domestic farmyard birds count towards the 60, too, so don’t overlook those areas.
Wild Boar roadkill. It’s just like birding in Florida! https://t.co/gT84IticOK
— The Birdist (@TheBirdist)
November 19, 2026
The most accurate aspect is the actual landscape. Having birded extensively across South Florida myself, the habitats are immediately recognizable, from the pebbly mangrove beaches at the Keys to the grassy swamps further north. The setting feels absolutely real, from the fonts on the roadside fruit stands to the roadkill alongside the highways. (I found dead wild boar and dead deer by the side of the road, and a Turkey Vulture somehow flew into a building I was in and died at my feet.)
So, if you’re up for the kind of funhouse-mirror version of Florida that the game presents, you can have a blast, and adding birdwatching into the insane free-for-all makes for some delightful moments.
This guy just wanted to look at a gull
but ended up chucking a woman off a pier. I’ve made myself laugh out loud by screeching to a halt in the middle of busy highways or intersections and jumping out of my car to look for birds while motorist behind me scream and swear. I love it.
easily my favorite thing to do so far is just screech to a halt in the middle of a busy intersection and start birding https://t.co/QsDOLmNfYq
— The Birdist (@TheBirdist)
November 19, 2026
As I was dodging dirt-biking rednecks to look for species in a northerly forest, I couldn’t help but compare birding in
GTA 6
to
birding in
Red Dead Redemption 2
(
RDR2
), the latest installment in Rockstar’s other huge franchise. Birds and birding are presented quite similarly in both games, including the binocular “study” mechanic and many of the same species, but the experiences are totally different.
RDR2
was set in the late 1800s, and players rode on horseback or locomotive through a comparatively wide-open and untrammeled version of America. There was mayhem in that game, too—outlaw gangs and marauders—but there were many peaceful moments, too, when a player could look out across wild landscape with nothing but nature as a soundtrack.

It is, I have to admit, a realistic depiction of birding in South Florida.

Not so in
GTA 6
. There’s plenty of birdsong on the soundtrack, but it competes with an endless racket of car radios, revving engines, swearing pedestrians, and blaring horns. There’s garbage almost everywhere, lapping the shorelines and blowing along the streets. There seems to be no inch of landscape in
GTA 6
that hasn’t been lessened by the touch of humans. It is, I have to admit, a realistic depiction of birding in South Florida.
Birders working to fill out their GTA VI wildlife checklists should know something I just found out: THERE’S A ZOO https://t.co/2xN0joPKcR
— The Birdist (@TheBirdist)
November 20, 2026
Though
GTA 6
provides what feels the most accurate version of modern birding ever put to screen, obsessing over the realism misses the point of having fun. Birders can, and should, visit the real South Florida to find the actual birds depicted in the game (and many more), but they can’t do it while also jumping over broken highway bridges on a stolen motorcycle. Birding is a bonus in
GTA 6
; mayhem is the draw.
I played for two hours after midnight, then about six straight hours Thursday before having to call it quits to write this column. In that time I found 50 of the 60 species listed in the “birds” compendium. I jumped back in this morning before work and found a huge chunk of species at a zoo (makes sense!) and on a farm, then found the 60th and final, an American Barn Owl, on a water tank in a town in the north of the map. Success!
The biggest thing I can confirm is that all 60 birds on this list are available immediately, without needing any story progression. In Red Dead Redemption 2, some bird species were only found in Guarma, only accessible later in the game
— The Birdist (@TheBirdist)
November 20, 2026
I felt a wave of satisfaction, and while I’m not certain if I was the first one to find them all, when I posted about it, a Rockstar designer replied with, “
History!
” I’d met my goal, and celebrated in a way that only
Grand Theft Auto
games allow: by driving my car full speed off a cliff into the ocean.

Honda
will begin standardizing some vehicle parts in an effort to lower production costs, according to a report by
Automotive News
.
The automakers will start with equalized quality criteria for steel, consistent protocols for plastics, and a universal color-coding scheme for wiring harnesses.
Discussions are starting with Japan’s domestic suppliers, though international suppliers will be looped in soon.
Japan’s three largest automakers have agreed to begin standardizing vehicle parts in an effort to reduce costs, according to
Automotive News
. The outlet reports that Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association chairman Koji Sato, who is also the vice chairman of Toyota, announced the decision at a news conference in Tokyo this week.
In the short term, the standardization efforts will begin with unified quality criteria for steel, consistent protocols for plastics and resins, and a universal color-coding scheme for wiring harnesses. In the long term, the Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association has plans to move to more components that cover the entire car. The three areas were chosen as the first to be standardized because they are parts that are generally not noticed by consumers, and they shouldn’t have an impact on any brand’s individual identity. All three are also areas that account for significant production costs for the automakers, meaning they can have an immediate impact.
