title: Let's Meet in the Middle
content:
I like making little tools that do one thing well and thing finding clever ways to combine them. It's the ethos behind a lot of the little software projects I have over at
Less Software
.
One of the first ones I made was a tool called
whereami
. Tongue-in-cheekly, I wanted to pitch it as the natural compliment to
whoami
. For that tool, the thinking was nearly every modern OS provides some kind of native API for geolocation. It felt silly to me that I could run a quick command from the terminal for so many things, but I couldn't run one that taps into this capability.
In the pursuit to make that tool cross-platform, one of the things I found myself navigating were the differences between them. Consistently, macOS tended to have a lot of extra niceties baked in, particuarly when it came to imagine recognition, natural language processing and accessibility tooling.
With geolocation, one of the nice things macOS provides that other OS-native approaches don't is a built-in geocoder (and reverse geocoder). So you can type in something like this:

That comment inspired me to make this list of "recipes" where I try to showcase different ways to combine these tools in surprising, useful and/or fun ways:
https://less.software/recipes/
But the one I want to write about specifically today is this "meet in the middle" idea.
I just showed you how you can use

How it works
It's three small tools, each doing one thing.
whereami
started life as a CLI that asks your operating system where you are. As of 0.4 it can also act like a reverse geocoder (on macOS):
$ whereami
"350 5th Ave, New York"
--json

{
"latitude"
:40.7482378,
"longitude"
:-73.9850579,

:0,
"address"

Looking up an address doesn't need location permission, because nothing is asking where you are.
jq
does the arithmetic. The
-s
flag slurps both JSON objects into an array, and the filter averages the coordinates:
{
"latitude"
:
40.7097896
,
"longitude"
:
-73.9743696
}
nearme
searches for places around a set of coordinates using MapKit, the search engine behind Apple Maps. It reads coordinates from JSON on stdin, and it only cares about
latitude
and
longitude
. It has no idea those numbers came out of
jq
and not out of a GPS.
Averaging two coordinates is not the "real" way to find the middle, but over a few miles trying to find a place to meet for coffee it's close enough. What does matter is that the midpoint has no idea what's actually there.
Make it a command
Typing that pipeline more than once get annoying quickly. It's more convenient to set it up as a function:

'{latitude: (map(.latitude) | add / 2), longitude: (map(.longitude) | add / 2)}'
|

"
${2:-coffeeshop}
"

"
${@:3}
"

}

Give it two addresses and something to look for. Anything after that goes straight through to nearme. Leave off the second address and it uses wherever you are right now, so
middle "123 Main Street" coffee
finds coffee between you and 123 Main Street. With only an address, it looks for a coffeeshop.
$ middle
"350 5th Ave, New York"

Caveats
It's macOS only.
nearme
is built on MapKit, and
whereami

It wants street addresses or city names, though landmarks will work soetimes. "Golden Gate Bridge" doesn't geocode but "350 5th Ave, New York" and "Central Park" and "Brooklyn Briddge" do (caveat emptor).
The math is a very literal and naive geographic middle, not taking travel-time middle or anything else into consideration.

title: Building a wireless network adapter for the Super Nintendo
content:
fig.0
An adapter that adds wireless connectivity to the SNES via the controller port, with no external power source needed. USB included for debugging.

00
Why?

01
Prototyping

02
Save sync

03
AI dialogue

04
Hardware

05
Enclosure

00
Why?

I always come back to the Super Nintendo (SNES). It was my first console and it’s still my most potent source of nostalgia.
It inspired my early interest in electronics as a teenager, designing circuits for mods and flash carts that I hoped to build one day.
I followed the launch of Hackaday, Adafruit, and the progress of bunnie Huang’s Chumby and knew exactly what I wanted to do.

I dropped out of my final years of high school to study hands-on electronics at college, and continued on to university. Then, finally equipped with those skills I’d aspired to, I went off-track and spent the next fifteen years working in data, ML and software. A lot has changed in that time but I’m back now, picking up exactly where I left off.

The Super Network Adapter is an exercise in ‘16-bit futurism’, it aims to be a faithful peripheral to the original SNES hardware and what we imagined the future might be back then: a wireless link to the net, sync’ing saves across devices and an uplink to AI.

01
Prototyping

The SNES never had a dedicated network port. The closest it came was the
Satellaview
, a modem peripheral connected to a hidden expansion port that could receive game broadcasts via satellite. There was also the
XBAND
, a modem that plugged into the cartridge slot and supported pass-through patching of specific games for online play. Reproducing the hardware of either of these today would be
challenging
, however most peripherals for the SNES took a much simpler route, they used one of the controller ports.

Controller Serial Link

The SNES controller ports are small synchronous serial buses that a game can control, setting and reading individual lines and driving the clock. These ports have seven lines but in a typical controller cable, only five tend to be present, with the wires for
D1
and
IOBit
left out. To make sourcing parts for this project easier, my design also only relies on the remaining five wires.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ ┌──────────────────────────────┐  ┌───────────────────────╮ │
│ │  ●       ●       ●       ●   │  │   ●       ●       ●   │ │
│ └──────────────────────────────┘  └───────────────────────╯ │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
1       2       3       4          5       6       7
5v     CLK    Latch     D0         D1    IOBit    GND

First I needed a protocol for talking over this serial link, which I iterated with
Mesen
and a virtual network adapter written in Lua simulating the controller port link. This protocol has the SNES writing to the
Latch
line and reading from the adapter on
D0
, one bit at a time (‘bit-banging’). Even with some optimisation (unrolling loops and ignoring mid-stream replies) this approach tops out at about 30 KB/s, but that’s enough for the ’90s.

Breadboard Version

The first physical prototype was built using a Pico 2 W dev board. The additional circuitry needed was very simple, just some pull-up resistors for
CLK
and
Latch
. The board’s
RP2350A
can handle the console’s 5v logic on its pins directly, and it has two cores: one can maintain the console link, while the other maintains the Wi-Fi network link, without juggling interrupts.

fig.1
The first prototype: a Pico 2 W on a breadboard wired up to a repurposed controller extension cable.

Controller port pinout

Pin
Signal
Wiring

1
+5V
feeds pull-ups only (Pico on USB supply for now)

2
CLK
GPIO pin and 4k7 pull-up

3
Latch
GPIO pin and 4k7 pull-up

4
D0
GPIO pin, open drain

7
GND
Shared GND

Warning

The prototype runs from USB, with the console’s 5v only feeding the pull-ups. I did not connect the SNES 5v to the Pico’s VBUS or VSYS while USB is plugged in. The Pico was powered on before the console so the RP2350’s pins were ready to handle 5v. The PCB design later can run on either supply.

02
Save sync

Adding Cloud Save or ‘Save Sync’ seemed the most practical use for a Wi-Fi connection. I often go back to the SNES and start a new game, but if I could continue playing that save file in RetroArch on my phone and then back to the SNES, it would fit into my life much more easily.

Game save data is stored in battery-backed SRAM and in order for a game to send that through my adapter, I needed some of my own code to run. I already have a programmable flash cart for the SNES, so I wrote a utility to patch ROMs and inject this ‘save sync’ code into the reset vector. At power-on and whenever the console is reset, it syncs the save data through the adapter to a WebDAV server as
saves/<core>/<name>.srm
(the same path RetroArch uses) so the console save can be continued on the phone, and vice versa.

Joining Wi-Fi

First though, the adapter needs to join the local Wi-Fi network. I wanted an era-appropriate UI that can be run from a setup ROM (fig.2), which has you pick a network and type its password with an on-screen keyboard, one letter at a time. That felt most ‘authentic’ but I also made a second iteration that shows the typical QR code on the TV for setup via mobile phone.

fig.2
The first setup ROM, recorded on a real SNES: pick a network, then type its password with the D-pad. Sound on for the chiptune.

The second version has the adapter set up a temporary network. Scanning the QR code with a phone joins the network and it then does the usual captive portal flow to open the adapter’s setup page, where the network and WebDAV auth details can be input in a much more user-friendly way.

fig.3
Setup from a phone using the QR code on the TV, and the adapter’s setup page joining the home network.

Pushing and Pulling Saves

An important detail to get right was checking whether the save on the cartridge was newest, or whether to download a newer one from WebDAV. RetroArch keeps a manifest file with a hash of every save, so the adapter updates that too, comparing hashes to decide whether the cartridge or the server has the newest save. If both sides have changed, nothing is overwritten and the cartridge’s save goes to a conflicts folder to play it safe.

SRAM saves are small but this sync still has to run whenever a game starts, potentially introducing a delay. To avoid this, the save is split into chunks that each have their own checksum, so only the chunks that have changed are sent over the controller port. In practice this makes the save sync delay imperceptible, and only when an existing save is pulled by the SNES for the first time is there a 1-2s load screen.

03
AI dialogue

Naturally in 2026, an internet connection also means a connection to LLMs. The dialogue in SNES-era games tends to be fixed and unresponsive. In A Link to the Past, the villagers don’t react when you smash their pots (unlike in subsequent Zelda games). With the network adapter though, we can hook the game’s dialogue text renderer to swap out the original text for an in-character line generated by an LLM.

fig.4
The castle guard getting fed up with Link, recorded on a real SNES. In the other images, the villagers complain about Link’s chicken-bothering.

In order to prompt for dialogue, the LLM needs to be passed the game context, such as the character being interacted with and recent events. Since Link to the Past has been fully disassembled, it was possible to patch it to accumulate this state in RAM and push it out over the controller serial to the adapter and on to an LLM (via a proxy I ran on a local machine that holds the API key).

I tried a few different models and settled on Claude Opus 5.5, as cheaper models would break character or leak spoilers despite being prompted not to. I used LLM as a Judge evals to measure the proportion of responses that fit the context - Haiku scored 66%, Sonnet 90% and Opus 98%. The challenge was the time to first token of the LLM, for Haiku it was about 0.8 s but for Opus it averaged 2.2 s.

To avoid game-breaking delays from the LLM response times, I switched to speculatively generating the dialogue when Link approaches an NPC, storing the responses in a cache and invalidating them as the context updates. The delay from using a larger model was hidden and most NPC interactions had the response ready. This is a great way to burn tokens so probably not something to do for the full game duration!

04
Hardware

When designing the PCB version of the adapter (fig.0) I replicated the same architecture as the prototype, an
RP2350A microcontroller
that handles the 5v lines and maintains the serial link, with an
ESP32-C3
Wi-Fi coprocessor that handles the Wi-Fi connection. These communicate with each other over UART, allowing each link to be maintained by a dedicated core.

┌─────────┐ port 2 ┌─────────┐ uart ┌──────────┐ wi-fi ┌────────┐
│ SNES    │──────▸ │ RP2350A │────▸ │ ESP32-C3 │~~~~~▸ │ cloud  │
│ 65816   │◂────── │
PIO
│◂──── │
TCP/TLS
│◂~~~~~ │
WebDAV
│
└─────────┘        └─────────┘      └──────────┘       └────────┘
3.58 MHz           150 MHz          160 MHz

A PIO state machine on the RP2350 watches
clock
and
latch
, queueing the data and filtering out glitches shorter than 100 ns. This frees up the cores to prepare data to be sent over
D0
while also talking to the C3.

fig.5
The RP2350A core, following Raspberry Pi’s minimal design: flash, crystal and USB on the left, the controller link and C3 pins on the right. Tap or click any schematic to enlarge it.

The USB socket was included not just for flashing the board but also to support debugging it while it is powered from the SNES. This means the board needs to safely support taking a 5v supply from either the controller port or USB, and avoid backfeeding if both are connected. This is done with a
LM66200
dual ideal diode. Supply can be taken from either source and we avoid the voltage drop that would come with using actual diodes. I’d seen some brownouts in tests on the breadboard, so designed the PCB with plenty of headroom for the LDO regulator even if the supply rail sags on a Wi-Fi burst.

fig.6
Power: the console’s 5 V or USB-C, whichever is present, through the LM66200 and on to a 3.3 V LDO.

Note

While prototyping I also had issues when using series resistors on the link lines. This may be related to
erratum RP2350-E9
in the A2 revision (stepping) of the RP2350A on my Pico 2 W. In the assembled PCB order I switched these to 0 Ω links, as they’re just for protection and I wasn’t sure which stepping the PCB would be assembled with. The boards turned out to have the fixed A4 stepping, so real resistors can go in next time.

fig.7
The controller port: the same pull-ups as the breadboard, and the 0 Ω links (R11–R13) where series resistors would go.

05
Enclosure

The case is just a tray and a lid that sandwich the PCB, though I did want it to nod toward an era-appropriate design language. It was generated in
code (
build123d
) using the PCB’s STEP files from KiCad, so that the design could be tested within a single 3D model.

fig.8
A render of the enclosure, about the size of a Zippo lighter.

The two halves join around the cable and the USB socket, and there are M2 pillars that align with the drilled holes in the PCB to hold everything together.

Since the PCB has a status LED, this design has a light pipe that channels that light up to become the dot of the etched Wi-Fi icon. It’s not the prettiest of designs, but I thought that was cute.

I’ve ordered a batch of these enclosures to be 3D printed and will update with actual photos once they arrive and the adapter is fully assembled. I’m also considering how to fabricate a single assembly that can insert directly into the controller port. Reach out at
[email protected]
if you’re interested!

06
Build log

2026-10-29
65816 toolchain, headless emulator tests

2026-11-02
Breadboard link to port 2 working

2026-11-09
First save uploaded from the console

2026-11-13
PCB designed and ordered from JLCPCB

2026-11-19
PCBs arrive and work perfectly!

2026-11-21
Ordered 3D printed enclosures

title: The next circle of security hell
content:
A few years back I wrote
“The modern packager’s security nightmare”
. Have things improved since? On the contrary, I feel like we’re slipping down a well-oiled slope with no end in sight. Vulnerabilities are reported at unprecedented rates. A lot of people are doing everything they can to patch them up, which doesn’t necessarily mean they’re not making things even worse. Complex software involves complex trees of dependencies, and every branch on that tree needs tending to. When they stop being reliable, people further down the tree start taking more weight. And there’s a limit of how much a single person can do, so what started as an effort to resolve an issue upstream may quickly become a weakness.

Is software less secure these days? It’s tempting to say yes. I’d love to blame the corporate sector for egotistically dumping low quality software on us. I’d love to blame marketing-oriented people developing stuff with the sole goal of making a profit. I’d love to blame Rust for getting people obsessed about memory safety, and ignoring the kinds of vulnerabilities that aren’t caught by the compiler. Finally, I’d really love to blame slop. But the truth is, I don’t know. That’s really beside the point.

The point is that nowadays everyone and their chatbot became security researchers. Projects are being flooded with vulnerability reports. Even though pretty much every bug bounty was discontinued because of slop, people aren’t stopping. And even if we disregard truly invalid junk reports, there’s a lot left, and you have to deal with them somehow. You have to figure out how important they are, and how to fix them (or more likely, whether the fixes submitted are truly valid and don’t introduce regressions), or if you should reject them and why.

In the end, security is tricky. We’re seeing lots of bugs like REDoS, or other kinds of “performance bugs”. Are they really vulnerabilities? Well, it depends on the attack vector. And that in turn depends on how the software is used. Some scenarios are really contrived, and feel like “shell can execute dangerous commands if you type them in”. But then, you also have really serious issues such as “timing attack can be used to guess user’s secret”. You need to know a lot to make that kind of judgment, and sometimes your judgment doesn’t really match users’ expectations.

In the end, what can project maintainers do? Even if they have the expertise and the energy to judge, if they can “know better”, there’s likely a CVE assigned already. It may have absurdly high score. All security scanners will complain unless you fix it, and users will come asking or complaining, or attacking, or forking. I mean, technology can’t handle nuances. More than once I’ve been doing unnecessary security stabilizations over vulnerabilities that didn’t affect Gentoo (for example, because we already unbundled the vulnerable dependencies), to avoid false positives from security scanners. I’ve been also doing meaningless version bumps (with no real changes or no changes that applied to Gentoo) so that our packages don’t get reported as being “outdated”. It’s a hassle and it sucks, but it saves people from worrying.

I’ve said this before and I’ll say it again: most projects aren’t really prepared to handle security issues. And it’s not just about triage. It’s about having LTS or security branches, it’s about making proper security releases with minimal changes. Unfortunately, it’s quite common for security fixes to be combined with new features, deprecations, API changes. In extreme cases, people are caught with their metaphorical pants down, and suddenly need to make a security release in the middle of a major rewrite, or along with barely tested new code. And then, people downstream discover that they need to quickly deal with major API changes to upgrade past a vulnerable version. These things keep piling up.

What happens next? The community reaches a breaking point. People can’t keep up. You discover you can’t rely on others, so you work around them. You start bundling more stuff. Soon enough your workload goes beyond your ability. Software development becomes “every chatbot for itself”. The nightmare becomes worse, and the wheel keeps turning.

Dirac's Theorem at a Dinner Party
content:
Dirac’s Theorem at a Dinner Party

Gabriel Dirac (the famous graph theorist) was the stepson of Paul Dirac (the even more famous physicist). Paul Dirac spent the last years of his career at Florida State University, and my father took his course in General Relativity in the 1970s.

Gabriel formulated an important theorem about Hamiltonian cycles. In this post I want to give a refresher on Hamiltonian cycles, and go over a fun proof of his theorem that involves a hypothetical dinner party.

Over the course of several decades, Dirac’s theorem was improved when mathematicians formulated similar theorems that work with a broader range of graphs. In the following figure, each theorem is more general than the one to its left. Each graph meets its own theorem’s condition, but none of the ones to its left, and its Hamiltonian cycle is blue.

Why am I writing about Dirac’s Theorem? Well, I wanted to write about a simple proof relating to Hamiltonian cycles as prep for my next post, which will be about Barnette’s Conjecture, one of my favorite graph theory conjectures. It got promoted to a theorem in the 6-Oct-2026 Mathocalypse. In my next post I’ll talk more about that.

A
Hamiltonian cycle
is a walk along the edges of a graph that visits every vertex exactly once and ends up back where it started. A graph that has one is
Hamiltonian
.

Hamiltonian cycles are related to the Traveling Salesman Problem (e.g. designing delivery routes for Amazon packages). But my personal favorite application is an old-school computer graphics problem: given a triangle mesh, can you render it using a single triangle strip?

Intuitively, it should be easier to find a Hamiltonian cycle in a graph that has lots of edges relative to its vertex count. In a way, that intuition is what Dirac formalized:

Theorem 1 (Dirac, 1952)

If a simple graph has
vertices, and every vertex has at least
neighbors, then the graph has a Hamiltonian cycle.

The following figure shows a random graph with 10 vertices, where every vertex has exactly 5 neighbors, so the theorem guarantees a Hamiltonian cycle. On the right, the same graph has been rearranged so that its Hamiltonian cycle runs around the outside…like a circular dinner table.

1.
Dinner party

To see why the theorem is true, first imagine a party where each guest is a vertex and each friendship is an edge. Friendship goes both ways, and nobody is their own friend, which is what
simple

guests, and every guest is friends with at least
of the others, then the guests can sit at a round table such that each one sits between two friends.

Here’s the plan. Seat everyone in random order. Two guests who sit side by side are
seatmates

gap

title: Don't keep your SSH keys on disk
content:
Although it's clear to me that some of the
panic is unwarranted
, all the recent security vulnerability reports and company breaches are a good reason to think about what you're doing to avoid risk, and to mitigate exposure if something bad happens.

I'm a pathological self-hoster and I've been running all kinds of systems, from old toy projects to fun tools, and over time I've accumulated a lot of them. This has changed in the last couple of months, where I've instead been pruning my running services. I've taken down unused old apps, because anything can be an entry point into your system. And they were
unused
anyway. I've also moved most of services behind my Tailscale, with some judicious use of
tailscale funnel
to poke little holes for specific things that do need to be publicly accessible. And I've been obssessively updating everything on my servers that can be updated.

That brings us to my personal computer. I've been trying to do the same kind of due diligence that I did for my servers, on my personal devices. I have been a long time user of password managers, and I recently wrote about
moving to Bitwarden
, and I am careful to always enable 2FA or passkeys on every service I use. But one area I've fallen behind is
SSH keys
.

A better approach to SSH keys

I was keeping copies of my private keys in my password manager, for safe-keeping, but I was still using the version on disk, loaded into memory with
ssh-add
. To just make this absolutely clear, this means that the private keys are vulnerable to be exiltrated by malicious code scanning my disk. After reading articles like
I deleted all my SSH keys
, I finally decided to take the next step and get them off disk.

I knew that for this to work for me, it had to be easy to use and the disruption had to be minimal, and so although things like the OSX Secure Enclave sounds incredibly cool, I needed something with better ergonomics. I already had Bitwarden set up, with the keys in it, and so that's the approach I ended up taking, and it has worked great for me.

Setting up the Bitwarden SSH agent

Ok, let's go through the steps. First, make sure your private keys are in Bitwarden. If they are not, you'll want to import them. Note that the Bitwarden UI for importing SSH keys is a bit awkward.

Create a new SSH key in Bitwarden, it'll automatically generate one for you.

Copy your existing private key into your clipboard, eg
cat ~/.ssh/id_rsa | pbcopy
.

On the Private Key header in the edit form, at the very far right of the asterisks hiding the value, there's an upload icon, click it.

Your private key has been imported. Give it a good name and save.

Once you're done with that, you can now move on to the next step, which is enabling the Bitwarden SSH agent. Note that these instructions are for the direct install, if you installed it through the App Store I think the
path is different
. Go to Preferences, App settings (all accounts), and find the checkbox for "Enable SSH agent". You'll also get the option of choosing how often it prompts you for permission, when something wants to use the key. I went for whenever the vault is locked, which I have set to every 4 hours, balancing security with convenience.

Next, add to your
~/.ssh/config
file:

Host *

IdentityAgent ~/.bitwarden-ssh-agent.sock

This tells
ssh
to use the Bitwarden SSH agent. This applies globally, so anything that calls
ssh
should now check the agent. Separately, you'll want to add this to your terminal config file, eg
.zshrc
:

export SSH_AUTH_SOCK=~/.bitwarden-ssh-agent.sock

This ensures anything that needs the SSH agent in your terminal, that isn't
ssh
, also go to the right place. This covers tools like
ssh-keygen
. Okay, now try it out with
ssh-add -L
. This should list all the keys loaded into
ssh-agent
. If you're confident you've copied all of your keys into your password manager, you can now delete the ones on disk.

Bonus: git commit signing

Git commits traditionally contain author information, but no proof that the author is who they say they are. This means it's trivial to impersonate someone else in a commit. It's still mitigated by the fact that git repositories generally have access controls, so a third party would not be able to push commits in the first place, but there is also a mechanism available for proving that the git originated from the claimed author: commit signing.

In the past, this was limited to GPG keys, but modern git supports signing using SSH keys. So I've set this up too, using a dedicated key that only has that job. This means that creating the commit and pushing it to the repo requires
two
separate SSH keys, and each one has to be authorized separately.

git

config

--global

gpg.format

ssh

git

config

--global

user.signingkey

"key::
$(
ssh-add

-L

|

grep

'YOURKEYNAME'
)
"

git

config

--global

commit.gpgsign

true

git

config

--global

tag.gpgsign

true

Go to a repo and create a commit, then run
git cat-file -p HEAD
, and you should see your signature there.

To have forges recognize your signature you have to teach them what it is. For Github that means going to
https://github.com/settings/keys
and adding it as a signing key. Tangled automatically trusts your configured SSH keys as signing keys. Gitea and Forgejo require some extra steps to trust your key, just follow their instructions at
/user/settings/keys
.

My experience after a couple of weeks

I've adjusted quickly. Everything just works out of the box, the only added friction is that now and then Bitwarden prompts me for permission to use keys, which if it's unlocked just means clicking "approve" on a dialog. If it's locked, I can unlock it with touch ID.

If any Bitwarden employees happen to be reading this, it would be nice if instead of clicking approve, I could use touch ID to approve use of the key. Or at least by hitting enter. As it is, I always have to move to the touchpad to approve. It would also be great if I could separately configure the vault lock interval and the same interval for keys. But that's just minor requests, overall it works just great for me, and it's not too disruptive.

And now I get to sleep a bit easier!

Written by
Johanna Larsson
.
Thoughts on this post? Find me on Bluesky at

@jola.dev

title: A Beginner's Guide to Local AI with Inkling, Qwen, and Unsloth
content:
A beginner's guide to Local AI with Inkling, Qwen, and Unsloth
We have AI at home! Set up your own free personal ChatGPT on your PC with Unsloth and Inkling or Qwen. It's private, and the whole house can use it.
By Jerry James
·
Nov 22, 2026
With the launch of
open-weight
models like Qwen, cloud-based LLM providers seem like they're more of infrastructure or appliance businesses when it comes to most routine tasks that an AI model can handle.
OpenAI and Anthropic have displayed a pattern of dropping model quality in the 'latest' version and controlling exactly what you're allowed to run on their models. Add to this ballooning costs and privacy concerns, and we get a pretty good case for moving away from this 'convenient' cloud experience.
That's basically where I was too. I wanted to offload certain token-heavy research, data collection, or coding tasks to an AI model without staring at usage limits all day. So, as any reasonable human being would do, I decided to set up my own
local AI
: a Claude and ChatGPT replacement that runs at home on my own hardware.
Since this was my first attempt, my primary focus was keeping it simple and hosting it on Windows. If you're a beginner, you can follow along to get one going on your home network too.
Once you have the hardware sorted, it takes about 10-15 minutes (excluding download times).
The short version
Install Unsloth Desktop, download a quantized AI model that fits your GPU's VRAM, set your context size, and turn on LAN access so everyone at home can use it.
What Do You Need to Run a Local AI at Home?
Not much (other than the hardware). Here's a short list:
A Windows PC with a graphics card (GPU).
The more video memory (VRAM) it has, the bigger the model it can run. I'm using an
RTX 5090
with 32GB VRAM for this setup.
Unsloth Desktop.
A free app that 'serves' the AI model to you through a chat interface.
Get it from Unsloth
.
An AI model sized to fit your GPU.
We'll pick one in the next section.
That's it. No terminal commands, Python environments, or subscriptions required.
Which AI Model Can Your GPU Run?
It depends on how much
VRAM
your graphics card has. As a rough guide, 8-12GB of VRAM handles smaller 9B-12B models, while 32GB comfortably runs 27B-35B models with plenty of room for long conversations.
On consumer-grade hardware, we'll need smaller models. The full-size Qwen model sits at around 56GB and won't really fit on a consumer graphics card unless you're running a Mac with unified memory. That's where quantization comes in.
What Is Quantization?
Quantization
shrinks a model by compressing weights and moving to a lower precision. You basically trade some accuracy for a model that actually fits on your GPU and runs faster.
The same photo stored at 8, 4 and 2 bits per pixel. A model's weights lose detail the same way going from Q8 to Q4 to Q2.
If you're wondering whether this tradeoff is worth it, well, it depends. You'll find that certain types of workloads don't really care and give similar outputs, while others may be nearly unusable.
Which Model Should You Run for Your VRAM?
For this guide, we'll be going with Qwen3.8-27B with 4-bit quantization on my system with an RTX 5090. Going up a tier is an option thanks to its 32GB of VRAM, but I wanted to allow for a larger
context window
(how much of the conversation the model can keep in mind at once) rather than cramming in the largest model that fits.
Qwen3.8-27B at each precision with a 128K context, from our
VRAM calculator
. At 4-bit, the model and the context fit a 32 GB card with room to spare.
If you want to run a model of this caliber with excellent performance, a hilariously overpriced RTX 5090 (remember when $1,999 felt too high?) is unfortunately still not a terrible 'deal' these days. The other option is way more expensive
enterprise-grade GPUs
.
If you're on a GPU with less VRAM, you can still get something very usable going right away. The table below gives you a rough idea of where you can start.

our calculator

GPUPartner's VRAM Calculator

Can You Run Inkling 2 on an RTX 5090?
Inkling 2 Mini, yes. Inkling 2 Small, no.
Inkling 2 Mini
is the newest model in this size class. Thinking Machines Lab released it on November 17, 2026: 26.4B parameters, Apache 2.0, vision support and a 1M-token context. Unsloth's recommended file, UD-Q4_K_XL, is 17.6 GB. That is within 0.1 GB of the Qwen3.8-27B file in this guide, so it sits on a 32GB card the same way and leaves about 14GB for context.
Nothing else in this guide changes. Update Unsloth Desktop first, because Inkling 2 needs a recent build, then search for Inkling 2 Mini in the same drop-down in Step 2.

Those figures are Unsloth's. They count RAM and VRAM together and cover the model alone, so a long context needs more. Inkling 2 Mini is a mixture-of-experts model with 5.4B parameters active, so the 4-bit file also runs on a 16 GB card with the remainder in system RAM, a little slower.
Inkling 2 Small
is small in name only. It is a 594B model, and the smallest file Unsloth publishes is 171.7 GB. That is unified-memory territory: a

Can You Run a Local AI on a Mac?
Yes. You'll find good alternatives in
Apple's Mac lineup
thanks to its
unified memory
. Macs are pretty good at running larger models, even if they don't offer the best performance. Just make sure you grab the MLX flavor that is custom-built for Apple Silicon.
The same trade applies to unified-memory PCs like the
MSI PRO MAX EDGE AI+ 11M
and NVIDIA's
DGX Spark
.
How Do You Set Up a Local AI with Unsloth Desktop?
It takes three steps: install Unsloth Desktop, download your model, and set the context size. I'll go over these steps in more detail below so you can follow along.
Step 1: Install Unsloth Desktop
First, we'll need a solution that 'serves' the AI model to you. My pursuit of simplicity narrowed my choices down to LM Studio or Unsloth Desktop. Both abstract away a ton of terminal commands and handle Python environments and dependencies behind a nice, simple UI, which makes them excellent picks for a first home setup.
I landed on Unsloth Desktop mostly because, well, I liked the name better. Also, it didn't try to push the very thing I was trying to escape when I opened its website: a subscription.
The community seems to like it overall too, so that's another point in its favor.
Once you've clicked through the installer and launched Unsloth, you'll see a window like this one.
Unsloth Desktop on first launch, before any model is loaded.
Step 2: Download a Quantized Model
On the top left of this main window, you can pick the model that you want to use from the drop down. We'll be using Qwen3.8-27B.
The model picker. Qwen3.8-27B is first on the Recommended list.
You should see a submenu like the one below when you click on a model. I'll be using Unsloth's UD-Q4_K_XL version. The M and S versions are smaller, but the XL version behaves much closer to the full-size model without filling up our VRAM, so it seemed like a good pick for my GPU.
Every quantization of Qwen3.8-27B with its download size. The gear next to the downloaded one holds the context setting.
Step 3: Set the Context Size
Once the download completes, you should see a gear icon to the right of the model as shown in the screenshot above. Here, you can set your context size manually or leave it on Auto if you aren't sure how much you need.
I'll be setting mine to 128K (unquantized) and might reassess after I've run the model through a few of my routine tasks for a few weeks. Again, you can use this
VRAM calculator
to help you with these numbers for
your specific GPU
.
At this point, our first local AI is up and running, and you can start chatting with it right inside Unsloth.
Remember, your mileage may vary depending on your setup.
How Do You Share a Local AI Across Your Home Network?
Short answer: Unsloth Desktop has LAN sharing built in. Set a Remote password, start LAN access, and share the address it gives you with anyone on your home network.
Once Unsloth Desktop is set up with a model, you might want to give family members or friends access too. For now, we'll only serve it over our local network, so my family can use it without needing physical access to this PC.
Head into Unsloth Desktop settings (gear icon on bottom left), and look for the 'Remote & LAN' tab.
Settings, Remote & LAN. LAN access is the second card. The Remote access card above it is for a later part.
Most of this section will be greyed out until you set a Remote password. Once you've set a password, you'll see a 'Start' button for LAN access. Click that and you should see an address that anyone on your home network can open in a browser to use a local AI model within a chat interface. They'll sign in as 'unsloth' with the Remote password you set.
Just keep in mind that the PC needs to stay on with Unsloth running for anyone to reach it.
Can You Access Your Local AI Across the Internet? Soon™
Not with this setup alone. Everything so far is limited to your local home network.
If you just need a chat interface like ChatGPT, Gemini, etc. to work within your home network, you're basically done at this point! You and anyone on your network can start talking to an AI model hosted on your machine right away.
In the next parts, we'll cover performance, tunneling, as well as setting up an agent that runs locally and uses only the web tools you allow it to use. This will let you automate more complex tasks like coding, research, and so much more without being tied to a subscription or usage limits and censorship.
As always, my focus remains simplicity that allows my family to use it without too much guidance or help.
PS. If you have any recommendations for agentic harnesses or even models to try, feel free to
let me know
and I'll give them a go!

title: Crafting Targeted MP4 Fuzzers
content:
+ All posts

In this blog post, I’ll discuss some challenges around fuzzing the MP4 container format with conventional mutation-based strategies, how I developed targeted fuzzers for GStreamer’s MP4 demuxer (the
qtdemux
element), and the vulnerabilities I found. This post is aimed at security researchers interested in developing more effective fuzzing techniques for the MP4 format, for GStreamer and beyond.

I was originally inspired to conduct this research by the blog post
Uncovering GStreamer secrets
from GitHub Security Lab, in which the author found 29 vulnerabilities in GStreamer by developing an MP4 corpus generator. While their strategy of producing small, structurally valid seed files was successful, it did not attempt to address a fundamental difficulty of fuzzing the format, which is the subject of this post.

Background

GStreamer is a widely used open source multimedia framework, supporting hundreds of media formats across its plugin sets. It consists of several command-line tools and a C library (with bindings for many other languages) that allow power users and developers to create arbitrarily complex encoding, decoding, and streaming pipelines.

From an adversarial standpoint, GStreamer’s expansive and decades-old media processing code, written in a memory-unsafe language, is a rich attack surface. Any system that sends untrusted data into a GStreamer pipeline is therefore a promising target for attackers. Prominent examples of such systems are the
GNOME desktop environment
, the
WebKitGTK browser engine
, the
webOS smart TV operating system
, and
Comcast’s RDK platform
for set-top box development, all of which use GStreamer to process media from potentially malicious remote sources.

Since MP4 is the most common media container format on the internet, it was logical to scope my efforts to GStreamer’s
isomp4
plugin, included by default in the
Good plugin set
.

Challenges with conventional fuzzing

When faced with the task of fuzzing a binary format like MP4, most researchers reach for a coverage-guided mutational fuzzer such as AFL++ or libFuzzer. This is a good instinct and is usually the right answer. However, the default mutation strategies used by these fuzzers tend not to be effective at achieving deep coverage for MP4 parsers, as we will see below.

An MP4 file can be represented as an n-ary tree consisting of nodes (referred to as
atoms
or
boxes
in the specification) that carry different kinds of data and metadata. Some atoms are parents to child atoms, while others are leaves that merely contain their own payloads.

Figure 1: Example MP4 Tree

To achieve this structure in a binary file, atoms are laid out in a depth-first sequence, each with a 4-byte size field followed by a 4-byte atom label. The size field accounts for the atom’s header, data, and descendants. When a fuzzer mutates the file by inserting or deleting data within an atom, the tree may become invalid unless the modified atom’s size field, as well as the size fields of each one of its ancestors, are corrected.

Figure 2: Fuzzer Mutation Invalidates MP4 Structure

Resultingly, a fuzzer that performs naive insertions and deletions (even on a coverage-guided basis) quickly starts failing on early validation code that checks the file’s structural soundness. For example, if a chunk of data is removed from the
mdia
atom, but the top-level
moov
atom still claims the original total size, the MP4 parser can reject the entire file because it is obviously invalid. After a while, the fuzzer can reach a plateau where it rarely makes it past those early routines, and deeper, more interesting code paths remain unexercised. This problem is exacerbated the more deeply nested the target atom is; the probability that a random, length-changing mutation will ever be seen by the relevant parsing code drops exponentially with the atom’s depth.

One way to counter this inefficiency is with structure-aware fuzzing, in which the fuzzer understands the format it is working with and uses a custom mutator to ensure that input files are at least loosely structurally valid before feeding them to the system under test (a good primer on structure-aware fuzzing can be found
here
). Developing a fuzzer that models the entire MP4 format is technically possible but complex to implement and would likely be much slower than a fuzzer targeting only a narrow, bug-prone subset of the specification. Such a fuzzer would also need to decide which of the many format invariants to enforce and which to break. With too much structural validity, the fuzzer may ironically miss some bugs that rely on malformed inputs. With too little, it may run into the original problem again.

Establishing a baseline

Before attempting to develop a structure-aware fuzzer, I first wanted to answer two questions: how much of
isomp4
is already covered by conventional mutational fuzzers, and is there any low-hanging fruit left? Since GStreamer is continuously fuzzed by the OSS-Fuzz service, I headed to OSS-Fuzz’s
code coverage report
to answer the first question. To my surprise, there was (and still is) zero pre-existing MP4 coverage because GStreamer’s fuzz targets were compiled
without the Good plugin set
(which includes
isomp4
). As a result, I needed to build one of the fuzzers locally and manually enable those plugins in order to establish a baseline.

I decided to use the general-purpose
gst-discoverer
fuzzer, which calls the GStreamer API to scan (“discover”) a media URI and extract as much metadata as possible from it with the appropriate plugin. The core logic for the harness is shown in the snippet below (comments my own). libFuzzer passes a single mutated input, represented by
data
and
size
, to the
LLVMFuzzerTestOneInput
function. Each mutation is coverage-guided but format-agnostic; neither libFuzzer nor the harness has any built-in awareness of the MP4 structure.
LLVMFuzzerTestOneInput
then sends the input unmodified to the GStreamer API’s
gst_discoverer_discover_uri
function for metadata discovery.

// Receives a mutated payload from libFuzzer

int

LLVMFuzzerTestOneInput
(
const
guint8
*
data
,
size_t
size
)

{

// ...

dc
=
gst_discoverer_new
(timeout
*
GST_SECOND,
&
err);

// ...

// Set global payload variables. Passed to GStreamer API via appsrc_configuration

fuzztesting_data
=
data;

fuzztesting_size
=
size;

// Discover mutated payload with GStreamer API

g_signal_connect
(dc,
"source-setup"
, (GCallback) appsrc_configuration,
NULL
);

info
=
gst_discoverer_discover_uri
(dc,
"appsrc://"
,
&
err);

g_clear_error
(
&
err);

if
(info)

gst_discoverer_info_unref
(info);

g_object_unref
(dc);

return
0
;

}

Figure 3: Stock Fuzzer’s Core Logic

After building the fuzzer with
-Dgood=enabled
to enable the Good plugin set, I ran it inside a virtual machine on my own hardware (Ryzen 9 3950X, 32GB RAM) for roughly 16-24 CPU-weeks. The input corpus was seeded with both complete MP4 files I found in various online corpora and minimal files generated by GitHub Security Lab’s corpus generator. Other than exercising
isomp4
, there were no functional differences between this fuzzer and the one continuously running on OSS-Fuzz.

Despite the fuzzer’s lack of structure awareness, this round succeeded in uncovering the five memory safety vulnerabilities listed below. The first two potentially allow attackers to disclose heap contents via crafted MP4 files, especially against applications that use the GStreamer API in non-standard ways. The remaining three enable denial of service against GStreamer or any application that uses its API to parse
TMPlayer
or
SubRip
subtitle files.

Heap out-of-bounds read in
qtdemux_parse_tree
(
CVE-2025-47183
)

Heap out-of-bounds read in
qtdemux_parse_trak
(
CVE-2025-47219
)

Null pointer dereference in
tmplayer_parse_line
(
CVE-2025-47808
)

Null pointer dereference in
subrip_unescape_formatting
(
CVE-2025-47807
)

Stack buffer overflow in
parse_subrip_time
(
CVE-2025-47806
)

Note that the fuzzer was never seeded with subtitle files; it discovered the TMPlayer and SubRip formats entirely on its own. This is a phenomenon intrinsic to coverage-guided fuzzers, discussed in more detail in the next section.

Pipeline-based fuzzing

The first fuzzer discovered vulnerabilities in two file types it was never seeded with because libFuzzer made random mutations toward the TMPlayer and SubRip formats over time, encouraged by coverage feedback telling it that those were new code paths to explore. Such drift is common with structure-unaware, coverage-guided fuzzing of any target that supports multiple formats, but whether it is desirable depends on the researcher’s goals. For this project, I was more interested in depth of MP4 coverage than breadth of formats, so finding bugs in other file types was an anti-goal.

One way to prevent format drift would be to disable support for all plugins except
isomp4
at compile time. However, to keep the build system compatible with other fuzz targets without maintaining different options for each one, I instead took advantage of GStreamer’s pipeline feature. Pipelines allow users to specify the exact sequence of elements that should be chained for operations such as demuxing, decoding, and playback. By defining a pipeline with
qtdemux
as the only demuxer, one could craft a fuzz target whose mutations converge on the MP4 format at runtime. This works because the pipeline fails early during demuxing on non-MP4 inputs, so libFuzzer sees no new code paths and does not consider those inputs worth mutating further.

Figure 4: GStreamer Pipeline Architecture (
source
)

To implement this, I wrote an
LLVMFuzzerTestOneInput
function that passed test cases to a pipeline defined as
appsrc name=src ! qtdemux ! fakesink
, as shown below. The
fakesink
element is a dummy sink that discards its input and is necessary to complete the pipeline.

int
LLVMFuzzerTestOneInput
(
const
uint8_t
*
data
,
size_t
size
)

{

// ...

fuzz_decode_mp4
(data, size);

return
0
;

}

int
fuzz_decode_mp4
(
const
uint8_t
*
data
,
size_t
size
)

{

GstElement
*
pipeline
=
gst_parse_launch
(

"appsrc name=src ! qtdemux ! fakesink"
,

NULL
);

if
(
!
pipeline)

return
0
;

GstElement
*
src
=
gst_bin_get_by_name
(
GST_BIN
(pipeline),
"src"
);

GstBuffer
*
buf
=
gst_buffer_new
();

GstMemory
*
mem
=

gst_memory_new_wrapped
(GST_MEMORY_FLAG_READONLY,

(gpointer)data,

size,

0
,

size,

NULL
,

NULL
);

gst_buffer_append_memory
(buf, mem);

gst_element_set_state
(pipeline, GST_STATE_PLAYING);

GstFlowReturn flow;

g_signal_emit_by_name
(src,
"push-buffer"
, buf,
&
flow);

gst_buffer_unref
(buf);

g_signal_emit_by_name
(src,
"end-of-stream"
,
&
flow);

// ...

return
0
;

}

Figure 5: Pipeline-Based MP4 Fuzzer

This pipeline-based fuzzer was faster than the stock one and found one bug the latter had missed: a heap out-of-bounds read in the
qtdemux_parse_uuid
function via an MP4 file with crafted PlayReady DRM metadata (
CVE-2026-46471
). An attacker could exploit this vulnerability to bypass address space layout randomization (ASLR) or leak the contents of files previously loaded by a GStreamer-backed process (see Atredis’ advisory
here
).

Structure-aware fuzzing

After investigating what was possible with conventional fuzzing, I started to conceptualize a structure-aware MP4 fuzzer. To avoid the complexities involved in modeling the entire MP4 format, I homed in on a small but valuable subset of the specification: the sample description (
stsd
) atom. This deeply nested atom is rich with variable-size sample decoding metadata contained in a number of sub-atoms, which are technically entries of one field called the sample description table.

Figure 6:
stsd
Ancestor Tree

Figure 7:
stsd
Atom Layout (
source
)

Within GStreamer,
stsd
is handled by the
qtdemux_parse_trak
function, which loops over the sample description table’s entries and parses each one using a mix of inline code and helper functions. The code tends to rely on manual pointer arithmetic and ad hoc bounds checking, making it a likely source of vulnerabilities. Additionally, coverage reports I generated after running the earlier fuzzing campaigns revealed that large, interesting regions of this code were never being hit. For instance, the section below, which parses a chunk of the video sample description, remained without coverage after extended runs of the stock fuzzer.

Figure 8: Example of Uncovered
stsd
-Parsing Code

A fuzzer that understands how
stsd
fits into the larger MP4 file and takes care to preserve the structure surrounding it could therefore be fruitful for finding bugs in this code.

As a proof of concept, I developed a partially structure-aware fuzzer with the following design: instead of mutating the entire MP4 file and passing it to GStreamer, as the stock fuzzer did, it would mutate
just
stsd
.
It would then randomly splice the mutated data into one of two static template MP4 files (either a video or audio track) containing
stsd
’s entire ancestor tree and update the ancestors’ size fields appropriately. This way, the overall structure of each MP4 file passed to
qtdemux
is guaranteed to be valid, while only the target atom is fuzzed. My hypothesis was that this would increase coverage for code sections like the one above.

Figure 9: Overview of Structure-Aware
stsd
Fuzzer

The basic implementation of this fuzzer is shown below. After receiving and minimally validating an input (a mutated
stsd
atom), the
LLVMFuzzerTestOneInput
function calls the
fix_outer_structure_and_fuzz
helper to adjust the ancestor tree based on the difference between the mutated atom’s size and its original size in the template.

int
LLVMFuzzerTestOneInput
(
const
uint8_t
*
data
,
size_t
size
)

{

// ...

Helper

While the basic concept works as is, it is somewhat counterproductive to always mutate
everything
inside
stsd
. Because the goal is structure awareness, fields like the atom type (label), size, and entry count should stay correct at least some percentage of the time, or we would re-encounter the problem solved by step three in the diagram above, just at the
stsd
level. At the other extreme, keeping the header valid 100% of the time could make us miss bugs stemming from disagreements between the size or entry count field and the contents of the payload (the sample description table).

We can compromise by adding a libFuzzer custom mutator to fix the atom’s size and entry count fields 50% of the time (arbitrary; there might be a more optimal value):

(mutated_size
<

+

=
((

%

==
0

if
(should_fix_stsd)

{

=

-
1

// Update stsd size field

write_uint32_be
(stsd_data, stsd_size);

size_t
stsd_entry_count
=
read_uint32_be
(stsd_data
+
12

if
(stsd_entry_count
==
0
||
stsd_entry_count
>
(stsd_size
/
8
))

{

(stsd_data
+
12
, (
rand
()
%
(stsd_size
/
16
))
+
1
);

}

}

return
mutated_size;

}

Figure 13: libFuzzer Custom Mutator for Structure-Aware Fuzzer (note:
rand
should ideally be seeded using the
Seed
argument to keep the function deterministic)

Instead of whole MP4 files, this fuzzer is seeded with a diverse sampling of
stsd
atoms, which I extracted from earlier runs’ corpora. All crash files and other libFuzzer artifacts are also
stsd
atoms and do not reproduce directly under GStreamer; they must be either spliced back into the right template first or passed to the fuzzer binary (which does the splicing automatically)
as positional arguments
.

This fuzzer ultimately yielded three new bugs: two division-by-zero vulnerabilities allowing denial of service with crafted audio tracks (
CVE-2026-46469
and
CVE-2026-46470
) and one global buffer overread without clear exploitability (
CVE-2026-46472
). As hypothesized, the coverage reports generated after a long campaign with this harness showed a substantial increase in
qtdemux_parse_trak
coverage, particularly in the section responsible for handling
stsd
.

Disclosure and remediation

As I verified and root-caused the crashes that accumulated, I reported them to the GStreamer developers per the project’s
disclosure policy
. This process entailed creating an account on
https://gitlab.freedesktop.org
and filing a confidential GitLab issue under the
GStreamer/gstreamer
repository.

The first batch of vulnerabilities, found during the stock fuzzer campaign, was fixed in the
1.26.2 release
on May 29, 2025. The single issue found by the pipeline-based fuzzer was fixed in the
1.28.1 release
on February 26, 2026. Finally, the three bugs raised by the structure-aware fuzzer were fixed in
version 1.28.2
on April 7, 2026. In addition to these point releases, GStreamer published patch files allowing end users to manually incorporate the remediations into older versions of the software. Further details on the disclosure and remediation timeline can be found in Atredis’ advisories.

I would like to highlight GStreamer’s frictionless disclosure process and the maintainers’ quick turnaround on my reports. The developers acknowledged each of my submissions within 24 hours, and internal fix commits were sometimes made even faster than that. This kind of response time is rarely seen from vendors, and I commend the GStreamer team for their attentiveness to security issues.

Limitations and future work

This blog post has shown that it is possible to extract more code coverage and vulnerabilities from MP4-handling targets using partially structure-aware fuzzers, even after extended fuzzing with a format-agnostic approach. However, the fuzzer I built had several design limitations that future research in this area should address. These include (but are not limited to) the following:

Single-atom focus
: The fuzzer only mutated
stsd
, leaving all other atoms alone.
stsd
is not the only complex atom, and its interactions with data in other segments of the MP4 file format might find code paths not yet explored by this work. A fuzzer capable of modeling a larger subset of the format and mutating different combinations of atoms (while keeping the overall file structurally valid) would search an exponentially greater input space and likely cover more code.

Static template
: While splicing
stsd
into a pair of unchanging MP4 templates simplified fuzzer development, it also likely blocked off code paths dependent on state set by
stsd
’s ancestor atoms. An approach that rotates between a variety of templates and injects randomness into fuzzed atoms’ ancestors is well worth exploring.

Limited subset of tracks
: The fuzzer mutated
stsd
only within two MP4 track types:
vide
(video) and
soun
(audio). Extending the fuzzer to support the full range of track types recognized by
isomp4
would not be difficult and, when paired with support for different atom types, could produce substantially more bugs.

Demux-only focus
: As stated in the introduction, this research focused on GStreamer’s MP4 demuxer in isolation. Codec parsing, decoding, encoding, and other elements of a full MP4 pipeline were out of scope but would also be expected to contain vulnerabilities. Future work should attempt to pass structurally mutated inputs to different pipeline configurations to exercise a broader range of GStreamer’s MP4 functionality.

In addition, this research occurred over several weeks between January 2025 and January 2026, just before the widespread adoption of AI agent harnesses for security research. As a result, all development, testing, debugging, fuzzing, and bug triage were done without the help of LLMs. The space has changed significantly in the past year. Frontier models are now capable not only of rapidly implementing and iterating on custom fuzzers, but also of spotting subtle vulnerabilities in complex codebases just by reading them. I would strongly advise anyone who picks up this work to enlist an AI agent and let it try both static and dynamic approaches.

title: Nespresso's project to reduce grams of coffee per capsule
content:
Information on Nespresso's Project Olympus.

Date:
November 1, 2026
Author:
Alvin Bunk

Introduction

The article is about Nespresso’s internal project to basically reduce the amount of grams per capsule that they produce. In August of 2026, I was informed by a Nespresso internal employee about “Project Olympus”. At first I didn’t think much of it and wasn’t sure how to deal with the information. It seems based on the docs that they were possibly improving the formulas, but I still questioned how that is possible with a reduction of grams of coffee.

The Documentation

The below text is the actual Project Olympus internal text for everyone’s reference to review:

PROJECT OLYMPUS: VERTUO
As part of our ongoing commitment to delivering an exceptional coffee experience, Nespresso is continuously innovating across every step of our process-while preserving the taste, quality, and consistency our consumers expect.

What’s changing?

Beginning in 2026, select Nespresso Vertuo coffee recipes will undergo a recipe optimization. Through advancements in grinding and roasting techniques, we’ve refined these recipes to achieve the same great taste and in-cup experience—using slightly less coffee per capsule.

This change will be rolled out gradually from Q1 through Q3 2026.

What’s staying the same?

While the capsule weight may be slightly reduced, the core elements of the coffee experience are unchanged:

Same taste profile consumers know and love

Same coffee volume per cup

Same caffeine levels, with only minor natural variation

Same high-quality standards across all affected coffees

These updates have been carefully validated from a sensory perspective to ensure no compromise in flavor or satisfaction.

Why are we optimizing recipes?

Innovation is at the heart of Nespresso. Our development teams are constantly exploring ways to improve how we roast and grind our coffees-while delivering the same consistent, high-quality results in every cup.

Project Olympus reflects this effort: a behind-the-scenes optimization designed to maintain excellence, even as we evolve our processes.

What if consumers ask questions?

In some cases, consumers may notice that certain capsules feel lighter than before or ask about possible changes. If inquiries arise, teams should emphasize:

Our commitment to quality and customer satisfaction

That the taste and experience remain the same

That the update reflects process innovation, not a reduction in value
The approved reactive statement and Q&A from the Project Olympus FAQ should be used to guide responses.

HQ development teams are continuously looking into innovating our coffee processes, whilst ensuring optimal and consistent in-cup quality.

We have optimized the grinding and roasting processes of some of our coffees, which has resulted to a slightly reduced capsule weight while providing the same consumer experience coffee lovers expect from Nespresso.

WAVE 1: Projected transition in market Q1 2026

Scope (6 SKUS): DOUBLE ESPRESSO SCURO, DOUBLE ESPRESSO CHIARO, DOUBLE ESPRESSO DOLCE, FORTADO, ORAFIO, RISTRETTO INTENSO

WAVE 2: Projected transition in market TBA

Scope (8 SKUS): MELOZIO, STORMIO, ODACIO, MO COSTA RICA, MO COLOMBIA, BIANCO DOPPIO, SOLEILIO, ARONDIO

Review attached memo and FAQ for additional information. No action is required as of right now.

Officially Whistle Blowing

On/about Sepetember 5, 2026, I noticed a post on
r/nespresso
asking about whether Nespresso had changed their recipes:

Did Nespresso change its recipe in the recent coffee pods?
by
u/Inevitable-Video9560
in
nespresso

I then decided to offically be the first whistle blower
about Project Olympus. A large number of Nespresso consumers were definitely not happy with Nespresso’s decision to reduce the number of grams per capsule. There are many users that are seriously considering to drop Nespresso and move to alternative coffee options.

Coffee Capsules Affected

There are a number of people that have asked which coffees are affected, and that’s a resonable question. From what is currently being observed, almost all the range of coffees are being reduced. The only ones that don’t appear to be affected are Lungos for OL, and Alto XLs (and other larger coffees) for Vertuo.

You can always use my spreadsheet to track any of the coffees that have been affected by Project Olympus:

https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1kZJCdTmqQla2ha3DDYyixQDIUuf9wLvt3122akBkhgM/edit?usp=sharing

Below are screenshots of a spreadsheet showing the currently affected capsules (as of November 12, 2026) showing the percentage change:

Please go to my ko-fi buy me a coffee page at:
https://ko-fi.com/alvinbunk
to support and donate to me for writing coffee reviews. Thank you

!

title: GPT 6.2 Astra Solves a Historical Mystery
content:
GPT 6.2 Astra Solves a Historical Mystery

Here's an interesting case-study in using GPT-6.2 Astra for historical research, from history professor Mark Humphries:

With only minimal prompting, GPT-6.2 Astra was able to autonomously identify the creator of an anonymous 1808 sketchbook held at
Yale’s Beinecke Library
. It did so extremely quickly (in just 22 minutes), using publicly available primary and secondary sources. To do so, it discovered a little known source in a paper archive, predicted that it would prove its hypothesis if examined and, in the end, it did. Not only that, but this new source turns out to be a major find on its own that will be of significant interest to both Canadian and fur trade historians.

Here's
the digitized sketchbook
.

Astra found a diary reference reference to a visit by the vicomte de Chabot dated five days before a date mentioned in the sketchbook at a nearby river, and suggested that Chabot's journal of his travels (only available by order from Cleveland State University) might confirm that the sketchbook was his work.

Are historians due for a round of
Deep Blue
? Mark thinks it will be mild:

But if the experience of mathematics is any guide, we can also anticipate that sometime next spring or summer we’ll face a sort of crisis of confidence as we struggle to understand how to respond to agentic systems that can do things human historians cannot. To be fair, that crisis will almost certainly be less profound for us than it is for math. The problem in mathematics, of course, is that solving hard math problems was the whole game. Historians, on the other hand, constantly reinterpret the past in light of an evolving present; we don’t chase a single universal truth. We also (in the ideal at least) write books and articles that are closer to works of philosophy and literature than they are to scientific tracts. Humanity is thus something of a requirement for the production of historical literature.

title: GLM-5.4: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer
content:
GLM-5.4: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer

GLM 5.4 is now available from Chinese AI lab Z.ai. It's their first model to use a looped transformer architecture, which they describe like this:

In a standard Transformer, each layer runs once per forward pass. In a Loop Transformer, a group of weight-shared layers runs for multiple iterations, refining the hidden states from the previous pass. This gives us a deeper network without increasing the parameter count.

This is the second mention of looped transformers I've seen in the past week - the first was
Inkling 2 Mini
from Thinking Machines Lab on November 20th, who said:

Inkling 2 Mini is a looped transformer, running the middle layers of the model three times for every token. This allows the model to apply more reasoning and reach the right answer with fewer tokens, especially on tasks such as agentic coding that depend on reasoning quality.

GLM 5.4 is not yet available as open weights:

We plan to open-source the model weights responsibly after completing necessary safety hardening.

I tried it out using the Z.ai API, for which I had to sign up for their
Coding Plan subscription
because 5.4 cannot currently be accessed through the regular API.

It turns out both coding plan and regular API share the same OpenAI-compatible Responses API (at
https://api.z.ai/api/v1
), and the API key for the coding plan worked with that and gave me access to the new model.

I built a
llm-glm plugin
, then realized that
llm-zai
by Tommy Hughes already exists! I've shipped mine purely because
llm-zai
doesn't yet support the new model, but I'll likely retire mine once that plugin catches up.

Here are
pelicans for GLM-5.4
on low, high, and max. This is the max one:

I realized I never ran pelicans for GLM-5.3, so
here those are
for the same effort levels. They look similar in quality to 5.4.

It's interesting how
GLM 5.1
and
GLM 5.2
produced radically different pelicans from other models. The pelicans for 5.3 and 5.4 are much more comparable to those I get from OpenAI or Anthropic models - the previous generations had their own distinctive look.

I made a
comparison grid
showing the four generations of GLM pelicans all in one place. The style transition between 5.2 and 5.3 is pretty stark.

title: Ladybird's first alpha release
content:
Ladybird
is an astonishingly ambitious project: a new browser, in 2026, with its own implementation of most of the key components - HTML parsing, CSS engine, layout, JavaScript, even WebAssembly. It still uses a few external components - things like
HarfBuzz
for text shaping,
Skia
for 2D graphics, ffmpeg for video, and SQLite for the things you do with SQLite. Everything else is part of Ladybird, or code brought in from Ladybird's even more ambitious predecessor project
SerenityOS
.

This morning the Ladybird project
released their first alpha
, which means you can now
install the browser
(on macOS or Linux) without having to compile it yourself!

I've been trying it out today, and it's very impressive. It feels fast, the UI is lightweight and intuitive, and most of the websites I've tried to load in it have worked as they should. It looks like this (showing my
video-compressor
tool):

Here's the process tree after I opened six tabs in one window and another tab in a second window (generated
by this script
, thanks Claude):

Ladybird (72925)  [240 MB]
└── Hub (72926)  [61 MB]
├── RequestServer (72927)  [29 MB]
├── ProcessReaper (72928)  [1 MB]
├── Compositor (72930)  [123 MB]
├── RequestServer (72953)  [36 MB]
├── WebContent (72984)  [819 MB]
├── MediaServer (73006)  [118 MB]
├── VideoDecoderServer (73007)  [20 MB]
├── WebContent (73052)  [144 MB]
├── WebContent (73057)  [73 MB]
├── WebContent (73073)  [166 MB]
├── WebContent (73094)  [70 MB]
├── WebContent (73112)  [116 MB]
├── RequestServer (73113)  [27 MB]
└── WebContent (73185)  [60 MB]

Ladybird runs different tabs in different processes, an isolation mechanism used by most browsers (well, technically Chrome uses a process-per-site).

I tried Ladybird against several of my more advanced tool examples - like the
video-compressor
shown above, which runs ffmpeg compiled to WebAssembly. I had it resize its own screenshot using my
image-resize tool
. It happily runs my
Pyodide REPL
(Python compiled to WebAssembly) too.

The one thing I tried that didn't work was
Datasette Lite
, which runs Pyodide in
a complicated arrangement
of service workers and web workers. Attempting to start Datasette Lite displays this error:

undefined is not a function (evaluated from 'navigator.serviceWorker.startMessages')

I filed
an issue about this
, then found
a FIXME annotation
in the source code.

The October explosion

The project has been leaning heavily into coding agents this year. On February 23, 2026 Andreas Kling published
Ladybird adopts Rust, with help from AI
, describing how they ported parts of their LibJS JavaScript engine from C++ to 25,000 lines of Rust in two weeks using Claude Code and Codex.

Here's
the GitHub contributions chart
for Ladybird over the past twelve months:

That uptick in October corresponds to the landing of a wealth of big improvements.

This Month in Ladybird — October 2026
describes what happened. In addition to moving style and layout to their own thread, landing a new JavaScript JIT, and replacing their C++ with Cranelift WebAssembly engine with new code that achieved a 7x boost on the
JetStream 3 WASM benchmark
, they gained 75,650 new passes on the ~2.25 million subtest
web-platform-tests
suite, beating Safari!

How did they do that? Coding agents:

Most of that gain came in five days, from about 2.12 million on October 22 to about 2.18 million on October 27. We pointed AI coding agents at WPT and asked them to fill in missing functionality. They made lots of small fixes, and those added up. Our biggest gains for the month were about 30,000 in
/css
and 10,000 in
/editing
.

I'm interested in what models they are using here - I know Andreas uses Codex and Claude Code, but I haven't seen him talk about specific model versions. Claude Opus 5.5 came out on September 22, 2026 and Claude Fable 5.2 on November 9, 2026 (after that window). I'd love to know what they were using for that huge leap in the last week of October.

Should you use Ladybird?

Here's what
Andreas says
about Ladybird's suitability for use as a daily browser:

This is an alpha, so some websites won’t work, and it will crash sometimes. When that happens, tell us! You can report a broken site from inside the browser. After a crash, you can read the crash report and decide whether to send it. Our
privacy policy
has the details.

We want security nerds to hack it! A new browser gets hacked, over and over, and that’s part of the process, so we make no promises about security today. When you pwn us, please
tell us how
so we can harden Ladybird!

Given how hard it is to secure a web browser, and the hostility of the environment they operate in, I won't be using Ladybird to sign into GitHub or Gmail or any of my other sensitive accounts.

I'm going to keep it around for anonymous browsing though, partly to participate in the testing efforts but mainly because it gives me a glimmer of optimism to see a promising new entrant in the stagnant browser engine market start to grow its wings.

title: datasette-charts 0.1a0
content:
Release:

datasette-charts 0.1a0

I've been thinking about this problem for over a year now, but on Sunday I finally fired up Claude Fable 5.2 to build an initial prototype. The prototype went so well that this is now a full plugin.

You can
try it out in Datasette Lite here
. It looks like this:

The new charts plugin works against any table or arbitrary SQL query in Datasette. It defines several different chart types (using vendored
D3
,
Observable Plot
, and
topojson-client
), each with a set of heuristics for identifying when they might be a good match for a specific set of rows.

Those suggestion thumbnails at the top are actual visualizations driven by the data, and selecting one pulls up the full chart along with tools for modifying it. You can also manually construct a chart from scratch.

As with other Datasette visualization plugins, the current state of your chart is persisted in a
#fragment
in the URL - so you can bookmark charts or share them with others.

The most important feature is that the charts take
all rows into account
. Previous charting plugins like
datasette-vega
would only show charts for the current page of results, generally up to 100 rows.

The new plugin compiles each chart to a SQL query that aggregates across the entire result set (potentially millions of rows) using GROUP BY, time bucketing, and window functions. Each query returns a result capped at 5,000 rows, suitable for display on the chart. The plugin uses sampling to help suggest charts for larger tables without evaluating the full result set.

I'm really happy with this initial release of the plugin. It's still very much an alpha, but it's the closest I've got to the dream of Datasette helping visualize data with as little required direction from the user as possible.
