title: GPT-6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities
content:
November 24, 2026
Science
Publication
GPT‑6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities
Read the paper
(opens in a new window)
Key findings:
Our GPT‑6 family of models can design new protein shapes and the sequence of their chemical building blocks using only reasoning and code, without calling specialized biology models to generate those designs.
An internal research model matched or outperformed specialized models on many protein design tasks. Researchers could also guide designs by prompting the model on where a protein should attach and what shape it should take.
In lab tests with Onava, proteins based on GPT‑6.2’s designs showed evidence of binding, or attachment, across five targets. Redesigned antibodies also retained binding. Specialized models helped supply sequences and select candidates for testing.
The models’ written reasoning and code suggest they draw on math, physics, chemistry, and biological knowledge to reason about protein shapes and interactions with other molecules.
In a preprint titled
GPT‑6 as a Universal Foundation Model for Protein Biology: Beyond Specialized Models
, we show that our GPT‑6 family of models has
intrinsic capabilities
for designing new proteins: the models can design new protein structures and sequences without relying on specialized biology models, using only reasoning and general-purpose coding tools.
Proteins do much of the work in living cells. They drive the chemical reactions that sustain life, carry oxygen through the blood, and defend the body against infection. Incorrectly shaped proteins can also cause disease and dysfunction. Proteins are made from chains of chemical building blocks called amino acids. The order, or sequence, of these amino acids helps determine how a protein folds into a three-dimensional shape, which in turn influences what it does.
Scientists often start with a clear idea of what they want a protein to do. They might want it to block a signal that helps cancer cells evade the immune system or to help capture carbon dioxide from the air. The challenge is to work out what three-dimensional structure would enable the protein to do its job and which amino acid sequence would give it that structure. Specialized biology models capable of generating three-dimensional protein structures and sequences have made this work more practical.
Using and coordinating these specialized models requires substantial expertise. Each accepts particular kinds of inputs and constraints, and these models cannot easily accept new kinds of information without changes to their software or additional training. In contrast, a general-purpose model capable of performing the work of multiple specialized models can easily adapt to new instructions and requirements.
Our research illustrates the potential power of pairing natural language with intrinsic protein capabilities. We could guide our models at scales ranging from a single bond between two atoms to the overall shape of a protein. For example, we asked GPT‑6.2 to predict where and how a small molecule would bind to a protein. When we already knew which two atoms formed a bond, we could give the model that information and ask how the rest of the molecule would fit. We could switch between these tasks simply by changing the prompt, without retraining the model. We also asked our models to design small proteins called minibinders and marked where each should attach to its target, and further specified how many coils or strands each minibinder should contain. An internal model followed that instruction with near-perfect fidelity in its three-dimensional designs.
Points farther from the center indicate better performance. Newer generations of models improved on many of the 14 protein tasks tested.
A closer look at our models’ protein designs
We ran computational tests of whether the GPT‑6 models series could design small proteins to bind given targets, build proteins around specified structural features, predict protein structures and molecular interactions, and rank how sequence changes affect properties such as stability and binding. Our latest models performed comparably to or better than specialized models on most tasks, although predicting a complete protein structure remained a clear weakness.
The models’ written reasoning and code offer clues to how they approach these tasks. They draw on mathematics, physics, chemistry, and coding alongside knowledge of recurring patterns in protein sequences and structures. For example, when designing a small protein intended to bind to IL-7Rα, the model proposed how the two proteins might interact, then wrote and executed code to explore different protein shapes and amino acid choices that could support that interaction.
The model’s written reasoning and code show it drawing on math, physics, chemistry and biology to design a protein intended to attach to IL-7Rα. It examines the target’s surface, arranges five coiled sections into a protein shape, and checks how the two proteins could fit together.
With our research partner,
Onava
⁠
(opens in a new window)
, we also tested the models’ structure and sequence designs in the lab. First, Onava made small proteins based on three-dimensional structures designed by a pre-released version of GPT‑6.2. Specialized models supplied amino acid sequences and helped select candidates for testing. For each of the five targets we chose, at least one protein showed evidence of binding in the lab. In separate experiments, GPT‑6.2 designed new amino acid sequences for existing minibinders and antibodies. Following candidate selection with specialized models, many of the redesigned proteins also showed evidence of binding to the same targets as the originals.
Laboratory Experiment 1: Designing small proteins that bind to a target
Our first laboratory experiment tested whether GPT‑6.2 could design small proteins that would bind to their intended targets. We compared computational measurements of quality against RFdiffusion, a specialized model for protein design, and found that GPT‑6.2’s three-dimensional designs scored slightly lower while our latest internal models scored higher. For the lab experiment, we made proteins based on GPT‑6.2’s designs and measured how strongly they bound to their targets.
We gave GPT‑6.2 the three-dimensional structures of five target proteins and marked where we wanted a minibinder to attach. It then wrote code to create three-dimensional designs for potential minibinders, without using specialized protein AI models.
To turn GPT‑6.2’s three-dimensional designs into proteins we could test in the lab, we needed amino acid sequences that would fold into the proposed structures. We used a specialized AI model called SolubleMPNN to suggest sequences for each design. Other specialized protein models helped us select candidates predicted to fold as designed and bind at the intended site on the target.
GPT‑6.2 designed shapes for small proteins intended to attach to chosen targets. Specialized models then proposed amino acid sequences—the order of the proteins’ chemical building blocks—and helped select designs for our research partner Onava to make and test in the lab.
We tested 322 minibinders against 5 targets in the lab. Of those, 35 (10.9%) tested positive for binding to their intended target. We found 5 hits for PD-L1 (a protein some cancers use to evade the immune system), 3 for IL-7Rα, 1 for TrkA, 8 for VEGF-A and 18 for IL-17A. The
original RFdiffusion study
⁠
(opens in a new window)
reported higher hit rates, but rates depend heavily on how strictly researchers filter designs before lab validation and their definition of binding. Nevertheless, our results provide early evidence that we can turn GPT‑6.2’s three-dimensional designs into proteins that bind to their intended targets in the lab.
An internal research model designed shapes for small proteins intended to attach to the target proteins shown in gray. The colored shapes compare each design with a computational prediction of how the protein would fold and fit against its target.
Laboratory Experiment 2: Designing new sequences for 3D protein structures
We tested whether GPT‑6.2 could design the sequences itself. We gave it three-dimensional models of how existing minibinders fit against their targets, withheld the original amino acid sequences, and asked it to propose new ones. Specialized models helped us choose which proteins to make and test in the lab.
For three targets, we started with computationally predicted structures of confirmed minibinders whose sequences Onava had collected from earlier studies. In our initial lab screens, we saw binding in 75 of 88 designs for MDM2 (85%), 26 of 42 for VEGF-A (62%), and 8 of 59 for PD-1 (14%). The amino acid sequences proposed by GPT‑6.2 also often differed significantly from the original minibinder sequences, with a median of 50% for VEGF-A, 43% for MDM2, and 15% for PD-1.
We also asked GPT‑6.2 to design new sequences for three unpublished minibinder shapes it had generated earlier: two targeting PD-L1 and one targeting IL-7Rα. A specialized model, ProteinMPNN, had already supplied one sequence for each shape, and proteins made from those sequences had shown binding in the lab. Of the 107 proteins made from GPT‑6.2’s new sequences, 14 (13.1%) showed binding.
Given an unpublished structure, GPT‑6.2 had come up with two substantially different sequences that both showed signs of binding to the same target. For the same PD-L1 minibinder structure, GPT‑6.2 designed two sequences different from the original in 52 and 58 out of 90 total amino acids. The two also differed from each other at 44 positions, nearly half the sequence.
The unpublished structures and substantial differences in sequence give us strong evidence that GPT‑6.2’s capabilities extend beyond memorization. The results also suggest we could use GPT‑6.2 to intrinsically design both a minibinder’s structure and its sequence.
Redesigning the parts of an antibody that bind to a target
Researchers often redesign an antibody’s binding loops to help it grip its target more tightly, a process called
affinity maturation
. They may also want it to bind more selectively, so it’s less likely to attach to similar proteins. We tested a first step toward those goals by asking our models to design new loop sequences that preserved binding to the original target.
We started with six small antibodies (VHHs) that bind to the same protein, IL-4Rα. For each antibody, we gave GPT‑6.2 its predicted three-dimensional structure and most of its amino acid sequence, leaving out the three loops that help the antibody grip its target. We asked the model to design new sequences for them. Of the 182 designs we tested, 128 (70%) showed signs of binding to IL-4Rα.
We then tested how precisely we could guide the model’s changes to existing therapeutic antibodies. This time, we gave the model the original sequences and asked it to change about half the amino acids in each of three binding loops while keeping the rest of the sequence intact. We tested the redesigned portions of the antibodies as fragments in the lab. Of 272 fragments based on five therapeutic antibodies, 179 (66%) showed binding to the original target, PD-1 or PD-L1.
What else can our models design and predict?
Precise control over minibinder structures for programmable structure design
A long-term goal of programmable structure-based design is to let researchers specify structural constraints in natural language. In our computational evaluations, our models consistently designed minibinders that contacted the required locations on the target. We could also specify the minibinder’s structural class (all helices, all strands, or a combination) and control the number of coils and strands with near-perfect fidelity. The same approach lets us express more detailed requirements for the binding interface, such as which target amino acids should be buried upon binding or whether the minibinder and target should interact through specific interactions such as “β-sheet–β-sheet”. As our model’s reasoning capabilities improve, we envision researchers guiding protein structure generation much as they guide image generation today, by describing the features they want.
Our model was asked to design small proteins with specified shapes: mainly coils (orange), mainly strands (blue), or a mix. Some instructions also specified how many coils or strands to include. The designs are intended to attach to PD-L1 or PD-1, shown in gray.
Building a protein around a specified structural feature
Most enzymes are proteins that speed up chemical reactions. When designing a new enzyme, researchers may know how a few key amino acids need to be arranged at the site where the reaction happens. Those amino acids can lie far apart along the protein chain. The challenge is to design the rest of the protein so that, as the chain folds, it brings them together and holds them in place.
We tested our models on 30 challenges from
MotifBench
⁠
(opens in a new window)
, including examples drawn from enzymes and from sites where proteins bind to one another. We gave the models a specific three-dimensional arrangement of amino acids, called a
motif
, and asked them to use coding tools to design the rest of the protein around it. This task is called
motif scaffolding
.
For each design, we used ProteinMPNN to propose eight possible amino acid sequences, and
ESMFold
⁠
(opens in a new window)
to predict how each would fold. We counted the design as a success if at least one predicted structure both preserved the motif and closely matched the overall structure the model had designed.
In a preliminary analysis, 43.7% of the designs we evaluated from our latest internal model met both criteria, compared with 27.8% for RFdiffusion. While laboratory experiments are needed to find out whether these proteins could carry out the intended function, such as speeding up a particular reaction, this provides strong computational evidence of our models’ intrinsic protein capabilities.
An internal research model designed protein structures around a small region whose shape had to stay fixed, shown in gold. The colored shapes compare the model’s designs with computer predictions of how the proteins would fold. Panels showing only gold had no design that passed the computer checks.
Designing a protein with a specified fold
In motif scaffolding, we specified how a few amino acids should sit relative to one another. We then determined whether we could also guide the design of an entire protein by specifying its overall fold. We gave our models a chain length and a code from
CATH
⁠
(opens in a new window)
, a system scientists use to classify protein structures. The models then had to work out where each amino acid should go in three-dimensional space.
Many designs captured the broad layout we asked for. The harder part was getting the chain to follow the right path through it. Two proteins can have several coiled stretches packed together in a similar bundle, for example, yet differ in the order in which the chain connects them.
We counted a design as a success if at least one amino acid sequence was predicted to adopt the requested fold and closely match the model’s three-dimensional design. Across 200 challenges, 18.9% of the designs we evaluated from our latest internal model passed, compared with 17.1% for Proteina, a specialized protein design model.
An internal research model was asked to design proteins with specified overall shapes, such as bundles of coils or layers of strands. The colored shapes compare selected designs with computer predictions of how they would fold, showing examples where the two closely match.
Predicting how chemicals and proteins fit together
Many medicines, including aspirin, are
small molecules
, chemical compounds much smaller than the proteins they act on. Predicting where a small molecule binds to a protein and how it fits there is called
docking
. These predictions can help researchers decide how to modify a drug candidate so it binds more tightly to its target. To test our models, we started with experimentally determined structures of small molecules bound to proteins. We digitally removed each small molecule and gave the models the protein structure along with a text description of how the molecule’s atoms were connected (a sequence of characters called SMILES). We then asked the models to predict where the molecule had been bound and how it was oriented.
For our first docking test, we used the
PoseBusters dataset
⁠
(opens in a new window)
, a collection of three-dimensional structures that show how small molecules bind to proteins. Researchers determined these structures experimentally, giving us a way to check the models’ predictions. Without being told where on the protein each molecule had bound, the models had to predict both where the molecule fit and which way it faced. GPT‑6.2 closely matched the molecule’s observed position and orientation in 93% of scored predictions, compared with 96% for our latest internal model and 50% for DiffDock-L, a specialized docking model.
In practice, researchers may already know something about how a molecule binds.
One major advantage of a GPT model is that we can give additional information directly in the prompt
. We tested this on 179 structures from the

Scarpino dataset
⁠
(opens in a new window)
, where each protein structure forms a chemical bond with a small molecule, tethering the two together. We told our models which two atoms formed the bond and asked them to predict how the rest of the molecule fit against the protein. GPT‑6.2 closely matched the experimental structure in

92% of scored predictions
⁠
(opens in a new window)
, and our latest internal model did so in 97%, while
DiffDock
⁠
(opens in a new window)
reached 60%.
An internal research model predicted where and how small molecules would fit against proteins, shown in gray. Purple shows the model’s predictions, and teal shows the molecules’ positions determined in earlier experiments. In these examples, the predictions closely match the experimental structures.
Predicting how antibodies bind to proteins
Where an antibody binds can help explain whether it blocks another protein from attaching to the same site. We tested how accurately successive generations of GPT could predict where an antibody binds and which way it faces. For hundreds of pairs of antibodies and targets, we showed the models the two proteins separately and hid some of the atomic detail (all side chains) on their surfaces.
With the side-chain details hidden, the mean DockQ score (a commonly used metric in which higher values indicate a closer match to the experimentally observed arrangement) increased from approximately 0.05 for GPT‑5.6 to 0.28 for GPT‑6, 0.57 for GPT‑6.2, and 0.81 for our latest internal model, at each model’s highest evaluated compute setting.
Because these structures were public, the models may have seen the same antibody-target pairs or similar ones during training. Even so, each generation of our models predicted more accurately how the two proteins fit together, even with all side-chain positions hidden. That progress gives us reason to be optimistic about harder docking problems.
Each row compares four models’ predictions of how an antibody attaches to its target protein. Colored shapes show the model’s prediction; dark gray shows the position observed in experiments. Results improved with each successive generation of model.
Predicting the effects of mutations
We can design far more proteins on a computer than we can make and test in the lab. Even after we settle on a promising structure, we may have many amino acid sequences to choose from. We tested whether our models could help researchers decide which versions to make first by predicting how changes to a protein’s sequence would affect its stability, activity, or ability to bind to a target.
We drew on four public datasets from experiments in which scientists had replaced one or more amino acids in a protein and measured the effects. For each test, we gave our models the sequence of the protein the scientists started with and the sequences of 50 modified versions. We told the models what the scientists had measured, withheld the results, and asked them to rank the 50 versions without using coding tools, by reasoning only.
In one study of protein stability, we asked the models to rank 50 versions of a protein by how likely each was to be folded at room temperature. We compared the predicted order with the order observed in the lab using a measure called
rank correlation
. A value of 1 means the rankings match perfectly, 0 means there’s no consistent relationship, and −1 means the order is exactly reversed. Across 265 sets from the stability study, each model generation improved, from 0.41 for GPT‑5.6 to 0.52 for GPT‑6, 0.57 for GPT‑6.2, and 0.66 for our latest internal model.
In each of the four datasets, GPT‑6.2 and our latest internal model produced more accurate rankings on average than ESM2-650M, a specialized protein model.
Early signals from our model’s protein structure predictions
Earlier, we relied on specialized models to predict whether an amino acid sequence would fold into the structure our models had designed. We wanted to see how close our models are to making that prediction themselves. We gave our models the amino acid sequences of proteins with known three-dimensional structures. Using only basic coding tools, the models predicted how each chain would fold in three dimensions. We evaluated their predictions using a measure called
TM-score
. A score of 1 means a perfect match to the real structure, and scores above 0.5 generally indicate that the prediction captures the overall fold.
The biggest gains are visible in individual examples. For some proteins, our latest internal model closely reproduced folds that earlier models missed. Across the full test, the average score rose from 0.16 for GPT‑5.6 to 0.26 for GPT‑6.2 and 0.38 for our latest internal model. The specialized model ESMFold2 averaged 0.93, so there’s still a substantial gap in how reliably our models can predict a whole protein’s structure from its sequence alone.
What if researchers already know most of the structure and want to fill in a missing piece? We tested this on 100 antibody fragments. For each one, we gave our models the amino acid sequences and the surrounding three-dimension structure, hiding the six loops that help the antibody recognize its target. Our latest internal model often predicted both the shape and position of those loops quite accurately. ESMFold2 was still more accurate overall, even working from the sequences alone.
Each model was given the same protein sequence—the order of its chemical building blocks—and asked to predict its 3D shape. The colored shapes show the predictions, and dark gray shows the structure measured in experiments.
Each model was given a partial structure and tasked with predicting the missing regions corresponding to the antibody CDRs. The colored regions show predictions from the internal model and ESMFold2 compared with the experimentally determined structures.
Limitations
It is important to note that our protein design campaign relied on specialized structure prediction models such as Boltz-2, OpenDDE, and ESMFold2 to filter candidates. Our results show that GPT models have intrinsic capabilities comparable to specialized models at two stages of the workflow: backbone generation, where researchers commonly use RFdiffusion; and sequence redesign, where they commonly use ProteinMPNN. Our results therefore do not yet establish that our models can generate de novo minibinders end-to-end in a zero-shot setting without help from specialized models.
Our work demonstrates yet again the jagged capability frontier. Predicting a complete protein structure from its amino acid sequence remains substantially harder for our models than several of the component tasks above. On that task, even our best internal models remained well behind specialized structure-prediction models.
Some benchmark results also require careful interpretation. In tests that asked models to infer amino acid sequences from protein structures, unusually high accuracy may partly reflect memorization or patterns left by the process used to generate those structures. Those results alone do not establish reliable performance on unfamiliar proteins.
The laboratory results provide a more direct test of whether proposed designs can work, but binding is only one step toward a useful research tool or medicine. Further work would need to establish properties such as specificity, stability, and biological activity, along with safety and efficacy for therapeutic applications.
What’s next
This work is an early step toward
programmable molecular design
at OpenAI. Our goal is to let scientists describe what they want a molecule to do in plain language and use our models to help design candidates to test in the lab. To make that approach useful for developing medicines, we want to make progress in three areas.
Find minibinders for harder targets.
We want to design molecules that bind to targets where our attempts so far have fallen short.
Design for what happens after binding.
We want to test whether the molecules we design can produce a specific biological effect, such as killing a cancer cell. We also want to design molecules that bind selectively to their intended targets and are practical to manufacture.
Design a wider range of molecules.
Our lab experiments focused on small protein minibinders and antibody fragments. We’d like to extend that work to molecules that bind to several targets at once, RNA, and small molecules, including a class called PROTACs that direct a cell to break down a particular protein.
As we work to accelerate scientific progress safely and responsibly, we also seek to evaluate and reduce risks, particularly those related to biosecurity. The same capabilities that help scientists design proteins for new medicines could also be misused. Our
Preparedness Framework
⁠
guides how we assess these risks and test safeguards to reduce them.
While lab testing remains a critical part of protein design, our goal is to provide powerful models that can shorten each round of design by giving scientists more control and flexibility, and reduce the total number of design-test cycles needed to find a functional protein. Ultimately, we envision enabling scientists to design proteins and molecules simply by prompting our models in natural language, massively accelerating the development of new biotechnologies and new medicines.

title: Searching for distant planets with Astra
content:
An illustrated view of HD 164604 b zooms out to the Milky Way. Boxes mark a selection of systems with confirmed exoplanets. Distances are scaled to the zoom and show the distance from Earth at the widest view. Hover over or tap a box to read its label. Use the arrow keys to browse labels and Escape to dismiss them.
November 24, 2026
Science
Searching for distant planets with Astra
Two amateur astronomers used Codex and Astra to look for signs of planets in public telescope data. Now they’ve given professional astronomers a few places to look more closely.
Astronomers have confirmed more than
6,400 planets beyond our solar system
⁠
(opens in a new window)
since the
first ones were announced in 1992
⁠
(opens in a new window)
. A worldwide community of amateur astronomers has long been part of that search. Some comb through public telescope data for small, repeated dips in a star’s brightness that could signal an orbiting planet. Others use their own telescopes to watch for the next dip and share what they see with researchers.
*Data from the NASA Exoplanet Archive’s
Planetary Systems Composite Parameters table
⁠
(opens in a new window)
. 2026 data are year to date through November 24, 2026.
Astronomers have used AI in this search for years. In 2017, researchers trained a neural network on 15,000 signals from NASA’s
Kepler Space Telescope
⁠
(opens in a new window)
that astronomers had already examined. From those examples, the model learned to recognize which patterns in starlight were most likely to come from a planet. When the researchers used it to examine weaker signals, one led them to an
eighth planet orbiting a star called Kepler-90
⁠
(opens in a new window)
.
Now, tools like Astra are helping amateur astronomers design and run searches of their own, often on data that has already yielded the more obvious exoplanet signals.
Kevin Bond, an engineer at OpenAI, came to astronomy through his love of photographing the night sky. He used Codex to search observations of about 100,000 stars from the Kepler telescope, a planet-hunting mission that ran from 2009 to 2018. Ethan Byrd, founder of the email infrastructure start-up Primitive, has always loved astronomy. Working independently of Bond, he tried several AI models before choosing Astra to help him analyze telescope data from about 19 million stars.
Both searches identified potential exoplanets. Bond and Byrd have now turned to astronomers for an independent assessment of their results. Bond contacted an astronomer at the SETI Institute, who ran an independent search and found two of the same signals in the Kepler data. Byrd sent one of his strongest candidates to researchers working on NASA’s Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) mission. It’s in line for further analysis, and two more candidates are awaiting submission.
Looking for dips in starlight
One of the most common ways to find an exoplanet is to watch the star it orbits. When a planet passes in front of its star from our point of view on Earth, it blocks a tiny amount of starlight. Astronomers call that crossing a transit. On a graph of the star’s brightness over time, known as a light curve, a transit shows up as a dip. If the dip keeps coming back at regular intervals, astronomers know when to watch for it again.
Searching for that pattern across thousands of stars is partly a coding problem. Astronomers have published methods for picking out faint, recurring dips in years of measurements. Bond used Codex to compare those methods, combine them in a search program, and test whether changes to the code improved the search. One AI agent scanned the light curves for promising signals. Another ran more detailed checks on the candidates the first one flagged.
Bond ran the program on public data from the Kepler Space Telescope. The search flagged more than 200 signals, including 10 from previously confirmed planets. Finding those known planets gave Bond confidence that the program could pick out the kinds of signals he was looking for.
Two stars stood out. The first, KIC 5689121, is a relatively cool star about half the size of our sun in the constellation Lyra. The Codex search found a dip in brightness every 13.8 days. If a planet is causing it, the amount of light it blocks suggests it could be about 2.4 times Earth’s diameter.
These four curves show the same Kepler observations aligned on a 13.77-day cycle.
The second star, KIC 6691030, is faint and lies in the northern sky. The Codex search found a dip in its brightness every 4.8 days, consistent with a planet smaller than Neptune. These were the two signals the SETI Institute astronomer found independently. Confirming what caused them could take months or years.
“Kevin’s work shows how citizen scientists, equipped with AI, can help astronomers explore the Kepler Bonus Catalog—a vast collection of stars beyond Kepler’s original targets. His pipeline has surfaced promising candidates in data traditional searches may have missed. Our initial checks are encouraging, and follow-up observations will tell us more.”
Vishal Gajjar, associate director for international SETI programs at the SETI Institute
Byrd used Astra to design two searches. One looked broadly for exoplanet candidates. The other focused on stars’ habitable zones. A habitable zone is the range of distances from a star where a planet with a suitable atmosphere could support liquid water on its surface.
Byrd then asked Astra to review published methods, build the search software, and run initial checks on promising signals. His searches drew on observations from TESS, which NASA launched in 2018, and from other public telescope archives.
Kepler watched one field for four years. TESS surveyed both hemispheres in its first 26 sectors, from 2018 to 2020. The star field comes from
NASA’s TESS mosaic through September 2025
⁠
(opens in a new window)
, clipped to that original survey footprint. The wider gap shows where TESS pointed farther north during six observing sectors. The inset marks
KIC 5689121
⁠
(opens in a new window)
in the original
Kepler field
⁠
(opens in a new window)
. See
NASA’s final prime-mission coverage maps
⁠
(opens in a new window)
and its
earlier field-of-view animation
⁠
(opens in a new window)
.
The first pass through the data turned up 49 candidates. Byrd sent one of his strongest candidates to researchers working on the TESS mission, where it is awaiting further analysis. His search is still running.
What does it take to confirm a planet?
When astronomers see a star dim, they have to consider what else might explain it. Two stars passing in front of one another can produce a similar dip. Even a change in temperature aboard a telescope can affect its instruments enough to make a star appear to dim.
Astronomers can use statistics to show that an exoplanet is the most likely explanation for a series of dips. They can also collect more observations, sometimes using a different method. For example, an orbiting planet’s gravity tugs on its star, causing it to move slightly toward and away from us. That motion, called radial velocity, shows up as tiny shifts in the color of the star’s light. Astronomers then publish their findings in a peer-reviewed journal so others can examine the evidence.
For Bond and Byrd, each candidate is a question that can be tested. If a planet is passing in front of the star in Lyra every 13.8 days, astronomers can watch for the next crossing. Further observations can help establish whether the dip repeats as expected, while additional checks can help determine what is causing it.
Photographs by Kevin Bond
Taking part in the search
You can contribute without owning a telescope. NASA’s
Exoplanet Watch
⁠
(opens in a new window)
lets you request data and learn to plot a light curve yourself. Its broader
exoplanet citizen science programs
⁠
(opens in a new window)
offer other ways to participate.
If you have access to a telescope, Exoplanet Watch walks users through how to collect data on transiting exoplanets and participate in observation campaigns.
AAVSO’s Exoplanet Observing Program
⁠
(opens in a new window)
can show you how to measure a dip in starlight and share your observations with the researchers studying that planet. And the
Unistellar Network Investigating TESS Exoplanets
⁠
(opens in a new window)
coordinates volunteers around the world with a certain type of telescope to observe the same star, helping astronomers catch transits that can last longer than a single night.
Astronomy has a long history of people around the world following their curiosity and sharing what they find. Bond and Byrd are part of that tradition. Their searches are still open, but they turned a love of the night sky into leads that other astronomers can investigate. We want more people to have that opportunity, in astronomy and across science.
If you want to follow along with new findings, practical guidance, and perspectives from researchers using AI to advance science
check out the OpenAI science blog

How Intentful uses dots to make more time for growth
How a small business founder’s dot helps her with research and proposals, while alerting her to critical messages and resolving issues.
Explore ChatGPT for small businesses
Company size:
SMB

North America

Marina Petrova is CEO and cofounder of
Intentful
⁠
(opens in a new window)
, a lean team that helps brands make their marketing interactive, with products such as ads that answer customers’ questions in real time and tools that make website information readable by AI. The company also advises and trains marketers on using AI.
In travel and tourism, Intentful works with destination organizations and local businesses such as hotels, restaurants, and attractions. A custom proposal is part of how Marina wins their business, showing prospects what’s possible and what it would take to deliver.
To keep Intentful growing, she needed more room for that strategic work, but she was spending too much time on research, hunting for files, and formatting decks. Her
dot
⁠
changed all that, taking on tasks and meeting Marina’s needs before she even had to ask.
“My dot makes me feel like I gained a new superpower.”
—Marina Petrova, CEO and cofounder, Intentful
From 300 websites to a proposal in hours instead of days
For one of Intentful’s tourism clients, Marina wanted to propose a package of Intentful’s AI services for hundreds of local businesses in the destination.

Before she could price the package, she needed to work out which businesses’ websites the package could cover and what Intentful had charged other clients for similar work.
She brought in her dot, which she named Aria, to help her get from research to a proposal she could put her name on in a few hours instead of several days. First, Marina gave Aria a spreadsheet of URLs and criteria for deciding which sites to include. For example, a site needed a readable sitemap listing no more than 3,000 pages.
“My dot looked through about 300 website sitemaps, helped me figure out which sites to include in a new offer for local businesses, and pulled pricing from past agreements.”
—Marina Petrova, CEO and cofounder, Intentful
Next, Aria helped Marina research pricing. Through
ChatGPT
⁠
(opens in a new window)
plugins, Aria reviewed Intentful’s sales data, including past engagements and discussions in HubSpot. It surfaced pricing from earlier agreements and context from Intentful’s plans for the following year.
Using that data, Marina and Aria then built a pricing model: page counts determined the pricing tier, and previous customer agreements also informed the price. “We worked through a custom pricing model together, and then Aria turned it into a one-page proposal I reviewed and edited,” said Marina.
When drafting proposals, Aria knows to use Intentful’s templates from Google Drive. Marina can also point Aria to an earlier proposal as a reference, so the draft follows Intentful’s style from the start. “I need to say what needs to be in a proposal, but I don’t need to spend an hour figuring out its layout. My dot handles that,” Marina says.
Aria can also spot things Marina hadn’t thought to check. When Marina asked Aria to reuse pricing from an earlier proposal, it noticed that the original renewal date didn’t match the timing she remembered. Aria flagged the discrepancy and left the date out of the new draft.
Staying ahead of messages, tasks, and team updates
Marina uses the Gmail and Slack plugins in ChatGPT to catch up on conversations, find open tasks, and see where the team needs her. Aria checks for messages that need Marina’s attention. While Marina was offline, Aria spotted a reply she had been waiting for and let her know it included an invitation for a call that morning.
Marina also uses Aria to talk through ideas, find conversations, check an account’s history in the CRM, or open and assign tasks in Asana. She often briefs Aria by phone while she travels.
“On a long drive, I call my dot and talk through what needs to get done. We chat through updates for client proposals, and my dot already knows the structure, the formatting, and what needs to be done.”
—Marina Petrova, CEO and cofounder, Intentful
Marina loves that her dot works in the tools she already uses. When Aria writes a draft, Marina can leave comments in Google Docs exactly where she wants changes. On longer documents, she asks Aria to use suggesting mode so she can see what changed.
Aria also keeps up with changes in shared work without being asked. For a conference presentation, Marina created the deck and a colleague added two slides. “Aria noticed the new slides, updated the speaker notes without being asked, and let me know,” Marina says.
Marina chooses which information Aria can access and always reviews outgoing email. She can keep work moving without handing over the final call.
Using dots to teach others about AI
When Marina prepared an AI 101 session on agents, she used Aria to help build the lesson. The process was itself an example of what she wanted attendees to learn: delegate a real task, give the agent enough context, challenge the result, and stay in control of what goes out.
Aria’s support continued even after the class. After a flight, Marina saw a participant’s request for access to a training file. When she checked with Aria, it had already shared the file. And after a session for 50 marketers, Aria noticed that a software glitch was preventing participants from opening the recording. It flagged the access issue and offered to fix it before the link was shared.
“With my dot, I can focus on strategic things. I can focus on ideas and growth.”
—Marina Petrova, CEO and cofounder, Intentful

content:

How iFood scales coding agents across 15,000 repositories

2x+
as many vulnerabilities fixed through the security platform
The Remote Agents Platform turned engineering tasks into API calls: teams delegate the work, execution takes place in a remote sandbox, and the result comes back as a merge request. In the internal security platform, the number of vulnerabilities fixed more than doubled.
The challenge isn’t the task—it’s the scale
iFood maintains more than 15,000 code repositories. Each periodically needs specific tasks performed: validating code to ensure it meets internal standards, fixing vulnerable dependencies, or running an analysis.
None of these tasks is difficult on its own. The challenge comes when those tasks multiply.
“Solving this for one repository is easy. The challenge is solving it at scale,” says Victor Coelho, Senior Software Engineer at iFood. “The Remote Agents Platform is designed to make it possible to solve this at scale across all 15,000 repositories.”
Before the platform, each team tackled the problem in its own way—and they all ran into the same obstacle.
“Before, we had fragmented solutions. Imagine several teams at iFood trying to solve different problems, but without this layer, this agentic runtime, available to them. In the end, those solutions always ran into the same problem.”
What was missing wasn’t intelligence or a use case. It was execution infrastructure. A dedicated
runtime
.
“Teams can focus on solving their business problems and delegate execution to our platform.”
—Victor Coelho, Senior Software Engineer, iFood
A coding agent in the cloud, accessible through an API
The team describes the Remote Agents Platform as an API that launches a remote agentic coding task. The cycle has three steps: the user submits a prompt and environment requirements through a REST call; the platform processes the task on a dedicated remote runner inside an isolated sandbox; and the result is retrieved later.
“The platform’s entry point, its interface, is a simple REST API. Users can use this API to create the runs they need. Internally, we handle and manage the entire lifecycle and delegate execution to isolated sandboxes,” he explains. Task progress can be monitored in real time.
The runner’s internal design alternates between two different types of steps—and that combination makes the overall workflow predictable.
Deterministic steps bookend the workflow: cloning the repository, importing the
skills
the agent can use, and setting up the working branch at the start; publishing the merge request and making the generated artifacts available at the end. In between is the agentic execution itself, running GPT‑5.6 Luna inside the sandbox.
“It’s a combination of those two things: deterministic steps and agentic execution within the workflow.”
The sandbox runs Ubuntu and includes the toolchains iFood’s ecosystem requires—Python, Java, Kotlin, C#, TypeScript, Rust, JavaScript, and Go—along with general-purpose tools. Beyond the sandbox, the agent can access Nexus, GitLab, Docker, Snyk, Kubernetes, and AWS.
Why GPT‑5.6 Luna
The model choice came down to three factors considered together, rather than just one.
“We chose GPT‑5.6 Luna because, among models at the same checkpoint, the benchmarks showed it offered a great balance of intelligence, efficiency, and execution speed—how quickly it could complete tasks. Those three qualities together led us to choose GPT‑5.6 Luna.”
That balance matters more for a platform built to scale than it would for a one-off use case. With tens of thousands of tokens being consumed, the average cost of four U.S. cents per run stops being a minor detail and becomes an architectural consideration.
“Given our plans to scale the platform across many use cases at iFood, the balance of efficiency and intelligence that OpenAI’s model provides ensures we can scale sustainably.”
—Victor Coelho, Senior Software Engineer, iFood
How to tell whether the agent completed the task
Delegating execution at scale creates a new challenge: automatically determining whether the agent did what it was supposed to do.
iFood’s answer comes in the step after the session. Once execution is complete, the result is processed using OpenAI’s Structured Outputs, which requires the output to conform to a predefined contract.
“We process the result using Structured Outputs, which ensures the response follows a predefined contract. From the agent’s session, we can identify the outputs within the response structure we expect. This helps reduce uncertainty and ensures we can always get a response from the agent’s session, whether positive or negative.”
—Victor Coelho, Senior Software Engineer, iFood
The first major user: security
The platform already powers an internal iFood security product that scans the 15,000 repositories for vulnerable dependencies and attempts to fix them.
The migration had a direct impact: “With our platform, the accuracy of those changes, those fixes, more than doubled,” says Coelho.
This use case illustrates the idea behind the platform: the security team didn’t need to build its own agentic runtime or become experts in agent orchestration. It needed to call an API.
Asynchronous execution gives developers their time back
The team emphasizes what asynchronous execution frees developers to do, rather than replacement.
Because the task is delegated and runs without supervision, the developer doesn’t have to stay focused on monitoring it.
“While they’re in a meeting, they can launch a code fix, a performance analysis, or another task that’s a little more routine—something they can delegate without having to monitor it at that moment.”
Routine work no longer competes for the team’s attention. That leaves time for problems that require judgment.
“You can unlock those productivity gains without necessarily having to monitor the work as it happens.”
—Victor Coelho, Senior Software Engineer, iFood
Modeled on the APIs that inspired it
The Remote Agents Platform was designed as an internal layer with similarities to the way OpenAI makes this type of task available to external customers.
“The Remote Agents Platform drew a lot of inspiration from OpenAI’s APIs, both the Batch API and the Agents API, which is an even more recent OpenAI product. We built a platform that resembles those products, but is internal to iFood.”
The inspiration went beyond the concept. It extends to the design of the interfaces, the organization of resources, and the approach to asynchronous execution with results retrieved later.
“These products directly inspired how we built our solution.”
—Victor Coelho, Senior Software Engineer, iFood
Results at a glance
The platform has completed more than 25,000 tasks, consuming more than 27 billion tokens, at an average cost of US$0.04 per run.
After migrating to the Remote Agents Platform, the internal security platform more than doubled both the accuracy of its fixes and the number of vulnerabilities resolved.
Coverage extends across iFood’s more than 15,000 code repositories.
All runs use GPT‑5.6 Luna, chosen for its balance of intelligence, efficiency, and speed.
Structured Outputs ensures that each session returns a result that follows a predefined contract, whether positive or negative.
Product teams have moved from building fragmented solutions to delegating agentic execution through a REST API.
Lessons for leaders
The bottleneck is often the runtime, not the use case.
Several teams already knew what they wanted to automate; they lacked an environment in which to run it.
Combine deterministic steps with agentic execution.
Cloning, publishing, and making artifacts available don’t require a model; the complex task in between does.
Treat cost per run as an architectural decision.
At scale, the cost per task determines what is feasible to automate.
Require outputs to follow a contract.
Without a structured response, there’s no way to know at scale whether the agent achieved its objective.
Asynchronous execution is the real productivity gain.
The value lies in not having to monitor the work, rather than completing it faster while watching over it.
Tips
Expose agentic capabilities through an internal API so other teams can use them without rebuilding the infrastructure.
Isolate each run in its own sandbox, with your ecosystem’s toolchains already installed.
Choose a model by considering intelligence, cost, and speed together, rather than a single benchmark.
Use structured outputs to classify success and failure automatically.
Start with an internal user with a clear pain point and high volume—at iFood, that was the security platform.
Next steps
The team plans to bring the platform to many more use cases across iFood, expanding the range of internal products that delegate agentic execution to it—with cost per task determining whether that expansion can be sustained.

title: OpenAI and Cisco introduce Shirudo
content:
November 23, 2026
Security
OpenAI and Cisco introduce Shirudo
An open-source runtime that helps operators protect running Linux systems without needing to wait for the patch or restarts
OpenAI and Cisco are launching Shirudo, an open-source runtime that helps teams protect Linux systems while they roll out patches. In a
controlled test
⁠
(opens in a new window)
, a Codex-generated shield blocked a Java4Shell exploit attempt against a running Elasticsearch service without requiring a restart.
We’re inviting developers, security researchers, and infrastructure operators across the industry to help develop the project further. The project brings together OpenAI’s frontier AI, security and infrastructure research and Cisco’s infrastructure and security expertise to help protect the systems people rely on every day.
Testing and deploying a patch can still take days or weeks. Protecting a service in the meantime can be challenging because an exploit and a legitimate request may rely on the same Linux operation. Blocking that operation entirely could take the service offline.
Shirudo (Japanese for “shield”) is designed to help security teams navigate this tradeoff. Teams can test whether a temporary safeguard, called a shield, blocks the behavior that exposes a vulnerability while allowing legitimate requests through. Once an operator approves the shield, it can be deployed while the service continues running.
“
We’re giving defenders better models and tools to find and fix vulnerabilities faster, but finding a bug today doesn’t mean you can patch every system tomorrow. We are partnering closely with Cisco on Shirudo to help teams protect the systems they need to keep running while they build and roll out a fix. So many teams rely on the same software that it makes sense to build these tools in the open. Now when one team finds a better way to protect a system, others don’t have to start from scratch.
”
Greg Brockman, President and Co-founder of OpenAI
How Shirudo works
Shirudo uses eBPF, a Linux technology that allows small programs to run at specific points inside the operating system. This makes it possible to observe suspicious activity and apply targeted security protections to running systems.
How the guardian agent observes and protects a running system with eBPF.
OpenAI and Cisco are designing Shirudo around four core capabilities:
Live protection:
eBPF shields can block vulnerable code paths without restarting the system. Security teams can monitor how a proposed shield would affect applications before enforcing it.
Defense at machine speed:
OpenAI and Cisco are designing Shirudo to give agents programmable controls to investigate vulnerabilities, develop targeted shields, and validate their effectiveness against exploits and real workloads. Security teams control what gets deployed.
Trusted deployment:
Shields are cryptographically signed and verified before loading. Linux's eBPF verifier checks eBPF programs against its safety rules, while kernel security controls restrict unauthorized changes.
Hardware-backed verification:
Shirudo uses a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) to support a verifiable record of protections being loaded or removed. Operators can use this evidence to check whether systems meet their security requirements.
The
Shirudo technical walkthrough
⁠
(opens in a new window)
from the Linux Plumbers Conference shows how to
apply a shield and verify it on the target host
⁠
(opens in a new window)
. The Java4Shell vulnerability is another example illustrating how a targeted shield can protect a running application while a permanent patch is being prepared. Using OpenAI's Codex, the team generated a shield that added an input check to Java's Base64 decoder and attached it directly to a running Elasticsearch process. When attempting to exploit the vulnerability, the shield rejected the malicious input, blocking the attack while Elasticsearch continued running. You can read more
here
⁠
(opens in a new window)
.
Rethinking infrastructure
Shirudo is a first step toward infrastructure that can adapt to emerging threats while remaining reliable. We want to strengthen the operating system foundations needed to deploy these protections at scale, including hardening the kernel and core services, limiting workload permissions, and making updates and recovery safer.
Our long-term goal is to enable defenders and AI agents to quickly identify affected systems, validate protections, and deploy eBPF shields that block exploits without disrupting workloads. Applications should run with only the permissions they need, governed by policies that are automatically generated and maintained.
We will combine frontier AI with security and infrastructure research to discover vulnerabilities and test defenses against realistic attacks. We aim to make it easier for operators to detect and contain compromises, prevent attackers from moving across systems, and restore services to a verified, known-good state. Hardware-backed attestation and independent network controls provide additional assurance even if individual systems are compromised.
Building in the open
OpenAI and Cisco are open-sourcing

Shirudo
⁠
(opens in a new window)
so developers, security researchers, and infrastructure operators can inspect the code, test protections, and contribute to its development. Shirudo is licensed under BSD 2-Clause, with its BPF programs dual-licensed under BSD and GPL.
Our goal is to make tested shields available alongside vulnerability disclosures, giving operators a way to evaluate and deploy temporary protections while preparing permanent patches.

to sign, load, and verify a test protection.

title: Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B
content:
Today, we’re introducing Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B, an upgrade to Ternary Bonsai 2 27B with substantially stronger agentic coding, multi-turn tool use, and multi-step task execution. Based on Qwen3.8 27B, it retains the previous release’s 5.9 GB model footprint while significantly improving the capabilities developers need to build agents that work with private files and tools on-device. The result is by far the strongest AI model of its memory footprint for agentic workloads.
With
Ternary Bonsai 2 27B
, we brought stronger reasoning, visual understanding, and tool use to local devices. Since then, we’ve focused on making the model more effective across long sequences of tool calls: interpreting results, adjusting when a step fails, and maintaining the task’s objective through the whole interaction. This release also continues our work to make Bonsai more practical by addressing excessive thinking and repetitive loops in the previous model. Compared with Ternary Bonsai 2, Ternary Bonsai 2.5 completes tasks in fewer turns, uses fewer tokens, and delivers results faster and more accurately.
Agentic workflows are particularly sensitive to model degradation: small errors can compound across successive tool calls and derail an entire task. Ternary Bonsai 2.5 significantly narrows the performance gap to the full-precision base model while retaining its compact footprint. Preserving this behavior through longer tasks is an important milestone in improving the intelligence density of models.
We evaluated Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B against both Ternary Bonsai 2 27B and the full-precision Qwen 3.8 27B base model, as reported in the full
whitepaper
. We see marked improvements in agentic execution, coding, and multi-turn tool use, as shown in the table below.
On a single NVIDIA H100, Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B achieves a generation speed of 291 tokens/s with MTP and processes a 2,000-token prompt at 3,200 tokens/s. Even on a consumer-grade RTX 4090, it delivers 204 tokens/s with MTP and a prompt processing speed of approximately 3,060 tokens/s. The demos below follow complete local workflows, from the initial request through intermediate decisions to the final result.
For products, this creates room to build assistance directly into the applications where work already happens: a coding assistant working through issues in a private repository, a document application that prepares reviewable summaries, or a desktop assistant that handles recurring analysis. Local deployment lets those products process sensitive material on the user’s device. Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B strengthens the model capabilities behind that experience while keeping the compact footprint that makes it practical.
Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B runs on NVIDIA and Intel GPUs via llama.cpp and on Apple devices (Mac, iPhone, iPad) via MLX.
Model weights are available today under the Apache 2.0 License.
Full technical details of our compression, evaluation, and benchmarking processes are available in our
whitepaper
.
We work with teams to tailor Bonsai models to their applications, from post-training on domain-specific data to optimizing inference for target hardware. If you’re building AI products with tight memory, latency, or power requirements, we’d love to explore how Bonsai can help. Reach out at
sales@prismml.com
.

title: Active intrusion campaign against Check Point security management servers
content:
GreyNoise tracks threat activity using our Global Observation Grid (GOG), a sensor network designed to attract adversarial scanning and exploitation attempts on our managed infrastructure. One might think of these sensors as conventional “honeypots,” but that doesn’t quite capture the variety, versatility, and scale at which we deploy and manage the complex fabric of the GOG. Unsolicited activity against our sensors is sketchy if not outright nefarious, and our approach allows us to capture end-to-end intrusions and analyze a broad swath of attacker infrastructure, tools, and tactics in near realtime, without waiting for lengthy incident response investigations. We fuse data from our sensor network with additional novel sources and methods to develop a comprehensive picture of adversaries.
‍
‍
We witnessed the GT13 actor use 99 IP addresses, all of which were either egresses through
ExpressVPN
or compromised victim Check Point devices, including activity over 1400+ network sessions, 800+ command line artifacts, and 1200+ files downloaded, uploaded, or created. We cannot cite all of the details here, but we can highlight observed GT13 adversary activities to illustrate their tradecraft and tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs).
‍
The GT13 threat actor used an automated scanning and exploitation pipeline to compromise an HFS server using
CVE-2026-61500
.
2026-10-02 13:17:45 UTC
- The actor scanned and began exploitation against the HFS server. Each POST to the HFS loginSrp1 endpoint returns a new signed session cookie containing a “sid” value drawn from JavaScript’s Math.random() function. Through conducting several logins in succession, the actor collected enough output to reconstruct the internal state of the V8 PRNG algorithm, and thus recover an HFS session-cookie signing key, then forge a signed admin session cookie. This allows the attacker to login as admin without a password.

CVE-2026-61500
for session forgery, which was not patched on this server. The actor now had control of the server.
Example HTTP POST request with forged cookie

Instead, the actor’s automated pipeline reused the HFS exploitation route to forge new session cookies and leverage the HFS server_code feature to attempt to download and install additional malware on the server. At this point, we can see that the actor intended to use the compromised server as a relay or “hop” for further intrusion operations.
Example of HFS command, which was preserved on the compromised server.

Example decoded base64 blob demonstrating that the actor was intending to download an apparent “ZULT” Linux implant to the compromised machine.
The malware download failed, and the adversary attempted to troubleshoot the download by checking running processes, invoking curl to access the resource, and viewing the network configuration.
Example of the actor following up, attempting to check on their implant
They couldn't figure out why their implant did not download, and the actor returned the next day with a direct SSH connection to continue setting up their relay.

The actor created a script (/root/exfil/srv_post2_<redacted>.py) which set up an unauthenticated HTTP server on the hop, after which the actor began to upload files. The first exfiltrated .tgz file contained results from scan of network routes from a compromised Check Point Security Management Server, demonstrating that the actor already had access to targeted victim assets.
The actor continued to set up their environment, uploaded and installed open-source tools like Nmap and
Chisel
, and then set up a Chisel server as a reverse proxy.
‍
Once the actor had the compromised server set up as a relay, they began to use it to manage their interactions with their previously compromised victim Check Point devices. There’s a lot of commingled victimology here, so we’ll refer to two sets of victims. During our visibility, the actor was actively working towards deepening their intrusion against Victim A, and we later observed bulk actions on 21 other victim Check Point devices.
Between October 20th and 26th, the adversary had one of their Victim A compromised assets download the Chisel program and run it in client mode allowing them to further scan and interact with the Victim A environment. Over the Chisel tunnel, and by using a script for
CVE-2026-16232
(Check Point SmartConsole auth bypass to Run Script), the actor launched over 100 management tasks on multiple Check Point Management Servers. This included copying the firewall database and the Internal CA, minting a new certificate (pivot.p12), and unloading security policies (which would disable the firewall). Further, the actor probed Citrix Netscaler, Ivanti Connect Secure, VMware vCenter, Microsoft Exchange, Oracle TNS assets and several domain controllers.
The bulk of the adversary commands and interaction is too voluminous to dig into here, but we can expose some of the adversary’s TTPs by taking a glimpse at their tooling. The actor used at least 30 Python scripts, many of which were helpers or launchers for other scripts, and several of them were probes for vulnerabilities or runners of exploits. Excerpts are provided below to illustrate the more specialized tooling and workflows.

title: The Spray Bottle
content:
When I first started designing this site, I would constantly look around my home for objects that I had never given a second thought.  Two products stood out to me as wonderfully mechanical and common: the mechanical pencil and the spray bottle.
The modern spray bottle emerged in the early 1970s, and by now there must be hundreds, maybe even thousands, of spray bottle designs out there in the world, with variations on their nozzle design, trigger mechanism and more. But they all utilize the same basic one-way-valve mechanism.
The main question we want to answer: How does fluid keep spraying out, pull after pull, every time you squeeze the Trigger?  Let's get into it!

title: Launch HN: Versine (YC F26) – MCP to send and receive money
content:
Versine is an MCP that sits in front of a wallet with a balance. With it, your agent can do things like:
- Send money to someone with your approval (via passkey in our app)
- Send and request money to/from up to 100 people at once
- Send money to people without a Versine account (they cash out to their bank in 2 mins)
- Pay people without your explicit approval to trusted contacts (you can set this)
Here’s a demo:
https://youtube.com/shorts/Q9X7zioEqi0
We started working on this because assistants are frustratingly hands-off when it comes to finance and money movement. You can have your assistant go through a receipt and map out all the amounts owed taking care of splitting the subtotal, taxes, tips, but at the end of it the assistant hands back work to you when you have to go out and make the Venmo transfer.
Our current solution is oriented towards power users: those who want to automate everything through their agent use us to split dinners, group trips, or settle poker ledgers. We see ourselves unlocking more value for the general consumer as
1. More people turn into power users of agents, and
2. We expand to a more complete banking solution: deposits, transfers, wires, everything you can (and more) do with your bank offered as an MCP.
Behind the scenes, each user has a self-custodial stablecoin wallet storing USDC on Base. With self-custodial wallets, users own their keys, meaning money can’t be sent without their approval.
Interestingly, we were almost forced into this solution because we had around 4 weeks to build this product (after a pivot), and traditional fiat with a partner bank would have caused far too many regulatory and compliance slowdowns.
Because of that, the only fast option that remained was using stablecoin wallets. It also ensures we aren't a Money Services Business (MSB) since we don’t hold control or access to the user’s funds.
Each call to the wallet creates what we call one-time or recurring standing permissions. For a one-time payment, your agent makes an MCP call, and you receive a notification in our mobile app. Once you swipe up in the app and approve with a passkey (or your device’s biometric method), we create a one-time permission that instructs your wallet to send $X to your recipient’s address.
Trusted contacts let your agent send money to people that you’ve previously authorized without explicit passkey approval. Generally, these are people that you’d trust to send your money back even if your agent made a mistake.
We’re also able to support sending money to someone off Versine using claim forwarding, where the user authorizes us to forward a specific amount to a future address (which we create once we verify a recipient's OTP).
Param worked on scaling vector search at Databricks and harness evals at Glean. Harshith worked on core Stripe Connect fee-processing infrastructure and built an AWS Fargate autoscaler at Amazon. Vishnu worked on intent-based agent testing infrastructure at Amazon. None of us were experienced in stablecoin or crypto infra before working on Versine but our distributed systems experience has helped us a lot.
We'd love for you guys to try it! It's available on iOS and Android and as an MCP on ChatGPT and Claude. We also support a public MCP and REST API for other agents.
Please let us know how you find it and if it works as you'd hoped!
https://versine.com

title: From CUDA and Jax to TorchTPU: Lessons from a Cayley Graph Solver
content:
From CUDA and JAX to TorchTPU: Lessons from a Cayley Graph Solver

Some time ago, I shared a
blog post
about working with Cayley graphs, where I solved combinatorial puzzles using AI coding agents, PyTorch on GPUs, and JAX on TPUs. Recently, Google
released
TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend for TPUs, and I wanted to see how well it works on the same task: whether a PyTorch-native TPU stack could match my A100 training pipeline and my JAX beam search in speed and solution quality, or maybe even beat them.

The short version: getting TorchTPU to work was easy; getting it to work efficiently was considerably harder. My initial training port was
1.65x
slower than the A100 implementation, while the first TPU beam search was
5.7x
slower than its JAX counterpart.

After optimizing eager execution, rewriting attention, eliminating dynamic tensor shapes, fixing a subtle deduplication bug, and investigating an attention-routing regression, the results changed substantially. Training reached comparable wall-clock performance to the A100, and the optimized TorchTPU beam search became
25% faster
per level than JAX on the same eight-chip v6e machine, producing the same total solution length across six test puzzles.

Along the way, the investigation improved the solver itself and resulted in an upstream TorchTPU GitHub
issue
that led to attention-routing fixes.

The code is available on Kaggle notebooks running on a free TPU v5e-8:

Training

Beam search, TorchTPU vs JAX

As in the previous post, the code and the experiments were done by coding agents (Claude Code and Codex): I decided what to port, what to measure, and how to judge the results, and they did the implementation and the profiling.

The problem

The
CayleyPy Professor Tetraminx
competition requires finding the shortest sequence of moves that solves 1000 scrambled puzzles. Formally, it is a shortest-path problem in a Cayley graph (each puzzle state is a node, and each of the 24 possible moves is an edge) with an 88-sticker state.

My solver uses beam search guided by a learned neural heuristic — a 3.4M-parameter
PieceTransformer
. Instead of treating the 88 stickers individually, it groups them into 50 physical pieces, turns each piece into a token, adds a class token (51 tokens in total), and runs four small transformer layers with eight heads of size 32. At the end, an all-neighbours Q head (a head that predicts, for each of the 24 moves, the distance to solved after that move) outputs 24 numbers. So the beam scores all 24 children of a state with one forward pass on the parent.

For training, the signal is a mix of cheap random walks and exact ground truth:

Random walks of 2–40 moves from the solved state. A state
p
moves into a walk has two known labels: undoing the last move gives distance
p - 1
, and continuing the walk gives
p + 1
.

Exact 24-way labels from a breadth-first search (BFS) table at depth 5 or less.

The puzzle’s 24 spatial symmetries, used as data augmentation.

On the A100, one epoch takes
142.7 seconds
. My best checkpoint is epoch 1500 of a 2000-epoch run, about 80 hours in total.

What is TorchTPU

TorchTPU is
not PyTorch/XLA
: there is no
LazyTensor
tracing, no
xm.mark_step()
, and no
xla_device()
. Instead, TorchTPU lowers ATen ops directly to StableHLO and runs through PJRT and
libtpu
(PyTorch’s core ops are translated straight into XLA’s input format and executed by the TPU runtime). Once you
import torch
,
"tpu"
works as a device string just like
"cuda"
.

It has three execution modes:

Eager (the default):
runs one op at a time asynchronously.

Fused eager (
TORCH_TPU_DEFER_AND_FUSE=1
):
defers ops and fuses them across op boundaries without needing
torch.compile
.

Compiled (
torch.compile(fn, dynamic=False)
):
graph compilation targeting the TPU backend.

Three rules matter in practice:

Static shapes were the reliable path: with the TorchTPU builds and operators I used, fixed tensor shapes and
torch.compile(..., dynamic=False)
worked best, and every new shape meant a full recompile.

Data-dependent output sizes were the most expensive: ops like
nonzero
,
masked_select
,
unique
,
bincount
, and even
x[bool_mask]
still run in eager mode, but they force a
.cpu().item()
host round-trip to learn their output size, and a compiled graph gets specialized to that one size, so each new size means another compile.

Nothing falls back silently to the CPU: an op that TorchTPU doesn’t implement raises an error instead of quietly running slowly.

Part 1: training, from 1.65x slower to 1.08x faster

I ran the first port on a Cloud TPU machine with four v6e chips, using DDP with one process per chip and a global batch of 512, so each epoch saw exactly the same number of samples as on the A100. Before the code could run on the TPU at all, I had to remove four GPU idioms (
masked_select
in the loss, boolean-mask indexing when expanding labels, 12
.item()
metric reads per step, and sampling training anchors on the CPU instead of keeping the 0.19 GB anchor table in TPU memory). This first working version took
234.8 seconds per epoch
, 1.65x slower than the A100. I was able to bring it down to 132 seconds with two changes.

Fused eager

The first win was practically free: turning on fused eager (
TORCH_TPU_DEFER_AND_FUSE=1
). Only the model’s forward and backward pass ran under
torch.compile
; the rest of the trainer (the random-walk sampler with its 40-iteration loop, label expansion, the loss, and the metrics) ran in eager mode, one op at a time. In default eager mode, that data pipeline took
61.3 ms per step
. Wrapping it in
torch.compile
brought it down to 29.7 ms, while fused eager, which fuses the ops at run time without any code changes, got it to
13.1 ms
. The pipeline is many tiny ops, and on this workload they fused better than they compiled; I didn’t profile why, since the cheaper option was also the faster one. Setting that single environment variable dropped the epoch time from 234.8 s to
176.5 s
.

The attention rewrite that was almost thrown away

Still, 176.5 s was slower than the A100, and the GPU profile didn’t help. On the A100, the input stage and embedding gradient took
67% of the step
; on the TPU, the same stage took only
0.96 ms (0.8%)
, and the model was spending
~90% of its time in attention
.

A roofline at the model’s own shapes explained why. A square 8192³ GEMM hits 361 TFLOP/s on one v6e chip, and the model’s QKV and FFN GEMMs hit 212–259 TFLOP/s, while attention ran at
3.0 TFLOP/s
. With
T = 51
and
head_dim = 32
, every attention matmul is 51x32x51 on a 128x128 matrix unit (MXU) — roughly
2.5% tile occupancy
. Padding
head_dim
to 128 or
T
to 64 actually made things slower (0.83x and 0.81x). As a result, attention is about 3% of the model’s FLOPs but about 90% of its time on the TPU.

If you want to keep the same model (for a fair comparison), you need to keep the same shapes and find other improvements. Standard
scaled_dot_product_attention
(SDPA) expects
(B, H, T, Dh)
, so the QKV tensor has to be permuted to move the heads to the second dimension. Rewriting attention with
torch.einsum
keeps the heads in their original dimension and avoids the permutes:

,

# heads never leave dim 2

The fp32 softmax is there for numerics. On the TPU, the einsum and SDPA versions disagreed by a relative 3.3e-3, so I checked both against a float64 reference on the CPU: both were about 4.6e-3 away from it, because the TPU’s matrix unit uses a single-pass bf16 multiply even for “fp32” matmuls unless you raise
torch.tpu.precision
. In bf16, keeping only the softmax in fp32 closed the remaining gap between the two versions.

This change was almost rejected. The agent first measured it on the forward pass only, where it looked slower (einsum 5.51 ms vs SDPA 4.56 ms), and discarded it on that basis. Thankfully, I decided to check the full forward+backward pass: the profiler attributed much of the backward-pass overhead to layout conversions around SDPA’s saved tensors, which cost far more than the forward pass saved. Across forward+backward, one layer dropped from
25.14 ms to 14.85 ms
(1.69x faster). That pushed the whole epoch down to
132.0 s — 1.08x faster than the A100
.

A checkpoint with deadlocks

The most confusing bug was in checkpointing. Saving a checkpoint only from rank 0 is a standard pattern:

if

is_main
:

torch
.
save
(
model

state_dict

path

# deadlocks under fused eager + DDP

Under fused eager, the tensors in
state_dict
are still deferred. When rank 0 reads them, it executes a graph that includes this step’s DDP collectives, while the other ranks are already waiting at the next barrier. The checkpoint file would grow to 1.1 MB, then 2.2 MB, and freeze forever while every rank sat busy. The fix is to move the tensors to the CPU on every rank and write the file on one:

The trap only fires in the mode that gives the speedup, which made it harder to find.
