On Kaggle’s free v5e-8 (eight chips, 64 samples per chip), the training notebook run 186 epochs in 7.41 hours, with a median of
142.4 seconds per epoch
against the A100’s 144.2 over the same epochs.

Over epochs 177-186, the training loss averaged 15.131 on the v5e-8 and 15.132 on the A100, and top-1 accuracy was 0.488 against 0.483. On exact labels, the TPU checkpoint at epoch 186 is on par with the A100 checkpoint at epoch 200: its best predicted move is truly optimal for 99.0% of states, against 98.9%. The best checkpoint trained eight times longer and is still better.

Part 2: beam search, first attempt

With training done, the second half was porting my beam search solver (
KhoruzhiiSolver
, the CUDA beam searcher from the previous post) to TorchTPU. Training needed targeted fixes; the solver needed a rewrite. It relied on
torch.unique
for deduplication, boolean-mask indexing, and dynamic tensor shapes (
cand.index_select(0, unique_pos[:B])
), none of which works well on a TPU.

So I wrote
beam_tpu.py
from scratch in pure PyTorch with fixed shapes across every step. Instead of dropping duplicates, I sort candidates by hash, flag adjacent matches, and assign duplicate scores
+inf
so
topk
simply never picks them:

sort_h
,

sort_idx

=

h
.
sort
()

dup_sorted

=

torch
.
cat
([
no
,

sort_h
[
1
:]

==

sort_h
[:
-
1
]])

dup

=

dup_sorted
[
sort_idx
.
argsort
()]

score

=

torch
.
where
(
dup

|

~
valid
,

BIG
,

score
)

To share a 1M-wide beam across chips, each chip holds an equal share of the beam slots, and a child’s owner chip is determined by its hash. Every step runs the Q-head forward on local parents, routes children to their owners via
all_to_all_single
, deduplicates globally on each owner, and runs
topk
for the next level. States are stored as
int8
, and the tree bookkeeping stays outside the compiled step so the level counter doesn’t trigger a recompilation.

The search doesn’t go all the way to the solved state: it stops as soon as a beam state appears in the exact depth-6 BFS table (27.8M states), and the table supplies the optimal last six moves. In the first TorchTPU version, this endgame tail (a Zobrist hash and a
searchsorted
over the table for each level, each ending in
.item()
) ran as eager ops on the TPU and took ~176 s after a 73 s solve. The JAX driver had always done it in NumPy on the host, so I did the same: identical moves on 3000 checked states, at under a millisecond per state. Running the model over fixed-size chunks inside a single
scan
didn’t change the step speed, but it kept one copy of the model in the compiled graph instead of one per chunk, shrinking the cached compiled code from 363 to 162 MiB.

I first tested an August pre-release of TorchTPU on six hard scrambles (1M beam, 4x v6e). It matched my JAX kernel on path length (186 vs 185 moves, every path replay-verified) but was 5.7x slower (1973 s vs 345 s). The profile showed that cross-chip
all_to_all
cost only 0.6 ms per step, while model inference took ~83% of the time. Then I moved to the public
torch_tpu==0.2.0
on Kaggle, and the results were surprising: the gap narrowed to 2.8x per beam level, but quality dropped, with TorchTPU finding
194 moves
where JAX reproduced its 185.

When a backend change exposed an algorithmic bug

Because Kaggle has a long TPU queue, I moved to Cloud TPU v6e to debug the 8 moves lost between the pre-release (186) and 0.2.0 (194). Two things had changed in
0.2.0
:
torch.topk
had reverted from a stable tie-breaking order back to an unstable default, and
bf16
attention on sequence lengths that are not a multiple of 128 no longer ran the whole module in
fp32
(more on attention below).

On eight v6e chips, forcing the old low-index tie-breaking in
topk
took 0.2.0 from 193 moves back to 187, the pre-release’s number there. But why should tie-breaking change path length at all? On four chips, every fixed tie order I tried (lowest index first, highest first, a random shuffle) gave 185 moves; only 0.2.0’s native order gave 188. Something in the beam was turning tie order into path length, and that something was my deduplication.

Because the Q head scores children from the parent, a state reached from two parents arrives as two copies with different scores. My dedup sorted candidates by hash and kept the first copy in each run, and since
torch.sort
is unstable on both builds, “first” was whichever copy the backend left in front. When 0.2.0 changed the tie order, good states started to disappear because their worse duplicate survived. JAX’s dedup uses a stable
argsort
on score-sorted buckets, so it keeps the better copy.

Replacing “keep first” with a segment-min over
(score, index)
(so duplicates always keep their best score) added 0.5% overhead and fixed the issue:

On ten more puzzles, this fix cut total moves from

My agent wrote up the measurements and

Conclusions

I started this experiment to see whether TorchTPU could replace my A100 + JAX setup, and on this task it can: the same model trains at the A100’s speed or slightly faster, and the beam search matches JAX on quality and is a bit faster per level.

However, a native PyTorch API does not eliminate the need for hardware-aware engineering. Static shapes, deferred execution, tensor layouts, compilation caching, and kernel selection all mattered considerably. Optimizations that helped training did not necessarily help inference, and seemingly minor changes in backend behaviour exposed a latent bug in my search algorithm.

The migration also improved both implementations: fixing deduplication reduced solution lengths, the attention investigation contributed to upstream TorchTPU improvements, and revisiting memory management enabled larger beams in JAX.

More broadly, this project demonstrated how AI coding agents can participate in experimental engineering rather than simply code generation. Claude Code and Codex implemented alternative approaches, profiled execution, constructed controlled experiments, investigated regressions, and prepared reproducible bug reports. My role was to formulate hypotheses, choose meaningful metrics, question misleading measurements, and decide which trade-offs were acceptable.

title: 2035 came early
content:
tl;dr

trynix.dev
boots GUI programs now. Try
solitaire
,
GL gears
,
xeyes
,
a voice
,
the weather over curl
, or
Firefox
.

I remember watching the talk
The Birth & Death of JavaScript
by
Gary Bernhardt
and falling in love with the whimsical yet dreadfully serious unfolding of the story of how JavaScript will come to dominate all software.

Others have noted the inevitability of JavaScript’s dominance, so perhaps it was not surprising that Atwood’s Law holds true.

Atwood’s Law
Any application that can be written in JavaScript, will eventually be written in JavaScript.
—
Jeff Atwood, 2009

I highly recommend watching the talk if you have not already seen it, but the short and skinny is a lookback from 2035 and how JavaScript came to be the defacto language for all software.

In Bernhardt’s retelling of events, the date is worked back from 2035, however unsurprisingly, large language models have rapidly sped up the timeline. What was once perceived to be the end-state at 2035 has arrived years earlier and you can witness it unfolding at
trynix.dev
.

One of the most impressive creations I’ve managed to build leveraging
nixpkgs-multiverse
is
https://trynix.dev
.

It still baffles my mind that I can run
any Nix package
, over 300,000 distinct package versions, straight from my browser. Truly insane capability.
I was however a little dismayed at the speed of the QEMU emulation in the browser. It was slow enough that the creation tipped more towards novelty than practicality.

I woke on November 20th and saw
Domen Kožar
sharing a single message in our
TacoSprint
Discord channel:
unkernel.dev

It was the fast browser Linux experience I had sought to achieve,
but with Nix
.

Aside

What is
unkernel
?
It is Linux compiled
to
WebAssembly, allowing the kernel and system components to run at wasm speed while only user programs are emulated. It was published by
Pooya Parsa
on November 19th, 2026.

In an AI induced manic frenzy, I adopted the new engine along with a slough of long-wished features almost immediately.

The proof is in the pudding: unkernel delivers remarkable speed improvements over
qemu-wasm
,
1
1
With a very healthy set of patches applied to make it even faster.
especially on first runs where kernel work dominates. The new engine is able to deliver 2x to 32x faster performance depending on the workload.
2
2
The
benchmark page
tracks both engines over time, measured through the real page and shell.

JavaScript & WebAssembly nirvana.

Amazingly not only does the kernel boot quickly, it also enables networking, full-fledged graphical and audio experiences directly in the browser.

Windows.
A program’s Wayland surfaces are composited in the page by
wland
, and they float over the terminal you started them from.

GL.
The VM includes a minimal Mesa build with only the virgl driver, compiled to WebAssembly, rendering through your browser’s WebGL2.

Sound.
The VM has an ALSA sound card, and can play audio through your browser.

Network.

curl
,
git clone
and
pip install
work. Each TCP connection goes over one WebSocket to a
Wisp
relay.
3
3
Thank you to
@_pi0_
for adding
trynix.dev
to his Wisp relay allow-list.

The best joke in Bernhardt’s talk is a browser running inside another browser: the Windows GIMP under Wine, in Chrome, in Firefox. Of course, I had to try it with trynix. 😈

Here is
Firefox in trynix
, and it loading
trynix.dev
, and then loading Firefox again inside itself.
4
4
Don’t get too excited: this took over 4 hours. The inner Firefox needed JIT disabled, the middle one ran without GL, and the outer page used a Wisp relay on my laptop since
wisp.unkernel.dev cannot reach itself
.

Sit and bask in that insanity. That is Firefox, on Linux compiled to WebAssembly, in a Firefox tab, loading the site and then loading Firefox again inside itself. 🤯

2035 came early.

title: Working with AI
content:
Nathan Wilmers, Maxim Massenkoff, Peter McCrory
Summary
How are businesses across the economy adopting AI? What bottlenecks and challenges have they faced? How can employers reorganize human expertise around increasingly capable models? To understand businesses’ experiences better, we conducted 66 interviews with 58 of Anthropic’s enterprise customers. We found:
Sources of AI value.
Companies are deploying AI across a dizzying range of knowledge work tasks. In particular, they are increasingly using coding agents to bring software capabilities to nontechnical roles. Interviewees report that most uses of AI add value by increasing their output, rather than by cutting costs. They attribute this both to AI accelerating
existing
work and to its role in introducing novel product and service improvements.
Impact on employment.
Across our interviews, we saw very few examples of domestic layoffs that were driven by AI automation. Although some companies reported hiring more due to AI, most companies reported hiring less due to AI. Many also reported reducing their use of contractors, particularly offshore ones. These reported cuts could be an early warning of job disruption in the international business services industry.
Bottlenecks.
Companies reported a range of bottlenecks, including experts resisting AI deployment and tasks that are not accelerated by AI. As coding speeds up, for example, other tasks—like code review, sales, and strategic decision-making—increasingly need to keep pace.
Limits to top-down and bottom-up approaches.
Many companies approach AI by identifying a workflow to automate and rolling out a top-down solution. This approach can lead to job insecurity, fears of workplace surveillance, and resistance from the experts needed to set up an effective and durable workflow. Companies that distribute AI tools and wait for bottom-up adoption see some valuable AI use but face bottlenecks from unequal adoption and single-task AI implementations.
Reorganizing for AI.
Interviewees described the highest-value uses as involving meaningful reorganization. Some companies are broadening their employees’ roles to ensure individuals can take ownership over whole workflows, and are redeploying employees to the “bottleneck” tasks that AI models cannot do. Some also seek to empower employees by building out infrastructure to support nondeveloper coding and by providing broad-based internal access to business data. These companies are reorganizing to take advantage of ongoing model capability improvements rather than settling on a fixed approach that assumes AI tools will remain as powerful as they are today.
Introduction
The use of LLMs has exploded across the economy. How are human organizations reshaping around these strange new collaborators? Consider an employee at a midsize law firm that we spoke to. For years, the firm’s mailroom had followed the same protocol: a scanner sent PDFs of incoming correspondence to an inbox; a mail clerk opened each PDF, skimmed it, clicked “Save As,” renamed it, and placed it in the firm’s file system. The process took five minutes per letter. One day, a senior developer visited the mailroom to watch the mail being processed. In a month, he built an AI system that eventually became two API calls, which name the document based on its first page and then assign it a place in the firm’s document system. The mail clerks “were blown away.”
An employee at another law firm we interviewed hoped AI would create “a second brain” for the firm. (“For higher-level stuff, it just opens up possibilities.”) But the firm struggled to get everyone to use AI effectively. Demand letters to potential defendants were filled with excessive em dashes and occasional errors. Attorneys building apps kept “running into the wall based on hallucinated menus or buttons that don’t exist.” Others worried about confidentiality and data security, or they just didn’t “have time to get onto this AI train.” A few power users inundated the firm with AI prose, “casually sending Claude-prompted seven-page instructions to the IT team.”
A third law firm we spoke to adopted AI early and achieved strong uptake. One of the firm’s early projects was an AI timekeeping system that saved attorneys work tracking billable hours. IT staff saw parts of their job automated, but they then focused on building secure infrastructure to host apps and manage context that served the rest of the firm. As AI tools spread, the firm realized that associates were no longer needed to write first drafts of certain legal documents. But without writing, “how does an associate know if that’s a good draft or a bad draft?” So it introduced a new workflow where junior lawyers were “required to really take that first [AI-written] draft and work with a senior attorney,” pairing off and marking up and editing the draft together.
These three firms applied the same technology in the same industry but in different ways. The first firm automated a workflow, creating efficiency gains but risking job displacement for the mail clerks. For the second, bottlenecks to adoption and effective implementation prevented job displacement but also blunted productivity gains that would benefit the firm. The third reorganized work without eliminating any jobs, because effective use of the technology required redeploying employees toward new tasks. The firm redesigned roles to maintain human expertise as a complement to increasingly capable AI models.
In this article, we explore the connections between AI-driven value and work reorganization through 66 face-to-face interviews conducted across 58 companies in the US, all of which are in the midst of adopting AI. We interviewed executives, managers, and individual contributors. We talked to employees at AI-native startups and 100-year-old businesses. We interviewed people at manufacturers and tech companies. We spoke with structural engineers, dentists, and accountants; employees at hedge funds, law firms, and private equity firms; a property manager, a trucking company, and a publisher. They’re all Anthropic customers, but many also use other AI tools. They were selected for this study because of their range across industry, size, and AI usage, though they are not a random or systematically representative sample.
As in other qualitative research, we present stories and a framework to organize them, with the expectation that follow-up quantitative research can test these ideas further. The interviews were done anonymously, both for the interviewees and their companies. Any names in the report are pseudonyms.
How are businesses adapting to AI?
In our interviews, we gained insight into how AI has become embedded in businesses across the economy. Some of the AI agents we heard about are sending faxes back and forth, as doctors’ offices refer and intake patients. Other agents are giving advice to technicians when an X-ray machine breaks, and still others are then marking up the X-rays to help patients better understand them. Agents are reading property deeds from the 1800s and working out delivery routes for gaming machines. Recently, an AI agent analyzed a company’s organizational chart and suggested departments where the company could add headcount: “Three heads here, we need to add two there, zero here.”
Mostly, agents are writing code. Interviewees described 100 pieces of software that they wrote with AI in enough detail that we could categorize them. Eighty percent of this software automated previously manual work, like spreadsheet-based financial updates or taking meeting notes. Another 20% replaced existing software, often previously purchased from outside vendors. Agents are building apps for private parking enforcement, 401(k) audits, and trademark checks for new product names. They are making dashboards to track portfolio companies, equipment repairs, and debt collectors’ phone calls.
How have human organizations harnessed these new assistants? We use our interviews to explore several aspects of these deployments. We begin by estimating how much value interviewees ascribe to AI deployments and relate that to a measure of how much organizational change they required to implement. Figure 1 plots nearly 300 AI applications that interviewees discussed in detail. We define an application as a specific AI use case in a specific company. We coded discussions of each application according to the value interviewees attributed to it and the extent to which the organization had to make significant organizational changes to accommodate it. These value assessments are primarily qualitative descriptions on the part of interviewees, not typically based on A/B tests or other quantitative assessments.
1
AI use cases by organization.
AI applications are arrayed by self-reported value to the business and the extent of organizational change interviewees reported. Self-reported value is coded on a scale from no value or net negative, convenience and small quality gains, material and measurable savings, to a large economic effect on the company. Organizational change was coded by an automated reviewer on a scale of 0 (only the user’s own work changed) to 100 (multiple roles or functions were merged or cut). The coder implemented this scale according to how deep a given change was, how many organizational changes were made, and how many different functions the change involved.
Figure 1 shows that many light-touch AI applications can fit into an existing organizational structure, like ad hoc data analysis or slide deck design. However, many of the simplest applications were rated as relatively low value by the employees who described them. Higher-value deployments tend to require changes to processes, like AI review of every code commit, or roles, like a marketing manager who edits skill.mds containing branding guidelines instead of designing individual documents.
Several interviewees described AI adoption as essentially a challenge of organizational change: flattening organizations, shifting reporting lines, or dropping functions. At one firm, for example, executives decided that junior analysts were no longer necessary because executives could complete their own SQL queries. As one accountant put it, “It’s a combination of process re-engineering and systematic discipline.”
There are several reasons why the most valuable applications led to significant organizational change. In some cases, the AI applications required a structural change in order to be successful, such as when a policy had to be clarified so that AI agents could rigorously apply it in an assessment workflow. In other cases, initial success spurred excitement about making larger organizational changes to further harness AI. In others, the success of using AI forced downstream changes. One commercial real estate company saw its staff start sending out client-facing documents themselves. But this meant they had violated company rules that asked employees to route external materials through the marketing department. As an IT director explained, “That’s good because, hey, we got another client. That’s bad because our standard operating procedures are starting to fall apart.” These stories echo academic research that shows that organizational change is necessary to
derive value
from
transformative technologies
.
Next, we studied what, exactly, value means in the context of AI adoption. Figure 2 shows that interviewees described most AI applications as adding value by increasing a firm’s output rather than cutting costs. Around half of the applications that increased output were due to AI accelerating or expanding existing work. The other half were the result of AI improving the quality of products and services or creating new products altogether. For instance, a medical group improved service quality by using AI to give patients an up-front estimate of after-insurance costs. A commercial real estate manager mocked up vacant units for potential tenants with their own branding (“Here’s what your sandwich place would look like in this space”). A dental company introduced an after-hours AI answering service, so patients’ midnight calls no longer went to voicemail.
How often different types of AI value come up in 66 interviews.
AI applications (use cases by firm) in which an interviewee specified whether and where benefits of the application appeared. Bars reflect the percent of applications that produced different types of value. An automated coder classified applications according to the surrounding discussion in interview transcripts.
In one-tenth of the use cases laid out in Figure 2, value was captured directly by employees, who were either doing more enjoyable work or were doing less work altogether. One manager described how bringing AI into his construction company meant that “work can be a joy again instead of a difficult, painful thing.” Senior engineers at an engineering consultancy described being thrilled to be free of tedious standards reconciliation work.
This sentiment was particularly common in cases where AI sped up peripheral tasks that were distracting to experts, like making pitch decks for product developers or preparing CRM reports for sales representatives. An employee at one construction materials company said they appreciated a whole series of small, personal automations that were “changing my life because now I do so much less work.” An executive at a food industry company remarked on “the number of people who just have thanked me because they could take a vacation.” (This is consistent with a Danish survey that found that around 10% of employees who save time with AI chatbots say they
take more breaks or have more leisure time
.) But some managers were less enthused. One frustrated executive described his employees as hiding their AI-enabled successes, saying, “They don’t want you to know, because they want to use those 10 hours a week to go walk their dog.” A private equity manager suspected that, among workers at companies in his portfolio, “some of them are working basically half days.”
Our interviews show substantial variation in the degree and kind of value companies derive from AI. The highest-value applications involve wide-reaching organizational change. These patterns warrant attention to the specifics of AI deployments across these companies. In the following section, we assess three common adoption strategies that we observed in our interviews: top-down automation, bottom-up experimentation, and a broader reorganization around AI.
Top-down automation
Mark racked his brain: had he messed anything up recently? As a paralegal at his law firm, he was rarely called into a partner’s office and even more rarely ended up in an office with two of the firm’s equity partners. They wanted to “talk about his AI use,” a topic that filled him with dread. He had already realized that models’ continued improvement would mean “the beginning of the end for my work.” He worried, “Why would anyone want to employ someone like me?”
Mark’s fears were understandable—and far from unique. This past year, AI has loomed especially large in performance assessments across industries. Some of the most sobering moments in our interviews were when managers described making difficult decisions to terminate employees who wouldn’t adopt AI. One engineering leader described experiencing a “morale hit” after the company terminated a developer who, they said, “just kind of shut down instead of trying to embrace it.” As one person at a financial services firm said of their company’s AI push, “You either get on board or don’t. And this might not be the place for you [if you don’t].” An engineering executive described grappling with the massive performance differences he saw emerging between AI users and AI resisters. Ultimately, he said, “we had a couple people who started off extremely anti-AI, and they moved a little along the spectrum, but not enough, and so we ended up letting them go.” But even heavy AI users were not immune to fears of losing their jobs or falling behind: one operations manager said she woke at 3 a.m., fearing for her career, and asked Claude, “How do I make sure I set myself apart so that AI can’t do everything that I do?”
These cases were rare. Overall, people at five companies described pushing out employees who would not adopt AI, and only two had seen AI automation fully eliminate a position and lead to someone losing their job. (By contrast, 10 companies reported
hiring more
due to AI, primarily into AI implementation roles and to bolster IT support, and others had grown rapidly for a variety of business reasons.) But layoffs weren’t the only adverse employment effect. People at two-thirds of the companies we spoke to reported
reduced
hiring due to AI: as one person put it, “We may not be firing, but we’re not hiring.” A third of these hiring declines were due to companies actively shrinking functions through attrition without backfilling the roles. But most were the result of companies forgoing hiring that, in the absence of AI, they would have needed to scale their businesses—a finding consistent with past work suggesting that
AI-native startups employ fewer workers
. As an engineering leader at a health management company put it, “We’ve added a lot of capacity by buying tokens instead of hiring people.”
Beyond terminations and reduced hiring, nine companies described cutting contracted software developers, customer service representatives, legal counsel, and a range of back-office functions, many of which they had already offshored. These outsourced jobs, which are based on modular tasks (self-contained pieces of work that can be handed off separately), sometimes without high expectations for quality, have been particularly vulnerable to replacement. An executive at a company that worked with an offshore design firm said, “We’ve since fired them because now we can get better quality things faster and cheaper” with AI. A finance company downsized well over 100 offshore data and developer contractors. An operations leader at a software company explained that with AI-driven contract reviews, their “legal bill has just completely disappeared.”
These reductions were often the result of top-down workflow automation. For example, one financial technology company adopted AI customer service agents and cut its offshore customer service contracts. Instead of managing human customer service representatives and fielding escalated calls themselves, customer service managers now review transcripts of conversations with the AI agents and edit the agents’ prompts, knowledge graphs, and general operating procedures. One company built an agent as part of a document review workflow. The agent reads submissions against the company’s approval policies and passes a structured analysis to human reviewers. Deploying the agent led the company to cut the number of reviewers it expected to hire for the coming year by more than 90%.
These agentic automations—in which AI agents are given instructions and then operate largely autonomously—are more advanced than the chatbots that still define many employees’ experiences with AI. AI-native startups take these automated workflows to the extreme, both in the products they offer and in how they organize their own work. One Chief Operating Officer walked us through his one-stop agentic portal for operations, noting that 90% of his operations budget was spent on AI tokens and 10% on headcount. He said of his approach, “Look, don’t hire anybody on the back office. I’m going to automate it.”
One AI startup founder told us bluntly that their company’s pitch was to replace the back-office workers their customers currently employed: “You’re trying to fire your [data] labelers, I guess.” A founder of a marketing startup described how their “marketing factory” had flipped from humans doing 80% of the work and AI doing 20% to the opposite. Another startup founder estimated that their company spent as much on internal AI use as on labor, and that it would need three times as many employees without AI. Overall, the six startups that gave us an estimate said they would need, on average, four times as many employees without AI.
Another top-down deployment involves using AI to monitor employees more closely. Under the Anthropic Usage Policy, employee monitoring and its scope must be disclosed to employees, and the monitoring must be limited to employers’ systems for security, safety, logistics, or compliance purposes. The policy further defines employment decisions, like evaluating an employee’s performance, as high-risk, and requires a human in the loop and disclosure to employees. The workplace monitoring we heard about appeared to be compliant with these restrictions, and did not always involve Claude.
One engineering executive explained, “You want to make your work legible to your manager. But nowadays I think you want to make your work legible to the agents your manager uses.” This executive, and others we spoke to, were ambivalent about the implications of these capabilities, seeing both the benefits of more accurate performance feedback and the risks of workplace surveillance—a “panopticon effect,” as one executive put it. An operations supervisor said he started each day by reviewing an AI report on the throughput and error rate of each member of his 12-person document extraction team: “If somehow there was a lag, then I can question back to them, ‘Okay, what happened this hour?’” Another operations director set up an AI-based assessment process for the firm’s customer service representatives. An agent codes their transcripts according to dozens of performance dimensions, then routes the results to a dashboard monitored by the customer service representatives’ managers.
Top-down deployments like these shift power from employees to executives and owners. But they can also be brittle, because they can quickly become out of date or obsolete. For example, the dozens of performance dimensions that customer service representatives were rated on are scored by a two-year-old model and are not taken seriously by managers. Similarly, a law firm built a series of automations for document management but ended up with a number of low-quality “zombie” apps that were hardly used. One engineering leader described a chatbot their company had built for customer service workers—an early experiment built on an open-source chat interface—as “super basic; just chat and answer.” They said the system was difficult to update and maintain, and that “we haven’t spent any more time or money on it.”
These systems are largely built by outside vendors rather than developed directly by internal users, and are marketed as targeted solutions for a specific industry and function. In interview after interview, companies described how improvements in model capabilities rendered these products outdated. As one employee said of one such system, “It’ll be obsolete in three months.” One executive despaired of the up-front investments needed to build top-down workflows as models rapidly improved: “It’s almost like we’re trying to throw darts at a spinning dart board.”
Similar problems emerge in even the most ambitious automation attempts, those targeting knowledge work that requires deep expertise. Standing up effective workflows in these areas typically requires experts to design the agents’ prompts and evaluate their outputs. But this means experts are effectively being asked to build and maintain the very systems that could replace them. One software engineer, who we’ll call Ellen, described her first encounter with automated coding: “I don’t think that my job is secure… software engineers are going to be obsolete.” Another employee put it even more bluntly: “If I’m open to this, I’m essentially building my own coffin.”
Managers also end up facing understandable
resistance

from employees
. Recall the company that used AI to automate an approval workflow. It intended to double the output of expert reviewers and reduce hiring by more than 90%. The human reviewers balked. As one executive put it, “Just because [a reviewer] can now do double the amount of cases, how do you incentivize them to do double the amount of cases?” The company considered offering gift cards to get reviewers to comply. At the time of our interview, the executive noted that while some reviewers were down to two minutes of review per submission, “there’s some that are hanging out in the 10-plus minutes.”
Likewise, recall the senior developer who’d automated one law firm’s mailroom. Fresh off that success, he told us, his COO put him on a more ambitious project: using AI to check for conflicts of interest among the firm’s prospective clients. Under the existing process, conflict staff would run a search, print out any hits, and pass “the buck right onto the attorney.” In under a week, he built a workflow that let attorneys request a check from an AI agent in plain language, which then routed the request through conflict-checking software. But the new workflow left it to the conflict staff to work through each potential conflict—and would often surface the types of complex and difficult conflicts that had previously been passed to the attorneys. Faced with this new work, the staff pushed back, the agent was shelved, and the firm returned to its old process.
Top-down AI deployment is already changing hiring and contracting patterns by automating whole workflows. It is also prompting resistance from experts and raising fears of workplace surveillance. That resistance can result in abandoned or fragile automations.
Bottom-up experimentation
For many companies, the problems of layoffs or the AI panopticon haven’t really arrived. Recall Mark, the paralegal who worried for his job after being called in to meet his bosses. The meeting was not the one he expected. Mark explained to us that at the meeting, the partners noted that his demand letters were better than others’ and asked him how he'd prompted AI so effectively. Mark said he’d felt hesitant about sharing his workflows. He remembered telling them, “That’s my secret sauce. I have my own workflow, my own process, and respectfully—please, do not take this the wrong way—I do not want to share with anyone.”
This pattern, of a few individual contributors thriving with AI, came up in many of our interviews, particularly for companies doing bottom-up deployments. Nontechnical knowledge workers with substantial expertise in a given domain often derived the highest value from such deployments. This is in line with
prior research on Claude Code usage
, which found that nontechnical experts had the highest task success rates. One accountant described “vibe-coding” an app that audits whether the 401(k) payments employers process actually end up in the investment fund they are intended for. This audit process requires matching payment records across dozens of different systems and providers and previously took accountants 80 hours. “I was able to show that to our team. They were like, ‘Wow, this is super cool,’” the accountant said. “They looked at me and they were like, ‘You built this?’ And I was like, ‘Sort of. I told Claude what I needed to do.’”
In these cases, coding tools clearly empower domain experts. A former airport operations manager told us about building a vehicle tracking app, saying, “I was wielding AI like Excalibur.” Quality assurance supervisors at a chemical plant built an app to monitor filtration rates despite having no coding experience: “They know they’re using Python because [Claude] told them.”
However, even the most dramatic success stories were often limited to changes that could be made from the bottom up. An employee at a manufacturing company explained, “We’re getting just these pockets of really cool stuff that could be great for our organization, but not necessarily a way to enable everyone to use that.” Swapping out a single software tool or building a new personal productivity app can be done by ambitious individual contributors. One investment manager at a real estate firm developed a deal tracker that replaced a third-party product that cost $10,000 per year. Another created a legacy Windows XP app that would have cost $250,000 to replace.
While many of these homegrown software replacements seem like notable upgrades at first, they still require review and ongoing maintenance—which means they can result in relatively small savings overall. How customized (and, therefore, how complex) does a deal tracker really need to be? An operations director at a large law firm considered building out dashboards to monitor their recruitment pipeline, but realized:
That’s small beans. There are plenty of SaaS [products] out there that can help you make dashboards. What is it—$30 a month, $50 a month, $100 a month, even? So, we can save that money by vibe coding. But the maintenance cost obviously goes up as well, and we have to get our talent manager to start maintaining a vibe-coded dashboard.
Likewise, an engineer at a government services firm considered using AI to customize their software but decided that even if it helped them win a few contracts, “we don’t think it’s super sustainable from the maintenance and support side still. It just requires a lot of staffing.”
Figure 3 summarizes the 140 pieces of software that interviewees described as being built with AI, broken down by the software’s purpose and the role of the person who worked with AI to build it. It shows that product features and technical infrastructure remain solidly within the purview of technical employees, while nontechnical employees focus on internal apps and dashboards. This implies that the bulk of software built by nondevelopers still requires support or infrastructure from technical employees.
Software built with AI, across technical and nontechnical functions.
Each piece of AI-generated software discussed in our interviews. Rows indicate the roles of the software’s authors; columns indicate the software’s purpose. Bubble sizes reflect the number of examples in each role by purpose. An automated coder classified both the software authors and the types of software according to the descriptions in the interview transcripts.
Beyond maintenance, these one-off, bottom-up coding projects can create substantially more work elsewhere in the organization, either in the last mile of production or through uneven acceleration across different tasks. The 401(k) audit app prototype mentioned above had to be implemented by a third-party vendor and was still not in active use months later. An engineer at an equipment manufacturer realized that AI could translate the text on their product surfaces into 10 different languages, but “we don’t have anybody that can answer the phone in those languages… So we ended up turning that [feature] off. We didn’t even ship it.” As coding accelerates relative to other functions, it hits bottlenecks: “Without the proper scaffolding in place, that bottleneck is immediate.”
These uneven changes in productivity can also run into organizational politics. As one manager put it, “In our world, it’s like Billy in Sales doesn’t trust Sally in Marketing.” Exacerbating these conflicts is the fact that the uneven adoption of AI can impose costs on nonadopters. Power users lob “Claude grenades” and shoot “Claude cannons” at the rest of the organization, while AI skeptics respond, “Guys, I’m not reading your AI email.” In one case, an AI agent put together a set of profit and loss projections that a Chief Investment Officer realized were based on outdated assumptions. As one frustrated executive put it, “A mediocre engineer with an AI is a menace to society.”
Figure 4 summarizes the bottlenecks to deriving value from AI discussed across the interviews. Many involve the uneven acceleration of tasks. The difficulty of reviewing AI outputs came up again and again, as their volume swamped scarce human attention. In one incident, an agent added an errant “S” to an API endpoint and broke a carefully planned feature release. In other cases, when coding accelerated, other functions could not keep up. Uneven employee adoption was also common, as the enthusiasm of power users failed to rub off on their peers. Companies also often noted that they lacked the necessary context and infrastructure to support AI-generated software. By contrast, customer skepticism and regulation were rarely cited as bottlenecks. The bulk of bottlenecks appear to emerge from the process of adopting AI within the organization itself.
Bottlenecks to getting value from AI.
All bottlenecks to AI adoption, diffusion, and value realization mentioned in our interviews. An automated coder searched interviews for any discussion of barriers and blockers to implementing AI.
These examples evoke
Paul David’s mill buildings
retrofitted with electric engines—a classic account of why productivity growth may lag technological implementation. Individual contributors can only revamp processes and decisions within their own small corners of an organization, while the broader division of labor remains in place. As one hotel services operations director put it, “The individual doesn’t have the authority to change the work. They can only apply it in their own area.” The head of AI at an investment firm voiced similar frustration with the bottom-up projects he had seen: “How can we upskill and tear down our workflows and rebuild like we were starting the company again now?… Not ‘Claude, write the email,’ but, ‘Why are you even getting the email?’”
One manager described the challenge of using AI agents to automate production planning. Setting output targets required input from a half-dozen functions spanning procurement, logistics, manufacturing, sales, and planning: “They’ve done a poor job at defining who has accountability and authority to make decisions.” The manager noted that only executive pressure could force change: “Getting them to imagine doing their job differently… can’t come from them. It has to come top-down.”
Reorganizing around AI
What is the alternative? Can AI deployment avoid both brittle automation of low-value tasks and the bottleneck of hobbyist projects the organization can’t absorb? Mark, the paralegal, ultimately agreed to share his approach with the partners and the rest of his firm. He had effectively automated the most relaxed part of his job—firing off AI-written demand letters. But he gained a new responsibility: supporting his firm’s AI transition and enablement.
Some companies are experimenting with complementary organizational changes in response to AI rather than just automating existing workflows or handing out AI tools. Here, we look at three ways companies have pursued these organizational changes: broadening roles to reduce coordination costs, redeploying employees toward “bottleneck” tasks, and building common infrastructure to support nontechnical builders.
Broadening roles
When firms broaden employees’ roles, individuals become responsible for an entire workflow rather than one narrow type of expertise. Engineers, for example, might start working across product, design, and even customer engagement. One healthcare startup asked all of its engineers—not just its business people—to speak regularly to medical professionals who used their product. Having a single employee or small team own an entire product or customer relationship limits the organizational friction and potential vetoes that can otherwise block AI acceleration. As one engineering leader put it, “Two people plus Claude is the most amazing thing… if two people agree on something, just ship it.”
As production—not just of code but also of legal research, data analysis, financial modeling, and other aspects of knowledge work—speeds up, agreeing on what to build across the organization can become slow and costly. But the more a single individual or a small team controls an entire workflow, the less these
coordination costs
appear. One executive described rethinking their lead sourcing, account executive, and customer success roles, merging them into a single role that handles the whole customer life cycle. AI tools made keeping up with the details of each step in the deal process easier, and made the “context loss” associated with handing a task off to a colleague more costly. One startup founder described exclusively employing individual contributors and giving each of them ownership over a distinct part of the product and business. At another company, a manager explained that “we essentially collapse designer, product manager, engineer, and QA, and even infrastructure, into a singular role.” Another engineering leader aimed at “more full-body contact of engineers with customers.” Figure 5 shows examples of roles broadening from specific functions to whole workflows.
Examples of role broadening.
Examples of role broadening across functions from our interviews. Some instances are changes to existing roles; others are new roles that combine tasks from multiple traditional functions.
Another
benefit of role broadening
is that even as some parts of a job are automated, experts have less reason to fear job loss. At current model capabilities, agentic workflows still typically
need active expert engagement and input to develop
. They also require ongoing maintenance as models improve and workflows change. For example, one engineer automated a system to respond to production-alert tickets, which had previously been a substantial part of his job. For two months after deploying the system, the engineer read transcripts of every conversation with the AI agent and tweaked the prompts, repaired broken integrations, supplied missing vendor documentation, and approved agents’ authorization requests. Six months in, with the system working well, he still sampled transcripts every two weeks to update and maintain the system. He also kept building on it. The alert agent became a company-wide Slack agent (“the company basically runs on it now”), and then an agent that keeps skills and context up to date on everyone’s laptop.
Some companies have also found creative ways to transfer employees to new roles and build their expertise. A financial services firm, for example, shifted its internship program away from its immediate business needs toward helping interns develop domain expertise, such that now the “sole purpose is to build expertise and domain knowledge for that person.”
Redeploying employees toward bottleneck tasks
Some companies respond to AI-enabled acceleration by shifting employees toward the tasks that are still bottlenecks. If employees can chase down bottlenecks, they can better complement the capabilities of AI models. Recall Ellen, the software engineer who was initially afraid she would lose her job to coding agents. She eventually accepted that “the entire job has switched right from writing code to making decisions.” At a consulting company, consultants helped automate the process of reconciling best practices and standards documents that conflicted with one another. The consultants then shifted to more “person-to-person consulting work instead of sifting through documents.” Likewise, an engineering director suggested that their team spend more time “talking to your PM [product manager] and helping your PM raise relevant questions against the user journey.” An operations leader said automation gave them “more time for the process change and the buy-in. Honestly, that is the biggest battle—that process change.” In these cases, the work shifted toward the interpersonal and strategic tasks that limit models’ productivity.
As another example, project managers at a construction company contributed to an agentic workflow for checking in across construction sites. Previously, project managers would call crew members at different sites every morning, put notes together, and write up a daily report for customers. Now, an AI agent pings crew members, who “talk to the robot” instead. The agent synthesizes the responses, reviews previous reports, drafts a new one, and sends it to the customer. Project managers said they got their mornings back to talk to customers about more pressing needs: “an excellent customer experience—that’s number one.” Similarly, one CTO shifted his product managers’ focus to aspects of the role that require more taste, or the ability to identify product-market fit. As the CTO put it, “Claude is a terrible product manager... So it’s a lot of taste deciding what features are important.”
For engineers,
code review became a critical bottleneck
, so many of them have worked on solving it. One engineer explained, “You find a bottleneck. Find out how to tackle that. Have someone own that. …Code’s no longer the problem. Let’s put time in user experience testing. Let’s put time in requirements gathering.” Some companies worked on automating code review, while others expanded the share of time engineers spent reviewing code. One company abandoned formal code review altogether but had developers work side by side with Claude to assess code.
The pressure to flexibly shift toward bottlenecks is especially strong with AI, because the models improve too fast for any fixed organizational plan to keep pace. As one HR manager put it, “You wait three months, and something new you didn’t think AI could do is now possible. And you’re like, ‘Well, okay, let me revise my whole plan.’” A CTO said, “If the world could just pause for a minute and let us get some harnesses in place, that would be great.” AI adoption benefits from scaffolding that makes role changes easier as the bottlenecks keep moving.
Figure 6 shows what these role changes look like across a variety of jobs. As software development becomes the purview of a whole gamut of nontechnical functions, engineers broaden their scope across design, product management, and even core business functions. At the same time,
new tasks emerge
: certified public accountants grade an AI finance agent’s outputs; marketing executives edit branding skill prompts; IT decides which nondeveloper apps to put into production; a client experience manager builds synthetic customers to pitch ideas to. Production planners, accustomed to poring over spreadsheets, become data labelers, providing qualitative context for AI agents to better understand the numbers: “You should be a journalist… you should not think about competing with AI.”
Representatives at the largest firms we interviewed said they were systematically inventorying employees’ skills and tracking shifts in their labor needs to formalize these changes. At one HR support firm, an agentic workflow automated the work of a team that had assessed clients’ employees for benefits eligibility. The team pivoted to client-facing work, answering calls and providing high-touch customer support, which the company had not previously had the resources to do. At a construction company, a contract administrator helped automate their own data-gathering work and was redeployed to integrate AI across the company and maintain agentic workflows. Redeployments like these can keep automation from leading to layoffs.
Task reallocation across jobs.
Cataloging task reallocations based on every description of a task change from our interviews. Each change is coded according to the person who previously performed it and the person who performed it after AI adoption. Red represents software engineering roles; blue represents other knowledge work; gray represents tasks that are introduced by AI.
Building common infrastructure
Several companies have set up common infrastructure that allows nontechnical people to build apps that do not expose security vulnerabilities or require substantial maintenance by engineers. “Every single employee now is a developer… creating additional attack surface every day,” a data security executive told us. The head of engineering at a real estate company said they “went from having a team of five developers to a team of [dozens of] developers that all want to release software.”
Perhaps the most important shared infrastructure is company data, which provides context both for increasingly autonomous agents and for employees across functions. With AI, an executive can query business data “at the moment of need” rather than waiting for a regular report from data analysts. A trucking company built an agent-accessible “data warehouse,” and managers across the company began creating their own analyses based on that data: “they’re absolutely addicted to it,” a person at the company said. Instead of a business intelligence or data science team mediating every request for analysis—“it would have ended up on the queue, sometimes a year or two”—a broad range of knowledge workers started running SQL queries themselves. At another company, a sales team leapt into data analysis, linking sales and finance data: “Anybody can do it. And so now everybody does it.” Without AI, one employee said, “they probably would have never seen [the data], or they would have never tried to do anything with it.” And the trust and safety team at an online marketplace used their new data analytics tools to identify fraud patterns. As one team member explained, “we can [now] go parse through all of our logs.” These examples all depended on companies first pulling in and consolidating their data so that AI had the context it needed. This is consistent with prior research on enterprise use, which found that more complex tasks tend to require more context from users (
measured in input tokens
).
Making data available to the whole organization can shift power downward. As one executive put it, “You have to trust the democratization of data.” At one company, the reporting team initially protested: “Hey, we have to stop Claude from accessing data. People are reporting on things that we normally report on.” But the AI advocates won out, and the work of the reporting and business intelligence teams changed. Rather than creating reports and building dashboards, the teams were able to offer advice and insight derived from more rapid and sophisticated analysis.
For AI-native startups, a structured pool of data is critical. Teams transcribe and graph customer calls and pull meeting transcripts into Slack and other public surfaces: “We just, like, transcribe everything.” An AI lead at an investment firm described urging employees to move out of direct messages and “work out loud.”
The same data and AI tooling can give executives more oversight of employees and give employees more leverage in the organization.
Prior research has found
that information technologies tend to push decision-making down to employees, while communication technologies tend to centralize it. Our interviews suggest that how organizations set up AI tools, such as who can access data, can tilt
a given technology
toward empowering employees.
Conclusion
The dozens of people we interviewed told us that AI has substantially automated a range of work at their companies, particularly in software engineering, customer service, and back-office roles. But we also heard about a variety of bottlenecks that prevented productivity gains on particular tasks from translating into overall benefits for businesses. As one executive put it, “The closer you are to the money, the harder it is for models to excel in that job.” If prototyping is fast but deployment is not, or production is fast but marketing is slow, then AI tools deliver far less than model evaluations and capabilities would imply.
The people working alongside AI face even deeper problems. In top-down deployments, automation and surveillance threaten to undermine employees. In bottom-up deployments, inconsistent velocity across the organization leads to inequality in performance between employees or teams.
Companies that reorganized around AI addressed the challenges associated with both top-down and bottom-up approaches. Developers broadened their remit across the full software stack, then shifted toward product, design, and quality assurance. Nontechnical employees found themselves needed for a whole range of novel tasks. The underlying approach was to shift people’s jobs toward the tasks that AI can’t yet accomplish. Broadening jobs also gave the people closest to the work the authority to redesign their workflows. And shared data and infrastructure helped knowledge workers collaborate with AI, extending the benefits of coding agents beyond engineers.
Our interviews suggest a path that could benefit both employees and employers. Given current model capabilities, experts are still critical to building and reviewing AI workflows. Interpersonal and strategic tasks are currently the central bottlenecks where humans are needed, but the details of these roles will continue to change as models improve. Employers that develop systems to redeploy employees in new roles and broaden their scope may be best placed to take advantage of these intelligence gains without displacing employees.
How can employers deliver on this potential? Our interviews suggest that some companies are already sharing the gains of AI deployments with their employees, using productivity gains to improve job quality and lighten tedious work. Sharing the gains in this way may also motivate employees to contribute their expertise to redesigning workflows for AI tools. Companies that commit to
internal worker reallocation
must plan ahead for where those workers could go. And they can give employees, including nontechnical ones, broad access to the data and infrastructure they need to make the most of new AI tools. Finally, model developers like Anthropic
must support these practices
by offering training and help to business customers. We hope the findings in this report will inform those efforts.
None of this is a guarantee against AI-induced job loss, and it will not replace a strong policy response in the event of substantial technological disruption. But the wide variation in how employers are deploying the same technology suggests they have some say in how AI changes work.
Appendix and references
For technical details on the study, see the Appendix in our
report PDF
.
The PDF also contains a full list of the sources used in this research.

title: Splitting USB-C: USB 3 and USB 2 on one port

Splitting USB-C: USB 3 and USB 2 on One Port
November 23, 2026
I started building
restorekit.org
dongles a few months ago at the
Recurse Center
. They are small inline USB-C boards that sit between a host computer and a target mac. They set the target mac into
DFU
Device Firmware Update: Apple's lowest-level recovery mode built into the boot ROM, so even a bricked Mac can be reflashed.
mode over
USB-PD
USB Power Delivery: the communication protocol over the CC wire used to negotiate power, roles, and vendor-defined commands.
without having to touch the target at all, and work with an open-source toolkit for restoring macs without the need for another mac.

The original board, the
Dongle-Lite
, is USB 2 only. A single USB 2 hub (
CH334F
) connects both the dongle’s MCU and the target mac through a single cable, while a
PD PHY
Physical-layer transceiver chip that encodes and decodes USB Power Delivery packets on the CC wire.
(
FUSB302B
) sends Apple’s DFU commands on the CC line.

I recently learned from timo at
Twocanoes
that newer Macs support USB 3 speeds for recovery. I obviously immediately wanted to support this on the hub for faster recovery, but the problem was cost. At first I designed a “proper” USB 3 board using a
GL3510
USB 3 hub and a pair of TI SuperSpeed muxes (
HD3SS3220
and
HD3SS3212
). It basically doubled the parts count, and
BOM
Bill of Materials: the full list of components and quantities required to assemble one board.
cost, required me to increase the size of PCB to ~100 mm, and topped out at 5 Gbps transfers between host and target (USB 3.1 Gen 1).

I really didn’t want to make a board that cost more than twice the Dongle-Lite just to get USB 3 speeds.

So with the 2nd version
Dongle-Pro
, I tried a kinda crazy USB-C experiment: drop the USB 3 hub completely, keep a cheap USB 2 hub on
D+
/
D-
, and route the USB 3
SuperSpeed
USB 3.x's dedicated high-speed TX/RX differential pairs, physically separate from USB 2's D+/D- wires.
lanes as a straight passthrough from host to target on the same USB-C port.  The idea being that
in theory
the USB 3 and 2 controllers on a USB-C are completely independent, and should work simultaneously.

Since high-speed USB 3 is super prone to interference I didn’t really have a choice other than to purchase a view boards and test it out.

Well… I just got the boards in from JLC and… THEY WORK! They establish a full
10 Gbps USB 3.2 Gen 2
connection while connecting the dongle’s USB 2 hub and MCU over the exact same port. After some aggressive cost optimization, the 10 Gbps board also ended up
cheaper and smaller than the USB 2 Dongle-Lite
.

Dongle-Pro v2 (21 x 48 mm)

A standard USB 3 hub chip like the
GL3510
is actually just two hubs in 1 package (a USB 2 hub and a USB 3 hub). On my first iteration of the Dongle-Pro, everything ran through that chip even though the dongle’s own MCU only speaks USB 2 Full Speed (12 Mbps) and has no need for the USB 3 speed.

2:1
mux
Multiplexer: a high-speed analog switch that routes whichever side of a reversible USB-C plug is active onto one pair of board traces.
. Each mux reads its own port’s
CC1
/
CC2
lines to handle cable flip and connects the active lane set to its common side. The two muxes sit in the center of the board, wired straight together through a short corridor with no hub and no
redriver
An active signal-conditioning chip that boosts and equalizes high-speed USB 3 traces to overcome cable and PCB insertion loss.
.

Pro v1 (hubbed 5 Gbps) vs. Pro v2 (split-bus 10 Gbps)

What Could Go Wrong

This sounded like it would work to me on paper, but there were a few things I thought could go wrong:

Two passive muxes in series with no redriver.
Every connector, ESD array, via, and switch adds insertion loss and reflections. I was hoping two
CH9441P
chips back-to-back would pass 5 Gbps. But hitting 10 Gbps is even better.

Sharing the target CC lines.
On the target port, the
HUSB311
PD PHY actively drives the CC lines to send Apple’s
SOP” Debug
A USB-PD packet framing addressed to a debug accessory rather than a normal device, required for Apple's DFU commands.

VDMs
Vendor-Defined Messages: custom USB-PD packets. Apple uses them to trigger DFU, reboot, and serial debug without touching the keyboard.
. The target’s
CH9441P
is also reading the lines to steer its lanes.

Host OS behavior.
Even though it made sense in theory, I really wasn’t sure if a machine would happily enumerate a USB 2 hub on a port’s
D+
/
D-
lines while a separate USB 3.2 Gen 2 device negotiated directly with the same port’s SuperSpeed lanes.

On the Bench

When the boards arrived, I immediately plugged one into my mac, plugged an iPhone into the target port, and inspected the bus with
system_profiler SPUSBHostDataType
and
ioreg -p IOUSB
.

Here is what macOS sees on a
single physical USB-C port
(
AppleT8132USBXHCI@01000000
):

One USB-C port on macOS: USB 2 hub on 0x01100000, 10 Gb/s target on 0x01200000

The raw
system_profiler SPUSBHostDataType
output shows both sides active at once:

USB 3.1 Bus
:

Location ID
:
0x01000000

Driver
:
AppleT8132USBXHCI

USB HUB
:

Location ID
:
0x01100000

Link Speed
:
480 Mb/s

USB Vendor ID
:
0x1a86

USB Product ID
:
0x8091

Dongle-Pro-v2
:

Location ID
:
0x01120000

Manufacturer
:
RestoreKit

Serial Number
:
DP2-C2BDF224

Link Speed
:
12 Mb/s

USB Vendor ID
:
0x16d0

USB Product ID
:
0x14f0

iPhone
:

Location ID
:
0x01200000

Manufacturer
:
Apple Inc.

Link Speed
:
10 Gb/s

USB Vendor ID
:
0x05ac

USB Product ID
:
0x12a8

0x01100000
is the USB 2 half of the physical port, and
0x01200000
is the SuperSpeed half of the same port. The iPhone enumerated straight through both passive
CH9441P
muxes at
10 Gb/s (USB 3.2 Gen 2)
, while the
CH334P
hub and
Dongle-Pro-v2
MCU enumerate at 480 Mb/s and 12 Mb/s on
D+
/
D-
.

Companion Ports

Splitting the bus required one interesting change in the host SDK (
restorekit
).

On the Dongle-Lite, whatever device you plugged into the dongle always showed up as a
child of the dongle’s hub
. That made it easy to tell which target Mac belonged to which dongle when you plugged in several at once.

On the Dongle-Pro v2, that breaks whenever the target connects at USB 3. Just like
iPhone@01200000
above, a SuperSpeed target bypasses the
CH334P
hub completely and shows up as a
sibling
directly on the host’s root hub.

Turns out the OS already tracks which USB 2 and USB 3 root ports share the same physical port and it exposes it directly:

On
macOS
, the USB 2 port’s
IORegistry
macOS's live kernel tree of hardware devices, ports, and drivers, which you can inspect with ioreg.
entry has a
UsbProtocolCompanion (3.x)
property containing the path to its SuperSpeed twin.

On
Linux
, the USB 2 port’s
sysfs
Linux's virtual filesystem at /sys that exposes kernel devices, USB hubs, and physical port peer links.
directory has a
port/peer
symlink pointing straight to the SuperSpeed port.

// On Linux, finding the SuperSpeed twin of the port our USB 2 hub sits on:

let
peer
=
fs
::
canonicalize
(hub
.
sysfs_path
()
.
join
(
"
port/peer
"
))
.
ok
()
?
;

let
port
=
fs
::
canonicalize
(dev
.
sysfs_path
()
.
join
(
"
port
"
))
.
ok
()
?
;

Some(peer
==
port)

So
restorekit
can still know with 100% certainty which 10 Gbps device is plugged into which dongle.

Cutting the Cost

I originally planned to have a Dongle-Lite and significantly more expensive USB 3 Pro, but that means having to maintain two hardware lines, so if I could cut the cost of the USB 3 version to be comparably priced to the original Dongle-Lite it felt like a no brainer.

After I removed the
GL3510
USB 3 hub from the original design, I went through the rest of the board to see what else I could cut:

SuperSpeed path:

HD3SS3220
($1.66) +
HD3SS3212
($1.55) +
GL3510
($1.23) came to
$4.44
on Pro v1 for 5 Gbps. Two
CH9441P
muxes cost
$0.47
total ($0.24 each) on Pro v2 for
10 Gbps
. Pro v1’s SuperSpeed chips alone cost more than the entire Pro v2 BOM.

MCU:
Swapped the
RP2354A
+ 3.3 uH inductor + crystal ($1.62) with a
CH32X035G8U6
($0.42), running off its internal 48 MHz
HSI
High-Speed Internal oscillator: an on-chip clock source that lets an MCU run without an external quartz crystal.
with no crystal, no external inductor, and a built-in ROM USB bootloader.

PD PHY:
Swapped the
FUSB302BMPX
($0.68) with a
HUSB311BLA
($0.51).

USB 2 hub:
Swapped the
CH334F
($0.53) with a
CH334P
($0.31), which integrates the crystal load capacitors and drops two more passives.

1.2 V SBU UART level shifters:
two
74AVC1T45
translators plus a dedicated
TLV70212
1.2 V LDO ($0.79) became two
HL2302
MOSFETs and a few resistors ($0.05) wired as common-gate level shifters.

Unified ESD and passive discipline:
swapped mixed
USBLC6
+
TPD4E05U06
parts for six
H5VU25U
flow-through arrays (JLCPCB Preferred Extended = $0 feeder fee), and limited the whole board to just
three resistor values
and
three capacitor values
.

These swaps resulted in a
72% BOM reduction
from original Dongle-Pro while
doubling
the SuperSpeed link rate from 5 Gbps to 10 Gbps, and a
42% BOM reduction
compared to the Dongle-Lite.

Conclusion

If you are building an inline USB-C tool where your MCU only needs a slow control channel and the host just needs fast passthrough to the downstream device, you might not need a USB 3 hub. USB-C gives you two independent buses in the same port.

Next up: A flash drive with USB 3.2 Gen 2 + 2 speeds?

title: An Italian folding bicycle design that fits into a suitcase

An Italian Folding Bicycle Design that Fits Into a Suitcase

The T&C Pocket Bici, from 1963

By
Rain Noe

-
October 29

in

Bikes

This T&C Pocket Bici is a folding bicycle made by Tresoldi & Casiraghi, an Italian metalworking firm, in 1963. Unlike the folding bicycles of today that split in half, the components here all fold into the racetrack-shaped frame. The whole thing then fits within its own suitcase. The bike's origin story is a bit murky; one auction site claims it was created specifically for the Chinese market, and that 2,500 units were sold. In contrast,

I could only find one video of the bike being unfurled:

title: Cloudflare hides shortcomings of the underlying infrastructure
content:
What Cloudflare Doesn't Tell You
Cloudflare has arguably done more to push modern internet technologies than any other company. The work they have done to enable TLS, IPv6, post quantum encryption, and other modern standards for millions of websites deserves a tremendous amount of credit.
While this is great, Cloudflare also hides many of the shortcomings of the underlying infrastructure from both users and website owners. Yes, you can connect to a Cloudflare website and it'll allow for IPv6, post quantum encryption, and TLS. But Cloudflare's connection to the origin server might be entirely unencrypted and rely exclusively on IPv4. This creates a huge mismatch between what is being presented to users and the reality of the connection.
One of my biggest problems with this is the fact that Cloudflare doesn't do enough to notify website administrators about these issues. While Cloudflare provides tools to inspect these, comprehensive visibility is lacking. The Cloudflare dashboard should notify you about each of these issues where Cloudflare is following better practices than your origin server, without website administrators having to dig through and specifically look for this information. Clear warnings and proactive alerts to administrators would help greatly.
Not only that, but according to
Cloudflare's own documentation
, they actively prefer IPv4 over IPv6 when making origin server requests, which is particularly disappointing for a company that has done so much to advance IPv6 adoption:
For proxied DNS records that have both an IPv6 and IPv4 origin address, Cloudflare will prefer the IPv4 address when connecting to your origin server.
Even when website administrators invest in deploying IPv6 on their origin servers, Cloudflare still prioritizes IPv4.
I also believe the industry should consider adding functionality so CDNs and other intermediate networks can expose origin TLS connection information alongside their own. This would allow users and network researchers to better understand the encryption state of the entire path and hold website owners accountable for bad security practices. A similar mechanism could expose which IP version is being used to communicate with the origin server.
Cloudflare has an opportunity to not only make modern internet technologies accessible to users, but also encourage adoption of those technologies throughout the underlying infrastructure. Cloudflare should be a catalyst for modernizing the internet, not a mechanism that allows website owners to avoid modernization indefinitely. Improving transparency would be a meaningful step toward achieving that goal.
