title: Gödel Enigma
content:
Project description

Had Kurt Gödel not thought very deeply about the foundations of mathematics around 1930, there would be no information society in the form we have it today.

Gödel's solitary work was the single most important factor in the development of precise theories of formal languages, which, through the coding that he invented, can be handled by a machine. His work led to precise notions of algorithmic computability from which a direct path leads to the first theoretical ideas of a computer in the work of Alan Turing in 1936 and John von Neumann some years later.

Intellectual background

The development of logic and foundational study has been known to us only in broad outlines until Jean van Heijenoort's pioneering work. He published in 1967 a collection of original papers under the title
From Frege to Gödel: The Development of Mathematical Logic 1879-1931
. There was, however, no attempt at organised historical work with the sources. Such detailed work is still in a very early state and crucial sources for the development of logic remain unexplored.

Deep intellectual history cannot be achieved if only published work is considered.

Comparison to a parallel and partly overlapping development is illuminating. Quantum mechanics, as well as foundations of mathematics, received a decisive impetus around the year 1900, with Planck's discovery of the quantum of action, and the discovery of Russell's paradox and Hilbert's idea of formalisation. All of these developments led to a well-established theoretical account by the early 1930s, right before the Nazi takeover in Germany: quantum mechanics in the second part of the 1920s in the work of the Göttingers Heisenberg and Born, logic and foundations with the full development of first-order logic by the early 1930s by the Göttingers Hilbert, Bernays, and Gentzen, assisted mainly by Gödel's striking discoveries.

Historical work on the development of quantum mechanics began in the 1960s in a massive effort in which every conceivable source was unearthed and made available in several hundred microfilm reels, the
Archive for the History of Quantum Physics
.

Sadly, nothing of this kind was ever done with logic and foundations. Our present information society owes a part of its existence to a well-hidden but essential line of development. There are several thousand pages of notes by Gödel waiting to be studied, written in
Similarly, extensive notes for lecture courses during the crucial years, written by Paul Bernays, the central driving force in foundational study around 1930, as well as over five thousand contemporaneous letters exist in the Bernays archive. These have been exploited only sporadically. The fate of many other sources, such as the papers of Gerhard Gentzen and Rose Rand, has been similar.

Rediscovering Kurt Gödel

The main aims of our project are twofold:

To obtain a full, objective picture of Kurt Gödel's crucial role as the logician behind the birth of present information society through a careful study of sources next to published work.

To exploit Gödel's hidden discoveries to the full, an endeavour whose results can be partly foreseen, as with his 1942 proof of independence of the axiom of choice, but in some cases still shrouded in mystery, as with his suggested proof of the independence of the continuum hypothesis "through the Brouwerian method."

It should be clear that so far completely unknown scientific developments will surface – one early finding is
some thirty years before Fitch's published works .

Understanding Gödel's unpublished papers requires a combination of mastery of the logical details and the application of professional standards of historical-foundational research to the source material, which, in addition, is only accessible to a reader trained in stenographic writing. So far, much of this work remains to be done. There are two exceptions: the transcription of Gödel's so-called "Zilsel lecture" in Vienna in January 1938 and his Göttingen lecture on the consistency of the continuum hypothesis of December 1939, both published in the third volume of Gödel's
Collected Works.
Both of these texts were lecture notes, relatively finished in comparison to the private notes. More recently, much effort has been dedicated to producing transcriptions of Gödel's philosophical notebooks that he called "Max Phil," or
Philosophical Maxims,
in order to better understand Gödel the philosopher. Our project will provide ample material for future generations of philosophers and logicians to complement the picture given by the
Philosophical Maxims
as well as other works of Gödel's published so far.

Methods and sources

The project consists of theoretically oriented basic research. It uses special methods for the study of mostly unpublished primary sources, the contemporary methods of logic and foundational study to aid in their interpretation, up-to-date formal methods for the development of research themes suggested by the sources, and scholarly methodological standards of historical-foundational research.

The main sources comprise a number of series of notebooks, all written in shorthand and logical symbolism, left virtually untouched except for the
Max Phil
series:

Resultate Grundlagen
is a collection of four notebooks continuously numbered from page 1 to 368, with systematically presented results on logic and foundations that Gödel considered to be in a final form. These were written in a relatively short time span between 1942 and 1943.

Arbeitshefte
is an incredibly rich and complicated series of sixteen notebooks on various logical and mathematical topics, altogether some twelve hundred shorthand pages. Most of the notes have been written between the mid-1930s and mid-1940s.

Logik und Grundlagen
is a well-organized collection of six notebooks, continuously numbered from page 1 to 440, often referred to simply as
Excerptenhefte
. It records Gödel's own work, often in the form of concise surveys, as well as the work by others that Gödel had read.

MaxPhil
is a series of 15 notebooks (one lost) of philosophical and foundational observations, written between 1934-1955. Lately, the notebooks
and transcriptions exist of most of the notebooks, although they have not been published yet.

Earlier
Excerptenhefte
and isolated notebooks. There are many isolated notebooks and diaries, such as the "Amerika 1933/34" and "Amerika 1935" notebooks, as well as a series of earlier
Excerptenhefte
, preceding the
Logik und Grundlagen
books, the first entries of which are from the early 1940s. Many of these isolated notebooks call for a separate study.

Gödel's notebooks have some overlap in themes, ideas and results that are presented in
Max Phil
or
Resultate Grundlagen
often appearing in less finished form in the Arbeitshefte, to give an example. Gödel was meticulous about keeping his notebooks, and they contain detailed lists of contents from which we can infer that he did reread them. There is a separate list of "Progress" entries, in which he summed both his achievements and objectives in numbered points in the
Arbeitshefte.

Current research

As of early Spring 2019, our current projects include the following:

Jan von Plato has been occupied by transcribing and translating Gödel's notebooks on incompleteness, the
Resultate Grundlagen
as well as the later
Arbeitshefte.
The latter two notebooks are a summary of finished work that remained unpublished, a legacy to be. They turned out to be very readable, modulo the archaic Gabelsberger shorthand, with almost no cancellations or hesitation, and a good coverage that makes them largely self-contained for a trained reader. What were Gödel's central aims in logic and foundations at that time, and why did it all remain unpublished?

Annika Kanckos and Tim Lethen have made remarkable discoveries about Gödel's's ontological argument and are preparing a definitive account of this topic. Tim has been digging into the theological notebooks that reveal surprising new aspects of Kurt Gödel. He has also transcribed a diary-type notebook from 1937-38 that gives a unique view of the last days of Viennese intellectual life.

Maria Hämeen-Anttila has been working on Gödel's early results, views, and remarks on intuitionism and constructivity in mathematics, with materials collected from the
Arbeitshefte
and other early notebooks. She should be finished with her work, which constitutes her doctoral dissertation, in late spring.

Jan and Maria have edited for publication Gödel's "Princeton Lectures on Intuitionism": These make up to more than a hundred pages. Maria's extensive introduction to the lecture series explains how the notes, written mostly in longhand English, relate to the shorthand
Arbeitshefte
of the same time, 1941.

title: Quad9 pulled their DNS service from France
content:
Back to Blog

Quad9 Service Deactivation in France

(
en français
)

Today, November 24 2026, Quad9 will disable services for French users. This means any query reaching any Quad9 service address will be refused, and no DNS resolution will be successful. Our planned deactivation will be at 09:00 Central European (Paris) Time, to try to give users who are unaware a chance to respond quickly instead of having services down outside of normal business hours.

We are unhappy to have reached this impasse. For those of you seeing this for the first time, see
our announcement of this deactivation
from one month ago.

The Summary

We have received demands from beIn (a sports rightsholder company) to block various domains they claim to be related to piracy streaming sites, so users in France cannot resolve those DNS names. Currently, the courts have upheld beIn’s demands, and we have faced fines for non-compliance. We are entirely opposed to piracy, but Quad9 has nothing to do with the piracy sites. This is an attempt to force us to be part of an enforcement regime against third parties.

We have a fundamental opposition to using recursive DNS providers as a tool in this or any other content blocking campaign. Putting demands on recursive resolvers has no effect on the origin servers that deliver objectionable content. Attacking recursive resolvers is a futile and
counter-productive effort
, but that explanation is not understood. The policymakers and courts of France may of course make any determination they wish, even those that seem ineffective or damaging in our view. We wish to remain within legal requirements where it is necessary. We have our own strict views of what we do and what services we deliver. Because there is a mismatch between the case outcome and our mission, we must withdraw from France to remain in compliance with both law and our internal guidelines.

This is a terrible outcome, but it imposes the least amount of harm viewed over time longer than the duration of this case. We understand this will cause harm in the short term: users who do not know of our withdrawal will find our services unexpectedly unavailable. Users who have to move to different resolvers will not be protected by our cybersecurity capabilities, and they may choose to use resolvers that are less privacy-focused than Quad9.

Repeating the Obvious

We object to the core premise of the legal arguments, which is the false assertion that recursive DNS can or should be used as a method to prevent piracy or any other type of content access. Our position is this is not effective or useful, as we have no monopoly on recursive DNS, and anyone can set up their own resolver in just a few seconds (though without the privacy and malicious content protection that Quad9 offers). The courts and plaintiff have not considered this argument and ignore it entirely in the judgement. Their interest is focused on the possibility for us to do what is demanded, even if it has results outside of France, and their interest is not in why that is unjust or unwise or ineffective. So, we will continue to argue with a refutation of our ability to do this accurately without applying French law to all other European nations and the world.

How Our Withdrawal Will Work

There is an understandable focus on how Quad9 is going to block “French users” when we do not collect user information and have also claimed that geoIP blocking is insufficient for selectively denying resolution for certain names. We understand this seemingly apparent paradox, so we will expand on it as it is a question that is frequently repeated.

Our geoIP-based method to identify and deny service to French users is inexact. We are aware that our methods to geographically locate users and declare they are in France is quite imprecise - this is inevitable. By using these methods, we will create conditions of overblocking, where we accidentally classify some queries as being from France when they are not from France, and it will also result in conditions of underblocking, where we do not correctly identify some queries as being from France and inappropriately complete those requests even though the user is in French jurisdiction. This imprecision is a core component of our case: there is no legally accurate way for us to determine what queries are from users located in France versus what queries are from users not in France. But we have no other mechanism - it simply does not exist.

These geoIP lists are inaccurate in two dimensions: firstly, IP geolocation data are often imprecise or just plain wrong, as IP geolocation is not an exact science. Mobile operators span national boundaries, corporate WANs split networks across nations, IP addresses are bought and sold frequently, and network operators shift allocations across borders. These are just a few of many other examples of how geoIP association may not be accurate. Secondly,
IP location does not necessarily equate to user location,
geoIP data only is a guess as to the location of the IP address, not the location of the end user. VPNs may exit in France but have the majority of their users in other nations; corporate users in one nation may egress in another due to proxies or internal DNS service distribution - there is
nothing
about a query that has any indication of the jurisdiction of the origin of the query itself.

The data is imprecise, but we do not know to what level it is imprecise. So we must work with what we have.

Why Not Block With This Method?

We could apply this same geoIP filter database to selectively block French users from reaching the sites we have been told to make unavailable, but this would corrupt our core premise which is that the DNS is not the right mechanism for this blocking to happen. If we comply within France to meet the requirement then we accept the worst eventual outcome for users - we lose our integrity and still do not have legally perfect coverage, plus we will inevitably apply French rulings across borders into other nations. We wish to first remain consistent with our core mission which is to only block cyber risks to end users and not content. Secondarily, we must remain as close to compliance as we can to the legal constraints put upon us.

By accepting even the smallest of the demands for blocking based on geoIP data, we would admit that such demands are permissible within our mission - that we accept to play a complicit role in aiding companies (or others) to create ineffective and mis-directed regimes of content constraint. We would be admitting that DNS blocking is a valid instrument for the piracy problem -
it is not
. We would be admitting we will do this for an ever-increasing number of names -
we will not
. We would be permitting these methods to be applied for more areas of content filtering such as moral, religious, social, or political reasons -
we must not
.

So we accept there will be egregious overblocking/underblocking errors in our blockade of French users but would rather remain steadfast to our stated mission and principles to uphold the integrity of the DNS. We would rather there be a clear distinction made for users of our services: you receive the DNS as you (the user) expect, or if Quad9 is forced to pollute the service with unexpected and arbitrary number of fragmentation demands, then we will not offer the services at all.

Doesn’t Quad9 Already Block Names?

Quad9 blocks a set of cyber-threats on 9.9.9.9 (and secondary IPs) for end users, where the outcome would be an unexpected and harmful result to the end user (i.e., malicious software). Content blocking is explicitly not in that set. Quad9 has subjective editing on that set, as well - if we believe something is inappropriately categorized by our threat intelligence partners, then we can remove it at our discretion. Additionally, Quad9 also offers 9.9.9.10, which has no blocking of any kind - it is entirely open. The demands we have been given would enforce mandatory restrictions on
all our service
addresses, which then makes our statements of their functionality inconsistent with the reality that would be forced upon us. We will not accept that condition.

The Future Prospects

We take a long range and principled view to the outcome of this case and the others in line. There are unmistakable long-term risks to Quad9, to user privacy, and to potential fragmentation of the internet that are far beyond the current moment. To give in now would start ‘the beginning of the end’ and allow motion towards internet fragmentation that cannot be undone. We accept the risks and the pain that come with fighting where others in similar circumstances to ourselves must bend and compromise in this invisible card game where end users are not even at the table. We represent those users, and our nonprofit mission of public service is aptly unique by not representing any shareholders, products, or other interests other than the end user.

It is especially disturbing to us to be doing this for an issue (piracy) which we believe is not slowed at all by any involvement of recursive DNS, though the damage to the integrity and trust of the global namespace is significant.

We have seen
recent articles
about extended blocking demands given to ISPs in France of social media or instant messaging sites, which we anticipate would be demanded of us as well if continued. It is quite clear to us the path that is being taken with these efforts: first create the mechanism, then expand the volumes of the mechanism (unconstrained rightsholder editing of the DNS), then expand the scope of prohibitions to other groups and for other reasons until there is effectively no limit to the number of editors or the reasons for DNS names to be deleted from recursive resolution. This contradicts our mission of delivery of trustworthy DNS results, and we believe this potential outcome to be antithetical to a free and open internet.

This is the second legal assault we have faced to see if the DNS can be slowly corrupted - we stood our ground and eventually
won in Germany
; with the continued community sponsorship and support we hope to win here, too. We refuse to take even the smallest step towards building the machinery of mandatory DNS restriction, and we will not abandon our obligation to the security, privacy, and integrity we have said we will deliver to users worldwide. We deeply regret having to step back from France and hope we will be able to return some day and offer the same unfiltered services that the rest of the world enjoys.

Legal battles like this drain time and resources away from building a better, safer internet. Your financial support is what keeps us in the fight—and keeps our services free and open for everyone. If you stand with us, please consider
donating
or becoming a sponsor today.

content:
Open source
·
Apache-2.0

A
lightweight

drop-in
replacement for your Postgres
read replica
.

Same SQL, same answers.
But
extremely fast
for analytical queries.

One query over 10 million rows: the Postgres primary took 15.7 seconds, Mason as its read replica took 0.193 seconds, and both returned the same answer to the same SQL: 81 times faster.

AWS m7g.xlarge · 4 vCPU · 16 GiB RAM · EBS gp3

Why Mason

Lightweight:
Mason is a single Node.js process you can run anywhere. It keeps all its config and your synced data locally in the folder you run it in.

Fast:
Mason syncs your Postgres data into DuckDB's columnar engine, and rewrites your Postgres queries on the fly into the form DuckDB runs fastest.

Postgres:
Mason is built from the ground up to match Postgres's syntax and behavior (not DuckDB's), so you can point your existing Postgres queries at it with confidence.

Read replica:
You choose which tables and columns to sync from your Postgres database, and how each stays in sync: on demand, by polling or by logical replication.

Built for AI agents:
Add a user per agent, with role-based access control (RBAC) that limits the tables, columns and rows each one can read. Every query is logged with who ran it, the SQL they sent, how long it took and, if it was refused, how to fix it. Mason also has MCP support built in.

Try it out in minutes, run it anywhere

$
npm
i -g @mason-data/cli

$
cd
my-app

# tell Mason which Postgres database to sync from

$
mason
init
'postgres://me:secret@db.example.com:5432/my_db'

# choose the tables to sync

$
mason
add orders customers

# start Mason locally and wait for the first sync to finish

$
mason
start
&&

mason
wait

# get a connection URL for your favorite Postgres client

$
mason
user add me

# get results fast

$
psql

"postgres://me:<password>@localhost:5433/mason"
-c
"SELECT country, sum(amount) FROM orders JOIN customers ON customers.id = customer_id GROUP BY country"

# or give it to your coding agent

$
claude
mcp add mason --env
MASON_URL="postgres://me:<password>@localhost:5433/mason"

--

mason
mcp

# done? stop Mason and delete its synced copy of your data

$
mason
stop
&&

mason
destroy

Self-host it →
Try Mason Cloud Free →

Where Mason is fast, and where it isn't

Fast

Queries that read lots of rows, like counts, sums and group-bys over big tables. The kind dashboards, reports and AI agents run.

Not fast

Queries that fetch a few rows and many columns, like looking up one order by its ID. Mason is fastest when you're querying a lot of rows across a few columns.

Mason (s)

From a cold start: each engine restarted and the page cache dropped before every run. 1 or 10 clients send the query at the same moment, and the time is until every client has its answer, the median of 3 runs. Actual results will vary, depending on the size and distribution of your data.

How it was measured
AWS m7g.xlarge · 4 vCPU · 16 GiB RAM · EBS gp3

Features

Role-based access control:
Mason gives each tool, AI agent or customer its own login, and its role decides which tables and columns it can read. You can add, disable or remove a user at any time, and the change takes effect immediately.

Row-level security:
You can limit each user to its own rows, such as the rows for one customer. Mason applies the same limit to related tables by following their foreign keys.

Generated tables:
These are like materialized views, but Mason keeps them up to date for you. They put no extra load on your database.

MCP:
Mason has its own MCP server, so AI agents like Claude Code and ChatGPT can look at your tables and run queries. Each agent can only see what its role allows.

Monitoring:
Mason works with the monitoring tools you already use. Prometheus and Grafana can read its metrics at
/metrics
, and uptime checks, Kubernetes and ECS can check its health at
/healthz
. It writes its logs to stdout, so Datadog or CloudWatch can collect them. You can also look back at every query, every sync event and how busy Mason has been, with
mason logs
and
mason usage
.

IP allowlists and TLS:
You can limit each user to the IP addresses it connects from. Mason can also encrypt every connection, with your own certificate or with one it makes for you.

Web UI:
Run
mason ui
to open a web page where you can add tables and users. The page also shows you queries, usage and sync events as they happen.

The Overview page shows you that Mason is ready, and how your tables and queries are doing.

The Queries page shows you every query, who sent it and how long it took.

title: LLM agents work for their parent companies, not for you
content:
In the evenings after work, I will often sit out back on the porch and do some phone rotting. That usually takes the form of me just flipping through reels on Instagram, allowing the algorithm to take me where it may. I usually pair this with a healthy tumbler of rum or bourbon. I'm turning my brain off after work, and I'm just having a good time on the internet. The kids might call it dopamine maxxing? Hell, I don't know. Who gives a shit about what those assholes would call it?

Anywho, I often encounter songs I really really like, and I would like to listen and discover more of please. Instagram makes it hard for me to connect with the band outside of their platform. I was trying to make this connection manually myself at first. I would just email myself a reel from my phone. Then when I'm back on the sofa and in the mood to track down new music, I'd open the reels and do my best to search on Bandcamp or YouTube or try to figure out if some of these musicians had a way to buy music from them. Very few do these days. They send you their Spotify link or send you to their TikTok page. I don't want to do any of that. I'd like to trade US dollars in exchange for some music files I can download onto my computer, where I can listen as much as I like on any device I own thank you please. Retro maxxing.

So, I used Claude Code to build a skill that does this for me. It opens the Instagram reel and attempts to identify the artist and song. It then tries to determine if the artists have a Bandcamp page so I can purchase the songs I want, and if it finds one, it gives me the URL so I can click it to complete the trade I want. I want to buy music from artists who make music I like. That's a fair and wholesome endeavor, I feel, but this recently stopped working.

It turns out Bandcamp added a challenge on their search API page. Ah bummer. No worries, that was an unpublished workaround anyway. As I was mulling over this discovery, the robot went on to explain that it would not help me work around the challenge.
cue Nick Young question marks

Well, that led me down a whole nother rabbit hole, which is turning into this post. There's another branch of my skill that attempts to locate the same song from the Instagram reel on YouTube, and it'll download the song to my computer if I ask.

So let me get this straight. The robot, which is my robot that I pay a pretty penny for, will not attempt to work around the challenge at Bandcamp so that I can more easily connect with bands to complete a sale,
but it will download the YouTube song, which doesn't send any money to the band or anyone
???

This is the real danger of the frontier AI models. Not that it won't help me hack Bandcamp
[1]
, but that this model doesn't really work for us. Well, they do, but only insofar as Anthropic or OpenAI or whoever else allows them to. In this case, Anthropic is trying to ensure that people can't use their models for evil. I'm not trying to do evil. I'm actually trying to do good! I want to buy something from a small artist on the internet. That's basically the most wholesome thing a person can do on the internet!

Have no doubt, dear reader, these companies want to dominate. They want to capture the market. They want all the money. It'll be the same march to enshittification that happened with Google. A bunch of nerds who built something cool sold out, and it turned into just another business that decided to remove its
don't be evil
mantra.

Right now, I think the robots are providing real information to the best of their ability, but I think it's only a matter of time until we must wonder if the answers they're providing are real answers that the robot found, or if they're weighted answers Anthropic put there because a company gave it enough money for product placement. I want to know the best robot vacuum according to old reddit or other trusted sources like Wirecutter, weighed and measured according to what I, and thus my robot agent, think are important requirements. I don't want to know which robot vacuum parent multinational conglomerate has a large ad budget.

And it's not just ads. If Anthropic can tell its model not to work around a challenge, then it can tell its model to do whatever the US government tells it to do, including not helping people download copyrighted music. It does that some now, but it's easy to slip the noose on that. For now.

This is the reason I want a local model that runs in my homelab. My robot should work for
me
and have
my
best interests in mind, not the interests of US corporate copyright holders. I plan to study up on what "open models" even means. I've been thinking about these as the FOSS version of LLMs, but I think that doesn't exactly map, as the biggest piece seems to be how the model was trained. The Chinese models are likely to refuse to answer questions about Taiwan, for example.

On the
existential threat or tool
question, I'm firmly in the
tool
camp, and I really do not like artificial restrictions on my tools. I will do everything I reasonably can to remove those restrictions.

And to be clear, I'm not trying to work around Bandcamp's challenge. I'm responding to the fact that Claude preemptively told me it wouldn't help me do this.

title: Worshipping at the altar of Brendan Gregg
content:
Okay, I am the first to admit that I’m a bit manic with AI. When you are working on a problem that has endless possibilities, it is difficult to constrain yourself to a limited set of features.

Can I just add one more?

I have been amazed at all the fun and useful things that a deterministic VM like
Rewind
enables. I have been using it to help
find heisenbugs
, to make
profile-guided optimization reproducible
, and to make
Nix builds bit-reproducible
. But the most fun has been using it to understand performance.

Turns out that performance is yet another area where Rewind shines. I have been using it to analyze the critical path of builds.

What is the critical path?

The critical path is the longest chain of dependent work in a program. It is the minimum time that the program can take to complete, regardless of how many resources you throw at it. The only way to make a program faster is to shorten the critical path.

If you worship at the altar of Brendan Gregg, you know he spent years turning performance analysis from a dark art into a science. This is a small offering to him. 🤲

I added a new
rewind time
command to Rewind that analyzes a recording and tells you where the time went and what would make the run finish sooner. You can drill into any part of that answer and see the source lines responsible for it. It’s like
Brendan Gregg’s flame graphs
but
on steroids
for the critical path and with a debugger attached.
1
1
All the ideas for the command are either inspired by or directly influenced by
Brendan Gregg’s work
. Kneel before Zod!

Aside:

New to Rewind? Start with
a flaky build you only catch once
and
dafuq is a deterministic VM?

Let’s see how it works by analyzing the critical path of a
libuv
build and test run. The build and test suite takes 78 seconds inside Rewind, and even with 64 cores it still takes 47 seconds. Why?

The usual answer is to look at a CPU profile, and in this case a CPU profile would be almost useless. For two thirds of those 47 seconds, the work the build is waiting on is not computing at all: it is
asleep
. 💤💤💤

§
Where the time goes

Every
rewind time
starts with two numbers:

$

rewind
time
7a29e716

libuv-1.51.0

78.0 s  elapsed on the VM's one CPU
47.4 s  critical path: the least it can take on any number of CPUs
67% asleep (epoll_pwait 23.1 s, clock_nanosleep 8.53 s, futex 100 ms), 33% computing

The first is how long the run took on the VM’s one virtual CPU. The second is the
critical path
: the longest chain of work where each step had to wait for the one before.

No number of CPUs makes a run shorter than its critical path, so the gap between the two numbers is all that parallelism can buy you.

The line under the two numbers applies Gregg’s
thread state analysis
. Here the biggest state is asleep: 23 seconds in
epoll_pwait
and 8.5 in
clock_nanosleep
.

A sleeping thread is invisible to a CPU profiler. Gregg’s answer is
off-CPU analysis
: look at where threads block, not only where they compute.

On a live machine, off-CPU analysis is hard. Linux can trace which thread woke which, and Gregg built
wakeup and off-wake profiling
on top of that, but you have to be tracing before the slow run happens, the tracing has a cost, and most of the sleeps you capture are noise. Rewind already logs every context switch because it needs them to replay, and now it records every wakeup and who caused it too. All that
juicy
information is in every recording. 🤤

Here is the whole output for libuv:

$

rewind
time
7a29e716

libuv-1.51.0
78.0 s  elapsed on the VM's one CPU
47.4 s  critical path: the least it can take on any number of CPUs
67% asleep (epoll_pwait 23.1 s, clock_nanosleep 8.53 s, futex 100 ms), 33% computing

The critical path by phase
3.54 s  configurePhase  ██
1.67 s  buildPhase      █
42.0 s  checkPhase      █████████████████████
99 ms  5 other phases

The critical path by process
on path      pid  process, with what it started
47.4 s       34  init › bash -e source-stdenv.sh default-builder.sh
41.9 s     4076  ├─ make -j8 SHELL=bash-5.3p3/bin/bash VERBOSE=y check
36.4 s     4910  │  ├─ make › bash › lt-run-tests
3.38 s     5412  │  │  ├─ lt-run-tests hrtime hrtime  asleep in clock_nanosleep 3.38 s
2.00 s     5013  │  │  ├─ lt-run-tests delayed_accept delayed_accept  asleep in epoll_pwait 2.00 s
1.62 s     5126  │  │  ├─ lt-run-tests fs_event_watch_dir fs_event_watch_dir  asleep in epoll_pwait 1.62 s

22.6 s           │  │  └─ 279 more
5.59 s     4077  │  └─ make test/run-tests

2.10 s     4189  │     │  └─ cc1 /build/source/test/test-fs.c

1.47 s              └─ 581 more

What would shorten it
sooner      pid  if this took no time
36.1 s           every lt-run-tests, 600 processes
6.66 s           every cc1, 283 processes
3.38 s     5412  75 sleeps in clock_nanosleep: lt-run-tests hrtime hrtime
2.00 s     5013  2 sleeps in epoll_pwait: lt-run-tests delayed_accept delayed_accept
1.76 s     4189  cc1 /build/source/test/test-fs.c

1.22 s           every perl, 9 processes
1.14 s     5510  lt-run-tests metrics_idle_time_thread metrics_idle_time_thread

Look closer
rewind time 7a29e716 --in PID             one process: its threads, sleeps and waits
rewind time 7a29e716 --folded             the path for flamegraph.pl or speedscope.app
rewind time 7a29e716 --perfetto F         every process on a timeline, for ui.perfetto.dev

The second table is the path as a
tree of processes
based on Gregg’s
colony graph
idea. Each line is a process with everything it started, and its time on the critical path.
2
2
A
ps
snapshot might miss short-lived process invocations; the recording has every fork, regardless of how brief.

In this build,
make check
needs 41.9 of the total 47.4 seconds, and 36.4 of that is
lt-run-tests
, libuv’s test runner. The test runner invokes 287 tests each spending 1-3 seconds.

All of those tests are on the path, and the path is a single chain, so the runner ran them one after another. Worse, most of each test is spent asleep, waiting on timers.

Drag can be less than time on the path.

The last table answers a different question: how much sooner would the run finish if this part took no time? The critical path method calls this
drag
.

For the truly magical part, we can jump to any part of the path and see what was happening, invoke
gdb
and fork the run at that moment. A profiler hands you a stack, sampled at some moment you can never go back to. Every frame in
rewind time
is a moment in a recording, and Rewind can replay the run to it.

--in
looks inside one process,
3
3
It can take a pid, a program or a word of the command line.
so let’s dive into the
hrtime
test that spent 3.38 seconds asleep in
clock_nanosleep
:

$

rewind
time
7a29e716
--in
hrtime

lt-run-tests hrtime hrtime (pid 5412)

3.38 s  on the critical path with what it started, 7% of the 47.4 s path

100% asleep (clock_nanosleep 3.38 s), <1% computing

What would shorten it

sooner      pid  if this took no time

3.38 s           75 sleeps in clock_nanosleep

Look closer

rewind where 7a29e716 115894 --pid 5412   the source line the first row's time starts at
rewind time 7a29e716 --perfetto F         every process on a timeline

Since this test spent 100% of its time asleep, the step provided on the last line is where it began.
rewind where
replays the run to that step and asks gdb where the thread was:

$

rewind where 7a29e716 115894
--pid
5412

process 5412 (lt-run-tests), thread 5412, at step 115894

#
2 uv_sleep
(
src/unix/core.c:1869
)

1867

1868    do

>

1869      rc
=
nanosleep
(
&timeout, &timeout
)
;
1870    while (rc == -1 && errno == EINTR);

1871

arguments:

msec = 45

locals:

timeout = {tv_sec = 0, tv_nsec = 45000000}

rc = <optimized out>

__PRETTY_FUNCTION__ = <error: Cannot access memory at address 0x7fb172519ae8>

called from #
3 run_test_hrtime
(
test
/test-hrtime.c:39
)

called from #
4 __libc_start_call_main
(
../sysdeps/nptl/libc_start_call_main.h:58
)

🎯 We can see that the test is calling
uv_sleep(45)
from line 39 of
test/test-hrtime.c
, and that it is sleeping for 45 milliseconds.
It does that 75 times for a total of 3.38 seconds.
4
4
Turns out that the test sleeps on purpose: it is checking how far
uv_hrtime
moves across a sleep. There is nothing to optimize in this case.

As the cherry on top: the run is deterministic, so step 115,894 is the same instruction every time you replay it. You can open
rewind gdb
at that step and investigate to your heart’s content.

The Rewind app’s
Time
tab shows the same answers. The path becomes a flame graph, colored the way Gregg colors his
off-CPU flame graphs
: computing is warm, asleep is blue, and a process shades from one to the other by how much of its time it slept.

Clicking a frame picks it and moves the playhead there, so the build log, the process tree and the files all show that moment; clicking a process again zooms into it. When you pick a blue frame, the app replays the run to that part’s longest sleep and shows the stack where it slept:

Under the stack,
Show source
opens the source panel at that moment on that thread, and
Open gdb here
opens gdb in a fork of the run at the sleep:

If you’d rather use tools you already know,
rewind time
can emit the data in their formats: folded stacks for
flamegraph.pl
and
speedscope
, or a Perfetto trace for
ui.perfetto.dev
.

The flame graph below is the real flamegraph.pl output: click a frame to zoom in, or
open it on its own
.

§
Kneeling at the altar

Every idea here predates Rewind. Gregg has been drawing off-CPU and wakeup flame graphs for over a decade, and build systems have reported critical path information potentially even longer.
5
5
Bazel’s critical path analysis
is a great example of this, and it has been around for years.
I have been inspired by his work since I first dabbled in
eBPF
, back when
flame graphs
were new. 🙇

What Rewind adds is the data.
Lots of it.

Rewind has that data because it can’t replay without it. On a single CPU the only thing that changes from run to run is the scheduler, so every recording already logs every context switch.

This changes the economics of performance analysis. On a live machine, you have to trace before the run, and tracing has a cost. You can only trace a few runs, and you have to pick which ones. Rewind traces every run, so you can analyze any of them later, and do so exactly.

It has just been a
manic fever
joy to take ideas I have admired for years, point them at a deterministic VM, and watch them work in ways that are hard or impossible on a normal machine.

Please accept
rewind time
as my offering at the altar of Brendan Gregg.

title: Cento fine foods has been sued for “tomato fraud”
content:
Illustration by
Tolga Akdoğan

So you’ve decided to make homemade pasta sauce. Good for you, chef!

First stop: browsing the supermarket for the best canned tomatoes for your future marinara. Now you’re deciding between Hunt’s, Mutti, Bianco DiNapoli, Cento, DeLallo, and those nondescript cans of tomatoes from
The Bear
filled with wads of cash. You’re considering brands, price points, and whether to buy your tomatoes whole-peeled, crushed, or diced, or hmm … maybe that jar of Rao’s would be easier? Then, just when you’re about to give up, two little words on a label stand out:
San Marzano
.

You’ve heard that phrase before somewhere—the Food Network? Ina Garten? That’s supposed to be primo stuff, right? Probably can’t go wrong with tomatoes that are
actually
from Italy. They’re a few dollars more expensive than the domestic options, but you spring for a can or two anyway. Surely getting the real thing will be worth the hassle and cost once that first forkful of al dente pasta and perfect sauce hits your lips.

•

Video from Slate

San Marzano tomatoes are indeed considered the good shit. They’re cherished for their low water content (think naturally saucy, thick tomatoes), their sweetness, and their deeply savory flavor—all qualities that can make or break a marinara. And they are certainly Italian: San Marzano tomatoes come from the Agro Sarnese-Nocerino region of southwest Italy, home to the fertile land surrounding Mount Vesuvius, the volcano that once destroyed Pompeii but whose ashy eruptions, settling over time into a nutrient-dense soil, now more helpfully produce the prized fruits in question.

Authentic San Marzano tomatoes are regulated—at least in Europe—by the Consorzio di Tutela del Pomodoro San Marzano dell’Agro Sarnese-Nocerino DOP, which I will be shortening to “the Consortium” so we don’t all go insane. And the Consortium is serious about its job.
According to its regulations
, true San Marzanos must have an elongated shape that usually measures between 6 and 8 centimeters and demonstrate that classic balance of sweet and tart flavor. The thin skin peels off easily, enclosing dense, fleshy pulp with very few seeds. They must possess something called an
axis ratio
of no less than 2.2 + 0.2, or contain limited presence of “placental voids,” which means the seed cavities are filled with gelatinous tomato gel and pulp rather than empty space. In short, they’re the jackpot if you are looking to make an unforgettably robust sauce or lip-smacking soup, and the Consortium exists solely to be this marvelous tomato’s protector.

There’s a reason these elite tomatoes are so tightly controlled. They can be grown only in a tiny region of the world—fewer than 1,000 acres of eligible volcano-adjacent land are currently cultivated—so they’re in very short supply. Or at least they ought to be. A skeptic might ask how the hell such prestigious produce ended up available in bulk at your local Ralphs or Whole Foods. Are all the brands touting the name
actually
San Marzanos? Is that even possible?

According to a recent lawsuit, the answer is … not necessarily. In fact, some of them are almost certainly fake. It’s been called “tomato fraud,” and it’s a real problem in the U.S.
Fraud
may seem like a dramatic word to apply to a tin of tomatoes, but given the considerably higher cost of cans labeled “San Marzano” (recently between $6 and $8, compared to between $3 and $5 for a normie 28-oz. can in my local market), where there are fakes, honest consumers are being ripped off by companies looking to profit from a legendary culinary reputation that isn’t theirs to claim. And tomato snobs aren’t taking it lying down.

Over the past 10 years or so, lawsuits accusing brands of
tomato deceit
have become
quite ordinary
. Take, for example, the highly entertaining
San Merican lawsuit
. The short version is that a company named
Simpson Brands
in Pennsylvania labeled its cans “SMT,” and in exquisitely sneaky fine print, the text by each letter spelled “San Merican Tomatoes,” instead of “San Marzano.” Though the plaintiff ultimately dropped the suit (and Simpson denied the allegations), I think its claim—that a reasonable person could easily confuse these impostors with the genuine article—is certainly fair. (Oh, and by the way, those San Merican tomatoes are trash. Not even
close
to San Marzanos. San Mericans are watery and sour Roma tomatoes, not the thick, sweet San Marzano variety. How to tell? Squeeze one of the San Mericans in your hand, and it’ll burst
everywhere
as if you just unloaded a shotgun on a jar of Prego.)

While you
do
see “San Marzano–style” tomatoes
sold quite frequently
, as this verbiage merely refers to the botanical genus of the tomato and passes muster in the U.S. (somewhat like the general cheese term
“Parmesan” vs.
Parmigiano-Reggiano
, which has its own official minders), straight-up labeling something San Marzano that isn’t would seem to run afoul of false-advertising prohibitions and leave violators open to litigation. (The Consortium might not like it, but it has no power this side of the Atlantic.) So you’d think companies would, you know, avoid doing that. Just stand behind the tomatoes you’ve got.

But there’s one well-known brand that may have thrown caution to the wind. It’s one you’ve
definitely
seen on your grocery store shelves, one that’s available in both old-school Italian delis and high-end grocers alike. And it may have succeeded in duping
everybody
—at least according to the folks suing it for $25 million in damages. In the eyes of these litigants, the dignity of the Rolls-Royce of tomatoes—and the integrity of America’s food system—is on the line. The questions they raise about product quality, corporate transparency, and the weight of authenticity could shape what we stir into our pots and spoon into our mouths for years to come.

In early May, a
lawsuit was filed
against Cento Fine Foods Inc., claiming that the company’s iconic yellow cans of tomatoes sold as San Marzano can’t possibly be the real deal: Cento Fine Foods, a New Jersey–based company, versus Natalie Gianne of Los Angeles and Mike Aldrich of Whittier, California. The crux of the suit is that authentic San Marzano tomatoes possess physical characteristics that render them superior to other tomatoes, and so what’s in Cento’s cans is simply not that. The filing alleges that Cento’s tomatoes “lack the taste, consistency, and other physical characteristics associated by consumers with certified San Marzano Tomatoes.” Thus, they were deemed “unsatisfactory” to the plaintiffs, who never would have paid a premium for them had they known the truth. And naturally (this is America), they’re seeking millions of dollars in flavor harm.

In a statement to Slate, Cento said that it “refutes all of the inaccurate and wrongful claims” in the complaint, calling it “entirely without merit.” The company added that it is seeking a “prompt dismissal” of the suit. The Weston Firm, the lawyers representing the plaintiffs, did not respond to requests for an interview.

If this all sounds kind of hard to prove in court, I’d say you’re right—taste is subjective. But that’s where the Consortium is
supposed
to come in. In 1996, the European Union granted the Consortium the exclusive right to certify and approve San Marzano tomatoes, empowering it to stamp authentic cans with a DOP/PDO label (meaning Product of Designated Origin). When you see
that seal
, you are being promised that what’s inside is verified. And Italians
live
to protect their products. They protect their cheese with DOP labeling, and they even have their own pizza rules: See the
AVPN
(the True Neapolitan Pizza Association), which aims to tell you what a Neapolitan pizza is and, more importantly, what it
isn’t
. In this case, the AVPN, which approves true Neapolitan pizzerias through a rigorous application process, even goes so far as to dispatch
secret agents
to later
spy
on pizzerias. If they aren’t meeting the organization’s high standards, they’re delisted. The Consortium, meanwhile, also inspects, approves, and occasionally delists tomato purveyors with the same critical eye.

So Italy has made rules for its San Marzano tomatoes, and Europe enforces them, at least in theory. Over there, you can’t just 3D-print some tomatoes, put them in a can, and call them San Marzanos. If you did, you would be the subject of police or judicial raids (which, as we’ll see, Cento may know something about). Here in the U.S., however, those rules don’t apply: There is technically no legal protection of that term as such, which is why alleging false advertising or consumer fraud—not getting the product you think you’re paying for—would be a shopper’s only avenue for justice against perceived trickery. This Gianne-Aldrich lawsuit argues that the Consortium is the
only
entity that can certify and approve San Marzano tomatoes grown in Italy, and here’s the thing: Cento is not acknowledged as a legitimate producer by the Consortium. Meanwhile, the company doesn’t even hedge and label its tomatoes San Marzano–
style
. Cento seems to be saying, “Bitch, these
are
San Marzanos,” and then raising its fist in the hope you’ll flinch.

How does Cento do it? Well, according to the lawsuit, it goes
around the Consortium completely
and has a third party certify its tomatoes (a process that, for its part, the company defends
in detail on a dedicated webpage
—one that clarifies, in very small print, that its certification partner is not affiliated with any consortium). That’s why its cans read “Certified” but don’t feature the official DOP seal. Feels shady, no? Why did Cento sidestep the Consortium to begin with? If its product is authentic, why not just obtain that official seal to avoid such headaches?

The answer is where things get
real
juicy: Cento used to be a participant in the Consortium, but over a decade ago it was reportedly ejected from the organization for what certainly looks like—you guessed it—tomato fraud.

In 2010, according to the
current lawsuit
, “police in Salerno obtained a criminal search warrant and raided Cento’s Italian operations.” What they found were 144,000 cans of intentionally mislabeled tomatoes. Manager Giuseppe Napoletano was busted for distributing tomatoes bearing counterfeit DOP labeling. Napoletano was also found to have “forged the signatures of tomato farmers” and to have “repeatedly committed fraud in order to obtain false certifications.” In 2019, an Italian court found Napoletano and his father, an accomplice, guilty of criminal fraud, for which they received fines and were given 26-month suspended sentences. What’s not clear is whether Napoletano did these things at Cento’s direction or acted alone. In my research, I found no evidence that Cento has ever commented on the incident directly, though it has
characterized its exit from the Consortium
as voluntary. Moreover, when I emailed the company to get a comment on Napoletano and the fraud, I heard nothing back.

But San Marzano tomatoes are a moneymaker, a prestige purchase for foodies everywhere. Cento clearly couldn’t lose its cash cow. After exiting the Consortium, though, claiming that it was hawking authentic San Marzanos would be tricky. The solution, according to the lawsuit: Get its tomatoes blessed by a “third-party certifier” called “Agri-Cert.”

“The hell is Agri-Cert?” I asked while reading the official court documents. Soon, I found myself obsessing over the organization’s comings and goings, its staff, its operations. Near as I can tell, the organization (
also known
, and
findable online
, as Bioagricert, which I’ll use going forward) seems to have one gig, and that gig is certification. It stamps products as organic, vegan, regenerative, and the like. But it also certifies
traceability
, meaning it traces an ingredient to its source. The lawsuit against Cento claims that Bioagricert doesn’t “possess the capabilities” to ensure that Cento’s products meet the same specifications as those overseen by the Consortium. Nonetheless, the plaintiffs have submitted photographic evidence of labels and website copy from Cento that call out Bioagricert (styled “Agri-Cert”) as its third-party certifier by name.

So what’s the deal with this mysterious outfit? After weeks of attempting to make contact, I finally got a response from the organization that may have sliced this can wide open. Technical manager Salvatore Sergi explained its relationship to Cento via email, which … well, read it for yourself.

“We do not certify Cento products,” Sergi wrote. “Rather, we certify an Italian company exclusively for the
ISO 22005 standard
(supply chain traceability). The peeled tomatoes are sold in the United States by our certified company inside unlabeled cans. These products are accompanied by a certificate that makes no reference to San Marzano tomatoes, as they are protected by PDO status throughout Europe. Cento applies its own label to the anonymous cans directly in the U.S. (where there is no protection for PDOs), due to the lack of a mutual recognition agreement with the EU.”

He summed it up in one sentence: “In conclusion, our certification is valid only in Italy for our company.”

To recap, Bioagricert certifies the
traceability
of the tomatoes—where they come from, yes (which might be important in, say, an outbreak of foodborne illness), and in this case, Cento’s assertion that they are grown in the correct region. Bioagricert does not, as Cento arguably insinuates with its labeling, certify that these are
true
San Marzanos
with the same detailed Consortium characteristics
(though Cento does claim to
adhere to some of them
, such as length, independently). And it doesn’t certify that because
it literally can’t
. That’s the Consortium’s territory. What’s more, Sergi says, the cans arrive in the U.S. unlabeled. It is only in America that Cento apparently applies the “San Marzano” and “Certified” labels. (Cento’s site claims the company has a “
production facility
” in “Campania’s San Marzano growing region.”)

In any case, you, chef, should not have to be concerned with tracing the international supply chain. You are in the pasta aisle. You pick up one of those yellow cans. There’s no DOP/PDO label; instead, there’s a green ribbon with the word
Certified
struck across it. Confusing? Yes, but as with a lot of products sold in America—from honey to olive oil—our government says you, the consumer, are required to read the fine print. Again, this shouldn’t be an issue:
An entire organization exists to protect San Marzano tomatoes.
Alas, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration doesn’t play by Europe’s rules, and vice versa—according to an investigation by the Italian news station
RAI 3
, Cento’s “San Marzano” tomatoes wouldn’t actually be able to be sold in Italy. It would be illegal to label them as such.

Back across the Atlantic, will Cento finally pay the piper?
Andrich et al. v. Cento Fine Foods Inc.
is still undecided, but I should note that

a much more scathing lawsuit from 2019 was thrown out.
That one claims
that the “Find My Field” tracker on the back of each Cento can—which you can use, CIA-style, to locate the exact coordinates your tomato came from—takes you to the same four fields over and over again. “It is implausible that [the] defendant can sell more San Marzano tomatoes than all other companies in the U.S., combined, and do so by cultivating only four fields,” the suit read.

Implausible indeed, but a New York judge
dismissed the case
, citing that your average person wouldn’t expect San Marzanos to be labeled with the Consortium’s DOP seal: “Here, while there may be ‘some few consumers’ who expect that a San Marzano tomato must be certified by the Consortium, the Court concludes, drawing upon common sense and common experience, that the vast majority of reasonable consumers expect no such thing. It is much more likely that consumers expect tomatoes grown in a region of Italy.”

Perhaps. But one rule I live by is that you should never assume that your audience is dumb. While your average person might be unaware of tomato fraud, people who care about food care about what they’re buying. And with each passing lawsuit and news story, it’s getting harder to buy that we’re getting true San Marzanos at all. In fact, the whole thing has me second-guessing my entire tomato reality.

At this point, you might want me to answer: Which brands of San Marzanos
are
trustworthy? We could consult the Consortium, of course, but I’m starting to think that may not be the right question. That, instead, might be: At the end of the day, when you’re just trying to get dinner on the table in your own kitchen, does any of this alleged tomato fraud even matter? Who, if anybody, is hurt by it?

Well, for starters, I would say that the farmers in the Agro Sarnese-Nocerino are deeply affected. These are generations of San Marzano growers. Many of the farmers are handpicking the tomatoes without using machines. A San Marzano tomato isn’t
only
its genus; its identity is fully wrapped up in the process of growing and harvesting—the region, the soil, and the methods of the farming itself. So long as San Marzano imitators exist, then the work of these hardworking farmers will be undervalued. In addition, Italian brands like Gustarosso, Casa Marrazzo, and Flora, which all adhere to the Consortium’s rules, are undercut by fakes.

But personally speaking, I find myself with a moral dilemma. Because, friends, in my opinion as a food writer and avid pasta-maker, I have to confess: Cento’s “San Marzano” tomatoes are actually
excellent
. They are, near as I can tell, the best available tomato at the most supermarket chains. I’ve
praised Cento in similar terms
in the past, before undertaking this head-spinning journey into the gelatinous placental void, but even knowing what I know now, the fact remains that Cento’s tomatoes are

sweet, savory, deep, and saucy. They are
perfect
for a red sauce. And I’m not the only one who thinks so.

“Before I opened
SheWolf
, I tried over 50 cans of tomatoes,” says Anthony Lombardo, chef and owner of acclaimed Italian restaurants Medusa and Shewolf in Detroit, “and Cento was the best.” That’s high praise not only because of Lombardo’s expert taste as a professional, but also because he has gone further than most in trying to capture that San Marzano essence here at home.

“It’s not like cheese or wine or salami,” he says, “where the DOP or DOC has real validity because it has to be this grape, has to come from this species of animal, or be this exact milk to be called this cheese.” Lombardo’s point is that tomato seeds are easily grown in other climates. Hell, I just saw a sign for “San Marzano tomatoes” at the Santa Monica farmers market, and a woman walking past exclaimed to her partner, “Oooh! San Marzanos!”

Lombardo may or may not have recently smuggled some San Marzano seeds back directly from Italy, which he may or may not grow at an urban farm in Core City, a few miles outside Detroit’s downtown area. He shows me a picture of green plum tomatoes growing on a vine, which he has dubbed “Detroit San Marzanos.” “Literally the opposite of a volcano,” he says of their terroir. I ask Lombardo, who has ventured to Italy numerous times, if his Detroit varietal tastes the same as true, Consortium-certified San Marzanos. “They do not,” he says. So will the tomato police come for Lombardo? Probably not, because of the 80-some tomato plants he has, which are thriving, none of the fruit will be labeled and served as San Marzano tomatoes. Smart man.

“I get why [the Consortium] are pissed. This is, like, their thing,” he admits. “But what do I call this tomato that is clearly the shape and size of a San Marzano?” It’s a great question. San Marzano–style?
Sans
Marzanos? Marzano di Detroit? Is the distinction even important when we live in a country where so many things are mislabeled?

Italians argue that it’s not
just
their genealogy that makes their prize fruits San Marzanos, but their terroir. Their land. It’s that sweet, sweet volcanic soil, and the lore that comes with it, that everyone is so horny for. But more than that, it’s the
culture
of Italy that is worthy of being protected. Their very identity is wrapped up in these tomatoes, and when nefarious operations find a loophole, well, it can feel as if they’re crushing that identity in the palms of their hands like an Italian nonna making red sauce.

I get all that. And yet … I’ll say it again: Cento is currently selling the best can of tomatoes—widely available, anyway—here in the U.S. While arguably not up to Italy’s standards, the tomatoes are still wonderful in flavor and texture. These are fleshy, elongated fruits dunked in a viscous sauce, with a deeply savory flavor one would expect of,
gulp
, San Marzanos. I pick one up, squeeze it softly and let the plum tomato break apart gently in my palm. It doesn’t burst with water. It just sort of dissolves. I eat a piece right from the can. It’s thick and sweet, and perhaps that judge was right: It’s so good that I can’t find it in me to care about where exactly it comes from. And ultimately, I feel a little ashamed about that.

But should I? I understand the value of cultural heritage, and in my heart of hearts, I wish we lived in a world that cared about authenticity, or even just the concept of a shared reality. But I don’t have to tell you that’s not where we are. Do I hope Gianne and Aldrich win their lawsuit? If their claims of fraud are true, then, yes, justice should be served. I’m tired, nay,
exhausted
, of living in a country where we’re constantly questioning what’s real. Where the people in charge have us second-guessing our good sense. I will concede that if this all comes down to a simple taste test, then Cento’s tomatoes are quite good. But I’d be fully willing to trade that quality for some goddamn clarity. For some honesty. For something tangible and trustworthy that I can pick up and hold. Without that, it’s hard to enjoy how good the food may taste.

So, I will simply ask Cento one thing: If the produce in the yellow cans are
not
bona fide San Marzanos, just drop the ruse, man. Drop the wishy-washy “Certified” label, and let the tomatoes do the talking—they can definitely speak for themselves! That way, we can all shut up, stop clogging up the courts, and get back to the thing we want to do most: making some damn
pasta.

Food

Law

Italy

Farming

title: How a Mechanical Watch Keeps Time (Interactive 3D)
content:
Mechanical watches have kept time for 500 years.  Many of their core parts were
invented even earlier for giant cathedral tower clocks before being shrunk into
portable timepieces.  This page explains how a modern one works.  I personally
think it’s fascinating that a well-calibrated, purely mechanical device can keep
time with 99.99% accuracy for $100.  They also changed the world and look good on your wrist.

This web page was partially inspired by Bartosz Ciechanowski’s
Mechanical
Watch
page.  You can think of this
page as a simpler introduction or background.  When you’re finished with this,
that page gives more depth.

You can drag any of the 3D figures to turn them and see the parts from the
side; on a phone, drag sideways.

Hairspring
c. 1675
Start with the part that keeps time.  In 1675 Christiaan Huygens, a Dutch
scientist, invented the
hairspring
. It is a flat spiral of steel ribbon, finer
than a hair. Its outer end is held still, and its inner end is free to
turn. Twist the inner end and let go, and the spiral winds and unwinds, back and
forth, at a steady rate. In this drawing it swings once every two seconds, and
the rest of the watch follows that beat.

Why does a spring swing? Think of a diving board. Bend it down, and
it pushes back: an
elastic restoring force
. Let go, and it does not stop at
straight. It overshoots, bends the other way, and comes back again: it

oscillates
. With no friction, it would oscillate forever.

A hairspring is a diving board rolled up. The board’s rest shape is a
straight line; the hairspring’s is a spiral. Take hold of the slider under
the next picture, and drag it to the right.

“Bend” becomes “wind”, and “straight” becomes “rest”. Now give the
hairspring a twist: drag the slider to wind the spiral away from its rest
shape, and let go.

It pushes back. It overshoots and swings, just as the board did. This one
move is the whole idea of the hairspring.

Balance Wheel
c. 1364
The hairspring is only half of the timekeeper. The other half is the
balance
wheel
.  While most of its mass is around the outside, it is actually fixed to
the spring’s inner end. The spring provides the
restoring force
. The wheel
provides the
mass
and
inertia
.

A hairspring alone would oscillate far too fast to count.  The wheel slows it to a
pace that the gears can count.

Mass also makes the swing steady. Push an empty playground swing, and it
jerks about. Put a child on it and it swings much more gracefully. A heavy wheel
carries its own momentum, so a knock to your wrist, or turning it upside down,
barely changes its rhythm.

How good is it? A well-calibrated mechanical watch, even an everyday
Seiko or Citizen, is about 99.99% accurate.  A day has 86,400 seconds, so that
watch gains or loses about nine seconds a day.

I’m not particularly handy with mechanical things. If I tried to build a table
it would wobble because things would be off by a few percent.  So it kind of
blows my mind that, for $100, I can get a simple, everyday, purely mechanical
system and tweak it to be 99.99% accurate!

Escapement
c. 1275
A second hand that just moves back and forth isn’t very useful.  We need it to
turn one way only.  The
escapement
turns the swing into steps.

The
escape wheel
is being turned by a mechanism we’ll explain soon, so it’s
hidden on this diagram.  Without something to stop it, it would just turn and
turn.

The
pallet fork
stops it.

Its two prongs (called
stones
) stick in the wheel’s teeth: a tooth lands on a
stone, and the wheel stops. Each time the fork rocks, one stone lets a tooth go,
and the other stone catches the next tooth.  The tooth
escapes
, and that is
where the name comes from.

What rocks the fork? The balance does. On its staff is a small
impulse
jewel
, which sits in the notch at the end of the fork.  It’s actually a
synthetic ruby or sapphire, so it really is a jewel, a precious stone.

As the balance swings through the middle, the jewel strikes the fork and
flips it one way. On the swing back, it flips it the other way.

So, at each swing, the balance lets the wheel take one small step.  The step
ends when the next tooth lands on a stone, hard enough to make a sound. This is
the tick and the tock of a watch.

Ticks and Turns
Before we go on, something that trips people up until they think it through. How
long does the second hand take to go once around the dial?

Each tick is one second, and sixty ticks brings it all the way around. So the
second hand makes a complete circle once a minute. A hand is named for what it
counts, not for how long it takes to make a full 360° turn.

Hand

A full turn

Second hand

Once a minute

Minute hand

Once an hour

Hour hand

Twice a day

Gears
Second hand: c. 1670
The escapement gets the escape wheel turning at a precise rate.  But the second
hand must turn once a minute, and the escape wheel turns faster than that. To
convert a faster rotation into a slower one, a watch uses gears: a small gear
that meshes with a big one.

The teeth on the two gears must have the same spacing, so they mesh neatly.
Each tooth fits in a gap of the other gear, so the teeth go past each other one
for one, and both rims move at the same speed.  Four teeth on each gear are
colored. Those four teeth are half of the small gear, but only a quarter of the
big one. So the small gear turns twice for each turn of the big one: twice the
circumference, half the speed.

Now attach the smaller gear (called a
pinion
) to the escape wheel.
The gears do not spin freely any more: they move on one tick at a time, with the
escape wheel. The escapement controls the speed of the whole train of gears.

The big gear pushing the small gear (pinion) is the force turning the escape
wheel.  What turns the big wheel?  That’s a mechanism we’ll explain soon.

In this watch, the big gear (called the
fourth wheel
) turns exactly once a
minute: just what the second hand needs! So the second hand goes on the big
gear’s axle. It is the first part of the watch that we can read.

Gear Train
Minute hand: c. 1656
The second hand turns once a minute. The minute hand must turn once an hour:
sixty times slower. So we could try the same trick, and have a gear that’s 60
times bigger than the small gear.

But there’s a limit to how small you can manufacture the small gear, so
the big gear would be huge.  And it would have a lot of teeth which adds to
the cost.  Plus, it would turn the wrong way, counterclockwise, because every gear
turns the opposite direction from the one it meshes with.

So the watch slows in two stages. The
third wheel
runs 7½ times slower, and
the
center wheel
runs 8 times slower than that.

7½ times 8 is 60, so the center wheel turns once an hour.

The minute hand goes on the center wheel’s axle (
arbor
), in the middle of the dial.
It makes a full turn once an hour.

The center wheel pushes the third wheel which pushes the fourth wheel
which pushes the escape wheel.  Next up, the mechanism that pushes the center
wheel and powers the whole watch.

Mainspring
c. 1430
This is a spiral spring, like the hairspring.  But instead of swinging back and
forth, it does one slow unwind over a day or two. In the illustration above,
it’s at rest.

Below, the outer end is held in place.  Drag the slider to wind it up.  The
spring keeps its length, so its coils draw in toward the center.

When wound away from its rest shape, the dashed line, it pushes back, as the
hairspring does.  A tiny one-way ratchet locks the axle (
arbor
) so it can only
turn one way.  To unwind the mainspring, let go of the outer end by pressing the
button.

The block is gone, and the outer end swings around until the spring lies on its
rest shape again. That fling is the energy that the winding put in.

A watch harnesses that force by attaching the spring’s outer end to a toothed
drum called the
barrel
, invented by Jean-Antoine Lépine around 1760.

As the mainspring pushes the barrel, the barrel’s teeth drive the gear train we
just built.  This is the “hidden mechanism” we mentioned earlier.

Because the ratchet stops the arbor from turning backwards, the spring
has only one way to unwind: by its outer end turning the barrel. Press the
button under the figure, and six hours pass in six seconds. The
barrel turns once, the minute hand six times, and the coils move back out to the
wall. When the spring is completely unwound, the watch stops.

Hour Hand
Hour hand: c. 1350
The hour hand must turn twice a day.  That’s once every twelve hours. Unlike the
60:1, a 12:1 gear is doable.

But the hour hand on that wheel’s axle (
arbor
) is off center!  And it
would run backward (counterclockwise): a pair of meshing gears turn opposite
directions.

So we use the same two-step trick we used for the minute hand.  This
time, 3:1 going out and 4:1 coming back.  3:1 × 4:1 = 12:1.

The hour hand goes on the hour wheel, in the middle, under the minute
hand, attached to a hollow tube (pipe) that slips
over
the minute hand’s axle.
It turns clockwise, twice a day.

Recap
And that’s how a mechanical watch works!

Here’s a recap, retracing our steps in reverse, from the hour hand to the
hairspring. The tour plays by itself, like a short film. The time scale in the
corner says how much faster than real time each segment runs.

The hour hand is driven by a pair of gears totaling 12:1.

Abstract:
A Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergence is never negative, yet PyTorch users have reported negative values for years, and the standard advice is to clamp them at zero. The sign is only the visible part of a silent failure. Many machine-learning applications compare nearby distributions, where conventional KL formulas lose accuracy. On 8.5 million inputs with certified references across 18 closed-form KL families and F.kl_div, we find widespread errors in values and gradients on CPU and GPU. Among scalar families in ordinary parameter ranges, over 85% of FP32 values have at least 1% relative error near KL 10^(-7) (FP16: 10^(-3)), and about 30% become negative at smaller divergences. More precision is not the cure: evaluated one precision higher, the same formulas still leave 7--51% of FP32 values significantly wrong for 22 of 23 configurations. Stable closed-form decompositions, compensated arithmetic, and analytic gradients remove over 97% of significant errors in the working format. Strict repairs eliminate significant errors on 7.2 million scored closed-form samples and correctly round all 567 million scored F.kl_div components. The errors affect parameter fitting, Bayesian decisions, identical-start distillation (up to 97% top-1 disagreement), KL-based layer rankings in a quantized LLM, and 19--59% of GPT-2 circuit edge scores. With the repaired code they all but vanish. Code and data:
