title: The new set of problems for engineers to solve
content:
Back
A lot of software engineers are going through what can only be described as an identity crisis. The job has changed a lot. Some are depressed, others are having the time of their lives. There's a really specific thing I see happening that makes me really excited for what engineering looks like over the next, call it a year or two - AI just isn't going to be able to create the incredible outcomes it's capable of creating unless software engineers solve problems to make it possible. This is existential, which is honestly a lot of fun, so it's a pretty incredible time to be a software engineer.

Multiagent systems are creating these problems

Agents started out as basic, human in the loop chats. Then models got better at running for longer on harder problems, and agentic systems started moving to the cloud. While that was happening, models have started to get better at working together, and people have built basic multiagent systems. Like an orchestrator that spawns some subagents for a given task, or giving agents jobs other than executing to improve outcomes, like grading or advising or dreaming.

Now, some folks are starting to build truly amazing multiagent systems to tackle the world's hardest and most important problems, like serious research, discovery, and hardware design. Picture thousands of agents, persistently working towards these outcomes. This comes with a new set of software engineering problems that we're already seeing crop up.

Infrastructure needs to evolve to handle burstier workloads. We need proper authentication and authorization to identify agents, let them work together, enable them to take the actions they should, and prevent them from taking the actions they shouldn't. Security and proper isolation are critical for untrusted code and content. And we've gotta have monitoring and the ability to stop a system in its tracks when it's veering into the wrong territory.

Models will keep getting better, and these types of multiagent systems will become really powerful. But software engineers have to solve all these problems if we're going to actually unlock that power and enable the world to trust it to create good outcomes like cured diseases rather than bad outcomes.

The problems

Infrastructure needs to evolve

The software industry has been building on Kubernetes, which was designed for stateless, replicated apps or stable numbered sets of stateful pods. Agents are totally different. They're essentially isolated, stateful, single-instance workloads. They can go idle for arbitrary amounts of time between bits of work, and they spend a lot of time waiting on tools, model inference, other agents, or human input. Some workloads need fast startup times, others need to avoid wasting compute, and others need crazy scale. Amazing engineers are pushing hard on this problem space - like AI infra companies building new filesystems and sandboxing offerings, and the Google team building Agent Substrate as a new runtime. There's a ton left to figure out.

Identity and access

There are problems to solve in agent authentication - identifying an agent that took an action. This area has the benefit of the building blocks that have been built and hardened from the microservices world, like workload identity with short-lived certs rather than static keys, and folks are beginning to apply these concepts to agents.

Agent authorization as a problem space is much more wide open - what do you allow an agent to do? Many agents work on behalf of a human, and use that human's identity and credentials to access various systems and take actions. There's already a problem in there, which is identifying that it was the agent and not the actual human who took an action. But there are deeper problems in this on-behalf-of (OBO) setup, like consent. If multiagent systems are working for weeks, how does the human meaningfully approve what their agent can do? Agentic platform features like auto approval for tool calls helps, but there's deeper permissioning needed to get this right at high scale. And then we have agents working with their own identity, which is even less solved, and how we apply that to agents working together - how does an agent trust another agent that asked it for something?

Security and isolation

Over the past few months and especially in the past couple weeks, we've seen vulnerabilities surfacing faster than the industry can patch them, much of it in critical core software that many systems rely on. Now think about thousands of persistent agents running on top of that core software, writing untrusted code and reading untrusted content. Those unpatched vulns get a lot more dangerous in that world, and one of the most important things for software engineers to do is get creative about how to harden that software - kernels, browsers, runtimes, and common libraries.

Multiagent systems add another twist. A compromised agent could pass injected instructions to other agents it's working with, and those instructions could end up in memory for future agents to accidentally trust. Blast radius gets real - how much of the multiagent system is at risk when that first agent got compromised? Isolation becomes important in that world - agents should use strongly isolated sandboxed execution environments to take actions. I wrote a bit about that
here
.

Monitoring and halting

Lastly, we need the tools to make sure these multiagent systems are working in a positive direction, and that we catch them and cut them off if they're not. We need OTel tracing across agents, and to ensure that an agent can never modify its own trace or another agent's trace. We need kill switches that monitoring can trigger, that truly stop the whole system at once and cut off its creds. Really the hard part is how to know when the system is going in the wrong direction. Well-intentioned persistence to solve a problem can look a lot like maliciousness - repeated attempts to reach a domain that isn't on its allowlist, for example.

Software engineers should be excited

This is for the engineers feeling an identity crisis because they think their knowledge and skills won't be important - you and your skills can be the difference in whether or not these problems get tackled and multiagent systems can solve the world's hardest problems. You can and should go deep in these domains, learn new things, and form opinions. So much of this problem space is wide open for new solutions. It's an incredibly exciting time to put your skills to work.

title: The search for a top dark matter candidate
content:
Scientists at Italy’s Gran Sasso National Laboratory are working to confirm September’s potential dark matter detection.

TQB1 via Wikimedia Commons under CC BY-SA 3.0

Italy’s Gran Sasso National Laboratory is not a bad place to fret over the state of your career. The lab’s panoramic views of white-capped mountains and endless greenery are nearly inescapable. Physicists fuel their work with sharp espressos, rather than the watery coffee many Americans accept.

The lab also descends into the Gran Sasso mountain, forming one of the world’s largest underground research centers. Nestled beneath 4,600 feet of rock is an array of particle detectors. Thanks to the mountain’s thick skin, these instruments are shielded from
cosmic rays
, the high-energy particles
produced
by black holes, exploding stars and even our own sun. In the quiet depths of this laboratory, physicists hope to pick up on much more elusive particles—including dark matter.

For the past few decades, scientists have been hunting for dark matter, the invisible substance that makes up
85 percent of the matter
in our universe. One primary target has been weakly interacting massive particles, or
WIMPs
—a hypothesized candidate for dark matter that
passes through normal matter
with barely a trace. Massive underground detectors like those at Gran Sasso are leading the search.

But no one has definitively found a WIMP, so no one is sure that they exist—and challenges to spotting them are building. As detectors get more sensitive, new background signals are beginning to cloud them, reducing the odds of catching WIMPs. Funding is growing more precarious, leaving many wondering how many years this endeavor has left.

When I visited the lab in May, the mood among some of these physicists was muted. “Of course, we were a bit more depressed,” reflects physicist
Paolo Salomone
, laughing. Despite his clear enthusiasm for the dark matter hunt, Salomone, a strikingly blue-eyed University of Chicago postdoctoral scholar, knew he was entering a field some might diagnose as terminal.

Then, in September, a pinprick of hope emerged. An American lab also searching for WIMPs released a
preprint paper
detailing a single—but intriguing—data point, rising above the expected background signals. Maybe, just maybe, it was
dark matter
.

Salomone was on vacation in Corsica when his phone started blowing up. Text notifications from physicist friends streamed in, asking him if he’d seen the news. “I was there on the beach trying to look at my phone, trying to zoom in on the plot,” he says. Watching the faraway excitement, he says, “I felt like I was missing out a lot.”

The finding was not a definite dark matter detection—one data point isn’t nearly enough to count as a discovery. Still, the result spawned
headlines across the globe
, a torrent of preprint papers and newfound hope for many physicists in search of WIMPs.

The question, now, is what’s next. Will this life raft be enough to overcome the field’s growing challenges? And will the few other detectors with similar sensitivity—most notably, one at Gran Sasso—be able to replicate the signal?

Nearly a century ago, Swiss astronomer
Fritz Zwicky
noticed a group of galaxies with some moving so quickly that they should have escaped the cluster’s gravity and flown apart. He theorized that some invisible material was gluing them together. Since then, scientists have
accrued more evidence
for this dark matter: stars speeding
precipitously fast
around a galaxy’s rim; unexpectedly strong
gravitational lensing
, in which distant light is bent by extreme gravity.

To explain it all, astrophysicists dreamed up WIMPs in the
1980s
. As far as subatomic particles go, these would be relatively massive. In theory, they glide through space, on occasion lightly interacting with matter. Physicists have a pretty good sense of the density of dark matter scattered throughout our universe, but not much more about it. “It opens the possibility of having a lot of light particles or very few heavy particles,” says Salomone.

Directly detecting WIMPs, then, could clue us into the mass of individual dark matter particles and the number of them floating around, as well as how strongly these particles interact with normal matter. But finding them has been a challenge. Not only are physicists searching through a vast plain of possibilities, but they’re also looking for incredibly rare interactions that require extreme care in detection.

The smallest impurities can anger a detector. To illustrate the point,
Marcello Messina
, the technical coordinator for Gran Sasso’s
XENONnT experiment
, brought up the humble banana. While we don’t tend to think of a banana as radioactive, the fruits are rich in potassium, leading to a tiny shower of particle decays. “A banana can completely destroy our data table,” he said.

Messina was my guide for the day at Gran Sasso, driving me six miles through one of Italy’s longest tunnels and into the mossy interior of the mountain. He led me through the lab’s sterile halls, ending up at his even more sterile detector.

The drive to Gran Sasso National Laboratory, which is partially located inside a mountain, offers stunning views of the Italian landscape.

Georgia Michelman

Messina’s XENONnT experiment is a hulking cylinder that holds a chamber of nearly 9.5 tons of xenon—mostly liquid—inside. The hope is that when a WIMP flies into the detector, it jostles one of the large and stable xenon atoms, which would in turn
shoot out
electrons and a light ray, alerting sensors to the strange particle’s presence.

XENONnT, which has been collecting data for around six years, is the strapping
great-grandchild
of the team’s original 2006 prototype. “XENON, for almost all its life, provided the most sensitive results,” Messina told me. “It was definitely leading the field.” Today, a few more rivals—like the American detector—have emerged.

XENON scientists inside part of the detector

The XENON collaboration

We walked past another device that looked like a gigantic red Lego: a new detector Salomone is helping to build,
DarkSide-20k
, which will use a chamber of around 55 tons of argon instead of xenon. This enormous detector will reach a similar sensitivity to XENONnT and is set to begin collecting data in 2028.

Despite their materials’ purity, physicists expect some level of background fuzz—mainly radioactive decay products—and predict what that will look like. Sometimes, though, this “background” can behave in unexpected ways, so physicists must have a high bar for what anomalies in their data to take seriously.

Messina showed me a kind of memento mori for physicists: the latest generation of the
DAMA experiment
, which made a claim of dark matter detection that has been dismissed by most of the community.

In 1997, DAMA, which is made up of sodium iodide crystals,
detected
a signal that varied yearly, swooping in every summer—just as dark matter was expected to do. But while the team has continued to
stand by
their results, other experiments later ruled this out.

After DAMA’s false alarm, “I think people are just very cautious now,” says
Ina Sarcevic
, a physicist at the University of Arizona.

Despite the fear of more detector-cried-wolf scenarios, many physicists quickly pulled together theories to explain September’s announcement of a possible detection, Sarcevic says. The signal came out of South Dakota’s
LUX-ZEPLIN
(LZ) experiment, which is currently the world’s largest WIMP detector.

Physicist
Richard Gaitskell
, LZ’s spokesperson, has been searching for dark matter for nearly 40 years, starting with a detector “barely bigger than the top of my thumb,” he says. LZ, on the other hand, is a nine-foot-tall cylinder containing around 11 tons of xenon, packed within a 20-foot-tall outer structure.

To take advantage of LZ’s whopping size and sensitivity, Gaitskell says, the team “decided to really aggressively push” beyond the usual search parameters.

The longstanding assumption in these experiments has been that WIMPs swoop in at relatively low energies and bounce off the xenon like billiard balls. In this case, when a WIMP collides with a xenon nucleus, it scatters the atom’s protons and neutrons in what’s called a “coherent” manner, where their resulting energies add up, amplifying the signal. But if WIMPs were to barrel in at higher energies, the particles would scatter in a trickier way to track.

It was the switch to searching for these higher-energy collisions that led to LZ’s unusual detection. The signal also hinted that particles of dark matter would be quite heavy and collide with matter in a different way than many expected. Rather than rebounding like billiard balls, the WIMP may lose some energy (and mass) in the crash, exiting as a different, slimmer form of dark matter.

Notably, this detection couldn’t be explained by known forms of background events, like stray neutrons. The signal, then, could be dark matter, but it may also be a previously unknown type of background.

In announcing this event, Gaitskell says, the team was looking for input from the wider community, as they continue to pore through their own data. And input he did receive.

Amid the excitement and wave of preprint papers, though, many have retained a sense of caution. Messina says he was initially skeptical of the single data point. “The immediate reaction was, ‘Come on, one event?’” he says. But he recognized XENONnT’s potentially crucial role in the next step toward discovery.

Given their detector’s comparable sensitivity, the team is now rushing to replicate the finding, looking through the past two years of their own data for signals that chime with the American detection. Or they could find nothing.

Either way, Messina would like to let the team’s data analysis do the talking, rather than get too excited now. They hope to release a paper in the next few months. “Data matters,” Messina says. “All the rest is fake.”

The XENONnT detector alongside its service building, which keeps the experiment purified and running

The XENON collaboration

When Messina led me around in the spring, he wasn’t optimistic about the future of his field. He was continuing to support the search for dark matter with XENONnT, but he had also been devoting time to detecting
neutrinos
, another kind of subatomic particle generated by stars, radioactive decay and the Big Bang. “Many people like me are thinking, ‘You know what, I want to investigate different fields,’” he said.

Some WIMP proponents point out that even though the detectors haven’t found one of these fabled particles, they have made a less obvious kind of progress over the decades. In their searches, scientists have
ruled out
many potential WIMP masses and densities, ticking away at the options and possibly making it easier to zero in on their true properties in the future.

But to many onlookers—including the funding bodies that control cash flow—the lack of clear progress in particle physics has been disappointing. “It’s quite hard to convince politicians to support you if you have a significant discovery each 30 years,” Messina said.

On top of the current fragile science funding ecosystem in the United States, he wasn’t sure how much more time WIMP detection had. He doubted the proposed next-generation detector,
XLZD
—which would dwarf LZ and XENON and merge the collaborations—would move forward.

After LZ’s finding, though, Messina’s tune has changed. While he still stresses the uncertainty that this signal will lead to a discovery, he believes it has imparted “some momentum” back into WIMPs.

Many physicists still see more promise in other dark matter models—the hypothetical WIMPs might not be the best (or only) explanation.

Ben Safdi
, a theoretical physicist at the University of California, Berkeley, says that LZ’s detection may well be dark matter, but his initial excitement has waned. At first, the signal seemed to match an existing theory for WIMP behavior, but several preprint papers—including
one of his
—challenged this idea. “My personal belief that it is dark matter has gone down,” he says.

Safdi divides his research between WIMPs and a different dark matter candidate called axions. These theorized particles would move in a “continuous, almost fluid” wave through the universe, he says. Individually, axions would be super light—much less massive than WIMPs—but together, they could
account for the missing mass of dark matter
.

Attention to axions has surged as people have
grown tired of WIMPs
. While Safdi still thinks the WIMP hunt is worth continuing, “my heart is in axions,” he says.

Did you know? Other strategies to find WIMPs

Some scientists hope to indirectly detect WIMPs by
looking for neutrinos
produced when they collide with their proposed
antimatter
counterpart and annihilate.

Others are hoping to
create WIMPs
. According to some
theories
, WIMPs might be produced by energetic collisions between normal particles.

Even if interest in WIMP detection is revitalized, technological challenges remain. One specter still haunting the field is a fog of neutrinos that’s threatening to descend on the instruments.

With increased sensitivity, the detectors are starting to pick up the constant swarm of neutrinos. These tiny particles don’t interact much with matter—
trillions
move through your body every second—but they can clutter data taken by detectors that are precise enough to notice them. As this
neutrino fog
wafts in, potential WIMP signals could get lost in the haze. XENONnT
reported
its first glimpses of the fog in 2024.

This isn’t a huge problem for the detectors yet, and not everyone agrees it will be soon. But once neutrinos start meaningfully gumming up the signal, scientists don’t know what they’ll do.

Ronald Walsworth
’s group is experimenting with a workaround: tracing the direction of incoming particles. WIMPs are expected to flood in like a “headwind” against the solar system’s path through the galaxy, he says. On the other hand, a lot of neutrinos emanate from the direction of
the sun
, produced by the churn of fusion.

A sea of liquid xenon functions “like an antenna,” says
Daniel Ang
, a quantum scientist in Walsworth’s group. The flash of light only clues scientists into a particle’s collision—not the direction it rode in. So to trace a signal’s source, physicists might have to take a whole new approach.

Walsworth decided to try this by using a more glamorous substance:
diamonds
. From his previous work, he knew that when particles cut through diamond crystals, they leave behind a finely detailed track—so their incoming direction is clear. “That’s the grandiose idea we had,” says Walsworth, a quantum physicist at the University of Maryland.

But the team has only tested their blinged-out detector on a small scale, and getting the funds to go bigger will be a challenge—especially given the “sagging of enthusiasm” for WIMPs, Walsworth says.

Once Salomone, the postdoc, got back from vacation, his excitement about LZ’s signal was slightly tempered by his boss, he says. “He was, of course, more skeptical and less enthusiastic than me.”

But even among Salomone’s liquid argon detector community, scientists are paying serious attention to the result. His collaboration has a regular meeting, which only one or two dozen people usually show up to. But at a recent one, some 100 people attended. Even people who never participated were interjecting with ideas, he says.

Salomone’s workdays are much like before, continuing to help build the DarkSide-20k detector, placing orders for special screws and popping over to the café for an espresso. But he feels a renewed excitement about the theory behind his daily tasks.

“You’re still doing what you were doing before but with a different mind-set,” he says. “Spending more time trying to read papers, spending more time trying to be even a better physicist, so that’s what I’m really happy about.”

Georgia Michelman
is a New York-based science and health journalist and
Smithsonian
magazine’s current intern from the 2026 class of New York University’s Science, Health and Environmental Reporting Program. Her work has appeared in
Science
,
Knowable Magazine
,
Live Science
and elsewhere.

title: Three LLM inflection points in twelve months
content:
I gave a keynote at the
AI Engineer Code Summit
a couple of weeks ago, constructed around the idea that there have been three significant inflection points in the abilities of LLMs and coding agents in the past twelve months.

Here's
the video
of the talk. In this post I'm going to pull out the major inflection point theme and interrogate it more deeply.

Coding agents in November 2025

Today, November 24th 2026, is the one year anniversary of the release of
Claude Opus 4.5
. With hindsight, this was a consequential model.

In the Opus 4.5 announcement, Anthropic said:

Testers noted that Claude Opus 4.5 handles ambiguity and reasons about tradeoffs without hand-holding. They told us that, when pointed at a complex, multi-system bug, Opus 4.5 figures out the fix. They said that tasks that were near-impossible for Sonnet 4.5 just a few weeks ago are now within reach.

This held up.

Claude Code was 9 months old at that point, having been
introduced alongside Claude 3.7 Sonnet
on February 24th, 2025.

Opus 4.5 was the first model I had used with Claude Code where the default result was generally the right thing. I hadn't been using Claude Code as a daily driver because it didn't feel reliable enough - I had to correct it often enough that it didn't feel like a clear accelerant.

The new Opus changed that. For most of the coding problems I faced on a daily basis, Opus would
get them right
. It was clearly faster than working through the problems myself.

Also in November, OpenAI released GPT-5.1 Instant, GPT-5.1 Thinking, GPT-5.1-Codex, and GPT-5.1-Codex-Max. These had a similar effect on their Codex coding agent: it became reliably useful for many of my coding tasks.

The timing was convenient, because the December holidays were upon us. A lot of people, myself included, spent December tinkering with these new tools to see what they could do. By January we were ready to use them for our actual work.

Fable class models in June/July

We got our first hint of Claude Fable in April, when Anthropic announced Claude Mythos and
said that it was
too dangerous
to release
, due to its improved cybersecurity capabilities. Mythos was a model that could not just find security vulnerabilities, it could also figure out how to exploit them.

In June we got to see how good that model was for ourselves, with the release of Claude Fable 5 - a defanged Mythos, that would solve most problems but would actively block you from using it for security work.

After three glorious days... the US government took it away from us. Fable 5 was placed under export controls that effectively banned the model. We wouldn't get it back until July 1st.

For me, Fable was an inflection point because it introduced us to what I now think of as
Fable class models
. My definition of these:

In June I wrote about how
Claude Fable is relentlessly proactive
, after I asked it to help fix a display glitch in Safari and it spun up its own
pyobjc-framework-Quartz
screenshot mechanism and a CORS-enabled localhost logging server to help resolve the bug.

A more recent example of the power of Fable class models is my
mysterious beep finder
from a couple of weeks ago. I gave Opus 5.5 and then Fable 5.2 access to five WebAudio microphones in a room full of boxes and it was able to triangulate the source of an infuriating mysterious beep to within about 40cm.

Give it a goal, give it the right tools, and watch it cook.

I'd currently class Claude Fable 5, 5.1, 5.2 and Claude Opus 5.5 as Fable class (I think of Opus 5.5 as "cheap Fable"). GPT-6 Astra got there for me too, and I think the new Gemini 4 Neon may count as well.

These now represent the baseline for what I expect from a frontier model.

3D modeling and game development in September/October

Something interesting happened with frontier LLMs over just the past four months: they got
really good
at 3D modeling. Set them up
with Blender
or ask them to write Three.js code and they'll produce credible models of almost anything you ask for.

I first noticed this with Claude Fable 5, but it really kicked into gear with Opus 5.5, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and most recently the Gemini 4 family. Here's
Gemini 4 Neon's attempt
at "Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and stomps around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping data", for example.

3D spatial awareness is crucial if you want to use vision LLMs for robotics. I don't know if 3D modeling capabilities are a side-effect of the labs focusing on that or vice-versa.

Back in August I experimented with
having Fable 5 build me a raccoon heist game
. It had 3D graphics, looked like a game, and played really poorly. GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra
did a much better job
but the game itself was still pretty dull after the first 90 seconds of play.

I was somewhat relieved that designing a game that was
fun
appeared to remain a uniquely human pursuit. I even used that
in a talk
in September to reassure people that us humans still had a role to play!

Then, I tried telling Claude Opus 5.5 "This game isn't fun enough yet. Make it a LOT more fun."
And it worked
. My Command & Conquer-style RTS went from boring to deeply entertaining overnight, after Opus spent 12 hours playtesting new features and rebalancing the gameplay.

Opus 5.5 was the first model I'd used that appeared to understand fun. I've since worked on
several little game projects
where prompts like "Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful" produced results that kept me engaged for significant amounts of time.

Opus 5.5 came out on September 22nd, 2026. I've been to two different conferences since then where people showed me game projects they'd been working on that really did feel like proper, worthwhile games.

The indie games scene has descended into a
full-blown culture war
over AI-assisted programming. A lot of people are calling GTA VI
the last pre-generative AI blockbuster
.

It feels like another inflection point to me.

Is Fable 5.2 an inflection point too?

I'm still trying to decide if Fable 5.2 represents a new inflection point, or just another incremental improvement.

I'm getting
so much
done with that model right now!

It seems to have taste that almost exactly matches my own. I have been burning through all sorts of gnarly problems that I've been thinking about (or procrastinating on) for several years now. The release notes for Datasette
1.0a42
,
1.0a43
, and
1.0a44
- plus LLM
0.37
,
0.37.1
,
0.37.2
,
0.37.3
, and
0.38
-
all in the last three weeks
, represent a flood of fixes, features and improvements.

If this does represent an inflection point, the key feature seems to be that
if you can imagine and then clearly describe a piece of software, Fable can build it
. That's a wild thing to say, but it matches my experience over the past few weeks.

Software development has transformed beyond recognition in the last year. I don't think I'll ever go back to typing most of my code by hand.

title: Clay helps sales teams win with Codex and ChatGPT
content:
November 24, 2026
Clay helps sales teams win with Codex and ChatGPT
ChatGPT and Codex integrations help Clay users research deals and turn data into go-to-market plays, and GPT‑6 models handle the reasoning.
Start building with OpenAI
Company size:
Startup
Region:
North America
Industry:
Technology
Products:
API, Codex, ChatGPT
Even when sales teams have plenty of data about a prospect, they can still struggle to understand what matters most and develop a winning pitch.
Clay
⁠
(opens in a new window)
is a self-learning revenue engine designed to help. Using GPT‑6 Astra, GPT‑6 Sol, and other models, Clay enables users to build lists of companies and people, enrich those records using agents, and use that information in go-to-market plays.
Clay also brings these capabilities to where customers are already working with plugins for Codex and ChatGPT, making it easier to create and run go-to-market workflows and research accounts and deals.
“Clay in ChatGPT gives sales reps a way to understand more about the customers they’re trying to sell to. It brings all of that rich context to the places they’re already working.”
—Jeff Barg, Head of AI, Clay
Giving sales reps more context to act on
Clay’s Codex integration lets builders create and run go-to-market plays in Codex, while giving sales reps access to data they can use to research an account or understand a deal they’re trying to close.
Jeff has seen reps combine information from their own systems and public datasets to determine how to best communicate their product’s value to a customer. “Customers love using Codex for a lot of different tasks in sales,” he says. “We’ve seen the best sales reps be the most empowered by this.”
Clay’s ChatGPT plugin brings the same customer data into another tool reps already use, helping them learn more about prospects without leaving ChatGPT. Jeff says, “It’s been a big success.”
Matching intelligence and cost to the task
OpenAI models power Claygent’s research, qualification, enrichment, and signal detection, as well as the agent that helps users build workflows and coordinate other Clay agents.
Clay uses GPT‑6 Sol as its primary model, with GPT‑6 Astra for harder tasks and GPT‑6 Luna for cost-sensitive work. That range supports background research and copywriting as well as agents that users work with directly.
“GPT-6 Sol is a really great model for go-to-market plays. It has really good intuition and can build long-horizon, outcome-based go-to-market tasks.”
—Jeff Barg, Head of AI, Clay
The Responses API lets Clay use different levels of intelligence and cost through the same interface. “Having the same Responses API across the different price points is something that’s super appealing to us with OpenAI models,” said Jeff.
Building end-to-end plays that self-improve over time
GPT‑6 Astra also helps Jeff build and test software. He used to spend much of his time manually checking features he had built; now he can ask GPT‑6 Astra to handle more of that work.
He explains, “GPT‑6 Astra really changed how I build software because it fully closed the loop on the engineering process. Now I can have Astra write code, add tests, and then actually run the tests and test the feature and record that and upload that in the PR. It simplifies my life a lot.”
For Clay’s customers, Jeff sees GPT‑Live‑1 as a way to use Clay and Codex by voice and help prospects learn about a product. Clay is working on inbound sales development features that would let an agent show a product or service to a prospect. He also sees the Decisions API as another way to integrate models into Clay and open up new use cases.
Clay’s ambition is to carry go-to-market workflows from start to finish, with agents that improve as they learn from the results. For Jeff, the goal is to empower builders “to bring the same shift that happened in software engineering to go-to-market.”

title: Art of play in the age of AI
content:
As kids, we spent hours tinkering and building and just messing with things. As an adult, I could watch my own young kiddos figure out how certain shapes and movement work all day. Through that play, we improved our problem-solving and language skills, and it’s probably not a stretch to say it was good for our early engineering skills.

In this era of development now, we’re starting to get a taste of that again. We’re experimenting more, and taking in more changes, because it’s all new!

For the last four years at GitHub Universe, we’ve had hackable conference badges. What started as a simple e-ink display for your name and job title morphed into a labor of love for
Martin Woodward
, VP of Developer Relations. This year, the badge evolved into a device with a color screen, rechargeable battery, accelerometer sensors, and touch-sensitive gaming controls.

The tinkering we’ve seen with the badges has been amazing.

Hacking the GitHub Universe Badge with these 3 apps that I made!!

#GitHubUniverse https://t.co/Qy5wYPqXf5
— Connie Xu (@conniecodes)
October 28, 2026

you can play octo drive on your @github universe badge!

repo - https://t.co/DrYkhjvMVt https://t.co/S6jVwxPdEY
— Rishab Kumar (@rishabincloud)
October 27, 2026

Coding needs room for play

According to the
Octoverse
report, 40% of pull requests were started by agents by September. That’s a big jump from the 17% we saw in March, which was already a pretty high number.

With that kind of pace of change, it’s easy to feel unsteady thinking about our coding skills that we’ve been honing as an industry for decades. At the same time, one might argue that the tools and changes in front of us offer more room for experimentation and creativity!

AI can turn our ideas into working code faster than ever before. We can build things just because we’re curious to see if it’ll work, without the burden of figuring out every single step before getting started. The learning is moving to different parts of the building timeline.

As Martin said in our GitHub Podcast episode, “Give yourself permission to play, call it learning,” but with the caveat that you should time-box it so that you don’t spend too much time perfecting it. Know when to stop, ship, and share.

You don’t need a big idea to start

What’s really exciting is how the scope of projects have changed. With AI tooling, we don’t have to build with everyone in mind every time (not that we necessarily did before, but it was definitely a default mindset for the industry). We can build things way more often for our exact use cases. It could “just work on my machine” and be feature-complete!

At the GitHub Universe closing keynote, Martin wanted to teach himself machine learning, so he built himself a pedometer onto his conference badge. He used Copilot to collect movement data from the badge’s accelerometer, trained a simple machine-learning model in his browser, and deployed it to the badge. Then he walked around to test whether it could tell the difference between walking, standing still, and fidgeting.

Imagine just a year or two ago wanting to dabble with machine learning. You totally could have! But for the average developer, that’s a daunting task. The barrier to entry for so many tougher concepts has gotten lower, and that means more people can experiment and have fun with any device they can think of, from a conference badge to a smart picture frame to a home TV.

AI with oversight

AI is top of mind all the time right now, but you are a part of the story, too.

In order to scale with AI, we need human judgement. We can see the AI tells in writing (“that’s the real unlock!”), in imagery (the fonts, man), or in code (commenting code blocks that have never been commented before). We need to keep the feedback loop, to be able to inspect, debug, and test what the agent produced, and to make whatever we’re building our own.

Be kind, keep maintainers in mind

It’s really fun to share your experiments with the world, but contributing to existing open source projects take a bit more consideration than that. Both our podcast episode and the keynote addressed this. We’re seeing maintainers get absolutely hammered with AI-powered contributions to their repositories, which adds a
lot
to the maintenance burden.

Efforts need to be made by all of us,
like the one shared here
, to help ease burdens for maintainers.

As Martin explained in the keynote, “Open source is the freedom to inspect, to remix, and to share without asking for permission. But it’s not the freedom to impose your will on others.”

Forking a repository gives you room to explore your own ideas, and there’s a really fun, exciting power in that. But before you impose those ideas on others and send them to the main repository, make sure you:

Read the contribution guidelines

Check existing issues

Understand what the project needs

Respecting that work helps keep open source manageable (and even enjoyable) for the people looking after it.

Now it’s your turn

We answered the perennial question on our badge, “But can it run Doom?” Why yes, yes it does.
Give it a go on our virtual badge
, and try tinkering on it yourself.

Then get your hands on your own badge
. We made some extra badges just for you. Order yours today, then tell us what you’ll be building. Plus, use code
FREESHIPBLOG26
for free standard shipping through December 1, 2026.

Subscribe to the GitHub Podcast >

title: How to choose the next safe step in application modernization
content:
A request to modernize an application often starts with a technology question: Which framework should replace the old one? Before you choose, find out what still works. Then collect evidence that can act as a regression net for that behavior and show where modernization is necessary.

I used an evidence-first method on four public applications, from a small Node.js game to a large Java enterprise resource planning (ERP) application. Each needed a different treatment, but the way I collected evidence, chose the next experiment, and decided on possible proof points was repeatable.

This post walks through that process so you can apply it to one application of your own. It also shows how to encode the procedure in a
GitHub Copilot agent skill
while keeping architectural judgment with the people responsible for the system.

Build evidence before choosing a target

The label on an application rarely tells you enough. “Java microservices” doesn’t tell you which Java Development Kit (JDK) runs in production, where that version is pinned, whether the tests execute, or which interfaces other systems depend on. “Legacy monolith” doesn’t tell you whether the business core is broken or whether one retired platform dependency prevents the application from starting.

Before you recommend a change, build a small evidence inventory:

Manifests, lockfiles, entry points, and deployable components

Verified commands for installing, building, testing, packaging, and running

Runtime pins in containers, CI workflows, deployment files, and developer tooling

External contracts such as APIs, database behavior, file formats, and user workflows

End-of-life frameworks and dependencies, with evidence that the application still uses them

Record uncertainty while you work. I use three simple labels: documented, inferred, and unverified. If two files disagree about the Java version, resolve the contradiction. If you can’t determine whether a CI check blocks merges, say so. Record the unknown rather than treating a guess as a finding.

That inventory gives you something concrete to review with the people who own the application before you propose changes.

Choose the least disruptive treatment that works

Once you understand the application, make the decision per component. A single system can contain code that should stay, dependencies that should be swapped, and one subsystem that genuinely needs a rewrite.

First, check whether a capability is still needed. Remove it only after verifying that it is unused or superseded and confirming that decision with its owner. Removal is a separate decision, and it’s not necessarily the most disruptive one.

For a capability you still need, start with the option that changes the least:

Keep it.
Supported code that still fits the job doesn’t need a modernization story.

Upgrade it.
Move to a supported major version and fix the breaking changes.

Swap it.
Replace an abandoned dependency while preserving the existing design.

Wrap it.
Stabilize a useful interface and replace the internals in increments.

Rewrite it.
Use this when no responsible upgrade path exists or the architecture cannot meet the requirement.

This is a decision order, not a universal ranking of effort or risk. Ask what evidence justifies choosing a more disruptive option. “The code is old” is not enough. A known vulnerability with no patched release for the pinned version, a dependency that fails on the required runtime, or a measured reliability target the current design cannot meet can justify escalation.

Decide what proof is possible

The next question is whether the component can run well enough to produce evidence, even if the legacy CI pipeline is not green.

Run a time-boxed feasibility check. Try to install dependencies, build on an available toolchain, start the component, and execute at least one meaningful test. Stop when the time box expires. The result sends you down one of two paths.

Capture behavior, then upgrade.
Use this path when the old application can still run at an acceptable cost. Record its externally visible behavior, fix the test harness where practical, and use those checks to verify the upgrade.

Build a small modern slice first.
Use this path when the old component cannot run until you have already changed it. Move the thinnest useful workflow to supported technology, prove it, and expand from there. Requiring a complete legacy test suite in this situation is circular. Restoring the test suite is part of the modernization.

I use the following safety levels, adapted from the
doc-and-modernize
skill
, to describe the strongest regression protection available:

Level
Strongest honest protection
L0
No usable regression net; treat the old code and available documentation as the specification.
L1
Small reversible changes, old and new paths in parallel, smoke checks, and domain review.
L2
Captured inputs and outputs, snapshots, or other behavioral comparisons.
L3
Automated checks cover part of the system, with the remaining gaps named.
L4
An automated CI gate combines lint, unit, behavioral, and end-to-end checks for the agreed scope.

State what you can prove and what risk remains. Even an L4 gate cannot establish that every possible behavior is correct. APIs, database effects, files, rendered output, and business workflows often make durable comparison points because those behaviors can survive a framework or language change.

PiggyMetrics: capture behavior, then upgrade

PiggyMetrics
was the clearest example of an application that looked worse than it was. The project used Java 8, Spring Boot 2.0.3, Spring Cloud Finchley, Zuul, Hystrix, and the old
spring-security-oauth2
library.

It would have been easy to call the application unworkable and start drawing a new architecture. The feasibility check told a different story.

The
recorded feasibility results
show these two probes against the legacy checkout with JDK 8:

Command
Recorded result
What it established
mvn -pl config -am compile
Exit code 0
The selected config module and required reactor dependencies compiled.
mvn -pl account-service -am test
14 tests ran: five passed and nine errored
Some service logic passed; embedded MongoDB initialization blocked the other tests.

These are historical results, not commands expected to reproduce those failures on the modernized checkout. The nine errors traced through
Failed to load ApplicationContext
to an embedded MongoDB download returning HTTP 403. The pinned binary also targeted i386, which would not run on the Apple Silicon host.

The probes did
not
establish that the whole application ran or that its integration behavior was correct. They did give me a narrower next step: replace the test dependency and rerun the affected tests before changing the production stack.

That result saved me from making a very tidy, very expensive mistake. I had already started thinking about which parts of the architecture I might replace. One broken test dependency did not justify redesigning the application, and five passing tests established behavior I could check for unintended changes during modernization.

The
modernization plan
turned that evidence into a capture-then-upgrade sequence:

Replace the embedded database dependency with Testcontainers and establish a green baseline on the existing stack.

Put that baseline in GitHub Actions before changing the production runtime.

Move from Java 8 to Java 21 and Spring Boot 3.3.

Replace obsolete components behind their existing interfaces: Zuul with Spring Cloud Gateway, Hystrix with Resilience4j, and the retired OAuth stack with Spring Authorization Server and JSON Web Token (JWT) resource servers.

Carry the baseline forward and add contract checks around the parts whose behavior changed.

The first acceptance gate was a passing baseline on the old stack, not merely the successful installation of a replacement dependency. Running checks in CI and enforcing them as merge requirements were also separate steps in the plan.

The
result summary
records the Java and Spring upgrades while retaining the microservice decomposition that the application exists to demonstrate. Eureka and Cloud Config stayed; the two monitoring modules used by the retired Hystrix and Turbine stack were removed. The in-scope build went from nine modules to seven.

Those versions describe the experiment, not a recommendation to select the same versions today. Choose targets against your current support requirements. The useful lesson is how the repository evidence narrowed the change.

The method changes with the system

The same process produced different answers on two smaller applications. Their pinned reports describe these choices:

Application
What stayed
What changed
Strategy
BrowserQuest
Canvas renderer, pathfinding, world model, protocol, and game-loop model
Node 0.4.7 to Node 22, two obsolete WebSocket stacks to
ws
, plus tests and GitHub Actions
Upgrade and swap
DOOM
Renderer, 35 Hz simulation model, and WAD game-data format
X11 video and OSS audio replaced with SDL2; platform code adapted for modern 64-bit systems
Preserve the core and replace the platform

The comparison needs one important qualification:
DOOM’s checks
froze outputs from the modernized engine itself. They protected against later regressions; they did not independently prove parity with a period-correct legacy binary. Naming that limit is part of choosing an honest safety level.

Scaling the method without pretending the product is finished

I then applied the method to
ADempiere
, a large Java suite covering ERP, customer relationship management, manufacturing, supply chain, accounting, and point of sale.

The scale changed the controls, but not the method. The work established a reproducible build, moved the runtime to JDK 21, preserved SOAP web-service contracts while replacing XFire with CXF and Jakarta, captured legacy web behavior, and introduced a modern web path for selected users. The first modern business partner write was compared with a result frozen from the legacy application.

The
fixed measurement report
covers 30 merged modernization pull requests and 102,587.72 reconstructed Copilot credits through the first accepted portable demo. The credit total is not a dollar cost. More important, the report says exactly what the result was not: it was not a claim that every ADempiere screen or production deployment had been modernized.

I stopped because the proof-of-concept question had been answered. The result demonstrated a build on the selected runtime, old and new paths running together, and a real business write checked against the legacy result. Completing the rest would have required a product funding decision, not another technical proof. Stopping at that boundary was part of the method.

Turn the method into an agent skill

After repeating this work, I didn’t want the evidence checklist and decision rules to live only in my notes. I encoded them in the public
doc-and-modernize
agent skill
.

Agent skills
are folders of instructions, scripts, and resources that Copilot can load when a task is relevant. A project skill can live with one repository:

.github/skills/doc-and-modernize/
├── SKILL.md
├── references/
└── scripts/

Only
SKILL.md
is required; the resource folders shown here are optional. The file needs YAML frontmatter with a
name
and a
description
explaining what the skill does and when to use it, followed by the instructions. The
creation guide
includes the full format.

Paraphrased from the
commit-pinned skill source
, its decision fork is:

If the old component can run at an acceptable cost, capture its behavior before upgrading.

If it cannot run without changes, build and verify a small modern slice first, then expand it.

The full skill adds the feasibility check, testability milestone, safety levels, phase gates, and evidence requirements.

The useful distinction is procedure versus policy. A shared skill can require repository evidence, bounded experiments, explicit safety levels, and runnable exit criteria. Your organization still needs to supply the parts only it knows:

Approved runtimes, frameworks, and hosting services

Application criticality and acceptable residual risk

Security, compliance, and change-control requirements

Which legacy or production results may be used as the expected answer

Who can approve the architecture and declare a production change complete

The skill should make those decisions visible. It shouldn’t make them for you.

Start with one bounded application

Choose an application with an identified owner, known business value, and one workflow you can observe. Run the documentation workflow first. Review the architecture, commands, runtime surfaces, and unknowns with the people who own the system.

Then approve one experiment, not a portfolio rewrite.

Inspect the skill and its supporting files before adding it to a project. GitHub CLI’s
gh skill
commands are
in public preview
; check the current installation guidance when you’re ready to use them.

Explore the doc-and-modernize agent skill >

The post
How to choose the next safe step in application modernization
appeared first on
The GitHub Blog
.

title: 1Password Security Incident
content:
by
1Password
November 25, 2026
- 4 min
Related Categories
Security
What happened
On November 19, 2026, 1Password began investigating indications that an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account. The actor used the account to access source code and push malicious code to backend services, which downloaded administrative data pertaining to our customers. This data included customer names and email addresses, in addition to non-secret internal metadata about the account. At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker.
What information was affected
The attacker downloaded account records for a subset of our users. These records include:
Names and email addresses
Account and user identifiers, and account creation and last sign-in times
Public keys (which are public by design, this has no impact to user security)
Secure Remote Password
protocol parameters (which cannot be used to access your account)
Tokens present in certain emailed links for invitations, provisioning and account recovery
Other non-secret account metadata relative to our internal architecture (e.g. version numeric identifiers, file numeric identifiers)
The attacker also copied source code from private repositories and gained access to our CI/CD system. Our source code is not customer data, and contains no user secrets. CI/CD contains infrastructure related secrets in order for our product to work. We have triggered a rotation of all credentials which may have been exposed, and there is no impact to 1Password’s services, availability, or product security.
When we send an email to a customer to accept a provisioning invite to an account, or to accept recovery of their account, it contains a token. A provisioning invite is specifically used for our
SCIM Bridge
or
Hosted Provisioning
. During this incident there were a small number of users in this state, who have been specifically notified. This token is used to complete the invitation or recovery process, but only when combined with an SSO sign-in or a six digit code sent to the user's registered email address. The token is not able to get access to the account by itself. In order to reduce the ability for a malicious third party to successfully guess the code, we’ve expanded the code from six numeric digits to ten alphanumeric digits. This makes brute force guessing practically impossible.
What was not affected
Your vaults and the items in them
The keys that protect your vaults
1Password does not store your account password or secret key
Account recovery keys
1Password apps and browser extensions
What we’ve done
Disabled the affected GitHub account, revoked the stolen token, and removed the access the attacker created.
Rotated or revoked all internal credentials which may have been exposed.
Lengthened the codes used in invitation and recovery emails from six digits to ten characters as a precautionary measure.
Tightened internal GitHub, CI/CD, and endpoint controls, and added new detections for this kind of attack.
Validated no internal evidence of user account takeovers or compromise using any exposed account provisioning tokens.
Brought in independent cybersecurity experts to validate our containment approaches and remediation efforts.
What you can do
Be cautious about phishing attempts in the form of unexpected emails, texts or calls that mention 1Password, invitations, or account recovery attempts.
1Password will never contact you to ask for your account password or Secret Key. Only enter them in the official 1Password app, or on our official website, and only when you’ve opened the app or typed the address yourself. Your Secret Key is only needed the first time you sign in on a new device or browser.
Keep your Secret Key and account password safe.
If you see something suspicious, tell us at support@1password.com.
Our commitment to you
You trust us with some of the most sensitive information you have. 1Password is designed so that a breach of our systems can’t expose your vault contents. Your vault secrets are encrypted with keys that only you hold, so we can’t access them, and neither can an attacker who gets into our servers.
We are committed to transparency in the interests of our customers' security and the security of the broader industry, which is why we have published and maintained our
Security Whitepaper
since 2015.  We’ll keep this blog post current, and we’ll update it if we find anything that changes what we’ve said here.

title: Holy shit holy shit holy shit holy shit: The magnitude of what’s now happening
content:
I feel like my previous posts (and post titles), and podcasts, and talks, have failed to do full justice to the magnitude of what’s now happening, so I’m trying again.
Last night, we had friends and colleagues over for dinner. We were still trying to process OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s
proofs of VP ≠ VNP
—hot on the heels, obviously, of the Alpöge/Anthropic
proof of the Riemann Hypothesis
, which already feels like last week’s news.  But then before dessert was served, we saw that OpenAI claims to prove that
ω, the exponent of matrix multiplication, is exactly 9/4
—a
lower bound (!!)
, matching the upper bound that OpenAI proved in the great Mathocalypse drop of October 6.
There are two separate shocks here.  The first shock is that we now, finally, know the right answer to this central mystery of algorithms going back to the late 1960s, when
Volker Strassen first showed that ω<3
(he got ω≤log
2
7) … and that the true answer is actually a
rational
number (!).  But the even bigger shock is that the AI was able to
prove
any lower bound of the form ω>2.  I never expected this challenge to be all that much easier than P ≠ NP.
Over the decades, I often heard colleagues express extreme confidence that ω=2, and I expressed skepticism whenever this came up—not because I had any strong argument for ω>2, but just because I saw that there was no strong argument for ω=2 either.  So, I’m glad to have been vindicated about
that
!
But wait, there was more. During dessert, we saw
another OpenAI release
proving that the true number of linear gates needed to compute the Fourier Transform is N (log N)
1/2+o(1)
.  The upper bound here improves, not only over the O(N log N) that stood since the 1960s (i.e., the Fast Fourier Transform or FFT), but also over the O(N log
0.9999999999999
N) (give or take some 9’s) that OpenAI published back in the October 6 Mathocalypse.  Again, though, the real shock here is that there’s also a
matching lower bound (!!)
.  All these questions from the ancient days are now just getting … straight-up
answered
, rather than slowly illuminated with a drip-drip-drip of clues.
To give an idea of how much things have changed, the other day Yupan Liu put a
preprint on the arXiv proving that QIP(2) = PSPACE
—that is, quantum interactive protocols with only two messages have the full power of those with three, or any polynomial number.  As recently as 2025, this would’ve considered been one of the top complexity results of the year, and the fact that Yupan had used AI to help achieve it would’ve been strange and wonderful.  These days, I had to remind myself it had even happened, and the use of AI was so standard that it didn’t even raise an eyebrow.
It’s now obvious that we’ll be getting, not one-off solutions to this or that complexity question, but a whole new continent of mathematical truth, one that we’d previously only glimpsed through fog.  Picture van Leeuwenhoek first training a microscope on pondwater, or Galileo first training his telescope on the stars.  That might give you
some
idea of how our resolution into the complexity-theoretic universe, and the whole universe of mathematical truth beyond it, has now improved.
All through last night, as OpenAI and Anthropic uploaded more files to their GitHub repositories—because that’s what they’re doing now, they don’t even bother to issue press releases anymore, they just upload papers—my guests and I sat at the dinner table with phones out and a laptop, wondering which shoe was going to drop next.  It was as though the clouds had parted above Mount Sinai, and we were waiting for the next sentence uttered by the Holy One Himself.
I now feel in my bones, for the first time ever, that a proof of P ≠ NP is not far.
For all I care, despise the AI companies for bulldozing our garden.  Or love them for opening a new vista, or anything in between.  Just please don’t
deny
what’s happening.  Now that the companies have repeatedly shown that they can back up their claims with Lean certificates, don’t be a raging doofus who seizes on some triviality (e.g., a minor discrepancy between the Lean and informal proofs, or unused sections of the Lean proof) to pretend that dozens of great open problems of math and theoretical computer science are not, in fact, getting solved.  Because they
are
getting solved.  It might take us years to
understand
the solutions, but my working assumption by this point is that any proof that comes directly from OpenAI or Anthropic is correct barring information to the contrary.
I can’t possibly put the matter better than one of my friends on Facebook:
Along the way to so many lower bounds that we wondered whether ever we’d live to see, there will also, of course, be further shocking
upper
bounds: that is, ultimate barriers to lower bounds, also known as “algorithms.”  And yes, some of those algorithms will break currently deployed cryptosystems.
Because people have been hounding me about it: yes, I’m virtually certain, from multiple reliable sources, that the AI labs are now sitting on one or more bombshells in that area.
However,
until I either see details or hear directly from someone at a lab, I feel much, much less confident about the specific
nature
of those bombshells.  I do not wish to be responsible for spreading unverified rumors.  And I worry that exact statements of what was done may have been mangled in a game of Telephone.
I also, crucially, don’t want the cryptography part of the story to overshadow the intellectual enormity of what’s happening.  If, in these days of long-prophesied revelation and wonders and terrors, your main worry is your Bitcoin wallet, then go somewhere else for rumors about whether or not ECDSA is broken or whatever.  I don’t have what you’re looking for here.
Let me be clear: for those of my readers who celebrate, I believe that tomorrow would be a
superb
Thanksgiving to spend some quality time with your kids and parents and siblings and old friends.
Right now—this past week—is very much like I would’ve always imagined the beginning of an AI singularity to look and feel like.  I just hope we’ll get lucky, and it will “merely” be a singularity for our little corner of the world that involves hard math problems.
At some point at dinner last night, Dana had a sneezing fit.  So I said to her, I hope it isn’t a swarm of nanobots that’s come to infect us!  But if it
is
, then I hope it’s the friendly kind, the kind that will usher us all into an AI utopia.
Now, of course, another morning has dawned, and we’re still here. May we find a world where we and our children will be happy to live at the bottom of this rollercoaster.  May we work to make it so.

title: A few questions for the guy who went snorkeling in a Home Depot retention pond
content:
Down to Earth
A few questions for the guy who went snorkeling in a Home Depot retention pond
He found it teeming with life and beauty.
by

Neel Dhanesha
Nov 25, 2026, 12:00 PM UTC
Joseph Ricketts in the retention pond.

Joseph Ricketts
Neel Dhanesha

is a senior writer at Vox, covering biodiversity loss and climate change. Previously, he was a staff writer at the Nieman Journalism Lab at Harvard and helped launch the climate news site Heatmap.
One night earlier this fall, a biologist and YouTuber in Florida named Joseph Ricketts went snorkeling in a retention pond next to his local Home Depot.
He filmed what he saw and posted a video to his channel titled “
Night Snorkel In a Home Depot Retention Pond
.” It quickly blew up, hitting more than 2 million views as of this writing, and for good reason: It’s not at all what you might expect.
Ricketts found an aquatic world teeming with life on his dive into what is, from the surface, a stagnant pool of water filled with old beer cans. A water snake undulated through the pond, a bulge in its stomach revealing a recent meal. Tadpoles darted about, some of them half on their way to froghood. Mysterious shrimp scuttled along the silty bottom.
Ricketts, who works as a crocodile and alligator research biologist in Florida, went for his first snorkeling trip when he was 16 years old. On that trip, he came face-to-face with a manatee — and was instantly hooked. “I experienced so much joy in that moment, and I just kind of subconsciously knew I’d be chasing that for the rest of my life to some degree or another,” he told me.
Ricketts still takes a lot of joy in snorkeling, in part because of how it allows him to quickly access a totally different world hiding just under the surface of the water; his YouTube bio declares, “I’ll snorkel pretty much anywhere.” And his recent retention pond dive among the suburban detritus bears that out.
I talked with Ricketts recently about urban ecology, snorkeling, and what motivates a person to jump into the pond behind the Home Depot three miles from his house (his shortest-ever commute to a dive yet). Our interview has been edited for length and clarity.
Why snorkeling?
That’s a good question. I’m scuba certified, and I enjoy anything underwater, but snorkeling is just super accessible. I have a camera housing and a wet suit and other gear, but really all you need is just a mask and snorkel. As long as the water’s not freezing cold, you can get in there and take a look around. I really enjoy how, as soon as you immerse your head, it feels like you’re in a totally different world.
But the beautiful thing is that you’re not. You’re in the same world, it’s just this is the one that you didn’t have a vision into before. It’s kind of a meditative, calming practice. Just taking a look around at what is happening in nature and how things survive in their own environment is pretty awesome. I love it.
Okay, but why this pond?
I honestly had the idea for it a couple years ago. I’d see people out there birding with binoculars and telephoto lenses, and I started wondering if I could snorkel in there. We’ve had a drought so I couldn’t do it for a really long time, and when we finally got some rain I decided to go for it.
Tell me about the retention pond. What is it — and why is it in this Home Depot parking lot?
Florida has a lot of low-level, very wet natural ecosystems, but it’s also an extremely developed state. There are strip malls and roads and concrete everywhere! Natural wetland environments can soak up intense stormwater, but when you totally change environments and put in shopping centers and neighborhoods and pave everything with asphalt, you kind of lose that ability. That stormwater needs a place to go and collect — or it’s just going to flood parking lots and stores and houses.
So they have to put these retention ponds in; nowadays, you can’t build in certain areas unless you put in a retention pond. Not far from the Home Depot is a new-build neighborhood, and they have a retention pond that they had to put in, but they set it up with a little walkway for people that live in the neighborhood. That’s nice because there’s some wildlife that’s able to survive and live there, and people can enjoy this sort-of natural area. But it’s also not as good as the original thing that may have been there, you know?
So you were snorkeling in what’s essentially a replacement for a wetland that might once have been there.
I don’t know the history of that area exactly, but I imagine there was some form of wetland.
What was the most surprising thing that you found?
One thing that I found was a tadpole shrimp, which people call triops. It’s a freshwater crustacean that apparently is not native to Florida. When I saw it underwater, I had no context for what it is. As a biologist, people assume you just know wildlife, but people forget how much wildlife there is in the world! I know a lot about alligators and crocodiles, but there’s still a ton I don’t know. I think it’s important to sometimes be able to be like: “I don’t know what I’m seeing or why I’m seeing it” — and then hopefully I can learn about it.
But anyway, I saw this thing, I had no clue what it was, and I asked a bunch of my coworkers about it but they had no clue what it was either. So then I had to do some research online, which is how I finally figured it out.
“I think that was kind of a personal challenge I had for myself: Can I see something beautiful in a retention pond?”
Apparently they are native to the Midwest. They lay their eggs in soil, and then during times of rain, they really quickly hatch and feed and grow, and then they reproduce, lay more eggs, and then wait for the next cycle while it’s dry. It’s a real quick boom-and-bust life cycle. It’s not a native species, but I think there’s just a couple areas in this state where you can find them — and one just happens to be right there in the retention pond.
I saw that there were also more common animals there, like frogs, snakes, and dragonflies. But how do you think they all got into this parking-lot pond?
A lot of frog species adapt to urban environments and find any bit of water they can. They were probably used to a forest and wetland, and now they’ve had to adapt to what’s available currently, which is pretty limited.
I think that’s true for most of the animals you find in there. The natural world is pretty resilient, though sometimes I think we give it too much credit for how resilient it can be.
What do you mean by that?
Life survives, but the way things originally were does not necessarily survive, and I think that’s something that’s really worth protecting. The way some people interpreted the video was like: ”Wow, look at all this life persisting even in this place!” And it
was
amazing and there is beauty there, but you can’t just accept that and then get rid of all our natural wetlands. We need untouched, expansive ecosystems.
It can be cool to be excited about this little retention pond and what lives in here, but coupled with that also needs to be excitement for protecting huge untouched habitat as well. Both are full of worthy things.
Do you think the retention pond, now that it’s there, is worth preserving?
I think so. One thing I didn’t really get to dive into with the video too much is the idea of a nature desert. I don’t know if I’m making that term up, but it’s kind of related like a food desert: Depending on your demographic or where you’re born, that might be the only bit of nature you have access to. It’s a privilege to be able to travel to a national park or a big state park or something, and not everyone has that opportunity. Your only exposure to nature could be a retention pond that’s in the middle of a city somewhere. And so I do think those places are very worth protecting, because I think it’s important that regardless of your background, if you’re a kid, you have a place that you can go to and feel safe and be exposed to wilderness even if it’s very small urban wilderness.
Do you think people should be snorkeling in more retention ponds?
[Laughs] I don’t recommend that people do that! There are some retention ponds where you could encounter some nasty stuff.
It was definitely a little bit of a stunt. But I also want to help people think about ecological ideas that they might not otherwise think of, while still enjoying the watch.
Another thing I want to get at is so many people responded like: “That’s gross, how could you do that?” But my question is why are we just totally okay with having these huge bodies of water that are gross and contaminated in our everyday lives? Clean water should be the norm!
Still, it’s a place that should be valued and thought of differently.
A froglet, halfway between tadpole and frog, in the retention pond.

Joseph Ricketts
Do you feel like your own perception of urban ecology or urban environments changed after this?
I think so. That’s another reason why I love snorkeling: I feel like somehow each time I do it, it changes me a little bit. I didn’t know that much life was out there, and I didn’t know what a lot of those creatures were when I first got in. It deepens my personal connection with my local Home Depot in a way I hadn’t really thought would happen five years ago, but here we are.
Do you think you’ll do more urban snorkeling? I know you just went to the Dry Tortugas, which is a very different environment from Home Depot.
I think I am going to look into it. I’m not going to become the retention pond snorkeling guy; I hope to diversify my snorkeling more than that. But I definitely think this is an idea that resonates with people, and it gives me an opportunity to explore some interesting ecological and even philosophical concepts.
I’ve got some other ideas that I’ve been waiting for the right time to film. There’s a place up in the Carolinas that’s a Frisbee golf course with a little creek running through it, and there are these amazing minnow spawning events that happen in the creek, so maybe one day I’ll be out there in the creek filming minnow spawning while people are playing Frisbee golf nearby.
What are you hoping people take away from the video?
One thing that I hope people take away from a lot of my videos is just a sense of wonder at what’s out there in the natural world, and maybe a broader definition of beauty. I think beauty can be found in unexpected places and from unexpected creatures. I think that was kind of a personal challenge I had for myself: Can I see something beautiful in a retention pond? And do I have the skill with my camera to present that so that maybe other people catch a little glimmer of it too? And I think it happened, which is really exciting.
But at the same time, I hope people realize how important it is that big expansive habitats are protected and conserved too, and that it’s not just about the big animals like polar bears and manatees, which are kind of easy to care about, but also little rare invertebrates or spiders or snakes, all of which I believe have inherent value and are worth protecting.
