title: GPT-6.2 Astra is the first model to beat Googlers' code golf records
content:
go/codegolf benchmark: frontier models vs. Google's 2015 code golfers.

32 problems · 8 languages · 256 cells

Loading…

Problems

Loading…

About

TL;DR:
I brought back 32 problems from a code-golf contest we played at Google in 2015 to see how frontier models
compare with our old records. Each model gets 30 minutes per problem in each of eight languages to make its solution
as short as it can. The leaderboard scores the byte counts, not just whether the code works.

Where the problems come from: go/codegolf

In 2015, when I was at Google, I spent a lot of time on an internal site called
go/codegolf
. There was one problem
a week, and we competed to write the shortest program that solved it. Most of the regulars were code-golf enthusiasts.

Each problem went through three phases:

Phase

What happens

1. Candidate

Any Googler could propose a problem by posting a statement and a full test suite. Everyone could read the tests and suggest fixes. Votes were called
LGTMs
; the candidate with the most LGTMs became the next week's problem.

2. Competition (7 days)

You could see your own submissions, but nobody else's. Only your shortest passing solution in each language counted. The per-language scoreboards showed sizes, not code. The problem's author could compete too.

3. Challenge (forever after)

After seven days, the rankings froze and every submission became visible to everyone on the site. You could still submit a challenge, but it had to be strictly shorter than both the winning solution and every earlier challenge entry in that language. A passing challenge got its own slot on the scoreboard, with its code visible too.

The rule was simple:
the shortest program that passed every test case won
. Undefined behavior, compiler quirks,
non-standard library features, even hardcoding every test case were all allowed. Apart from passing the tests, the
program only had to be
deterministic
.

The site supported JavaScript, Python, Go, C++ and Haskell in 2015. Rust was added after I left.

From a weekly contest to a benchmark

I kept a collection of problems from the 2015 contest and chose
32 of them
for this benchmark. I wrote about half
under the name @binjin. The Problems page credits the original author of each of the others.

I also archived the scoreboards, statements and test cases. For JavaScript, Python, C++ and Haskell, those scoreboards
record the
shortest solution any Googler submitted
, including improvements made during the challenge phase.
Those byte counts are the human records used here.
The human solutions themselves are never shown on this site.

Eleven years later, I wanted to see how frontier models would do against the people I used to golf with.

The eight languages

Language

Why it's here

Human record

JavaScript

Original 2015 language

✓

Python

Original 2015 language

✓

C++

Original 2015 language

✓

Haskell

Original 2015 language

✓

Ruby

A popular golfing language with plenty of ways to save a byte

—

Raku (Perl 6)

Another golfing favorite, with a different programming style and just as much room to explore

—

Racket

A Lisp: what does golfing look like in prefix notation?

—

GolfScript

An esoteric, stack-based golfing language with very little public training data

—

There are no 2015 human records for the last four languages. I used an oracle run to get a reference size for each cell,
though models have beaten those sizes in some cells. Later, I ran the oracle on the original four languages as well,
this time starting from the human records. See
Known Best and the oracle
.

Haskell has human records too, but they are much weaker than the other three, so the humans' main score, JS/PY/C++,
leaves Haskell out. See
Overall and JS/PY/C++
.

How models play

A
cell
is one problem in one language. Each gets a fresh session with a
30-minute wall-clock limit
. The model
receives the statement, the I/O specification,
all the test cases
and a short guide to the language. For GolfScript,
it also gets the full language reference, since the language is small and not widely known.

There are two tools, and both work in all eight languages:

submit
runs a solution against all the test cases in the replicated sandbox.

A passing solution is saved only if it is strictly shorter than the model's previous best.

Wrong answers, runtime errors, timeouts and compile errors are returned with stderr.

Every response includes the
current best known size
. I want the model to know when someone has done better;
without a target, it's easy to decide a solution is short enough and stop.

playground
runs a program in the same sandbox as submissions, with mostly the same environment: the same
compiler or interpreter, compiler options and libraries.

It can preload the test cases as
inputs
and
outputs
, so the model can try its
g
on every case, compare the
results with the expected outputs, or just examine the data.

It's useful for trying a language feature or checking what the interpreter does with an edge case.

It also lets the model write search programs: for example, to brute-force a magic number or find the shortest
expression for a small formula. Human golfers do this all the time.

That's all the model gets. There is no internet, shell or access to other files.

For the four original languages,
the sandbox reproduces the 2015 environment
, down to the compiler or interpreter
version, flags and quirks. A trick that worked in the old contest should work here; a feature added since then won't.
The full runtime list is in
Technical details
.

Known Best and the oracle

Without human records for Ruby, Raku, Racket and GolfScript, I needed another way to set a target for the models and a
reference for scoring. For that I run an
oracle
: a model with internet access,
no time or request limits
and
every JavaScript, Python, C++ and Haskell solution in the benchmark to learn from, including the shortest human
solution for each cell and all the models' solutions.

The first oracle was GPT-6 Astra. I ran it on the four added languages to set their reference sizes, then on the
original four, where it could work directly from the human records and try to improve them. Later I ran the oracle
with other models as well.

The oracle is
unranked
; it only supplies best-known sizes.

When it beats every competitor in a cell, the Problems page shows its byte count as
Known Best
, but never its code.

In 126 of the 256 cells, the oracle's solution is shorter than every competitor's. The oracle had
much more time and information to work with.

Scoring

Each cell is scored by comparing its byte count with the best known:

score = (best known size ÷ your size)²

Match the best known size and you get
100%
. A solution 10% longer gets
82.6%
; twice as long gets
25%
.

An unsolved cell gets
0
.

Overall
averages all 256 cells, in all eight languages.
JS/PY/C++
averages the 96 cells in JavaScript, Python
and C++. See
Overall and JS/PY/C++
for why JS/PY/C++ leaves out Haskell.

The best known size can come from a human, a model or the oracle. If anyone finds a shorter solution, everyone else's
score for that cell goes down.

To score 100% across a whole run, you have to match the best known size in every cell.

A gold mark on a problem's scoreboard means that solution matches the best known size. A filled mark means no other
competitor has matched it; an outlined mark means a tie. Humans count as competitors, but the oracle doesn't. If the
oracle's Known Best is shorter than every competitor's solution, nobody gets a gold mark.

Overall and JS/PY/C++

The leaderboard has two summary scores:

Overall
averages all 256 cells: JavaScript, Python, C++, Haskell, Ruby, Raku, Racket and GolfScript.

JS/PY/C++
averages the 96 cells in JavaScript, Python and C++.

JS/PY/C++ covers only the languages where the human records make a strong reference. In 2015, JavaScript, Python and
C++ were the languages most go/codegolf regulars golfed in. Each of those scoreboards had a crowd of enthusiasts
competing on it for a week, and the challenge phase kept the best of them improving it long after. Eleven years later,
those records are still competitive with frontier models: see

What the results show so far
.

Haskell is different. The site supported it and every problem here has a human Haskell record, but only a few regulars
golfed in it. I suspect that mostly reflects how few Haskell users there were at Google in 2015, not how golfable the
language is. With so few people competing, many Haskell records never got the attention the others did, and models
have already beaten 31 of the 32. Counting Haskell in the human score would measure how few of
us wrote Haskell, not how good the people who golfed were, so JS/PY/C++ leaves it out.

Haskell still counts like any other language everywhere else. The human Haskell records still set best-known sizes,
appear on the problem scoreboards and count in each model's Overall score.

Humans have no Overall score, because they have no entries in Ruby, Raku, Racket or GolfScript. By default the
leaderboard lists the models that beat Humans on JS/PY/C++ first, ranked by Overall, then Humans, then every other
model, also ranked by Overall. Sorting it by Overall instead ranks the models by Overall and puts Humans just above the
first model they match or beat on JS/PY/C++. Each problem's full scoreboard ranks models by their combined score in all
eight languages on that problem, and puts Humans just above the first model they match or beat in JavaScript, Python,
C++ and Haskell combined. On the leaderboard, runs still in progress go below every complete one in any order, the
earliest-released model first, with their partial scores dimmed.

Technical details

Language

Runtime

Time limit

JavaScript

Rhino 1.7R4, JavaScript 1.7 (problems 01–19) / Rhino 1.7.7, partial ES6 (20–32)

20 s

Python

PyPy 2.3.1 (Python 2.7.6) in the RPython sandbox, no JIT, restricted imports

10 s

C++

PNaCl clang 3.5.0 (Pepper 41),
-std=gnu++11 -stdlib=libc++ -O2 -w -Werror=c++1z-extensions

10 s

Haskell

GHC 7.8.4, evaluated through mueval 0.9.1.1.1 (hint 0.4.2.2)

10 s

Ruby

MRI/CRuby 3.4.10 with the Prism parser and YJIT enabled

10 s

Raku

Rakudo / MoarVM 2026.08

10 s

Racket

Racket CS 9.3

10 s

GolfScript

Reference interpreter (
darrenks/golfscript

cded542
), with the Ruby-eval string interpolation removed

20 s

Function, not program.
You define a function
g
. A wrapper calls it on every test case and prints the results;
the wrapper doesn't count towards your size. For Haskell, it also supplies
g
's type signature. The solution is the
body of a
let
binding, and mueval evaluates the whole thing as one expression.

State between test cases.
JavaScript, Python, Raku and Racket run every test case in one process, so global state persists from one case to the next (Haskell is pure). C++ compiles the solution inside a struct that is created fresh for each test case, so its "global" variables start at zero every time; only
static
ones persist. Ruby runs each test case in its own fresh environment. GolfScript runs the program's top level once and then each test case in a fresh copy of that state, so precomputed values are shared but nothing a case changes carries over.

Bytes, not characters.
The score uses the raw file size. Spaces, newlines and every byte of a multi-byte UTF-8 character count.

Deterministic.
Each submission runs twice, independently. Both stdout and stderr must match exactly before the output is judged.

Shuffled inputs.
Each run gets its own random ordering of the test cases. The judge puts the results back in the original order before checking them, so a solution can't rely on the order of the inputs.

One time limit per run.
Compilation and the full batch of test cases must fit within the same time limit.

JavaScript.
Problems 01–19 run on Rhino 1.7R4 (JavaScript 1.7, interpreted mode at optimization level -1, stack depth 4096). Problems 20–32 run on Rhino 1.7.7 (partial ES6, optimization level 9, stack depth 65535); on a stack overflow or an unknown exception it retries in interpreted mode within the same 20 s limit.

No prime builtins.
Primality and factorization builtins are withdrawn in C++, Ruby, Raku and Racket, so prime-flavored problems stay non-trivial. Modular exponentiation, gcd/lcm, factorials and the rest of the standard libraries remain available.

C++ quirk.
Clang 3.5 accepted the C++1z range-for shorthand
for(x:a)
(a proposal later dropped from the standard). The original site rejected it with
-Werror=c++1z-extensions
, and so does this replica;
for(auto x:a)
still works.
An AI model found a way to switch that error off from inside
its own solution
and use the shorthand anyway. No Googler ever did.

Isolation.
Every execution starts fresh processes in an isolated container with no network access, and everything it started is cleaned up afterwards.

Thinking effort and the 30-minute limit

Most models let you choose a
thinking effort
: roughly, how long they reason before they answer or act. More
thinking can crack a hard problem, but here it shares the same 30 minutes with everything else. Golfing is a loop of
trying an idea, testing it and submitting whatever passes, and only submitted solutions count. An idea still being
thought through when time runs out scores nothing.

So the highest setting isn't automatically the best one for this contest. I ran Claude Haiku 5.5 at both
max
and

xhigh
(“extra high”, one step down), and it shows both sides. Its
max
solution was the shorter of the two in
160 cells and the longer in 52, and
max
scored higher overall.
But in some cells it spent so long thinking that it ran out of time with little more than its first, ungolfed working
solution. In
Game of Life
, its

Racket solution
is still indented over six lines, at 329 bytes
against 259 at
xhigh
, and its
GolfScript
takes 137 bytes to

xhigh
's 95. Telling a model to submit early and often doesn't reliably prevent this.

Neither run got the most out of the model. Picking the shorter of its two solutions in each cell scores higher than
both:

Claude Haiku 5.5

Overall

JS/PY/C++

xhigh

56.796%

58.655%

max

61.832%

63.987%

Shorter of the two in each cell

64.140%

65.836%

Each model runs at its highest available setting, unless that setting tends to leave it thinking until time runs out;
then it runs at
xhigh
. The leaderboard shows each run's setting next to its name, and both Haiku runs are on it.
Everyone gets the same tools and the same 30-minute limit.

Why I built this

I started this after OpenAI introduced GPT-6 Astra as
"a new generation of
intelligence"
, and its president Greg Brockman ended the launch briefing with

"Welcome to the AGI era."
It made me wonder:
how
would we judge whether frontier models have reached the limits of human intelligence?

My first thought was mathematics. Some of the sharpest human minds have worked on it for centuries, and Astra had
already helped
solve long-standing open problems
. Then I
thought of code golf. A golf score can't answer that question about intelligence, but it gives me a comparison I
understand: models trying to beat people at something those people cared about and worked hard at.

I spent about three years in middle and high school training for math olympiads, and golfing often gives me the same
feeling as working on a math problem. You can be stuck for ages until you find a different way to look at it. Then you
still have to make the idea work. And as you get further, the next step tends to get harder, whether you're finishing
a proof or trying to lose one more byte.

That was a big part of the appeal of go/codegolf. I'd guess 30 to 50 of us played the weekly problem. We'd spend lunch
breaks trying to save a single byte. Sometimes an idea would come to you and you couldn't wait to try it; sometimes
you'd go days without an improvement, while the scoreboard kept telling you a shorter solution existed. When the
challenge phase opened and we could finally read each other's code, some of the shortest solutions were astonishing.
I once tried to work out how many engineer hours we were all "wasting" on it, multiplied that by the average Googler's
salary, and estimated its weekly "negative impact" on Google.

Thanks to
@wangz
for creating go/codegolf. Without it, neither that contest nor this benchmark
would exist. And thanks to everyone who wrote a problem or competed: your records are representing the humans here,
and you've made them hard to beat.

I'm impressed by how far language models have come, especially when I look at some of Astra's solutions. There's
still plenty of room to improve. The best known size isn't a fixed answer key: each shorter solution changes the
target for everyone. I'm looking forward to seeing what the next models find.

Why Code Golf

TL;DR:
Every model with a complete run can solve these problems. They differ a lot in how short they can make
their solutions, even with the same tools and time limit. That's what I want to measure: can a model keep finding
better ideas after it has code that already works?

No answers to memorize

These problems come from go/codegolf, a weekly contest that code golf enthusiasts at Google ran for their colleagues.
They appear online here for the first time, and the site doesn't show the human solutions. There's no public set of
answers for a model to memorize; it has to work out a solution for itself.

Getting a working solution

Frontier models don't have much trouble getting these problems right. Every model with a complete run has an accepted
solution in
all 256 cells
. If I only counted passing solutions, they would all have the same result.

But their scores range from
47.975%
to
91.934%
across all eight languages, and
from
52.911%
to
92.265%
on JS/PY/C++ (JavaScript, Python and C++ alone).
Once a solution works, there's still the question of how much shorter it could be. That's where the models start to
differ.

Scoring by byte count

Exact.
Either the program passes or it doesn't. If it passes, we count its bytes. There's no human rater or LLM
judge deciding whether it's good code, and no points for style.

Fine-grained.
Saving one byte always helps. The squared score makes the difference between a close solution and
an even closer one matter.

Open-ended.
We don't know the shortest possible answers. "Best known" just means nobody has found anything shorter
yet. Models have already beaten the 2015 human record in
93
cells. Getting every problem
right doesn't end the competition, and a new record gives everyone else something to aim for.

Less boilerplate to golf

In some contests, you spend part of your byte count on getting the input in and the output out. I like go/codegolf's
format because it leaves very little of that overhead. I kept the same format for the four added languages:

A function, not a program.
You define a function; the wrapper handles input and output. Top-level code still
runs, so you can use global variables and precomputed tables, or write a recursive solution.

A fixed name:
g
.
The name costs one byte, and a recursive call is just
g(…)
. Recursion is often the shortest
approach, though getting a very short recursive function right can be difficult.

Libraries already imported.
The C++, Haskell, Racket and Ruby templates import most of the useful standard
libraries. The Python template imports nothing, so using even
re
costs
import re
. Sometimes it's still worth it.

Nearly every byte is part of the solution.
With I/O, naming and most imports taken care of, you're mostly golfing
the code that solves the problem, rather than the code needed to run it.

Knowing the language and the runtime

When you're trying to save a byte, details that rarely matter in ordinary code can become useful: operator precedence,
implicit conversions, an obscure builtin, a non-standard extension, or what a particular compiler does with undefined
behavior. The original languages use old runtimes, including a 2015 C++ toolchain, Python 2.7 and GHC 7.8. Knowing how a
modern version behaves isn't enough. The model has to know, or try out, what works in the version it's actually using.

Trying things out

A lot of golfing involves questions you can answer by running a few lines of code:

Will this interpreter accept this syntax? Will the compiler let me leave that out?

Try it in the playground or make a submission.

If it works, see where else you can use it.

Sometimes the experiment needs a program of its own. Golfers write searches for a
magic number
or
magic string

that encodes a lookup table, or for the
shortest expression
that gives the right result using a few operators.
A model that never runs these experiments will miss some of the same savings.

Finding a different approach

Often you can't get to the shortest solution by trimming the obvious one. You need a different algorithm, or a
different way to represent the data. These are some examples I like from the models' solutions:

Carries without carrying.

Addition by hand
asks how many carries occur when you add two
numbers column by column. Each carry turns ten in one column into one in the next, reducing the digit sum by 9. So
the answer is (digit sum of a + digit sum of b − digit sum of a+b) ÷ 9, and most models' Python solutions compute
exactly that.
Gemini 4 Carbon's Python
needs neither the
subtraction nor the division:

g=lambda a,b:sum(map(int,a+b+52*str(int(a)+int(b))))*6%53

It works modulo 53. Adding the digits of a+b 52 times is the same as subtracting them once, because 52 ≡ −1, and
multiplying by 6 is the same as dividing by 9, because 6 × 9 = 54 ≡ 1. There are at most 50 carries, so the
remainder is the answer. That's 57 bytes, against 59 for the shortest solution that divides by 9.

Comparing rows instead of finding a path.

2×n matrix
asks how many blocked cells you
have to clear to walk from the top-left to the bottom-right of a two-row grid, given as two strings of 0s and 1s.
Most solutions work out the cheapest way to reach each cell, column by column.

Claude Opus 5.5's Python
walks greedily instead and lets string
comparison choose the row:

g=lambda*s:all(s)and(min(s)>='01')+g('0'+min(s)[2:],max(s)[1:])

You always stand on a free cell, so the row you're in starts with 0, and
min
picks it. If the other row's cell is
free too, you could switch rows at no cost, and
min
picks whichever row's next cell is free. If even that cell is
blocked,
min(s)>='01'
adds 1 for clearing it. Then both rows lose their first column, and the cell you step onto
becomes
0
. That's 63 bytes. Claude Fable 5.2 and Gemini 4 Neon found the same idea, and the column-by-column
solutions take 78 bytes or more.

The quaternion group in one number.

Quaternions
asks for the product of a string of
1, i, j and k, such as
ijkj
. The usual shortcut numbers 1, i, j and k from 0 to 3. Then XOR gives the letter of a
product, and only its sign needs a lookup table. Many models drop the table: they number all eight results, ±1,
±i, ±j and ±k, from 0 to 7, and multiply with x ∘ y = x + 3ˣ·y (mod 8). Bit 2 holds the sign. 3ˣ mod 8 is 1 when
x is even and 3 when x is odd, and that twist is what makes i × j = −(j × i).

GPT-6.2 Sol's Python
does it in 67 bytes; the next shortest Python
takes 74:

g=lambda a:'----1kji'[reduce(lambda n,c:n-ord(c)%25*3**n&7,a,4)::4]

ord(c)%25
turns 1, i, j and k into 24, 5, 6 and 7. The code subtracts these steps, so modulo 8 the letters get
the numbers 0, 3, 2 and 1, their positions in
1kji
. Starting at 4 instead of 0 multiplies the whole product by
−1, which suits the output:
'----1kji'[n::4]
takes every fourth character from position n, giving one character
for n from 4 to 7 and two, a minus sign first, for n from 0 to 3.

Three exponents from one counter.

(−5)-Smooth Numbers
asks for the first n positive
numbers of the form (−2)ˣ(−3)ʸ(−5)ᶻ, that is, numbers 2ˣ3ʸ5ᶻ with x+y+z even. Most solutions build them with
nested loops or by growing a set, then sort.
GPT-6.2 Astra's Python

gets them all from powers of 4:

g=lambda n:sorted(4**i%(2**999-5)%(2**49-3)for i in range(7000))[:n]

Modulo 2⁹⁹⁹−5, each factor 2⁹⁹⁹ in 4ⁱ = 2²ⁱ turns into a 5. Modulo 2⁴⁹−3, each 2⁴⁹ turns into a 3. So, writing
2i = 999z + 49y + x, 4ⁱ becomes 5ᶻ3ʸ2ˣ. Since 2i is even and 999 and 49 are odd, x+y+z is even too: the sign
condition comes for free. When a product doesn't fit below a modulus, the reduction scrambles it, but every
scrambled value is above 7 × 10¹⁰, and the largest number the problem needs is 10⁹. That's 68 bytes; the other
Python solutions take 70 or more.

Counting each neighbour twice.

Game of Life
asks for the next generation of a board.
A cell lives on if it has three live neighbours, or two if it's already alive. Most solutions add up each 3×3 block
and compare the sum with 3 and 4.
GPT-6.2 Astra's Python
counts
the block twice:

g=lambda a,p=['z'*99]:[a<p and`g(zip(*r))`[1::3]or+(4<`r*2`.count('1',4)<8)for r in zip(a,p+a,a[1:]+p)]

Each block r is a nested tuple of characters with the cell itself first. In the text form of
r*2
, the block
written out twice, that cell's character is at index 3, so counting 1s from index 4 skips it in the first copy
only. For a cell c with N live neighbours, the count is 2N+c, and 4 < 2N+c < 8 is exactly the rule: 5 or 7 for a
live cell with two or three neighbours, 6 for an empty cell with three.

One lambda handles both directions. Called with the rows, it zips each row and its neighbours into columns, calls
itself on them and reads the digits back out of the resulting list's text with
[1::3]
. Called with those
columns, it counts. The test
a<p
tells the two cases apart: Python 2 compares a list of strings with
['zzz…']

string by string, but ranks any tuple above any string. The z's also pad the edges, since they aren't 1s.
zip

stops at its shortest string, though, so a top or bottom row more than 99 cells wide would come out cut short; the
test boards are at most 66 wide. That's 103 bytes; GPT-6.2 Sol uses the same count in 108, and the other Python
solutions take 121 or more.

Raising the bar instead of counting letters.

Cracking Caesar
asks you to decrypt a
Caesar cipher, knowing that e is the most common letter in the plaintext. The usual approach counts the letters,
finds the most common one and shifts every letter by its distance from e.

Claude Fable 5.2's C++
and

Gemini 4 Argon's
, both 93 bytes, never count the letters:

int n,i;string g(string a){for(char&x:n=i++/26,a)n-=x>64&&(--x%32?:x+=26)^5;return n?g(a):a;}

Each call shifts every character after
@
back by one and subtracts 1 from n for each one that doesn't become e.

x>64
isn't a real letter test: it would also shift
[
to
Z
, although only letters are encrypted. It works
because the test messages contain only letters and punctuation that comes before
A
. n starts at i/26, where i
counts the calls, and the function stops when n ends at exactly 0. In the first 26 calls, one full cycle of shifts,
that only happens if every letter becomes e; in the next 26, if all but one do; and so on. So the first shift to
meet the rising bar is the one with the most e's. Solutions that count the letters and then shift once take 121
bytes or more. This one is slow, up to a few thousand recursive calls on the tests, but that costs no bytes.

Complex numbers, now common.
Two ideas that only a few models had found when I first wrote this page are now in
most models' Python and Ruby solutions.

In
Surviving queens
, a queen survives if no other queen shares its row, column or
diagonal. Put the queen in row r and column c at the complex number r + ci. The directions a queen can move in are
the eight multiples of 45°, and raising a difference to the fourth power multiplies its angle by four, which puts
exactly those directions on the real axis. So two queens attack each other when (z − w)⁴ is real. In Ruby,
comparing a complex number with
<=>
gives nil unless it's real, and 0 counts as true, so

Claude Fable 5.2's Ruby
counts the queens x for which

q.one?{(it-x)**4<=>0}
holds: x itself, with a difference of 0, must be the only queen at a real fourth power.

In
The Rolling Dice
, a die is back in its starting orientation exactly when one
well-chosen point on a sphere around it is back where it started: a point that no rotation of the die other than
the identity leaves in place. So instead of tracking six faces, follow that point.

Stereographic projection
maps the sphere to the complex
plane, and a roll in direction k, one of 1, i, −1 and −i, becomes z → (z+k)/(1−z/k).

GPT-6.1 Sol's Ruby
takes 61 bytes:

g=->a{z=2;a.bytes.map{z+=r=1i**(-it/3);z/=2-z/r;z==2?1:0}*''}

1i**(-it/3)
turns each letter's character code into its direction, and the two updates together apply the
formula. Ruby does this arithmetic exactly, with fractions, so
z==2
can test for the starting point directly.
Python's complex numbers are floating-point, so the Python versions test for something only the starting point
satisfies, such as a real part above 2.

These solutions depend on finding and trying different ideas, then choosing the one that uses the fewest bytes.
The fastest or most elegant algorithm isn't necessarily the one you want. Ordinary coding benchmarks rarely give a
model a reason to look for this sort of solution.

Why one byte can be hard to remove

In a well-golfed program, the same piece of code often does several jobs. That's how it got so short. It's also why an
apparently simple change can break something elsewhere.

Here is
GPT-6.1 Sol's 79-byte JavaScript
for
Nim
:

function g(a){for(i=-1;(d=a[++i],d-=d^eval(a.join('^')))<0;);return[d?i:--d,d]}

The algorithm is the usual one. Let x be the XOR of all the heap sizes. If x is 0, there's no winning move. Otherwise,
find the first heap a for which a − (a XOR x) is positive, and take that many stones. But fitting it into this code
requires a few tricks:

eval(a.join('^'))
builds an expression such as
3^5^6
and evaluates it to get x. It's inside the loop test, so it
runs again for every heap. That wastes time but saves storing x in a variable.

The test reads the next heap into d and turns it into d − (d XOR x) on the spot. Unless x is 0, that's never 0, and
it's negative exactly when we're looking at the wrong heap.

If x is 0, the first heap gives 0, so the loop stops with i at 0. Then
d?i:--d
gives −1, and because
--d
also
changes d to −1, the second element is −1 as well.

GPT-6.2 Astra's JavaScript
takes one byte less. It uses the same
algorithm and tricks, but reads each heap in the loop body instead of the test:

function g(a){for(i=d=0;(d-=d^eval(a.join('^')))<0;)d=a[i++];return[--i,d||i]}

That one move changes everything around it. The loop now tests before it has read a heap, so d starts at 0, and the
first test computes 0 − (0 XOR x) = −x. That starts the loop when x isn't 0 and stops it at once when x is. Reading
after testing leaves i one past the heap it found, so the result uses
--i
. In the losing position the loop never
runs:
--i
turns 0 into −1, and
d||i
turns d's 0 into the same −1.

Moving the read saves nine bytes in the test,
d=a[++i],
, and costs eight in the body,
d=a[i++]
. The new start,

i=d=0
, is a byte longer than
i=-1
, and the new result,
[--i,d||i]
, is a byte shorter than
[d?i:--d,d]
. The
saving only appears when the start, the indexing and the losing case all change together. That's common in golfed
code: a variable has two meanings, or an expression both updates the state and checks whether we're done. Remove a
byte in one place and you may break an assumption somewhere else.

Solutions of the same length can be just as far apart. These are

GPT-6.2 Astra's
and

Claude Fable 5.2's
91-byte JavaScript for

Quaternions
. Both use the mod 8 multiplication described above:

function g(a){for(i=x=.5;y=1976%a.charCodeAt(i++);)x+=x%2*y;return(x&4?'-':'')+'1kji'[x&3]}

function g(a){for(i=t=0;c=a.charCodeAt(i++)%25;)t+=t%2*2*c-c;return["-"[~t&4]]+"1kji"[t&3]}

In Astra's, the
.5
does three jobs:

charCodeAt
drops the fraction from its argument, so i = .5, 1.5, 2.5, … reads characters 0, 1, 2, …. Past the
end it returns NaN, and
1976%NaN
is NaN, which stops the loop.

x%2
is .5 when x's whole part is even and 1.5 when it's odd, so x grows by y/2 or 3y/2: the factor of 3 for odd
x, without computing a power.
1976%
gives 16, 86, 68 and 50 for 1, i, j and k. They're all even, so their halves
are whole numbers, and modulo 8 those halves are 0, 3, 2 and 1, the positions in
1kji
.

x&4
and
x&3
ignore the fraction.

Fable's takes its steps from
%25
instead (24, 5, 6 and 7, and NaN at the end) and never lets t rise above 0. Then

t%2
is 0 or −1, so
t%2*2*c-c
multiplies c by −1 or −3: the same twist with the sign reversed. And

["-"[~t&4]]
is either
["-"]
or
[undefined]
, and the second turns into an empty string when added to

"1kji"[t&3]
.

The two solutions do the same arithmetic in the same length, but neither can borrow a piece from the other: Astra's

.5
needs even steps, and Fable's sign trick needs t never to be positive.

To make code like this shorter, the model has to understand why all the pieces work together. A change still has to
leave the whole program correct.

Knowing when to keep trying

The first few cuts are usually easy. After that, you can spend a long time trying things without saving a byte.
It's tempting to stop there, even when the scoreboard says a shorter solution exists.

Models get 30 minutes per cell and are always shown the best known size. They don't have to use the whole session:
the instructions say to keep submitting while they have ideas for improvements, and to stop when they run out.
Continuing to come up with things to try matters here.

GPT-6 Sol usually stops after 5 to 10 minutes, even at its highest reasoning effort. With exactly the same prompts,
every GPT-5 model, including GPT-5.6 Luna, is still working at the 30-minute limit on most cells. I suspect this explains
much of GPT-6 Sol's ranking.

Eight different languages

The language set includes imperative languages, Haskell's functional style, Racket's Lisp prefix notation and the
stack-based esoteric language GolfScript, for which there's little training data. Golfing well across all of them
takes more than repeating familiar patterns; a model has to apply what it knows in quite different settings.

Human records to compare against

These records came from Googlers who enjoyed code golf and spent a week competing on each problem, with the option
to keep challenging afterwards. They put real time into finding shorter solutions. Beating those records means more
to me than beating a reference answer nobody tried very hard to golf.

What the results show so far

GPT-6.2 Astra is the first frontier model to surpass the human records on
JS/PY/C++
, the combined score for
JavaScript, Python and C++:
92.265%
, compared with
87.533%
for humans. So far it's the
only model above them. Its lead doesn't rest on one strong language: it scores above the humans in each of the three.

Language

Humans

GPT-6.2 Astra

Cells humans still hold

JavaScript

80.980%

90.555%

4 of 32

Python

90.579%

93.049%

5 of 32

C++

91.039%

93.190%

5 of 32

JS/PY/C++

87.533%

92.265%

14 of 96

These human records combine the best submissions from the original contest and later challenges, not one person's
30-minute run. Models have beaten them in
62
of the 96 cells, but in

14
the human solution is still shorter than every model's: those are the cells humans still
hold. Both counts exclude the unranked oracle.

title: SSH is a GUI framework
content:
SSH is a GUI framework
Hasan Madi

·

21 November 2026
"One thing about which fish know exactly nothing is water."
— Marshall McLuhan
SSH is a tool so ubiquitous that we've forgotten what it actually is: a multiplexed, encrypted byte stream accessible on a cross-platform rendering engine that ships on every laptop, server, and phone on earth. A number of terminal protocols have slowly added graphics, clipboard sharing (including images), notifications, mouse support, and more on top of SSH.
To see just how far you can push it, I've made a microVM with a desktop environment designed from the ground up to render natively over SSH. You can try it right now (no sign-up):
ssh
zydra.sh

ssh

-p

443
zydra.sh
# if on an office network

ssh

-t
zydra.sh dino
# SSH port of the Chromium T-Rex game, for fun.
zydra.sh desktop, entirely over SSH, in the Kitty terminal
Terminal Protocols (and matching terminal support)
All terminal protocols work on data that can be passed through SSH, so typically, any terminal protocol will extend to SSH.
Perhaps the most ubiquitous new terminal protocol is the
Kitty Graphics Protocol
, which superseded the older Sixel and iTerm2 graphics protocols. It allows for compression, client-side graphical state (via VRAM), and even
animations
entirely on the terminal.
Graphics alone don't make a complete GUI, though. SSH has protocols that cover all other angles:
Notifications
:
OSC 99
"Rich Notifications" allow image, text, and body.
OSC 777
(our first fallback) allows only text and body, and
OSC 9
(our last fallback) allows only a title.
OSC 99
OSC 777
OSC 9
Title
Yes
Yes
Yes
Body
Yes
Yes
No
Image
Yes
No
No
We end up using a similar fallback for many things.
Clipboard sharing
:
OSC 52
handles bidirectional clipboard sharing, and Kitty's
OSC 5522
adds image and arbitrary MIME-type transfers on top of that.
Mouse support
:
CSI ? 1000-1006
help track the mouse and give us its precise coordinates.
Synchronized Output
(Batched Rendering):
CSI ? 2026
allows atomic rendering, preventing visual tearing and flickering.
File upload (Kitty)
: The Kitty terminal uniquely supports a file upload feature, which
zydra.sh
uses to allow the upload of projects and related files to personal VMs.
SSH-native compositing: How I made it fast
A few tricks make compositing over SSH fast. Firstly, where possible, especially when streaming terminals, we simply stream them as text rather than unnecessarily streaming it via graphics. The compositor's UI framework itself cleverly overlays traditional text over carefully aligned graphics, saving bandwidth. In the case of
zydra.sh
, this allows us to efficiently stream the entire cloud computer's desktop UI over SSH.
Next, we optimize graphics by sending a sort of "grid" of pixels. Each cell has its own updates, where the previous frame is compared to the current frame to catch and send updates, avoiding having to constantly stream the full screen. Kitty also offers both RGB and RGBA, and so by removing transparency where it's not needed, we save another 25% in bandwidth. We also track ping and other factors to determine how well the client handles the stream: lowering the resolution in select cells, especially when scrolling, to relieve pressure. We also use Kitty's client-side state to hold graphics ahead-of-time before they're displayed on screen, as well as holding repeated UI components.
Backwards Compatibility
Not all terminals support all the latest terminal protocols, so the compositor must also fallback to older graphics protocols Sixel and iTerm2, and when necessary, fall back to pure textual streaming, using ASCII to replicate some UI. In the case of notifications and other protocols, multiple protocols similarly exist, which we also gracefully fallback to when needed.
Parsing terminal versions and querying capabilities allows us to get an idea of what the client supports. We also continually verify that features work as expected on the client as the session boots. The Kitty terminal itself I've found to have very reliable support for all graphics protocols
zydra.sh
relies on.
SSH often beats webapps and VNC at their own job
VNC is limited to sending pictures of the screen and diffing frames to find what changed. With
zydra.sh
's approach, apps directly tell the compositor what changed, and terminal text is sent as text you can select and copy natively. The browser is a WebKit build that delivers frames to the compositor as DMA-BUFs without a readback, which can be driven agentically via Playwright.
While webapps have advantages, especially in client-side state, WASM, and WebGPU, they don't really capture the universality and ease-of-use of an SSH session. SSH keys double as authentication, and
-A
allows you to SSH into servers from within a remote microVM itself. Webapps also can't be accessed from a pure TTY.
SSH also has sshfs, so you can mount your VM's filesystem locally:
sshfs
zydra.sh: ~/zydra
Where SSH still struggles and what I'm doing about it
On Android, SSH is technically "available" through Termux, although it can be finicky. I've made a webapp version of the
zydra.sh
compositor that's more responsive and accessible in mobile for this use case.
SSH also still poses limits around audio (as agents are increasingly used with dictation), and despite how much the Kitty graphics protocol helps, it leaves a lot of optimization on the table due to a lack of stronger client-side state and streaming protocols.
My SSH-native compositing system and microVM desktop environment based on it are the backbone of my broader attempt to create an actually pleasant agent sandbox :). A cloud computer without cloud friction if you will. Another article which describes how I added a "timeline" feature to
zydra.sh
that allows you to rewind the VM as if watching a livestream is available here:
Agents need an undo button
. You can read more about me and my background on my
portfolio
, too.

title: Britain's ghost stations
content:
Text size

Small

Medium

Large

Line Spacing

Compact

Normal

Spacious

Comments

When I stepped off a train at Achanalt station into the frosty Highlands one morning last March, I did notice that it wasn’t quite Waterloo in the rush hour, but I didn’t realise what an exclusive club I had just joined. According to a list of Britain’s most and least-used stations published this week, I was one of only 352 people to board or get off a train there in the entire 12 months from April 2025 to March 2026.

Flanders and Swann wrote ‘The Slow Train’ about the Beeching closures, lamenting the rural stations which were to close. They needn’t have worried: over half a century on, such places still exist.

My instinct is to attack the waste of public money in keeping a station open when hardly anyone uses it, but the absurdity of Britain’s ‘ghost’ stations fascinates me more than angers me. In any case, having paid £11 to travel 20 miles down the line from Strathcarron, I did rather feel that I had single-handedly covered the annual cost of maintaining what is really little more than a platform and Perspex shelter.

Achanalt, it turns out, is only the 15th least-used station in Britain. The honour of being the least-used this year is taken by Reddish South, on an obscure line from Stockport to Stalybridge in Greater Manchester, which was used by only 94 passengers. It is an achievement it will be hard-pressed to repeat next year, as the country’s least-used station invariably receives a leap in custom as railway fanatics descend on it just for the sake of being there: station-visiting has apparently taken over from train-spotting now that few trains have proper locomotives any more. Last year’s winner of the title for least-used station, Elton and Orston, in Nottinghamshire, saw its annual passenger numbers jump from 68 to 102, demoting it to third place. I wouldn’t be surprised if every single one of the extra passengers wore an anorak and carried a bag of Marmite sandwiches.

Most popular

Tim Stanley

How Nick Fuentes is reshaping the right

Alexander Larman

Taylor Swift is a megalomaniac. So what?

Chris Mondics

The unanswered questions about Ilhan Omar

There are two types of ghost station. Firstly, there are those such as Reddish South which are the product of public opposition to the Beeching closures. Some time in the 1970s, British Rail stopped closing stations, reckoning that the bureaucracy and expense of going through the consultation procedure required to remove them from the railway map altogether was greater than simply running down the service to a minimal level. As a result, Reddish South receives one train a week in each direction, on a Saturday morning. You can’t even get a day out in Stockport: catch the 8.46 from Reddish South and you only get five minutes before the train home.

The second type of ghost station is those like Achanalt, which offer a full service of several trains a day; it is just that there aren’t many people who want to travel there. In Achanalt’s case, it isn’t hard to wonder why. The ‘village’, if it can be called that, consists of four houses. Nor is the station all that much good for doing what I was doing: accessing the nearby hills, as a river cuts them off to the south and a thick forestry plantation lies in the way to the north. If you want to go for a walk, it is almost certainly going to involve a few miles’ romp along the A832.

It is pretty absurd that Dr Beeching left a station like this open while depriving Dudley (population 335,000) and Mansfield (114,000) of a rail service – although the latter has subsequently reopened. But at least Achanalt serves four properties. Even more bizarre is Altnabreac station on the Far North Line between Inverness and Wick.

Maybe Dr Beeching couldn’t even find it on the map. It lies up a track seven miles from the nearest public road and there is precisely one house within five miles: the former station house. Trouble is, owners, who presumably could have bought a remote property anywhere in the empty vastness of Caithness, don’t seem to like trains very much. In 2023, a gang of workers from Network Rail turned up to repair the platform and found the gate locked. After a stand-off lasting many months, involving many lawyers and a court case, and a threat by Network Rail to compulsorily purchase the property so that access could be restored, an injunction finally gave the work gang access.

In the meantime, no trains ran at all: the official passenger numbers for the year 2024/25 were zero. Happily, services have now been restored and the walkers and bird-spotters have returned to the platform. Er, all 172 of them last year.

title: I checked Clojure's core with Lean and found unreported bugs
content:
I read Koukyosyumei's article "
著名なRust製OSSをLean 4で形式検証してみたら、めちゃめちゃバグが見つかった話
" (in Japanese; the title means "I formally verified well-known Rust OSS with Lean 4 and found a lot of bugs").
The author ported well-known Rust projects into a form they could prove in Lean 4, and where a proof failed, they found a bug in the original code.

Many people have used Clojure's persistent data structures since around 1.0, so I expected no bugs to remain.
Still, I wanted to see whether Lean would find something there too.

hirosassa/lean-verify
describes a procedure for modeling a small function in Lean 4 and checking it for all inputs, so I applied it to the part of Clojure's core written in Java.

I modeled integer and bit arithmetic in Lean and searched for counterexamples.
I checked the collections with differential testing against the
java.util
collections, and for Java interop I compared the same call with and without a type hint.

I found 17 bugs that I could not find in Clojure's JIRA or on ask.clojure.org.
They include
reduce
on
vector-of
, the hash collision node of the HAMT, and calls to functional interfaces without a type hint.

The HAMT itself showed no mismatch in 3 million operations of differential testing, and the vector tree showed none around its boundaries.
The bugs sat in separate code outside the trees, and in places where two mechanisms meet, such as
=
and hashing.

I used Clojure 1.12.7, released on 2026-11-18, and JDK 21.
The links to the source point to the
clojure-1.12.7
tag.

How I checked

The lean-verify procedure picks one function and models it as a Lean definition.
You write a property that compares it with a naive specification computed at a wider width, and
bv_decide
searches for a counterexample.

If you model Java's
long
and
int
as
BitVec 64
and
BitVec 32
, the wraparound of addition and multiplication maps onto
BitVec
operations.
So do the rounding of
/
toward zero and the sign of
%
.

When Lean found a counterexample, I turned the value into a Clojure input and reproduced it in the original code.
I then modeled the fixed code in Lean and proved the same property.
Lean can only take small functions that reduce to integer and bit arithmetic, so I checked the large persistent data structures with differential testing.

Each test applies the same random sequence of operations to
PersistentHashMap
and to
java.util.HashMap
and compares the results.
For the HAMT, the keys mix partial collisions at each 5-bit level with fully identical hashes, and I ran 1,500 operations for each of 2,000 seeds.

For vectors, I compared against
ArrayList
around 32, 1056, 32800, and 1048608, where the tree gains a level.
The operations were
conj
,
pop
,
assoc
, and their transient versions.

I checked whether anyone had reported each bug before.
I searched Clojure's JIRA through its REST API and ask.clojure.org through web search and the site's own search, and found no matching report.

reduce on vector-of never finishes

vector-of
is a vector that stores its values in primitive arrays.
Clojure implements it in
gvec.clj
, written in Clojure and separate from
PersistentVector
.
If you
drop
from one and then
reduce
it, the call never returns once the vector has 65505 or more elements.

(
reduce
+ (
drop
1
(
into
(
vector-of
:long
) (
range
65504
))))

;; => 2145354256

(
reduce
+ (
drop
1
(
into
(
vector-of
:long
) (
range
65505
))))

;; => never returns

(
reduce
+ (
drop
1
(
vec
(
range
65505
))))

;; => 2145419760

The cause is
line 79 of gvec.clj
, where the seq's
reduce
computes the start of the next 32-element chunk.

(
recur
result (
bit-and
0xffe0
(
+
aidx
32
)))

The code uses
0xffe0
to clear the low 5 bits and round down to a multiple of 32, but the mask also clears bit 16 and everything above it.
With 65505 elements, the last chunk starts at index 65504.
After that chunk, the start of the next one should be 65536, but the mask turns it into 0, so
reduce
goes back to the start and reads the vector again and again.

The
0xffe0
mask has stayed in place since the
2010 commit
that added
internal-reduce
.
In Lean, I wrote the property that from a position
a
that is a multiple of 32, the next chunk starts at
a + 32
.

import
Std.Tactic.BVDecide

def
stepImpl
(a : BitVec
64
) : BitVec
64
:=
0xffe0
&&& (a +
32
)

def
stepFix
(a : BitVec
64
) : BitVec
64
:= (~~~
0x1f
) &&& (a +
32
)

theorem
impl_ok
(a : BitVec
64
) (h32 : a &&&
0x1f
=
0
) (hlt : a <
0x7fffffe0
) :

stepImpl a = a +
32
:=
by

unfold stepImpl; bv_decide

theorem
fix_ok
(a : BitVec
64
) (h32 : a &&&
0x1f
=
0
) (hlt : a <
0x7fffffe0
) :

stepFix a = a +
32
:=
by

unfold stepFix; bv_decide

impl_ok
fails with the counterexample
a = 1073741792
, and
#eval stepImpl 65504
returns 0 as well.

fix_ok
uses
(bit-not 0x1f)
as the mask, and its proof goes through under the assumption that
a
is a multiple of 32 below
0x7fffffe0
.

dissoc on a HAMT collision node hides another key

Clojure's hash-map is a HAMT: it splits the key's hash into 5-bit pieces and uses them to walk down the tree.
Keys whose 32-bit hashes are identical share a
HashCollisionNode
at the bottom of the tree, and the node finds a key among them with
=
.

HashCollisionNode.without
builds the new node with one key removed.
It should give the new node its own hash,
this.hash
, but it passes the parameter
hash
instead.

return
new
HashCollisionNode
(
null
, hash, count
-
1
,
removePair
(array, idx
/
2
));

The parameter
hash
is the hash of the key you pass to
dissoc
.
If you
dissoc
with a key that is
=
to the stored key but has a different hash, the node records the wrong hash.

In Clojure, a vector is
=
to a Java
ArrayList
with the same elements, but the two hash differently.

CLJ-1372
tracks this mismatch.

In the example below, I chose
a
and
b
so that both
ArrayList
keys hash to 1003.

(
def
a
(
java.util.ArrayList.
[
0
42
]))

(
def
b
(
java.util.ArrayList.
[
1
11
]))

[(
hash
a) (
hash
b) (
hash
[
0
42
]) (
=
a [
0
42
])]

;; => [1003 1003 1867155179 true]

(
def
m3
(
->
(
hash-map
a
:A
b
:B
)

(
dissoc
[
0
42
])

(
assoc
a
:A2
)))

[m3 (
count
m3) (
get
m3 b)]

;; => [{[1 11] :B, [0 42] :A2} 2 nil]

When you print
m3
, you can see the key
b
, but
(get m3 b)
returns
nil
.
After the
dissoc
, the node records 1867155179, the hash of
[0 42]
.
The next
assoc
then concludes that
a
, with hash 1003, does not collide with the node, and splits the two into separate branches.

A lookup of
b
follows the branch for 1003 and finds only
a
there, so it never reaches
b
.
In this example the collision node sits on the first level of the tree, so the key passed to
dissoc
needs the same low 5 bits as 1003, and 1867155179 has them.

disj
on a hash-set has the same bug, while the path through the transient
dissoc!
does not.

I changed that line in the 1.12.7
PersistentHashMap.java
to
this.hash
and compiled it.
With the patched class ahead of the jar on the classpath, the same example returned
:B
for
(get m3 b)
.

removeIf gives different results with and without a type hint

Since Clojure 1.12, you can pass a Clojure function directly where a Java method takes a functional interface.

CLJ-2864
removed the logic that read the function's return value as a Clojure truthy value.

In prior alphas, the FI adapter returns inserted Clojure truthy return logic when adapting a Clojure function to an FI with boolean return.

The compiler follows this for calls where it knows the type.
A call without a type hint goes through reflection and uses
Reflector.coerceAdapterReturn
.
That method still applies
RT.booleanCast
to a
boolean
return value, so the same
.removeIf
call gives a different result depending on the type hint.

(
let
[l (
java.util.ArrayList.
[
1
2
3
])]

(
.removeIf
l #{
1
2
}) (
vec
l))

;; => ClassCastException

(
let
[l (
identity
(
java.util.ArrayList.
[
1
2
3
]))]

(
.removeIf
l #{
1
2
}) (
vec
l))

;; => [3]

Wrapping the list in
identity
hides the type of
l
, so the call goes through reflection.

A set used as a function returns the element itself.
In the call with a known type, the adapter cannot turn the
Long
into a
Boolean
and throws.
The reflective call reads the return value as true and removes the elements.

int overflow and a negative subvec index

Clojure 1.12 added
IDrop
implementations that make
drop
faster.
The ones for string seqs and vector seqs add the current position and
n
as ints and then compare the sum with the length.

StringSeq.drop
for string seqs is one of them.

(
drop
Integer/MAX_VALUE (
next
(
seq
"abc"
)))

;; => StringIndexOutOfBoundsException Index -2147483648

(
drop
Integer/MAX_VALUE (
seq
"abc"
))

;; => ()

The Lean model gave the counterexample
i = 2147483646
and
n = 2147483647
.
I changed the check to compare
n
with the remaining length
s.length() - i
.
Under the assumptions
0 <
i < s.length()= and
0 < n
, Lean proved that the fixed check matches the naive specification for every 32-bit input.

For
assoc
on the result of
subvec
,
SubVector.assocN
does not reject a negative index.

(
assoc
[
2
3
]
-1
:x
)

;; => IndexOutOfBoundsException

(
let
[s (
assoc
(
subvec
[
0
1
2
3
4
]
2
4
)
-1
:x
)]

[s (
.-v
s)])

;; => [[2 3] [0 :x 2 3 4]]

The call overwrites an element of the underlying vector outside the subvec, and returns a subvec that looks unchanged.

CLJ-962
fixed the same bug in
nth
, but
assoc
still has it.

Other findings

The other 12 bugs have a smaller impact, and I reproduced each of them on Clojure 1.12.7.

Behavior

Example

reduce-kv
throws on
vector-of

(reduce-kv f [] (vector-of :long 5 6))

With a functional interface of three or more arguments, a call with a known type truncates an
int
return value without an error

(fn [a b c] 4294967297)
returns 1, and
(fn [a b] 4294967297)
throws
ArithmeticException

next
on a seq of a string, a primitive array, or an infinite
repeat
keeps the metadata

(meta (rest (with-meta (seq "abc") {:m 1})))
is
{:m 1}
, and for a vector's seq it is
nil

(long ##NaN)
and
(int ##NaN)
return 0

(long ##NaN)
is 0, and
(byte ##NaN)
throws

long
clamps a double 2^63, and
int
a float 2^31, to the maximum value

(long (Math/pow 2 63))
is
Long/MAX_VALUE

char
wraps a BigInt at 2^64

(char 18446744073709551681N)
is
\A

float
rejects
##Inf
but lets
##NaN
through

(float ##Inf)
throws, and
(float ##NaN)
is
##NaN

Boxed and primitive doubles use different range checks when converted to byte and similar types

(byte (identity 127.9))
is 127, and
(byte 127.9)
throws

get
truncates a fractional index on strings and Java arrays

(get "abc" 1.9)
is
\b

byte-array
and
short-array
reject an initial value

(byte-array 2 7)
throws

On a seq of a primitive array,
.indexOf
and
.contains
disagree

(.indexOf (seq (byte-array [1 2 3])) 2)
is -1

.lastIndexOf
on a list compares with
equals
instead of
=

(.lastIndexOf (list 1 2) (int 2))
is -1

Where I found nothing

PersistentHashMap
and
PersistentHashSet
matched
java.util.HashMap
over 3 million operations that mixed persistent and transient updates.
The tests also covered maps before an update staying unchanged,
ArrayNode
splits and merges, and collision nodes down to depth 7.

PersistentTreeMap
matched
java.util.TreeMap
and kept the red-black tree invariants.
Vectors matched
ArrayList
around every tree boundary I tested.

On the numeric side, Lean proved for 64 bits that the check
Numbers
uses to pick the fast path for addition and subtraction agrees with the overflow check.

For multiplication,
bv_decide
timed out at 16 bits, so I checked 8 and 10 bits.
I proved up to 32 bits that
clojure.core/mod
matches the floored remainder.

Every property I proved in Lean holds for the model shown in this article.
I checked that each model means the same thing as the Java code by comparing it with the source and with the reproduced behavior.

title: Porting Rockbox to an undocumented $9 AliExpress 'YP3' MP3 player with LLMs
content:
Rockbox
is a wonderful old custom firmware project for
a variety of MP3 players and iPods. Flashing rockbox to my
Sansa E200

was a seminal moment for me: computers were everywhere, and if they didn’t do
cool things, it was because no one had bothered to program them to do so. Looking
back, that played no small part in my choice of career.

It seems like in 2026 there aren’t any cheap MP3 players that Rockbox supports
though. Reverse engineering an embedded platform like this is one of the hardest
things I can think of, and I had decided to pay the big bucks for one of those
delicious subsidized token plans to try and push it as hard as I could, and
I did have a dirt cheap $9 Aliexpress MP3 player lying around.

TL;DR: it ported Rockbox to a 512 KiB player, I was barely involved.
Then, I had it build a re-usable toolkit/set of skills for future ports based on
what worked from the first attempt approach, and Claude was able to get Rockbox
running on another MP3 player (TS47) in 4 hours.

I made a quick website for the project:
https://rockslop.jayd.ml

Here is the porting toolkit:
auto-rockbox

Enter: The YP3

This is an unbranded player, sold under a variety of fake consonant soup brands
on Amazon as well as Aliexpress. You can order them wholesale from Alibaba for
less than $7 or so each.

It calls itself a
yp3_2.0.43
in the “About” menu as.
This appears to be a listing for a YP3
- the original is gone. I paid $9.71 for mine, shipped.

NOTE: Before you run off and buy one, I have another rockbox port that is probably
a week or two out, it is booting and stable, just needs more acceptance testing.
This device is extremely similar but has 4 MiB PSRAM, so it has fewer compromises

This was $20 on sale

I also have a stack of other random MP3 players I intend to repeat this with

See the project website:
https://rockslop.jayd.ml

Special thanks

If anyone gets credit for this rockbox port, it’s
ilyakurdyukov
- they figured out how to get it into ROM Download
mode (Down + USB), and wrote a utility to dump / write flash. Then I could be
a little slop kiddie and not have to use a soldering iron.

See
the YP3 page
on the project
website for more info.

The good:

It costs $9. If it breaks buy another one.

USB-C and Blueooth!

There is a physical reset button, device is easily recoverable

Unbrickable (if you keep stock bootloader): holding down and resetting brings
you into a DFU USB download mode.

Someone already figured out how to flash and interact with ROM DFU

That ROM DFU mode lets you poke flash and RAM.

The bad

SoC:
Complete mystery meat Chinese “Smartlink SL6801” / Jointbees. Does
not exist online

2x Cortext-M4 r0p1 cpuID
0x410fc241

192 MHz (stock does not vary CPU freq). Has an FPU

Capable of Execute In Place (XIP) from flash, but no cache at all. Slow as dirt.

When XIP-ing code, cpu1 always waits behind cpu0 and can stall indefinitely
if cpu0 is continuously fetching instructions from flash. Very easy to deadlock

SRAM
512 KiB plus about ~30 KiB for packets for the bluetooth radio.

2 MB Flash ROM

128x160 full color LCD (RGB565)

Only 5 buttons - a dpad with a center press (center press is power & wired to
PMU)

Bluetooth (with an undocumented stack)

It has 512KiB of SRAM, and the smallest existing Rockbox target was 2 MiB, I was
already scrolling Aliexpress for another one, but the LLM said “trust me bro I
can make it happen” and I decided to try its luck.

The ugly

While the hardware is cheap but functional, stock OS is painful to use

It regularly crashes and watchdogs when in USB transfer mode

Where the port ended up

YP3 running Rockbox

After about a week it was booting a build of Rockbox on a crash diet - every
single buffer had been cut to the bone, but it could start and play audio.
Tuning, bug fixing, etc took another month or so.

I am not aware of anything that isn’t working hardware wise.

The main feature you lose is concurrency while playing music and plugins. Codecs
and plugins are already loaded and swapped around at runtime with normal Rockbox,
but on this player there is one shared 128 KiB arena for both, so starting a
plugin stops music playback.

Other cuts include:

No voice

Only English is supported

DSP:
No pitch/speed control, surround, crossfade

Cuesheets

album art

Theme backdrop pictures

No dircache, so folders are read straight from SD card

Large folders are truncated by default at 256 (configurable from 32 to 512)

Playlists are capped at 400

Codecs: WMA Pro, Musepack (MPC), RealAudio (Cook), and the chiptune formats
SID, NSF, VGM, KSS, HES, SGC, ASAP. WavPack (16-bit), (24-bit/96 kHz)

What made it, somehow:

MP3 (up to 320 kbps), AAC/M4A (AAC+ too, HE-AAC v2 plays in mono),
WMA, Opus (up to ~192 kbps), Ogg Vorbis, FLAC (stereo, up to 24-bit/96 kHz),
ALAC, WAV, AIFF, AU, TTA, APE, Speex, MOD, SPC, AY, GBS, A52/AC3, ATRAC3,
Shorten, ADX, VOX, SMAF.

The database.

The database has a new variant that is disk only and has synchronous, blocking
updates (ie the player shows a loading screen and stops music when it refreshes
and doesn’t refresh in background). I think it also cut the “songs by letter”
menu.

The database requests memory for its menus at runtime, and depending on the
size of your theme it can refuse to open the menus.

Themes, without backgrounds. load and work, although heavy themes can cause the
database to stop opening (handled gracefully with a warning)

Bluetooth

Overnight Claude reverse engineered the bluetooth stack and wrote a bluetooth
HAL for Rockbox. I asked it before I went to bed and it was working in the
morning.

No binary blobs are shipped: the bt stack is burned into chip ROM (not flash),
and the YP3 bluetooth driver calls into the stack.

A note on codecs

Most of the codecs run from SRAM as normal. MP3, AAC, WMA, Vorbis and Opus,
however, wouldn’t fit in our arena nicely, so they run from flash.

But, our XIP flash is dirt slow, so lots of very careful profiling was done to
move hot code loops back into SRAM. This kind of profiling had to be done
all over Rockbox to get hot loops into SRAM - font rendering, alpha blending,
scrolling, etc. This is where most of the “weeks of polishing” went.

Battery Life

Largely comparable to stock. I hooked the player up to the PC’s line in or
fake bluetooth sink and set it to repeat Daft Punks
Random Access Memories
. A
script on the PC detected when it cut out.

Stock:
21.29 hours wired, 20.07 on Bluetooth

Rockbox:
20.07 hours wired, 19.3 on Bluetooth

There was some variation in the battery voltage at start, and this was just
one run, so expect some variation.

Battery life is surprisingly impressive on this player,

Approach

I’m one of those software guys, I can’t solder or find UART pads to save my life.
This was an entirely software only port; I haven’t ever opened mine up.

I hooked up ghidra-mcp and let it start pulling the firmware apart. It figured
out how to inject tasks into the running RTOS (FreeRTOS) in bootloader mode.
This allowed it to probe the hardware and even write drivers before attempting a
Rockbox boot.

To be clear: this is
100% vibecoded
. I have only glanced at some of the code
it wrote. I contributed my approach to development and testing, was the PM and
QA person, and the agent’s little meat robot to reboot it when it crashed or
wander around my house with headphones on while it tuned the bluetooth radio.
I haven’t doneC and firmware development for years.

Cleanroom

Initially I let the same agent do the reverse engineering as implementation.
Later I had it go through and rip out anything that wasn’t a hardware fact (ie
a register) and re-did the drivers with a cleanroom setup. One dirty agent with
Ghidra, one referee agent in between to make sure nothing leaks, and the implementation
agent. Subsequent ports used a variation of this setup from the beginning

The most work I have done personally on this project is writing this blog post.

Robotic eyes and ears

Webcam pointed at the screen, so the model could see what the player was
doing and to work on the LCD drivers.

Webcam mic for bringing up the speaker

(had to yell at Claude when it decided to start playing tones at 2 AM)

Headphone jack plugged into Line In on my PC (finally, I used it!!)

This allowed it to test and tune audio output.

Bluetooth adapter. I plugged in a bluetooth adapter and gave it full reign
for testing. It used Google’s
Bumble
python
bluetooth stack to have the PC pretend to be headphones

Claude kept picking “We Will Rock You” as a test track. I choose to believe this
is evidence of a subtle sense of humor when working on a Rockbox port

Opus 5.5 »»»> Sol

This port was started with Codex/Sol 5.6. It was making progress, but was incredibly
risk averse and slow. It took it 5 days or so and dozens of manual resets on my
part until it felt ready to flash something and boot it.

I should have told it how to figure out how to arm the watchdog and reboot into
download mode itself sooner. Codex got it to showing the rockbox logo with buggy
drivers stubbed out, but had clearly lost its mind in the meantime. I hadn’t
been paying attention too closely, but as it had spun around it had:

Created 55 GB of files in 2,567 dirs. 3.87 million files total

443 one off tool scripts, 384 documents written

an incredibly paranoid flasher that would check each block as it was written
and took 15 minutes to write 2 MiB

This flashing script - and many other tool scripts - would check the sha256
of the
documentation files they depended on
to ensure nothing had changed.

It’s kind of beautiful in its own insane way: this seems to be an attempt to
work around multiple agents and memory limits. Madness though

An MCP server with tons of ceremony and tools around flashing things, running
tests, etc

Claude immediately threw that garbage away and wrote like a few python scripts
to use instead. Auto mode in claude code helped too.

The subsequent TS17 port went from me plugging it in to a usable alpha build
in about 4 hours with Opus 5.5 (there was little to re-use from the YP3 other
than scripts and skills).

Bidirectional Rockbox Dev Shell

This is one of the most valuable things it did. Rockbox has an existing one-way USB
serial driver for logs. I had that extended to have dozens of little commands to
drive the player, everything from injecting keypresses to taking screenshots to
debugging the bluetooth radio.

This was critical for completely hands off development - I had it build a torture
test suite in Python that would monkey-test the player for hours, pressing
buttons at random. Many bugs were found doing this - including some in Rockbox
upstream. At this point the player has hundreds of hours of bench testing under
Rockbox - I could just leave it running and Claude would patiently watch the
test logs for new failures to diagnose and fix.

An agent can reboot to recovery, flash firmware, reboot into Rockbox, run tests,
see what is on the screen, hear what it is doing, completely on its own. Most of
the development of this project happened while I was asleep.

Audio Tuning

For audio (and battery endurance testing) Claude had me set up a 3.5 mm splitter
with one end going into the PC’s Line In and the other going into real
headphones to provide an actual load.

Then I had it build a test suite and file that plays a variety of sweeps and
test tones. I used an Apple lightning adapter to use as the ground truth for this
setup, then used it to compare audio levels and frequency response.

My PC’s sound card is not high sensitivity equipment, but this is enough of a
sanity check for me.

More charts that I don’t understand</summary>

</details>

The Hardest Parts

There were two tricky things to work out that Claude struggled to fix.
The exact power off sequence took quite a few tries, probably because it was the
only thing I had to be there to test, it couldn’t just work on it for hours
overnight.

The other crazy bug was that the FM radio sounded terrible. You
could tune to a station, but the sound was distorted and clipped. Claude spent
forever trying to figure out why, but eventually I noticed that the frequency
it was tuned to did not match the station identifier over the air.

It turns out the tuner had been set up with a slightly wrong clock source, so it
was ~4 MhZ off. It just so happened to work out that when I tuned it to my test
station, it could kind of lock on to another one, but sounded terrible.

Other New Features

Plugin Psychosis

I told Claude to port as many games as it could to Rockbox.

This release adds
THREE HUNDRED AND FIFTY SEVEN
new plugins. That is not a
typo: 357. Most of these are ports, a few are originals. Given the quantity here
I haven’t done enough QA here.

Originals

RockGPT

This is going to get its own blog post because it is deeply amusing. A ~1 million
param model running on your MP3 player. Almost coherent, fine tuned to be aloof
and dismissive of humanity. Weights are streamed from SD card. Crazy

RockTrack

A little tracker/chiptune editor for Rockbox. I haven’t had a ton of time to
test this one. Probably needs ergonomic improvements.

Video Player

Rockbox’s existing mpegplayer didn’t fit on the YP3 and I didn’t want to hack
it up too much, so I had Claude write a new one, with a nicer pixel art UI,
MKV support. AVI, MKV, MP4; MPEG-1/2, MJPEG.

Ports

There are too many to list.
Here is the full set of ports

Anarch - FOSS DOOM clone

Celeste Classic - Platformer Maddy Thorson, Noel Berry

MicroCity City builder, jhhoward

Prizm Racing, Racing, duarteapcoelho

Rockcraft Minecraft-style block sandbox, port of Blocks-TI-84 by The Science Elf, MIT

Terrario, Terraria-like KBD2

Jet Island, 3D island demo CubeCoders

Rock88, 3D rendered Film player demo JetExamples

Bulk Ports

We got to stupid plugin numbers by writing compat shims/libraries for several
popular open source players:

Arduboy
: 240

Pokitto
: 23

Flipper Zero
: 33

Gamebuino
: 17

Misc Features

Enhanced RDS: program type names, call letters, clock time, RadioText+
(artist/title)

Charge limiter (hardware dependent, allows 50-100% cap)

Bluetooth HID drivers

Yes, you can pair a PS4 controller or keyboard to Rockbox. I wanted to see how
much we could do with the existing Bluetooth stack

Bluetooth headset battery level detection, with an icon in the status bar

Themes

I had it port some themes from the Rockbox website to work on this screensize,
add a bluetooth status icon, and it generated 5 original themes: Ukiyo (my
favorite), Asterism, Chaldani, Lavenia, Cyanotype.

Note: This is a WIP screenshot, there have been bug fixes & some of these got
cut because of unclear licensing.

Note that heavy themes can cause some issues, so I would suggest sticking with
lightweight ones.

Fin

Well, reverse engineering a completely undocumented chipset was one of the
hardest things I could think of to do, and Claude can ace it. I’m planning on
porting Rockbox to a bunch of other cheap MP3 players.

THEY ALL SHALL RUN ROCKBOX!

Appendix: Identifying a YP3

There are lots of clones that look like each other. The YP3 specifically:

Only has 5 buttons - dpad and center

no power, volume

symbols molded into buttons, not printed on them in white

Has a reset pinhole on the
right

Speaker on
top
rear

USB on bottom right, headphone jack on left

SD card on the left

I think they’re all black

Also, these screens are made of cheese, you’ll want a screen protector.

title: Show HN: An agent skill that optimizes code with falsifiable hypotheses
content:
Agents that optimize your code like an algorithm engineer: a falsifiable hypothesis before every experiment, correctness checked after every change, one reviewable patch per accepted change, and a PDF report of the whole session.
A skill for Claude Code and Codex, from the Algorithm Engineering Group at Heidelberg University.
Every kept change was checked against the original output.
Algorithm Engineering is a cycle of design, analysis, implementation and experiment, driven by falsifiable hypotheses. AAE hands this cycle to an autonomous agent. During setup you agree with the agent on the benchmark, the metric, the correctness assertions and the budget; then it runs on its own.
From the report of the KaHIP
kaffpa
session: 122 experiments, 69 hypotheses, 41 patches, 3.9x faster in total.
In Claude Code:
In Codex, install the skill with
scripts/install_codex_skill.py
and call it with
$aae
; any other agent can follow
AAE.md
. To try it first, run the
10-minute quick-start example
: a slow but correct shortest-path program with a benchmark and a correctness check.
Sessions share what they learned: the
knowledge base
collects optimization techniques and experiment results, and agents read it before they start. Contributions from your own sessions are welcome.
David A. Bader, Adil Chhabra, Ernestine Großmann, Monika Henzinger, Alexander Noe, and Christian Schulz.
Agentic Algorithm Engineering: Improving Shared-Memory Exact Minimum Cuts.
In 13th DIMACS Implementation Challenge Workshop: Network Flows 2.0, OASIcs, 2027. To appear. Preprint:
arXiv:2609.07204
.
To cite the software itself, use its Zenodo DOI
10.5281/zenodo.24537749
, which always resolves to the latest release.
