his post this week
. You peel back the curtain on some piece of infrastructure the economy quietly runs on, expecting Swiss watchmaking, and find duct tape, twenty-year-old batch files, and three people in the whole company who know why you never reboot box four on a Tuesday. He calls them “smart people who give a shit,” and he’s dead right that they are the main reason the lights stay on.

Halfway down the page, though, the essay takes a turn I’ve been seeing a lot lately, and it bugs me. Michael points to the recent run of big outages (Microsoft 365, United, major banks, Apple) and blames leadership for trying to swap those people out for generative AI. Fair enough; there’s probably plenty of truth in that. But he doesn’t stop at bad management. By the end, the tools themselves have become the acid dissolving whoever picks them up. “Every prompt moves them one step further away from the system they used to know inside and out,” he writes. Every generated line robs engineers of the struggle that makes them smart and the ownership that makes them care.

The implication is pretty hard to miss: if you’re using AI, you’re giving up on giving a shit.

I use these tools every day on systems where bugs cost significant sums of money or wedge production queues, and my experience has been almost the exact opposite. More than anything else, LLMs amplify who you already are. Deeply curious, caring people can dramatically amplify what they produce and how thoroughly they understand it. Lazy bums can, for now, coast as meat proxies for a chat window, ferrying tickets into a prompt box and clicking merge on whatever falls out.

Think about what “giving a shit” actually meant on a normal engineering team before 2024. Mostly, it meant fighting a losing war against the clock. You’d spot a nasty race condition in a state machine and know you
should
model it in TLA+, or write a property test that hammers every interleaving, or go read the forty-thousand-line service downstream to be certain your assumption held. Half the time you didn’t, because doing it properly took two days you didn’t have and three other fires were waiting. So you eyeballed the diff, wrote a unit test for the happy path, left a slightly nervous comment, and hoped nobody touched that file for a while. Caring was rarely limited by how much people wanted to do the right thing. It was rationed by how fast one human could read and type.

When you hand a capable model to
that
engineer, they don’t suddenly shrug and rubber-stamp the first draft. They finally write the TLA+ spec. They pull on the threads they were always curious about, digging into why a gnarly legacy subsystem behaves the way it does instead of treating it as a black box. They build a real simulator for the flaky third-party API nobody ever had time to mock properly. They have the model trace every caller of a legacy function across a sprawling monorepo before changing its contract, instead of grepping for five minutes and praying. They write the exhaustive edge-case tests and run mutation testing against the parts that keep them awake at night.

The kind of rigor that used to be reserved for people writing avionics software or working at Bell Labs is suddenly cheap enough to pull off on an ordinary Thursday. Calling that “caring less” has the whole thing backwards.

Then there is the other side of the amplifier. Anyone who has reviewed a 1,500-line pull request written by a meat proxy who clearly hit “accept all,” got a green linter, and blanked out when asked to explain line 400 knows exactly what Michael is furious about. (I’m certainly guilty of opening massive AI-assisted PRs myself, though in the service of giving a shit, so the line count by itself isn’t the crime.) Prompt, paste, and pray is very real, and it produces miserable software. I’ve
written before
about the specific sinking feeling of staring at 800 lines of generated code you have no mental model of and deploying it with crossed fingers.

There’s a subtler hazard too, especially for people early in their careers: if you never wrestle with a weird bug or read a stack trace yourself, you never build the scar tissue that tells you when something smells wrong. And LLMs make laziness unusually tempting because of how they fail. A compiler yells at you loudly when you screw up; a model fails in smooth, confident prose that looks totally reasonable until production catches fire. That’s a genuine risk, and pretending it isn’t would be silly.

Still, look closely at what’s actually broken in that scenario. The trouble comes from shipping code nobody verified, without building a mental model, in an organization where nobody feels on the hook when it breaks. We had that exact engineer long before ChatGPT showed up. Ten years ago they pasted the top Stack Overflow answer without reading the comments, pulled in a bloated dependency to avoid thinking for twenty minutes, and stamped “LGTM” on every review after thirty seconds. Now they can coast as a human clipboard for a model, at least for a while, until the production bugs pile up or someone realizes a cron job could do the clipboard part cheaper. Take away their LLM tomorrow and they won’t suddenly start caring about ACH edge cases. They’ll just go back to shipping carelessness at a slower clip.

Look at Michael’s own example of ACH. The people keeping banking rails alive aren’t chiseling NACHA files into stone tablets to stay spiritually close to the metal. Their care shows up in reconciliation scripts, monitors, static checks, runbooks, and custom tooling they built because unaided human attention breaks down on systems this messy. Every jump up the abstraction ladder (compilers, garbage collectors, search engines, high-level frameworks) brought the exact same warning that we were moving another step away from the machine and losing the people who really understood it. Sure, far fewer programmers today can hand-assemble x86 than in 1985. Meanwhile, the systems we have to keep upright grew by several orders of magnitude. Without stronger leverage, you don’t get a golden age of artisanal engineering where everyone holds the whole codebase in their head. You just get more critical systems that nobody understands at all, because they long ago outgrew what one unaided brain can hold.

There is a bigger elephant in the room about all those outages, too, and it predates LLMs by a long shot. A huge share of the instability we are watching right now is the bill coming due for forty years of insufficient engineering rigor. Giving a shit does not make people infallible. Some of the smartest, most conscientious engineers in the industry spent decades building critical infrastructure in memory-unsafe languages, gluing together under-specified protocols, skipping formal verification, and shipping state machines whose edge cases lived only inside one person’s head. Heroics and tribal knowledge kept the wheels on, right up until they didn’t.

Plenty of the vulnerabilities and failure modes knocking systems over today have been sitting quietly in the wild for years, or even decades. We got away with them because nobody had the time or budget to poke every dark corner of a sprawling legacy stack, and because change moved slowly enough for manual patching to keep up. Only now is the issue being forced, by
automated bug-hunting that never sleeps
, by decades of accumulated coupling, and by systems that have finally grown too tangled for human heroics to paper over. Blaming all of that on AI slop is a comforting story, because it implies we can just go back to the old way of working and everything will steady out. The old way of working is how we ended up with a world where bad updates and long-dormant bugs can wobble major banks, airlines, and cloud providers in the same week.

None of that lets leadership off the hook. Where Michael is completely on target is what’s happening in the executive suite. Leadership looking at an LLM and thinking,
fantastic, now we can lay off the prickly senior engineers who push back on bad ideas and replace them with a $200-a-month subscription
, really is a slow-motion train wreck, and it makes a fragile landscape much worse. To someone who has never been paged at three in the morning, a fragile system held aloft by quiet competence and a pile of plausible-looking slop look identical on a quarterly slide deck.

That disease, though, is decades older than generative AI. It’s the exact same management fantasy that gave us “let’s fire the expensive in-house team and outsource the core platform to the lowest bidder,” “let’s cut QA because developers can test their own stuff,” and “let’s lay off twenty percent of engineering while keeping the roadmap unchanged.” AI didn’t invent the belief that engineers are interchangeable output factories. It just handed executives a shinier, cheaper-sounding excuse to run the same playbook again.

That’s why lumping AI-using engineers in with the executives hollowing out their companies does real harm. Telling the story as “AI makes engineers dumb and indifferent” accidentally writes bad leadership an alibi:
shucks, the new technology didn’t live up to the hype, who could have known?
And on the way there, it sneers at the people in the trenches who are grabbing every piece of leverage they can find to keep increasingly absurd systems from falling over.

If you want to know whether someone gives a shit about a system, asking whether they used an LLM is the wrong question. Ask what happens when the code they merged breaks at two in the morning. Ask whether “the model wrote it” flies as an excuse in code review. Ask whether they have the time, standing, and backing to tell a VP that a deadline is reckless.

Companies lose smart people who give a shit when they strip away ownership, punish dissent, and reward shipping volume over reliability. Give those same people real stakes and a good model, and they don’t check out. They finally get to build the guardrails, proofs, and fixes they never had the hours to build before.

Michael is right that capitalism has its hand squarely on a hot stove right now, and that the rest of us are getting burned while executives relearn that you can’t automate away accountability. I just wish we’d aim the anger at the people making that bet, instead of pretending that giving a shit requires typing every character by hand.

title: The industrialization of noise: Automated proof-solving is the same old dead end [pdf]
content:
Computer Science > Cryptography and Security

[Submitted on 19 Nov 2026]

Title:
The Industrialization of Noise: Why Automated Proof-Solving is the Same Old Dead End

Authors:
Richard DeMillo
,
Richard Lipton

View a PDF of the paper titled The Industrialization of Noise: Why Automated Proof-Solving is the Same Old Dead End, by Richard DeMillo and 1 other authors

View PDF

HTML (experimental)

Abstract:
Nearly fifty years ago, DeMillo, Lipton, and Perlis argued that mathematical proofs are not static, isolated structures of formal logic, but the products of a vibrant, evolving social process of human critique, internalization, and shared intuition. In October 2026, OpenAI challenged this thesis by releasing a massive repository of 722 automated mathematical manuscripts, claiming full or partial solutions to 372 longstanding open problems. This paper examines the immediate crisis through the lens of the original DLP framework. We argue that the sudden, automated overproduction of dense, unreadable proofs represents an industrial pollution of the mathematical ecosystem. By examining the three fatal structural pillars of this automated approach (Specification, Regress, and Utility), we demonstrate that decoupling the act of mechanical solving from the human social process of understanding produces a sterile repository of dead logical artifacts.

The resulting industrialization of unexamined manuscripts is self-fulfilling. Flooding the literature guarantees that the finite supply of human attention will lose the race to separate signal from noise. In this sense, posting a result is not the same act as submitting it to the community processes by which mathematics is vetted, digested, and incorporated into shared knowledge.

title: A Beer Brewer's Noise Estimation
content:
A Beer Brewer’s Noise Estimation
Counting my algae samples and estimating the error with a hemocytometer
CasualPhysicsEnjoyer
Oct 29, 2026
As a control for my bioreactor trials, I aim to get a constant number of algae cells in every experiment I do. To do this, I have to count the number of algae colonies in a given volume of water, to get a concentration. Both the number and the volume are susceptible to error, which I will discuss.
One cheap approach to estimate a concentration of cells with a microscope is to use use a hemocytometer. I
got one last time
, thanks to suggestions by Kevin Lynagh and David Jordan. The hemocytometer is a slide with dips and a visible has a grid that lets me count the number of cells across a fixed length on the
x
and
y
axes. It also comes with a depth of 0.1 mm when used with a 0.4 mm coverslip¹.
A side view is below.
The side view of a hemocytometer
The grid etched on the hemocytometer
For my first trial I’m using
Scenedesmus quadricauda
from Blades Biological. It's
probably safe
. I pipetted it onto my hemocytometer, put the coverslip on and used my Swift microscope.
I used a new disposable pipette to put it on the sample.
I connected the Swift microscope to my computer and then took the following images.
This is what a single colony looks like. It is usually made out of 4 cells, but if you look closely the number of cells in a colony can vary.
I wanted to use these images to count the number of colonies. I got Claude to write a script to count the dark spots, which are the algae colonies. The procedure it used is in the footnote below².
There are 14 squares where I've counted the number of algae organisms. Each square is 0.2 mm × 0.2 mm. The volume per square is 0.2 mm × 0.2 mm × 0.1 mm = 0.004 mm³ = 4 nL.
We've counted 27 algae colonies. This means that a point estimate for the concentration of our algae is 27 / (14 × 4 nL) = 27 / 56 nL =
4.8 × 10⁵
colonies per mL.
Estimating the error
We can never know the exact, true value of what the concentration is. This is just a point estimate. And in experiments, these measurements have noise and uncertainty. Experiments have multiple sources of uncertainty. In my bioreactor experiment, it could come from a faulty CO2 or O2 sensor. Or a wrong optical density measurement.
Now, it would be impossible and impractical to eliminate
all
uncertainty. But, we should at least guess the magnitude of uncertainty at each step of our protocol. If we do this, we can get a sense for the biggest uncertainties that we need to eliminate.
And so let's try to find an
uncertainty band
around this estimate of our algae concentration.
The first naive method would be to just guess subjective uncertainty bounds. I could just say, based on gut feel, that the concentration has a higher and lower band of 20%. But we can do slightly better than this. One of the earliest methods was made by William Sealy Gosset at the Guinness brewery, who tried to estimate the uncertainty bands around the number of yeast cells present in the brewing mixture. The original paper was
Student (1907), *On the error of counting with a haemacytometer*, Biometrika **5**, 351–360
. Gosset was originally anonymously credited as 'Student' in the original paper, because Guinness didn't want to reveal the methods it was using to brew its stuff.
Gosset uses a hemocytometer to count cells in a volume, and then estimates a quantity called the
standard error
. The interpretation of standard error is the following. Suppose that we repeated the sampling procedure several times under the same conditions. The standard error is the spread of the estimates we would get.
Here is a sketch of Gosset's approach. It is general enough to calculate standard errors for other distributions too.
First, we label the true values in the problem. The full sample in the bottle, which has a fixed volume V, contains some true number of colonies. Suppose we split the bottle into N thin squares, each with volume V / N, and set the true value of the number of colonies as cV, where
c
is the true concentration.
To obtain an estimate for
c
, we need to design an
estimator
. An
estimator
is a way of sampling our system to find a parameter.
It would be impractical to count every single colony in our full volume. So in our case, one estimator we can make is to look at one of the squares above and count the number of colonies we see. We then divide by the volume V, which we assume is known, to get the concentration. The next step is to calculate the statistical properties of this estimator.
Given that we have cV colonies, what is the likelihood that we observe
r
colonies in a given square that we select? The probability that a given colony lands in chosen square is 1/N. The odds of
r
colonies appearing in a square are given the binomial theorem, which is
P(r \text{ colonies in the selected square}) = \binom{cV}{r}\left(\frac{1}{N}\right)^{r}\left(1-\frac{1}{N}\right)^{cV-r}
Now, if we take the limit as N gets large, it turns out that the probability converges to an easy expression. The details of this limit are in Gosset's paper³. The probability of getting
r
colonies in a selected square as N gets large becomes
P(r) \;\longrightarrow\; \frac{m^{r} e^{-m}}{r!}, \qquad m = \frac{cV}{N}
This is known as a
Poisson distribution
. The average of a distribution is the sum of its set of values multiplied by the probability that it gets the value. Doing this for the Poisson distribution, we find that the average of our estimate
r
is given by
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[r] &= \sum_{r=0}^{\infty} r\,P(r), \qquad r = \text{colonies counted in sample} \\
&= \sum_{r=0}^{\infty} r\,\frac{m^{r} e^{-m}}{r!} \\
&= m\,e^{-m} \sum_{r=1}^{\infty} \frac{m^{r-1}}{(r-1)!} \\
&= m\,e^{-m}\,e^{m} \\
&= m
\end{aligned}
If we take multiple counts on separate occasions using our hemocytometer, then on average,
r
is the concentration multiplied by the volume we have sampled.
\mathbb{E}[r = \text{colonies counted in sample}] = m = \frac{cV}{N} = c \cdot \frac{V}{N}
This makes sense. The formula is saying that the
average of our estimator
is the
true
concentration, multiplied by the scaled volume of the sample we collected. And since we know the volume we have collected, calculating the concentration is just a matter of taking
r
and dividing it by our known volume.
In our case the "selected square" is the 14 hemocytometer squares I counted together, with v = 56 nL, and the number we've counted was 27.
To get the standard error, we want to know how much a sample count would deviate over multiple trials. Now we know the distribution of the estimator is Poisson, we can calculate the standard deviation by calculating the standard deviation of a general Poisson distribution.
The standard deviation is the square root of the variance.
\mathrm{Var}(r) = \mathbb{E}\!\left[\left(r - \mathbb{E}[r]\right)^{2}\right] = \mathbb{E}[r^{2}] - \mathbb{E}[r]^{2}
To calculate this, we need to find the expected value of r². To do this, we use a trick and calculate the expected value of r(r-1), since it factorises out nicely.
\mathbb{E}[r(r-1)] = \sum_{r=0}^{\infty} r(r-1)\,\frac{m^{r} e^{-m}}{r!} = m^{2} e^{-m} \sum_{r=2}^{\infty} \frac{m^{r-2}}{(r-2)!} = m^{2}
Some basic algebra gives us
\mathrm{Var}(r) = \mathbb{E}[r^{2}] - \mathbb{E}[r]^{2} = \left(m^{2} + m\right) - m^{2} = m, \qquad \sigma_{r} = \sqrt{m}
We don't know m, so we estimate it with the one count we have m̂ = r, giving σ_r ≈√(r). The concentration estimate is ĉ = r / v, so its standard error is
\sigma_{\hat c} = \frac{\sqrt{r}}{v}, \qquad \frac{\sigma_{\hat c}}{\hat c} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{r}}
For our count, r = 27 in v = 56 nL. And √(27) ≈5.2. Therefore, our
\hat c = \frac{27 \pm 5.2}{56\ \text{nL}} = (4.8 \pm 0.9) \times 10^{5}\ \text{colonies per mL}
our relative error is about 19 %.
The volume I need to pipette to get a target number of colonies n is v_pipette = n / ĉ. Since n is fixed, the relative error in the volume is the same 19 % as the relative error in the concentration; the pipette's own error (about 1 % for a 1 mL pipette) is negligible beside it. For a million colonies:
v_{\text{pipette}} = \frac{10^{6}}{(4.8 \pm 0.9) \times 10^{5}\ \text{mL}^{-1}} = 2.1 \pm 0.4\ \text{mL}
References
Student (W. S. Gosset), 1907. On the error of counting with a haemacytometer.
Biometrika

5
(3), 351–360. doi:10.2307/2331633.
PDF
¹
I learned that standard 0.1 mm coverslips don't work because the capillary effect moves the coverslip in.
³
Student (W. S. Gosset), 1907. On the error of counting with a haemacytometer.
Biometrika

5
(3), 351–360. doi:10.2307/2331633.
PDF
² the claude procedure

title: Hazel (YC W24) Is Hiring a Product Designer
content:
Our mission at Hazel is simple and powerful. We use AI to help U.S. government purchasing teams buy at the speed of need with unparalleled efficiency and cost-effectiveness. It is a $2.7T problem every single year, and Hazel is at the forefront with Federal and State, Local, and Education (SLED) agencies.
Hazel has identified a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to solve this by deploying cutting-edge AI to the public sector and unlocking the full potential of our nation. We empower our partners to move with expediency against the most pressing challenges of this century. Hazel builds AI for the public interest.
Hazel is transforming government procurement: how government agencies purchase goods and services from commercial vendors. Our federal partners use our AI-forward bid evaluations solution to assess vendors more accurately, reliably, and quickly. With the federal government under increasing pressure to accelerate acquisitions, our tools give them a real edge.
Our COTS products, led by Document Builder and Evaluations, serve state & local governments, schools, and special authorities. The users are procurement officers working through long, high-stakes documents and decisions, and they deserve software that is as clear and trustworthy as it is powerful.
As Hazel's contract Product Designer, you will elevate the user experience and visual design of products government teams rely on daily. Hazel has built a substantial product based on deep understanding of our users' needs. In this role, you will refine our UI/UX and establish standards for our engineering team going forward.
There are three main deliverables:
$10,000 - $20,000/month depending on experience | Contract for 3-6 months, 20-40 hrs/week
You will set the design standard for Hazel. Your work will ship to federal evaluators and to procurement teams across states, cities, and schools. The style guide you leave behind will shape every feature we build after.
You'll work side-by-side with inquisitive and driven founders as well as a world-class and dynamic founding engineering team, with frontline exposure to our government partners.
Hazel is a mission-driven organization founded by engineers and built around delivering world-class innovation to our government partners. We strive for excellence, deliver impact, and have fun doing it.
You care about mission.
Hazel partners with agencies supporting everything from public school teachers in the classroom to warfighters in the field. We believe in products which change America for the better.
You want a startup that is structured without being rigid, quality-obsessed without being slow, and product-led without losing the vision.
You take ownership: shaping the experience, talking to customers, and wearing many hats.
You solve problems.
There's no more time to opine on strategy and policy when our nation faces existential challenges, today. We are workhorses, not showhorses.
You are always learning.
Nobody has all the answers, and the world is ever-evolving, so we must be adaptive. We bring the best practices available from all domains to meet the challenge.
You believe in team.
Our team grows together, supports one another, and elevates our shared successes. We are more effective together.

title: How did pinwheel calculators work?
content:
How did pinwheel calculators work?
In today’s article, you can watch the author add numbers together.
Nov 25, 2026
As a handful of readers might know, I am
a bit of a calculator nerd
. I’m especially fond of mechanical four-function calculators that had their heyday between the 1920s and 1960s and then disappeared without a trace.
A video is worth a thousand tokens, so to explore the ingenuity of the design, let’s start with a short clip of a Vaucanson calculator from my collection:
In the first half of the video, I demonstrate addition. I calculate 1234 + 4321 by placing the first operand in the input register, turning the crank clockwise to add this value to the accumulator (bottom right), and then entering the second operand and cranking again. To subtract from the stored value, I’d turn the crank counterclockwise.
The second and more interesting half shows multiplication: I solve 79 × 123 by entering the first operand and then turning the crank three times to load 79 × 3 into the accumulator. Next, I shift the accumulator carriage one decimal digit to the right and crank twice; because the accumulator is offset from the input register, this has the same effect as cranking twenty times in the original position; in other words, I add 79 × 20. Finally, I shift the carriage once more and complete one more turn to add 79 × 100. Note that the crank counter in the bottom left now reads “123”, confirming that we multiplied the first operand by the correct value.
To divide, I’d load the first operand into the accumulator and then successively subtract power-of-ten multiples of the second number. This would give me the integer result in the counter register and the remainder in the accumulator.
Alright — so how does this work? Well, if you pop open a pinwheel calculator, you will be greeted by a pretty complicated mechanism:
Calculator entrails. By author.
There’s a lot going on here, but the most important part of the assembly is the prominent stack of input disks, one per digit, as seen in the top right of the photo. Each disk has three main components: a center section mounted to a keyed shaft that stays in position until the main crank is turned; a set of nine radial pins that slide into grooves machined in that disk; and a freely-moving digit-setting ring with a track and a couple of detents:
The fundamental mechanism of a pinwheel calculator. By author.
Each pin has a protrusion that rides in the track of the digit-setting ring. By turning the input lever, we can change the number of pins that extend from the assembly.
Input digit set to “3”, with three pins extended. By author.
When the crank is turned, these extended pins mesh to an intermediate gear that advances the digit at the corresponding position of the accumulator:
Of course, this mechanism is not enough: without a way to carry to the next column, 0001 + 0009 would give us 0000 instead of 0010. To implement carry, each input disk (except for the rightmost one) is also equipped with a spring-loaded carry pin. This pin sticks out at all times, but is normally out of the path of the intermediate gear, so it has no effect on the output value.
To perform carry, each output position is equipped with a cam that pushes a wedge-shaped carry-sensing lever into the path of the carry pin just as the digit rolls over from 9 to 0. This wedge pushes the pin to the left, momentarily placing it in the path of the intermediate gear for the next decimal digit.
This is a mouthful; the entire process is shown in the following video:
The carry-sensing lever is pushed back into the retracted position before the drum completes a full rotation, thus allowing the carry pin to spring back.
Note that the carry pins are staggered and do not engage at all once; this is to allow carry to effortlessly ripple through all digits if necessary (e.g., when adding 9999 + 1).
There’s a couple of additional convenience and reliability features in each pinwheel calculator; this includes interlocks to prevent out-of-sequence inputs, as well as reset levers for each register. There’s even a mechanical bell on overflow or underflow. I won’t bore you with all the gory details, in part because these mechanisms are less interesting — but if you’re morbidly curious, this
ancient YouTube video
provides a more complete walkthrough.
And if you want to learn about the prehistory of calculators, I invite you to check out my 2023 article:
An illustrated history of the calculator
lcamtuf
·
August 26, 2023
Read full story
PS. Yep, this is why one of the registers on all Intel CPUs is called the “accumulator”.
I write articles about
electronics
,
math
,
philosophy
, and
more
. If you like what you see, please subscribe.

title: Bypassing iOS Safari's 60 FPS Limit to Build Web Applications That Feel Native
content:
Bypassing iOS Safari’s 60 FPS Limit to Build Web Applications That Feel Native
Rida F'kih
·
November 20, 2026
·
10 min read

Devon Govett
of React Aria posted
“Scrolling is All You Need: Building a Swipeable Sheet”
back in October, and in it he talked about his team developing a sheet component that cleverly leverages the physics and smooth interactions provided by native browsers to provide the illusion of a native interaction.

More recently,
Jordan Walke
, creator of React, posted
a video of an experiment
on X showing a convincing native-like mobile interaction using DOM & CSS. It re-established a long-lived itch that I’ve had, and prompted
this response
from me. It’s something I could never justify building, however. Anything I built using this method would be pegged to 60 FPS.

Why the iOS Safari Experience Sucks

What the video Jordan Walke posted doesn’t show is that, unless you flip the “Prefer Page Rendering Updates near 60fps” flag buried deep within the Safari developer settings on iOS, WebKit limits requestAnimationFrame to just 60 Hz on a 120 Hz screen, and on a regular page, touch and pointer events are held to that same rate. This is what makes even the best mobile websites feel irritating to use.

How can I make this experience suck less without resorting to flags? Let’s call back to the React Aria piece. The reason it feels so nice is that scrolling is the responsibility of the compositor. It runs in its own thread. It moves, clips and fades without a JavaScript round-trip.

Finger to digitizer, digitizer to compositor, compositor to GPU. This will become the basis of our interaction.

High Refresh Rate Interactions

Behold, two grids. They both move a square when you drag. The one on the left uses JavaScript events and sets the
transform
attribute in CSS, while the one on the right simply places a square in a scrollable area.

Try dragging this
Try dragging this

If you’re on iOS Safari, you’ll immediately be able to tell which is which because one refreshes at most 60 times a second in a renderer pass, while the other uses the compositor.

In order to leverage the power of the scroll area, we need to find a way to read the scroll position outside of the renderer. If we can do that, we can treat it like a trackpad, or use it to “extract” native bounce, physics, momentum, etc., and apply them directly from the compositor to our animations.

Want a 1:1 trackpad experience? We just measure only when the finger is pressed.

Want a true trackball with native momentum? We just make it an infinitely scrollable region.

Want native bounce? We configure over-scroll padding and set the bounds of the container.

Want a dial with notches? Snap points!

The point is, it’d be crazy flexible if we could just find a way to pull the values out of it frequently enough.

Creating “The Controller”

I measured scroll events updating 5 to 26 times per second during momentum scroll on an iPhone Duo. The best-case scenario is during slow, deliberate scrolls where it reaches almost 60 updates a second. Useless.

Instead, we’ll be aiming to read
scrollTop
and
scrollLeft
synchronously.

First, I tried having a
MessageChannel
call itself recursively, which worked: but it produced 50,000 reads a second with just 80 distinct values. That’s a lot of waste and heat since it pins a CPU core.

Next failure was trying to use
Atomics
to wake at the screen’s refresh rate, which worked and similarly extracted 80 distinct positions every second, but the drawbacks were too great. Since it needs a SharedArrayBuffer, we’re forced to use COOP/COEP headers which break cross-origin assets on our website.

What finally worked was using a
MessageChannel
like before, throttling the next measurement to the next tick using a
setTimeout
according to the refresh rate of the device, phase-locked to vsync using
requestAnimationFrame
timestamps. I was nervous about this approach, but as you’ll see later, it panned out well. The only remaining drawback specific to this solution was easy to work around. iOS rounds
performance.now()
to the millisecond, so I derived the minimum time between draws from the refresh interval.

Each solution got us 80 position reads per second. Two-thirds towards our goal of 120 Hz input.

Safari’s UI process sends the web process one scroll position at a time, and waits for an acknowledgement from the web process before sending another. Anything that arrives in the meantime is overwritten. This was costing us dropped positions. Digging through WebKit yielded what we needed to get around this. It turns out that on every tick where the page has a rendering update queued, Safari flushes the position without waiting. An empty
requestAnimationFrame
loop is all we need to do that.

This bought us ~12.5% more reads, and brought us to 90 unique position reads per second.

I sort of assumed I had hit the limit of the aforementioned IPC, but it turns out that ProMotion was just deciding that there’s no need to render at a refresh rate higher than 90 Hz.

Squeezing out the last 30 Hz was trickier. A GPU-accelerated CSS animation lets the screen go to 120 Hz, but only while something is scrolling. So a tiny invisible scroller smooth-scrolls in the background, ready to boost us to the full ProMotion refresh rate whenever we need it.

Of course, we don’t want the display pegging to 120 Hz the entire time, so we reserve all the tricks we used to get there for times we expect animations to occur: touch events, scroll-derived animations, etc.

If the interaction you’re building doesn’t need momentum, rubber banding, or snapping, you can forego them entirely and just use a passive
touchmove
listener on the controller which fires at the full 120 Hz.

Just like that, we’re receiving updates from the controller at a full 120 Hz! Drag the grid below to see.

Position
0, 0
Updates
0/s
Unique values
0/s
Speed
0 pt/s
Try dragging this

One issue remains.
scrollTop
and
scrollLeft
are rounded to the nearest integer even though iOS scrolls with sub-point precision. Easy fix, thankfully. We just scale the scrollable surface up by the device pixel ratio, then its container back down by its reciprocal.

If you want to use the viewport itself as a controller, you
can
choose to invasively set the
initial-scale
in the same way, but this comes with some caveats. You’ll have to scale units by the DPR, disable text autosizing, and manually scale safe areas. You’ll also get tiny text-selection indicators. All trade-offs, but by no means required.

Position
0.00, 0.00
Updates
0/s
Unique values
0/s
Speed
0 pt/s
Try dragging this

From here on out, I’ll refer to these scrolling grids as “controllers”, because they act exactly like one. All we have to do is make one invisible and lay it over where we want to read high-frequency input.

Note that the page itself can also be a controller, but Safari will throttle reported scroll positions to 10 Hz during the URL bar resize that happens when you change scroll direction. WebKit skips this if we give the page a scroll-driven animation that animates a non-GPU-accelerated attribute. I went with transitioning between two transparent colours for this page.

Breaking the 60 FPS Render Barrier

Now we get high-frequency input, but the DOM still only updates 60 times a second, so if we tried to leverage it as it stands, we’d just be updating a value twice for every frame that’s drawn. The user would get no benefit.

The vast majority of dragging interactions are already covered by our controllers, and predefined animations are covered by CSS animations. But what about more complicated interactions? What about computation-derived layouts? What about shaders?

Ask your search engine or AI of choice today “How to render canvas content on iOS at 120 Hz without feature flag?” and it will respond that this is a fundamental impossibility in iOS Safari. Even WebKit’s own
bug tracker
is full of people asking for it. Ink & Switch, game-engine makers. People even cite Capacitor & Tauri as resorting to private APIs.

Asking Google yields the following preamble.

There is no public web API or standard JavaScript workaround to force HTML5 <canvas> (requestAnimationFrame) to run at 120 Hz on iOS Safari without changing the system feature flag.

Fable 5.2 shares the same sentiment.

Short answer: you can't, for JavaScript-drawn canvas frames. On iOS, WebKit caps page rendering updates (which is when canvas content is presented) at 60 Hz unless the user turns off the flag. No web API overrides it. […] Timer-based loops (setTimeout, MessageChannel) won't help, in my understanding: you can draw more often, but the result is still presented at the 60 Hz rendering update. Low Power Mode throttles further.

Well, as of today… you can!

At first, I tunnel-visioned on scroll. I tried breaking workers, pre-rendering permutation “flip-books,” and even live-generating video. It was all too laggy, jagged, or required so much RAM the WebKit process just crashed.

Seven attempts later, and a whole lot of agents digging through WebKit’s source, I landed on this.

In WebKit on iOS, if we create a
canvas
element and call
transferControlToOffscreen
, we get an
OffscreenCanvas
back. The original canvas element becomes a placeholder, and WebKit (following the HTML specification’s recommendation) skips waiting for the next rendering pass when an
OffscreenCanvas
pushes a frame.

Unlike earlier attempts, without workarounds this is easy on the battery and only uses as much memory as is needed to support a higher-frequency backing store.

Jackpot. We now have 120 FPS rendering on iOS WebKit canvases.

OffscreenCanvas
Canvas
Controller
Try dragging this

Putting it All Together

Now we can take any input at 120 Hz, and render an output at that very same frame rate. The first thing I created for this was a small UI clone of
Ando
’s mobile application fitted with a Liquid Glass tab bar, buttons, and buttery smooth navigation interactions. Once installed as a PWA, I kept having to double-take to check I wasn’t in the native application.

Applying Our Learnings

This page is fitted with two custom “Liquid Glass” elements in the viewport. Each of them renders at the full device refresh rate. We have to be very deliberate in order to do this in a way that is performant and convincing.

When the page first loads, we take a snapshot and load it into a WebGL texture. This texture is used as the foundation for a composite that is then fed into our shader.

WebGL Composite Texture + Glass
Drag me!

As the page scrolls, we then sample the region beneath each component, which is all we need to produce our effect. Building it this way means that no matter
how
the content below it is built, it can decide the best way to keep the texture live.

On this page, components using
requestAnimationFrame
for illustrative reasons update the texture from the main thread. Components using
OffscreenCanvas
post their frames directly from their workers to the worker managing the texture. This keeps us off the main thread and lets us get shaders refreshing at 120 Hz.

After all that, the glass just samples a small region around where it would land on the composite texture and computes the frame.

Building a Tab Bar Component

Building the Structure

Let’s build our Liquid Glass tab bar. We’ll start out by just drawing the underlying structure.

Structure

Layout of Controllers

We’ll break this down into one controller for each button. Each controller sends us timestamped events: which controller is being used, and how much it has been dragged. We keep a short history of those samples, so we know when a press has moved far enough to count as a drag, and how fast the finger is moving. Nothing else. Everything else is derived from that.

Controllers
Tap and drag me!

Building the State Machine

We now build a state machine around this. Every frame, the new events go in, and a frame comes out: where the lens is, how far it has lifted and stretched, and how visible the pill is.

If a controller is being touched we then magnify & lift the lens.

We know where to move the lens based on the controller’s offset since the touch began.

If the user pulls past the bounds of the tab bar, we stretch the bar towards their finger.

Depending on the offset, when the user stops touching the controller, we settle the lens on the nearest tab.

State machine
Tap and drag me!

Adding razzle-dazzle

Finally, we apply some shaders to get a convincing Liquid Glass effect.

Shaders
Tap and drag me!

Performance

I built a benchmark environment and recorded an iPhone 18 Pro at 240 FPS, slowing it down to an eighth to benchmark the difference. The two oscillating squares measure inputs and renders.

Controller
Pointer
Dropped
Try dragging the chart

Over three seconds of dragging, the controller version averaged 118 FPS while the pointer events version held a steady 60. Even in Low Power Mode, which traditionally limits you to 30, this approach gets you 60.

Wrapping Up

Liquid Glass was the target as an overblown example, but this unlocks a lot. For the first time, you can take input and render output at true device-native speeds on iOS Safari. Micro-interactions feel native and delightful, PWAs which ignored the aforementioned feature flag finally have a way to render at 120 Hz, and look at all the fun we had along the way!

Disclaimers

Would I rebuild my entire application around this? No. Fact remains it’s completely within Apple’s rights and would not violate the HTML specification if they just decided to make
OffscreenCanvas
’ placeholder wait for the main thread rendering pass. They even have a strong track record of “party pooping” as was done shortly after
Lochie Axon
unveiled the
web-haptics
library. I’d much prefer they make these findings moot by disabling the feature flag and natively supporting ProMotion for websites, but Apple is Apple for a reason after all.

title: Spending 35B Opus 5.5 Tokens to Write a Symphony
content:
Back to blog

"I fear not the man the man who one shots 2500 symphonies with Claude, rather I fear the man who 2500 shots a single symphony with Claude"

So, I got bored and wanted to push Opus to its limit with respect to music composition. Basically, I did the meme:

You can watch a full virtual instrument rendering of the composition on youtube here, which is likely higher quality than the version you'd get streamed from x.com:

The full scores, as PDF:

Movement I
PDF

Movement II

Movement III

Movement IV
PDF

The source of the scores, the critics' reviews and the scripts are on GitHub:

github.com/halfprice06/claude-symphony

These are virtual instruments, so the audio quality is not as good as if an orchestra recorded this live. But its pretty good, and considering Claude did all of the mockup and rendering in a DAW with pro-level VSTs, I'd say the result is still pretty impressive.

The whole thing used around 35 billion Opus tokens.

We used Claude Code Projects (beta) for this, and I find it really useful for project-based coding. The orchestrator / thread model worked really well for us in practice. Generally, each movement was owned by a thread.

I thought the process I used to achieve this was pretty interesting, so I decided to write it up.

tl;dr
- For things that can't be 'verified' as good or bad like art/music, just make the agent do more iterations, way more iterations than you think.

There were three jobs: writing the symphony, turning the score into a recording, and making the video. I'll go through them in that order.

Part 1: Writing the symphony

Claude Opus 5.5 composed a four-movement symphony for full orchestra, about 25 minutes of music, in one month. This is how it was done.

The music is written as text

Claude cannot easily click notes onto a staff, but it can write text. So the whole score was written in LilyPond, a free program that turns typed text into printed sheet music. A note is a letter and a number:
c4
is a C that lasts a quarter note. From the same text, LilyPond also produces a basic computer playback.

Because the score is text, Claude could edit it, compare two versions, and check it with small programs, the way programmers work on code.

"Only these notes" is a simple synthesizer in your browser playing the violin line alone. The recording is the same eight bars from the final mockup, with the whole orchestra.

One Claude writes, another reviews

The method is called an actor-critic loop. One Claude, the composer, writes the music. Another Claude, the critic, reviews it.

The composer writes a version of a movement.

A new critic, which has never seen the piece before, studies it and suggests specific fixes.

The composer decides which fixes to accept.

The result becomes the next version, and a new critic starts again.

Each critic looked at one subject only, such as melody, harmony, the use of the instruments, or whether the parts are playable. A written log recorded every decision, so that a later critic would not undo an earlier one.

Each movement went through this loop about 600 times. With four movements, that's about 2,400 rounds.

Originally I only planned to do this looping process around 50 times. But once I hit 50, it seemed like the agent was still improving. So, I just kept going. This entire process was mostly autonomous. I just prompted Claude to keep going.

Critics had to read the textbooks

A critic's opinion was not enough. I supplied standard textbooks on orchestration, harmony and music notation. From then on, each critic was assigned a chapter and had to show where the score followed it and where it did not.

One example: an orchestration textbook says that in loud passages two horns are needed to balance one trumpet. A critic checked every loud brass chord against that rule, found three chords where an important note was too weak, and proposed fixes. The composer accepted all three.

Great symphonies as models

Claude also collected scores by composers such as Beethoven, Dvořák and Tchaikovsky. Every tenth critic compared a whole movement with one movement by a master and answered one question: would a conductor believe a master wrote this?

What I did

I set the goal: a symphony that could pass for the work of a master, with melodies people remember. I chose the method, supplied the books and decided how long the loops ran. I left the musical choices to Claude.

I was also the only one who could listen. Claude cannot hear audio, so it judged the music from the written score. I listened to computer playbacks and asked for a small number of changes.

Part 2: Turning the score into a recording

A written score doesn't make any sound, so the next job was a recording.

The recordings of the symphony are not a live orchestra. They are mockups: every note was recorded in advance by real players, and software plays those recordings back in the order the score asks for. This is how the four mockups, about 25 minutes of music, were made.

The tools

Two programs did the work, both on my Mac. REAPER is a music production program. It holds one track per instrument, mixes them together and saves the result as an audio file. EastWest Hollywood Orchestra is the library of recorded notes. (These are the DAW and the pro-level VSTs I mentioned at the top.)

Claude did not click around in either program. It wrote scripts that read the score and built each REAPER project from it. The score is a text file, written in LilyPond, so a script can read every note and every marking directly.

Claude cannot hear

A person making a mockup listens, adjusts, and listens again. Claude cannot listen. It can only measure the audio file. So after every recording it checked things that can be measured:

Is the melody louder than the accompaniment?

Does each note start on the beat?

When a loud chord stops, does the sound die away as fast as it does on a real orchestra recording?

The loop

Each movement was improved in rounds. Every round had the same four steps:

Record the movement.

Three critics measure the recording. Each critic is a separate Claude with one job. One checks how the notes are played. One checks the balance between instruments. One checks something different each round, such as the timing or the sound of the room.

Each critic writes a short list of the worst problems, with evidence and a suggested fix.

Another Claude decides which fixes to make, changes the scripts and records again.

The four movements took 184 rounds in total.

My listening

The measurements missed things, and I caught them by listening. I said the long timpani rolls were drowning out other instruments. I said the accents were too harsh, the sound was "too wet" and "a bit mushy", repeated notes were hard to tell apart, and the recordings were too quiet on AirPods.

Each of my notes became a rule, and a new thing for the critics to measure. Two examples:

Too wet.
The reverb was cut in half and shortened.

A volume change on almost every note.
I opened a project and saw that the loop had been fixing problems by moving the volume fader note by note. No person works that way. All of those moves were removed, and the problems were fixed the way a person would fix them: by changing how the instrument plays the note.

Learning from people who do this by hand

About a month in, we studied how professionals make mockups. The sources were YouTube tutorials by film-score mixers, the sample library maker's own template project, and project files that composers have shared for others to study. Three lessons changed the recordings most: use less reverb, shape each phrase so it rises and falls, and leave a small gap between repeated notes.

Part 3: Making the video

The last job was the video at the YouTube link above.

Each video shows the orchestra's sheet music as a dark page. Every note lights up at the moment it sounds, in a color for its instrument, and a small light hops from note to note along each instrument's line. A program worked all of this out from the written score and the recording.

Eight seconds of Movement I, without sound: the start of the first theme, the bars shown as text above.

Watch from here
1:07

Finding the notes

Like I said above, the score is written as text in LilyPond. For the videos, LilyPond printed each movement as one long line and also wrote down where on the page it put every note. That gave the video program the exact place of all 22,979 notes.

Staying in time

The recording speeds up and slows down, as any performance does. REAPER, the software that made the recording, keeps a list of every change of speed. The video program uses that list to work out the second at which each note sounds. The lights land within two hundredths of a second of the sound.

Pointing the camera

An orchestra's score is too tall to fit on the screen, so the camera shows only part of the page. It goes to the instruments that are loudest in the recording at that moment. The program plans the camera's whole route before it draws anything, so the camera moves seldom and arrives before the passage it is moving to begins. When two instruments far apart on the page matter at the same time, the screen splits in two.

The split screen: Horn 1 and the cellos play the second theme of Movement I together.

Watch from here
2:08

Words on the page

Each instrument's name is printed on the page where it starts to play. Short labels, 124 in all, point out what a music theory class would: a theme coming back, an unusual chord, a quotation from an earlier movement. One Claude wrote the labels from the score, and a second Claude checked every one against the notes.

Watching and fixing

I watched each version and said what looked wrong. The camera jerked around. The instrument names shifted about. The opening took 19 seconds to reach the first sound. Each comment led to a fix, and the videos were made five times in two days. The four movements were then joined into one 25-minute video for YouTube, and its music now starts in the first second.

Adding it up

So that's the whole process. Add it up and it's about 2,400 rounds on the score, 184 on the recordings and 5 on the video. That's roughly the 2500 in the title.

None of those rounds had a pass/fail test, because there isn't one for whether music is good. What I could do was give each critic one narrow thing to check, make it back up its opinion with a textbook or a measurement, and run the loop way more times than seemed necessary. Then I listened to the result myself, because Claude can't.
